en: General Chronological Treatise on the Compilation of Buddhist History (Lǒngxīng Fójiào Biānián Tōnglùn) Catalogue Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zǔxiù of Shíshì Monastery in Lǒngxīng Prefecture Volume One

the śramaṇa An Shigao; and the śramaṇa Zhi Loujiachen and Zhu Foshuo.

Mouzi’s *Zi Xu* (Self-Narrative) and the twenty chapters of the *Li Huo Lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts);

During the Eastern Jin dynasty,
Minister of State Yu Bing proposed that śramaṇas should pay homage to the sovereign; however, He Chong,
the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and others argued that they should not be required to prostrate.
Yu Bing proposed for a second time that one should pay respects; He Chong and others proposed for a second time that one should not pay respects.
Yu Bing proposed for a third time that he must insist on paying respects; He Chong and others proposed for a third time to refute this, arguing that one should not pay respects.
[The petition was signed by] He Chong, Minister of the Secretariat, and the Dharma Master Zhu Fajian.

Emperor Gaozu of the Tang issued an edict inquiring about the benefits and harms of Buddhism; and Prime Minister Xiao Yu debated the matter in court.

Volume Eleven of the *Treatise*,

Emperor Taizong admonished Fu Yi for disparaging the Buddha; he issued an edict to swallow locusts;
he ordered that Buddhist temples be established at every site of battle;
and he reduced the number of death sentences throughout the empire to twenty-nine.
The Fourth Patriarch, Master Xinxing, expounded the Dharma for Chan Master Rong;
the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang took leave to travel to the Western Regions;
and by imperial decree, Master Chongwan was ordered to survey the provinces and prefectures throughout the realm to determine the fixed number of monks and nuns to be ordained.
Zhang Shiheng’s Response to the Imperial Prince’s Inquiry Regarding the Vinaya Master Huiren;
an Imperial Decree; the Dharma Master Zhishi’s Dispute Not Being Granted;
and the Discourse by Minister Yu Shinan.
The Dharma Master Huìjìng debated doctrine with the Daoist Cài Zǐhuáng;
the Dharma Master Huìlín and the monks of Tàiyuàn requested that the Emperor visit them in person;
and the Chancellor Xiāo Yǔ issued an edict prohibiting the sale of Buddhist images.
When Emperor Taizong visited Hongfu Temple, he bestowed silk upon Dharma Master Fashun and Dharma Master Xuanzang;
they subsequently entered the kingdoms of Kīra and others. At Yuanzhou, an auspicious stone was presented, containing the *Wenlun* (Treatise on Writings) in twelve fascicles. Volume Twelve.

When the Dharma Master Xuanzang returned from the Western Regions and had an audience with the Emperor at the Eastern Capital, he presented the newly translated sūtras and śāstras and requested that the Emperor compose a preface for them.
Emperor Taizong issued an edict declining the request; the Dharma Master Xuanzang then submitted a memorial requesting that the Emperor compose the preface once again.

The Dharma Master Hui-ling and the practitioner Li Chunfeng were summoned by Emperor Taizong, who commanded that Master Xuanzang cease his monastic life to assist in governance; Xuanzang declined resolutely and was granted exemption.
By imperial decree, he was ordered to transcribe the newly translated scriptures and treatises, which were then distributed as gifts to the nine provinces.
The Imperial Preface to the Tripiṭaka of the Holy Teachings by Emperor Taizong; the Memorial of gratitude from Dharma Master Xuanzang;
the Postscript to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra by the Crown Prince; the Imperial Edict bestowing a *mò-nà* (patchwork robe) upon Dharma Master Xuanzang;
and the Imperial Edict ordering each monastery throughout the realm to ordain five monks.
An imperial edict was issued to establish the Translation Court within the palace, where Dharma Master Xuanzang remained to discourse on the Way.
Prince Zhaoye established the Great Ci'en Monastery. Upon the demise of Emperor Taizong (Biography and Eulogy), [the author] discusses the Fourth Patriarch and Grand Master Xin.

It is like the great ocean, which can only be entered through the guidance of a master. Since the transmission of the Dharma from the West, there have been many who have expounded its meaning. Among these, the various commentaries on the source of Chan (*Chan Yuan*) are particularly significant. I have collected and edited these works to form this compendium, hoping that those who seek the Way may find a clear path therein.

I, Pei Xiu, have long been devoted to the study of the Buddhist teachings. I have observed that while the scriptures are numerous, their essential meaning often remains obscured by complex terminology. Therefore, I have sought out the most authoritative treatises and commentaries to clarify the true nature of Chan. This collection serves as a bridge for those who wish to traverse the ocean of the Dharma, providing them with a reliable guide to the ultimate truth. May all practitioners rely upon it to realize the nature of their own minds and attain liberation. [End of Preface]

The Second and Ninth Volumes of the Treatise by Chan Master Qingliang Wenyi (Appended: The Imperial Preface to the Holy Teachings composed by Emperor Taizong of the Sacred Dynasty) [The following is the translation of the "Imperial Preface to the Holy Teachings" (Shèngjiào xù): The Buddha’s Dharma is profound and subtle; its essence is vast and boundless. It transcends the realm of words and thought, and lies beyond the reach of the mundane mind. Yet, because it is not separate from the mundane mind, it is manifested through the mundane mind. Because it is not separate from words and thought, it is revealed through words and thought. Now, the Tathāgata appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings. He taught that all phenomena arise from conditions and that the nature of the mind is originally pure. He showed that the five aggregates are empty and that the six sense objects are illusory. He opened the gate of liberation for those who are deluded and led them to realize the path of enlightenment. Since the transmission of the Dharma to the East, successive sovereigns have revered the teachings with utmost sincerity. They have established monasteries, honored the Sangha, and promoted the study of the scriptures. This is truly a manifestation of their filial piety and benevolence. I, [Emperor Taizong], have long been devoted to the pursuit of the Way. I have examined the various sutras and commentaries, seeking to understand the ultimate truth. Although my wisdom is shallow, I am determined to propagate the sublime doctrine. Therefore, I have composed this preface to record the origins of the holy teachings and to encourage future generations to uphold and practice them. May all beings, by reading and reciting these words, attain awakening and realize the nature of their own minds. Written on the first day of the first month of the second year of the Zhenguan era (628 CE). [End of the Imperial Preface] [The following is the beginning of the "Treatise on the Essentials of the Dharma" (Fǎyào lùn) by Chan Master Wenyi: The Great Master Qingliang Wenyi says: The Dharma of the Tathāgata is like the great ocean; its depths are unfathomable. To enter this ocean, one must rely upon the guidance of a skilled navigator. Thus, I shall now discuss the essentials of the Dharma, drawing from the profound meanings of the various sutras and treatises, to provide a clear path for practitioners. [End of Volume 29 of the Treatise by Chan Master Wenyi]

compiled by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of Shishi Monastery in Lōngxìng Prefecture.

In the seventh year of the Yongping era of the Eastern Han, Emperor Xiaozong Xiaoming dreamed one night of a golden man sixteen feet tall, with a solar disc adorning his neck, arriving by flying through the air, its radiance illuminating the palace courtyard.
In the morning, he questioned his ministers; at that time, the Grand Master for Ceremonial Affairs (Daxue) heard of it.
The courtier Fu Yi stepped forward and said, "In the past, during the reign of King Zhao of Zhou, a sage appeared in the Western Regions named Buddha.
His appearance and radiance were exactly as described in the dream; I suspect it must be him.

Thereupon, the Emperor dispatched the Commandant Qin Jing, the Doctors Wang Zun and Cai Yin (pronounced *yin*), and others as envoys to the Western Regions to seek out the Buddha-dharma. Jing and his companions...
In the border regions of India, [Emperor Ming] encountered the śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan, who had obtained Buddhist scriptures and images.
He subsequently ordered them to return east with him, arriving in Luoyang in the eleventh year. Mātanga and Falan presented themselves in the robes of śramaṇas; the Emperor was delighted.
He stayed at Baima Temple. There were the practitioners of the arts (fangshi), Fei Shucaí and Chǔ Shànxìn, who were jealous of him.
With a few words, they declared him to be wrong. Tèng Lán reported this to the Emperor, saying: "The Dharma of our Buddha that appears in the world cannot be destroyed by water or fire.

I request to put it to the test with these practitioners. The Emperor granted his request and issued an edict for Shucaí and the others to produce all their marvelous scriptures and secret instructions.
He ordered that the scriptures and images brought by the śramaṇas be burned. When the fire was lit, the śramaṇas' scriptures alone remained intact and were not consumed by the flames.
The fangshi bowed their heads in respectful admiration, and the Emperor marveled at this even more. Consequently, Teng Lan studied the Chinese language.

After some time, he translated five scriptures: the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*, the *Ten Stages of Severing Bonds*, the *Buddha’s Jātaka Tales*, the *Treasury of the Dharma Ocean*, and the *Buddha’s Past Deeds*.
The Emperor once visited his monastery. Teng Lan reported, saying, "What building is that to the east of the temple?

The Emperor replied, "In the past there was a mound that rose up without cause; when it was leveled, it appeared again. At night there were strange lights, so the people called it the 'Sacred Tomb' and offer sacrifices there."

They suspected it was the spirit of Luoyang. Teng said, "According to the records of Tianzhu Jinzang Quan, King Aśoka enshrined relics of the Tathāgata throughout the world in eighty-four thousand locations.
Within the borders of Zhina (China) and Zhendan (China), there are nineteen such sites;
this is one of them. The Emperor was greatly astonished and that very day set out for the sacred tomb, accompanied by Teng and Lan.
As he proceeded to pay his respects and rose, a circular halo suddenly appeared above the tomb, and within the light, the three bodies manifested. The attendants cried out, "Ten thousand years!
The Emperor said with joy, "Had I not encountered these two Great Beings, how could I have known of the surviving blessings left by the Supreme Sage? He then issued an edict to build a stupa over it.
He received the imperial decree from Teng Lan. The stupa was completed with nine tiers and stood two hundred feet high. The following year, light appeared once more;
a golden hand emerged from the top of the stupa for a span of about one chi, visible as if seen through lapis lazuli. A celestial fragrance wafted intensely.

The Emperor traveled there in person to pay his respects and gaze upon the light, circumambulating it in accordance with its movements. The light persisted from the fifth watch until the seventh before vanishing. At that time, the Emperor’s younger brother, the Prince of Chu, [was present].

Yingxi observed the fasts and precepts of the Buddha and once offered silk to redeem his transgressions; the Emperor returned it to him to assist in providing the sumptuous feasts for the *upāsakas* and *śramaṇas*.
The commentary states: In the past, the teaching of the sages of the Western Regions could not have been brought about by the rulers of the declining Zhou or the tyrannical Qin.
However, although the two or three eminent rulers of the Western Han possessed the virtue capable of attracting him, the Sage did not arrive.

He appeared only in a dream to Emperor Xianzong. Generally, the eminent monks of recent antiquity have all maintained that the Sage passed away more than a thousand years ago before his teaching arrived;
yet there has never been any formal examination or record [to support this]. The virtue of Emperor Xianzong was such that it would inevitably have moved the Sage.
This is the reason for composing this general discourse on principle. Now, throughout the two Han dynasties that ruled the world, twenty-four generations passed;

yet those who possessed sovereign virtue were merely two founders and four emperors. As for the two founders, they were the sovereigns who established the ultimate standard, and thus there is nothing to be debated regarding them.
As for the three emperors, each possessed their own merits, yet none could avoid their respective shortcomings. Only Xian... [text ends]
This dynasty has reached the pinnacle of excellence. It possesses the beauty of Emperor Taizong’s reverence and frugality, yet surpasses him in literary refinement and majestic dignity.
It holds the merit of Emperor Shizu’s strategic management of the four barbarian tribes, yet is free from the corruption of his later years.
It shares the clarity of Emperor Chengzong’s governance, yet excels in its veneration of Confucianism and esteem for virtue. Thus, it truly combines the strengths of these three emperors.
Yet it is free from the shortcomings of the three schools [of historiography]. For this reason, Ban Gu and Fu Yi praised his meritorious achievements as being the most magnificent in the Han dynasty.
Nevertheless, scholars of the world do not regard Ban and Fu as reliable authorities;

seeing only that the biography of Zhongli Yi states the Emperor’s nature was narrow and scrutinizing, and that he delighted in using secret surveillance of the ears and eyes to manifest his "enlightenment," they consequently take this to be the case for Emperor Xianzong.

True Record. Alas! How could this not be considered a profound discourse? In the past, Confucius expounded and deliberated upon the administrative instruments of the Five Emperors and Three Kings to bequeath them to posterity.
Yet, following his passing, these teachings were subjected to the ravages of the violent Qin dynasty’s book burnings; it was only until the reign of Emperor Shizong that they were partially restored.
It was not until the time of Emperor Xiaozong that the arts of the Confucians were first personally practiced, as he honored and nourished the "Three Elders" and the "Five Virtuous Men."
When the ritual of feasting and archery was completed, the Emperor sat upon his throne and lectured in person. The various Confucian scholars held their scriptures and engaged in debate.

At that time, scholar-officials wearing their ceremonial caps and girdles gathered around the bridge-gate; those who came to observe and listen numbered in the hundreds of millions. How magnificent it was!
How vast and expansive! Since the Three Dynasties, the flourishing of Confucian culture has never been more profound than during the Yongping era.
Following the ZHANGHE period, scholars established academies to transmit the Way, and those registered as students numbered well over a thousand.

Indeed, the influence of the Yongping transformation was like the response of the "Qilin and Zhi" ode in the *Zhou Nan*. Although legal disputes were initially frequent and complex, [the transformation prevailed].
When the Emperor ascended the throne, he applied himself with deliberate intent to judicial adjudication, exercising rigorous severity.

This was truly the realization of the principle of "rewarding the good and punishing the evil," much like when Confucius served as Minister of Justice and executed Shao Zheng Mao within seven days, or when he briefly presided over Mount Jia and had all the jesters and performers put to death.
This truly cannot do without the exercise of benevolence and forbearance; to call it "partial scrutiny" would be an error.
I say that were Confucius to be born again, he would surely declare: "As for Emperor Xianzong, I have no cause for criticism.

This is because Emperor Xianzong encompassed the excellence of the three emperors of the Western Han and personally practiced the Way of the ancient sovereigns; this is why his spiritual essence is so vibrant.
Our Buddha’s spiritual resonance and penetration have caused the holy teachings to reach the Central Plains;
thus, they complement Confucianism and spread goodness throughout the world. How could this possibly be a mere coincidence?
In the second year of the Jianhe era, the śramaṇa Anqing of the country of Anxi arrived in Luoyang. Anqing’s courtesy name was Shigao;
he was originally the crown prince who was destined to succeed to the throne, but he abdicated it to his uncle, renounced the world, and became a monk.

Having reached the capital of Luoyang, he translated twenty-nine scriptures totaling one hundred and seventy-six fascicles. He ceased his work in the third year of the Jianning era of Emperor Lingdi, as he happened to be embarking on a boat.

While traveling along Mount Lu, he arrived at Gongting Temple. He moored his boat beneath the shrine. The deity of the temple was most efficacious and capable of dividing the wind to favor ships coming and going in turn.

There was once a man who begged for a bamboo pole from the deity; though it was not granted, he cut it down anyway. The deity grew angry and capsized his boat, causing it to drift to the spot where the bamboo had been felled.
Passersby would hold their breath in awe and break into sweat. When the boatmen offered sacrifices and prayed for blessings, the deity would invariably descend.
The attendant said, "Did the śramaṇa not come along with you? When Gao arrived below the temple, the deity descended again and spoke to Gao as before.
He then wept and said, "Your disciple’s family resides at this lake; the thousand li around are all under my jurisdiction. Because of my habitual abundance of anger,"

"Currently, my manifested form is extremely ugly, and moreover, I am on the verge of death day and night; I shall certainly enter hell. I have a thousand rolls of silk and various precious playthings;
I wish to build a temple and a stupa for them as a merit for the afterlife. Senggaokao consented to this. Xu then said, "Can you manifest your physical appearance and endure the hardship?
The spirit replied, "My form is hideous; how could I do that? Gaokao said, "Just manifest it. Thereupon, he emerged from within the curtains.
It was a giant python. Hui-gao recited mantras in the Sanskrit language to subdue it; the python shed tears like rain and suddenly vanished.
Before Hui-gao’s boat had even departed, a youth knelt before him. Hui-gao again recited mantras for him, and he departed. The boatmen asked, "Whose son are you?

Hui-gao replied, "The temple deity has already cast off his python form; that is why he came to express his gratitude. Hui-gao reached Yuzhang and built a monastery, which is the present-day Da'an Monastery.
It was also [founded] by him; it became renowned for its height and is considered the beginning of the temple towers in the Jianghuai region.
In the third year [of the Jian’an era], the Śramaṇa Lokakṣema from the country of Yuezhi—also known as Zhi Chen—arrived in Luoyang.

After a short time, he practiced the local language and became thoroughly proficient in the Chinese tongue, subsequently translating scriptures. By the Zhongping era, there were twenty-one works totaling sixty [rolls].
In three fascicles:
In the first year of the Yongxing era, Emperor Huan cast a golden stupa and an image of Laozi within the palace, covering them with a canopy of a hundred jewels.
He personally offered sacrifices to them; consequently, the common people were drawn toward this transformation, and their devotion to the Buddha became increasingly flourishing.
In the first year of the Jiaping era, the Indian śramaṇa Zhu Foshuo arrived in Luoyang and translated the *Dàoxíng Bānrě Jīng* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra).

He discarded the ornate style in favor of the essential, thereby capturing the profound meaning of the sūtra. During the Guanghe period, he collaborated with Zhi Chen to translate the *Bānzhōu sānmèi jīng* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra) in three fascicles.
In this year, the lay devotee (upāsaka) Anxuan, the Commandant from the kingdom of Parthia, arrived at Luoyang.

Together with the lay practitioner Yan Fotiao, they translated seven scriptures. At that time, there were also the śramaṇas Zhi Yao, Kang Chen, Kang Mengxiang, Tan Guo, and Zhu Dalie, all of whom were proficient in local dialects.
Throughout the Han dynasty, they translated a total of more than three hundred scriptures.
During the Chuping era of Emperor Xian, there was a man named Mouzi—his personal name is unknown—who was popularly known simply as Mouzi.

Having studied the Classics and Histories, he took pleasure in all the various philosophical treatises (*zǐshū*), whether great or small. Although he did not delight in the art of war, he nevertheless read it;

and though he read books on the immortality of the transcendents (*xiānshén*), he suppressed his inclination to believe them, regarding them as empty and extravagant. This was during the time following the death of Emperor Ling.

Below, there was turmoil; only Jiaozhou was relatively peaceful. Eccentric persons from the north all came there, many practicing the arts of the immortals, such as abstaining from grain and seeking longevity.
Mouzi frequently challenged them with the Five Classics; none of the Daoist practitioners dared to respond.
Prior to this, Mouzi had fled the world with his mother. At the age of twenty-six, he returned to Cangwu to marry a wife. At that time—
The Governor heard that he was devoted to learning and requested him to take up an official post. At that time, he was in the prime of his youth and his will was focused on scholarship;

moreover, seeing the world in turmoil, he had no intention of serving in office and ultimately did not accept. At that time, the various prefectures and commanderies were suspicious of one another, and communications were blocked and cut off.

The Governor, because of his extensive learning and vast knowledge, sent him to pay respects to the Governor of Jingzhou. Mouzi considered that honorable rank and titles are easily renounced, and thus he... [sent him].

Mao Mi declined the command on the grounds that it was too dangerous. At that time, Mao Mu’s younger brother, the Governor of Yuzhang, had been killed by Ze Rong, who served as a General of the Household.
Mao Mu dispatched Liu Yan, a Cavalry Commandant, to lead troops to his aid. Fearing that those outside the capital might become suspicious and prevent the army from advancing, Mao Mu said to Mouzi:
"My brother has been slain by a rebel; the pain of this loss to our own flesh and blood stirs up my liver and heart with indignation. I have already sent Liu..."
The Commandant was on an official tour. Fearing that there might be doubts and difficulties beyond his jurisdiction, he thought that travelers would not be able to pass through.
"You," he said, "are endowed with both civil and military virtues and possess the talent for diplomatic missions. I now wish to request your presence in Lingling and Guiyang;

how would it be if you were to take this route as a way station? Muzi did not wish to go against his wishes and consented. However, shortly thereafter his mother passed away, and so he did not proceed. After some time, he sighed and said: "Laozi [declared]..."
The sage abandons worldly wisdom, cultivates his person, and preserves his truthfulness. Myriad things cannot disturb his will, and the whole world cannot alter his joy.
Thus, even the Son of Heaven cannot make him a subject, nor can the feudal lords make him a friend; therefore, he is worthy of honor. Thereupon, he applied his keen resolve to the Way of the Buddha.
He also studied the *Laozi* in its five thousand characters. He took its profound mysteries as his wine and draughts, and enjoyed the Five Classics as if they were zither music.

Many among the worldly folk criticized him, claiming that he was turning his back on the Five Classics to lean toward heterodox paths. If he wished to argue with them, it would not be in accordance with the Way;
yet if he wished to remain silent, he could not. Consequently, amidst his writing and brushwork, he briefly cited the words of the sages and worthies to provide proof and clarification.
It is titled *Mouzi Lihuo* (Mouzi Resolving Doubts). It asks:

"Why is he specifically called 'Buddha'? What does 'Buddha' signify? Mouzi replied: "Buddha is a posthumous title (a designation), just as the Three Sovereigns were called 'Divine' and the Five Emperors were called 'Sages.
Buddha is the primal ancestor of the Way and its Virtue, and the ancestral lineage of the spiritual and the intelligent."

"Buddha" means "Awakened. He manifests through mystical transformations, dividing his body and dispersing his form; he may appear or vanish, be small or large, round or square, old or young, hidden or manifest.
Treading upon fire he is not burned; stepping on blades he is not wounded; dwelling in filth he is not defiled; encountering calamity he remains unharmed. He reaches destinations without traveling;
he radiates light without acting. Therefore, he is titled: [The Buddha] (The Awakened One) (Note: The original text ends with "Therefore, he is titled," implying the title "Buddha" follows.)

[He replied: "The Buddha. [The questioner] asked: "What is meant by the Way (Dào)? What kind of thing is the Way? Mōuzi said: "The word 'Way' means 'to guide. It guides people toward non-action (wúwéi).
If one pulls it forward, there is no front; if one draws it back, there is no rear; if one raises it up, there is no top; if one suppresses it..."
Look down at it and it has no form; listen for it and it has no sound. It is greater than the four quarters of the universe, winding and twisting beyond them;
it is finer than a hair’s breadth, interweaving within them. Therefore, it is called the Dao.
Question: Confucius took the Five Classics as the Way, teaching that they could be chanted with folded hands and practiced through conduct.
Now you speak of the Way as empty, non-existent, and elusive; its meaning is not seen and its matters are not pointed out. How does this differ from the words of the Sage? Mouzi replied:
One must not consider what one is accustomed to as important and what one seeks after as trivial. To be deluded by external appearances leads to the loss of the truth.
In this regard, when establishing affairs within the human realm, one must not lose sight of the Way and its Virtue (Dao-De), just as one tunes strings without losing the notes of Gong or Shang.
The Way of Heaven follows the four seasons; the Way of Humanity follows the Five Constant Virtues. Laozi said: "There was something undifferentiated and complete, born before heaven and earth.
It may be regarded as the Mother of the world. I do not know its name; I have tentatively called it the Dao. As for the substance of the Dao, it can be found within the home."
By means of it, one serves one’s parents; by it, a ruler of a state can govern the people; by it, one who stands alone can cultivate the self.

To practice and carry it out, it fills heaven and earth; to abandon it and not employ it, it vanishes yet remains inseparable from us. If you do not understand this, what difference could there possibly be?

Question: Now, the ultimate reality is not adorned with ornamentation, and the ultimate expression is not embellished. Words that are concise yet reach the essence are elegant; matters that are few yet convey the meaning are clear.

Thus, pearls and jade are precious because they are rare, while tiles and pebbles are base because they are abundant. The sages composed the foundations of the Seven Classics in no more than thirty thousand words, yet all matters were fully contained therein.
Yet now, the Buddhist scriptures are counted by the tens of thousands of fascicles, and their words number in the hundreds of millions.
[The number] is such that it cannot be sustained by the power of a single person. I consider this to be cumbersome and lacking in essential purpose. Mouzi said:
"The reason the rivers and seas differ from puddles is their depth and breadth; the reason the Five Peaks are distinguished from hills and mounds is their height and magnitude.
If their height did not surpass that of ordinary hills, even a lame sheep could scale their summits. [If their depth...]

The flow of the waters never ceases. A young child bathes in its depths; yet the qilin does not dwell within a walled garden, nor does the fish that swallows a boat roam in a stream only several *ren* deep.

To cut open a three-inch insect to seek the pearl of the bright moon, or to search the nest of a thorny jujube tree for the fledgling of a phoenix—these will surely be difficult to obtain. Why? Because the small cannot contain the great. Thus it is with the Buddha.
The Sūtra first speaks of events spanning billions of years, yet it subsequently reveals the essentials for ten thousand generations.

Before the Great Primal Chaos had arisen and before the Great Beginning had been born, when Heaven and Earth were first emerging, its omens could not be grasped and its subtleties could not be entered.

The Buddha has completely encompassed that which lies beyond the vast and great, and has analyzed the profound and wondrous within; there is nothing he has not recorded. Therefore, his scriptures are [as follows].

They number in the tens of thousands; it is said they are counted by the hundreds of millions. The more there are, the more complete they become; the more numerous they are, the more abundant they grow. How could there be anything that is not included?

Although this is beyond the capacity of any single individual, it is like one who comes to a river to drink water: once satiated, he is content with himself; how could he know what remains beyond his reach?
Question: The Buddhist scriptures are numerous. One wishes to obtain their essentials while discarding the rest, speaking directly of their substance while removing their ornamentation.
Mouzi replied: "No. Now, the sun and moon both shine, yet each has its own illumination; the twenty-eight lunar mansions each have their own domain;
a hundred medicines grow together, yet each cures a different ailment; a fox-fur cloak prepares one for the cold, while fine linen wards off the heat. A boat..."

Carriages differ in their paths, yet they all serve to transport travelers. Confucius did not compose the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and the *Classic of Filial Piety* because the Five Classics were already complete;
rather, he wished to broaden the scope of the Way and allow people’s minds free rein. Although Buddhist scriptures are numerous, their ultimate aim is one and the same.

This is just as the Seven Classics, though diverse, are likewise one in their exaltation of morality, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness. As for why the teachings on filial piety are so varied, it is because they follow...

One bestows [instruction] according to the person's conduct. When Zixia and Ziyou both asked about filial piety, yet Confucius answered them differently, he was attacking their respective shortcomings. How could there be any abandonment [of either]?
Question: The Buddha-way is most supreme and most great. Why did Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius not cultivate it? It is not seen in the words of the Seven Classics.
Since you are already devoted to the Odes and Documents and take pleasure in the Rites and Music, why do you further favor the Buddha-way and delight in heterodox arts?
Could these possibly surpass the Classics and Commentaries or excel the noble achievements of the sages? I privately believe that you, my friend, should not adopt them. —Mouzi.

It is said: "Books need not be the words of Confucius, and prescriptions need not be the formulas of Bian Que; that which accords with righteousness is followed, and that which heals illness is excellent.
A gentleman extensively gathers all that is good to assist his person. Zigong said: "What constant teachers did our Master have?
Yao served Yinsou; Shun served Wusheng; Dan studied under Lü Wang; and Qiu (Confucius) studied under Lao Dan."

Furthermore, [the Buddha's teachings] are not found together with them in the Seven Classics. Although the four masters were sages, when compared to the Buddha, they are like white deer compared to the qilin, or common swallows compared to the phoenix. Even Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius were surpassed by him;

how much more so, then, could one abandon the Buddha’s physical marks, his transformations, and his boundless supernatural powers without studying them? As for the matters and meanings of the Five Classics...
"If there were some omissions that the Buddha did not record, what is there to be so strangely suspicious about?
A questioner asked: 'The Buddha is said to possess the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; how can they differ from those of ordinary men so greatly?
This is likely the talk of the wealthy and the learned, not a statement of reality. Mouzi replied: 'A proverb says that those who have seen little imagine themselves to have seen much.'"

What is strange is this: seeing a camel, one calls it a horse with a swollen back; Yao had eyebrows of eight colors, Shun had double pupils, Gaoyao had a beak-like nose, King Wen had four nipples, Yu had three openings in his ears, and the Duke of Zhou had a hunched back.

Fuxi had a dragon’s nose, Zhongni (Confucius) had a reversed forehead, Laozi had a sun on his brow and a moon suspended above him, two pillars on his nose, ten marks held in his hands, and the numbers two and five marked upon his feet. This...
Are they not different from ordinary people? Why then should one doubt the Buddha’s marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*)?
A questioner asks: "The *Classic of Filial Piety* states that one's body, hair, and skin are received from one's parents and must not be mutilated or injured.
When Zengzi was on the verge of death, he opened his hands and feet [to show they were intact]. Now, śramaṇas shave their heads; how can this be so contrary to the words of the Sage?"
"This accords with the way of a filial son. You, sir, have always delighted in debating right and wrong and leveling crookedness and straightness;

yet do you now turn against what is good? Mowzi replied: "To slander the sages and worthies is unkind; to level things without hitting the mark is unwise. Being neither kind nor wise, how can one cultivate virtue?
When virtue is not cultivated, one is of the same class as the stubborn and the arrogant. How easy is it to engage in such debate? Formerly, in Qi..."
A man was crossing a river by boat when his father fell into the water. His son rolled up his sleeves, seized his father by the head, and turned him upside down to force the water out of his mouth;
thus, the father’s life was restored. Now, seizing the head and turning one upside down is an act of unfiliality beyond measure. Yet, it was done to preserve the father’s body.
Had he stood with folded hands, merely practicing the conventional rites of a filial son, the father’s life would have perished in the water. Confucius said, "This may be done."

One who has attained the Way may not yet be able to exercise discretion (*quan*); this refers to what is appropriate for the timing of a given situation. Furthermore, the *Classic of Filial Piety* states:

"The ancient kings possessed supreme virtue and the essential Way. Yet, Taibo cut off his hair and tattooed his body to conform to the customs of the Wu and Yue peoples, thereby contravening the principle that one's body, hair, and skin are received from one's parents.
Nevertheless, Confucius praised him, saying that he could indeed be called one of supreme virtue. Confucius did not—
It is because they cut their hair to signify their renunciation. Viewed from this perspective, if one possesses great virtue, one is not constrained by minor matters.
A śramaṇa diminishes family wealth and abandons wife and children; he does not listen to music or gaze upon beautiful forms—this may be called the ultimate in yielding.

How could this contradict the words of the sages or fail to accord with filial piety? (Consider) Yuzhang who swallowed charcoal and lacquered his body, Nie Zheng who disfigured his face and maimed himself, and Lady Bo...

To walk upon fire, perform high acrobatics, or mutilate one's appearance—though a gentleman may be brave enough to die for the sake of righteousness, we have never heard of anyone being censured for such self-destruction.
To compare the śramaṇa, who shaves off his beard and hair, with these four types of people—is this not going too far?
Question: Now, in matters of merit, none surpasses having an heir; in matters of filial piety, none exceeds being without progeny.
Yet the śramaṇa abandons wife and children, squanders wealth, and remains unmarried for his entire life. How does this contradict the practice of merit and filial piety?
To suffer for oneself is no marvel; to save oneself is no distinction. Mouzi replied: "He who is long on the left must be short on the right; he who is large in front..."

One must certainly narrow one's focus on the future. Meng Gongchuo would have been more than sufficient as an elder for the Zhao and Wei houses, yet he could not serve as a high official in Teng or Bi.
Wife, children, and wealth are the remnants of the world; a pure personage acting without artifice is the subtle essence of the Way. Laozi said: "Between reputation and the body, which is dearer?
Between the body and wealth, which is more valuable? He further said: "Observe the lingering customs of the Three Dynasties and examine the Confucians."
The Way and arts of the Mohists consist of reciting the *Shi* and *Shu*, cultivating ritual propriety, exalting benevolence and righteousness, and maintaining purity and cleanliness.

When their reputation spreads and overflows among the people of the village, this is what the middle-ranking scholar practices; it is something those who are tranquil and indifferent do not concern themselves with.
Thus, if there were a pearl from Suizhou before and a roaring tiger behind, one would see them and flee without daring to take [the pearl]. Why? Because they prioritize their own lives.
As for their legacy, consider Xu You, who nested in trees; and Boyi and Shuqi, who starved on Mount Shouyang.
The Sage Confucius praised them as virtuous, saying they were those who "sought benevolence and attained it. He never heard of him criticizing them for having no descendants or wealth.

When a śramaṇa cultivates the Way and virtue to exchange it for the pleasures of worldly wandering, and befriends the virtuous and wise to borrow joy from them instead of from wife and children—is this not extraordinary? Who would fail to recognize it as such?
To act in accordance with this is to be extraordinary; if one does not act contrary to it, how can one be considered different?
A questioner asked: "The Yellow Emperor hung his robes and fashioned garments; Jizi set forth the *Hongfan*, wherein appearance is the foremost of the five matters."
Confucius composed the *Classic of Filial Piety*, which begins with the three virtues. It further states: "Rectify one's robes and cap; dignify one's gaze.
Even though Yuan Xian was poor, he did not discard his elegant cap; when Zi Lu encountered peril, he did not forget to tie his neckband. Now, the śramaṇas shave their heads and wear saffron robes;
when they see people, they lack the etiquette of bowing and rising, nor do they possess the decorum of graceful movement. Why is this?
Regarding their violation of the regulations for appearance and dress, and their departure from the refinements of the scholarly class, Mouzi said: "Laozi stated:
'Those of the highest virtue do not claim virtue, and thus they possess it; those of lower virtue do not lose virtue, and thus they lack it.
In the era of the Three Sovereigns, people ate meat and wore skins, dwelling in nests and caves to honor simplicity and substance. How could they have required the *zhangfu* cap or the *quqiu* robe?"
...such refinements! Yet those individuals were reputed to possess virtue and be profound and vast; they were upright, sincere, and non-actionist.

The conduct of the śramaṇas resembles this. Someone said: "If what you say is true, then the likes of the Yellow Emperor, Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius would be abandoned as unworthy of emulation.
Mouzi replied: "One who sees extensively will not be deluded; one who hears clearly will not be confused."
Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius cultivated worldly affairs; the Buddha and the filial son, however, were dedicated to the realization of non-action (*wuwei*).
Zhongni wandered restlessly through more than seventy states, while Xu You, having heard of the abdication, washed his ears in a deep pool.

The way of the gentleman is such that he may either emerge from seclusion or remain there, and he may either speak in silence or remain silent. He does not overflow his emotions nor does he distort his nature; therefore, the nobility of his Way lies in what he values.

"How can there be anything discarded? He asked, "The teachings of the Buddha say that when a person dies, they must be reborn. I do not believe this statement to be true. Mouzi replied, "When a person is on the verge of death, their family climbs onto the roof and calls out to them. Once they have died, whom would you call? Someone said, "One calls for their spirit. Mouzi said, "If it is the spirit, then it has already departed from the body. If it is the body, then it is already dead. Whom, then, do you call? The other asked, "What is the meaning of this? Regarding the *hun* and *po* spirits, Mouzi said: "When the spirit returns, there is life; when it does not return, where does the spirit go?
One says it becomes a ghost or spirit. Mouzi said: "This is so. The soul-spirit is certainly not extinguished; it is only the body that decays and rots.
The body is like the roots and leaves of the five grains, while the soul-spirit is like the seed and fruit of the five grains. The roots and leaves must inevitably die, but the seed..."
