This refers to those who perform not a single day’s good deed yet seek lifelong renown. When one possesses the Way, though they die, their spirit returns to the Hall of Blessings;

when one commits evil, upon death, their spirit shall suffer the calamity. The foolish are ignorant of what has already been accomplished, while the wise and virtuous anticipate it before it has even sprouted.
The difference between the Way and its opposite is like gold compared to grass; the distinction between calamity and blessing is like white contrasted with black. How could it be otherwise?
It is not different [from what you claim], yet you ask how it could be so easy.

The questioner says: Confucius said, "If one has not yet been able to serve the living, how can one serve the spirits? If one does not yet know life, how can one know death? This is what the Sage recorded.
Now, the Buddhists constantly speak of the matters of birth and death, and the affairs of ghosts and spirits. This—
This is surely not the speech of a sage or a wise man (*zhé*). Now, one who treads the Way ought to be empty and tranquil, returning their will to simplicity and plainness.
Why, then, do you discuss life and death to disturb the mind, and speak of the secondary matters of ghosts and spirits? Mouzi said:
"What you say is like seeing the exterior while failing to recognize the interior. Confucius was critical of Zilu..."

I do not inquire into the origins or the details; I merely restrain [the argument] with this. The *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "Establish ancestral temples so that they may receive offerings as spirits;
perform sacrifices according to the seasons so that they may be remembered in due time. It further says: "In life, serve them with love and respect; in death, serve them with grief and sorrow.
Does this not teach people how to serve ghosts and spirits and understand life and death? When the Duke of Zhou petitioned for the life of King Wu, he said: "Dàn possesses many talents..."
To perform many arts and serve the spirits—what is the purpose of this? Is it not the very path of birth and death described in the Buddhist scriptures?
Laozi said: "Once you know the child, return to guard the mother; throughout your life, you will not face peril. He also said:
"Use its radiance and return to its luminosity; do not leave behind calamity for the person. This is the way in which birth and death proceed, and the source of good fortune and misfortune.
Regarding one’s dwelling: the essential point for reaching the Way truly prizes stillness and silence. How could the Buddha’s teaching delight in talk?
Yet, when a question is posed, one cannot help but respond. Do bells and drums ever sound of their own accord? They produce sound only when the mallet is applied.
Question: Confucius said, "The having of a ruler by the barbarians is not equal to the lack of one among the various states of the Central Xia.

Mencius, in censuring Chen Xiang for studying the arts of Xu Xing, said, "I have heard of using the Xia to transform the barbarians, but I have never heard of using the barbarians to transform the Xia.
You, sir, studied the Way of Yao, Shun, the Zhou, and Confucius when you were in your early twenties; yet now you abandon it to study [something else].
"The arts of the barbarians—are they not utterly delusive? Mōuzi replied: "These are merely the remnants of my own words from before I had understood the Great Way.
You may be said to perceive the outward splendor of ritual regulations while remaining blind to the reality of the Dao and its Virtue;
you have caught a glimpse of the light of a torch, yet have not beheld the sun of the celestial court. What Confucius spoke was intended to reform the ways of the world; what Mencius [spoke]..."
It is simply a matter of being swift and single-minded. Formerly, Confucius wished to dwell among the nine tribes of the Yi, saying, "When a gentleman dwells there, what is there that is uncivilized?
Furthermore, when Zhongni was not tolerated in Lu and Wei, and Meng Ke was not employed by Qi and Liang, would they have gone on to serve among the barbarians?
Yu emerged from the Xiqiang and became a sage-philosopher; Gusou fathered Shun, yet he was stubborn and arrogant; Youyu was born [among the Rong].
The Di people established a hegemony over Qin; Guan and Cai spread rumors from the region of the Yellow and Luo Rivers. The *Zhuangzi* states:
"The North Star is at the center of heaven and to the north of humanity. Judging by this, the territory of Han was not necessarily the center of heaven.
According to what is taught in the Buddhist scriptures, all sentient beings throughout the universe, from the zenith to the nadir, belong to the Buddha. For this reason, I have returned...
Revere and study them. Why should you abandon the Way of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius? Gold and jade do not harm one another;
a raw stone and a polished jade disk do not obstruct each other. To call others deluded is, in truth, to delude yourself.
Question: Confucius said, "Extravagance leads to insolence; frugality leads to parsimony. Between insolence and parsimony, it is better to be parsimonious.

Yu Sun said, "Frugality is the foundation of virtue; extravagance is the height of evil. Now, the Buddhist school makes the emptying of wealth for the sake of almsgiving its name and considers the giving away of all one's possessions to others as noble. How can there be any merit in this? Mouzi replied: "That was for a different time."

This was one such occasion. Confucius’s words criticized extravagance and the lack of ritual propriety; Yu Sun’s discourse satirized Duke Zhuang for his carving of the tubs. These were not prohibitions against giving.
When Shun farmed Mount Li, his benevolence did not reach his own neighborhood; when the Grand Duke (Tai Gong) slaughtered oxen, his kindness did not extend to his wife and children.
Yet once they were employed by the state, their benevolence flowed to the eight wildernesses and their favors were bestowed upon the four seas. This was because they possessed abundant wealth.
Much wealth is valued for its ability to aid the poor; frequent poverty is valued for its adherence to the Way.

Xu You did not covet the four seas; Boyi did not find his own state sweet. Yu Qing abandoned a fief of ten thousand households to rescue the urgent plight of the destitute—each acted according to their own will.
Xi Fuji preserved the entire neighborhood where he lived through the kindness of a meal from a jar; Xuan Meng [saved] with a single... [text fragment].
Because he provided him with food, he preserved his invaluable life. A secret act of kindness was performed unexpectedly, yet the manifest reward is as bright as the midday sun.
How much more so when one exhausts their family wealth to give rise to a benevolent mind; such merit is as towering as Mount Song and Mount Tai, and as vast as the rivers and seas.
Those who harbor goodness are answered with blessings; those who harbor evil are repaid with calamity. It has never happened that one might sow rice...
Yet one obtains wheat; this is one who brings misfortune upon themselves but reaps blessings.

A questioner asks: "In living in this world, there is no one who does not prefer wealth and honor while detesting poverty and low status, nor who delights in joy and ease while fearing toil and exhaustion.
Even the Yellow Emperor considered the five delicacies the highest for nourishing his nature, and Confucius said, 'In eating, do not disdain what is refined; in minced meat, do not..."
[The opponent said: "I loathe these trivialities. Today’s śramaṇas wear red cloth, eat but once a day, and shut off the six sense-faculties;

if they thus bring their lives to an end, what joy can there be in such a state? Mouzi replied: "Wealth and honor are what people desire, yet if they are not obtained through the proper Way, one does not dwell in them.
Poverty and low status are what people detest, yet if they are not removed through the improper Way, one does not depart from them."
Laozi said: "The five colors blind the eyes; the five notes deafen the ears; the five flavors dull the palate;
racing about for hunting and the chase makes the heart go wild; rare treasures obstruct one's conduct.
The sage provides for the belly, not for the eyes. Are these words not indeed true? Liu Xiaohui did not [covet] the position of the Three Ducal Ministers.
They exchanged their outward appearances. Duan Ganmu did not exchange his person for the wealth of Lord Wen of Wei;
Xu You and Chao Fu dwelt among the trees, claiming to find peace within the imperial domain; Boyi and Shuqi starved at Mount Shouyang, claiming to be satiated by the virtues of Kings Wen and Wu.
It was simply that each attained his own will—how could there be anything lacking in this?

Question: If the Buddha’s sutras are so profound, subtle, and elegant, why do you not discuss them at court, debate them with your sovereign and father, cultivate them within the domestic gate, or share them with your friends?
Why instead study the Confucian classics and read the various philosophical treatises?
Mouzi replied: You have not yet reached its source, yet you ask about its currents. It is like setting out ritual vessels and sacrificial stands upon a stack of mats.

To raise banners and standards in the court while wearing a fox-fur robe to face the *ruibin* (the fifth month), or to don fine linen and hempen garments to withstand the *huangzhong* (the eleventh month)—
though these may not lack beauty, they are misplaced in their setting and mistimed. Thus, to enter the gate of Shang Yang with the arts of Confucius,
or to present the doctrines of Mencius at the court of Su Qin and Zhang Yi, results in no merit whatsoever, while the transgressions are measured in fathoms.

It is but a foot [in length]. Laozi said: "The superior man, upon hearing the Way, practices it with diligence; the man of middle capacity, upon hearing the Way, is as if it exists and as if it does not;
the man of inferior capacity, upon hearing the Way, laughs at it loudly. Fearing such loud laughter, I do not discuss it.

One who is thirsty need not wait for the Yangtze or Yellow River to drink; the water of wells and springs—what is there that will not satisfy one’s thirst? For this reason, I have once again examined the classics and commentaries.
[The King] listened. He asked, "Laozi said, 'The wise do not speak; those who speak are not wise. He also said, 'Great eloquence appears like stammering;
great skill appears like clumsiness. A gentleman feels shame when his words exceed his actions. If you śramaṇas possess the ultimate Way, why do you not practice while remaining seated?"
Why do you further discuss right and wrong or argue over what is crooked and straight? I consider this to be a thief of virtue. Mouzi said:

"If one were to say, 'Next spring there will be a great famine,' yet one does not stop eating this autumn; or if one were to say, 'The Huangzhong note portends cold,' yet one wears heavy furs during the Ruijin month—though such preparations may be made early, they cannot avoid being foolish.
This is what Laozi meant when he spoke of those who have attained the Dao; it does not apply to those who have not attained the Dao.
How could one know this? A single word of the Great Way brings joy to the whole world; is this not the ultimate eloquence?
Does the Master Laozi not say, "When the task is accomplished, the body withdraws—this is the Way of Heaven"?

Once the body has withdrawn, what more need be said? Yet the śramaṇas of today have not yet attained the Way; how can they refrain from speaking? Even Laozi spoke; had he remained silent, he would have been no different.
What could five thousand words possibly express? If one knows and yet does not speak, that may be permissible. But if one neither understands the text nor can speak of it, such a person is a fool.
Therefore, one who can speak but cannot act is a teacher of the state; one who can act but cannot speak is a useful servant of the state;
and one who can both act and speak is a treasure of the state. Each of these three types has its own appropriate application. Why would they be considered enemies of virtue?
Indeed, it is only those who cannot speak and yet cannot act who are thieves.

A questioner asked: "According to your words, one should merely study eloquence and cultivate the art of debate; why then should one further cultivate one's emotions and nature, or practice the Way and its Virtue?
Mouzi replied: "How can you be so extremely slow to understand? For speech and discussion each have their own proper time."
Qú Yuàn said, "When the Way prevails in the state, one acts straightforwardly; when the Way does not prevail in the state, one rolls up [one's talents] and keeps them within.
Níng Wǔzǐ said, "When the Way prevails in the state, one is wise; when the Way does not prevail in the state, one is foolish.

Confucius said, "To fail to speak with one who can be spoken to is to lose the person; to speak with one who cannot be spoken to is to lose the words. Therefore, wisdom and folly each have their own proper time. As for discourse..."
Each has its own purpose. Why should one engage in mere discourse without putting it into practice? Question:
It is said that the Buddha-way is most supreme, most blissful, unconditioned, and tranquil. Yet many scholars of the world mock and disparage it, saying:
"Its doctrines are vast and empty, difficult to apply; they are void and nihilistic, difficult to believe. Why is this so? Mouzi replied: The ultimate flavor...
It does not accord with the ears of the multitude; a great sound is not in harmony with the ears of the masses.

When the *Xianchi* was performed, the *Dazhang* established, the flutes were sounded, and the nine-part melody was chanted, none could join in harmony. Yet when the strings and songs of Zheng and Wei were spread—the music of the times and customs—people would inevitably clap their hands without being asked.
Thus Song Yu said: "When a guest sang a song of the lowest rustic style in Ying, those who joined in harmony..."

When a thousand people were led by the *shāng* and *suǐ* notes, none of the multitude responded; these were all those who delighted in depraved sounds and did not understand the Great Standard (*dà dù*).
Hàn Fēi slandered Yáo and Shùn with the limited vision of one peering through a tube; Jīe Yū reviled Zhòng Ní based on a distinction as small as a hair’s breadth.
Both were those who indulged in the trivial while neglecting the great. Indeed, it was like hearing the *qīngshāng* note and calling it the *jiǎo*.

It was not the fault of the lute strings; it was the lack of acuity in the listener. To see the *hebi* (Harmony Jade) and call it stone is not because the jade is base, but because the observer lacks clarity of vision.
A divine serpent can sever itself and then reconnect, yet it cannot prevent others from severing it.
The numinous tortoise appeared in a dream to Yuan of Song, yet it could not avoid the net of Yu Qie. The Great Way has no...
It is not for the sake of being seen by the common world; it is not made noble by those who praise it, nor debased by those who revile it. Whether it is employed or not is determined by Heaven;
whether it is practiced or not is a matter of the times; whether it is believed or not is a matter of fate.

The questioner asked: "My son, you have used the principles of the Confucian classics to explain the teachings of the Buddha. Your language is rich and its meaning manifest; your prose is brilliant and your exposition beautiful.
Is it not possible that these are not the truth? Truly, this is merely your own eloquence. Mouzi replied: "I am not being eloquent."
"It is because one has seen extensively that one is no longer deluded. The questioner asked, "Is there a method for seeing extensively? Mouzi replied, "It is through the Buddhist scriptures.
Before I understood the Buddhist scriptures, my delusions were even greater than yours. Although I had recited the Five Classics, they served merely as ornamental flowers and did not yet bear fruit.
Once I had beheld the teachings of the Buddhist scriptures and examined the essentials of filial piety, I maintained a state of tranquility and detachment."

By nature, one contemplates the practice of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). When looking back upon worldly affairs, it is like standing at a deep well and gazing into a valley, or ascending Mount Song or Mount Dai and beholding a mere mound of earth.
The Five Classics are the five flavors; the Way of the Buddha is the five grains.
Since I first heard the Way, it has been as if clouds were parted to reveal the bright sun, or as a torch was brought into a dark chamber.
Question: You employ the language of the classics and commentaries, along with flowery rhetoric, to praise the Buddha’s conduct and extol his virtues.
Your loftiness surpasses the blue clouds, and your breadth exceeds the boundaries of the earth. Is it not that you have overstepped the source and exceeded the reality?
Yet your criticisms, sir, seem to hit upon a sore spot; what is this ailment? Mōuzi replied: To call me... [the text continues].
I, Bao, am like adding dust to Mount Song or Mount Dai, or collecting morning dew and casting it into the rivers and seas.

Your slander is like grasping a ladle or a cup and wishing to diminish the rivers and seas, or taking up a plow and wishing to damage Mount Kunlun, or holding up a single fist to obscure the light of the sun.
"Raising a clod of earth to dam a breach in the river—what I praise cannot make the Buddha higher, nor can your disparagement cause him to sink lower.

The commentary states: Muzi’s *Lihuolun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) consists of thirty-seven chapters; the Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang dynasty included it in the *Hongming ji* (Collection for Propagating and Clarifying).
The *Mingji* (Collection on Illumination) may be said to have originated from a distant antiquity.

Observing how it extols virtue, discerns delusion, restrains depravity, and wards off insult, while bringing forth the brilliant radiance of the Great Teaching, its author was clearly a gentleman of vast learning and extensive knowledge. At that time, however...
In the very beginning when the source of our Buddha-dharma first emerged, there were no more than ten Western śramaṇas who arrived in China, starting from Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.
The newly translated scriptures numbered over three hundred fascicles, all belonging to the Hīnayāna teachings.

If even the most subtle Mahāyāna sūtras have not yet reached this point, yet Mouzi is able to perceive it through profound insight and attain awakening, thereby harmonizing with the core of the Buddha’s mind and attaining such a deep flavor of the Dharma—when compared to figures like Mi Heng, Chen Yuanlong, and Kong Daohai of the late Han period, who vainly possessed extraordinary talents but ultimately failed to hear the Way and were nothing more than... [a mere... (one-sided person).
The worldly scholar has passed away. Thus, Mouzi was indeed a worthy man; it is a pity that his writings could not be recorded in their entirety.

I have selected twenty chapters to supplement this comprehensive treatise. For the most part, as for the delusions of the world, even when the World-Honored One was present in the world, there were still those who could not be free from them;
how much more so now, when more than two thousand years have passed since the Sage? [If one wishes] for the world to be cleared of such confusion...
That all could have attained correct faith—how could that have been possible? Nevertheless, this book must certainly be transmitted to posterity.

In the "Treatise on the Western Regions" of the *Hanshu*, the court historian Fan Ye’s commentary states: "Regarding the records of the climate and soil of the Western Regions, previous histories had not [yet provided them]."
I have heard it said that Zhang Qian conceived the strategy for reaching distant lands, and Ban Chao exerted his will to attain the rank of marquis;

in the end, they were both able to establish merit in the western regions and bring foreign domains into submission. From those who were subdued by the majesty of our military power to those enticed by wealth and bribes, there was none who did not present rare treasures from their regions and offer their children as hostages.
With shorn hair and crawling on their elbows, they turned eastward to pay court to the Son of Heaven. Therefore, the *wù* [military] stations were established.
Each official was assigned to his respective duty, and the establishment of the Protector-General (Du-hu) centralized the command and authority over them.

Later, Gan Ying reached Tiaozhi and traveled through Anxi; he gazed upon the Great Qin from the Western Sea. Spanning more than forty thousand *li* from the Yumen and Yangguan Passes, there was nothing he did not thoroughly investigate.
As for the excellence or deficiency of their local customs and dispositions, and the products they produced— [The text continues with a description of these matters.]

The distinct categories of things, the origins of rivers, valleys, and mountain ranges, the seasonal variations of coolness and heat, the paths of climbing mountains and crossing gorges by rope-bridges or wading through sands,
and the regions plagued by bodily fevers, headaches, wind-disasters, and demonic calamities— all these have been exhaustively depicted according to their actual conditions,
with their fundamental realities thoroughly investigated. As for the rise of the Buddha’s Way and divine transformations from the land of India, [it was likewise recorded].
In the two Chinese regional gazetteers (*fangzhi*), there is no mention [of this land]. Zhang Qian merely recorded that the region is hot and humid and that its inhabitants fight on elephants.
Although Ban Chao listed that they venerate the Buddha and refrain from killing, the merits of their refined texts, excellent Dharma, and guidance have not been transmitted or described.
I heard this from later accounts. That kingdom is as prosperous as the Central Lands; its "jade lamp" [the harmony of the four seasons] is temperate.
The Qi is where the spirits and sages descend and gather, and where the worthy and virtuous are born. When divine traces are strange and extraordinary, their principle transcends the realm of men;

when responses and verifications are clear and manifest, the events arise beyond the heavens. That there are those who have surpassed others yet remain unheard—could this not be because the Way was secret during past eras and its destiny has opened only in these later years?
Otherwise, why such extreme slander against the extraordinary? Since the Han dynasty, from the time of the King of Chu...
The Duke of Ying first flourished the sacrifices of fasting and purification; Emperor Huan further cultivated the adornments of the "flower-canopy" (huagai).

Is it because the subtle meaning had not yet been translated that they merely venerated the divine spirit? If one examines in detail the teachings on purifying the mind and casting off burdens, and the school that simultaneously discards both emptiness and existence—

It is a derivative of the Daoist scriptures. Furthermore, because it prizes benevolence, abhors killing, eliminates corruption, and exalts goodness, many worthy and enlightened gentlemen have come to cherish its teachings.
Yet, its proponents favor the grandiose while disregarding canonical authority; its marvels and deceptions are endless.

Even the eloquence of Zou Yan in his discourse on Heaven or Zhuang Zhou’s treatise on the space within a snail’s horn would not suffice to encompass even a ten-thousandth part of it. Moreover, its accounts of spirits arising and perishing—
Because causes and retributive marks follow one another, those who understand yet remain obscured are often confused by this; thus, many people have been perplexed.

This is because there is no fixed method for guiding the secular world, as the suitability for things varies according to their different circumstances. If one adopts the principle of returning to the same source and sets aside doubtful doctrines, then the Great Way will be realized.

Sengyue (Skt. *Vasudhara*), whose courtesy name was Weizong, was born at the end of the Jin dynasty and served under the Song. It was from Sengyue that the tradition of scholarly discourse on Buddhist matters within historical records first began.
Yuan Hong’s *Han ji* states: In the eleventh year of the Yongping era, there was the term "Futu," which refers to Buddha. In India, a land of the Western Regions, there is the Way of the Buddha.

"Buddha" (Fo) means "Awakening" in the language of Han; it signifies one who brings about the awakening of all living beings. His teaching takes the cultivation of goodness and a compassionate heart as its core;
he does not kill and is solely devoted to purity. Those who are most refined among his followers are called śramaṇas, which in the language of Han means "those who have ceased [evil]."
The mind. This means to stifle the thoughts, eliminate desires, and return to non-action (*wuwei*).
Furthermore, they hold that when a person dies, the spirit is not extinguished but follows along to receive another form. Whatever good or evil one performs during life all has its retribution;

therefore, what is valued is the practice of goodness and the cultivation of the Way, refining the spirit without ceasing until one reaches non-action and attains Buddhahood. The body of a Buddha is tall...
He was one zhang and six chi tall, of golden hue, with the light of the sun and moon adorning his neck. His transformations were boundless, and there was nowhere he could not enter;
thus, he was able to manifest through all things and bring great salvation to all living beings. Initially, Emperor Ming dreamed of a tall golden man with the light of the sun and moon upon his neck.
He questioned his ministers about it, and some said, "In the west there is a deity whose name is Buddha."
His stature was tall and large. Consequently, he dispatched an envoy to India to inquire about their spiritual arts and to procure images of their deities to bring back.

There were several tens of millions of scrolls of scriptures, which take "non-being" (*xūwú*) as their fundamental principle; they encompass both the subtle and the coarse, leaving nothing uncomprised.
They excel in producing discourse that is vast, expansive, and far-reaching; what they seek lies within the single body, while what they clarify lies beyond the reach of sight and hearing.
Ordinary people of the world may consider this to be empty and exaggerated; yet, it ultimately returns to the profound and subtle, so deep and far-reaching that it is difficult to fathom.
Thus, when princes, dukes, and great officials contemplate the juncture of death, life, and karmic retribution, there are none who do not startle and lose their composure.
The Eastern Slope Recluse of our dynasty said: "This is likely the speech of those who first came to know of the Buddha in China.
Though it is shallow and simple, its essential points are fully present. It is like a rustic man who, having caught a deer, simply boils and eats it;

later, he sells it to a townsman, who then places it in the imperial kitchen to be prepared in a hundred ways. Yet, as for the inherent excellence of the deer itself, it has not changed by even a single thread."
"‘Mao’ (rarely) refers to the occasion when [the Buddha] ate boiled food. (Regarding Yuan Hong’s *Han ji* discussion of the Buddha’s era, the complete text is not extant.

The "Yuan Hong’s Discussion on the Buddha" cited in the *Dongpo Dazhuanji* is actually a passage from the commentary by Prince Zhanghuai of the Tang dynasty on the biography of Chu Wang Ying in the *Hanshu*. It should be understood that this complete passage from the *Han ji* is the correct version.)
*Comprehensive Chronicle of Buddhism from the Longxing Era*, Volume One;
*Comprehensive Chronicle of Buddhism from the Longxing Era*, Volume Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of the Stone Chamber in Longxing Prefecture.

In the first year of the Huangchu era of the Cao Wei dynasty, Emperor Wen received the abdication of the Han at Fan Chang and subsequently established his capital at Luoyi. This lasted until the first year of the Xianxi era of Emperor Yuan;
five sovereigns reigned for a total of forty-five years. During this period, six śramaṇas from the Western Regions produced various sūtras and vinayas.
The *Karmavācanā* (羯磨) consists of thirteen sections in twenty-five fascicles.
The treatise states: Since the Han dynasty, the empire has been unified; however, following the Jian’an era, the realm began to divide into three contending powers.
Yuan and Cao vied for supremacy in the Central Plains, while Liu and Sun contended for the "deer" [the throne] at the Yangtze Gorges. The Five Peaks were shrouded in dust, and the Nine Provinces...
Clouds gathered like armies. Some established imperial designs within two sacrifices; others laid the foundations for hegemony through the division of the realm into three.
Thus, the Founder of Wei held the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords, while the House of Liu relied upon Jian Gate to plot the containment of the imperial carriage.

The brilliant strategy of the Sun clan raised high the barriers of the Yangtze River, employing the martial power of their "claws and fangs" and the might of the Sleeping Dragon to separately occupy a domain and swallow up [their rivals].

To "devour" (shi) refers to the mind. Each [ruler] spans the borders and frontiers, fortifying the passes and barriers; they extensively recruit men of talent and virtue to serve as their limbs and assistants.
The worthy and capable were honored with generous gifts as treasures of the state; thus, master craftsmen and wondrous teachings returned once more here.

When Saṃghadeva arrived in Wu, the śarīra relics manifested their spiritual brilliance in the region east of the Yangtze; when Kālaya traveled to Wei, the prohibitive precepts were first inaugurated in the capital of Luoyang.

The observance of the precepts flourished greatly from this point onward, and pagodas were erected everywhere. Translators followed local customs by retaining the original dialects; as scriptures were produced according to the times, titles were assigned accordingly.
Thus, there arose the *Wu-pin* (Wu-version) and the *Shu-pu-yao* (Shu-version of the *Prabhūtaratna Sūtra*). It was from this that the practice of re-translating and re-editing began;
the proliferation of divergent versions and the loss of the original translations originated here. Furthermore, at that time, the Three Kingdoms stood as separate entities.

Why is it that the single capital of Western Shu alone lacks a record for its era? Now, as we compile the chronicles of Great Wu, the monastics and laypeople of the Wei court are all listed below to the left.
In the second year of the Jiaping era, the Indian śramaṇa Dharmakāla arrived in Luoyang and translated the *Sangīti-vinaya-mātṛkā*.
The flow of the Dharma began to spread; at that time, bhikṣus merely shaved their hair, as there was yet no formal code of discipline (*vinaya*).

All ritual matters for the upoṣadha were conducted like sacrificial rites. Dharmakāla first produced the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, taking the precepts as his sun and moon, and further invited a Brahman monk.
Dharmatrāta and others established the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures); thereby, the source was clarified and resolved, and the Way of the Dharma subsequently flourished.
Thus, the monastic precepts in the Middle Kingdom began from this point onward.
In this year, the Indian śramaṇa Kang Seng-kai arrived at the Baima Monastery in Luoyang and translated two sections of the sutras.
At that time, there was an Indian śramaṇa named Dharmagupta (translated into Chinese as Fazang). His teacher was Kātyāyanīputra, who was the ninth-generation disciple of Ānanda.
Dharmagupta followed in his lineage and was profoundly skilled in the Vinaya school; he brought the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* with him.
In Luoyang, during the Zhengyuan era, the śramaṇa Tandi from the kingdom of Anxi arrived; he was also well-versed in the Vinaya studies.
Consequently, at the Bai-ma Temple, he was requested by the assembly to jointly translate one fascicle of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
In the first year of the Tianning era (the *Ganlu* period), the Śramaṇa Bo Yan arrived at Luoyang from the Western Regions and translated six scriptures in nine fascicles.
In that same year, the foreign Śramaṇa Zhi Jianglianglou— whose name means "Fearless" (*Abhaya*)— translated the *Dharmapada-samādhi-sūtra* in one section and six fascicles at Jiaozhou.

Prince Si of Chen, Cao Zhi, styled Zijian, was the middle son of Emperor Wu. At the age of ten, he could recite over one hundred thousand words from the *Shi* and *Shu* classics and was skilled at composing prose.

When Taizuo saw him, he marveled at him and asked, "Did you have someone else compose this for you? Cao Zhi replied, "Speech issues forth as ready-made discourse; when the pen touches the paper, it forms a finished composition.
If you wish to test me on the spot, how could I have relied on another? As he grew up, he became proficient in the various arts of the world.
His skills were refined beyond measure. When Han Dan-chun saw him, he was struck with awe and sighed in admiration, calling him a "heavenly man.

Whenever Zhi read Buddhist scriptures, he would linger over them, sighing in appreciation and playing with the text, regarding them as the ultimate pinnacle of the Supreme Way. He chanted the seven musical tones, their rising and falling, their twists and turns;
the world all followed his intonation as a model. At Mount Yu, he heard a sound that was exceptionally extraordinary—pure, resonant, plaintive, and elegant.

Consequently, he imitated those sounds to create the *Banzan* (Brahman-chant). The *Gyozan-banzan* (Yushan Brahman-chant) found in Buddhist liturgical rites today is the very legacy of his performance.
Initially, when Emperor Wu of Wei wished to appoint him as his successor, Cao Zhi avoided it by disgracing himself through excessive drinking.

Emperor Wen was somewhat envious of his talent and suppressed him so that he would not be employed. Cao Zhi once sought to prove his own worth, but the Emperor did not grant permission. Subsequently, within eleven years, three times—

He moved his residence to Fán. Cài died with his ambitions unfulfilled at the age of thirty-one. Initially, while atop Yú Mountain overlooking Dōng'ā, Cài sighed deeply, vowing to spend his final days there;
he subsequently prepared his grave and left instructions to his son to conduct a simple burial. During his lifetime, Cài did not place great faith in the teachings of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi;

he expressed his views in the "Discourse on Discerning the Way" (*Biàn dào lùn*), which is now included in the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification [of Buddhism]) within the Buddhist canon.
Sun Wu’s ruler was Sun Quan, styled Zhongmou. He was a native of Fuchun in Wu Commandery. Above his family’s eastern tomb, there were frequently divine lights and vaporous clouds.
When Quan was born, his eyes possessed an extraordinary radiance; he had a square jaw and a large mouth. His father, Sun Jian, marveled at him, saying:

He was a vessel for both kingship and hegemony. After Sun Ce passed away and Wei Wen received the abdication of the mandate, in the second year [of Yellow Dragon], Sun Quan assumed the title of King of Wu and established the first year of the Huangwu era.
By the third year of Taihé of Emperor Ming of Wei, he subsequently ascended the imperial throne. Initially, the capital was at Wuchang;
it was next moved to Moling, and then again to Jianye. Under four successive rulers, the state endured for fifty-nine years before its territory entered the Jin dynasty.
There were four individuals, both monastics and laypeople. It is said that they translated a total of one hundred and eighteen works in one hundred and ninety fascicles.
The śramaṇa Vighna—here translated as "Obstruction"—was a native of India.
Together with the śramaṇa Zhu Lüyán, he arrived at Wuchang Commandery and translated two works. After Vighna passed away, Lüyán further translated three works at the capital of Yangdu.

Three fascicles. At that time, there was the lay devotee Zhi Qian, whose courtesy name was Gongming. He was a native of the country of Yuezhi. Initially, he traveled to Luoyang and studied under Zhi Liang;
Liang’s courtesy name was Jiming, who had studied under Zhi Chen. The world said that no one in the realm possessed such broad knowledge as these three Zhis.
Qian was widely read in the classics and scriptures; as a man, he was slender, tall, dark, and thin, with eyes that were mostly white.
His eyes were yellow. At that time, people said, "Zhi Lang’s eyes are yellow; though his physical form is slight, he is a treasury of wisdom.
When he fled to Wu to seek refuge, the Ruler of Wu saw him and was pleased with him. The state of Wu appointed him as a *boshi* (Doctor of Literature).
He translated one hundred and twenty-nine scriptures in one hundred and fifty-two fascicles.
In the fourth year of the Chiku era, the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui arrived in Jinling from the kingdom of Kangju.
He constructed a thatched hut, established an image, and practiced the Way. When the people of the country first saw the śramaṇa, they were struck with wonder and astonishment.

An official reported this to Sun Quan, the Ruler of Wu, saying, "Is this perhaps the lingering influence of the Buddha-spirit dreamed of by Emperor Ming of the Han? A decree was issued for him to appear and explain his situation. Senghui advanced...
He said, "The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has been in parinirvāṇa for a thousand years; yet his sacred relics and śarīra manifest divine responses without limit.
In the past, King Aśoka enshrined them in eighty-four thousand stūpas—this is the legacy of that transformation. I shall use this as a means to demonstrate my own prowess, saying:
'If the śarīra can be obtained, I shall build a stūpa for them; if there is no proof, the state shall impose its regular punishments. I request that a date be set."

After seven days, he said to his attendants, "The rise or fall of the Great Dharma depends on this single undertaking. You must apply yourselves with focused intent, purify your hearts, and pray with sincere devotion.
When the appointed time came and no sign appeared, he extended the period to fourteen days (two weeks). Still there was no response. Huiquan said, "Go ahead and cook it.

Huihui silently recited the Buddha’s name, thinking, "The Buddha is truly compassionate; how could he ever fail me? He further requested an extension of the time, praying with the resolve to die. Again—

Seven days passed; the assembly was so terrified that they lost their color. At the fifth watch, they heard a sharp metallic sound. Rising to look, they saw five-colored rays flashing forth from within the jar.

He cried out in a loud voice, "Truly, my wish has been fulfilled! At dawn, he presented it [to the Emperor]. The high officials gathered to observe it and sighed in admiration, saying, "A rare omen for this age.
Huì further stated, "The majestic spiritual power of the śarīra is such that nothing in all the worlds can surpass it."
When it was broken, he had a strong man strike it with a hammer; though the anvil shattered, the radiance remained as before.
Thereupon, a stupa was erected at Fotuo-li, and a monastery was named Jianchu, where [Dharmakṣema] took up residence.
Kàn Zé, courtesy name Dérùn, was a native of Shānyīn, Huìjī. His family had been farmers for generations. Zé was fond of learning;

though living in poverty and lacking resources, he often supported himself by working as a hired scribe. Once a transcription was finished, he could immediately recite it from memory. Consequently, he read extensively across all the classics and histories.
When Yú Fān saw him, he praised him, saying, "The young Mr. Kàn is outstanding and exceptional; he is of the same lineage as Zhōngshū and Zǐyún. He entered government service...
Wu. [Kang] Senghui entered Wu while serving as the Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince. The Ruler of Wu then asked Kang Sengze: "In what year of the Han Ming era did Buddhism enter China?
For what reason did it not reach the East earlier? Sengze replied: "The Dharma first arrived in the eleventh year of Yongping;
calculating from the present, the fourth year of Chihu, it has been one hundred and seventy years. It was the fourteenth year of Yongping..."
The Daoist master of the Five Peaks, Chu Shanxin, and others requested to compete in dharma with the Western monks. Thereupon, Shanxin died of his own delusions;

his disciples carried his corpse back to be buried at Mount Nanyue. Generally speaking, those of the Central Kingdom were not permitted to leave home [to become monastics], so there was no one to propagate [the teachings].
Furthermore, having suffered through years of turmoil, they only reached their own country now. The Ruler of Wu said: "Confucius composed and transmitted..."

"The Classics and Instructions serve to educate future generations; Laozi and Zhuangzi cultivate the self for personal enjoyment, wandering freely among mountains and forests with their hearts set on tranquility.
Why, then, should one serve the Buddha? Zhe said: "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi take Heaven as their model and regulate their applications, not daring to disobey Heaven.

The Buddhist teachings are that the various heavens practice them and do not dare to disobey the Buddha. By this one may see the difference in their relative excellence" (from Zong Bing’s *Mingfo lun*).

In the first year of the Tianning era [260 CE], Sun Hao, the ruler of Wu, ascended the throne. He proceeded to destroy shrines to the spirits, and his persecution extended even to Buddhist monasteries.
His ministers remonstrated, saying that the former emperor had established these temples because he was moved by auspicious omens, and thus they should not be destroyed.

Thereupon, he dispatched his minister Zhang Yu to confront Kang Senghui. Senghui refuted his arguments with such sharp eloquence that Zhang Yu could not humble him; returning, he reported that Senghui’s talent was extraordinary.

Now, the śramaṇas are single-minded and devoted in observing the precepts, and their observance of ritual propriety is likewise uniform. As for the intensity with which they observe these precepts—

They sacrifice their bodies without hesitation; how could they dare to treat their physical forms with negligence toward ritual reverence? Whenever they see incense being burned for prayers, they invariably prioritize the state first.
Their desire to provide comprehensive blessings and abundance is boundless and inexhaustible. Their service to the sovereign and their profound obedience arise spontaneously.
The simplicity of their rituals is intended solely to maintain focused adherence to the Dharma; therefore, when the former sages governed the world, they followed this principle without alteration.

This is indeed a change. Yet, the heavenly net is vast and wide; though its mesh is sparse, nothing escapes it. We, your subjects, with our humble and sincere devotion, believe that not requiring [the recipients] to pay their respects would not violate the law.
By bestowing grace according to what is beneficial to them, you ensure that both the wise and the ignorant dare not fail to apply their whole hearts [to virtue].
Thus, above, there will be the bounty of Heaven’s covering and Earth’s supporting; below, there will be those who maintain integrity and cultivate goodness. We respectfully submit this again.
He set forth his own ignorance and shallowness, wishing to be granted a review of his proposal; thus, the debate on the water supply was finally shelved.

He Chong (courtesy name Cidao), a native of Qian in Lujiang, was the grandson of Wei Yan, a Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. From his youth, he was renowned for his literary talent and mastery of the classics.
Initially, he served as a clerk under Wang Dun. When Wang Dun’s elder brother, Wang Han, governed Lujiang with greed and corruption, Dun once, during a formal assembly—
He remarked, "My elder brother is surely doing well in the commandery. Lu Jiang’s scholar praised him for this. He Chong, maintaining a stern expression, said, "I am a native of that very commandery;
what I have heard differs from this. Hui Dun remained silent, and all the guests felt uneasy, yet He Chong remained composed as usual.
Once, Minister of State Yu Liang recommended him to Emperor Ming, saying, "He Chong’s character and capacity are broad and upright."

He was the object of the hopes of ten thousand men. If he had been able to preside over the court as a deputy to the aged ministers and serve as the Minister of State (Shangshu Ling), he would have exerted his abilities for the public good rather than privately cultivating personal favors;
thus, he was highly esteemed by the world. Once, Ruan Yu jokingly said to him, "Your ambitions are as vast as the universe, and your courage surpasses that of former ages.
When Xun Chong examined the meaning of these words, Ruan Yu replied, "I am merely plotting to obtain a commandery of several thousand households."
He had not yet attained [his goal]. "Is it not also great for you to aspire to become a Buddha? he asked. He passed away at the age of fifty-five.
Thereafter, his family members served the Buddha with great devotion. His grandsons Shangzhi, Dian, Yin, and others all established great principles and elucidated the Buddha-dharma.

In the second year of the Xingning era, Emperor Ai issued an edict for the Dharma Master Zhu Qian to lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā* within the imperial palace. He once arrived wearing leather sandals;
those inside the hall gathered to watch him, admiring his lofty character and moral integrity, initially unaware that he was in the marketplace of court.
At that time, Sima Jianwen was acting as regent. Liu Tan (tán) of Pei State once encountered Zhu Qian during a session with Sima Jianwen and mocked him, saying, "Monk..."
"Did you also frequent the gates of noble mansions? He replied, "You yourself see them as vermilion gates; to this poor monk, they appear as thatched huts.

When he took his leave to return to Mount Shan, Zhi Dun sent a letter requesting to purchase a small ridge on the island for him to retire in seclusion. Huiqian replied, "If you wish to come, I shall provide for you.
I have never heard of Nao and You purchasing a mountain to go into hiding. He passed away in the second year of the Ningkang era. Emperor Wu issued an edict stating:

His realization of the profound principles of the Dharma was vast and far-reaching, and his discernment was pure and lofty. He renounced the glory of being a high minister to don the simple white robes of a monk.
Dwelling in the mountains beyond the secular world, he was diligent and tireless. Just as we were relying on him to proclaim the Way and save all living beings, he suddenly passed away.
He took this to heart with deep sorrow. Consequently, he granted one hundred thousand strings of cash to assist in the construction of a stupa for the remains. Huiqian’s courtesy name was Fashen;
he was the first among the Chinese śramaṇas to receive imperial burial honors.
The Dharma Master Zhi Dun, style name Daolin, was on intimate terms with Xie An, the Grand Marshal (Taifu) of the Eastern Jin, and Wang Xizhi, the Right General (Youjun).
When Xie An was serving as Governor of Wuxing, he sent a letter to Dun, which read in brief: "My longing for you has accumulated day by day, becoming even more intense these days.

I know you intend to return to Shan County to manage your own affairs; at this, I am deeply moved. Human life is but a temporary lodging. Since the time of [Wang] Xiang, matters of refined elegance and worldly success have been..."
All things have been worn away and exhausted; only the constant, lingering sorrow remains. I hope you will come once to dispel it with conversation, so that a single day may feel as a thousand years.
When Zhu Qian took his leave of the court, an imperial edict was issued for Zhu Dun to succeed him in preaching the Dharma within the palace precincts.
At that time, prominent scholars such as Yin Hao, Xi Chao, Sun Chuo, Huan Yanbiao, Wang Jingren, He Chong, Wang Tanzhi, and Yuan [Shi]...

Yanbo maintained formal friendships with both of them. Those throughout the world who wished to see their refined character would visit Liu Xi at Baima Temple to discuss Zhuangzi, where they took the "free and easy wandering" (*xiaoyao*) to mean the fulfillment of one's nature.
Huidun said, "Not so. Jie and Zhi took cruelty and tyranny as their nature; could that also be called 'free and easy wandering'?

Thereupon, he wrote a commentary on the "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter, which scholars took as their authority. Wang Meng... [text ends]... Once, [Hui] Meng had exerted his utmost concentration and composed several hundred words. He presented them to Huidun, who said, "We have been parted for a long time, yet you have not improved at all; why is this? Meng, flushed with shame and perspiration, replied, "What is the King of the Red Alms-bowl like? Xi Chao once asked Xie Taifu: [The passage continues: "I have heard that when Wang Dao was young, he was already known for his brilliance.

When he first entered the capital, he went to visit the Prime Minister Wang Dun. Dun said to him, 'I have not seen you for a long time; why is it that you have not grown at all? Dao was ashamed and perspired, saying, 'What is the King of the Red Alms-bowl like? Xi Chao once asked Xie Taifu:

Hui Dun remarked, "How does he compare to Xi Kang, the Director of the Central Secretariat? The Grand Tutor said, "Xi Kang could only manage half of it. He then asked, "How does he compare to Yin Hao?
The Grand Tutor said, "In his tireless debate and argumentation, he likely surpasses [Yin Hao] in his transcendent insight and profound source;

Yin Hao possesses a virtue that falls short. Later, Hui Chao wrote in a letter to his relatives and old friends: "Master Lin has attained the Way of the Divine Principle; his profound extraction and solitary awakening are such that [his] numerical..."
For a hundred years, he alone has succeeded in propagating the Great Dharma and ensuring that the True Principle does not perish.
In the second year of the Taihe era, while Emperor Haixi was on the throne, Huida submitted a memorial requesting to return to the mountains.
An imperial decree provided him with provisions, and various high officials were dispatched to see him off at Zenglu Pavilion. Cai Zishu arrived first and sat down near Daolin; just as he rose—
Xie Wan hurried toward him. Zishu turned back, joined his bedding together, and lifted Wan up, throwing him to the ground. Wan said, "I nearly damaged my face.
Zishu replied, "I did not initially consider your face at all. Such was the way he was admired by those of his time.

In his later years, he resided at Mount Yin and lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*, with Xu Xun serving as the presiding lecturer (*dùjiǎng*). Whenever Zhu Tún expounded a single point of meaning, the assembly believed that Xu Xun could not refute it;
yet when Xu Xun posed a challenge, they further believed that Zhu Tún could not resolve it. Thus, the challenges between guest and host continued endlessly.

Among the listeners, many claimed to have grasped Zhu Tún’s intent, but upon being cross-examined, they invariably lost their way. He authored the *Jísè yóuxuán* (Wandering in the Profound through Immediate Form) and the *Shèngbù* (Treatise on the Sage).
In his treatises on the discrimination of knowledge and other matters, there was one who gave him a horse; he kept it, saying, "I simply love its noble beauty. There was another who gave him a crane;
he released it, saying, "A creature that soars toward the heavens—how could it be a mere plaything for the ears and eyes? The gentleman [Zhu Daoqian] praised him for his profound understanding.

Upon his death, Dai Kui passed by his stupa and sighed, saying, "The sound of his virtuous teachings has not yet faded, yet the arched timbers [of the tomb] are already overgrown. To calculate the principles of the spirit..."
"Continuous and enduring, it does not perish along with the cycles of the qi.
Xi Chao, courtesy name Jiabin, possessed a transcendent breadth of character from his youth. His discussions on principles and meanings were refined and subtle;

he set his aspirations upon the Buddha and was particularly fond of practicing *dāna* (charity). He was recruited as a military aide by the Great General Huan Wen. At that time, Wang Xun served in the same administration. Xun...

Xiao Chao was the Adjutant (Cānjūn), while Xiao Xun was the Secretary (Zhǔbù). Chao had a long, beautiful beard, whereas Xun was short and small in stature. Within the commandery, they were known by the saying:

"The Bearded Adjutant and the Short Secretary can make the Duke smile, and they can make the Duke angry. When Xie An and Wang Tanzhi visited the residence of [Wang] Wen, Wen first ordered Chao to lie within the curtains to listen to their discussion of affairs.
Suddenly, a breeze stirred and the curtains opened; An laughed and said, "Mr. Xi may truly be said to have entered [the room]."

He was a guest of the imperial court. Chao Xiyin delighted in reclusion; whenever he heard of one who had "shaken off their robes" (renounced worldly life), he would invariably build a house for them and provide them with utensils and implements.
Zhi Daolin often remarked that his achievement in penetrating the subtle was sufficient to rank alongside the era of the Zhengshi period, and he held him in high esteem.

Furthermore, he was on close terms with Dharma Master Tai. They once made an agreement that whoever died first should inform the other of any karmic retributions encountered in the realm of the unseen. Shortly thereafter—
Tài passed away. One night, [the deity] appeared in a dream and said, "The matters of retribution that I previously promised you have now all proven not false.

I hope you will not forget to cultivate virtue so as to deliver your spirit to higher realms. From this point on, Chāoyóu followed the Way with ever-increasing devotion and consequently composed the *Wǔjiè wén* (Text on the Five Precepts).
Its summary states: "By not killing, one attains long life; by not stealing, one enjoys constant peace; by not engaging in sexual misconduct, one remains pure."
If one does not deceive others, people will always respect and trust them. If one does not become intoxicated, the divine principles of the mind will be clearly understood.
Having practiced the five precepts, one should then cultivate the monthly and seasonal fasts. The three seasonal fasts occur in the first, fifth, and ninth months;

on each of these months, one observes the fast from the first day to the fifteenth. The six monthly fasts occur on the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days. In all cases...

On days of fasting, one must not taste fish or meat, nor consort with a wife or concubines. One should eat before midday; once midday has passed, one must not taste anything sweet, fragrant, or delicious.
One should cleanse the mind to contemplate the Way, take refuge in the Triple Gem, repent and reproach oneself, and practice the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
One should distance oneself from the chamber, remain unattached to the six desires, refrain from whipping or scolding others, and avoid riding oxen or driving [beasts].

The men wear their armor and carry weapons; the women likewise discard their unguents, powders, and ornamental hairpins. They rectify their hearts and align their intentions, striving to maintain gentleness and compliance.
Those who observe the fast do so universally for the sake of deceased ancestors, present acquaintances and relatives, and all sentient beings alike.
By means of this sincere devotion, once a mutual resonance is awakened, they shall be liberated from the suffering of transgressions. Therefore, [this practice embodies] loyalty and filial piety.
Those who are virtuous must apply themselves with even greater diligence. This is truly because the merit of salvation does not reside within oneself alone.

In the first year of the Ningkang era of the Eastern Jin dynasty, the Dharma Master Dao’an constructed a stūpa and cast a bronze image at Tanchi Temple in Xiangyang.
He was able to manifest his supernatural powers and travel to Mount Fang, where he halted. His radiance illuminated the heavens, and the entire capital turned out to gaze upon him in worship;
their joyful shouts shook the mountains and valleys. Fu Jian, the ruler of Qin, sent a foreign gold-adorned reclining image and a Maitreya statue with golden threads and pearls.

Whenever Dao’an gave lectures, he would set up [statues] to serve as witnesses. One night, light emanated from the statue and illuminated the room; upon inspection, it was found that there were *śarīra* relics within its crown.
Xi Zuochi, a man of high integrity from Xiangyang, had previously established friendly relations by means of a letter.

He then went to visit Dao’an, introducing himself as “Xi Zuochi of the Four Seas. Dao’an replied, “Shi Dao’an who covers the heavens. They took great delight in meeting one another. Dao’an then sent a letter to Xie Dong.
Mount [Shan]. He was called An, a truly eminent and superior man; it is only a regret that you have not met him once. When Emperor Xiaowu heard of An’s reputation, he issued an edict stating:
"The Dharma Master illuminates both gods and men through his virtue and the Way, causing the Great Dharma to flow and spread, serving as a reliance for all living beings.

It is fitting that he receive the stipend of a Prince every day. The relevant authorities were ordered to provide these provisions at the appropriate times. An firmly declined and would not accept them. Not long after,

Fu Jian attacked and captured Xiangyang. Upon obtaining Dao’an, he was delighted and said to his attendants, "With a hundred thousand troops, I have taken Xiangyang, yet I have gained but one person and a half.
His attendants asked who they were. He replied, "Master An is one person; Xi Zuochi is half a person.
When Dao’an entered the Guanzhong region, the tens of thousands of śramaṇas all took their master’s surname as theirs and adopted his name. Dao’an said, "Do not let the Master [Fu Jian]..."
He was like the Buddha, the World-Honored One. It was appropriate that the śramaṇas should take "Śākya" as their clan name.
When the *Ekottarika Āgama* arrived, it stated: "The four rivers enter the sea and no longer have different names; those who leave the home life from the four castes are equally called Śākyas.
Thus, [the tradition] came into accord with the sutra, and the world increasingly revered him. Furthermore, an ancient bronze cauldron was found in Lantian, with a capacity of twenty-seven hu.
There were also seal-script inscriptions that no one at court could identify. When someone asked Dao’an about them, he replied, "These were cast by Duke Xiang of Lu.
Consequently, Fu Jian decreed that the scholars of the Three Academies should take Dao’an as their teacher whenever they encountered doubts. A proverb arose among the people of the state:

"In study, if one does not take Dao’an as one’s teacher, the meaning will not be free from difficulty. At that time, the Fu clan’s dominion extended east to the Bohai Sea and westward it annexed Kucha.

To the south it encompassed Xiangyang, and to the north it reached the desert; only Jiankang remained unsubdued. Fu Jian’s long-standing ambition was to seize and possess it, yet he would not listen when his ministers remonstrated against him.
One man, the Grand Marshal Fu Rong, knelt and implored him for the sake of the common people, saying: "Please grant An [Shigao] a single word of favor."

Fu Jian sent for Dao’an at the Eastern Garden and ordered him to ascend the carriage to travel together with him. The Minister of Works, Quan Yi, stepped forward and said, “I have heard that when the Son of Heaven travels in his formal state carriage, the Secretariat Director must accompany him as an attendant.

Now, Dao’an has destroyed his physical form [as a layman]; how can he be permitted to join such a retinue? Fu Jian replied in anger: [...]* *Note: The original text fragment ends with "Fu Jian replied in anger," indicating the remainder of the dialogue was not included in the source provided.*
"Master An’s virtue and character are worthy of the highest honor. I would rather exchange the empire for him; the splendor of this carriage does not truly match his merit.

He immediately issued an edict for the attendants to support An as he ascended the carriage. Thereupon, the attendants knelt and assisted him. Fu Jian turned to An and said, "I intend to travel south with you to Wu and Yue.
I shall marshal the six armies on a tour of inspection, ascend Mount Kuaiji, and gaze upon the vast blue sea."
[The Emperor] said, "I am also pleased. [Ji Kang] replied, "Your Majesty responds to Heaven and governs the world, possessing the wealth of the eight provinces.

From your central seat, you command the four seas; it would be fitting for you to settle your spirit in non-action (*wuwei*) and rival the glory of Yao and Shun. Now, you wish to lead an army of a million to seek out lands of the lowest grade.
The regions of the southeast have low terrain and pestilential vapors; in ancient times, even Shun and Yu traveled there and did not return."
The First Emperor has gone forth and does not return. From my humble perspective, I do not see this as being appropriate. Yang Gong is a close relative and Shi Yue is a high-ranking minister;
both are profoundly concerned for the state, and their arguments are worthy of being heard. Fu Jian said: "It is not that the realm is not vast enough.
I merely wish to gauge the will of Heaven and clarify where the Great Mandate resides. There is a time-honored maxim regarding touring the lands in accordance with the seasons."
"If it were as your lofty argument suggests, would there not be records of emperors inspecting the various regions? An said, "If you must go, you should halt at Luoyang.

Rest your spear and harbor your sharpness while sending out proclamations to the south of the Yangtze. If they do not submit, it will not be too late to strike them. Fu Jian did not accept this advice.
In the seventh year of the Taiyuan era, Fu Jian personally led a hundred thousand cavalry and infantry to the outskirts of Shouchun, where he encountered the Jin forces of Xuzhou.
He was defeated by the Provincial Governor Xie Xuan and fled back on a single horse. Dao’an constantly expounded upon the meanings of the scriptures, always seeking authoritative proof from the Sage.
One day, he was moved by the descent of a venerable elder with bushy eyebrows. Dao’an brought forth his own compositions and presented them;

the elder marveled at them, deeming them to be in complete accord with the Buddha’s mind. He further promised to provide secret assistance in propagating the teachings. Dao’an recognized him as Piṇḍola and consequently prepared...
Originally, offerings were made daily for the ancestral sacrifices; it was from the time of An that offerings were first made specifically for Piṇḍola.
Among his disciples who mastered his teachings, there were several dozen, the most renowned among them being Fayu, who transmitted the doctrine to Changsha and had several hundred followers.
When one of Yu’s disciples drank wine privately, Yu let him be and did not reprimand him. An knew of this and immediately sealed a thorn branch and sent it to him. Yu embraced the thorn branch and—
Weeping, he said, "I, Dongzhong, have been unworthy and have caused my Master distant grief. Thereupon, he prostrated himself and accepted his reprimand.

On the final day of the first month in the fourteenth year of the Taiyuan era, Dao’an ordered his disciples to prepare for a ritual bath. Suddenly, he saw a strange monk entering and exiting through a crack in the wall.
When Dao’an asked him where he resided, the monk pointed toward the northwest; immediately, the clouds parted, revealing a multi-storied pavilion that appeared like a phantom.
He emerged and said, "That is Tuṣita Heaven. That evening, several hundred small children all came to bathe and then departed.
Those who recognized him considered them to be companions of an Arhat. On the eighth day of the second month, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Hui'an's appearance was plain and his complexion dark; yet he was widely learned and skilled in literary composition. A popular proverb says: "The lacquer-clad monk startles the four quarters."
His neighbor [had a mark]; on his left arm there was a square inch of flesh that protruded like a seal. He was thus called by the time-honored title "Seal-Hand Bodhisattva.
He composed twenty-four articles concerning the monastic rules for monks and nuns and the regulations for the Dharma gates, which the world has followed and practiced ever since.
The treatise states: At the very beginning when the source of the Dharma was still in its infancy, it found security through Fotudeng; from Fotudeng, it reached Master Huiyuan.

The transformative rituals and models of these three great beings were in no way different. Yet as for their respective ways of entering or withdrawing from the world and their personal conduct and aspirations, why do they appear so contradictory?
Generally speaking, following Emperor Ming of the Jin dynasty after the court had moved south of the Yangtze River, when...
Although the rulers of those times were not particularly praiseworthy, the court’s institutions, regulations, and laws had never faltered.

It was precisely during such a period that Master Huiyuan was able to pursue his lofty aspirations; when the Son of Heaven visited Xunyang, he issued an edict but could not induce him to leave the mountains.

In their respective positions, they looked up and down and yielded to circumstances as required. Would Shi Le and Fu Jian have been willing to tolerate someone reclining in the mountain forests and refusing to bow before them?
This is what the ancients meant by "if one were in their place, one would act the same. The Three Great Sages possessed this quality;
it was for this reason that Mencius praised Bo Yi, Yi Yin, and Liu Xia Hui, all calling them sages. Indeed, it is excellent.

This was because his Way was comprehensive and he excelled at adapting to the times. The world claims that the integrity of Fotudeng and Dao’an did not equal that of Master Yuan (Huiyuan), but I do not believe this.
Sun Chuo, styled Xingong, whose father Sun Chu possessed great renown, was a man of broad learning and elegant literary talent. Together with Xu [Xun] of Gaoyang—
Both Xun and [Zhu] Taoqian possessed noble aspirations. Initially, they lived in seclusion at Mount Xi, letting their spirits roam amidst the mountains and waters.

He composed the "Fu on Realizing My Initial Intent" (*Suichu fu*) to manifest his resolve. When Zhi Daolin asked Xun, "How do you compare to Xu? he replied, "As for his lofty sentiments and far-reaching ambitions, I have long since internalized them;
however, regarding his poetic compositions, I would place myself beneath him as his disciple. He once composed the "Fu on Tiantai" and showed it to his friends.
Ren Fan Rongqi said, "Try tossing it on the ground; it ought to produce a golden sound. Rongqi replied, "I fear this 'golden sound' does not accord with the notes of the Gong and Shang scales.
Nevertheless, whenever he encountered an excellent verse, he would invariably remark, "This must be the speech of our own kind.

He composed many treatises concerning our Way, all of which can be found in the *Hongming ji* and other collections. He died at the age of fifty-eight. The court historian praised him, saying he was "exceedingly talented."
His integrity was not merely a matter of literary elegance.

Xu Xun, courtesy name Xuandu, was a native of Gaoyang and the great-grandson of Xu Yun, the Grand Commandant of the Central Army during the Wei dynasty. He purified his mind through the study of Buddhism.
He was greatly admired by the high officials of the Jiangzuo region. Emperor Wen of the Jin dynasty held his character in high esteem;

whenever the moon was bright and the wind was calm, and he desired to contemplate profound speech and subtle principles, he would surely visit him. When he spoke with tireless eloquence, Emperor Wen unconsciously moved his seat forward until dawn, forgetting all weariness.
The Emperor said to his close friends, "Xuan-du’s talent and temperament are truly not easily found. Liu Zhen-chang was a man of his time..."
Tan Zong formed a bond of pure friendship with him. He often said to others, "Had I not met Xuandu, I might have become a frivolous magistrate.

He also once remarked, "How could I not think of Qingfeng and Mingyue? When Xuandu first went into seclusion on Mount Yongxing, offerings from lords and nobles of the four quarters arrived in a continuous stream.
Someone remarked, "Mount Ji was not like this. Xu replied: [The text here implies the comparison between the two mountains].
Carrying baskets and bundles, he was thus light in his movements throughout the world. Xu Jian was capable of ascending steep heights;

at that time, it was said that he possessed not only superior spirit but also the equipment necessary for such feats. He often remarked that since the time of the worthy scholars Sima Xiangru, Wang Bao, and Yang Xiong, the world had come to favor the style of fu and song.

Once, he visited the seat of Dharma Master Dao’an along with his younger brother Huidi. Upon hearing the teachings on supramundane dharmas, he took delight in them and exclaimed, "The nine schools of thought are but mere chaff.

Hui'an dispersed his disciples, instructing and exhorting them all with earnest and repeated counsel before sending them on their way. Huiyuan alone was not addressed with a single word. Huiyuan asked in wonder why;
Hui'an replied, "If it were you, what would I have to say? He then departed from Jingzhou for Mount Luofu.

A wind and thunderstorm uprooted trees and tossed sand and stones, leveling the foundation and carrying the wood to the top; at the time, it was considered a divine maneuver.
Originally, when the Grand Marshal (Taishou) Tao Kan was stationed at Guangzhou, a fisherman caught a statue of Mañjuśrī at sea and sent it to Sèxī Temple.
