Ten men could not lift it. Subsequently, when Huicong exerted all his strength to place it on a boat, the boat immediately sank; thus, the image was lost. At that time, a popular saying went:
"Tao Kan was preeminent only for his sword; the image is distinguished by its spirit. It can be brought forth through sincerity, but it is difficult to summon through force.

When Huiyuan established the monastery and prayed for it with a sincere heart, the image then arrived of its own accord, cool and silent. At that time, the Jin dynasty was in decline, yet this was a marvel throughout the world.
Huiyuan possessed great talent but lived in seclusion and did not serve in office.
Liu Yimin of Pengcheng, Lei Cizong of Yuzhang, Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen, Bi Yingzhi of Xincai, Zong Bing of Nanyang, Zhang Shimin, Ji Shuo, and others followed Huiyuan on his excursions.
Together with more than a thousand śramaṇas, he formed the White Lotus Society. Before an image of Amitāyus, he established a vegetarian feast and made a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land.
Upon hearing that Dharma Master Kumārajīva had entered Guanzhong, he looked toward him from afar, paying respect through his reputation and sending a letter to establish friendly relations.
The letter read: "Last year, I received a letter from the Right General Yao [Sengchong], through which I fully learned of your virtuous renown. You, O Benevolent One, formerly in a distant land..."
Transcending external objects, at a time when phonetic translations had not yet been exchanged, one rejoiced upon hearing of the wind [of the Dharma].

Recently, having learned that one who possesses such treasures has come to travel here, I have galloped forth nine times in a single day. Though my feelings delight in the sublime flavor, there is no way to exhaustively convey it;

I can only gaze toward the road as my weariness increases in waiting. Indeed, when sandalwood is transplanted, it shares its fragrance with other things; when the *maṇi* jewel emits its radiance, it illuminates all manner of treasures.

Accumulating merit for oneself and fulfilling one's vows, you do not monopolize such excellence for a single generation. How could Nāgārjuna alone be virtuous in following the tracks of his predecessors?
Now, as you have sent this gift of a robe cut according to the proportions of the body, I pray that you ascend the high seat and wear it for me. Kumārajīva replied:

"Since we have not yet spoken face-to-face and our literary expressions are separated by vast distances, the path for communicating the mind is blocked and the conditions for attaining mutual understanding are severed. I shall now transmit your gracious gift."
I have briefly described the fragrance of your virtues. How could I possibly provide a complete account? Hearing a single path is sufficient to encompass a hundred others.

The Sūtra states that at the end of time, there shall be a Bodhisattva in the East to protect the Dharma. Be diligent, O Benevolent One, in widely propagating this task! Now, wealth has five prerequisites:
merit, precepts, extensive learning, eloquence, and profound wisdom. Those who possess all of these see the Way flourish; those who lack them remain stagnant. You, O Benevolent One...
These matters have been fully prepared. Thus, by means of words, we convey our goodwill; through translation, we transmit the mind—how could this possibly be exhaustive?
It is merely a rough response to your kind intentions. Regarding the robe you sent for comparison, which you wish me to wear when ascending the Dharma seat, it accords with the Tathāgata’s intent;
however, I am ashamed that the person does not match the object. Now, I shall take the brass double-mouthed washbasin I usually use...
The jar may serve to complete the number of ritual objects. He also sent a verse, which said: "Since you have already abandoned defiled pleasures, has your mind attained proper restraint?
If it does not wander or scatter, has it deeply entered the true mark (*dharmatā*)? Within the ultimate mark of emptiness, your mind finds no delight.
If you find joy in dhyāna and wisdom, this is the non-illumination of the *dharmatā*. All things are empty, deceptive, and without reality."

"This is not a place for the mind to rest. I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will graciously reveal the essentials of the Dharma you have attained. Yuan replied with a verse: "From where does the primordial root ultimately arise?
Its arising and ceasing lie beyond the limits of existence and non-existence. A single atom, once it enters the realm of movement, creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain."

Delusive thoughts multiply one after another; when encountering the Principle, one naturally encounters stagnation. Although causes and conditions have no master, the path opened does not belong to a single lifetime.
Since there is no enlightened master at this time, who will grasp the profound seal? Your inquiries still linger in the distance; let us together look forward to the final years.
Initially, in China, there was no teaching regarding the eternal abiding of *nirvāṇa*. [Dao]an merely stated that the Buddha’s lifespan lasted for many kalpas.

Huiyuan said: "The Buddha is the ultimate; that which is ultimate is unchanging. How could the principle of the unchanging have an end? He then composed the *Faxing lun* (Treatise on the Dharma-nature), of which a brief excerpt says:
"The ultimate takes non-change as its nature; attaining this nature takes the realization of the ultimate as its core tenet. When Kumārajīva saw it...
The Treatise (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) praises him, saying: "Though Kumārajīva had not yet seen the sutras, he darkly accords with their principles; how marvelous this is!

King Yao Xing of the Qin sent a letter and presented Kumārajīva with a fine-woven image from Kucha as an expression of his profound respect. Yao Song, the Marquis of Ancheng, offered a pearl-adorned image and submitted a preface to the *Śāstra*, stating:
"The *New Record of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* was composed by Nāgārjuna; the Dharma Master shall now place it at the head [of his collection]."
This preface is written to clearly demonstrate that throughout ten thousand generations, the practitioners of this land shall alike hold this in reverence and hear it.

Huiyuan declined the request on the grounds that the Great Treatise was too extensive, humbly refusing to consent; he therefore abridged its essentials into twenty fascicles and composed a separate preface for them.

When Huan Xuan governed as regent, he urged Emperor An to purge the ranks of monks and nuns. The imperial edict stated: "Among the śramaṇas, there are those capable of expounding and transmitting the scriptures."

He expounded upon the principles of the Dharma and his monastic conduct was refined; those capable of propagating the Great Transformation were permitted to remain according to their training, while all others were ordered to disrobe.
The only exception was Mount Kuang, the abode of those possessing the Way and its Virtue, which was not subject to this screening. Yuan then sent a letter to Xuan.
Yang Zong attempted to seize control, but Yin stopped the imperial edict. Huiyuan once examined the origins and lineages of the *Chanzong biezhuan* (Separate Biography of the Chan School);
it was found that its accounts perfectly accorded with those concerning the arrival of the Patriarch Bodhidharma.
When Tao Yuanming lived in seclusion at Chaisang, he sought the Way from Huiyuan and held him in deep admiration. Xie Lingyun applied for membership in the community, but Huiyuan refused him.

They did not accept this internal [position]. Subsequently, Zong Bing authored the *Mingfo lun* (Treatise on Clarifying Buddhism); Yan Yanzhi analyzed the *Daxing lun* (Treatise on the Realization of Nature); Zhou Yong refuted the *Yixia lun* (Treatise on the Barbarians and the Chinese);
and Zheng Daozi authored the *Shen bumie lun* (Treatise on the Immortality of the Spirit). All of these were received from Huiyuan as their standard of correctness.
By the time of the Long’an era, Huan Xuan reiterated the views of Yu Bing, desiring that śramaṇas pay full homage to the sovereign; the court followed this trend.
Zhitu’s views accorded with those of Xuangao. Consequently, he asked Huiyuan: "This is a momentous matter for the present age; we must not allow the imperial court to lose its dignity.

I have received a letter from the Eight Seats [the high ministers] which they now seem to entrust to you. You should provide a detailed discussion on each point regarding the meaning of 'non-prostration' to resolve their doubts, so that the matter may then be implemented.
Huiyuan replied to the letter and composed the *Shamen bujing wangzhe lun* (Treatise on the Śramaṇa Not Prostrating Before Kings).
In his treatise in five sections, [Fayuan] set forth in detail the reasons why he would not perform the ritual prostration. Daoyuan’s intention remained firm;

however, upon receiving Fayuan’s treatise, he immediately relaxed his stance. Before long, he usurped the throne and issued an edict stating: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and expansive, such that it cannot be fathomed."

Reflecting on the sentiment of serving one's lord, he wished to inspire reverence; yet now that the matter rested with himself, he ought to embody humility and refrain from receiving formal salutations from the various monastics.
When Emperor An retreated from Xuan and reached Xunyang, he issued an edict for Huiyuan to visit him at his temporary residence.
He Fei, the Protector of the State, urged Huiyuan to go out once, but Huiyuan firmly declined on the grounds of illness. The Emperor sent a second edict to inquire after his well-being.

An imperial edict was issued to the Governor of Jiujiang to provide annual offerings of rice for his support. He resided there for thirty years; his shadow never left the mountains and his tracks never entered the secular world.
Whenever he saw off guests, he used Tiger Creek as the boundary. His younger brother, Huichi, also possessed noble conduct;
among the several thousand members of the Lotus Society, Huichi occupied the foremost seat. Wang Xun, the Grand Commandant, once questioned Fan [Yuan], the Regional Inspector of Yuzhang...
"Which is superior, Master Huiyuan or Sengchi? Ning said, "They were both virtuous brothers. Sengxun said, "Even to have a brother like him would be difficult to encounter;
how much more so to have one who is truly virtuous. When Huiyuan was nearing death, his disciples offered him honey water. Fearing he might violate the Vinaya rules, Huiyuan declined it.
He ordered his attendants to examine the Vinaya; before the scroll was finished, he joined his palms, faced west, and passed away at the age of eighty-three.
Xie Lingyun composed his funerary stele inscription. His *Kuāngshān Collection* in thirty fascicles circulates in the world.
The Master Mingjiao of our dynasty, Qisong, visited the Hall of Distant Reflection and inscribed six points upon it. His words were as follows:
"Lu Xiujing was a scholar of heterodox teachings, yet he saw [Huiyuan] off beyond Tiger Creek; this shows that one does not reject the words of others merely because of who they are."
Tao Yuanming was addicted to wine, yet [the Master] associated with him; this was because he overlooked minor details and valued his spiritual attainment.

The eminent monk Buddhabhadra was expelled for manifesting supernatural powers, yet [the Master] invited and praised him; this was because he deeply respected those of true insight and corrected the envy of the unvirtuous.
Xie Lingyun was not accepted due to his impure mind, and he indeed perished by the law; this was because [the Master] recognized the man’s capacity.
Yet they were cautious regarding their final end. When Lu Xun intended to rebel, he clasped [Huiyuan’s] hand and sought an old friendship; this was because he personally believed in the Way.

When Huan Xuan displayed his awesome majesty, [Huiyuan] confronted him and did not yield; this was because he possessed great integrity. Generally speaking, human nature throughout antiquity and today is such that few fear neither authority nor seek to avoid it through expediency;
few forget righteousness while shunning suspicion; few value reputation over substance; and few tolerate the influence of factions.
Guzhi adorned his conduct yet feared entanglement; he considered himself right while deeming others wrong—who could have followed him based on a few words?
Who could have esteemed one generation as a sage-teacher and been willing to follow that man with a single phrase?

Who could have been endowed from youth with superior virtue, devoted to pure conduct, and yet be willing to associate with a drunken official while admiring his attainment? Who could have humbled themselves to treat a teacher of men with such courtesy, only to cast him out?
Could one who is a guest truly manifest their worthiness? Who could refuse a man of great reputation and not allow him to participate in instruction, yet still complete his life with integrity?
Who could, out of righteousness, avoid calamity, cultivate intimacy with old friends, and maintain the Way?
Who could, facing the majesty of generals and commanders at a time of execution and violent punishment, uphold the Way without yielding and preserve their integrity? This—
Indeed, Master Huiyuan’s insight and magnanimity were so far-reaching and vast that he stood alone among those of past and present.

As for his upholding of the ultimate teaching and broadening the Great Way to bestow lasting benefits upon both gods and men—was it not only through his profound wisdom that he was able to exhaustively fulfill these tasks? Was he not a sage, or at least a paragon of virtue?

How magnificent! The Great Mass of Earth sighs forth its breath, and the six realms are filled with pure wind; such is the renown of Master Yuan’s fame. The autumnal colors of the four seas rise high amidst the divine mountains;
such is Master Yuan’s purity and loftiness. A dragon among men and a phoenix among monks, he bows long to those like Chao Fu and Xu You;
such is Master Yuan’s exemplary conduct. White clouds and crimson ravines, jade trees and precious herbs; such is the place where Master Yuan dwells.
The treatise states: One hundred years after Confucius passed away, there arose Mencius. During the time of Mencius, the Way of Confucius was nearly in decline;
Mencius therefore exerted himself to practice it and revitalized it. Three hundred years after the Great Teaching flowed eastward, there appeared Master Huiyuan.
During the time of Master Huiyuan, the śramaṇas were gradually flourishing, yet none had yet emerged who stood out as uniquely eminent.
Huiyuan alone established a code of conduct and an exemplary model that served as the patriarchal authority for all under heaven;
through him, our Way first began to flourish. It may be said that Huiyuan rendered a great service to the Buddhist tradition, much like Mencius did for the school of Confucius.
Liu Chengzhi, courtesy name Zhongsu, was a native of Pengcheng. Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with such filial piety that it became renowned.

He took pride in his literary talent and would not submit his spirit to the conventions of the age. Although he suffered from cold and hunger while power and fortune lay before him, his resolve remained as deep and unshakable as ever.
The Minister of Education Wang Mi, the Chancellor Huan Xuan, the Palace Attendant Xie Hun, and the Grand Marshal Liu Yu all praised his worthiness and wished to recommend him for office.
Chengzhi declined their offers with great firmness and retired to Mount Kuang to seek refuge under Master Huiyuan. Huiyuan said, "Your official rank is lofty; why do you go there?
Chengzhi replied, "Ruler and subject suspect one another; those with excrescences and tumors harm one another. The House of Jin has no..."
Though as firm as a bedrock, the nature of things carries the peril of a tower built upon stacked eggs. What could I do? Yuan Xian agreed with his reasoning.

Because Dai Xiang’s character was profound and his will was unbending, the Grand Marshal Huan Yu also joined the assembly of eminent officials in deliberating upon the title "Surviving Subjects" (Yimin) to honor him.
At that time, Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi, Bi Yingzhi, Zhang Xiushi, Zong Bing, and others were likewise [engaged].
Relying on Master Huiyuan, he said: "In coming here, how could you gentlemen forget the journey to the Pure Land?
Those with such a heart should redouble their efforts; there must be no delay. He had Chengzhi compose a text to record this event, titled "The Vow of the Lotus Society.
Its words are as follows: "In the year of the Jiǎwù cycle, the seventh month, the first day being Wùchén, on the twenty-eighth day..."
On the day of Yiwei, the Dharma Master Shi Huiyuan’s profound resonance with the mysterious and his frost-like resolve were uniquely inspired.

He then invited one hundred and twenty-three like-minded companions who had stilled their minds and possessed correct faith—such as Lei Cizong, Liu Chengzhi, and others—to assemble before the image of Amitābha at the Bore Terrace Monastery on the southern slope of Mount Lu. There, they led the way with incense and flowers in reverent worship.
Having made these offerings, we take this oath: "The principle of conditioned transformation is already clear, and the transmission through the three periods of time is manifest.

Since the patterns of shifting influences correspond, the retribution for good and evil is inevitable. Inferring from those who have vanished in the blink of an eye, one realizes that the arrival of impermanence is urgent;
examining how the two types of retribution press upon one another, one knows that the perils of saṃsāra are difficult to extricate."
This is why our fellow seekers of the Way have been vigilant at dusk and diligent through the night, looking upward in thought for a means of salvation.
For the spirit can be reached through resonance but cannot be sought through outward traces. If there is a substance to that resonance, the path to the unseen realm is but a few inches away;

yet if one seeks it without the proper method, it remains as vast and distant as the ford of the Yellow River. Now, fortunately, we have resonated without prior consultation, with our minds in perfect accord.

In the western region, the *Kou pian* (Preface to the Inquiries) opens up faith and clarifies the heavenly mind. Thus, the spiritual mechanism and its manifestations were communicated through dreams; joy was as great as that felt at the arrival of a son.
Thereupon, the cloud-patterned diagrams displayed brilliance, and their splendor equaled divine creation. This merit arose from the harmony of principle, not from human effort.
This is truly a case where Heaven has revealed its sincerity and the mysterious destiny has gathered [the response). How can one not be diligent in heart and mindful in thought? Revere this!
One must refine one’s thoughts to concentrate the mind. Yet, as illustrious achievements vary and merits differ, though our morning aspirations may be the same, our evening returns are far apart.
This is truly lamentable for the bond between us, my teachers and friends. Therefore, with deep sighs, we have gathered and adjusted our robes in the Dharma Hall;
with equal single-mindedness, we contemplate the profound depths of the Way, vowing that we, as fellow men, shall together—
Wandering through remote frontiers, there are those who, possessing world-shaking insight and peerless virtue, first ascend to the divine realm;

they do not seek solitary excellence upon the cloud-capped peaks, nor do they forget the preservation of all beings in the secluded valleys. Those who have advanced shall follow as others ascend, diligently contemplating the Way of collective advancement.

Only then will one contemplate the sublime ordinances with wondrous insight, opening the mind to true illumination. Through cognition, awakening is renewed; through form, transformation is achieved. One may then rest like a lotus in the midst of the stream.
Shading myself beneath the jade branches, I chant my words; my ethereal robes flutter through the eight directions. Amidst the fragrant winds, I spend my years until the end;

my body forgets comfort yet remains profoundly serene, and my mind transcends worldly joy to find its own delight. Facing the three paths of suffering, I offer a distant farewell; looking with pride upon the celestial palaces, I bid them a long adieu.
Continuing the track of the multitude of spirits, I point to the Great Expiration as my destination. To investigate this Way—could it not be so?

How magnificent! Chengzi established a separate meditation hall at the northern stream of Xilin, where he cultivated his aspirations, lived in contented poverty, and investigated the profound mysteries of the Dharma with tireless diligence.
Fully observing the prohibitive precepts, he was admired and looked up to by Zongzhang and others.

Devoting himself exclusively to seated meditation, after only half a year had passed, he beheld within samādhi the Buddha’s light illuminating the great earth, all of which was the color of pure gold. Once—

After emerging from meditative absorption, he felt even greater joy. Having lived in the mountains for fifteen years, while practicing *nienfo*, he again beheld the body of Amitābha Buddha, purple-gold in color, with rays of light radiating from his *ūrṇā*. With hands extended downward, the Buddha comforted him and appeared before his chamber.
Chengzhi, filled with relief and gratitude, wept as he spoke of his own situation, saying, "How may the Tathāgata stroke my head and cover me with his robe? Suddenly—
Then the Buddha stroked his head and drew out his *kāṣāya* robe to cover him. As Xi Ri constantly recited the Buddha’s name, he again saw himself entering a pool of the seven treasures.
In the pool were lotus flowers, all of which were a mixture of blue and white; the water was deep and clear, as if it had no banks or shores.
In the midst of it stood a person with a halo around the neck and the *svastika* (*śrīvatsa*) marked upon the chest, who pointed to the pool and said to Cheng: "The eight meritorious qualities..."
"Water! You may drink it. He then cupped his hands and drank; its sweetness was extraordinary. Upon waking, he still perceived a sublime fragrance emanating from his pores.
He sighed and said, "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have now arrived. Who has brought this assembly of the six harmonies to provide me with witness?
Thereupon, the monks of Mount Lu all gathered. Chengzhi faced the image, burned incense, and prostrated twice, offering these prayers:
He said: "By virtue of the Bequeathed Teaching of Śākyamuni, I know that there is Amitāyus Buddha. This incense shall first be offered to Tathāgata Śākyamuni;

next, it shall be offered to Amitābha Buddha; thereafter, it shall be offered to the assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the Lotus Assembly, extending even to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions. I pray that all sentient beings may be born together in the Pure Land."
He then took leave of the assembly of eminent monks. Facing west, he sat upright with his hands folded and passed away at the age of fifty-nine.
Zhou Xuzhi, Zong Bing, Lei Cizong, and others—whose biographies appear in the *Nanshi*—practiced together in the Lotus Society and were known in the world as the "Eighteen Worthies.
Bai Juyi’s "Record of the Grass Hall on Mount Lu" states: "In the past, there were eighteen men such as Huiyuan, Huijiao, and Lei..."
People entered this mountain together, dying there of old age without ever returning.

At the beginning of the Taiyuan era, during the height of the Fu Qin dynasty, auspicious stars appeared repeatedly. The Grand Astrologer reported: "A wise man from a foreign land shall enter to assist our state.
When King Fu attacked Xiangyang and captured the Dharma Master Dao’an, he rejoiced, believing him to be the one who had fulfilled the prophecy. Dao’an, however, declined with humility.
He did not dare accept. Consequently, he urged the Lord of Qin to welcome the Kuchean Dharma Master Kumārajīva.
Yao Jian followed this advice and immediately dispatched General Lü Guang of the Xiaoqi Command with seventy thousand armored cavalry to invade Kucha.

He instructed him, saying, "If you capture Kumārajīva, send him back by express courier. When Lü Guang’s army arrived, Kumārajīva said to the King of Kucha, Bai Chun: "The fortune of your nation is declining."
"Now that a powerful enemy has descended from the land of the Sun, you ought to receive him with hospitality; do not oppose his vanguard. Śrīghoṣa did not accept this advice and rejected it.

Consequently, he was utterly defeated by Yao Xing and captured Kumārajīva. Upon seeing that Kumārajīva was young in years, Yao Xing treated him with worldly levity and gave him the daughter of the King of Kucha as a wife.
Kumārajīva earnestly declined, saying it was improper, but Yao Xing forced him to drink strong wine and confined them both in the same room.
In the meantime, he was coerced by [Fu Jian]. When the light returned, Fu Jian had already been defeated. Consequently, [Fu Jian] usurped the throne in Guzang;

father and son succeeded one another, both being men of mediocre talent who did not understand the Way. Kumārajīva possessed profound understanding, yet he lived amidst this chaotic state and had no opportunity to propagate his teachings.
The ruler of Qin, Yao Chang, was a Qiang of the Western Rong. Following the defeat of Fu Jian, Chang, serving as a veteran general, led his own tribesmen in rebellion.
When Fu Jian fought him and was unsuccessful, he was subsequently strangled to death by Chang at a Buddhist temple.
Chang usurped the throne and established his capital at Yongguan, changing the name of Chang’an to Cháng’ān. He reigned for eight years. Fu Jian led a host of ghost-soldiers.
At midday, he entered the palace, where a dagger pierced his private parts; he bled for over a *shí* and passed away.
His son Xing ascended the throne, demoted the imperial title, and styled himself "Heavenly King. Before long, the blades of war were laid to rest and the transformation of customs flourished.

Auspicious omens appeared one after another, including the growth of trees with interlocking branches within the palace courtyard, which all regarded as an auspicious sign of a wise man entering the state. Thereupon, Yao Shuo was dispatched...
When Devaliang succeeded Lülong, he welcomed Master Kumārajīva. The ruler of Qin treated him with profound courtesy and honored him as National Teacher.

He extensively expounded the sūtras and śāstras. From the time of the Former Qin until the reign of Fu Qin, including the period of Master Kumārajīva and others, a total of over eight hundred fascicles of the Tripiṭaka—comprising sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras—were translated and propagated throughout the land of China.
In the fourth year of Long’an, the Heavenly King of the Yao Qin established the Xiaoyao Garden within the Western Palace and commanded Master Kumārajīva to proclaim and translate various scriptures.
As these were all texts he had mastered through oral recitation, the King, during the intervals of his administrative duties, personally engaged in translation with Kumārajīva.
Upon examining the existing translations, he found many errors and discrepancies; Kumārajīva corrected them. There were eight hundred śramaṇas, including Sengrui and Sengzhao, who assisted.

Other people transmitted and received his teachings, further producing over three hundred scrolls of sutras and śāstras in total. The śramaṇa Huìzuì possessed refined discernment and far-reaching insight;
he followed Kumārajīva in transcribing the texts. Whenever Kumārajīva spoke with Huìzuì, he would say: "In the Western regions, literary form is especially valued.

Their tonal patterns and rhythms are considered excellent when they can be adapted for flutes and strings. Whenever one has an audience with a king, there must be hymns of praise and verses of scripture."
These are all his models. When Kumārajīva was young, he could recite thirty-two thousand words daily.

He left the household life following his mother and traveled extensively through the Western Regions, where he mastered a vast array of scriptures. He was particularly adept at the Mahāyāna and was intent upon its propagation and exposition.

He once sighed, saying, "Were I to compose a Mahāyāna Abhidharma, it would not be comparable to that of Kātyāyanīputra. At that time, there was no one with deep insight [to appreciate this], so he desisted in sorrow.

He composed two scrolls titled *A Solemn Discourse with the King of Qin on Reality*. He once lectured on the sutras at Caotang Temple, where the king, court officials, and several thousand śramaṇas listened with solemn countenances.
The king said to him, "Dharma Master, your talent and brilliance are of transcendent realization; you are peerless within the four seas.
How could it be that the lineage of the Dharma is not to be continued? He then coerced Kumārajīva by sending ten palace women to compel him to accept them.

It is also said that whenever he gave lectures, two young boys would climb onto his shoulders to shield him from view. From then on, he no longer resided in the monks' quarters but established a separate residence for himself.
When other monks objected to this, Kumārajīva filled his alms bowl with needles and said, "If you wish to emulate me, you must be able to eat these;
only then may you maintain a private dwelling. Having said this, he ate the needles as if they were ordinary food. The monks felt ashamed and desisted.
Originally residing in Kucha, whenever the kings of neighboring countries assembled, they would invariably request Kumārajīva to preach the Dharma;

they would always kneel and prostrate before his seat, commanding him to step upon their shoulders to ascend. He once visited the Venerable of the Northern Mountains in the country of Greater Mozhishi with his mother.
Beishan said to his mother, "Protect this śrāmaṇera well. At thirty-five years of age, he will be without flaw in the Vinaya;
he will deliver others like Upagupta, or otherwise, he will be a truly eminent Dharma Master.

When the bhikṣu Beidu heard in Pengcheng that Kumārajīva had entered Guanzhong, he sighed and said, "I have been separated from this youth by play for three hundred years; our meeting once again seems as distant as ever."
It was merely that his end had been delayed until a future life. He fell ill while residing in Qin for only nine years.

From his mouth, he uttered the Threefold Divine Incantation (*traidhātuka-mantra*), ordering his foreign disciples to recite it to save themselves. Before he could exert himself [in practice], he felt his condition growing increasingly critical.

Thereupon, despite his failing strength, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell, saying: "We have met through the Dharma, yet we have not fully exhausted our hearts' intent. As we are about to part for the next world, my grief is profound."

"How tragic it is to say! Out of my own ignorance and inadequacy, I have mistakenly served as a translator. Among the sūtras and śāstras I have produced, only the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* has not yet had its redundancies edited.
If my interpretation accords with the Buddha’s mind, may my tongue not be scorched or destroyed on the day I burn my body. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
On the day of his cremation, his tongue remained as red as a lotus flower and did not decay.

The treatise states: "When Emperor Guangwu of the Han was born in Nanyang, there were no base men in Nanyang; when Kumārajīva arrived in Guanzhong, men of extraordinary talent gathered from all quarters.
The Sūtras declare that whenever sages and worthies appear in the world, they do so because of shared practice during their causal stages.
The scholar followed [the Buddha] down into birth to assist and support his transformation; this is truly not a false claim.

From the Wei and Jin dynasties onward, when the Great Dharma was in its incipient and obscure stage, the śramaṇas who arrived from the Western Regions invariably manifested their transformative teachings through miraculous traces.

Although there were occasional extraordinary and eminent figures among them, most were constrained by their attachment to external studies. It was only upon the arrival of Master Kumārajīva that [the true teaching] finally flourished.
The source of the Dharma was originally profound; scholars were thus able to devote their hearts fully to the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings while looking down upon Laozi and Zhuangzi.

Indeed, Master Kumārajīva exerted great influence within the Dharma-gate—how could his contribution be considered anything less than substantial? Yet, due to the burden of past karmic obstructions, he resided in Guanzhong for only nine years.
Of the vast treasury he possessed, not even one-tenth was put into practice, and he did not attain longevity. King Qin [Yao Xing]...
Although Kumārajīva’s achievements were such that his excellence could not be fully realized, alas! Had Master Kumārajīva’s lofty virtue and pure conduct been equal to his inner potential,
and had he attained a long life to bring the succession of the Great Teaching to glory, what more could even Maitreya’s appearance in the world have added?

The Dharma Master Daoli was esteemed by the Ruler of Qin for his devotion to the Vinaya and his ascetic rigor. Since Master Kumārajīva entered Guanzhong, the number of monks and nuns had reached ten thousand;
as their transgressions and excesses became numerous, the Ruler of Qin grew concerned. He subsequently established the position of Sengzheng (Monastic Rectifier) and issued an edict stating:

"The Great Dharma has now reached its zenith in its migration to the East. As the number of monks and nuns increases, it is fitting to establish a governing framework. One must proclaim and transmit far-reaching regulations."

To restore the collapsing traditions, Dharma Master [Shi] had long possessed the spirit of learning; in his later years, he was renowned for his virtue. He should be appointed as the National *Sengzheng*.
He shall be provided with a carriage, attendants, and the stipends of a *Shizhong*; two persons each shall be assigned to deliver imperial edicts and to pull the sheep-drawn carriage.

Furthermore, Sengqian and Chanhui shall serve as the *Yuezong*, while Faqin and Huibin shall serve as the *Senglü*. Their ranks shall be differentiated accordingly, and they shall subsequently be granted the privilege of an escort of trusted guards.
Each of his attendants was dressed in white, and there were thirty men from each group.
At that time, there was a Brahmin in the Kingdom of Siṃhala named Cui-ming (Clever), who was a leader among the heterodox sects.

Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he loaded his books onto a horse and arrived there, requesting to debate with the monks. The śramaṇas of Guanzhong looked at one another with a sense of inadequacy. Kumārajīva said:
The Dharma Master Daorong said, "You may take on this task. Daorong looked at the non-Buddhist scriptures; though he had not yet read them, he secretly had someone record their titles.
Upon a single glance, he could recite them from memory. He set a date for the debate. The Ruler of Qin assembled with his high officials and ministers.
The Brahmin boasted of his extensive learning, but Daorong enumerated the titles of those books as well as the three categories of scriptures and histories of the land of Qin.
[The Brahmin] doubled [his wager]. Kumārajīva, seizing the advantage, taunted him, saying, "Have you not heard that in the Great Qin there are those of profound learning?
How dare you come from so far away with such arrogance? Thereupon, the Brahmin was filled with shame and submission; he bowed twice at the feet of Sengrong and departed.
The Dharma Master Daoheng was renowned for his filial piety while serving his stepmother in his youth. After his mother passed away, he became a śramaṇa and followed Master Kumārajīva.
Kumārajīva cherished his talent, and Daoheng attained a reputation equal to that of Daobiao.

When the Lord of Qin heard of the two men’s mastery of the arts of governance and scholarship, he ordered the Minister Yao Xian to proclaim an imperial decree, earnestly urging them to abandon the monastic life and assist in the administration. Daoheng and Daobiao submitted a memorial to present their circumstances and resist the command.
The Emperor said briefly: "Emperor Guangwu of the Han dynasty perfected the integrity of Yan Ling; Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty preserved the loftiness of Guan Ning.
Your Majesty’s sagely nature is divinely bestowed, and your deliberations have always sought to place you far beyond the likes of Yao and Shun.

How is it that these two men, wearing only their head-covers and robes, must now fall beneath the status of Guangwu and Emperor Wen? He then commanded Kumārajīva and others to earnestly exhort them, desiring that they surely fulfill their aspirations."

[The Emperor] sent his heart [to him]. Kumārajīva, Senglang, and others respectfully presented a memorial recounting these events, stating briefly: "Only a sage can penetrate the wills of all under heaven."
Sengbiao had already discarded his hair and beard and was wearing improper robes; now to place him in the court of scholars and officials was contrary to his aspirations.
Furthermore, as the Great Qin has risen and extraordinary talents have emerged in succession, those such as Sengbiao are not considered preeminent.

When the King issued another decree, the entire assembly earnestly petitioned for his release, and only then was the matter laid to rest. Sengbiao sighed and said, "My reputation has advanced, but my true [nature] remains."
The burdens of the Way were thus cast aside, and he entered Mount Langya, never again emerging for the rest of his life.
The Dharma Master Sengrui had enjoyed great renown from his youth; when he followed Kumārajīva to receive instruction, his profound realization was peerless.
Once, King Yao Xing asked Minister Yao Song, "To whom can Master Sengrui be compared? Yao Song replied, "I have yet seen anyone to whom he could be assigned. When the court...

When the high officials and great assembly gathered, Daoxuan’s (Sengrui’s) spirit and demeanor were brilliant and penetrating. The King pointed to him and said to Sengsong, "He is the foremost hope for the monastic community throughout the four seas.
When Sengrui lectured on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, Master Kumārajīva said, "In this treatise of debate, there are seven points where it refutes the *Abhidharma*.

Can you explain them? Sengrui raised his hands to respond to the questions, and in every case, he hit the mark. Kumārajīva sighed in admiration and said, "You truly possess refined discernment. (Recorded in the *Biographies*)
"There is reward for those who appreciate the sound [of the Way]; what cause for regret could I have?

The Dharma Master Sengzhao was poor in his youth and worked as a copyist for others; he subsequently read widely across the classics and histories, and was particularly adept at the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*."

This was merely his outward appearance. At the age of twenty, he became a śramaṇa, and his reputation shook the Three Commanderies. When Master Kumārajīva was in Guzang, Sengzhao went there to rely upon him.

Upon conversing with him, Kumārajīva was struck with amazement and said, "He is a dragon or an elephant among the Dharma. When they returned to Guanzhong, he meticulously determined the meanings of the sūtras and śāstras.

Scholars from all quarters flocked there like the spokes of a wheel, launching difficult challenges and attacking one another; yet Sengzhao resolved them as easily as slicing through meat with a blade, and all [the solutions] emerged [from his pen].
Daoyi composed the *Prajñā-nirjñāna-śāstra*. When Kumārajīva saw it, he said, "In my understanding, I do not surpass you; in literary style, however, I must bow to you.
He transmitted this treatise to Mount Kuang, where Liu Yimin presented it to Master Huiyuan. Upon reading it, the Master struck his thigh and sighed deeply.
It was thought that such a thing had never occurred before. He further composed treatises such as "The Non-transmigration of Things," all of which exhaustively capture the subtlest nuances.
The ruler of Qin held his writings in especially high esteem and issued an edict to disseminate them throughout the empire. Sengzhao died at the age of thirty-two;
those of his time lamented his untimely passing.
The Treatise states: Mingbai Juefan remarked, "When Kumārajīva arrived in Guanzhong, men of extraordinary talent gathered there in full.
Thus, the Great Dharma flourished suddenly. In overseeing general affairs, there was Senglang; in penetrating the subtle meanings to the divine, there were Sengzhao and Daosheng;
in using wisdom to repel insults, there was Daorong; and in embellishing the scriptures with refined rhetoric, there was Sengrui."
As for those whose eloquence and wit astounded their peers like Tanyi, or whose resolute will remained unyielding like Daobiao and Daheng—such individuals were still many.
Now, when a millipede loses its legs it can still move because those assisting it are numerous.
That Mingbai criticized Kumārajīva for "losing his legs" while attributing all merit to the many sages—how could he be said to understand the art of speech? As for those such as Seng... [text ends]

The two masters, Sengzhao and Daosheng, attained sudden enlightenment regarding their original nature and realized the Buddha-mind lineage, adorning the Great Teaching with refined brilliance; their writings remain extant.
How could they have merely achieved a mastery of profound meanings that enters the divine?
In the first year of the Yongxing era, the Indian Venerable Puṭhagoda arrived in the Qin territory, followed by several hundred śramaṇas specializing in the study of doctrine.
At Zhong Temple, they produced the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Before Kumārajīva had translated half of it, Puṭhagoda passed away.

The śramaṇa Dharmaruci arrived; he was also well-versed in the Vinaya. When Master Huiyuan of Mount Kuang heard of this, he rejoiced and sent a letter to Guanzhong, urging Dharmaruci to bring forth the remainder of that Vinaya to complete it. Dharmaruci then continued the work with Master Kumārajīva until its conclusion.
From this point on, the Vinaya regulations became fully established.
When the Indian Venerable Buddhayaśas arrived at Guzang, he heard that Master Kumārajīva had accepted palace women from the Qin court.

He sighed and said, "Kumārajīva is like fine cotton; how could one allow him to enter thorny brambles? When Kumārajīva learned that Yaśas had come from afar for his sake, he feared they might part ways and return home.
He urged the King of Qin to welcome him. Once the envoy arrived, Yaśas said, "Your gracious decree has descended from afar; I shall immediately..."

He traveled by relay carriage. This was to reciprocate the donor’s diligent hospitality toward scholars. [The King thought: "If he were treated with the same courtesy shown to Kumārajīva, then this poor monk would surely remain in the northern mountains.
When the envoy returned, the King’s longing did not cease; he dispatched another messenger to extend full honors to bring him there. Only then did Guṇabhadra consent to come.
The King went out to meet him at the outskirts of the capital and built a separate vihāra for his residence, providing him with offerings befitting a king. Guṇabhadra...
He accepted nothing; when the time came for alms, he took but a single meal. He was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā* treatises and had red whiskers, so he was known at the time as "Red-Whiskered Vibhāṣā.
Later, he traveled to Kuāng Mountain, where he was highly esteemed by Master Huiyuan.
Huiyuan personally carried iron to the summit of Zixiao Peak to cast a stupa, in which he enshrined relics of the Tathāgata’s true body. It remains there to this day.

In the first year of the Yuanxing era of the Eastern Jin, during the reign of Emperor An, the Grand Marshal Huan Xuan sent a letter to the eight high officials, reiterating the arguments of He Chong and Yu Bing regarding the matter of śramaṇas not paying homage to kings.
He stated that while Yu Bing’s intention was to honor the sovereign, his citation of ritual precedent was incomplete; so too was that of He Chong.

To emerge from biased faith and subsequently sink into [a fixation on] names and forms—now, although the Buddha’s transformation of beings is vast and boundless, extending beyond the reach of sight and hearing, he takes reverence as his foundation;

thus, there is no difference between his presence in the world and his withdrawal from it. It is simply that what they aim for differs; it does not mean that reverence and respect should be abandoned.
Laozi places kings and lords among the "Three Greats"; if one traces the reason for their importance, it lies entirely in their providing sustenance.
The Way of Life and its Universal Operation: How could it be that the Sage alone occupies the throne and is thus compared to the Two Polarities?
Rather, it is because the Great Virtue of Heaven and Earth is called "Life," and the power to penetrate the principle of life and regulate all things rests with the Sovereign.

Therefore, while the sacred vessel [of kingship] is honored, the actuality of the rites is truly exalted. This is not merely a matter of empty veneration; the meaning lies in the ruler’s governance. As for why the śramaṇas—
All living beings rely on these for their survival; they also employ these principles and mandates in their daily lives.

How could one receive such virtue yet neglect its corresponding rites, or enjoy such bounty yet abandon the respect due to it? At that time, many renowned scholars and worthies of the court responded;

although their words did not yet fully awaken [the truth], each was contemporaneously possessed of excellence. They all exhausted what they harbored within, yet the underlying principle remained latent in their feelings. Yuan was thus [convinced].
He hurriedly recorded his inquiries and submitted them to the Dharma Master Huixiu, known as Master Yuan of Huxi. The Master sighed with deep regret and said, "How tragic!
This is precisely the origin of mutual ruin and a period of stagnation for a thousand years.

Fearing that the Great Dharma would soon sink into confusion and that past events might be forgotten, I have composed five treatises to thoroughly expound my subtle intentions, hoping that future gentlemen will revere and honor them."
Buddhists may examine this in detail.
In the first section, "The Theory that Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Homage to Kings," concerning those who dwell at home:
To begin with, the principles elucidated by Buddhism primarily distinguish itself by taking renunciation as its hallmark. There are generally four types of such renunciants.

As for the propagation of the teachings and their penetration among sentient beings, their merit is equal to that of emperors and kings, and their transformative influence encompasses the ways of governance. As for moving the common people and awakening the times, there has been no age in which this did not occur.

However, depending on the circumstances they encountered, there were times of active engagement or withdrawal; thus, it was through these cycles of decline and flourishing that they appeared or remained hidden.
Regarding those who may be discussed herein, let me speak briefly: Laypeople who revere the Dharma are subjects who follow the transformative influence [of the state].

Their sentiments have not yet changed from worldly customs, and their traces remain within the secular realm. Consequently, they possess the affection of kinship and the etiquette of serving a sovereign.
Since ritual reverence has its root, the teachings are thereby established upon that foundation. If one examines the origin of these causes, the merit derives from the past. Therefore:

By means of intimacy, one teaches love, so that the people may know there is a natural benevolence; by means of solemnity, one teaches reverence, so that the people may know there is a natural gravity.
The arrival of these two states truly arises from a hidden resonance (*miṅyìng*). Since this resonance does not reside in the present moment, one should seek its source.
Thus, taking offenses as their counterparts constitutes punishment, causing people to be cautious only after they have been struck with fear; taking paradise as their rank constitutes honor.
They offer rewards so that people may be pleased and subsequently act. All of this clarifies the teaching by means of the retribution of shadows and echoes;

it takes accord with conditions as its path and does not subvert what is natural. Why is this? For those who cherish their persons and preserve their lives, taking possession of things creates stagnation.

Their accumulated roots are deep and firm, and their attachment to the self remains unextinguished; they are currently treating sensual desires as their pleasure gardens and sounds and colors as their playgrounds.
It is for the purpose of wandering and observing; being immersed in worldly pleasures, one is unable to exert oneself to transcend them.

Therefore, that which the teachings restrain takes this as its boundary, and does not clarify what lies beyond it. Since what lies beyond is not clarified, it remains largely in accord with the natural flow of transformation.
Therefore, one must not receive their virtue while neglecting their ritual propriety, nor accept their bounty while abandoning respect.

For this reason, those who delight in the spirit of Śākyamuni invariably first serve their parents and honor the sovereign. Those who transform their secular ways and cast aside their hairpins must wait for the proper mandate before acting in accordance with it.
If the sovereign or their parents harbor doubts, they withdraw to seek the fulfillment of their own aspirations until there is mutual enlightenment. This is indeed...

The reason Buddhism values the sustenance of life and assists in the king’s transformation of the people within the Way of Governance is that the fundamental intent and outward appearance of the arguments established by its proponents share certain commonalities.
Therefore, I shall distinguish between the internal and external realms to clarify the resolve of those who stand in the threefold relationship [to their sovereign].
I will briefly recount the purport of the scriptures to express and entrust my own sentiments.
On the Śramaṇa Not Paying Homage to Kings, Part Two: Leaving Home.
Those who have left home are guests from beyond this world; their traces are severed from mundane things. Their teaching is this:

they realize that suffering and entanglement arise from having a physical body, so they do not preserve the body in order to end suffering. They know that the continuous cycle of birth arises from receiving the transformations of destiny, so they do not follow those transformations...
Seeking the ultimate principle does not depend on following the process of transformation; thus, one does not value the resources for sustaining worldly movement.
Ceasing suffering does not depend on preserving the physical body; thus, one does not prize the benefits of enriching life. This is where principle diverges from form and the Way opposes the mundane.
For such a person, their vow begins with the removal of the hairpin, and their resolve manifests in the change of robes. This is...
Therefore, all who have left the household life do so to withdraw from the world in order to seek their aspirations and to transform their customs in order to realize the Way.
Since they transform their customs, their robes and insignia cannot conform to the rites of worldly codes; since they withdraw from the world, they ought to elevate their conduct.

It is by being thus that they can rescue the drowning masses from the deep current, uproot the hidden seeds of suffering from across kalpas, and provide a distant passage to the ferry of the Three Vehicles.
This broadly opens the path for devas and humans. If even a single man were to perfect his virtue, then the Way would permeate his six kin and its bounty would flow throughout the world.
Although he does not occupy the rank of king or noble, he has already harmonized with the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji) and granted repose to the people.
Therefore, while internally he diverges from the gravity of natural kinship, he does not violate filial piety; externally, while lacking the formal reverence due a sovereign, he does not...
They lose their reverence. Judging from this, we know that if one seeks the fundamental source by transcending the realm of transformation, the principle is profound and the meaning is earnest;
yet if one speaks of benevolence while merely observing the sighs of the world, the achievement is trivial and the grace is shallow.

If this is so, even those who turn their steps toward the dark mountains [of the West] might still feel ashamed to hear of such a wind; how much more so for those subjects who follow the flow of transformation and merely draw a salary?
...whose virtue was such that his filial piety and reverence were identical to those of the sages.
In the third section of the *Treatise on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Reverence to Kings*, titled "Seeking the Ultimate Source Rather Than Following Transformation," the question is asked:
"If we examine the intent of Laozi, Heaven and Earth take the attainment of the One as their greatness, while kings and lords take embodying compliance as their principle."
It is honored as supreme. Because it is one, it serves as the root of the myriad transformations; because its essence accords with [the Way], it possesses the merit of pervasive movement.
Thus, clarifying the fundamental principle must reside in realizing the ultimate essence, and realizing the ultimate essence must proceed from accordance with transformation.
For this reason, the former sages regarded this as a noble discourse, which no other arguments can alter. Any view that differs from these arguments has no basis for its meaning. And yet, it is said:
Why is it that some do not conform to transformation? The answer is: All things existing within the realm of phenomena equally receive their birth from the Great Transformation (*mahāpariṇāma*).
Although the myriad species differ in their complexity and their essential natures vary—whether refined or coarse—from a comprehensive perspective, there are only two categories:

the sentient and the insentient. That which possesses sentience has an emotional engagement with transformation; that which lacks sentience has no such engagement. For that which lacks engagement with transformation, once the transformation is complete, its life comes to an end.
Birth does not arise from emotion; thus, when the physical form decays, it transforms and ceases. Sentient beings, however, are affected by transformation and are moved by external objects.

Such movement necessarily proceeds through emotion, and therefore their birth is never-ending. When birth is never-ending, their transformations become ever more extensive and their physical forms ever more accumulated.
As the passions become increasingly stagnant, the burdens grow ever deeper. How can the extent of their affliction be fully described?

For this reason, the Sūtras state that Nirvāṇa is unchanging and takes the exhaustion of conditioned existence as its abode, while the three realms are in constant flux and take sin and suffering as their field. When the exhaustion of conditioned existence accords with causes and conditions, the flux is forever stilled;

yet when one remains in flux, suffering is experienced without end. How is this so? It is because birth— (Note: The source text ends abruptly. The translation provided reflects the available portion.)

The physical form acts as a shackle and fetter. Life arises through transformation; when transformation is driven by emotional attachments, the spirit becomes stagnant in its source and wisdom darkens its illumination.
When one is rigidly confined by boundaries, all that remains is the self, and all that is encountered is movement.
Consequently, the reins of the spirit are lost, the paths of birth open up daily, and one follows along the long current of craving—how could this be merely a single lifetime? This is so.

Therefore, those who return to the root and seek the ultimate source do not allow life to burden their spirit; those who transcend and fall away from worldly constraints do not allow emotions to burden their life.
When emotions do not burden life, then life may be extinguished; when life does not burden the spirit, then the spirit may enter stillness.
Because the spirit enters stillness and the realm is severed, it is called *nirvāṇa*. How could the name *nirvāṇa* be a mere empty designation?

Ah! Please allow me to extend this argument and substantiate it. Although Heaven and Earth take the constant generation of life as their greatness, they are unable to ensure that those born do not die.
Although kings and lords take the preservation of existence as their merit, they are unable to ensure that those who exist are free from affliction.

Therefore, the previous discourse stated: "One realizes that the accumulation of afflictions stems from having a body; by not preserving the body, one brings afflictions to rest. One knows that the continuous generation of life arises from...
In receiving transformation, one does not follow the transformation in order to seek the ultimate principle; this is where the meaning lies. This is where the meaning lies.

This is why the śramaṇas treat the sovereign of ten thousand chariots with equal courtesy, exalting their own vocation, and why they do not accept rank from kings or lords yet partake in their bounty.
The Fourth Treatise: On Why Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Homage to Kings; On the Ultimate Reality Being Beyond Dual Service. Question:

Examining the annals of past history from the time of the August Sovereigns onward, those who occupied the throne and held the position of patriarchal authority have never differed regarding the fundamental source.
Since the source cannot be twofold, for a hundred generations the same codes have been followed and the imperial line has remained unified. As it is said: "Only Heaven [is the ultimate]."
The Great [Sage] alone took Yao as his model. If this is so, it is not that wisdom has something it does not illuminate; rather, there is simply nothing external to be illuminated.

It is not that principle has something it does not exhaust; rather, there is simply no principle left to be exhausted. By inferring from this, one sees that beyond seeing and hearing, the vast expanse has nowhere to lodge.
When principle has nowhere to lodge, the ultimate source can be clarified. Yet, the śramaṇas of today do not awaken to the meaning beyond the words.
Yet, as for the texts that express these teachings, their errors are already extreme. Should they furthermore possess manifest verification, this would indeed be a rare occurrence in the world.
He replied: "The profound principle is vast and remote; the divine way is subtle and refined. It can be sought through reason, but it is difficult to interrogate through mundane affairs.
Since it involves the realm of teaching, it is to be verified by its adaptation to the times. Although it is a means for responding to the world,"

There are ten thousand differences in superiority and inferiority; yet, in the process of bringing all things to completion through their specific applications, one aligns with the hearts of the people and accords with their respective capacities.
When these capacities reach their limit, one simply halts where wisdom cannot know further, without interfering in what lies beyond.

If this is so, it is not that those who embody the ultimate do not encompass all things; rather, it is that one who encompasses all cannot manage everything simultaneously. Therefore, when the ancients spoke of the "Great," they meant this.
As for the Way: through five transformations, its forms and names can be set forth; through nine transformations, its rewards and punishments can be discussed.

These are merely the gradations within the realm of the mundane, yet even they cannot be explained all at once—how much more so that which lies beyond it! Let us further extend and broaden this to encompass its distant categories.

Regarding that which exists beyond the six directions of the world but is set aside without discussion: it is not that it cannot be discussed; rather, if one were to discuss it, it might lead to confusion.
It is so. Among the six realms of the universe, there are matters discussed but not debated; it is not that they cannot be debated—it is that debating them might lead to doubt.

In the Spring and Autumn Annals, which records the world and embodies the will of the former kings, there are matters debated but not deliberated upon; it is not that they cannot be deliberated upon—it is that deliberating on them might lead to disorder.
In all three cases, these matters take as their pivot points things that do not reach the ears or eyes of the individual, yet they do not fail to command attention.
To listen is to look beyond the external. By seeking the intention of the sages through this means, the ways of the internal and the external can be harmonized and clarified.
I have always maintained that the Way of the Dharma and the teachings of names, as well as the Tathāgata and Yao or Confucius—though their manifestations differ, they secretly influence one another;
though their modes of engagement with the world are truly distinct, their ultimate aim is the same. If one examines and distinguishes them in detail, their final destination can be understood.
Observation reveals that, according to principle, there may be those who first harmonize and later diverge, and those who first diverge and later harmonize.

Those who first harmonize and later diverge are the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. Those who first diverge and later harmonize are the successive monarchs who have not yet realized the ultimate—this is their category.
How is this clarified? A sutra states: "The Buddha possesses spontaneous, divine, and wondrous [powers]."

This is the Dharma of transformation through skillful means (*upāya*). Adapting to beings according to their capacities, he manifests in various forms: sometimes as a divine immortal (*ṛṣi*) or a universal monarch (*cakravartin*);
sometimes as a high minister, a state preceptor, or a master of the Dao. Among such manifestations, kings and gentlemen do not know who he truly is.
This is what is meant by "first being in harmony and later becoming estranged. Or there are those who first establish a great enterprise and achieve merit...

The transformation has not yet been fully accomplished; because their traces differ, that which they receive is likewise different. Some expect merit after death, while others manifest response within their own lifetimes.

The number of sage-kings who have relied upon these [teachings] to establish their instruction is beyond counting. Although their methods of restraint and guidance are manifold, they must ultimately converge at the same path.
This is what is meant by "first diverging and later converging. If one were to allow them to remain divergent...
Only after they have been unified can one proceed along the common path; thus, those who intend to traverse this shared way must certainly not limit themselves to a single standard.
If one were to first unify them and then allow for divergence, it would be evident that the ultimate goals of Śākyamuni and those of Yao and Confucius are no different.
Therefore, if one seeks their unity from their divergence, one knows that their convergence in principle must be identical; yet, if one seeks their divergence from their unity—

The realization of the manifold aspects of the ultimate essence is something that those who perceive only outward forms cannot encompass; thus, they become confused by the various paths and are startled by their differences.

Observing from this perspective, one sees that the Way of Heaven and Earth exhausts its efficacy in the process of transformation, while the virtue of the sovereigns [exhausts its efficacy in governance].

The principle reaches its ultimate in accordance and penetration. If one compares it with the peerless teaching and the immutable doctrine, it is clearly evident that they cannot be ranked as equal in terms of their superiority or inferiority. This is also self-evident.
The Fifth Treatise: On Why Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Homage to Kings. Question:

The purport of this treatise holds that the exhaustion of transformation constitutes the ultimate; therefore, those who reach this ultimate must necessarily oppose transformation in order to seek the fundamental source.

Seeking the ultimate principle does not depend upon following the process of transformation. Therefore, [the author] cites the monarchs of successive dynasties to show their alignment with Buddhism, so that sovereigns who have realized the ultimate may exercise temporal governance through skillful means. This is the foundation of your elegant discourse, and it must necessarily lead to great penetration.
Yet, while this may seem correct when sought superficially, in principle it is not so. Why? Because the endowment of vital energy culminates in a single lifetime; once that life is exhausted—
Thus, they dissolve and merge into non-existence. Although the spirit is subtle and wondrous, it is certainly a transformation of yin and yang.
Having been transformed into life, it is again transformed into death; having gathered together to begin, it disperses to end.

Inferring from this, we know for certain that spirit and form are both transformed and originally share no different governance; the refined and the coarse are one qi, and their beginning and end dwell in the same abode.
When the dwelling is whole, the vital energy (*qi*) gathers and becomes spiritual; when the dwelling is destroyed, the energy disperses and its illumination ceases.
To disperse is to return to the original source bestowed by Heaven; to cease is to revert to non-existence. This cycle of recurrence and exhaustion is merely the natural order of things.
Who could have created it? If their origins were different, then their energies would be distinct; yet since their numbers coincide, they merge and undergo the same transformation. Thus it is.
The spirit abiding in a physical form is like fire residing within wood. As long as it lives, it necessarily persists; when it is destroyed, it necessarily extinguishes.
Once the form departs, the spirit disperses and has no place to lodge; once the wood decays, the fire becomes still and has no support. Such is the nature of principle.

Even if the distinction between identity and difference is obscure and difficult to clarify, the discourse of existence and non-existence must depend upon gathering and dispersing. Gathering and dispersing are transformations of the vital breath (*qi*).
This is the general name for the arising and ceasing of the myriad transformations. Thus, Zhuangzi said: "The birth of a person is the gathering of vital energy (*qi*);
when it gathers, there is life; when it disperses, there is death. If life and death are merely matters of that [energy], then what cause for concern should I have?
Those of antiquity who were skilled at speaking of the Way must have attained this truth. If this is indeed so, then the ultimate principle culminates in a single life. Life...

If [the spirit] were entirely not transformed, its meaning could be sought. The answer says: What, indeed, is this "spirit" (shen)? It is that which is numinous through the ultimate refinement of the essence.
Being the ultimate refinement of the essence, it is not something that can be diagrammed by trigrams or images. Therefore, the Sages spoke of it as a wondrous entity.
Even those of superior intelligence cannot definitively determine its physical form or exhaust its profound subtleties; yet, those who discuss it rely only upon conventional knowledge.

To harbor doubts is largely equivalent to self-confusion; the extent of such misrepresentation is already profound. Were one to wish to speak of this, it would be to speak of that which cannot be spoken.
Now, within this ineffable realm, we shall again speak of it in a vague and approximate manner. That which we call "the Spirit" (shen) responds universally without a master;
its subtlety is ultimate and beyond naming. It moves in response to things and proceeds by way of numerical patterns. In responding to things...

It is not a substantial entity; therefore, while entities transform, they do not perish. It is provisionally designated by numbers, yet it is not a number; therefore, though the numbers may be exhausted, it remains inexhaustible.
That which possesses emotion can be moved by entities; that which possesses consciousness can seek through numbers. Because numbers have degrees of refinement and coarseness, their natures differ;
because wisdom has degrees of clarity and obscurity, its illumination varies. Reasoning from this, one knows that transformation occurs through emotion.
Response: The spirit transmits through transformation; emotion is the mother of transformation, while the spirit is the root of emotion.

Emotion possesses the way of meeting with objects; the spirit possesses the power of subtle shifting. It is only that those who have attained thorough awakening return to the source, whereas those who are deluded regarding principle pursue external objects.
Even among the ancients who discussed the Way, there was no single consensus. Let me cite them to clarify this. Zhuangzi uttered profound sounds from...
The Grand Master said: "The Great Clod toils me with life and rests me with death. Furthermore, he regards life as being bound by others and death as returning to the True.
This is what is meant by knowing that life is a great affliction and taking non-birth as the return to the root.
Wenzi quotes the words of the Yellow Emperor, saying: "The physical form wears away, but the spirit does not transform. By means of this non-transformation, one rides upon transformation."
Transformations are infinite. Zhuangzi also said: "One merely assumes a human form and yet still rejoices;

if this human form undergoes ten thousand transformations without ever reaching an end—this is what is meant by knowing that life does not terminate with a single transformation, and thus one pursues external objects without returning.
Although the arguments of these two masters have not fully exhausted the reality of the matter, they have nonetheless approached the fundamental principle and gained some insight into it.
Alas! Debaters do not investigate the teachings on the various modes of birth and death, yet they treat the cycles of aggregation and dispersal as occurring within a single transformation.
They fail to reflect that the Way of the Spirit possesses the numinous power of wondrous beings, yet they claim that both the refined and the coarse perish together. Is this not tragic?

The analogy of fire and wood originates from the sacred scriptures; having lost its transmitted lineage, its profound inspiration can no longer be sought, and these subtle words have consequently sunk into the realm of the mundane.

The teaching causes those who discuss it to rely upon it to form doubts. Had there not been masters of the time who awakened to the fundamental principle, one would not have known of the brilliance of prior enlightenment or the merit of its secret transmission;
it would have perished without being heard for generations. Why is this? For when emotional dispositions and numerical phenomena interact, their transformations are without end.
Causes and conditions are subtly structured and secretly replicated; were it not for those of penetrating vision, who could recognize these changes?
Were it not for one who possesses penetrating insight, who could recognize their convergence? Let me provide an argument for the sake of the debater to verify this.

Just as a real fire is transmitted to kindling, so is the spirit transmitted to the physical form. The transmission of fire to different kindling is like the transmission of the spirit to different forms.

Since the former kindling is not the latter kindling, one knows the subtlety of the principle that "when the finger is exhausted [the light remains]. Since the former form is not the latter form, one awakens to the numerical law of the emotions.
How profound this realization is! Those who are deluded see that the physical form perishes within a single lifetime and consequently conclude that spirit and emotion perish along with it;

they are like one who observes fire ending when a piece of wood is consumed and concludes that its duration has come to a total end. This is merely to follow the discourse on the preservation of life (*yangsheng*), rather than seeking out its true nature through distant inquiry.
To follow your argument, even if we assume that form and spirit transform together, originating from the primordial source of Heaven, whether one is foolish or wise—
Regarding the means of sustenance, all beings alike receive what they are given. One must ask: is that which is received received by the physical form, or is it received by the spirit?
If it were received by the physical form, then all things possessing form would transform into spirits.
If it were received by the spirit, this would mean that spirit transmits to spirit; in which case Danzhu would be equal in sageliness to Emperor Yao, and Zhonghua would be equal to Gusun.
"Is it possible for the spirits of the blind musicians [the *sou*] and others to be so? Is it possible?

If it were not so, we would surely know that the convergence of hidden conditions was established in the distant past, and the distinction between light and darkness was fixed at the very inception of form.

Even though the spirit of Qu Yuan possessed skillful governance, he could not alter the naturalness of one's nature; how much less so for those who have come down from that time? To verify this through principle, it is a subtle teaching."

There is evidence. By examining this through concrete affairs, one may avoid being deluded regarding the Great Way. After the treatise was completed, there were guests living in retirement who walked by moonlight on a night excursion;
they gathered together in the Dharma Hall and asked: "We respectfully examine your elegant discourse, and its great purport is clearly visible;
indeed, there is almost nothing to dispute. Yet, if we were to attempt a further investigation for a day, there might still be a few points that have not been fully exhausted."
I grant your point. I consider that the virtuous standards of a śramaṇa are an extraordinary regulation for transforming worldly customs; they are the distinguished implements of the Daoist path.
It is fitting that when applied to sovereigns and parents, formal reverence should be set aside. What I now doubt is this:

you have recently initiated a difficult undertaking and look far toward the achievement of merit beyond this world. Its hidden benefits lack manifest efficacy in the present dharma, and its future retribution remains profound and obscure.
[The host] replied: "It would indeed cause kings and dukes to present offerings and lay devotees to humble themselves. Would it not be a failure to receive their virtue while remaining seated?
Would it not lead to the burden of premature judgment, or result in receiving their bounty in vain, thereby inviting the reproach of those who eat the bread of idleness?

After a long silence, the host finally replied: "I beg to offer an analogy for you gentlemen. Suppose there were a person here who, on behalf of the imperial mandate, traveled far to communicate with foreign lands..."
In the customs of the nine translated regions, when asked whether the King should provide them with provisions and grant them carriages and robes, the answer was:
"Yes. The host said: "The pattern can now be sought. As for those called *śramaṇas*, what does this mean?

It means they are able to dispel the dark ignorance of the common world and open the profound path beyond transformation. They are about to employ the Way of universal forgetting (*jīwàng*) to [attune] with Heaven..."
Those below followed suit. May those who aspire to the heights pay homage to his lingering influence, and may those who rinse their mouths with mountain streams savor its residual essence.
If this is so, then even though the great enterprise has not yet been completed, by observing the traces of his transcendent strides, that which is realized is already vast indeed.
Thus, the merit of his active engagement and the benefit of his preservation have not yet repaid the resolve of his initial vow; how much less could they answer for the three karmas?
"How wearying! Furthermore, as for such a person, though their physical form depends upon sustenance, their spirit has no proximate attachment.
To them, the four types of offerings appear like gnats and mosquitoes passing before one's eyes; how much less need be said of the kindness of moistening ears with droplets?

Thereupon, the assembly of guests first realized that on the path to the unseen realm, opening a track is the true merit, and that for those who have stilled their minds, purity and completion constitute the Way. Thus they rejoiced.
Nevertheless, they withdrew with their hearts gladdened by the verses they had recited.

The commentary states: In the year following the Master Yuan’s composition of this treatise, Emperor An was ultimately usurped by rebellious traitors and went into exile in the region south of the Yangtze River.

It was only after three years that he returned to the throne. At that time, it may truly be said that the age was in decline and the fortunes of the realm were at their lowest; such was the state of men.
Huiyuan was deeply concerned. He alone maintained the sacred Way with solemnity, tracing its origins back to show that our Buddhist tradition shares the same spirit as that of Yao and Confucius.

Consequently, the worthy men of his time found solace through him. As for the debate regarding the veneration of rulers, my humble arguments and refutations were simply unavoidable, given the burden of upholding the religious teachings. Once Huiyuan’s treatise was published, not only...
At that time, all the prevailing opinions were discarded, providing a standard for reference for ten thousand generations. Alas!

When Kumārajīva spoke of how the śramaṇas of the Western Regions would invariably turn toward the wind at dawn to pay homage, calling him the "Dharma-protecting Bodhisattva of the East," how could he have failed to believe this?
