In the second year of the Yixi era, the Venerable Buddhavarman from India arrived in Chang’an. Master Kumārajīva hurriedly stepped out of his shoes to welcome him, regretting that they had met so late in life.
Their discussions were often as medicinal as a prescription for the soul. Buddhavarman remarked, “The translations you have produced do not exceed the reach of ordinary minds;
how then have you attained such a high reputation? Kumārajīva replied, “I have merely served as a scribe for those who have already mastered the learning.”

Is it appropriate to vainly embellish appearances and conform to public opinion merely to be considered eminent? [Instead,] one should calmly resolve the meanings that remain unsettled, thereby further increasing sincerity and reverence.
Prince Yao Hong of the Qin dynasty invited Kumārajīva to the Eastern Palace to discuss the Dharma with him. Kumārajīva asked: "How is it that dharmas are empty? He replied:
"The various subtle elements (paramāṇu) compose form; since form has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva), form is itself emptiness. He asked again: "Since..."

[The opponent asks: "If form is destroyed by means of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) to establish emptiness, how then is that single atom itself destroyed? [The respondent] answers: "Because of the single atom, the multitude of atoms is empty;
because of the multitude of atoms, the single atom is empty. The śramaṇa Baoyun translated these words but did not comprehend their meaning.
Everyone assumed that the subtle atoms (paramāṇu) calculated by Bhadra were eternal, so they requested him once more for clarification. Bhadra said: "Dharmas do not arise of themselves;
they arise through the convergence of conditions. Because there is one atom, there are many atoms. Since atoms lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva), they are empty."

"Would one not rather say that not even a single atom has been destroyed? At that time, the Qin court held the profound teachings (xuanhua) in high esteem, and several thousand śramaṇas entered and exited the imperial palace.
Buddhabhadra remained composed and indifferent. He once casually said to his disciples, "Yesterday I saw five ships from India set sail together; they should have arrived by now.
Furthermore, his followers claimed for themselves that they had attained the first fruit (srotāpanna). Sengzheng and Daoji remarked, "The Buddha..."
He was not permitted to speak of the Dharma he had attained himself. What could the theories of the five ships possibly clarify?

His disciple’s light words were deceptive and misleading, and they violated the Vinaya; their interpretations did not accord. Thereupon, Guṇabhadra crossed the river and entered Kuāng Mountain to see Master Huiyuan.
Huiyuan did not yield to Dao’an’s arguments. Dao’an held him in high esteem and sent a letter to Guanzhong to clear his name of the injustice.
Later, while at the Sīkōng Monastery in Jiangdu, he translated the sixty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

He was moved by two youths dressed in blue who would emerge daily from the pond in the courtyard to light incense and replenish the vases, never leaving his side; at night, they would secretly return to the pond. Day after day...
He regarded this as a constant occurrence. When the translation of the scriptures was completed, he vanished without a trace for seven years.

During this time, the Dharma Master Faxian returned from the Western Regions. Initially, in the second year of the Long’an era, Faxian had entered the Western Regions to seek the Dharma together with Huijing, Tanzheng, and others.
Having crossed the shifting sands, they lost their way; using the sun to determine the east, they looked toward the west.

He proceeded through a place strewn with human bones, where he was not seen by the fierce winds or evil spirits. Upon reaching the Onion Range (Pamir), amidst the accumulated snow, there were venomous dragons and flying sands;
he advanced along a path suspended in mid-air. Below, the precipices were all ten thousand *ren* high and extremely perilous; it took him seven days to pass them by means of ladders.

The river was eighty paces wide, and those who crossed it by treading upon a rope bridge did so with great difficulty. It was a place that neither Zhang Qian nor Gan Ying of the Han dynasty had ever reached.
Beyond this lay the Lesser Snow Mountains, where the cold was extreme; Huijing’s thighs shook with cold and he died.

Faxian wept for him in deep grief, then wiped away his tears and journeyed alone through over thirty more kingdoms until he reached Central India. He was thirty *li* from Rājagṛha when he entered [the city].
At a certain monastery, he asked for the way to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. The monks said, "The sun is setting; there are many lions there that devour men, so you must not go.
Faxian thought to himself, "I have come wishing to behold this sacred site. It is unfortunate that I have arrived late. If I were to die tonight, my lifelong ambition would remain unfulfilled.
My body is not what I cherish—how could I fear lions? Once Faxian arrived, the sun had already set, and he remained on the mountain for the night.
Shedding tears, he bowed and said, "I did not know of my own accord that I had reached this point. He sat beneath a tree reciting a sutra.

At the third watch of the night, a lion crouched before him, licking and gnawing at him. Hui-xian traced its body with his hand and said, "If you desire my flesh, wait until I have finished reciting the sutra.
Thereupon, the lion tucked its tail and departed. The next day, when he returned, an old monk stood leaning on a staff; when Hui-xian bowed to him, the monk did not respond.
He departed slowly. A youth approached, and Xuán asked the elder who he was. He replied, "I am the *dhūta* Mahākāśyapa. Xuán pursued him to the mountain;
there was a stone blocking a narrow crevice, preventing him from proceeding further. Upon reaching South India, he obtained the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and other scriptures.
He remained for three years to study the Brāhmī script. He then entrusted the scriptures and images to merchants and traveled to Siṃhala.

In that country, his companions were all gone; he halted there of his own accord. It happened that someone offered him a silk fan for the Buddha, which moved Hui Xian to thoughts of returning to the East.
Two years later, he arrived in Qingzhou, where the Governor, Li Yi, personally went out to welcome him.
He was escorted and brought to the capital.
In the eighth year, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema arrived at Guzang from Kucha. King Juqu Mengxun of Liang had long been a devoted follower of the Great Dharma.
After Dharmakṣema had resided there for some time, he became fully proficient in the Chinese language and translated the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra and the Mahāsannipāta-sūtra.

The text comprised more than six hundred thousand words; yet, as the number of chapters in the *Nirvāṇa* section was still incomplete, he returned to the Western Regions to seek it out and obtained it.
Upon arriving in Liang, he translated it into forty-two fascicles, totaling ten thousand verses. Kumārajīva displayed many divine wonders.
At that time, King Tuoba Gui of Zhongshan, having heard of Kumārajīva, desired to pay him homage and dispatched an envoy to welcome him. However, Kumārajīva did not go.
Xu Hu granted permission. He dispatched Gao Ping Gong Li Shunce to confer upon Sun the title of King of Liang and bestow upon him the nine emoluments (*jiu xi*).
He instructed him, saying, "Tanwuchen’s virtue and wisdom are vast and profound; I wish to have an audience with him. You should send him here by express courier.

Sun replied, "I serve the imperial court with total loyalty and owe it nothing. My previous memorial requested that Tanwuchen be allowed to remain, and now I have come again to escort him back. He is my teacher."
"If he has already died, that is the end of it; if you wish to go [to him], it is no longer possible.

Shun said, "The court has gathered the King’s loyalty and righteousness, and therefore has openly bestowed upon him extraordinary honors. Now, because of a mere Daoist, you would ruin such a great achievement.

Unable to endure a momentary fit of anger, you have uttered what should not be said, thereby losing the intent behind the court's treatment of you. I truly consider this unacceptable for Your Majesty. Xun said:

"What Your Excellency says is indeed excellent; however, I fear that one's inner disposition may not match such words. Daoxun ultimately did not leave behind any prophecies (*chan*). Consequently, Tuoba Gui harbored a grudge against him.
When Daojin arrived, he sought to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from Daoxun. Daoxun said, "You must repent for seven days before you come back. Subsequently, Daojin went to see Daoxun.
Daoxun suddenly became angry and said, "This is due to past karmic obstructions (*zhàng*). Thereupon, Daojin practiced with meticulous diligence.
After three years, he experienced a vision in a dream in which Śākyamuni Buddha bestowed the precepts upon him. That evening, more than ten people had the same dream as Jin had seen.
Thereupon, they went to visit [Seng]chan again; seeing them from afar, Chan was greatly delighted and said, "Excellent! You have already received the precepts."

I now bear witness for you. When he firmly declined and prepared to return to the West, Liu Sun was enraged that he was departing from him; he secretly dispatched his trusted confidants to assassinate him on the way.
When Daocheng first passed through the frontier pass, he said to those escorting him, "The time for my karma has arrived;
even a supreme sage cannot escape it. It is not that I cherish death or wish to distance myself from you. Not long after, Liu Sun felt remorse and regret in broad daylight.
He saw a ghost and stabbed it with his sword, whereupon he died. His country was subsequently annexed by Wei.

Nine years later, the Dharma Master Daosheng was divinely endowed with marvelous insight. Before the latter chapters of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* had arrived, Daosheng read them repeatedly for a long time and declared:
"Persons of *icchantika* nature shall naturally attain Buddhahood; it is simply that this scripture has not yet reached its conclusion. Thereupon, the text...

Master Zhi attacked him from all sides, falsely accusing him of propagating heterodox teachings and declaring that he should be banished according to the law. Daosheng addressed the assembly with a vow, saying:
"If what I have taught does not accord with the meaning of the sutras, may I receive an evil retribution in this very body.

If it truly accords with the Buddha's mind, may I occupy the Lion’s Seat at the time of my death. Thereupon, with his hands tucked in his sleeves, he traveled south and entered Mount Huqiu, where he erected [a stupa].

The rocks became his audience. When he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* upon reaching the passage concerning the Buddha-nature of icchantikas, he asked, "Does the meaning of what I have explained accord with the Buddha’s mind?

All the rocks nodded their heads in agreement. Later, while traveling to Kuāngshān and residing at Xiāojiǎng Yán, he heard that Dharmakṣema had retranslated the later chapters of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in Nányīng; indeed, it stated that all icchantikas possess Buddha-nature.
He was filled with such joy and comfort that he could not contain himself;
he vowed to serve the Dharma even unto death. The śramaṇa Sengqun resided at Mount Huo on Lujiang. The mountain rises steeply from the midst of the sea;

there is a stone shaped like a basin, several *zhang* wide and six or seven *chi* deep, containing a spring of exceptionally sweet water. Sengqun drank of it and was able to remain without hunger, whereupon he ceased consuming the five grains. Taishō... [text fragment] ...too great.
Shou Liu Kui followed the group and begged for some of their water; Qun gave it to him immediately. However, once they left the mountain, the water smelled foul. Kui went to visit Qun in person.

At the time they were crossing the sea, the weather was clear and bright, but upon reaching the foot of the mountain, a wind and rain suddenly arose, darkening the sky. They remained there for several days unable to proceed.
Kui sighed and said, "This must be because the spirit of the mountain has turned back my worldly carriage. He then departed. Beside Qun’s hermitage, there was a small footbridge.
One day at Dubenquan, a duck with a broken wing crossed a narrow footbridge with its head held low. The community wished to strike it away with a staff but feared injuring the bird;
consequently, they did not drink for several days and subsequently passed away. He was over one hundred and forty years old.
At the time of his death, he said, "In my youth, I once playfully broke the wing of a duck; this is likely the retribution manifesting now."
The Treatise says: Chan Master Gui of Mount Song said, "The Buddha cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma.
He also said, "Even fixed karma is not eternal or firm. How true! If karma is not eternal or firm, there is the principle that it can be extinguished through repentance.

Yet, although the spiritual wonders of Dharmakṣema were renowned and he was suspected of having attained the fruits of sainthood, he nonetheless suffered the calamity at the hands of Juqu Mengxun; likewise, Sengqun abstained from grain.
Drinking from mountain streams and practicing pure cultivation for a hundred years, they still could not avoid the retribution of having their wings broken. Why was this?
When Sengjin advanced in the Way through three years of diligent effort, he was moved by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni bestowing the precepts upon him.

When Daosheng attained refined awakening and entered into a profound resonance with the Buddha’s mind, he was moved by a stone nodding its head in approval. Thus, were these four masters all recipients of provisional teachings established for specific purposes? If it were Jin...
The case of Yu Shenggai shows that extraordinary matters can be achieved through sincerity;
the cases of Chen and Qun show that one must not treat the retribution of karmic offenses as illusory and thus act with negligence.

Were it not for this, how could there be one who does not betray the realms of both the unseen and the seen by sacrificing a body of inestimable value for the sake of a single minute object? Truly, such a person is the highest in all under heaven.
He was a man of action. As for the Yuan Wei dynasty: his original surname was Tuoba; he was a Xianbei barbarian. During the chaos of the Western Jin, there was a Tuoba Lu who settled in Loufan.
The Jin court enfeoffed him as King of Dai. Subsequently, his tribes dispersed, and more than sixty years passed.
Reaching the period of Lu Sun, Shi Yi was replaced by Sha Gui. The *Weishu* states that Gui was none other than Wei Taizu, Emperor Daowu.
In the first year of the Taiyuan era, he went out to occupy Shuozhou and built a city three hundred li to the east, naming it Heng’an.
He served as the Protector-General (*hujun*) under Fu Jian; after Jian’s defeat, he then assumed the true imperial title. Upon the death of Taizu, Taizong Mingyuan Di ascended the throne. Mingyuan...

Upon the passing of the founding ancestor, Emperor Taowu was established on the throne. From that point, after four more sovereigns had succeeded him, Emperor Xiaowen, the World-Honored One, moved the capital to Luoyang.
He changed the family name to Yuan, discarded the Hu attire and headgear, abolished the barbarian language, and honored Chinese customs.

At that time, there were only two states in the world, known as the Northern and Southern Dynasties. Throughout the entire duration of the Wei dynasty, there were sixteen rulers for a total of one hundred and sixty-one years.

In his reign, the number of monks reached two million, and there were over thirty thousand monasteries. A total of one thousand nine hundred and more fascicles of translated sutras, vinayas, and śāstras were produced.
From antiquity, no Buddhist undertaking regarding images, stupas, or temples has ever surpassed this in magnificence.
Qi Zhaozuo composed the "Buddhist and Daoist Annals" (*Folaozhi*) for Wei Shou’s *History of Wei* (*Weishu*). Its summary states:
"The study of Śākyamuni was heard of during the Yuanshou era of Emperor Wu of the Former Han. During this time, Huo Qubing captured the King of Kanyue and a golden man approximately one zhang tall.
The Emperor regarded him as a great deity and enshrined him in the Ganshan Palace, where he burned incense and prostrated before him. This was the origin of the flow of Buddhism."
This was the gradual beginning of its dissemination. Upon the opening of the Western Regions, Zhang Qian was dispatched as an envoy to Da Xia;

upon his return, he reported that the kingdom of Shendu (India) possessed the teachings of the *Futu* (Buddha). During the Yuanshou era of Emperor Ai, Jing Xian received an oral transmission of the *Futu jing* from the King of Great Yuezhi.
Later, during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, he dreamed of a golden man with a halo of light atop his head flying through the palace courtyard. [Dong] Zhongshu and [Fan] Leji...
It began with the Emperor’s audience with the Buddha. The Emperor dispatched the Court Gentleman Cai Yin and others as envoys to India to transcribe the legacy of the Buddha’s teachings.
They subsequently returned to Luoyang together with the śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, bringing back the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* and a standing image of Śākyamuni.
The Emperor ordered court painters to produce copies of these, which were placed at the Qingliang Terrace and the Xianjie Mausoleum and sealed away.
It passed through the stone chamber of the Lan-tai (Lantai) Palace. *Futu* is sometimes called *Buduo*; this is a shift in phonetic transcription. It is translated as "Pure Awakening" (*Jingjue*).
This signifies that by extinguishing defilements and clarifying the Way, one attains holy enlightenment.
The essential purport of these scriptures generally states that all categories of living beings arise from their karma;
there are the three periods of past, present, and future, and the consciousness never perishes. Whatever good or evil one performs will inevitably entail its retribution.

Gradually accumulating superior karma, they refine away their coarse and vulgar nature; passing through countless forms, they polish and purify their spiritual intelligence until, reaching the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*), they attain the Buddha-way.
During this interval, the stages and levels of mental cultivation are not uniform; all proceed from the shallow to the profound.

To transform the obscure into the manifest generally depends upon accumulating benevolence and compliance, purifying desires and cravings, and cultivating emptiness and stillness to achieve pervasive illumination.
Thus, when first cultivating the mind, one relies upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—known as the Three Refuges—which are like the three things a gentleman fears.

Furthermore, there are the Five Precepts: abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants; their general significance is akin to that of benevolence and righteousness.

Ritual propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness are the same in this regard: if one upholds them, one will be born in the superior realms of devas and humans; if one violates them, one will fall into the various sufferings of ghosts and animals.
Furthermore, there are six paths of rebirth where good and evil lead one to be born.

Those who follow this Way shave their hair and beards, cast off worldly burdens, and leave the household life. They form the relationship of teacher and disciple, observe the rules and regulations, and dwell together in harmony.
Governing the mind and cultivating pure conduct, they beg for alms to sustain themselves; these are called *śramaṇas*. Alternatively, they are called *sāman*, as the sounds are similar.
Their fundamental capacities and practices differ, which are termed the "Three Vehicles": the *śrāvaka*, the *pratyekabuddha*, and [the bodhisattva].

It is called the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna) because it takes that which can be mounted and driven to reach the Way as its name. Those of superior faculties cultivate the six perfections and advance in the myriad practices;
they ferry across billions of streams over vast expanses of time, ascending to the realm of enlightenment and being designated as Buddhas.

His original name was Śākyamuni, which is translated here as "Capable Benevolence" (Néng-rén). This signifies that his virtue is full and his Way complete, such that he can govern and deliver all things.
He descended as the son of the King of Kapilavastu in India on the eighth day of the fourth month, emerging from his mother’s right side.
His physical appearance was transcendent and extraordinary, possessing thirty-two marks; likewise, thirty-two auspicious omens descended from heaven in response.

He entered nirvana on the fifteenth day of the second month. This is called "extinction" (mie-du) or "eternal bliss, self, and purity" (chang-le-wo-jing), clarifying that there is no further transmigration or the burden of suffering.
Furthermore, it is said that all Buddhas have two aspects: the first is the ultimate reality (zhen-shi).
This refers to the ultimate essence, which is wondrously transcendent and free from all constraints; it cannot be anticipated by spatial location, nor can it be limited by physical dimensions.

When there is a stimulus, there is a response, yet its essence remains eternally serene. Second is provisional response: this means blending one's light with the six realms and sharing the dust of the myriad categories.

Birth and extinction occur according to the times, and longevity or brevity respond to conditions. Form arises through stimulation, yet its essence is not substantially existent. This is provisional form.
Although the true essence has departed, it does not transmigrate; however, because there is no subtle resonance at this time, one is unable to see it constantly.
This clarifies that the Buddha’s birth is not a real birth, and his extinction is not a real extinction.
Once the Buddha had passed away, his body was cremated with fragrant wood. His sacred relics were divided into fragments, large and small like grains of rice;

they could not be broken by striking them nor consumed by burning them, yet they possessed radiant light and divine efficacy. These are called *śarīra*. His disciples collected and enshrined them, exhausting themselves in offerings of incense and flowers and paying them the highest respect.
Out of devotion, they constructed edifices for them, which are called *stūpas*, much like ancestral temples. Therefore, they have been referred to as "towers" (*ta*) since ancient times.

This refers to the temple. A hundred years later, there was King Aśoka, who by means of his supernormal powers divided the Buddha’s relics and commanded various spirits and deities to construct eighty-four thousand stupas throughout the world, all of which were completed on the same day.
Today, there are temples of King Aśoka in Luoyang, Pengcheng, Guzang, and Linzi; these likely preserve his legacy. And...
His shadow, footprints, nails, and teeth remain in India; those who travel back and forth there all say they have seen them.
Initially, the teachings were expounded orally, and later they were all committed to writing. Having thoroughly examined their profound significance, nothing has been omitted or lost.
Thus, the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are like the various systems of the Nine Schools; their ultimate convergence is fundamentally rooted in the Three Vehicles. Hereafter...
Arhats and Bodhisattvas composed treatises in succession to elucidate the meaning of the sutras and refute the heterodox schools.

All of these relied upon the great principles of the various *piṭakas* and *nikāyas*, employing hypothetical external questions to explain them through internal teachings. These were transmitted to China and gradually spread widely.
At the beginning of the Han dynasty, śramaṇas all wore red cloth; later, they changed to garments of variegated colors.

Emperor Taizu was born with innate knowledge and believed in Buddhism. When he first pacified Zhongshan and traveled through various states, he paid his respects to all śramaṇas he encountered and prohibited his military forces from committing any offenses against them.
In the first year of the Tianxing era, he issued an edict stating: "The rise of the Buddha-dharma has come from afar."
The merit of his salvation and benefit extends invisibly to both the living and the deceased; his divine traces and bequeathed Dharma may truly be relied upon as a refuge.

By imperial decree, the relevant authorities were ordered to construct and adorn a sacred image within the capital and to refurbish monastic quarters, so that those who follow with faith and devotion might have a place to dwell.

When Emperor Taizong ascended the throne, he established images throughout the capital and the four quarters of the realm, and further commanded śramaṇas to instruct and guide the customs of the people.

During the Huangshi era, the śramaṇa Faguo of Zhao Commandery, whose observance of the precepts was refined and supreme, expounded the scriptural canons. By imperial decree, he was summoned to serve as the *Sengtong* (Patriarch of the Monks).

His words were frequently met with approval and satisfaction. Successively, he was granted the titles of Duke of Yicheng for Assisting the State, Marquis of Zhongxin, and An... (the title was subsequently elevated).
He repeatedly declined the title of Marquis of Cheng. Emperor Taizong once visited his residence; because the gates and lanes were too narrow to accommodate carriages, the Emperor had them expanded.
He died at the age of over eighty. The Emperor attended his funeral three times and posthumously conferred upon him the title of General Laoshou and the posthumous title of Lord Ling of Zhao Hu.

The Treatise says: During the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, after the *Book of Jin* had already been compiled, there were again those who urged the compilation of the histories of the seven dynasties of the North and South.
Because the *Book of Northern Wei* was already extremely detailed, Taizong specifically refused [the request]. Examining this with the present day, it is indeed so.

Generally speaking, the scriptures and teachings of Buddhism and Daoism are considered heterodox studies (*wàixué*) by Confucian scholars; should one wish to encompass them both, it is not possible—unless...

Having long been perfumed by the power of matured vows, his return to this world was such that even the most discerning could not perceive its likeness, let alone those who sought to penetrate his ultimate purpose and trace the lineage of his teachings.
How extraordinary it is that the "Buddhism and Daoism" chapter of the *Wei Shu* gallops between Sima Qian and Ban Gu without needing to cross a horse’s stride;
it brandishes its banner to press against the fortresses of Xunzi and Yangzi, moving with a dignified and graceful gait.
Consider this: Wei Shou combined the difficult-to-master studies of three sages and possessed a mind of equanimity toward the four founders [of the schools].
That his writings alone have been trusted by posterity—is this not truly magnificent?

At that time, Cui Hao, the Wei Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was slandered. Emperor Taizu ordered Hao to return to his private residence as a commoner, whereupon he devoted himself to the arts of nourishing the body and cultivating the nature through medicinal elixirs.
Previously, the Daoist Kou Qianzhi of Mount Song had practiced the techniques of Zhang Daoling;

he claimed to have once encountered Laozi descending to bestow a mandate upon him. Qianzhi succeeded Daoling as the Celestial Master (*Tianshi*) and was granted the transmission of methods for abstaining from grain and lightening the body.

He compiled twenty fascicles on these arts and precepts to purify and organize the Daoist teachings. Furthermore, he encountered the divine being Li Puwen, who claimed to be a remote descendant of Laozi.
Li bestowed upon him more than sixty fascicles of diagrams, registers, and direct scriptures (*zhijing*), as well as the methods of the *Tiangong Jinglun*.
Kou Qianzhi presented these texts to Emperor Taiwu; however, many within both the court and the commonalty did not yet believe in them.
Xin was the sole teacher to whom Cui Hao devoted himself, following him to receive his arts. Hao also submitted a memorial extolling and clarifying these matters.
Emperor Taizu was delighted and dispatched an envoy with jade, silk, and sacrificial animals to the Mount Songyue to welcome [Tao]qian.
Qian established the Tianshi Daoist monastery south of Pingcheng on a five-tiered terrace; from this point on, the followers of the Way flourished.
The late Sima Wenzheng of our dynasty said: "The general purport of the texts of Laozi and Zhuangzi is to seek identity between life and death and to treat coming and going with indifference;
yet those who practice the arts of the immortals ingest elixirs and engage in refinement to seek levitation, and they smelt herbs and stones to produce gold and silver."
Their methods are fundamentally contradictory. For this reason, Liu Xin’s *Qilüe* categorized Daoism among the "Treatises" (*Zǐzǐ*) and relegated the arts of immortals to "Techniques" (*Fāngjì*).
Later, there emerged the arts of talismanic water and prohibitive incantations; by the time of Kou Qianzhi, these were finally merged into one, a practice that persists to this day.
The corruption of this tradition is extreme. Although Cui Hao disliked the scriptures of Buddhism and Daoism, he placed his trust in Qianzhi.
As for these words, what is their reason? Formerly, when Zang Wenzhong sacrificed to the *yuanju* birds, Confucius considered it a lack of wisdom.
For one such as Qian, his devotion to the *yuanju* was even greater. Of the three hundred poems of the *Shijing*, they can be summarized in a single phrase:
"Let your thoughts be without deviance. How can a gentleman not be cautious in choosing his methods?
The Dhyāna Master Xuangao resided on Mount Maiji. He was a close friend of the śramaṇa Tanhong.
Hearing that Dharmapriya had come from the Northern Mountains to Liang to practice wondrous dhyāna contemplation, Xuangao went to attend upon him. Within ten days, he attained realization;

Dharmapriya marveled at his extraordinary progress and considered him superior to himself. When Dharmapriya returned to the West, a wicked bhikṣu, jealous of Xuangao, slandered him to the King of Henan.
Zi Man said, "Gao is now gathering disciples and will become a threat to the state. Zi Man believed him and wished to kill Gao, but his father would not permit it.

Consequently, Gao was banished to the north of the River, where he dwelt on Mount Tang in Linyang. This mountain was the abode of terrestrial immortals (*dìxiān*); at night, the sounds of bells and stone chimes were heard there.
Among Gao’s more than one hundred disciples, Xuan Shao stood out as preeminent and possessed supernatural powers. Once, he pointed toward the ground...
He drew water from the spring to provide for the community. There were eleven others who succeeded him. King Hénán went out to welcome Tánhóng;
upon arriving, he asked the King why he had excluded Gāo, saying, "That man is a rare omen of this age. The King received him with great courtesy.

When Gāo wished to comply with the summons, the trees and grasses in the mountains collapsed and lay prostrate, and jagged rocks blocked the path. Gāo said, "My will is to propagate the Way. From that point on—
It was of no benefit to remain stuck in the rocky caverns; the path could now be traveled. The King came out to the outskirts of the city to welcome him and honored him as his teacher.
Later, he traveled to the land of Liang, where Juqu Mengxun treated him with even greater courtesy. A disciple named Sengyin claimed to have attained the fruit of an Arhat;
he falsely attributed supernatural powers to himself, causing [the Master] to see, while in meditative concentration, the world of the Ten Powers and hear various...
The teachings expounded by the Buddha are each distinct; even during a single summer, he could not exhaustively investigate what he had seen, whereupon he felt a sense of shame and trepidation.

The following year, a Wei envoy invited Daohigh to enter Pingcheng. While Tuoba Tao was on the throne, his sincerity and reverence increased further, and he commanded Crown Prince Huang to serve him as a teacher.
*General Annals of Buddhism During the Lōngxìng Era*, Scroll Four;
*General Annals of Buddhism During the Lōngxìng Era*, Scroll Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zǔxiù of Shíshì in Lōngxìng Prefecture.

In the third year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the divine monk Beidu first emerged from Jizhou. Appearing like one who was eccentric or mad, he carried a wooden cup and would invariably ride upon it when crossing water;
thus he was named Beidu (Cup-Crosser). He once traveled from Mengjin, riding his cup across the riverbank, all the way to Jinling.

At that time, he was about forty years old. His appearance was haggard and impoverished, and his moods were inconsistent. Whenever it grew intensely cold, he would immediately bore holes through the ice to bathe;
at other times, he would climb mountains wearing wooden clogs, or walk barefoot through the marketplace. Carrying a single reed basket, he would occasionally visit Yanxian Temple.

The śramaṇa Fayi encountered him with even greater diligence. Suddenly, [the deity] abandoned him and departed. As Fayi traveled to Guabu and was about to board a boat, the boatman did not respond immediately;
he then boarded a bowl and crossed to the northern bank. At that time, a member of the Li family in Guangling was providing a meal for monks; Fayi crossed directly and entered.
He placed a reed ring in the courtyard upon his seat, and the assembly gazed at it with wide eyes. As he crossed over it, he remained composed.

A person in the assembly who was angry saw that the reed ring was obstructing the path and tried to move it; though he possessed great strength, he could not budge it. After the meal was finished, Hui-du took it up and departed, saying with a smile, "The Four Heavenly Kings.
At that time, a young boy secretly saw four small children inside the ring, each about several inches tall.

His eyebrows and eyes were like a painting. When they went to search for him, he had vanished from his location; from this point on, his traces became manifest. After his death, there were still times when people saw him and said: [as follows].
In the sixth year, Guṇabhadra of India arrived at Jinling. Emperor Wen sent an envoy to welcome him from the outskirts of the capital.

Guṇabhadra’s spirit was clear and transcendent; when the Emperor saw him, he was greatly pleased and ordered him to reside at Qihuan Temple. He repeatedly invited him into the palace to receive offerings.
The Vice Director He Shangzhi, Prince Yikang of Pengcheng, and Prince Yixuan of Nanqiao all served him as their teacher.
They requested that he lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Because Guṇabhadra had not yet mastered the Chinese language, he prayed to Avalokiteśvara for increased intellectual power.

That night, he dreamed that a divine warrior replaced his head; upon waking, he felt a great deal of pain, yet he subsequently became thoroughly proficient in the Chinese language and immediately lectured for the assembly.
At that time, because of the sublime Mahāyāna principles of Guṇabhadra, he was given the title Mahāyāna.
In the ninth year, Emperor Wen visited Dazhuangyan Monastery to convene a great assembly, personally sitting on the ground together with the fourfold assembly.

When it came to the meal, the assembly feared the sun had passed noon and did not dare to set their chopsticks down. The Emperor said, "It is only just noon. At that time, Master Daosheng was present.
Xie Jizhi said, "The bright sun adorns the heavens; now it is precisely midday according to the celestial reckoning. Why do you say it has passed?
He raised his bowl and began to eat, and the entire assembly followed his example. The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict to have Daosheng remain in the capital.

At that time, eminent figures such as Wang Hong, Fan Tai, and Yan Yanzhi all visited his door to form friendships with him. Daosheng often felt that the scriptural texts had not yet reached their full meaning.
Regarding the intent of the Buddha, many scholars remained mired in mere hearsay and superficial observation.

Consequently, he composed the *Treatise on Good Deeds Not Being Rewarded*, the *Treatise on Sudden Enlightenment and Attaining Buddhahood*, the *Treatise on the Two Truths*, the *Treatise on the Permanence of Buddha-nature*, the *Treatise on the Formlessness of the Dharmakāya*, the *Treatise on the Buddha Having No Pure Land*, and the *Treatise on the Existence of Conditions for Response*.
These works comprehensively gathered ancient doctrines to reveal their profound depths; they became as revered as the sun and stars. Furthermore, in the following year’s first month...

On the *gengzi* day of the month, he ascended the Dharma seat; his voice was clear and resonant, and those who heard him were enlightened and delighted. Suddenly, his fly-whisk fell to the ground, and leaning upon his armrest, he passed away.
In the eleventh year, the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman from India first renounced his kingdom to enter the monastic life and mastered the four Āgamas.
His mastery of the Tripiṭaka was profound, and he could recite several million words. The kings of the various vassal states all followed him to receive the precepts and refuge.

He would often say to the kings: "The Way lies in profound mastery; when one encounters conditions, one should respond accordingly. It is sufficient simply to rely on compassion and refrain from intentionally harboring harmful intent.
While traveling in the kingdom of Śrīvijaya, its king wished to renounce the world and serve Guṇavarman, but his ministers earnestly petitioned against it.

This was not permitted. He then issued a decree throughout the land, saying: "If all within the realm receive the Great Monk’s returning-to-the-precepts [ordination], do not commit acts of killing or harm, and provide relief to the poor and destitute, I shall grant your request. Thereupon, the ministers, officials, and commoners bowed their heads and obeyed his command.
The court had long heard of his reputation, so the śramaṇas Huiguan and others petitioned Emperor Wen, requesting that an envoy be sent to bring him back. An imperial edict was issued accordingly.
The Regional Inspector (Zhōu Cāishǐ) of Jīn dispatched the śramaṇa Dàochūn and others by sea to invite him. When Chūn arrived, Guṇavarman joyfully boarded the ship and reached Guangzhou.
By imperial decree, he was permitted to travel to the capital by post station; on his way, he passed through Shìxīng. Finding that its mountains resembled Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he remained there.
At nightfall, there was a Bǎoyuè Hall in the monastery; Guṇavarman playfully depicted the Buddha Dīpaṃkara on the eastern wall.

The image of the youth with his hair spread out was exquisitely marvelous; it would frequently emit light at night. Once, while he remained in meditative concentration for several days without leaving the temple, the monks sent a novice to observe him.
The novice saw a white lion looking up and pawing at a pillar while playing, and the air was filled with blue lotus flowers. Startled, the novice ran back and shouted loudly;
the temple monks rushed there together, but there was nothing to be seen. When he was brought to Jinling for an audience, the Emperor went out to welcome him.

[The Emperor] was deeply moved by his earnestness. He then asked him with composure: "I have often wished to observe the fasts [of the uposatha], yet I am unable to fulfill this wish while engaged in governing the world.
Now that you, Dharma Master, have come from afar, I am fortunate to have you here. How may you instruct me? He replied: "The Way resides in the mind, not in external affairs;
the Dharma arises from oneself, not from others. Furthermore, the cultivation practiced by a sovereign differs from that of a commoner. As for the commoner—

One whose status is lowly and whose name is obscure lacks the authority for their words to carry weight. If one cannot overcome oneself and practice rigorous self-discipline, what purpose can they serve?

When a sovereign takes the four seas as their home and the myriad people as their children, a single noble word causes both officials and commoners to rejoice, and the promulgation of a single virtuous policy brings harmony among all ministers.
When punishments do not shorten lifespans and labor does not exhaust strength, then wind and rain will follow their proper seasons.

Cold and heat respond to their proper seasons; the hundred grains flourish and the mulberry and oak trees grow lush and thick. To observe the fast and refrain from killing on this basis is already a great achievement.
Why must one first cease half a day’s meal and save the life of a single bird before it can be considered a vast act of salvation?
The Emperor leaned on his desk and sighed, saying, "The laity are deluded regarding profound principles, while the monastics stagnate in superficial teachings.

As this Dharma Master’s words suggest, he is one with whom it is possible to discuss the realm between heaven and humanity. He then commanded that he reside at Qizhi Temple to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the "Ten Stages" chapter.
The Emperor personally led the high officials to assemble daily beneath his seat; such a magnificent assembly for the Dharma had never been heard of before.
In the twelfth year, the Capital Prefect Xiao Mozhi requested permission to establish monasteries and cast Buddhist images.

The Emperor asked the Palace Attendant He Shangzhi and the Minister of Personnel Yang Xuanbao, saying: "I have not read the scriptures extensively since my youth; of late, I have had even less leisure."

The matter of cause and effect remains obscure and unexamined; this is why I have not dared to propose a divergent view—simply because your honorable contemporaries are for the most part faithful and respectful.
Fan Tai and Xie Lingyun both stated that the laws and regulations of the Six Classics are fundamentally intended to save the world.
One must seek the wondrous Way, taking the Buddhist scriptures as one’s compass for north and south.

Having seen Yan Yanzhi’s *Analysis of the Treatise on the Nature of Sentient Beings* and Zong Bing’s *Refutation of the White and Black Treatises*, their explanations are vast and brilliantly illuminate the ultimate truth.
If the people throughout the realm were all to cultivate this transformation, then I would sit and achieve Great Peace. What else would there be to do? Regarding Xiao Mo’s request yesterday...

The Emperor decreed: "I shall present these [drafts] to you for your consideration regarding what to add or omit. Only when they contain means to restrain and suppress frivolity and excess, without harming the promotion of the Great Dharma, should they be committed to writing.
Shangzhi replied: "In this world of mortals, there are those who are intermittently disrespectful and lacking in faith.

As for me, being of mediocre and humble capacity, I possess only my foolish diligence; I truly fear that my deficiencies will bring disgrace upon the Great Dharma. That I have instead been honored with such praise and deliberation fills me with profound shame."
I have heard it said that the eminent figures of previous dynasties did not fail to respond to enlightened edicts. Since the crossing of the Yangtze River,
there have been Wang Dao, Zhou Yi, Yu Liang, Wang Meng, Xie An, Xi Chao, Wang Tanzhi, Wang Gong, Wang Mi, Guo Wen,
Xie Shang, Dai Kui, Xu Xun, as well as my late ancestors and brothers, the brothers Wang Yuanlin, Fan Wang, Sun Chuo, Zhang Xuan, and Ao.
Kai. Some were prime ministers whose crowns shone brightly; some were paragons of human ethics who served as the ceremonial ornaments of society;
some devoted their hearts to the realm between Heaven and man; and some set foot beyond the clouds and mists. There was none among them who did not turn their minds in refuge [to him].

Among these, there are those comparable to Lan Huokai and Qian Yuan, who withdrew into the deep abyss and sought the sublime heights—both of whom followed in the footsteps of the Yellow Emperor, or perhaps they were men of unfathomable depth. This is how the monastics and laity have recently debated the matter.
It is so. If one were to list them all, the eminent and extraordinary figures who emerged throughout China and the barbarian lands during the Han and Wei dynasties would be beyond counting.

Huiyuan said: "The transformation wrought by Śākyamuni is such that there is nothing it cannot encompass. Adapting to the Way is certainly the source of his teaching; bringing all things into harmony is likewise a vital task.
I have humbly savored these words and find they accord with the ultimate truth. Why is this? Because among the officials of the hundred schools, ten men uphold the five precepts.
If ten people are pure and prudent, then in a village of a thousand households, if one hundred people practice the ten wholesome deeds, those one hundred will live in harmony.

If this moral influence is propagated throughout the world, then among a population of billions, there will be a million benevolent people. Now, to perform a single good deed is to eliminate a single evil;
to eliminate a single evil is to bring rest to a single punishment. When one punishment is brought to rest within a family, ten thousand punishments are brought to rest.

Within the kingdom, this is precisely what is meant by the imperial edict’s statement that "peace will be brought about through inaction. Thus, when Tancheng arrived in Zhao, the two Shi rulers were reduced in their violence;

when the light emanated from the Spirit Tower, Fu Jian diminished his cruelty. That the divine Way assists in transformation is clearly visible. As for Mou’s request for regulations, it cannot be said to be entirely wrong;
however, the harm and decay suffered by both the clergy and the laity stem fundamentally from those monks and nuns who lack proper conduct. Nevertheless...

It is difficult to distinguish between the sincere and the hypocritical, and it is not easy to decide what to accept or reject. As for works of earth and wood, although they may seem wasteful, one must continue to cultivate merit and repay kindness;
these activities cannot be abruptly severed. Your servant has recently deliberated on whether to proceed or withdraw, yet remained uneasy.

Today, having personally received Your Majesty’s gracious edict, I am truly filled with joy and gratitude. Yang Xuanbao stepped forward and said: "This discourse concerns the study of Heaven and Man; it is not something within the humble capacity of this servant."

I, Lou, ought to be permitted to hear this. I fear that when Qin and Chu discuss the arts of strengthening their armies, or when Sun Tzu and Wu Qi exhaust their schemes for annexation, they will find nothing of value here.
The Emperor said, "This is not the tool of the Warring States; it is truly as you say. Shangzhi said:
"Indeed, when the rites honor the recluses, the warrior spirit subsides; when benevolence and virtue are esteemed, the martial air vanishes.
If one were to take Sun Wu as one's model and aspire to conquest and annexation, then one would find nothing to value in the Way of Yao and Shun—how much less so in the teachings of Śākyamuni!
The Emperor was pleased and said to Shangzhi, "The Buddhist community having you is like the school of Confucius having Ji Lu."
From then on, the Emperor applied his mind to the Buddhist scriptures and grew increasingly reverent toward the profound transformation.

When Yan Yanzhi composed the *Lishi lun* (Treatise on the Separation of Consciousness) and the *Lunjian* (Examination of Treatises), he commanded Dharma Master Huiyan to distinguish between their similarities and differences. They debated back and forth throughout the entire day, whereupon the Emperor laughed and said, "You gentlemen are truly not to be shamed by [the likes of] Zhi Dun and Xu Xun."
In that year, Xie Lingyun was executed by the "market" (public execution) for plotting rebellion. Initially, Lingyun was equal in fame to Yan Yanzhi;
his prose was more expansive, brilliant, and inspired than Yanzhi’s, though he did not reach the latter's depth.

He inherited the title of Marquis of Kangle and resided in Kuaiji, where he indulged in unrestrained pleasure with the recluses Wang Hongzhi and Kong Chunzhi. The Prefect, Meng Yi, [was a devout Buddhist].
The Buddha was earnest and sincere, yet he was held in low esteem by Lingyun. He once said to Huiyi, "To attain the Way requires the accumulation of wisdom;
you, my elder, shall be reborn in heaven before Lingyun, but you will certainly become a Buddha after him. Huiyi harbored a deep resentment over these words.

When Huiyi entered the imperial court, [Lingyun] repeatedly suppressed him, preventing him from being summoned for service. Later, Huiyi served as the Interior Historian of Linchuan, where he lived a life of leisure and wandering in the district.
His conduct was unlawful, and he was denounced by the authorities. The Minister of Education dispatched Zheng Wangsheng, an official of Suizhou, to arrest Lingyun.
Lingyun immediately raised troops and fled in rebellion; having thus harbored treasonous intentions, he was pursued and captured by Wangsheng and sent to the Court of Judicial Review.

The Emperor, appreciating his talent, commuted his death sentence to exile in Guangzhou. Subsequently, he rebelled again and was ordered by imperial decree to be executed in the marketplace. He died at the age of forty-nine.
In the thirteenth year, the Emperor visited the Qu-shui (Flowing Water) Park. The high officials and ministers all assembled there, and the Emperor commanded them to compose poems.

The śramaṇa Huiguan’s poem was completed first and presented to him; its lines possessed a marvelous and elegant resonance. The Emperor was delighted and showed it to the hundred officials, all of whom marveled at his talent.
Huiguan, together with Huiyan, Xie Lingyun, and others, meticulously edited the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, significantly revising and augmenting its phrasing.
In a dream, he was rebuked by a divine being who said, "How dare you, with your ordinary sentiments, presume to treat the sacred scriptures with such irreverence?
Guǎn and the others were struck with fear and ceased their actions. At that time, Huìlín gained favor with the Emperor due to his talent and learning;

he participated in the decision-making of state affairs and was popularly known as the "Black-Robed Chancellor. His gate was so crowded with carriages and canopies that there was often no room for a foot to pass. Lín became arrogant and overbearing; when he saw [Guǎn],...

The high officials were capable of nothing more than exchanging pleasantries. [Wang] Chengzhi authored the *Baihei lun* (Treatise on White and Black), in which he slandered the Buddha and rebelled against the teachings. As a result, he experienced immediate retribution:
his flesh and skin rotted away, and he died after several years.
The treatise states: Worldly wisdom and eloquence are what people admire and cherish as marks of genius and spirit.

Yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, considers these among the eight difficulties (aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ). Why is this? Lingyun relied on his talent to act with arrogance toward the world and was executed for plotting rebellion.
Huilin disfigured his appearance by donning the saṃghāṭī robe of a monk, yet he exhaustively involved himself in court politics. Having thus betrayed the Teaching, they fell into calamity.
Furthermore, they proceeded to disparage the Buddha and consequently suffered the retribution of death. Alas! It is clear that the perils of worldly wisdom are indeed formidable.
Consider the noble and sublime conduct of the two masters, Yan and [Dao]an; yet they recklessly used ordinary sentiments to lightly judge the sacred scriptures.
Had they not encountered a divine person who rebuked them, it is likely that the perils of worldly wisdom would have been almost unavoidable.

How magnificent are the words of the responses and compositions by Ba Mo and Shang Zhi! They may truly be called an exhaustive exploration of the grand principles and a thorough realization of the subtlest details—a universal discourse for all under heaven.
In that year, Emperor Wen issued an edict seeking śramaṇas capable of expounding the meaning of Master Daosheng’s doctrine of sudden enlightenment.
The Provincial Governor, Yu Dengzhi, recommended Shi Fayuan. He was summoned for an audience and questioned; Fayuan presented his arguments with detailed clarity. He Shangzhi sighed and said:

"I had thought that with the passing of Master Daosheng, the subtle words [of the Dharma] would be forever lost. Now, once again, I hear discourse on that which transcends the phenomenal world—this is truly what is called..."
Heaven had not yet destroyed these cultural arts. Before long, Tianbao Temple was completed, and by imperial decree, Huai was appointed to preside over it.

When Wang Jingwen arrived, he encountered him while he was lecturing. Jingwen sighed in admiration, saying: "Everything he cites is unheard of; everything he points to transcends the ordinary mind. He is truly a dragon among the Dharma.
When Xianggong Temple was completed, Huai was moved there again to reside. The Emperor visited in person to listen to the Dharma. At that time, because...
This was for his honor.

In the sixteenth year, the Dharma Master Lingche passed away. Lingche had shaved his head under Master Huiyuan; because he was profoundly versed in the sutras, śāstras, and literature, he enjoyed great renown in the world.
He once traveled to the south of Mount Kuang, where he leaned against a withered pine tree and let out a long, resonant whistle as the valley wind [blew].

When Huiyuan reached Mount Lu, the mountain birds sang in harmony; he felt a sense of transcendence and self-attainment. Upon his return, Sengche asked him, "The monastic precepts prohibit pipes and strings.
Is it permissible to sing or chant? Huiyuan replied, "To let external objects stir one's thoughts is to disturb the emotions and obstruct the Way; such things ought not to be done.
From this point on, Sengche abandoned his brush and inkstone and lectured upon the Great Dharma, becoming a master revered by his disciples.

In that year, Wei Crown Prince Huang was slandered, and Emperor Taizu became suspicious of him. Huang sought the mercy of the śramaṇa Xuangao, who performed the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* repentance ritual for him.
Emperor Taizu then dreamed that his deceased ancestor reproached him, saying, "You ought not to suspect the Crown Prince on account of slander.
Upon waking, he told the dream to his ministers; all the officials declared that the Crown Prince was without fault, and they treated him accordingly.
It was as before. At that time, Cui Hao feared that the Crown Prince would bring harm to him. He said to Emperor Taizu: "The Crown Prince indeed had a plot previously;
he allied with Xuangao and used his arts to bring about the death of the late Emperor, surely for the sake of Your Majesty.

If he is not executed early, he will certainly cause great disaster. Emperor Taizu was greatly enraged. He arrested Xuangao and Huichong and put them to death. Xuangao’s disciple, Xuangao... [text fragment]

When Xuanchang was residing at Yunzhong, he heard that Daogao had been killed. He galloped six hundred li in a single day to the gates of the Wei court, where he wept and said, "The Dharma Master possessed supernatural powers;
surely he shall rise for my sake. Thereupon, Daogao opened his eyes and said, "The Great Dharma manifests through transformation, flourishing or declining according to conditions.

While flourishing and decline pertain to its outward traces, the underlying principle remains eternally constant. I only regret that you all do not practice as I did. This was said solely to Xuanchang.

He crossed southward to the river. "After you have passed away, the Dharma shall surely flourish again. Cultivate your minds well so that you do not feel regret later. Having finished speaking, he immediately vanished.
The śramaṇa Fajin cried out, "The Sage has departed from this world; what use is there for me to live? At that very sound, he saw Senggaohao appear amidst the clouds.
Fajin prostrated himself and begged for deliverance. Gaohao said, "I do not forget anyone; how could I possibly abandon you alone?"
He asked, "Where were you and Master Chong born together? Daoxiao replied, "I went to the evil realms to rescue and protect sentient beings, while Master Chong has already returned to An-yang.
Having finished speaking, he vanished from sight.
In the twenty-second year, the Wei ruler and Cui Hao both placed great trust in Kou Qianzhi and followed his Way. Hao particularly disliked Buddhism;
he frequently spoke to the Wei ruler, claiming that the Buddhist teachings were empty and exaggerated, a source of waste and harm to the world, and that they should be completely eliminated.
When the Wei ruler’s army reached Chang’an following the defeat of Gai Wu, he entered a Buddhist temple, where the śramaṇas drank from the vessels of the attending officials.
Wine. He entered the monk’s quarters and saw a great quantity of weapons. Upon coming out, he informed the Wei ruler. The ruler said in anger, "This is not what a śramaṇa should possess;
he must have conspired with Gai Wu to incite a rebellion. He ordered the officials to arrest and execute all the monks in the monastery.
When they inventoried the property, they found a large amount of brewing equipment as well as goods entrusted by the governors and magistrates of the provinces and prefectures.

The number reached ten thousand. He also constructed underground chambers to hide women. Daohao then advised the Emperor that he should execute all the śramaṇas of the empire and destroy all scriptures and images.
The Emperor followed his counsel. Kou Qianzhi earnestly remonstrated, deeming it improper, but Daohao would not listen.

First, execute all the śramaṇas in Chang’an and burn their scriptures and images. Furthermore, issue an edict to the subordinate offices throughout the four directions, commanding them to follow the laws of Chang’an exactly.

The imperial decree stated: "In the past, the decadent rulers of the Later Han dynasty believed in and were deluded by heterodox and false teachings, thereby throwing the natural order of Heaven into chaos.
From antiquity until now, nothing like this has ever occurred within the Nine Provinces—a boastful and grandiose claim that does not accord with human nature. In these degenerate times..."

Throughout the world, none were not deluded by this. Consequently, governance and transformation failed to take root, rites and righteousness fell into utter ruin, and the lands within the nine circuits were reduced to desolate ruins.
I, the Emperor, succeeding to the heavenly mandate, desire to eliminate the false and establish the true, restoring the governance of the ages of Fuxi and Nonghuo.
All else shall be swept away and its traces obliterated. From this day forward, should anyone dare to serve the spirits of the Hu or create their images, [they shall be punished].
Those who possess clay or bronze images shall be executed by the extermination of their entire clans. The authorities shall proclaim this to the generals of the garrisons and the regional inspectors:
all Buddhist statues and foreign scriptures are to be smashed and burned; no śramaṇas, whether old or young, are to be spared, but all shall be buried alive. Great!

The Prince had long been devoted to the Buddha-dharma. Although he repeatedly remonstrated [with the Emperor], his advice was not heeded. He then deliberately delayed the proclamation of the imperial edict so that those far and near might hear of it in advance and each could devise a plan for themselves.
Consequently, many śramaṇas managed to escape and hide, thereby avoiding capture, and they collected and preserved the scriptures and images.
However, as for the stūpas and temples located within the borders of Wei, not a single one remained.
In the twenty-seventh year, Emperor Taiwu of the Wei personally led the vanguard with an army said to number one million to destroy the Song.

Emperor Wen issued an edict dispatching General of National Assistance Xiao Bin and others to resist them. When the army reached Kaoyao, the vanguard commander Wang Xuemo was unskilled in managing his troops;
the soldiers were cowed and retreated, fleeing even before the battle had begun. Xiao Bin, enraged, bound Xuemo within his tent.
He was about to be executed. Xuánmó dreamed that someone told him, "If you recite the name of Avalokiteśvara one thousand times, you will be spared. Upon waking, he began to recite it;

having reached the thousandth repetition, he did not cease even as he approached the blade. Just then, Wáng Qìngzhī urgently remonstrated, saying, "The Wei barbarians' power shakes the world, and they command millions of drawn bows.
How could Xuánmó possibly withstand them? To execute him before his orders have even been presented would be a grave error."

To appoint a deputy commander for oneself would be to weaken one's own position; this was not a sound strategy. Tanbin realized this and immediately granted him his life. Xuannu continued to lead the troops as before. (This is recorded in the *Nanshi*).
In that year, the Wei Minister of Education Cui Hao relied heavily on his own talent and strategy, as well as the favor he enjoyed from the Wei sovereign.
He assumed exclusive control over the authority of the court. The Wei ruler appointed Hao as Supervisor of the Secretariat.

One of his partisans, Min Zhan, urged Hao to engrave the national history he had compiled onto stone to manifest his upright penmanship. Hao followed this advice; consequently, the stones were engraved and erected at the suburban altar.
The accounts of the Wei’s past affairs were all detailed and factual. Those who passed by and saw them all spoke of it, saying that among the Northern people there was...

They were not resentful or angry, but instead praised Hao to the Emperor, claiming he was publicly exposing the evils of the state. The Emperor was greatly incensed and ordered the relevant officials to investigate Hao’s crimes.
Hao was bewildered and unable to respond; consequently, Hao and one hundred and twenty of his subordinates were executed, and all were subjected to the extermination of their five clans.
Previously, Hao had already encouraged Emperor Taowu to eradicate the followers of Śākyamuni and destroy the scriptures and images.

[The statue] was discarded. Whenever Hao encountered discarded images while traveling, he would invariably stop his carriage and submerge them in water. When his clan was executed, no one came forward to collect his corpse.

Furthermore, because he had accumulated such resentment among the people, they vied with one another to drown his body until it had completely decomposed before they finally desisted. (Seen in the *Beishi*).
The Treatise says: The lack of wisdom in Cui Hao has been discussed in detail by Sima Guang.

Generally speaking, when the Tuoba clan first arose from the Sha-se region, before they had moved their capital, their nature was cruel and violent; they regarded killing people as if consuming sweet food and drink.
Such was their habitual custom. Initially, when Crown Prince Huang was slandered, several monks including Sengxuan were executed. To a considerable extent...
To see their innocence and yet, upon the dissolution of the Śākya śramaṇas, to execute and bury them alive—how can one adequately describe such cruelty?

Although this was due to the savage nature of the barbarians, it was also because when Cui Hao held power, he applied the law in such a manner. Subsequently, Hao was slandered and his crimes were exposed;
they were largely the result of errors made while compiling the history. Had this occurred in the Tang era, he would have been no more than demoted from office.
□Rong was merely exiled to a remote frontier. Even had he been executed, it would have affected no more than a single individual.
Yet, you proceeded to exterminate his entire five-clan lineage. Why was this?
It is because when one inflicts harm upon others without cause, the retribution returned to oneself will surely be severe. This is the constant law of Heaven that never changes. As for me...
The scriptures and images of Śākyamuni were indeed a source of harm to Hao Yong. Yet every time Hao saw them, he would invariably stop his carriage and drown them.
Before Hao had even turned his heel, the corpse was likewise drowned by someone else, until it reached a state of complete putrefaction and disintegration.
Alas! How Hao dares to disregard the words of the Sage and deceive Heaven to such an extent!
Therefore, Heaven has again brought swift retribution upon him to serve as a warning to the world of men. Should one not be cautious? Should one not be cautious?
In the twenty-eighth year, during the New Year’s assembly at the Wei court, the śramaṇa Tanshi arrived at the palace gate shaking his monk’s staff.
The officials informed Emperor Taowu, who said, “Execute him immediately! When the blade fell upon him, he was not wounded. They reported this again as he approached the palace steps;

Taowu grew enraged, drew his sword from his girdle, and struck him himself, yet it could not wound him. The sword left only a slight mark like a thread. He ordered the man arrested and cast into a tiger cage.

In the midst of this, the tigers were all cowed with fear and did not dare to blink. His attendants requested that he test them with the Heavenly Master (Laozi). The tiger immediately let out a roar. Emperor Taiwu was greatly alarmed;

he invited Shi to ascend the hall, where he prostrated twice and apologized in repentance. The *Folaozhi* (Record of Buddhism and Daoism) in the *Wei Shu* states: "The śramaṇa Huishi was the son of the Zhang family of Qinghe.
Having first heard that Kumārajīva was translating scriptures, he went to Chang’an to see him and studied under him."
Shi Shi practiced dhyāna-concentration north of the White Canal. During the day he entered the city to listen to lectures; at night he withdrew to a secluded place in the Three Prefectures (Sanfu).
Those who understood him held him in high esteem. When Emperor Wu destroyed the Yao clan, he left his son Yizhen to garrison Chang’an.
When Yizhen was defeated by Helian Chujiu, Shi Shi was the first to have his body struck by blades yet remain unhurt. Enraged, Chujiu summoned Shi Shi before him and [took] what he wore...
He struck himself with his precious sword, yet it could not harm him; he then prostrated himself in fear and apologized. Later, during the Wei dynasty, he transformed and guided many.

From the time he first practiced meditative concentration until his death, more than fifty years passed without him ever lying down to sleep. He walked barefoot, yet his feet were never stained by the mud.

He became increasingly radiant and white; the world called him the "White-footed Arhat" (Bai-zu A-lian). Emperor Taiwu treated him with profound reverence. From the beginning, he knew the time of his end.
Purifying himself through fasting, he sat upright; as his disciples filled the space around him, he passed away in serene stillness. His body lay for ten days without change in complexion.

More than ten years later, when his remains were exhumed for reburial, his features remained as if he were still alive. The entire world marveled at this wonder. On the day of his burial, those who escorted him...
More than ten thousand people wailed for him in profound grief. Gao Yun, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, composed a biography to extol his virtue.
In the twenty-ninth year, Emperor Taizu of the Wei dynasty passed away. Prince Wu ascended the throne but died shortly thereafter.
Emperor Wencheng, the High Ancestor, then took the throne; he was the grandson of Emperor Taizu. The ministers urged the restoration of the Buddhist faith, and an edict was issued stating:

Now, those who act as emperors and kings must reverently serve the enlightened spirits and manifest the Way of benevolence. If one can bestow kindness upon the living and provide relief and benefit to the various classes of beings, their heroic deeds will be recorded and their legacy celebrated, even if they lived in antiquity.
For this reason, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* rejoices in rites that clarify and honor [the divine], and the *Canon of Sacrifices* records the lineages of those who have bestowed merit.
How much more so for the Buddha’s teaching, wherein the Tathāgata’s merit has rescued the great trichiliocosm and his grace flows forth.
Regarding the realm of sensory objects, those who seek the nature of birth and death praise its profound insight; those who examine its textual meanings value it as a marvelous gateway.

It assists the prohibitions and laws of royal governance and augments the virtuous nature of benevolence and wisdom. It repels the various heterodoxies and expounds upon perfect enlightenment; thus, from previous dynasties until now, there has been none who did not hold it in high esteem.
Furthermore, it has been that which our nation’s imperial house has always revered and served. This was [the case under] Emperor Taizu Wudi and Emperor Shizu Taizu Wuhuang.
The Emperor has opened up the remote frontiers and his virtuous bounty has spread afar.
Śramaṇas and Daoists of pure conduct and sincere integrity—such as those like Huishi—have reached every distant place. Their mutual influence through moral integrity is as vast as a forest.

Yet, how could the depths of mountains and seas avoid harboring the wicked and licentious who find pretext for their presence within monasteries and temples? Thus, there have arisen factions of the malevolent; for this reason, the Emperor first...

In the past, when the Emperor Zhao pressed for a temporary halt to executions of those who had committed crimes, the relevant authorities misunderstood his intent and prohibited [the practice] altogether.
Emperor Jingmu often lamented this matter; however, as the state was beset by many affairs of war, he had not yet been able to restore it.

I, the Emperor, having inherited the great legacy and presiding over the myriad realms, intend to fulfill the former will in order to promote this Way. Now, it is decreed that in all places where people reside in various provinces and commanderies, each...

He granted permission for the construction of one Buddhist monastery. Those who delighted in the Dharma and wished to become śramaṇas, whose character and conduct were naturally sincere and well-known to their neighbors, were permitted to leave the household life. Thereupon, throughout the realm, people followed this wind of change;

before the morning had even passed, the monasteries and temples that had previously been destroyed, along with their scriptures and images, were all restored and repaired. Among them was a śramaṇa named Shi Xian, of the royal lineage of Kaśmīra.

He traveled east to Liangcheng and reached Wei, where he encountered the suspension of monastic ordinations. Although he was temporarily deprived of his medical arts, he maintained the Way without wavering.
On the day ordinations were resumed, he immediately became a śramaṇa. Five of his peers had their heads shaved by Emperor Gaozong in person. He then appointed Sengxian as the Sanghasthavira.
The following year, an imperial decree was issued to cast a statue of Śākyamuni at the Five-Tiered Great Temple for the five emperors beginning with Taizu.
There were five statues, each one zhang and six chi in height, made from twenty-five thousand jin of red gold (as recorded in the "Buddhism and Daoism" chapter of the *Wei Shu*).

The treatise states: The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) of the Liang dynasty records the deeds of Tanshi, which differ significantly from the account in the "Buddhism and Daoism" chapter (*Folao zhi*) of the *Wei shu*.
Here, I have combined both accounts and recorded them together. Generally speaking, Tanshi, Xuangao, and Huichong all attained sanctity through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Observing their guidance of the common people—transcending death and entering life with unimpeded ease—it is clear that this was no mere coincidence.
Was this not the manifestation of the power of vows by the ranks of sages and worthies? Emperor Gaozong eloquently recounted the will of Crown Prince Huang, who was unjustly imprisoned and died;
he personally witnessed how Cui Hao’s madness and transgressions led swiftly to retribution. He issued an edict to restore the Buddhist teachings and caused the civil laws to shine forth.
This truly accords with the manifest spirits—how magnificent! It may be called the deed of a wise monarch, perfectly suited to the occasion.
By manifesting the Way of Benevolence according to the needs of the times, did he not bring about the tireless diligence of all under heaven?
In the first year of the Xiaojian era, when Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty raised troops to execute the "Great Tyrant" (the rebel), Guṇabhadra fled into the common people.
Subsequently, when Wang Xuemu’s army reached Liangshan, Emperor Xiaowu ordered that anyone in the ranks who captured Guṇabhadra should be rewarded with a fast courier.
He galloped to the palace and soon found him; he was sent to Jinling for an audience. The Emperor said, "I have long yearned for your virtue, and only now do we finally meet.

Having endured such hardships to return here, do you harbor any regrets? He replied, "I have no regrets; I only think that through past affinities, I have encountered this and thus brought my practice to fruition.
The Emperor comforted him and jokingly asked, "Do you still think of Prince Qiao? He replied, "The ancients did not forget [their former lords]."

"A single meal! How could I dare so quickly forget that the King fed me for ten years? Now I shall request from Your Majesty to serve as the abbot of the King’s temple to cultivate merit for the afterlife.
The Emperor looked upon him with a sorrowful expression and changed countenance. When Zhongxing Temple was completed, an imperial decree ordered him to reside there as its head.

The Emperor held a banquet at the Eastern Palace where the high officials were all assembled; he summoned Guṇabhadra, who appeared white-haired, pure, and emaciated. Emperor Xiaowu saw him from afar and said to Xie [Luan]:...
Zhuang said, "Mahāyāna possesses ready wit and eloquence; we should test him, for he will surely be able to awaken the people's understanding.
Bodhidharma ascended the steps, and the Emperor said, "Mahāyāna has not come in vain from afar. There is only one thing remaining.

He immediately replied, "This poor monk has eaten the food of the Sage Dynasty for twenty years; your benevolence and virtue have been profound. What I lack now is but death. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
They shifted their seats to urge him forward, and the entire assembly leaned in with rapt attention.
In the second year [of the reign], Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict appointing the śramaṇa Daoyou as the presiding Dharma Master of Xin’an Temple.

Initially, Emperor Wen had asked Huiguan which of them possessed the true understanding of the principle of sudden enlightenment; Huiguan replied that it was Daoyou. By imperial decree, he was summoned into the inner palace, where he was received with great honor.
He gathered renowned scholars; his expositions were systematic and orderly, and his elucidation of the Dharma and its meaning was brilliant. Those who heard him attained awakening.

Whenever there were those who raised challenges or objections, Huigou would invariably refute them with skillful explanations. The Emperor patted his thigh in praise, saying, "Excellent. By this time, he served as the Preceptor of the Dharma for all under heaven, fully meeting the high expectations of the age (like the jade discovered by Bian He).
The Dharma Master Bao Liang resided at Zhongxing Temple. Yuan Can, the Secretariat Director, beheld him and marveled at his extraordinary nature.

He sent a letter to Li’s master, Daoming, which stated in brief: "Recently, I have observed that Master Liang is no ordinary man. Day after day I hear what I have never heard before, and I am unaware that the year is drawing to a close.
Yet, when pearls are born in Hepu, people from Wei take them to illuminate their carriages; when jade is found in Handan, those from Qin [seek it out]."
People requested that he adorn the state; the treasures of the world cannot be monopolized by oneself—they must be shared with others.

From this time on, Sengliang’s reputation grew increasingly weighty. In his later years, he resided at Lingwei Monastery, where his lecture hall was preeminent in the capital. He had more than three thousand disciples.

Sengliang’s brilliant spirit was ever more imposing, and the sharpness of his rhetoric was swift and soaring. Whenever a debater was obstructed by a principle, Sengliang would resolve it; none [could withstand him].

It was not until the ninth month of the sixth year of the Daming era that the Right Counselor submitted this memorial: "Your servant has heard that profound seclusion and solemn residence are not intended merely for loftiness;
prostration and kneeling are not simply for the sake of reverence. Rather, they are meant to illuminate the four quarters and establish order within the six realms. Therefore, although..."

The various branches of Confucianism and Legalism, as well as the different streams of the Mo school, do not differ in their principles regarding the veneration of parents and the strict observance of superiors;

however, only the Buddhist teaching is uniquely exceptional in this regard. It transgresses and destroys ritual propriety, and its practitioners dwell in a state of arrogance toward their honored kin, thereby losing the subtle traces of adapting to local conditions.
I am captivated by the profound beauty of this transformation. Your servant has heard that the Buddha disciplines himself through humility and frugality, and takes loyalty and obedience as his path.

The Bhikṣu Puṇyālaṅkara would bow to anyone he encountered; the Great Being Maudgalyāyana paid homage when meeting those of seniority. How could one who bends his knee before the fourfold assembly fail to offer ritual respect to his two parents?
Or how could one who prostrates himself before monks of advanced seniority fail to lay his head at the feet of the Ten-Thousand-Wagons [the Emperor]? Thus, during the Xiankang era...
