The original proposal was made at the beginning of the Yuanxing era and restated thereafter; yet the matter was thwarted by partisan factions, and the Way was truncated by petty divisions.

Now, as the vast source is thoroughly cleansed from afar, the myriad streams look up to it as their mirror; the Nine Immortals present their treasures, and the hundred deities stand alert in their offices.

Yet within the capital precincts there remain subjects who do not acknowledge their sovereign, and among those seated at court are guests who refuse to observe the proper rites. I fear this is not the way to clarify and unify social customs.

The regulations provide detailed instructions on exemplary standards. Your servants have deliberated and propose that when śramaṇas are received in audience, they should all manifest an appearance of utmost reverence.
If they follow their own original customs, the court’s prestige will remain orderly, and the governance of the realm will extend far and wide. This was decreed as acceptable.
Upon hearing this, the Dharma Master Sengyuan sighed and said, "I shaved my head to become a śramaṇa; I originally left home to seek the Way.
What concern is this of emperors? That very day, he brushed off his robes and returned to the mountain valleys.
In that year, Zhu Lingqi of Wu Commandery returned from Goryeo. His ship was driven by the wind to an island where there was a mountain;
following his intuition, he climbed it for over ten li and heard the sound of midday chanting, knowing thereby that there was a monastery. The monastery was constructed of the seven precious gems.
Lingqi saw that the several monks were all stone statues. As he was about to turn back, someone called out to him. Lingqi prostrated himself twice and received food;
the flavor of the food was fragrant and exquisite, unlike anything found in the mundane world. Someone said, "This place is more than twenty thousand *li* from Jinling.
Have you ever known the Dharma Master Beidu? Lingqi replied, "I know him. The person pointed to a bag, a bottle, and a monk’s staff against the north wall and said: [End of provided text]
"It is merely his almsbowl. He then took it to give to you along with this letter, and further presented him with a green bamboo staff, saying, "Give this to Bei-du as soon as you see him.
He ordered a novice monk to escort them to the ship. The novice monk, Lingqi, placed the bamboo staff before him in the water, and they arrived at Shitou on the Huai River in three days.
Thereupon, the bamboo staff was lost. After a short while, Bei-du arrived and recovered it.
Fotu laughed loudly and said, "I have not seen this bowl for four thousand years. He tossed it into the clouds, caught it again, and departed.
Fotu frequently manifested his passing into nirvana, yet subsequently returned to wander in the world.

Later, he arrived at the home of Qi Xie, where he was joined by the three great adepts Lü Daohui, Du Tianqi, and Shuiqiu Xi. Qi Xie was greatly astonished and immediately prostrated himself twice before Fotu.
He said, "This year will be a time of great calamity; do not forget to cultivate meritorious deeds. A man of the Way named Fayi possesses high virtue; you may rely upon him to avert disaster.
Suddenly, a monk called out from above the lintel, "Cross over! Looking up, [the master] saw him and he immediately departed, never to be seen again.
In the second year of the Taishi era, the Great Being Baozhi traveled between Mount Wan and the Jian River;

he went with shaven head and bare feet, wearing a brocade robe, and the common people called him Gong Zhi. His face was square and translucent like a mirror, and his hands and feet were all marked with black claws.

Originally, the wife of a man surnamed Zhu from Dongyang in Jinling heard the crying of a child within an eagle’s nest on the day of Shangsi. She climbed the tree, retrieved it, and raised it as her own son.
At the age of seven, he entered the monastic life under the śramaṇa Sengjian of Mount Zhong, where he specialized in the practice of dhyāna and contemplation.

It was at this point that his miraculous manifestations became evident; he would hang scissors, a ruler, and a whisk upon the tip of his staff and carry them as he traveled. Thus it is recorded in the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*.
The children of the village clamored and pursued him. Sometimes he would beg for a little wine; at other times, he would go without food for several days.
Once, when he encountered someone eating minced fish, he asked for some. The eater shared some with him, but with a sense of disdain, he spat it into the water.
It all became live fish. From time to time he would compose poems; at first they seemed unintelligible, but later they were all proven true.

At that time, there was a man named Shao Shi who was originally from the country of Kangju. He had large lips and ugly eyes, appearing as though he were mad; children would often treat him with contempt.
From time to time, he would join wine-drinkers and enter taverns to drink to excess. Later, he became a śramaṇa and was known as Master Shi. He was on the closest terms with [Seng]zhi.

Whether entering or leaving, walking or practicing meditation, they did not inquire whether it was night or day. Whenever Shi wished to do so, he would depart to travel through the various regions of Yizhou.
In the county, he was known for his witty and humorous speech, which could provoke laughter in others; through this, he would then exhort them toward goodness, and every household delighted in him.

As he was about to die, he said to the śramaṇa Fajin, "I wish to have my remains exposed beneath a pine tree; however, my two feet must be shod with sandals. Fajin agreed. Shortly thereafter, he passed away.
They carried his corpse out to expose it, but when they went to look the following day, it had vanished. A short while later, someone came from...

A person from Dan County came and said, "Yesterday I saw Master Shuo walking through the marketplace wearing only a single shoe. He said, 'Tell Master Jin for me that I have been deceived by this child;
he gave me only one shoe. Master Jin was startled and questioned the novice, who replied, 'When we were carrying the corpse, one shoe fell off.
We walked so hurriedly that I did not have time to tie it on.'"
In the third year, Emperor Ming issued an edict appointing Sengjin as the Sangzheng (Director of Monks) for the realm. He resided at Linggen Monastery.

The Emperor harbored many taboos and would invariably execute anyone who offended them; yet Sengjin constantly offered corrective counsel and remonstrance, and it was thanks to him that many were spared from death.

At that time, the masters of the capital had established three schools regarding the doctrine of the Two Truths, each with differing tenets. Thereupon, Zhou Yong of Ru’nan composed the *Sanzong lun* (Treatise on the Three Schools).

He sought to reconcile these differences; however, fearing censure, he did not dare to transmit them. The Dharma Master Zhilin, who possessed the highest reputation and influence, sent a letter to Tanyong. It read in brief:
"I have humbly heard that the *Sanzong lun* (Treatise on the Three Schools) probes the profound and seeks out the hidden, exhausting the sentiments of all sentient beings;

it broadens and clarifies the path, fulfilling the intent of all Buddhas. This ensures that the lamp of the Dharma shall have manifold benefits that are inexhaustible. Even were it to [fall to] the state..."

"How can the giving of one's city, wife, and children compare to this gift? The transmitter [of the text] believed that the donor (dānapati), fearing the criticism of the assembly, wished to stop midway.

How could he allow himself to be uniquely entangled by the obstacle of doubt and manifest it as an active affliction? When Sengyong received the letter, he was struck with awe and attained realization.
This treatise subsequently circulated in the world. Lin also sent a letter commending it, which stated in brief: "Holding the fly-whisk, you have come for the fourth time..."
For over ten years, I have seen many records of the various schools, yet among these [practitioners], not a single person—whether monk or layperson—has attained it. This caused me great distress.
I never expected that this sound would so unexpectedly enter my ears.
Zhou Yong, whose courtesy name was Bolen, was successively promoted to serve in the palace chambers as a *zhishì*. He enjoyed the profound favor and patronage of Emperor Ming.

The Emperor was quite fond of metaphysical principles (*xuánlǐ*), yet his conduct was often cruel and harsh. Zhou Yong did not dare to offer open remonstrance; instead, he would recite passages from the sutras concerning the causes and conditions of sin and merit. This somewhat dampened the Emperor's ardor.
To the west of Mount Zhong, Zhou Yong established a separate vihāra (monastery), where he would retire whenever he took leave from official duties.
Whenever he gathered with guests and friends, he would sit in an empty chair to converse; his speech flowed like a stream, and those who listened forgot their fatigue.

Whenever he met Zhang Rong, they would engage in profound discourse that would detain them for days without resolution. Pure and poor, with few desires, he maintained a vegetarian diet throughout the year.
Although he had a wife and children, he lived far away in a mountain hermitage. When the Chancellor Wang Jian asked him, "What do you eat in the mountains?
he replied, "Red rice with white salt, green chives with purple dock. Xiao Zixian jokingly asked, "Of all the flavors of vegetarian food, which is best?
Yong replied, "Early spring chives and late autumn kale. Such was his lofty character; he cast off his official cap during the height of his career.
He lived in the mountains until his death at the age of fifty-five.
In the fifth year [of the reign], the Wei envoy Li Daogu came to court. The Emperor, noting that the monk Zhong of Zhongxing Temple possessed eloquence, summoned him to serve as a guest attendant.
As he conversed with Daogu, the sun reached its zenith, yet Zhong had not eaten. Daogu asked, "Why do you not eat?"
Zhong said, "The bequeathed Dharma of the former Buddhas is that one does not eat after midday. Guo said, "Is this not merely the way of the Śrāvakas?
Zhong replied, "For those who should be saved by appearing as a Śrāvaka, he manifests the body of a Śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them. At that time, this was considered a famous rebuttal.
The Treatise says: Formerly, when Zilu’s army was defeated, Shi Qi and Yu Yan struck him with a halberd, severing his cap-ribbons.
Zilu said, "A gentleman dies with his cap intact. He then tied his ribbons together and died. Zilu may be said to have maintained the Way of the Master until death.
Sengzhong wore robes of undyed color and ate from an earthenware bowl, maintaining the tradition of the former Buddhas.
Observing the precepts is also his duty. When receiving guests, he does not eat until midday. Alas!
Zhong’s adherence to the Way places him in the same category as Zhong You; he is truly worthy of esteem.

As for those such as Beidu and Master Bao, they were world-transcending sages and worthies whose traces cannot easily be judged by mere outward appearances. How virtuous was Zhou Yong, who manifested the possession of wife and children.
Yet his traces are entrusted to the clouds and mists, and his name is inscribed upon the tablets of the scholar-officials; yet his principle exhausts the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Examining his conduct in both seclusion and office, he was truly one who possessed the Way (*mārga*). How could one afford to place him as a brother above those of the Xiyang era, or treat him as a junior to the vast and indeterminate?

In the seventh year, Emperor Xianzong of the Wei dynasty was intelligent from an early age, possessed a resolute will, and was stern in his judgments; yet he took a profound interest in the study of Buddhism.

He frequently invited court officials and śramaṇas to discuss profound metaphysical principles. Having a natural distaste for wealth and status, he constantly harbored a desire to transcend the mundane world.

Because his paternal uncle, Prince Zixun of Jingzhao, was grave, refined, benevolent, and virtuous, and had long enjoyed a reputation for excellence, [the Emperor] wished to abdicate the throne to him.

Regarding the imperial throne, he convened the high officials for a grand deliberation. The ministers earnestly petitioned, saying, "If Your Majesty truly intends to renounce worldly affairs, then the Crown Prince should succeed to the legitimate line.
If you were instead to confer it upon a collateral branch, we fear this would not accord with the intention of the former sages.
The Emperor then said, "In establishing the Crown Prince, what is there that prevents the high officials from assisting him? He subsequently abdicated the throne and styled himself...

The Retired Emperor immediately established Luye Monastery within the Northern Garden. To the northwest of the garden, he practiced *dhyāna* meditation for several hundred days alongside several hundred Zen monks.
In the second year of the Yuanhui era, the śramaṇa Tamlan was residing at Mount Chicheng in Shifeng when a man several [feet] tall suddenly appeared.
Zhang called out to Hulan, saying, "You should leave now. Furthermore, strange beasts appeared, manifesting hundreds of anomalies. Hulan sat in meditation as if nothing had happened;
he then prostrated himself twice and said, "You have truly deceived me. My maternal uncle is currently at Mount Weiqing.
I am going to visit him to offer this to the Honored One," whereupon [the apparition] vanished. Three years later, the sound of carriages and cavalry was heard, and a man wearing—
Xi (the head-dress). He addressed him as "Shuqiwang" (King Who Surpasses Others) and requested an audience.

The lady and twenty-three of her sons and daughters were all elegant and refined, like the celestial retinue of the Queen Mother of the West depicted in secular paintings. They all wished to receive the precepts for returning to the faith.

Senglan asked, "Where do you reside? They replied, "On Mount Weiqing in Anle County. Thereupon, Senglan held the incense burner and straightened his demeanor, bestowing the Five Precepts upon each of them.

The section on the precepts concludes. He departed after making an offering of ten thousand coins and two jars of honey. Several dozen disciples of Lan were attending him at his side and witnessed this exchange.
(From the *Liaozai jiaojing bianian tonglun*, Volume Five).
*Comprehensive Annals of the Buddhist Teachings during the Lōngxìng Era*, Scroll Six.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zǔxiù of Shíshì Monastery in Lōngxìng Prefecture.
Qi Dynasty.
In the second year of the Jianyuan era, the High Ancestor had business at Mount Zhongshan and consequently visited the residence of the śramaṇa Sengyuan.
Sengyuan sat upon his couch and declined [the visit], citing his old age and illness as reasons he could not come out to welcome him. The High Ancestor intended to go beneath the couch to see him;

however, his attendants pointed out that the chamber was too narrow to accommodate the carriage and canopy, so the Emperor halted there. He dispatched an envoy to inquire after his health and comfort while he lay ill before departing. Sengyuan—
He dwelt in the mountains for over fifty years. At first he still had food to eat, but later his provisions were no longer sustained.

For more than twenty years he drank from mountain streams. The world looked up to his noble conduct. Upon his death, Emperor Wu sent a letter to the śramaṇa Faxian, saying: "I have learned that Master Yuan has passed away.
During the night, I already knew that Master Yuan had departed to a most excellent place; such excellences are not merely one."
I shall no longer increase my sorrow. Only when I have seen the Dharma Master for a time can I recount the auspicious dream.
I am currently performing meritorious deeds specifically for you; please provide a detailed list of whatever is required.

In the second year of the Yongming era, an imperial decree appointed the śramaṇas Faxian and Xuanchang as the Patriarchs of the Monks throughout the Land. On another occasion, they were assembled before the Emperor;
when addressed by imperial command, they called themselves by name but did not sit, nor did they rise. When the temple monks’ bell was struck, they addressed the Emperor as "this poor monk" (pindao).

Emperor Wu was surprised by this and questioned Wang Jian of the Secretariat. Jian replied: "During the Han and Wei dynasties, the Buddha-dharma had not yet flourished; thus, there are no such precedents in the historical records."
As for this practice, it first flourished during the Song and Wei dynasties. Many śramaṇas styled themselves "the Poor Wayfarer" (píndào) and were permitted to sit among the assembly.

During the Jin dynasty, both Yu Bing and Huan Xuan sought to compel them to do otherwise, yet in the end it could not be enforced. Today they still style themselves "the Poor Wayfarer. The Emperor said:

"The two masters Xiàn and Chàng possessed such spiritual conduct that they still addressed themselves by name. I believe that addressing them by name is what is appropriate. You may establish this as a formal decree."
As a permanent record: Initially, Duke Mu, aspiring to the Dharma, traveled westward. Departing from Ba and Shu, he went through Henan and passed through the kingdom of Rouran to reach Khotan.
He intended to cross the Pamir Mountains, but encountering the suspension of the plank road, he was unable to proceed. There, he obtained a single tooth of the Buddha.

He returned with fifteen grains of śarīra relics, along with Sanskrit manuscripts of sūtras and śāstras. Master Chang investigated the sūtras and vinaya with great precision and was extensively versed in the teachings of the Confucian classics, histories, and the hundred schools of thought.
At a time when the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* had no commentaries, Chang was the first to compose one, providing scholars with a foundation for their studies.
Furthermore, he could extend his hand to emit fragrance and cause water to flow from his palm. His character was lofty and simple, and he propagated the Way.

They rendered meritorious service to the state throughout their lives, and in their later years, they were uniquely permitted to enter the imperial hall in a sedan chair; thus, they were celebrated as the "Two Heroes in Black Robes.
A Zen Master of the Mingjiao school of our own dynasty remarked: "In recent antiquity, eminent monks did not address the Son of Heaven by name. When they received pre-arranged edicts,"
They were called "Master" and "Duke. Sengyuan of Mount Zhong remained seated on his couch and did not rise to welcome the imperial carriage when it reached his gate;

Huayan Huiyuan of Tiger Creek did not leave the mountain despite the Son of Heaven’s visit to Xunyang and his summons. At that time, they were treated with such honor because their virtue was so revered;
thus, the Way of the Sages was revitalized, for their disciples esteemed virtue. When Confucians say they "value virtue," how is this different? It is because [Buddhism] is close to it.
This is the Way. Those who admire the lofty monks of later ages cannot even participate in the rites of a lower official when interacting with ministers and high officials;
their conduct in public and private life does not equal the self-contentment of an ordinary man, let alone the encounter between Huiyuan and the Son of Heaven, or the composure of Sengyuan himself.
Looking toward the flourishing of our Way and the cultivation of us people, can this truly be achieved?
Alas! To preserve the teaching while not requiring the person—how can preserving it possibly be of benefit? Thinking of this, I have never failed to shed tears.
The Discourse says: "The reputation for clarifying the teaching held by the two [monks] Yuan does not diminish the excellence of Confucius, Bo Yi, and Shu Qi; they are truly worthy of emulation."
As for my sighs lamenting the times, they likely arose from being deeply stirred by such circumstances.
Since the Huángyù era, many among our circle have been granted imperial summons; these were merely coincidental opportunities at a particular moment.
Consequently, there were indeed those whose cultivation was inherently deficient, who could not find the proper course in their advancement or withdrawal. Only Yuántōng...

When Master Shoune was serving as the Chancellor of the State Academy (*Taixue*), the administration of the empire was extremely stable and his official duties were mostly at leisure. He longed to engage in conversation with one who possessed the Way.

Shoune was the first to receive this summons, yet the Master’s Way could not be bent. Nevertheless, the imperial mandate could not be flatly disobeyed; thus, he recommended a member of his own school.
The monk Huai-lian went in his stead. When Liàn entered the court, Emperor Ren treated him with the courtesy due to a Dharma friend, and they shared a profound mutual affinity.

Consequently, both the court and the common people were filled with admiration and longing. That Nǜ could thus recognize others and value himself in such a manner shows that our Way was furthered by him.
How magnificent! Alas! Master Neng’s grasp of the essence of the Dharma may serve as a teacher for ten thousand generations; the two Yuans were not enough to be considered many.

The paths of the two masters Xian and Chang were also ultimate, yet their lowering of their aspirations and their adoption of secular names resulted in the loss of the dignified character of the Great Teaching.
As for the two "Jie" (Xuanzang and Daoxuan), their fame is well-established and their merits are worthy of being adopted.
After seven years, the Emperor became enraged that the Great Master Baozhi was deluding the masses; he had him arrested and imprisoned in Jiankang.

On that day, the people of the country all saw the Great Master wandering through the markets and streets. Upon inspection, however, he was still found within the prison. That evening, he said to his attendant:

Outside the gate were two carriages with food; golden bowls filled with rice were inside. "You may take them," [the Master] said. Indeed, it was then that Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince Jingling sent offerings.
Lü Wenxian, the Magistrate of Jiankang, reported this to the Emperor. The Emperor expressed regret and apologized, welcoming [the Master] into the imperial palace.
Shortly thereafter, an imperial decree was issued to clear the inner palace for a banquet with his family. Sengzhi followed protocol and temporarily left with the crowd;
yet, she was still seen walking in the Xianyang Hall, followed by seven bhikṣus. The Emperor was startled and dispatched an official to inquire about her.

The official reported that Huizhi had been out for a long time in the inner palace; when he went to look for him, his body was as if smeared with ink. The Emperor’s reverence and awe toward him increased all the more.
Later, while in Huālín Garden, Huizhi suddenly wore three layers of cloth caps, and it was not known from where he had obtained them.
Not long after, the Emperor passed away, followed in succession by the death of Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince Yuzhang—exactly as had been foretold.
The Prophecy: A śramaṇa named Bǎoliàng of Lingwei Monastery wished to give a patched robe to him, but before he could speak, Sengzhì suddenly arrived, pulled the robe away, and departed.
When Wáng Zhōngxióng asked what position he would attain in office, he did not answer; instead, he simply untied the left-hand cord from his staff and gave it to him.
Zhōngxióng initially did not understand this, but later he indeed rose to the rank of Left Vice-Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuóchén). This was at the end of the Jiànwǔ era.
At dawn, he went out the gate, suddenly drawing up his robes and running past it, saying, "There is the smell of blood upon the gate.

When Emperor Ming was subsequently assassinated, his corpse was indeed carried out through this very gate in an ox-cart to the residence of the eunuch Xu Longju. Blood flowed from the Emperor's neck, staining the threshold of the gate.
Previously, as the Yulin Emperor had frequently harmed members of the imperial clan, the eminent scholar Jiang Bi feared for the safety of Prince Nankang.

He asked Daoshi about his own past lives. Daoshi covered the ashes in the incense burner and showed him, saying, "It is all gone, with nothing remaining. When Xu Ling was a child, his father took him to visit Daoshi.
Daoshi patted him and said, "This is a stone qilin from the heavens. Later, Xu Ling indeed became prominent in the world.
The śramaṇa Jingdu abstained from grain and consumed pine resin. He was capable of lecturing on and reciting the sūtras, dhyāna, and vinaya.

While traveling through the region of Guanghan, he once fell ill while reciting the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*. Having recited half of it, he requested his attendant to take over. He passed away after reading through the entire text.
Those both near and far all saw a precious horse in the sky carrying his coffin away.
The śramaṇa Puheng was fond of dwelling in secluded places to collect and restrain his mind. He was a close friend of the śramaṇa Tao of Shu.
He once entered the *tejo-dhātu-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi), which extended from between his eyebrows down to the *vajra-maṇḍala*.

Within that light, he beheld various forms and images, including the karmic retributions of his previous lives. When he passed away, a servant saw that his [robe] was half-removed, and thus came to believe in him with great conviction.

This was not permitted. He then bent three fingers of his hand. Throughout his life he had been dark-skinned and emaciated, but at the time of his passing, his complexion became white. Those who understood this knew that he had attained the third fruit of the path.

As for the path of the śramaṇa’s Dharma, it was shared by both [Hui]heng and [Hui]si. Once, while in meditative absorption, Dao entered the Inner Court and beheld Maitreya emitting light from his navel that illuminated the three miserable realms.
Inspired by this, he exerted himself with diligence, remaining constantly seated without lying down. At the time of his death, the auspicious omens were beyond compare with those of Heng.
Furthermore, there was a monk named Shi Sengding, who claimed to have attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmin). At that time...

The Abbot of Zhongxing Temple gathered a crowd to investigate the matter thoroughly and ordered him to manifest his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Ding replied, "I fear that doing so would constitute a violation of the precepts.

The Abbot said, "According to the Vinaya, there are four causes and conditions by which one may manifest supernatural powers: first, to sever the net of doubt; second, to destroy false views; third, to eliminate arrogance;
and fourth, to accomplish meritorious virtues. Despite this, Ding was ultimately unable to do so, and he was consequently expelled.
The śramaṇa Huikai traveled to Chang’an. After staying there for some time, he departed to practice dhyāna-concentration in the mountains and valleys.
One night, a headless ghost suddenly appeared before him. Huikai said, "Since you have no head, you are free from the affliction of headaches;

how joyful this must be! The ghost then vanished. It subsequently returned in the form of a bellyless ghost. Huikai said, "Since you have no belly, you are free from the affliction of hunger and thirst; how joyful this must be!"
He hurried to comply. Suddenly, one night, there was snow. Someone knocked at the door seeking lodging; when he lit a candle to look, it was a beautiful woman.
She bowed twice before him and said, "I am a celestial maiden. Because you, Venerable Sir, possess the virtue of the precepts, Heaven has sent me to console you.
Sengwei said, "Since I have seen you, you should depart of your own accord. You are an obstacle to my path to enlightenment. Thereupon, the woman ascended into the air.
He departed. He sang this song: "The River Water may run dry; Mount Sumeru may be toppled. But that Superior Man cannot be moved.
During the Yongming era, Emperor Wu summoned the recluse He Dian to serve as Secretariat Director. Dian declined and did not go. The *Nanshi* states:
"Dian’s family had served the Buddha with great devotion for generations. He maintained a 'square-and-round' friendship with Zhang Rong and Kong Zhigui. [He] invited...
Accompanied by eminent companions and renowned śramaṇas, he composed poetry and engaged in refined discourse, living in leisure and self-contentment.

When the Chancellor Wang Jian wished to pay him a visit, he realized that he could not be seen and desisted. Prince Yi of Yuzhang ordered his carriage to go to [Hui]dian; however, Dian fled away through a rear gate.
Upon hearing this, Prince Ziliang of Jingling remarked, "If even Prince of Yuzhang could not catch up with him by following the dust of his tracks, how could I?"
He intended to retire from worldly affairs at Wangxiu. Later, while residing at Falun Temple, Xiao Ziliang went to visit him.

As he ascended the seat with his headband tied back, Ziliang faced him and was filled with inexhaustible joy. He left behind for Daodian the wine cup of Xi Shuye and the wine ewer of Xu Jingshan before departing.
Daodian had once suffered from a chronic thirst in his youth that did not cease for many years; later, while at Shifo Temple in Wuzhong...
While lecturing on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, he fell asleep in the lecture hall during the day. He dreamed of a śramaṇa with an extraordinary appearance who gave him a handful of something;

he consumed it in his dream and was immediately cured. At that time, it was considered a response to his pure virtue. Later, when Cui Huījǐng rebelled and besieged the palace city, [he remained there].

Huijing had long been fond of Buddhism and admired Sengqian. Sengqian refused him, not permitting their association. When Huijing now summoned him by force, Sengqian tore his skirt to make trousers and went to attend the lecture on the sutras;
he did not concern himself with military affairs. When Huijing was defeated, Emperor Donghun became enraged at Sengqian and intended to execute him.
The minister Xiao Chang remonstrated, saying: "Sengqian previously did not entice the rebel; that they lectured together cannot be easily underestimated. For this reason [he was spared].

He said, "If you speak of this, you shall surely receive a fief. Emperor Donghun accepted his words and desisted. Xiao Dian’s younger brother, Xiao Yin, was a man of broad learning with a great reputation.
He once entered Zhongshan Dinglin Temple to study the Buddhist scriptures (neidian), mastering them all. During the Jianwu era, he was appointed Secretary of the Palace Secretariat (Zhongshuling).
Hearing that Xie Fei had resigned from his post as Governor of Wuxing and would not return, Yin feared he might be left behind; he immediately submitted a memorial to resign from his office.
He did not wait for a reply. Emperor Ming was enraged; though he pursued him, he could not catch up. An imperial edict was issued granting him permission to leave.

Zhiyin, noting that Kuaiji was full of numinous wonders, went there to travel. He resided at Yunmen Temple on Mount Ruoye. Since he had retired together with his elder brother, they were then known as Dadian (the Great Mountain) and Yin (the Small Mountain).
Subsequently, he moved his residence to Mount Qinwang, where he established a lecture hall; the site was already formed by the surrounding forest. Thereupon, Yuan [assisted him].
Yan constructed a separate small pavilion on an island and took up residence within it; he personally opened and closed the door, allowing no servants to enter.
His lofty reputation surpassed that of the entire world. Previously, Huiyin had been extravagant regarding flavors, requiring his meals to fill a square zhang.

At this time, Zhou Yong of Runan sent him a letter urging him to eat vegetarian food, saying: "Among great transformations, none exceeds that of life and death; among things most precious to life," [none exceeds food].
Nothing exceeds one's own life and nature. Life and nature are of the utmost urgency for that [other world], whereas the flavors within me may be postponed.
It would be fortunate if it could be said that the principle of the three periods of existence is false.

However, if this Way is indeed true and the receiving of form does not cease, such that going and coming through birth and death are constant affairs, then the bitterness of heartache will surely reach you as well, O Elder, regarding the taste of blood.
Although one may not personally practice such things, even regarding the morning wild geese and the night carp, how could one fail to take precautions at the butcher’s door?

When wealth and possessions have passed through the hands of thieves, they are still rejected by the upright; when the nature of life is once opened to the golden blade, how could it ever be tolerated by a compassionate heart?
Though the zhouyu stag is hungry, it will not eat grass that has not died naturally. Hearing of its character—
Does this not cause one to feel much shame? You, Elder, have long possessed such realization; I have merely offered these few words to provoke your reflection.
From this point on, I shall completely sever my attachment to the flavor of blood.
As for the śramaṇa Huian, it is unknown where he was from. In his youth, he was a captive; he was sold to a wealthy family in Jingzhou to perform manual labor.
By nature, he was prudent and sincere, so his master loved him. At the age of eighteen, he was permitted to leave home and become a śrāmaṇera. He resided at Pipa Temple in Jiangling.
Being a rustic man judged by his outward appearance, whenever the assembly of monks sat down, he would invariably rise to serve water, starting from himself and proceeding upward.
The water used for washing never failed. The assembly marveled at this. When he received full ordination (*upasampadā*), his spiritual manifestations became even more pronounced.

Once, while ascending the hall with the śramaṇa Huìjì for the *poṣadha* ceremony, the doors of the hall had not yet opened; Hui’an grasped his hands and entered through the wall, and his exit was likewise.
Huiji was so struck with terror that he did not dare speak. After a moment, [the monk] took his leave of Huiji, saying, "I am about to travel far; I now bid you farewell.

Huiji looked up and saw beautiful flowers filling the air, accompanied by the sound of pipes and strings, while a celestial fragrance permeated everywhere. Huiji became even more terrified. Dao’an said:
"I have been traveling with you; regarding what we have seen, do not speak recklessly. To speak thus would bring retribution.

Only in the southeast is there a Bodhisattva in white robes who has newly resolved his mind; he is one with whom you may speak. Thereupon, [the monk] took his leave and joined a merchant caravan to enter the region of Xiang.

On the road, he suffered from dysentery and was on the verge of death. He said to the merchant, "When I die, my spirit-body shall remain upon the bank; there is no need to prepare a coffin. He asked...
The reason for this was that he said, "I wish to give [this body] to the insects and birds. The merchants followed his instructions and cast the corpse onto the bank.
At night, flames would constantly emerge from its body, and the merchants were greatly terrified. They steered their boat toward Xiangzhong, where they found An had already arrived there.
When they wished to approach him to speak, he had already vanished from his location. Later, when Jì arrived at Zhǐqǐ Temple, he stayed overnight with the hermit Liu Qiū.
When the matter was mentioned, Xiu immediately prostrated from afar and said, "This is one who has attained the Way;
it is the Samādhi of the Fire Light. As for the śramaṇa Tanchao, he dwells on Mount Lingyuan in Qiantang. One night, a strange man arrived and said:

'This region owes its blessings to the Master’s protection of the common people. However, the people of Fuyang have, without cause, excavated the foot of the mountain, thereby severing and destroying the multitude of dragons.'"
The dragon was resentful and failed to send rain; it has now been two hundred days. We wish for the Dharma Master to go once and instruct the dragon, to pray for the blessings of all living beings.
Do you have the intention to do so? Sengchao said, "This is the concern of the donor; what can I possibly do?
The spirit said, "I, your disciple, am able to emit clouds by my own power, but I cannot bring forth rain. Sengchao gave his promise, and he went to Mount Chiting to [deal with] the dragon.
He was preaching the Dharma when a heavy rain suddenly fell. Consequently, he stayed by a stream. When the magistrate heard that Hui-chao was there, he dispatched a boat to welcome him.
That very day, Hui-chao fled back to Lingyuan.

The recluse Liu Qiu, courtesy name Lingyu (also styled Deming), was a native of Nanyang. He was a seventh-generation descendant of Liu Qiao, the Jin-era Governor of Yuzhou, and had moved his residence to Jiangling.
From youth, Qiu maintained high principles and was devoted to learning; he intended to retire into seclusion as soon as he obtained a salary.

During the Taishi era, he served as the Magistrate of Dangyang. Upon retiring from office, he returned home to live in quietude. He commonly wore a deerskin tunic and abstained from grain, subsisting instead on medicinal herbs.

[He studied] arts and sesame cultivation. When Emperor Qi assumed the throne through abdication, he summoned [Liu] Qiu with a carriage drawn by a *pú* tree and bundles of silk to serve as a *Tongzhilang*, but Qiu did not accept.
Prince Jingling sent a letter to convey his intentions; Qiu replied: "In four seasons I lie ill from disease; in three seasons I tend to irrigation and planting."

He spent his remaining years among mountains and marshes, entrusting his twilight sentiments to fish and birds. Was this not the profound grace of the ages of Tang and Yu, and the vast dispensation of Zhou and Shao?
Longqiu was most sincere and clear in his faith toward the Buddha-dharma; his understanding surpassed that of ordinary people in plain robes, whom he could not endure.

He composed a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, judging its teachings according to the two gates of sudden and gradual, which has been adopted by various schools to this day. He also annotated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
He personally lectured on the sutras, and whenever he did so, everyone held his character in high esteem.

In the second year of the Jianwu era, while he was ill, white clouds hovered about the eaves during the day, and within the doors there was the fragrance of incense and the sound of chanting. On that day, he passed away at the age of fifty-eight.
The reclusive scholar Gu Huan lived in seclusion and did not serve in office; he revered the teachings of Huang-Lao.

The *Nanshi* states that because the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism were different, students would mutually disparage and slander one another. Consequently, Gu Huan composed the *Yixialun* (Treatise on the Barbarians and the Chinese).

Its summary says: "To distinguish right from wrong, one should rely upon the sacred scriptures. The *Daodejing* states: 'When Laozi entered the region of Tianzhu [India], the Queen of King Vīrasena...'"
It is said that [the Buddha] was named Jingmiao (Pure Subtlety). Laozi, taking advantage of his daytime sleep, mounted the solar essence and entered Jingmiao’s mouth.

Four years later, on the eighth day of the fourth month, he was born from the incision of the right armpit. Upon falling to the ground, he immediately walked seven steps. Thereupon, the Way of the Buddha flourished.

This appears in the *Xuānmìo nèipiān* (Inner Chapters on Mysterious Subtlety). The Buddhist scriptures state that there have been as many Śākyamunis attaining Buddhahood as grains of sand in the Ganges; some acted as rulers of states.

The Master [Huiyuan] is the patriarch of the Daoist scholars and the Confucian forest. He produced the *Ruiying* and *Benqi* [sutras]. Let us examine this: among the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns, it was unheard of that there was a Buddha;
among the National Preceptors and Daoist Masters, none surpassed Laozi and Zhuangzi; and as for the patriarchs of the Confucian forest, who could surpass the Duke of Zhou and Confucius?

If Confucius and Laozi were not sages, who else could be? Yet, if what is taught in their two scriptures accords like the joining of tally-marks, then the Way is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the Way.
Their sanctity is identical, though their traces appear contrary; perhaps they harmonized their light to manifest in a manner accessible to the mundane.
Some manifest brilliance to demonstrate their reach; because they deliver the world through the Way, there is no region they do not enter.

Because their wisdom encompasses all things, there is nothing they will not do. Their entries differ, and their actions must necessarily vary; each fulfills its own nature without altering its function.
Thus, the formal robes and sash-belted gowns are the attire of the Central Kingdoms, while the shorn hair and wide-sleeved garments are the dress of the various frontier tribes.

The tradition of preserving one's form and observing propriety continues the spirit of inheriting goodness; the practice of disfiguring one's appearance and altering one's form is the study of severing evil.

How could this apply only to fellow humans? It extends even to other beings without end. Throughout the world, sages arise in succession: some illuminate the Five Classics, while others propagate the Three Vehicles.
When among birds, one utters bird cries; when among beasts, one bellows beast cries. To instruct the Chinese, one uses Chinese speech; to transform the barbarians, one uses barbarian tongues.

Although boats and carriages are equal in their capacity to reach distant places, they each have their proper domains—rivers and land respectively. Likewise, while the Buddha-way is identical to other teachings in its ability to bring about transformation, there remains a distinction between the "barbarians" and the "Middle Kingdom.
If one were to claim that because their ultimate goals are equal, their methods may be interchanged, it would be as if one thought a carriage could be used to ford a river.

If a boat can travel upon a river, can it also travel upon dry land? I have frequently seen Buddhist monks who "carve marks on boats" and Daoist practitioners who "wait by the stump," each contending over what is minor or major and mutually disparaging one another.
Some confine the Way into two distinct paths, while others blend the secular with the One;
thus they force the different into the same and shatter the same into the different. This is the source of discord and contention, the root of confusion. Let us therefore examine this matter...

Although the Noble Path is the same, the teachings have their respective orientations. Beginning from no origin and ending at no terminus, *nirvāṇa* and transcendental transformation (*xianhua*) each constitute a distinct method.
Buddhism is termed "Correct Truth" (*zhengzhen*), while Daoism is called "Correct Unity" (*zhengyi*). Unity returns to non-death; Truth accords with non-birth.
In name they diverge, but in reality they converge. However, the teaching of non-birth is remote, whereas the transformation of non-death is immediate.

The Buddhist teachings are elaborate and manifest; the Daoist scriptures are concise and profound. Being profound, the subtle gate is difficult to perceive; being manifest, the correct path is easy to follow. This is the distinction between these two systems.
The Sage’s craftsmanship is without fixed form, yet the square and the round each have their own substance. As vessels differ in their utility, so too do the teachings differ in their application.
Buddhism is the method for destroying evil; Daoism is the art for promoting goodness. To promote goodness is to act spontaneously.

The High [Way] values courage and vigor in destroying evil; the Buddha’s traces are grand and luminous, suitable for transforming others, while the traces of the Way are subtle and profound, suitable for one's own cultivation.
The distinction between their superiority and inferiority lies roughly herein. Although I rejoice in both as being the same Dharma, my inclination favors the teachings of the Way.
Minister of Education Yuan Can commissioned the śramaṇa Tong Gong to refute this. His summary states: "The light of the sun pauses its radiance and the fixed stars conceal their illumination;

The nine-tiered pagoda had its foundations built down to the Yellow Springs; it was ninety *zhang* high, with a *śikhara* (finial) atop it another ten *zhang*.
Every night at stillness, the sound of its bells and chimes could be heard for more than ten *li*. The Buddha hall was like the Taiji Hall, and the triple gate like the Duan Gate.
The thousand columns of the monks’ quarters were adorned with jade beads, brocade, and embroidery that captivated both the hearts and eyes of men. Before long, there was thunder, lightning, and fire.
They cremated the stupa, and those far and near all saw it rise into the air amidst the smoke and flames before vanishing.

More than a month later, someone arriving from the eastern region reported that on that very day they had seen the stupa flying through the air over the sea; those gazing out at the ocean also witnessed it at the time.
In the eighteenth year, the śramaṇa Huìjiǎo of Kuàijī, finding that the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* compiled by Bǎochàng was somewhat superficial and diffuse,
subsequently composed the *Biographies of Exalted Monks* in fourteen fascicles, covering the period from the tenth year of the Yǒngpíng era of the Eastern Han dynasty down to that year.
In total, there were four hundred and fifty-three years [of history], comprising two hundred and fifty-seven individuals, with more than two hundred others mentioned in passing.
To elucidate their virtues and achievements, they have been categorized roughly into ten sections. Their own preface states: "In previous compilations, most are titled 'Famous Monks' (*ming seng*).
However, fame is but the guest of reality. If one’s true practice remains hidden from the light, one may be eminent yet remain unnamed; if..."
One of meager virtue who happens to be timely gains fame but not eminence; since such fame is not eminent, it is here recorded for its historical significance.
One who is eminent but lacks fame is included here for completeness. This is considered by the world to be a definitive judgment.
Shi Senglang was a man who constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra. His demeanor was serene and profound; his eating habits were irregular. Whenever he went out, a dog and a monkey would follow him.
Each day, as he wandered for alms, whatever food and drink he obtained, he would place it in a wooden bowl. Once finished eating, he would take the leftovers to feed the monkey and the dog.
He was skilled at performing the "tortoise-retraction" (kūrma-saṃkoca); at times, he would withdraw his feet, hands, head, and neck entirely so that they could not be seen. Furthermore, he once...
They boarded the boat. At first, there was no power from oars or poles; Lang sat within it while monkeys and dogs remained docile by his side, and the boat ascended against the current on its own.
When Dharma Master Daoying was first practicing meditation in seclusion on Mount Taihang, tree branches entwined together like a canopy to cover him.

After living there for a long time, he left and traveled to Longtai Lake. There, observing the swimming fish, he took a liking to them; he immediately undressed, entered the water, and sat in meditative absorption.

He emerged from a deep abyss after seven days. Furthermore, once during the height of winter, he beheld severe ice; admiring its crystalline clarity, he lay down upon it and rose after two nights and one day.

Later, while residing at Pujisi Temple in Puzhou, one day as he was lecturing on the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) up to the section on the Gate of Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*), he suddenly passed away.
The assembly thought he had departed this life, but the presiding lecturer recognized him and immediately said to the crowd: "This..."
He entered a state of cessation through perception; it was only after three days that he revived.
In the first year of the Putong era, the Emperor constructed a circular altar within the palace precincts, intending to receive the *śaraṇa* precepts.

He carefully selected those of exceptional virtue and conduct to serve as his preceptors. The court deliberated that Dharma Master Huiyue possessed the highest reputation, and an imperial edict summoned him. Huiyue, according to the rites—

Huiyuan declined, refusing permission. On the day of Ding-si in the fourth month of summer, the Emperor went to pay his respects and requested that Huiyuan accept him as a disciple and confer upon him the full ordination (upasaṃpadā).
During the performance of the *karmavācanā*, sweet dew descended upon the courtyard; two three-legged birds and two peacocks came down the steps, tamed and submissive.
The Emperor was greatly delighted and bestowed upon Huiyuan the honorary title "Zhìzhě" (The Wise One). From then on, whenever he entered court, a special seat was always prepared for him.

The Imperial Throne was situated beside him. In total, there were forty-eight thousand people—including princes, dukes, high officials, monastics, and laypeople—who followed [the Master] to receive the precepts.
Although the śramaṇas were already advanced in age, they nonetheless received the transmission once again. Only Master Fayun said:
"I have already taken my vows; how could I employ the Buddha-dharma for worldly affairs? Thereupon, those who deliberated on the matter held him in high esteem.
At that time, there was a Chan Master named Da who had attained the water-contemplation samādhi (*āp-samādhi*).

Whenever he entered this meditative absorption, those who peered inside saw only clear water pooling and filling the room. The śramaṇa Daoxian followed Da and attained the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*). Regarding his [Daoxian's]...
The chamber where he resided was brightly illuminated even during the deep of night.

The Emperor applied his mind to the Dharma-gate, yet at that time many śramaṇas were unrestrained and dissolute; the presiding monks were weak and unable to discipline them, which troubled the Emperor.

He wished to personally conduct the affairs of the Sangha-rectifier (Sengzheng) according to the Vinaya. When the imperial decree was issued, none of the great virtuous ones (Dade) in the capital dared to offer counsel;
only Dharma Master Zang considered that the Buddha-dharma is profound and vast, such that it cannot be exhausted by a single person, and he steadfastly refused to comply with the decree.

The Emperor was surprised by this and summoned him into the Guanghua Hall to question him on the matter. Zang presented the general principles face-to-face with firm justification, and the Emperor could not [prevail over his resolve].
Duo then followed his lead. After Zang had withdrawn, he said to the monks, "The Master takes the Buddha-dharma as his own responsibility;
we ought indeed to defer to him. Yet, even ten youths from noble families cannot all act in accordance with their fathers' wishes.

Now, you are a mixed multitude from the five directions, yet you are being constrained by the likes and dislikes of a single individual. The precepts and regulations will surely fall into ruin. Do you not consider this?"

"What is this? asked the Emperor. Dharma Master Fayun sighed and said, "The profound significance of the scriptural principles cannot be fully expressed; for a single day’s affair, I am truly filled with shame and must submit.

The Emperor himself received full ordination and lived and slept much like a śramaṇa. Although he was within the palace precincts, he always allowed the monks free access for their excursions and sightseeing. Only...
The imperial throne was strictly forbidden [to others], yet one day Master Zang ascended and took his seat upon it.

His attendants shouted to stop him, but Zang said, "I, a poor monk, am a descendant of King Dingguang of the Golden Wheel; how could I feel ashamed of this seat? Even if I were to be killed, I have no concern that I would lack a place of rebirth.
When the Emperor heard this, he let the matter rest and did not punish him. After a short while, Zang passed by a physiognomist, who said, "The Dharma Master’s lifespan will not exceed..."
31. Xuanzang was apprehensive. Daily he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. When the appointed time arrived, he dreamed that the man from before came again and told him:
"Dharma Master, by the power of the *Prajñā*, your lifespan has been doubled. Furthermore, he frequently dreamed that Vimalakīrti descended into his room and conversed with him.
Upon parting, Vimalakīrti left him a white *cāmara* whisk and departed. From then on, Xuanzang’s profound eloquence flourished daily.

The Treatise says: Formerly, King Wu of Zhou faced north to receive the Great Plan in Nine Categories from Jizi. Once the King had finished receiving the text, Jizi was merely granted a fief of the fifth rank.

Later, during the reign of Emperor Shun of the Later Han, he issued an edict for the scholar-recluse Fan Ying to prepare an altar and mats to perform the ritual of seeking counsel on the Way and to consult him regarding matters of gain and loss; yet, in the end, Ying possessed no special ability whatsoever. Thus...
The scholar-recluses (*chushi*) throughout the realm were all subjected to the reproach of being "pure thieves" who trafficked in empty reputations.
When Emperor Wu received the precepts from Master Dao-yue, thereafter whenever Dao-yue entered court, the Emperor provided him with a special seat for his placement.

The Emperor would sit beside him, honoring him as his teacher until the end of his life. Alas! The Emperor’s embodiment of venerating teachers and valuing the Way has been passed down since the Han dynasty.

Such a thing has never occurred before. Yet, since Master Zang was not the Imperial Preceptor, it was merely a matter of him marveling at being a descendant of the Golden Wheel King and occupying the Throne of the Grand Ultimate (*Taiji*).
That the previous histories regard this as a glorious tale is incorrect. Our school takes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnya*) as its throne.

If Master Zang were able to honor himself through the Dharma, then he would have responded to conditions and met with sentient beings everywhere without exception, while always remaining in [the state of]...
As for this Bodhi seat, why wait until one occupies the throne of a sovereign to find glory? To say that [the Emperor] was ignorant of this would be to claim he lacked understanding.

As for his declining the decree of the Imperial Preceptor Sengzheng and appearing in a dream to the spirit of Māgha—such instances suggest that he possessed a day’s worth of seniority over the monks of the present age.
In the eighteenth year, Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty underwent the capping ceremony. He commanded śramaṇas and Daoists to lecture on the Way within the palace.
At that time, the Daoist Jiang Bin and the śramaṇa Tanmujue engaged in a debate. The Emperor asked, "Did the Buddha and Laozi exist at the same time?
Jiang Bin replied, "According to the *Kaotian jing*, when Laozi entered the West to convert the barbarians, the Buddha served as his attendant; this makes it clear..."
At that time, Tanmuzu asked, "In which year of the Zhou dynasty was Laozi born? Bin replied, "He was born in the third year of King Dingwang;
he entered government service in the Zhou in the fourth year of King Jianwang; and in the fourth year of King Jingwang, at the age of eighty-five, he went west to convert the barbarians.
Tanmuzu said, "Our Buddha was born in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of Zhou, and in the fifty-second year of King Mu..."

The World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa. From the time of the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa until the third year of King Ding’s reign, exactly three hundred and forty-five years passed before Laozi was born.
Furthermore, when Laozi traveled westward in the first year of King Jing’s reign, four hundred and twenty-five years had already elapsed since the World-Honored One manifested his passing.
Given this vast chronological distance, is it not erroneous to claim that he converted the barbarians?
Bīn asked, "The Buddha was born in the era of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty; what textual records exist for this?

Zuì replied, "The *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou) and the *Han Fa Ben Neizhuan* (Inner Biography of the Origin of the Dharma in the Han) both contain explicit accounts. Bīn asked, "Confucius established his own system of laws, yet there are no records whatsoever concerning the Buddha.
Why is this so? Zuì replied, "Confucius possesses the three 'completions' and the ten classics, which refer to Heaven, Earth, and Man. As for the words of the Buddha, they..."
When this was fully explained, Sengbin asked, "Confucius was a sage; why did he rely on divination? Sengzui replied, "The Buddha is the king of all sages.
He understands the past and future limits, as well as the fortune and misfortune, the end and beginning, of all sentient beings; thus, he does not rely on divination.

As for other minor sages, although they may perceive what is yet to come, they must depend upon the milfoil stalks and tortoise shells to discern auspiciousness and calamity. At that time, Liu Teng, the Palace Attendant, proclaimed an imperial decree.
The Emperor said, "Jiang Bin’s discourse lacks a central tenet; he should retire from his seat. He further asked, "From where did you obtain the *Kaitian jing*?
Who is its author? Bring it here at once. When the scripture was brought forth, the Emperor commanded his ministers to examine its authenticity in detail.
At that time, over one hundred and sixty officials, including the Grand Marshal Xiao Zong, the Grand Tutor Li Shi, and other dukes, ministers, and scholars, finished reading it.
The indictment stated: "Laozi composed only the *Wenzi* (Five Thousand Words) and has no other teachings. What Jiang Bin now relies upon consists of vulgar language and erroneous tenets;
it both defiles the former master and deceives the imperial hearing. His crime is that he deludes the masses. An edict was issued to sentence him to criminal punishment.
Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci memorialized that Jiang Bin should be specifically exiled to Mayi. Tánmó... [text ends]
He was most excellent in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles and possessed the practice of the Vinaya.

Initially, while expounding the Vinaya in Handan, he moved sixty-odd extraordinary bhikṣus to leave their seats and listen to the precepts. Whenever Ratnamati saw them, he would call them "Bodhisattvas of the East."
The "Buddhist and Laoist Records" (*Fó-lǎo-zhì*) in the *Wei Shu* states: "The source of the Daoist school originates with Laozi. Regarding his own words:

he was born before Heaven and Earth to provide sustenance for the myriad species. Above, he dwells in the Jade Capital (*Yùjīng*) as the patriarch of the divine jade beings; below, he resides in the Purple Microcosm (*Zǐwēi*) as the lord of the flying immortals.
Undergoing a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, he possesses virtue yet does not claim it. Responding to things according to their occasion, his traces are ever-changing."

He transmitted the teachings of Xuanyuan at Mount Emei and instructed Emperor Ku at Mudé. Great Yu heard the secret instructions for longevity, and Yin Xi received the essential meaning of the *Dàodé jīng*.

As for the scriptures concerning the cinnabar book and purple characters, the ascent to the profound and the soaring steps, as well as the discourses on jade, stone, golden light, and the wondrously numinous caverns—they are beyond counting. Their teaching is one that entirely purges away all that is heterodox.
They repeatedly cleanse their spirits and accumulate virtuous conduct to establish merit and increase goodness. Thus, they attain ascension to heaven by day and eternal life in this world.

For this reason, the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han devoted themselves with unceasing resolve, exhausting their minds and thoughts in pursuit of it everywhere, yet in the end they could not achieve it;
they later regretted their failure, leading to the execution of Luan Da and Xu Family. Nevertheless, as for that Way—
Those who deluded others by imitating these practices were not few. Emperor Ling established the *huágài* canopy at Zhaolong Palace and set up an altar to perform rituals.
When Zhang Ling transmitted the Way at Heming Mountain, he passed down two thousand and twenty copies of the *Tiāngōng zhāng*.

His disciples transmitted them to one another, and the practice flourished greatly. Rituals for the ancestral sacrifices and prostrations each had their established methods; thus, the Three Primal Origins and Nine Offices [were organized].

The one hundred and twenty palaces are all governed by various deities. Furthermore, they borrow the terminology of kalpas from Buddhist scriptures, claiming that at the end of such a kalpa, both heaven and earth will perish together.
Their texts contain many prohibitions and secrets; those who are not their disciples may not peruse them at will.
As for their methods of transforming gold and melting jade, as well as their practice of talismans and the command of water, there are myriad and myriad strange formulas and wondrous arts.

It is said that those who ascend undergo "feather-transformation" (*yùhuà*) and fly to heaven; next, it is claimed they eliminate calamities and extinguish misfortunes. Consequently, those who delight in the extraordinary often venerate them.
Initially, when Emperor Wen entered into the service of the Jin dynasty, his attendants reported that he had ascended as an immortal at Yique.

Emperor Taizu delighted in the words of Laozi, reciting and chanting them without weariness. During the Tianxing era, Dong Mi, the Director of the Court of Ceremonial, presented the *Fúshí xiānjīng* (Scripture on Food and Elixirs for Immortality).
He composed several dozen chapters. He then established the office of the Immortal Doctor (Xianren Boshi) and founded the Immortal Ward (Xianfang) to decoct a hundred medicinal herbs.

He sealed off the Western Mountains to provide firewood for his incinerations and ordered those facing capital punishment to consume these medicines; however, most died without any miraculous effect. After some time, Emperor Taizu’s interest grew somewhat lax, and he ceased the practice.

During the era of Emperor Shizu, there was a Daoist named Kou Qianzhi, courtesy name Fuzhen, a native of Yongzhou. From an early age, he was fond of the Way of the Immortals and practiced the arts of Zhang Lu.
Although he spent years ingesting medicinal elixirs, they yielded no effect. A xianren named Cheng Gongxing sought to become his disciple;
together they entered Mount Hua to dwell in a stone chamber. There, Gongxing gathered medicinal herbs for Qianzhi to ingest, and he was able to [attain longevity].
[Da]qian’s skin [became smooth]. Furthermore, they entered a stone chamber on Mount Song together. Shortly thereafter, a strange person brought medicinal substances to Daqian;
these were all poisonous insects and foul-smelling things. Frightened, Daqian fled. Sengxing sighed and said, "The Master has not yet attained immortality;

he can only serve as a teacher to emperors. Not long after, Sengxing departed as an immortal. Daqian remained at Mount Song to maintain his resolve when he suddenly encountered a great deity riding upon clouds and drawing a dragon.
A hundred spirits led the way and assembled at the mountain peak. Addressing himself as the Most High Lord Lao (Taishang Laojun), he said to Xuankun:
"Since the passing of the Heavenly Master Zhang Ling, the office upon earth has remained vacant. You possess a refined physique and upright principles;
therefore, I confer upon you the rank of Heavenly Master. I bestow upon you the twenty fascicles of the New Code from the Clouds, which have not been transmitted since the beginning of creation."
"Worldly one, you shall proclaim my new regulations to purify and rectify the Daoist teachings.

Eliminate the spurious methods of the Three Zhangs, as well as the collection of rice, money, and taxes, and the arts of male-female *heqi* (union through breath). The Great Dao is pure and void; how could it contain such things?
I shall take ritual propriety as the primary focus, supplemented by dietary practices and disciplined training, so that the Nine Doubts and Twelve Jade Maidens may grant instruction to Xuanzhi."
He was introduced to the oral instructions (*mukhāgama*), whereupon he attained the ability to abstain from grain; his vital energy flourished and his complexion became radiant and beautiful.
The *Treatise* states: "The Wei History recounts the origins and development of the Way (*Daojiao*) and the life and career of [Ge] Qianzhi as follows.
Thus, Qianzhi’s contributions to the Way were not comparable to those of the Three Zhangs. Furthermore, the Sima Wen..."
Zheng Gong once compared Qianzhi to the *yuju* (great sea bird). Now, the *yuju* mentioned in the *Zuozhuan* was neither wise nor spiritual;
it was merely a strange bird. Qianzhi, however, personally encountered the Old Lord [Laozi], who transmitted secret instructions to him in person, thereby reviving the Daoist teachings.
This ensures that scholars of future generations may follow and transmit his teachings.
Even if Qian were not among those who attain the status of immortals, he was nonetheless an exceptionally eminent gentleman. To compare him with the *yuanyu* (wild goose) is surely excessive.
Nevertheless, when the Duke Wenzheng said that his words serve as teachers for a hundred generations and his conduct as a model for the world, his intention must have been directed toward Qian.
The spirits encountered therein are precisely those of which Confucius did not speak.
That this transmission has flourished and spread throughout the world, and that Wen Zhenggong declined to participate in it, is only fitting. Alas!
If even one who prizes humility and abides in equanimity and simplicity would remain aloof, how much more so should those beneath him?
In the eighth year of the Putong era, the Great Master Bodhidharma, the first patriarch from India, arrived in Jinling.

The Master was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India in the Western Regions. Upon the king’s death, he entered the monastic life and encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, who entrusted him with the Great Dharma.
Thereupon he asked: "Now that I have attained the Dharma, which country should I go to transform? Prajñātāra replied: [The remainder of the text follows].
Rāhula said, "After you have attained the Dharma, more than sixty years after my parinirvāṇa, you shall go to the land of China to propagate the teachings.
Rāhula asked, "Are there those in that land who are vessels for the Dharma capable of continuing my lineage? Will there be calamities during the kalpa thousands of years hence?
Mahāsthāmaprāpta said, "The number of those in the regions you convert who shall attain Bodhi is beyond counting. After my parinirvāṇa, there shall be those who remain..."
[The Master] said: "Difficult indeed. Wenbu, who is skilled in water, shall subdue it himself. When your time comes, you must not remain long in the south. Listen to my verse:
'Traveling along the road, crossing waters and meeting sheep; All alone and desolate, one secretly crosses the river.

At sunset, how pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses; Two young cassia trees flourish for a long time. He further recited eight verses, all of which were premonitions of future events. [This continued] until many [verses].
When Rāhula entered nirvāṇa, the Master propagated the Dharma in his native land. At that time, his nephew, King Hsien-chien, disparaged the Triple Gem.

The Master dispatched his disciple P’o-lo-ti to manifest supernatural powers and convert him, leading him back to the correct path. The Master then perceived that the conditions for China had ripened.

He then parted from his followers. King Yi-jian (Heterodox View) visited the Master in person and said to him, "You should diligently cultivate meritorious deeds and protect and uphold the Triple Gem.
It will not be too late for me to depart; I shall return in eighteen days. The King wept and said, "Since you, my elder brother, have karmic ties there, I cannot detain you.
I only pray that you will not forget your native land and return early once your affairs are concluded. Thereupon, he prepared...

The great ship was filled with various treasures. The King personally led his ministers and officials to escort them to the seashore. The Master, together with the merchants, boarded the vessel and reached the South Sea.
Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, provided him with lodging and submitted a memorial to the throne. By imperial decree, he was summoned for an audience.
The Master entered the imperial court. The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting.

What merit do these deeds possess? The Master replied, "They possess no merit. The Emperor asked, "Why is it that they possess none? The Master said, "These are the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas;
they are causes tainted by outflows (*āsrava*). Though they exist, they are not real. The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Master replied, "Purity..."
"Wisdom is wondrously luminous; its essence is inherently empty and quiescent. Such merit is not sought within the world. The Emperor asked, "What is the ultimate meaning of the Noble Truth?
He replied, "Vast emptiness—therein is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me? He replied, "I do not know.
The Emperor did not grasp the profound purport. The Master lingered for several days and then crossed the river to Wei, where he stayed at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.
He spent his entire day in wall-contemplation (*bi-guan*) alone. There was a monk named Shen Guang who, prompted by a divine being, came to visit the Master.
The Master sat upright and did not look back. It happened that there was a great snowfall; Shen Guang stood in the snow until the accumulated drifts reached above his knees.

The Master took pity on him and asked, "Why have you been standing in the snow for so long? What do you seek? Shen Guang replied, "I only pray that Your Great Compassion will open the gate of the ambrosia (*amṛta*)."
"The Gate opens wide to deliver all classes of beings. The Master said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas is difficult to encounter even throughout vast eons.

How can those of meager virtue and limited wisdom, with a frivolous or arrogant mind, hope to attain the True Vehicle? Your diligent toil would be in vain. Upon hearing these exhortations, Huiguang was overcome with joy;
he immediately took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Master. The Master said, "At the very beginning, the Buddhas..."
"One who seeks the Way values the Dharma above all and forgets the self. Since you have now severed your arm before me, your seeking is indeed permissible.

Huiguan accepted these words and was immediately renamed Huike. He asked again, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? The Master said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.
Huike said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to bring it to rest. The Master said, "Bring forth your mind."
"I have given you peace," he said. "You may say: 'I sought the mind, but it is ultimately unattainable. The Master replied, "I have finished giving you peace.
After some time, he briefly expounded for Heshang Ke and others the four practices for entering the Way according to the Mahāyāna. His words were as follows:
Now, there are many paths for entering the Way; yet, to summarize them, they do not exceed two kinds: first, entry through principle (*li-ru*); second, entry through practice (*xing-ru*).

Entry through principle means awakening to the fundamental essence by relying on the teachings. It involves deep faith that all living beings share the same true nature, which is merely obscured by adventitious delusions and cannot be fully manifested.
If one discards delusion to return to the truth and remains steadfastly absorbed in the "wall-contemplation" (*bi-guan*), there will be neither self nor other.
Ordinary beings and sages are of one and the same rank; remaining steadfastly immovable, they no longer follow the teachings of culture and education. This is in accord with principle.
Being without discrimination, tranquil, and non-active—this is called "entry through principle. There are four types of "entry through practice": first, the practice of requiting resentment;

second, the practice of following conditions; third, the practice of seeking nothing; and fourth, the practice of conforming to the Dharma. Regarding the practice of requiting resentment: as for ordinary beings...

When a practitioner of the Path undergoes suffering, they should reflect: "Throughout countless kalpas since antiquity, I have abandoned the fundamental for the peripheral and wandered through the various realms of existence, giving rise to many enmities and grievances and committing infinite acts of harm.

Although I have committed no offense now, this is the ripening of the fruits of my own past calamities and evil karma; it is neither bestowed by gods nor by men. I shall accept it with a willing heart and endure it without resentment."
Regret. When one contemplates in this way, it accords with principle; by embodying resentment and advancing on the Path, it is called the Practice of Repaying Resentment.
As for the Practice of Following Conditions: sentient beings have no self and are all driven by conditions and karma. Suffering and joy are received equally, as both arise from conditions.

If one obtains superior retributions such as honor and fame, these are all evoked by past causes from former lives. Once the conditions are exhausted, they vanish back into nothingness. What [is there to cling to]?
In the existence of joy, gain and loss follow conditions while the mind neither increases nor decreases. When the wind of joy does not stir, one should accord with the Way;
this is called "acting in accordance with conditions. As for the practitioner who seeks nothing: worldly people are long lost in delusion, greedily attached everywhere.

The wise awaken to the truth and settle their minds in non-action (*wuwei*). All phenomena are empty and there is nothing to hope for. Dwelling long within the three realms is like being in a house on fire.

All bodies are suffering; who can find peace therein? To thoroughly comprehend this point is to still the mind and cease seeking. Thus, a sutra says: "Where there is seeking, there is suffering; where there is no seeking, there is bliss.
This is the practice of the Way through the truth of non-seeking; therefore, it is called the Practice of Non-Seeking (*apraṇihita-caryā*).
Regarding the "Practice in Accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānusāri-caryā*): the principle of intrinsic purity is termed the "Dharma. This principle is empty of all marks and devoid of...
In the state of non-attachment, there is neither "this" nor "that. As the Sūtra says: "Dharmas have no self, for they are free from the defilement of self.

The wise who believe and understand this principle should act in accordance with the Dharma. Since the essence of dharmas is devoid of stinginess, one should practice the giving of charity through body, life, and wealth, with a mind free from parsimony.
Having realized the three kinds of emptiness, one does not rely on or cling to anything; one acts solely for the sake of transforming sentient beings through the example of Vimalakīrti.
To give birth [to these practices] without grasping at signs is both for one's own cultivation and for the benefit of others; it adorns the path to enlightenment.

Just as it is with the perfection of giving (*dāna*), so it is with the remaining five. To practice the six perfections in order to eliminate deluded thoughts while having nothing to practice—this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmacaryā*).
In the tenth month of the second year of the Dàtóng era, the Master was about to manifest his passing away.
Dào Fù, the nun Zǒngchí, Dào Yù, Huìkě, and others were attending at his side. He said, "The time has arrived. Why do you not each speak of what you have attained?

At that time, Dào Fù said, "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, yet I do not depart from words and letters, taking them as the functioning of the Way. The Master said, "You have attained my skin."
The nun Zongchi said, "What I have now seen is like Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha; once seen, it is never seen again.
The Master said, "You have attained my flesh. Chan Master Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist;
