He then looked toward Ka and said, "The World-Honored One entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Mahākāśyapa, and it was passed down through successive generations until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it. I also grant you this robe as a token of the Dharma. Ka knelt.
He accepted the robe and requested instructions. The Master said: "Internally, the Dharma-seal is transmitted to accord with the true mind;
externally, the Dharma-robe is bestowed to establish the fundamental tenet. In future generations, when the world becomes degenerate and doubts arise in competition, people will say:

'He was in the Western Land while you are from this land; on what basis did you receive the Dharma, and by what means do you have proof? Should such difficult circumstances be encountered, simply produce this robe to serve as a token."
Believe that his transformation was unimpeded. More than two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the transmission of his robes will cease, yet the Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra;
there will be more than ten million who secretly correspond with and intimately accord with it. You must propagate this transformation and never slight those who have not yet awakened.

A single thought that turns the faculty [of mind] back to its source is identical to what is originally possessed. Listen to my verse: "I came to this land To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One..."
"The flower has opened its five petals; the fruiting occurs naturally. He further said, "I have also these four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* which I entrust to you.
This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground. Since I left South India for this Eastern Land, I observed that the Great State of China possessed the atmosphere of the Mahāyāna;
thus, I crossed seas and deserts to seek the Dharma and find a person worthy of it. Our meeting is now timely."
Previously, I was as unrefined as a fool and as reticent as one who stammers. Now that I have received your transmission, my purpose is fulfilled.
Thereupon, he went with his disciples to Qiansheng Temple at Yumen. The Governor of Qicheng, Yang Xuanzhi, asked him: "In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, the masters are revered as patriarchs;
what is their Way like? The Master replied: "To clarify the mind-source of the Buddha and to ensure that practice and understanding correspond—this is what is called [the Way]."
Zu said, "I, your disciple, have long venerated the Triple Gem, yet my wisdom has been clouded and dull. I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will reveal the essential principles.
The Master replied to him in verse: "Do not harbor aversion upon seeing evil; do not strive to practice virtue merely by observing it.
Do not abandon wisdom to draw near to folly; do not cast away delusion to pursue awakening. To realize the Great Way is to transcend all measures; to attain clarity..."
The Buddha’s mind brings forth deliverance; it does not share the same entanglements as ordinary beings or even sages. Transcending all, he is named the Patriarch.

Upon hearing this verse, Xuanzhi prostrated himself and said, "I pray that you, Master, will abide in this world with compassion and patience for a long time. The Master replied, "My karmic conditions for transformation are already exhausted."
"The Dharma has been entrusted to the right person; I shall now pass away. On that day, he sat upright and entered nirvana.

His disciples enshrined his entire body for burial at Dinglin Temple on Mount Xiong’er. The following year, when the Wei envoy Song Yun returned from the Western Regions, he encountered the Master on the Pamir Mountains.
Carrying a single sandal in his hand, he strode forth alone and elegant. When Huìyún asked him where he was going, he replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven.
When Huìyún returned to the capital, he related these events in detail. When the disciples opened the tomb, there was only an empty coffin and the single sandal remaining.

Upon hearing that the Master’s miraculous manifestations had begun and ended in this manner, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty personally composed an inscription and carved it upon a stone at Mount Zhong.

The commentary states: Formerly, Song Mingjiao composed the *Zhengfajingzongji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma), in which he claimed that Bodhidharma remained in the world for several hundred years.

It is certain that he had already attained the fruit of sainthood and possessed a mind-born body (*manomayakāya*), and was thus not constrained by the death and rebirth of the fragmented stages (*pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa*).
When he arrived in this land and manifested his passing, his entire body was returned after the funeral rites were completed;

thus, the duration of his life is certainly not something that can be fathomed by worldly standards. The *Chuan Deng Lu* states: On the twenty-first day of the ninth month, the Master arrived in Guangzhou.
The Regional Inspector submitted a memorial to inform the Emperor, who dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial edict to welcome him. On the tenth...
On the first day of the month, he arrived in Jinling. However, from Guangzhou to Jinling is a distance of no fewer than three thousand li.
While the messenger had gone and returned, the Master was only then setting out; how could he have traversed three thousand li within ten days?
Furthermore, it is said that Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty admired the Master’s extraordinary character and thrice extended imperial summons, yet the Master ultimately did not go.
He descended to Shaolin. When the Master passed away, Song Yun was returning from the Western Regions; he encountered the Master on the Pamir Mountains.

Emperor Xiaozhuang issued an edict ordering the opening of the tomb. This was the eighth year of the Putong era of the Southern Dynasties history, which corresponds to the first year of the Datong era.
Emperor Xiaoming passed away on the day of Guichou in the fourth month of that year. The Master arrived in Liang in the tenth month. Thus, it appears that the Master...
Before the Wei dynasty arrived, Emperor Xiaoming had already passed away. Not long after his son ascended the throne, he was assassinated by Erzhu Rong, who then installed Emperor Xiaozhuang.
From this, the Wei state fell into great chaos. Three years later, Emperor Xiaozhuang died;
five years after that, the realm was divided into Eastern and Western Wei. Thus, while my ancestor was at Shaolin, [the world was in turmoil].
The time coincided precisely with that period of turmoil. By the time Song Yun returned, more than five or six years had passed since Emperor Xiaozhuang’s death;
his kingdom had long since been partitioned. How could there be any truth to the claim that Emperor Xiaozhuang ordered the opening of the tomb?
The *Old History of the Tang* states: "At the end of the Later Wei, a monk named Bodhidharma came by sea. After he passed away, in that same year, the Wei..."
When Song Yun returned from the Pamir Mountains, he visited [the Master] there; when his disciples opened the tomb, they found nothing but a single shoe.
This is indeed an authentic record. Furthermore, it is said that the Vinaya Master Guangtong and Bodhiruci repeatedly administered poison to harm the Master, yet the Master did not save them.
Alas, how tragic! Guangtong and Bodhiruci were the dragon-elephants of the Dharma-gate; how could they—?
Can it truly be so? This is entirely due to the errors of those who formulate their doctrines.

Nevertheless, the matters of our school from time immemorial have been as clear as the sun and moon moving across the sky. Thus, after the Second Patriarch had performed three prostrations, he stood in his place.
At that very moment, he sealed kalpas as numerous as motes of dust within a single instant; he penetrated the ocean of lands within the tip of a hair. One must directly accept this.
The entire body bears the burden. As it is said, "At the summit of Tongxuan Peak, it is not of this world. Having entered this gate, one knows nothing of conceptual understanding.
Furthermore, how could there be any distinction to be made between movement and stillness, coming and going, self and other, or time and circumstance?

Composed by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of Shishi Monastery in Longxing Prefecture.
The Great Being of Shuanglin in Yiwu, Wuzhou, during the Liang Dynasty, was surnamed Fu and named Xi; his Dharma name was Shanhui.
At the age of sixteen, he took Liu Miaoguang as his wife, and they had two sons, Pujian and Pucheng. Once, there was a man from the Western Regions...
The śramaṇa Śaṅghadatta saw the Mahāsattva and said, "I and you both made a vow together at the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.
Now, the robes and alms bowl remain in the Tuṣita Heaven; on what day shall we return? Thereupon, he accompanied him to the edge of a pond to observe their reflections.
Seeing the Dharma of the Circular Halo and Jewel Canopy flourishing most vigorously, the Great Being smiled and said, "The forge produces much dull iron;
the gate of a skilled physician is filled with the sick. To deliver sentient beings is my urgent task; why dwell on that pleasure?
Not long after, he constantly saw the three Tathāgatas—Śākyamuni, Suvarṇapuṣpa, and Dīpaṃkara—emitting light that enveloped his body. The Great Being rejoiced and said, "I..."
Having attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he immediately abandoned his fields and houses and sold his wife and children. With the fifty thousand coins obtained, he established a Dharma-giving assembly.
He subsequently founded a monastery atop Mount Songshan at the site of the twin *śīrīṣa* trees and resided there; it was named Shuanglin (The Twin Forests).
By day he engaged in manual labor, and by night he practiced the Way. There is a verse that says: "Empty-handed, grasping a hoe; Walking, yet riding."
Water buffalo. A person passed over the bridge; the bridge flowed, yet the water did not flow.

On another day, while walking on the path around twin trees joined at the roots on a mountain peak, he was moved by the appearance of the seven Buddhas following him. Śākyamuni led the way, and Vimalakīrti followed behind.

Only the World-Honored One Śākyamuni repeatedly turned to look back and converse with the Great Being (Mahāsattva). From this, his extraordinary traces became manifest daily. The fifth year of the Great Tōng era, the tenth day of the first month.
On the fifth day, he dispatched his disciple Fu Yang to deliver a letter to the court. The text read:

"The Great Being of Good Wisdom, who shall attain liberation hereafter beneath the twin śāla trees, addresses the National Sovereign, Bodhisattva Savior of the World: I now wish to cultivate the good of the superior, middling, and inferior grades."

I hope you will be able to receive and uphold this. Regarding the highest good: briefly, it takes a humble and open mind as its foundation, non-attachment as its principle, the signless (*animitta*) as its cause, and *nirvāṇa* as its fruit.

Regarding the intermediate good: briefly, it takes the cultivation of the self as its foundation, the governance of the state as its principle, and the peaceful and happy retributions of the heavens and the human realm as its fruit.
Regarding the lowest good: briefly, it consists in protecting and nourishing sentient beings, overcoming violence and abolishing killing, and [bringing peace] universally.
He caused all the common people to observe the six fasts. Now, hearing that the Emperor honors the Dharma, he wishes to present his arguments on its meaning, yet has not yet fulfilled his intentions;
therefore, he has sent his disciple, Fu Yang, to inform you. Yang delivered the letter to He Chang, the Director of the Court of Imperial Music, who said:
"Master Yao has already submitted his petition. Xi is merely a local official and not a senior elder; since he shows no humility at all, how could I dare to present it?"
Dáhuì burned his hand on the imperial road. Chāng then galloped to Tóngtài Monastery to consult Dharma Master Hào.

Hào urged him to present it immediately. On the eleventh day of the second month, the book was submitted. Upon reading it, the Emperor hastily dispatched an edict to welcome him. Once he had arrived, the Emperor asked:
"Whom have you served as a teacher from the outset? He replied, "I come from nowhere; I have come from nowhere. My service as a teacher is likewise.

Prince Zhaoming asked, "Why does the Great Being not discuss the principles of doctrine? He replied, "That which is spoken by a Bodhisattva is neither long nor short, neither broad nor narrow, neither finite nor infinite. Since it is the suchness of the true principle, what further words could there be? The Emperor [asked].
[The Emperor] asked, "What is true permanence? He replied, "It is cessation without extinction. The Emperor said, "Cessation without extinction implies the existence of form (*rūpa*).
Because there is form, it is dull. If this is so, then you, Master, have not yet escaped the common worldly ways. He replied, "When facing wealth, one does not seek gain by dishonest means;
when facing danger, one does not seek escape by dishonest means. The Emperor said, "Master, you possess great knowledge of propriety (*li*. He replied, "All dharmas are..."
There is neither being nor non-being. All forms and images within the great trichiliocosm are entirely empty.
Just as the myriad rivers flow together but do not exceed the sea, so too the immeasurable sublime dharmas do not transcend True Suchness (*tathatā*).

For what reason does the Tathāgata alone transcend the ninety-six paths within the three realms? He regards all sentient beings as his own infants; for there is nothing in the world that is not the Way.
Feeling uneasy and finding no joy in what was contrary to propriety, the Emperor remained silent. The Great Being (Mahāsattva) took his leave.
On another day, while the Emperor was lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in the Shouguang Hall, Zhigong remarked, "The Great Being is capable of this.

The Emperor immediately summoned the Great Being, who faced the Emperor holding a clapper-board and lectured on the sutra, chanting it in forty-nine verses. He then returned to the Shuanglin Temple. This occurred in the first year of the Taizhuan era of the Chen dynasty.
In the fourth month of that year, as he was about to pass away, he said to his disciples: "This body is utterly loathsome, a gathering place for all manner of suffering.
The essential point is to guard the three karmas and diligently practice the six perfections; otherwise, if one falls into hell, it will be extremely difficult to escape.
One must constantly perform repentance. He further said: "After my passing, do not move my bed. On the seventh day, there shall be a venerable man named Faming."
He brought a statue and a bell to settle there. A disciple asked, "After he has entered nirvana, what will become of his physical remains?
He replied, "Burn them on the mountain peak. The disciple asked, "If that cannot be done, then what? He replied, "Do not use a coffin for interment.
Simply pile bricks to form an altar, place the corpse upon it behind a screen, surround it with crimson silk canopies, and build a stupa above; install it as you see fit."
He stood up. [The Emperor] asked again, "When all Buddhas pass into parinirvāṇa, they invariably proclaim their merits. May I hear of the origins of the Master’s own manifestation?
He replied, "I have come from the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven to deliver you all. I am next in line to succeed Śākyamuni. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
'There is a bodhisattva who comes from Tuṣita Heaven; his faculties are sharp and keen, and he swiftly accords with Prajñā. This refers to none other than myself."
"This is my body. Having spoken these words, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away at the age of seventy-three.
On the seventh day, the venerable monk Famen brought a woven image of Maitreya and a nine-milk bronze bell to enshrine them at the site of the grotto;

yet, in an instant, more than ten articles belonging to the Great Being (Mahāsattva) vanished. During the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, the King of Qian opened the stupa and took out the sacred relics.

There were six pieces, all of a purple-gold color. Together with the ritual implements, they were brought to Longhua Temple, built south of the capital city, where statues were fashioned and installed.

The Great Being once composed a single piece titled "The Inscription on the Mind-King" (*Cittarāja-nāma*), the text of which says: "Behold the King of the Empty Mind, profound and subtle, difficult to fathom.
Nameless and formless, it possesses great spiritual power. It can extinguish a thousand calamities and bring to fulfillment ten thousand virtues. Its essential nature..."

Although it is empty, it can bestow the principles of the Dharma; when observed, it has no form, yet when called upon, it has sound. It acts as the great general of the Dharma, transmitting the sutras through the precepts of the mind.
Like the taste of salt in water or the presence of blue pigment within its color, it is certainly existent, yet one does not see its form.

The King of the Mind is likewise: it resides within the body, entering and exiting through the gateway of the face; responding to objects according to circumstances, it is sovereign and unimpeded in all that it does.
All shall achieve completion. Realize the fundamental consciousness-mind; with this consciousness-mind, one sees the Buddha. This mind is the Buddha; this Buddha is the mind.
In every thought-moment, it is the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha. If you wish to achieve success early, restrain yourself through the precepts.

Purify the discipline, purify the mind; the mind itself is the Buddha. Apart from this sovereign mind-king, there is no other Buddha. If you seek to attain Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing. The nature of the mind—
Although it is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real. Entering this Dharma-gate, one sits upright and attains Buddhahood.

Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*. A true seeker of the Way observes their own mind; knowing that the Buddha is within, they do not seek outwardly. Mind is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself the mind.
When the mind is clear, one recognizes the Buddha; when one understands, one recognizes the mind. Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha [there is no mind].
It is not the mind; neither Buddhas nor others can fathom it. It has no functional capacity; those who cling to emptiness or stagnate in quiescence drift and sink within it.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace in this [conceptualized] mind. The Great Beings who have clarified their minds awaken to this profound principle:

the nature of body and mind is wondrous, and its functioning cannot be altered. Therefore, the wise let go of the mind with ease and freedom. Do not say that the Mind-King is empty and devoid of essence, for it is capable of...

The physical body may manifest as either deviant or correct; it is neither existent nor non-existent, its appearance and concealment being indeterminate. Although the nature of the mind is empty, it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely.
Therefore, I urge you: take care to guard yourself well. Every moment of action leads once again to drifting and sinking.

The pure and clear mind-intelligence is like the gold of the world; the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā resides entirely within one’s own body and mind. This unconditioned Dharma-jewel is not something shallow.
It is not profound. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized this fundamental mind; for those who encounter it through the conditions of affinity, it is neither of the past, future, nor present.
The commentary states: When the Great Being (Bodhisattva) sent a letter to Emperor Wu, wishing to set forth the superior, middling, and inferior forms of goodness, his intention was indeed excellent.

However, these were not practices that could be implemented within China. Upon meeting Emperor Wu, he found that the Emperor’s views did not harmonize well with them, until finally he encountered Master Bao.

When the Great Being (Bodhisattva) was invited to lecture on the sutras, those who recounted the story remarked that twenty-one years had passed since the Great Being entered the court and Dharma Master Bao passed away.

Nevertheless, Master Bao’s spiritual wonders were so renowned and manifest that even after his death, he frequently descended and appeared within the imperial palace to speak of matters to the Emperor;
thus, there is no cause for doubt here. How magnificent is the *Inscription on the Mind-King*! Its phrasing and intent are sublime.
Exquisite! Its purport accords with the path of the Chan school, and its Way shares the same source as the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Were it not for the manifestation of Maitreya himself, how could such a work have been achieved? In the past, Shan谷 (Shangu) once said:

"If one understands this treatise on the Twin Trees and then reads the *Analects*, it will be like eating roasted meat and knowing its flavor for oneself. To claim to understand the chapters and sentences of the *Analects* without knowing the mind is impossible.
"I do not believe it. Even if there were authors in later generations, they would not alter my words. One may truly say that Shan Gu was one who understood speech.
At that time, there was a recluse named Ruan Xiaoxu, a native of Chenliu. His family had served in officialdom for generations; his father, Ruan Yan, was an attendant to the Grand Marshal (Taishou).
Zhonglang. At the age of thirteen, Xiaoxu mastered the general principles of the Five Classics. At sixteen, he encountered a family tragedy;

after completing the mourning period, he entered Mount Zhongshan to attend lectures. After some time, his mother fell ill. While at the lecture hall, Xiaoxu felt a sudden shock in his heart and returned home. To prepare medicine, she required fresh ginseng.
He went into Mount Zhongshan himself to search for it but had not yet found any when, suddenly, a deer appeared before him. He was struck by this as extraordinary. Upon reaching...
While he was at the Deer Breathing Retreat (Luk-sik-chu), he obtained ginseng; when his medicine was prepared, his mother’s illness was cured.

When Wang Yan, the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat of the Qi dynasty, came to visit him, Xiao Xiu (Haoxu) loathed the man and fled by breaking through the fence. When Wang Yan was subsequently executed, Xiao Xiu was spared because he was not a member of the faction.
He once used a deer forest as a vihāra, surrounding it with groves and ponds to sever all social ties; thus, few in the world were able to see him.
Ren Fang, the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat and Censor-in-Chief, wished to visit him but did not dare to approach.

He pointed toward the deer forest and said to his elder brother, "The dwelling is near, yet the man is far away. From this, the nobles of the court ceased all visits and requests, and he remained in solitude, only with—
He was on friendly terms with Pei Ziyě. Toward the end of the Tianjian era, he was summoned repeatedly but did not go.
The Emperor considered that he was merely establishing a hollow reputation to seek prominent fame; thus, both of the He brothers were able to fulfill their lofty aspirations.
Nanping Yuanyang said to him, "In the past, your grandfather declined an invitation to come and visit, thereby bringing reproach upon my younger brother. Why did you alone persist in such a resolve?"
Xiaoxu said, "If deer and elk were all fit to be harnessed alongside a carriage, how would they differ from the steed Lujì?
The Prince of Zhonglie of Poyang was his sister's husband; though the prince sent him seasonal offerings, he accepted none of them. He was a contemporary of Liu, the Court Annalist."
Liu died. Xiaoxu said, "How much longer shall I remain? He then settled his funeral arrangements and passed away several days later at the age of fifty-eight.
Xiaoxu had read extensively across all branches of literature, finding nothing he did not find excellent; his vigor and powerful memory made him a model for scholars.

Upon his death, his disciples conferred upon him the posthumous title of "Wenzhen Chushi" (Scholar of Literary Integrity). Initially, Liu Xin of the Han dynasty had composed the *Qilüe* (Seven Summaries), and Wang Jian of the Qi dynasty had composed the *Qizhi* (Seven Records).
In the fourth year of the Putong era, Xiao Xiaoxu composed the *Qilu* (Seven Catalogs).

The first five were called the "Inner Section," the sixth was the "Buddhist Records," and the seventh was the "Records of the Way of the Immortals," which he termed the "Outer Section. As for Liu Xin’s *Qilüe*, he classified the School of the Way as...
My sons, regarding the pursuit of immortality as a mere technical art, Wang Jian’s *Qizhi* places the Daoist before the Buddhist,
whereas Xiao Xiu’s *Qilu* places the Buddhist before the Daoist. This difference in what they venerate likely stems from the varying depths of their respective teachings.
The seven catalogs comprise a total of forty-four thousand five hundred and twenty-six scrolls of internal and external books and illustrations;

indeed, all the lost books and secret records of the world are contained herein. The internal Buddhist catalog consists of five divisions—Sūtra, Vinaya, Śāstra, and so forth—totaling five thousand four hundred scrolls.
During the Renshou era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, there were thirty-seven scrolls of books in the Jiaze Hall.

Ten thousand scrolls. During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, the Imperial Library organized its holdings according to the four categories of Jia, Yi, Bing, and Ding, arranging them into the four treasuries of Classics (Jing), History (Shi), Philosophy (Zi), and Literature (Ji).
Together with the works composed by Tang scholars, these totaled eighty-two thousand three hundred and seventy-four scrolls.
Today, the "Treatise on Arts and Literature" (Yiwenzhi) in the *Jiu Tangshu* records five thousand two hundred scrolls across these four categories.
One thousand one hundred scrolls. Those not recorded in the catalog number twenty-seven thousand six hundred and thirty scrolls, totaling seventy-nine thousand eight hundred and thirty scrolls.
Among these, the Śāstra section specifically lists the works composed by twenty-five monastic and lay authors, amounting to only three hundred and ninety-five scrolls.
These are the figures for books from both ancient and modern times.
In the first year of the Dàtóng era, Dharma Master Huìyuē delivered his final admonitions to his disciples; having finished speaking, he joined his palms and passed away.
The Emperor suspended court for three days and, dressed in plain mourning attire, wept for him. He was buried to the left of Zhìgōng’s stūpa.

Those who had once received the *śaraṇagamana* precepts from Huìyuē numbered forty-eight thousand people; all wore the five-month mourning dress and wept as they escorted him to the stūpa. Huìyuē habitually rode a blue ox.
They shed tears and wailed piteously. Subsequently, a pair of cranes circled the stupa, weeping mournfully for an entire month before departing.
In the fourth month of the third year, Crown Prince Zhāomíng passed away. The prince’s posthumous name was Tǒng, and his courtesy name was Wéimó.

He was born at the Báfǔ residence in the first year of the Tiānjiān era; three days after his birth, Jiānkāng was pacified. Those who understood the signs considered him to be one upon whom the mandate of Heaven had converged. From childhood, he was intelligent.
At three years of age, [Prince] Rui received instruction in the *Classic of Filial Piety* and the *Analects*. At five, he had read all five classics and was able to recite them from memory.
At eight, he lectured on the *Classic of Filial Piety* in the Shouguang Hall; eminent scholars and high-ranking officials gathered in full around him.

The Crown Prince’s speech was elegant and fluent, its profound source flowing without obstruction; everyone admired him and regarded him as a sagely child. At the age of twelve, he adjudicated legal cases within the Inner Office.
His judgments were fair and equitable; from then on, he was frequently dispatched to preside over legal cases, and those whom he saved through his mercy were beyond counting.
By nature, he was compassionate and filial, possessed of refined demeanor, and could read several lines of a book at once. He could recall and recite everything he had seen without error.

Since the Emperor had set his heart upon the Buddhist scriptures and personally lectured upon them, the Crown Prince, who by his natural disposition was also devoted to Buddhism, perused almost all the sūtras and śāstras of the Śākya school.

Everywhere. In the Eastern Palace, he established Huiyi Hall specifically as a place for the assembly of the Dharma. He summoned renowned monks to compile liturgical manuals for Buddhist rites and to establish the principles of the Three Truths and other doctrines;
the world praised him for this. When his mother passed away, he wept so bitterly at every funeral rite that he fainted repeatedly and refused all food and drink.
The Emperor commanded his attendants to proclaim an edict, saying: "To destroy oneself so as to extinguish one's nature is not the way of the sages."
This was what he had been constrained to do; unable to overcome his grief, he felt it akin to a lack of filial piety. "How could I, being here, bring myself to such self-destruction?

he thought. He then forcibly proceeded to drink rice gruel. When the Prince began to consume the gruel at the Emperor's command, his body, which had previously been stout with a waistband of ten spans, had by this time diminished by more than half.
The Emperor soon entrusted him with the affairs of state and the military; the Prince adjudicated matters without delay. He led...

He recruited the extraordinary talents of the empire, bestowing his favor and affection upon them without weariness. The Eastern Palace possessed some thirty thousand scrolls of books, and a multitude of eminent scholars gathered there;
such a flourishing of literary elegance had not been seen since the Jin dynasty. Once, while traveling on the rear pond in a gorgeously decorated boat, he plucked lotuses and water plants for sport.
His consort caused the boat to capsize, and she emerged drenched. He was stricken with illness, and his thighs began to throb with pain; fearing [the consequences],...
He did not inform the Emperor of his illness, thereby causing the Sovereign anxiety; he subsequently passed away. The people of the world wept for him as if they had lost a close relative.
A man of letters named Liu Xie was highly esteemed by the Crown Prince. He composed the *Wenxin Diaolong* (The Dragon Carving of the Literary Mind) in fifty chapters.

Being poor, he did not marry and lived in reliance upon the śramaṇa Sengyu, through whom he came to master the sutras and treatises extensively. He categorized the various classes of texts and composed prefaces for them, establishing their definitive order.

The library of the forest monastery was his own compilation and arrangement. Shen Yue, the Chief Secretary of the Palace Secretariat, held his writings in the highest esteem and would often place them upon his desk.
All the inscriptions for the monasteries and stupas in the capital, as well as those for famous monks, were composed by his hand.

Having served successively as a Chamberlain for Ceremonial Affairs, he submitted a memorial requesting to leave the household life. He first burned off his beard as a vow of self-dedication, which the Emperor praised; he was subsequently granted the dharma-name Huìdì.

In the fourth month of summer, in the third year of the Taicheng era, the rebel Hou Jing breached the Tai City. Accompanied by five hundred armored guards for his own protection, he entered the hall with his sword girded on.

Having completed his prostrations, the Emperor remained composed in countenance and gesture; he ordered him to be led toward the seats of the Three Dukes and addressed him, saying, "You have been in the military for a long time;
are you not weary? Hou Jing was so struck with terror that he could not respond. Stepping outside, he said to the Left...
The man on the right said, "Whenever I mounted my horse to face the enemy, amidst the clashing of arrows and stones, I felt no fear at all.
Now that I see Lord Xiao’s envoys, I am struck with awe and dread; is this not because his celestial majesty is difficult to defy? I shall never see him again.

When Liu Ying proclaimed himself Grand Chancellor and his demands became incessant, the Emperor grew indignant and subsequently fell ill. Nevertheless, he did not slacken in his observance of fasts and purifications, day after day.

In the evening, he recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing from his lips. Only the Crown Prince attended at his side. On the *bingchen* day of the fifth month, his condition grew grave and he could no longer take food.
After a long time, his mouth became bitter and he asked for honey; before it arrived, he raised his hand and said, "He-he," and then passed away in the Jingju Hall at the age of eighty-six.
The Emperor remarked that [the King] had the features of a horned dragon, the lines on his tongue formed the character "eight" (*bāzì*), and a fleshy protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his neck.
His body was radiant; when he stood facing the sun, he cast no shadow. The patterns on his right hand formed the characters for "Wu" (Martial).

In his youth, he once walked upon the void, and the room where he dwelt was constantly filled with cloud-like vapors. Anyone who encountered him would invariably feel a sense of solemn awe and trembling.

Throughout his life, he received more than sixty instances of imperial mandates and auspicious omens. Upon ascending the throne at the Taiji Hall, six dragons were constantly present, each guarding one of the pillars. His...

These miraculous and extraordinary omens were unprecedented among sovereigns since the inception of written records. From his youth, he was fond of learning; he was proficient in all six arts of the classics.

His skill in chess reached the highest rank. Furthermore, he thoroughly mastered the subtleties of the *Yīngyáng* (Yin-Yang) and *Wèihòu* (astrological portents), as well as divination, physiognomy, calligraphy in both cursive and clerical scripts, correspondence, horsemanship, and archery.
Although he ascended the great throne and was occupied with the myriad affairs of state, he never ceased to hold a book in his hand.

He lit candles by his side for illumination until the fifth watch of the night. He compiled the *Tongshi* (Comprehensive History) in six hundred fascicles, the *Jinhai* (Golden Sea) in thirty fascicles, and commentaries on the meanings of the Five Classics along with lecture notes totaling more than two hundred fascicles.
Furthermore, he produced one hundred and ten fascicles of miscellaneous writings, including eulogies, prefaces, imperial edicts, inscriptions, dirges, admonitions, odes, and memorials.
In his later years, he followed the Buddhist path, eating only once per day, and his meals contained no fresh meat.
His diet consisted only of bean soup and coarse rice; occasionally, when pressed by affairs and unable to find time for a meal, he would rinse his mouth and sit as soon as midday had passed.
He composed several hundred fascicles of commentaries on the meanings of various sutras, including the *Nirvāṇa*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Triśikṣā* (Three Wisdoms).
During intervals between study and lecture, he would deliver expositions at the Chongyun Hall and Tongtai Monastery. Eminent monks and great scholars from the four [directions]...

The assembly of his followers regularly numbered more than ten thousand. He wore garments of plain cloth or cotton and used black curtains for his quarters. His crown lasted three years, and his robes two.
Beyond the age of fifty, he abstained from sexual intercourse. He did not drink wine nor listen to music;

except during ancestral temple sacrifices, great assemblies, banquets, and various religious rites, he never allowed musical performances. He was diligent in his administrative duties, particularly during every winter month.

At the end of the fourth watch, he would immediately issue an edict to hold up candles to examine the documents. Holding his pen in the cold, his hands became chapped and cracked. Nevertheless, his benevolence was unceasing;
he frequently pardoned the transgressions of his kinsmen and those close to him who were favored by him. Because of this, the administration of government and justice fell into disorder.

Whenever he adjudicated a death penalty, he would always feel deep compassion and shed tears before the case could be submitted for imperial approval. By nature, he was upright and principled; even when staying in a small, dimly lit hall, he remained steadfast.
In his private quarters, he always wore his cap and robes; even when sitting for a short while during the hot months, he never bared his arms.

Although he was surrounded by palace attendants and minor officials, he treated them as if they were solemn guests. He was posthumously titled Emperor Wu, and his temple name was Gaozu (from the *Nanshi*). The court historian Wei Zheng said:
The High Ancestor was truly guided by Heaven’s decree; his intelligence was profound and he examined the ways of antiquity, ranking him among those born with innate knowledge.
His learning encompassed all things, and he was truly both civil and martial, possessing many arts and manifold talents. From his days as a student, his character was unrestrained;

when the treacherous and cruel ones ravaged the land and the bonds of kinship were struck by calamity, he gathered a righteous army to avenge his family’s grievance. Proclaiming that "Zhou may be overthrown," they assembled spontaneously like dragons meeting.

He leaped over the barriers of Fan and Han, striking like lightning upon Xiang and Ying. He severed the disunited virtues as easily as shaking down withered stalks; he seized the solitary ruler as if picking up a fallen trifle.
His heroic talent and grand strategy are truly beyond the scope of praise. Having already hung the head of the enemy upon the white flag, he was truly responding to the favor of the August Heaven.
He distributed bounty and practiced benevolence, gladdening those near and attracting those from afar, opening the path of the Great Way and transforming all that was corrupt.

The customs of the Shang region were refined; literature was extensively cultivated and ritual decorum grandly adorned. They fanned the profound breeze of the Way and propagated the scholarly vocation of Confucianism.
Using benevolence and righteousness as armor, they neutralized threats at the banquet table. Their fame shook the entire realm, and their bounty reached the distant frontiers.
For several decades, weapons of war remained sheathed; such a flourishing and magnificent state had not been seen since the Wei and Jin dynasties.

Yet they were unable to cease the branches to restore the root, or to hew away the ornate to return to the uncarved simplicity. They vied for fame and sought out novelty, exalting the frivolous and the ornate;
they suppressed Confucius and Mozi while lingering over Śākyamuni and Laozi. Some could not sleep until the end of the night, or would not eat until the sun hung high in the sky.

This was not to propagate the Way for the benefit of all beings, but merely to adorn their own cleverness to startle the ignorant. Moreover, their hearts had not yet cast off worldly glory, as they vainly occupied the positions of those who should serve as "blue-clad" attendants.
In rank, he spoke loftily of casting off one's shoes [to become a recluse], yet in the end he remained attached to the dignity of the imperial yellow canopy.
For a person, the great desires lie in food, drink, sex, and procreation; as for carriages, official robes, halls, and palaces, these are not matters of immediate personal necessity.

That the High Ancestor cast aside his cravings yet remained attached to carriages and robes—he attained what is difficult while being stalled by what is easy; it may be said that there were certain things even the spirit could not penetrate.
There are things that even wisdom cannot fully penetrate.
The commentary states: Wei Zheng’s discourse on Emperor Wu of Liang may truly be called the words of a benevolent man in all under heaven.
Furthermore, the "Biography of Xiao Yu" in the *New History of Tang* (Xin Tang Shu) also concludes with a praise stating: "The rise of the Xiao clan of Liang in Jiangzuo was indeed meritorious."
The people, in the end, committed no great evils; because [the state] declined gradually and became minute before perishing, its remaining blessings reached its descendants.
By this, one can verify that Master Zheng’s discourse is all the more detailed and accurate. Yet Han Yu once said: "Emperor Wu of Liang starved to death at Taicheng.
This was likely because he had screened off his sensual desires, ceased eating after noon, and even observed fasts and purifications until his final moments.
"Decadence. To those who indulge their passions in the enjoyment of abundance, this [simplicity] appears almost like starving to death.
It is like when Confucius spoke of Bo Yi and Shu Qi starving to death on Mount Shouyang; his subtle intention was precisely to perfect their excellence.

How could it be said that he died of hunger because he failed to obtain food? To deliberate upon gain and loss, success and failure, as Wei Zheng did, accords with the principle of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* to hold the worthy to a higher standard of accountability. How could this not serve as a standard of public justice for ten thousand generations?

In the first year of the Chengsheng era, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha was preparing to return to India. Upon arriving in Guangzhou, the Provincial Governor (Cishi) Ouyang Wei invited him to stay at Zhizhi Temple.
There, the śramaṇas Huikai and others requested that he translate treatises such as the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Paramārtha possessed a noble bearing and a spirit that was fresh and transcendent. Ouyang Wei’s son, Ouyang He, resided in a separate villa on the banks of the river; Paramārtha visited him there frequently.
He would spread his sitting mat upon the surface of the water and sit cross-legged atop it, traveling back and forth with such ease that the mat was hardly moistened at all.

At times, when he did not spread a mat, he would simply fold lotus leaves to cross over. Those who were devoted to him often depicted these events in paintings and offered them as objects of veneration.
The Layman of Jing Mountain, Lu Fahe, lived in seclusion during his youth on Mount Qingxi in Jiangling. He served the śramaṇas with devotion, observing the etiquette of a disciple.
Upon reaching adulthood, he traveled abroad; his speech was in the dialects of Ba and Chu, and his countenance was extraordinary.

Because his conduct was peerless, he was held in high esteem by Xiao Gang, the Prince of Xiangdong of the Liang dynasty, who granted him a noble rank of leisurely retirement. He was deeply revered by the various lords. Initially, when Hou Jing first...
Huan Xingjing surrendered. Fǎhé knew he would surely rebel and told Zhū Yuánīng of this; however, Yuánīng did not grasp his meaning. Before long, Huan Jing besieged the capital.
Yuánīng sought a strategy, and Fǎhé said, "To gather fruit, one must wait for it to ripen. Jing dispatched the general Rèn Yuē to attack the Prince of Xiāngdōng.
Fǎhé requested troops to oppose him, and they drew up their lines at Chìshā Lake. The rebels took advantage of the wind to launch a fire attack.
As the fire burned the thatched huts, Fǎhé waved a white-feathered fan to summon the wind; the wind immediately reversed its course, and Yuè’s army was utterly routed.
The soldiers sought Yuè but could not find him. Fǎhé said, "There is a water-stupa on the edge of the island; Yuè is beneath it. You may go and capture him.
Indeed, they found Yuè embracing the stupa, with his head tilted upward so that only his nose protruded. Fǎhé released him and said to the King, "In the future, he shall..."

He gained great influence. Based on his future results, he established the method for efficacy. Wherever he traveled along the rivers and lakes, he invariably established fish-release ponds and strictly prohibited the slaughter of living beings.
When Xiangdong ascended the throne—this being Emperor Yuan—he appointed Fǎhé as the Imperial Protector of Yǐngzhou.
Initially, Fǎhé wished to launch a grand campaign to pacify the Wei dynasty, but the Emperor did not permit it. Fǎhé laughed and said, "I have never aspired to the status of Śakra or Brahmā."
"The place where the King sits—could he possibly covet the rank of a human king? It is simply that he has a karmic connection with the Buddha *Kongwang* (Empty-King).

If it cannot be utilized, what can one do about one's karma? When Emperor Tai of Qi was defeated and returned to Qi, Emperor Xuan of Qi rejoiced at his arrival, enfeoffed him as Grand Marshal (*Taishou*), and granted him a premier residence.
Fahuo requested that it be converted into a Buddhist temple; he himself lived in a side chamber, holding an incense burner in his hand and walking about every day.

He practiced the Way, prostrating to the Buddha and burning incense, sitting in meditative concentration while anticipating the day of his death. When the time arrived, he sat and passed away; his corpse shrank by about three chi. He had inscribed on the wall:
"Ten years as Son of Heaven is still tolerable; a hundred days as Son of Heaven is urgent as fire;
a year as Son of Heaven is merely a succession of seats. He further wrote: "Two mothers give birth to three heavens; two heavens together make five years," referring to Empress Dowager Lou Da.
People were terrified; they scraped it away from the walls, yet in the end, they could not remove it. Its spiritual anomaly was such as this. Later, Qi Xu stated:
"During the Yuan Wei dynasty, General Li Qizu brought about the collapse of the Suzong era. Emperor Xiaoming held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem. The barbarian..."
The Empress Dowager personally presided over the affairs of state; within a single decade, the empire was at peace.
Upon the death of the Emperor and the Empress Dowager, Gao Huan executed the rebel Erzhu Rong at Ye and burned the palaces of Luoyang. He then escorted Prince Li of Qinghe to the throne at Ye.
For seventeen years in total, he supported and protected the Wei court. This continued until the third year of the Taiching era, when Emperor Wu passed away. Gao [Huan]...
He, too, passed away first. His son, Prince Cheng, succeeded him as the Prince of Xiang, but he died shortly thereafter.
Emperor Jing of the Wei dynasty then abdicated the throne to Gao Yang, who was the third son of Gao Huan. His clan was from Wuchuan, and he continued to reside in Ye.

His spirit was extraordinary and unconventional, possessing a mixture of wisdom and folly. Within a decade or so, the Buddhist teachings were revived, and the number of monks reached over two million.
There were approximately forty thousand monasteries in total. The six rulers succeeded one another for twenty-eight years before the state was destroyed by the Zhou.

In the third year of the Chengsheng era, Emperor Gao of the Northern Qi issued an imperial decree summoning Master Sengchou. As the master was about to set out on his journey, the mountain peaks resounded with echoes and the birds and beasts cried out in distress;
this continued for three days before ceasing. When Sengchou arrived at the capital, the Emperor halted his carriage in his honor.
He was received with honor and commanded to enter the palace to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. All five-farm falcons, dogs, and instruments for harming living beings were halted;
slaughter within the imperial precincts was prohibited. Sengchou remained in the palace for forty days before departing to reside at a monastery outside.

Shortly thereafter, an edict was issued to disband the lecture halls and to require all śramaṇas to practice meditation and contemplation exclusively. Sengchou entered the inner court to remonstrate with the Emperor, arguing that the propagation of the teachings and principles must proceed gradually.

"Inducing the young and ignorant to learn relies entirely upon formal instruction; I pray you do not forbid it. [The Emperor] followed his advice. When Emperor Xuan ascended the throne, he once paid a visit to Huida.
Huida sat upon his bed and did not rise to welcome him. One of his disciples urged him to rise, to which Huida replied:
"In the past, when the Venerable Piṇḍola welcomed King Aśoka, he rose and walked seven paces, causing the king to lose his kingdom for seven years. Although my virtue is meager, I hope..."

The Emperor obtained blessings from this; however, he was soon slandered on account of it. When the Emperor went to the temple intending to enter again, he planned to suppress [Hui]chou for his lack of respect and execute him.
Hui[chou] became aware of this and, upon the Emperor’s arrival at the temple, went out to wait for him some ten *li* away. The Emperor asked him in surprise why he had come.
Tanyou said, "I feared that my own blood would defile the monastery; therefore, I have come from afar to meet the blade. The Emperor was struck with awe and repented, apologizing for his error.
He said to his minister Yang Zun, "I was not clear-headed and recklessly insulted the Holy Master. I shall now treat him as before.
Thereupon, he spoke with composure, saying, "Your Majesty was a rākṣasa in a previous life; your current fondness for killing is surely a residual habit. The Emperor asked why this was so.
Having realized this, Zhòu requested that a basin be filled with water and he perform a self-consecration over it. He then commanded the Emperor to come and observe;
indeed, the Emperor saw his own reflection in the form of a rākṣasa, followed by a swarm of other rākṣasas. The Emperor was greatly alarmed.
From then on, he abstained from meat and spent his days in seated meditation, prostrating before the Buddha and practicing the Way with the vigor of a whirlwind.
Du Bi, courtesy name Fuyan, was a native of Quyang in Zhongshan. At the age of thirteen, when the jinshi candidate Zhen Chen questioned him on a policy essay, his pen flowed like a stream.
Upon seeing his response, Wang Cheng sighed and said, "He possesses the talent of a king’s minister. He served Gao Huan and was held in high esteem and frequently commissioned for missions.

When the Wei Emperor learned that Du Bi had a profound understanding of Buddhist principles, he asked: "In the scriptures, what is the difference between Buddha-nature and Dharma-nature? Du Bi replied: [text continues]
"This is precisely one principle. The Emperor asked, "Some teachers say that the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is broad while the *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) is narrow;
what do you say to this? Bi replied, "In being broad, it becomes broad; in being narrow, it becomes narrow. If we discuss the essence of nature (*xingti*), it is neither broad nor narrow.
The Emperor said, "Since you say it becomes broad and becomes narrow, how can it be neither narrow nor broad? Bi replied, "If it were definitively broad, it could not become narrow."
If concentration were inherently narrow, it could not become expansive; because it is neither narrow nor expansive, it can be both expansive and narrow.

Although that which is accomplished differs, the means by which it is accomplished remains constant and singular. The Emperor said, "Excellent. Having returned after his mission was successful and met with the Sovereign's approval, Wei Xiang asked him for the essentials of governance.
Bei replied, "Among the great affairs of state, none exceed the two ends of punishment and reward. By rewarding one person, all under heaven rejoice."
"Punishing a single person and the whole world submits; these two matters attain the Mean, and thus naturally achieve the utmost excellence.
Wen Xiang said with delight, "Though your words are few, their principles are most essential."

In the first year of the Shaotai era, the Daoist Lu Xiujing and others had previously been dismissed by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and subsequently fled to the Wei state; by this time, their influence had become quite prominent.

However, when Emperor Xuan of the Qi dynasty began to practice Buddhism once more, Lu Xiujing and his followers became envious. They went to the imperial palace and requested permission to compete in religious debate with the Buddhist monks.
An edict was issued ordering the Sangha Head (Sengshang) to set a date for the contest. On the appointed day, high officials and nobles gathered in great numbers. Lu...
Jing and his associates used sorcery to cause the monks' robes, alms bowls, and the beams and pillars of the palace to fly up and shake violently.
The monks looked at one another in stunned silence, unable to counter them. Thereupon, the multitude raised a clamor, declaring that the Daoist master had emerged victorious.
Xiu Jing and the others leaped for joy like fish at the sight of bait; they looked up with pride and self-importance, considering themselves to be among the ranks of the immortals.

They further remarked, "When the śramaṇa manifests one, we manifest two; he is merely using minor arts to entice us. The Emperor turned to the Imperial Preceptor (Shangtong) and said, "Is there truly no one in the Buddha-dharma?
Simply seek them out; they shall face you separately on another day. Thereupon, the matter was dropped. Not long after, the Imperial Preceptor...
He sought out the Dharma Master Tanxian and submitted a memorial requesting that Dao Liu be invited to adjudicate between them regarding who was authentic and who was false.
On the first day of the tenth month (the *yibao* day), they assembled in the main hall; the hundred officials were present as witnesses.

Tanxian, having consumed wine, stepped forth from the assembly and said, "I have heard the Master say that if a śramaṇa manifests one, I shall manifest two. Is this truly so? Xiu Jing replied, "It is so. Thereupon, Tanxian raised one finger.
Zu said, "I shall manifest one; I request that you, sir, manifest two. The Daoist remained silent and did nothing.
Xian rebuked him, saying, "Lately you have encountered no formidable opponents and have dared to indulge in your minor arts with self-satisfaction.

He then placed Master Chou’s *kāṣāya* on the ground and commanded the Daoist practitioners to join forces in performing their rites. After more than an hour, they were unable to move it. The Emperor ordered his attendants [to intervene].

He took the robe, but even ten men together could not lift it. Xian then took it himself and placed it between the rafters; he commanded his disciples to cast spells upon the beams and pillars, yet they could not move it.
His followers shrank back in shame, their faces devoid of color. Du Xiu-jing then sought once more to surpass him with his eloquence.
He then said, "The Buddhist school designates itself as the 'Inner Teaching. Since it is inner, it is small. We, the Daoist school, designate ourselves as the 'Outer Teaching.
Since it is outer, it is great. Xianying replied, "If that is so, then the Son of Heaven, residing within the nine-layered palace, should also be smaller than his hundred officials.
Jingqi remained silent and offered no response. The assembled ministers all cried out "Ten-thousand-year reign! and departed with joyful leaps. Xian did not [speak further].
It was unknown who he was; his character was vast and expansive, and his inclinations were unfathomable. His end was not known thereafter.

On the *bingchen* day of this month, Emperor Xuan issued an edict, saying: "The Dharma-gate is non-dual; the True Doctrine resides in oneness. Seeking it by the correct path, one takes profound stillness as the foundation."

As for those who call themselves "Sacrificial Masters" (*jìjiǔ dào*), they have falsely assumed this title since the middle ages; worldly people, failing to realize this, continue to revere them. Their use of fermented grain and malt is a corruption of the true flavor that obscures the essence of the Dao.
Since they deviate from the source of benevolent sacrifices and further contravene the formalities of the sacrificial canons, they should be prohibited and their custom no longer followed.
As for those Daoists who claim to have attained the state of immortality (*xiān*), they may ascend the Three-tiered Terrace (*Sānjué tái*) and fly upward.

Those who could not do so were all exhorted to abandon their delusions and return to the correct path; they were then sent to the Chief Administrator of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuan Shangtong) to undergo tonsure and enter the monastic life.
Consequently, the stream of the Way within the borders of the Qi dynasty gradually declined.
The Treatise says: At the end of the Jin dynasty, Lu Xiujing visited Master Huiyuan of Mount Kuang. The Master escorted him beyond Tiger Creek.
Later, during the Southern Qi dynasty, Prince Ziliang of Jingling also presented him with a white-feathered fan. Such was the appreciation and esteem shown by these two gentlemen.

Thus, Xiujing was indeed an extraordinary man. From the Jin dynasty until the Northern Qi, a period of some one hundred and seventy years, the methods used by [the masters of] Xian were extremely crude and vulgar; it is doubtful that they were actually devised by Xiujing himself.
Yet, both the *Lunheng* of Master Xuan of Nanshan and the *Shenqing Beishan Lu* contain this account. (2)
Laozi was not one to deceive people. Now, Xiu Jing has reportedly lived for nearly two hundred years;
if this were indeed true, he must surely possess extraordinary arts. In my view, among the followers of Xian, those who took Xiu Jing as their model have already been defeated.
Therefore, these two gentlemen falsely assumed his name to condemn him, and this I cannot fail to clarify.

The Dharma Master Fashang’s virtue and character were preeminent among his contemporaries. Emperor Xuan issued an edict establishing the ten *zhaoxuan* lineages and appointed Shang as the Grand Master of State (*Guoshi*).

An altar was constructed within the palace, and the full ceremonial protocol for seeking instruction in the Way was prepared; the Emperor requested that Shang confer upon him the *śaraṇagamana* precepts.

The Emperor spread his hair upon the ground and commanded Shang to step upon it before ascending the seat. Once the Emperor had completed receiving the Great Precepts (*mahā-śīla*), [the ceremony concluded].
Next, he commanded the high ministers of the Eight Seats, as well as the consorts, empresses, and their relatives, to all receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
He founded Baode Temple and appointed the Emperor as its presiding master. By nature, the Emperor was frugal and simple;

although he held the position of National Preceptor during his reign, he wore tattered robes of coarse cloth and never rode in a palanquin. The world increasingly held him in high esteem, and a proverb arose: "The Sage-Wang (Venerable One) of the Four Seas."
Dharma Master Fashang was at the site of practice when Emperor Wu abolished the Buddhist teachings; Fashang went into hiding in the mountains and marshes, yet he never ceased his lectures.

At the beginning of the Daxiang era, Emperor Xuan of the Zhou dynasty restored the teachings; Fashang rejoiced greatly. He was just reciting the Śrīmālā-sūtra when, halfway through it, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.

In the *Qi Shu*, the court historian Wang Shao described Buddhism, stating: "The teachings of Śākyamuni are beyond the reach of a narrow view through a tube; to speak of them rashly and recklessly would be a grave error.

He further cited the *Lie Yukou* regarding the account of Lord Shang’s Grand Chancellor questioning Confucius on the matters of the sages, as well as the passage concerning the Yellow Emperor’s journey to the land of Huaxu.
He noted that the land of Huaxu is merely equivalent to the realm where a Buddha wanders in spirit.

What is here spoken of bears a resemblance to that of the Buddha. During the Yao Qin dynasty, the stone-scriptures were translated and subsequently expanded. This was likely intended to pacify and subdue the hearts of men;
thus, many parables were employed as skillful means (*upāya*). One cannot know what kind of divine marvels they contain, for they are exceedingly vast and profound.

Their discourse concerns the good and evil of the human body and mind, as well as the causes and conditions of worldly affairs, employing [the four immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity at all times.
The *Lèwǒjìng Shū* (Treatise on Delight, Self, and Purity) distinguishes the ultimate essence; its clarity is like that of the sun and moon. Who but a Perfectly Awakened One could certify it?

All who follow the head of the Dharma take refuge in it without exception. Those who have attained realization guard their body and speech and cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom, reaching the equality of liberation and the ultimate Bodhi.
As for those who are deviant and practice it, they cannot penetrate the underlying principle; they merely labor in vain and exhaust themselves.
The pursuit of wealth, power, profit, and utility leads to turbidity; it is as if the Six Classics all have their deficiencies—it is simply that one has not delved deeply into them.
Thus it was said by Chen.
The Preface says: The fortunes of the Liang dynasty were precarious, and calamities arose from within. The rebel Hou Jing of Eastern Wei took advantage of a rift to flee to our territory.
The High Ancestor proposed that he be admitted, and he was enfeoffed as the King of Henan. Relying on this favor, he incited a rebellion and subsequently seized the Imperial City.
Prior to this, the Prince of Xiangdong of Liang had been stationed at Jingzhou and Shanzhou, and he dispatched Wang Sengbian, Chen Baxian, and others to pacify Jinling. Not yet...
Shortly thereafter, Xiangdong was destroyed by the Western Wei. After Hou Jing had been executed, Xiao Sengbian was in turn killed by Xiao Baoyin.
In the first year of the Taiping era, the Emperor of Liang abdicated the throne; Baoyin ascended the imperial throne at Jinling and established a state with his own surname.
He was originally from Changcheng in Wuxing and belonged to a prominent aristocratic family. His natural endowment was extraordinary, standing nine chi and two cun tall with a beard three chi long;

his hands reached below his knees when hanging down naturally. He possessed a lofty and liberated spirit that was highly esteemed by all. Having assumed the Great Treasure (the imperial throne), he restored the administration of the Liang dynasty and held the Śākya teachings in high honor.
Previously, there were more than seven hundred monasteries in Jinling, but they had been burned and destroyed by Hou Jing.

After how long did it perish? When Emperor Gaozu of the Chen dynasty ascended the throne, he restored everything. The translation of scriptures and the lecturing on the Way continued without interruption from the previous dynasty.
From the founding of the state until the third year of the Zhengming era, there were five emperors for a total of thirty-three years. The country was then absorbed by the Sui.
For twenty-four years it shared governance with the Northern Zhou, and for nine years it shared governance with the Sui. At that time, in the kingdom of Ujjayinī in India...

The Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman—whose name means "True Truth" (Zhendi) in the Chen language—translated forty-eight works, totaling two hundred and thirty-two fascicles, including sūtras, śāstras, commentaries, and biographies, over a period of fourteen years at various locations. It is said that he produced these works as follows: [list of titles].

The Chan Master Huiming once extracted the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* from the Tripiṭaka. Upon opening the scroll, he attained a wondrous realization of its essential meaning and immediately prostrated from afar to Nāgārjuna as his teacher.
Later, Huisi relied upon this [text]; within twenty-one days, he attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), yet his residual outflows (*āsrava*) were not yet exhausted.
Subsequently, while in meditative concentration, he relaxed his body and leaned against a wall; before it even reached the wall, he experienced a sudden, expansive awakening.

He attained entry into the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and the *āvartana-dhāraṇī*. Consequently, he observed the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-śaraṇa-śīla*) and did not wear silk or cotton.
When suffering from the cold, he would simply apply mature mugwort (*ai*) to his seat. His practice became renowned, and at that time he was called Master Sita (Great Contemplation).
When asked why he did not descend the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings, Sita replied: "The Buddhas of the three periods..."
"The Buddha has been swallowed by me in a single mouthful; what sentient beings remain to be transformed? He was frequently ill. Thereupon he reflected:
"Illness arises from karma; karma arises from the mind. If the conditions of the mind do not arise, what form can external objects take?

Karma, illness, and the body are all like clouds and shadows. Having made this contemplation, his body became light and at ease. Emperor Gaozu of the Chen dynasty summoned him to the capital and settled him at Xi.
He visited Xuansi Temple and received great respect and greetings from its community. After a long time, he took his leave to return to Mount Nanyue.
Dharma Master Hongyan was highly esteemed by Emperor Wen; when the Qi envoy Cui Wuzi came to court, Wuzi possessed such exceptional diplomatic talent that the court stood in awe of him.
The Emperor, recognizing that Hongyan excelled both in talent and learning, ordered him to serve as the guest master for Wuzi.
Zi returned home after sighing deeply. Consequently, the court deliberated on how to compel him to change his resolve, intending to bury him wearing a ceremonial cap and sash.

When Huiyan heard this command, he immediately ceased eating and swore an oath to die. The Emperor, recognizing his firm sincerity, granted his request. At that time, he was celebrated for his "Four Excellences":

his dignified appearance, his virtuous conduct, his literary compositions, and his mastery of the cursive and clerical scripts. As he approached death, he said to his disciples, "The people of this world are driven by greed."
The mind is shrouded in darkness. Being greedy for oneself, one begrudges even the loss of a single hair; yet being impoverished toward others, one never knows satisfaction.
Upon the death of the body, one makes the tomb high and the outer coffin heavy, surely believing that beneath the nine springs one will still form ties with one's neighbors.
How lamentable! Now that his eyes have closed, he has offered his humble body as dried meat for the birds and beasts.
Upon his death, his disciples followed his instructions. His collected writings comprise twenty scrolls, which by imperial decree were deposited in the Secret Library.

The Dharma Master Baoqiong was appointed as the Sanghasthavira by Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty. He managed the community with disciplined propriety, and the fourfold assembly found peace under his guidance.

He frequently entered the Chongyun Hall to lecture on the Way, and the Emperor honored him as his teacher. Initially, during the Liang and Wei periods, the Sanghasthaviras had ostentatiously adorned themselves with staffs and insignia that imitated those of government officials;
it was at this time that Baoqiong petitioned for their abolition. Whenever he went out, he was accompanied by several *dhātus* (monks) carrying staffs and alms-bowls.

Thus it was. At that time, twelve kingdoms to the east of the sea, hearing that Master Qiong’s virtue and character were beyond compare, sent envoys together to offer gold and silk in search of a portrait of Qiong. Such was the reverence and admiration he inspired throughout the world.

Upon his death, the Dharma Master Tanyan succeeded him as the Sangheśvara (Sengtong) and likewise possessed great renown. From the moment Tanyan was born, forty teeth had already fully formed. He raised [his hand]...
The World regarded this as extraordinary.
*Lōngxīng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Eight.
*Lōngxīng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Nine.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Zuxiu of the Stone Chamber in Longxing Prefecture.
Zhou Xu said: The ancestral master of the arts in the Zhou dynasty, whose courtesy name was Wenjue, was the eldest son of the Grand Chancellor Tai of the Wei dynasty.
Tai enthroned Gao Yang as emperor and moved the capital to Chang’an, establishing the dynasty known as Western Wei. This lasted for eighteen years.
The emperor was deposed and replaced by the Prince of Qi as emperor; four years later, Tai passed away. Jue succeeded to the Wei mandate, but he was himself deposed that same year.
He enthroned his younger brother, Yu, as Emperor. Four years later, he passed away, whereupon his younger brother Yong was established on the throne; this was Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou.
After more than ten years had passed, at the beginning of the Jiande era, he became deluded by the heterodox words of the Daoist Zhang Bin and others.

Fearing the prophecies concerning those in "black robes," he abolished and suppressed Buddhism, destroying more than forty thousand monasteries and compelling all three million monks to return to lay life.
Upon the extinction of the Qi dynasty, the reign title was changed before long. [Wenxuan] died in the fifth month of Xuanzheng. Crown Prince Yǒn ascended the throne, styling himself Emperor Tiānyuán.
He passed away in the fifth month of the second year of Dàxiàng. Crown Prince Yǎn succeeded him; the following year, in the second month, he abdicated the throne to the Sui.
Thus, five Zhou emperors reigned for a total of twenty-five years before the state was extinguished. Initially, when Yuwěntài and the Grand Chancellor...

Yuwen Hu also held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem. Together with more than ten Tripitaka masters from the Western Regions, he translated sutras, śāstras, works on astronomy, and other texts, totaling approximately one hundred scrolls.
In the second year of the Tiānhé era, Emperor Wǔ commissioned the Confucian monk Dào Shēn to describe the benefits and defects of the Three Teachings.

The śramaṇa Dào’ān composed twenty chapters of the *Èjiào Lùn* (Treatise on the Two Teachings), in which he categorized the nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism as "Outer Teachings" (*wàijiào*) and Śākyamuni’s teaching as the "Inner Teaching" (*nèijiào*).

His intention was that in ancient times, when simplicity prevailed, the expositions of the *Féndiǎn* had not yet spread; however, as the pure customs gradually became diluted, the teachings of Kūn and Suō...
The patterns were thus manifested. Encompassing the seven canons and synthesizing the nine schools, all serve as strategies for governing the state and are instruments for cultivating the self.
If one were to branch them out and divide them, their number would indeed be nine; yet if one were to consolidate them into a whole, they all belong to the single tradition of Confucianism.
Now, within a single transformation, the nine schools vie like competing rivers; in an age of the Great Way, they allow for only minor accomplishments.
This competitive debate surely harms the supreme wind of the Imperial Way above, while opening the door to the base and dissolute evils of confinement and license below.
When he expounded upon the Inner Scriptures (Buddhist texts) and submitted them to the court, no response was received for a long time. Dao’an was diligent in serving his mother;

regarding all matters such as water, firewood, and food and drink, he personally provided for them with his own efforts. When one of his disciples attempted to take over these tasks, Dao’an said, "This is my mother."

"How could he have been one who toils for worldly affairs? When Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty abolished the teachings, he wished to appoint Dao’an to an official post because of his esteemed reputation;
however, Dao’an refused resolutely on the grounds of death. Shortly thereafter, as the Great Teaching was being suppressed, he died in a state of wailing lamentation.

In the second year of the Jiande era, Emperor Wu first intended to abolish Buddhism entirely. He accordingly assembled his hundred officials and ordered the śramaṇas to debate their relative merits with the Daoists.

He had previously instructed the Daoist Zhang Bin to employ deceptive rhetoric to defeat the Buddhist monks, hoping that they would be defeated on the grounds of their own doctrines and subsequently cast out.
At that time, Dharma Master Zhixuan confronted the Emperor, responding with eloquence and articulating refined arguments.

It was formidable. Emperor Gaozong’s intention was to have Bin suppress him, but Bin could not restrain himself; he immediately displayed his imperial majesty and issued a stern command. His attendants shouted at Xuan, telling him to listen to the imperial decree.

Xuan responded with composure and dignity, and as he expounded upon the principles of righteousness, they grew ever loftier. Among the high ministers present, there were none who did not move with emotion, filled with reverence and admiration.
The Emperor could not humble him. The following day, an edict was issued to abolish the Daoist teachings concurrently with Buddhism.
The Dharma Master Jing’ai, hearing that the edict had been issued, sighed with indignation and said, "To consume the grain of the Zhou dynasty while forgetting its service—can this be called loyalty?

He immediately went to the palace gate to present a memorial requesting an audience. Emperor Wu granted his request. When he was summoned for an interview, he spoke at length regarding the destruction [of the Daoist teachings].

He taught the matters of the retribution of fortune and calamity, providing clear evidence and verification. The Emperor changed his expression and, seeing that the karmic consequences were already established, realized that once an edict was issued, it could not be revoked;
he therefore took leave of him and dismissed him. Da’ai withdrew and wept, saying, "The Great Teaching is being obstructed;
how can I bear to witness this? He then fled into Mount Zhongnan. The Emperor soon wished to appoint him to office and dispatched guards to search for him.

Fawei heard of this and moved to Mount Taiyi. The guards were unable to capture him and returned. Fawei lamented the extinction of the Dharma, weeping day and night for seven days without ceasing his voice.

He compiled the *Sanbao lu* (Record of the Three Jewels) in twenty fascicles, employing the roles of host and guest to skillfully modulate the arguments and demonstrate the soaring and settling of the discourse.
He extensively gathered scriptural texts and meanings to propagate and praise the Mahāyāna, while also recording the facts of what he had seen and heard;

he concealed these within mountain caves, hoping that they might be revived by future generations. He then told his disciples: "In my life I have contributed nothing to the world; I shall now perform the practice of self-sacrifice."

The multitude wailed and wept, refusing to let him go, yet he ordered his attendant to leave the mountain. Fayai then wrote a verse with his own blood and sat upon a flat rock, leaving behind only an inner garment.
He sliced his own flesh and spread it over the stone, drawing out his intestines and entrails to hang them from the branches of a pine tree until all five viscera were exposed.
The remaining flesh, muscles, hands, feet, head, and face were all mangled and torn apart; he used a knife [to finish the task].
He cut out his heart and presented it, and then passed away. When the attendant returned to the mountain, he still saw him sitting there, holding the heart.
Of the remaining remains, there was no blood at all; instead, white milk flowed alongside them and congealed upon the rocks. Among those who heard of this, there were none who did not shed tears.
He was forty-five years old at the time.
In that year, during the reign of King Wu of the Zhou dynasty when scriptures and images were being destroyed, there was a certain Minister of the People’s Department named Mr. Ren.
While dining with his subordinates, he looked up and saw six segments of an object, indistinctly appearing and then vanishing amidst the clouds.

The smallest one among them soared through the air like a banner and suddenly fell right upon their location. Mr. Ren took it and examined it; it was the nineteenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. From—
The fact that flames issued from between them without being consumed was kept secret. Emperor Xuan again gave instructions, and Ren submitted it to the throne;
the Emperor was then nineteen years of age.

Six years later, Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty extinguished the Northern Qi and occupied the capital of Ye. He assembled the monks and issued a decree on the abolition of the Buddhist teachings, which stated in brief:
"The secular laws and the three teachings have long-standing traditions. Upon examining their ultimate principles, [Buddhism] contains many errors regarding transformative cultivation.

The Six Classics of Confucianism provide a thorough understanding of the way of governance; its rites, righteousness, loyalty, and filial piety are appropriate for the world and must be preserved. Furthermore, the True Buddha does not..."

Your letter, expressing sincere respect from afar, clearly reveals the purport of the scriptures. However, the world today vainly venerates stupas and temples, adorning monasteries with exquisite ornamentation in the pursuit of merit.
Foolish people, believing and complying, exhaust their precious wealth in empty inducements and wasteful expenditure. Consequently, all such scriptures and images are subject to destruction.
That śramaṇas do not revere their parents—who owe them boundless and infinite kindness—is the height of rebellion and perversity. This must be addressed.

"Monks, nuns, and Daoists should all return to their secular dress to honor filial piety and support their parents. This is my intention. If you have any other reasoning, you may state it fully; do not withdraw or harbor slanderous words.

The Dharma Master Huiyuan stepped forward from the crowd and replied: [The Emperor said: "Monks, nuns, and Daoists should all return to their secular dress to honor filial piety and support their parents.
