This is my intention. If you have any other reasoning, you may state it fully; do not withdraw or harbor slanderous words. The Dharma Master Huiyuan stepped forward from the crowd and replied:
Your Majesty presides over a great nation, attaining the position of supreme honor and establishing the statutes for the Three Teachings.

Yet Your Enlightened Edict states: "The True Buddha is formless; this is truly as Your Imperial Decree declares. However, the common people rely upon the scriptures to hear of the Buddha, and they depend upon the teachings to manifest the Truth.

If these were to be abolished, there would be no means by which goodness could be promoted. The Emperor replied: "The True Buddha exists inherently within the void of space; why should one rely upon scriptures?"

Xiang Yuan said: "Before the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han, scriptures and images had not yet reached this land. Among the common people, none were known to have spoken of a 'True Buddha' as being the void.

If one could know [the truth] without relying on the teachings, then prior to the Three Sovereigns, when written characters did not yet exist, one ought to have naturally understood the Five Constant Virtues.
If you claim that serving clay images—which are insentient—is of no benefit, then [consider that] in ancient times, people lived in caves and dwelt in the wilds."

If one dwells in a place where benevolence and righteousness are not practiced, yet the Five Emperors observed the patterns of nature to establish their teachings—divinizing them to transform the people so that they would take them as models—then how can the current Emperor’s establishment of the seven ancestral temples, which likewise constitutes a path of reverence and obedience, ever be abolished?

Furthermore, the Imperial Decree dispatches monks to return to lay dress to honor filial care. Confucius said: "Establish oneself and practice the Way to bring glory to one's parents. This is filial piety.
This is the ultimate [principle]. For one who practices benevolence and wisdom, how could filial piety necessarily begin with residing at home?
Tanyuan opposed the Emperor’s decree from afar; his anger was evident in his words and countenance. Tanyuan remained solemn and fearless, replying further:

"Your Majesty may employ your power to disparage the Great Teaching at will, yet the Buddha taught that the retribution of calamity and fortune in the unseen world does not depend on whether one is noble or humble. I, this poor monk, privately [fear]..."

The Emperor cherished him and commanded his attendants to lead him away; dissatisfied, he ended the interview. At that time, more than two million monks and nuns within the borders of Qi were ordered to return to secular dress.
Having conquered Qi, Emperor Wu of Zhou’s prestige shook the world, yet Fayuan alone opposed him with unyielding integrity.
The Emperor held his steadfast rectitude in high regard and did not punish him for his defiance. Consequently, Fayuan fled into the western mountains of Jiji Commandery. Fayuan...
His appearance was full and handsome; his waist measured ten spans, and his voice was like a bell. Whenever he presided over a lecture hall, those who saw him felt a sense of solemn reverence.
He composed commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, and other sutras. During the revolution that established the Sui dynasty, he was held in high esteem by Emperor Wen.
In the seventh year, Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou passed away, and his son, Emperor Xuan, ascended the throne.

At Mount Zigai in Zhongnan, the śramaṇa Fazang shaved his hair, donned the full monastic robes, and entered the capital. The relevant authorities reported this to the Emperor, who said with great joy:

"I have desired to restore the teachings of Śākyamuni, and yet a monk has come from Mount Zigai. He immediately summoned him for an audience and asked: "I have already issued orders to repair the Shizhu Peak."
The temple authorities were about to restore the Buddhist teachings, but the court deliberated that what had been practiced by the previous dynasty should not be easily altered so abruptly.

They asked, "Since you have come from afar, Master, how will you instruct us? Paramārtha’s words and intentions were shallow and blunt, greatly offending the Emperor's sentiments; he was consequently expelled.
Previously, one Ren Daolin, whose learning was profound and extensive, gained the favor of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou.

For over twenty days they engaged in debate, exchanging views seventy times. Although Emperor Wu exhausted his refined reflections, he could not defeat him; the Emperor once promised to restore the Buddhist teachings on his account.
The previous assembly had failed to achieve its goal when it collapsed; now, Daolin renewed his petition with particular vigor. The Emperor followed his request.
On the twenty-sixth day of the second month, he issued an edict stating: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and sublime, revered by all throughout antiquity.

How could it be appropriate for it to remain hidden and neglected? From this day forward, from the princes and dukes down to the common people, all shall practice and serve it. Let them know my intent."
On the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month, another edict was issued, stating: "The principles of the teachings are profound and mysterious, and their spiritual wonders are vast and great.

Although the rituals for broad conversion have been extensively opened up to facilitate the practice of cultivation, those who venerate [the Dharma] need not shave their hair, lest they deviate from the Great Way."
It was appropriate to establish the ritual protocols for Bodhisattvas, with ceremonial robes, crowns, and sashes; thus, the relevant authorities drafted a formal code of conduct.
Thereupon, Senglin and others carefully selected one hundred and twenty veteran śramaṇas whose virtuous conduct was pure and refined, and whose reputations were preeminent.

They entered Zhuhusi to continue their residence there as before. Before long, the Zhou dynasty declined, and Emperor Wen of the Sui overthrew it, restoring the teachings of Śākyamuni on a grand scale.
The treatise states: When Master Xuan of Nanshan recorded the debate between Ren Daolin and Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty, there were over seventy rounds of exchange.
Yet Emperor Wu frequently used the scriptures and other treatises as pretexts to obstruct Daolin. Among these, there are indeed points worthy of consideration.
Just as the Six Classics were transmitted to the world for the purpose of assisting the sovereign and benefiting the people, yet Wang Mang utilized them...

This is a literary fabrication; how could it not be erroneous? How magnificent was Master Lin’s insight! Having followed the Emperor in abandoning the monastic path, he presented himself in the coarse robes of a lay scholar.
When he was questioned regarding the imperial edict, he synthesized the teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism to elucidate the principles by which they bestow blessings upon both heaven and man.
His gentle and enlightening discourse nearly dispelled the delusions of Emperor Zhou Wu. Yet, before long, the Master passed away.

That Emperor Xuan was able to issue such edicts was also due to his power. Had Senglin been established in court at a time of crisis, even Chen Ping or Li Ji (Diliang Gong) could have added nothing to him.
The two masters, Xuan and Yuan, exerted themselves with upright and resolute speech; they revered the Dharma and forgot their own bodies.
While Zhou Wu relied on titles and rank to encourage rewards for the world, wishing to bestow wealth and honor upon others, those superior men—
Could these two gentlemen indeed be of such a class? When the teachings of the masters An and Ai were preserved, they flourished; when their teachings ceased, they perished.
Alas! They were truly worthy men, following in the tradition of Yan Hui and Duan Zhu.
The Mandate of Heaven has bestowed upon the Sui the succession of these five dynasties. The Sovereign Lord, graced by divine favor, dwells within these nine provinces.

Thus, at the very moment of his birth, a divine radiance shone forth; and since he ascended the throne, auspicious omens have vied with one another to arrive. Therefore, the celestial signs were manifested through the tortoise.

Wen Water floats in five colors; the earth opens to reveal sweet springs, and the mountains resound with cries of "Ten Thousand Years. Clouds bring auspiciousness, dew is sweet, pearls become luminous, and stones undergo transformation.
The deaf hear, the blind see, the mute speak, and the lame walk. Birds and beasts witness extraordinary omens, while plants and trees manifest portents beyond record.
Thus we know that the seven treasures heard of in antiquity were not confined to the Golden Wheel [of a Cakravartin King]; today, such divine wonders pervade the four seasons.
I know the King’s illumination. In the past, in the year of *chìruò* (赤若), he governed the imperial throne from within the yellow-canopied carriage.

When the element of Earth suppressed the movement of Water, the sun of the Buddha was eclipsed by destruction; when the element of Fire ascended the cycle of Wood, the auspicious title of Kāi huáng (開皇) was inaugurated.

In the second year of the Great Peace (*Dàdìng*) era of Emperor Jìng of the Zhou dynasty, a yellow dragon descended upon his former residence, and auspicious clouds (*qīngyún*) appeared at the city gates on the thirteenth day of the second month.
The Zhou dynasty returned the imperial mandate through abdication to the Sui. As the Great Mandate descended, the yellow robes replaced the black.
The Six Ministries of the Zhou were abolished, and the Three Departments of the Han were adopted. The Sun of the Buddha shone once more, and the Water of the Dharma flowed secretly.

That winter, a monk from the Zhou dynasty arrived at the appointed time, bringing more than two hundred Sanskrit scriptures from the Western Regions. An imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities to seek out translators. Thus, [the era of] Kai... was opened.

In the second year of Huang, during the second month of spring, the proclamation was issued. In the final month of summer, an edict was promulgated that the mountains, rivers, plains, and valleys of Longshou were magnificent and the flora and fauna flourished there;
thus, it was deemed fit to establish the capital. All city walls, palaces, gates, commanderies, gardens, and monasteries were named Daxing.
From this point on, the compassionate transformation of the Triple Gem began to flourish, and the benevolent influence of the empire spread far and wide across the ten thousand nations.
Monasteries stand tall and majestic, their halls facing one another; bodhisattvas shoulder to shoulder, and those of faithful heart flock together.

When the Renshou era began and the precious stupas were erected, auspicious responses were manifested across more than a hundred provinces. At that time, the four seas were calm and the nine regions were free from dust.
The number of ordained monks and nuns reached nearly three hundred thousand, and the temples and monasteries being renovated and constructed numbered close to five [thousand].
[The number of] thousand [volumes]. Twenty-four monastics and laypeople served as translators, producing nearly five hundred fascicles of sutras and śāstras.

When Emperor Yang succeeded to the throne and established his capital in the Eastern Metropolis (Luoyang), he subsequently established a Translation Hall at Shanglin Park on the banks of the Luo River.

At that time, the four types of offerings were provided without lack. Now, I shall recount the thirty-seven years of two reigns under one dynasty, [and the achievements of] the ancestral masters and eminent scholars.
There were fifteen eminent masters of the monastic community who manifested the flourishing prosperity of our teaching during the Sui dynasty.
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, there was the Dharma Master Tanyan, whose physical presence was extraordinary; he stood nine chi and six cun tall, with his hands hanging down past his knees.
His gaze was directed outward. His reputation and wisdom were equal to those of Huiyuan. He composed commentaries on the meanings of various sutras.

Critics remarked that while Huiyan excelled in outlining the essential points and headings, Huiyuan surpassed him in the elegance and appropriateness of his phrasing. Emperor Taizu of the Qi dynasty followed his advice, seeking his counsel and providing him with a monthly stipend.
It happened that the Zhou envoy Zhou Hongzheng arrived on a diplomatic mission; the high officials recommended Huiyan to serve as the host for the reception. Hongzheng...

He had previously relied solely on his own talent and standing above others; upon meeting Daoyan, his pride was naturally dispelled. Upon returning home, he sought out Daoyan’s portrait as well as the commentaries and treatises he had authored, and brought them back with him.

The Emperor held him in even greater esteem, promoting him to the rank of Upper Patriarch of the Zhaoxuan Monastery. This occurred before Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou abolished the Buddhist teachings.
Fayan fled into Mount Taihang. When Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty ascended the throne through the rite of abdication, Fayan shaved his hair that very day and went to pay his respects as a śramaṇa.

Emperor Wen was greatly pleased and issued an edict restoring his monastic status. After some time, there was a drought; by imperial decree, Fayan was ordered to lead the assembly in praying for rain.

The rain did not fall. The Emperor asked for the reason. He replied, "The matter depends on 'one' and 'two'. The Emperor immediately dispatched Su Wei, the Governor of the Capital, to inquire about the meaning of "one" and "two.
Yan said, "Your Majesty personally manages the myriad affairs of state, while the various ministers exert the strength of your limbs."
Although they were both capable of governing the state, they both fell short of the profound transformation [of the people]. Whether it rains or does not rain depends on these two factors.

The Emperor perceived their intent and issued an edict to the relevant authorities to select an auspicious day to establish the ritual in the main hall. He commanded Yan Shou to bestow the Eight Precepts upon him;
once the ministers had received them in succession, the scorching heat was like a burning fire when a great rain poured down in torrents. The Emperor was delighted, and from that time on—

Whenever Fayen entered the court, he would personally present the imperial provisions to serve the Emperor. At the time of his death, he submitted a memorial to take leave of the Emperor, entrusting him with external protection.
The Emperor wept for him most bitterly. On the day of the funeral, the various officials attended in white mourning garments to see him off.

The Palace Secretary Xue Daoheng composed a written offering of sacrifice, which stated in brief: "In the past, when the Way fell into ruin and the dark threads of governance were loosened, you took refuge in the secluded crags with an unshakable resolve."
High rank and generous emoluments could not turn his thoughts; stern authority and rigorous laws were insufficient to intimidate his mind.
Whether walking or sitting in meditation, he remained unchanged in both prosperity and adversity. His precepts and virtuous deportment were consistent from beginning to end.

When the Sage Emperor initiated his mandate and the Semblance Dharma flourished once more, this eminent monk in black robes rose as the preeminent leader. He humbled himself before the gravity of imperial majesty to uphold the principle of the teacher-disciple relationship.

Through her, the Three Jewels were propagated and protected; by means of her, the Two Truths were proclaimed. Her faith was sufficient to allow her to follow in the footsteps of Fotudeng and Kumārajīva, and to surpass Dao’an and Huiyuan.

As for the nun Zhixian, she was the daughter of a commoner from Puzhai in Hedong. She left home to become a nun in her youth and maintained strict observance of the precepts. In her maturity, she attained profound understanding.

In her meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), she spoke of matters concerning fortune and misfortune, success and failure; there was nothing that did not prove wondrously accurate. She resided at Bore Monastery (*Prajñā-vihāra*).
It happened that Emperor Wen was born in this monastery during the peak of the summer heat. His wet nurse suddenly fanned him, and the Emperor was so chilled that he nearly died;
he could not cry. Those around him were greatly alarmed. The nun went to examine him and said, "This child is protected by Heaven and the Buddha; you need not worry. Immediately—
Lifting him up, she called out, "Nārāyaṇa," and thus he was given that as his childhood name. She carried him to the Great Ancestor (Taizu) and said, "The origins of this child are beyond compare;
an ordinary household is defiled and unsuitable for him to remain in. I request that you raise him.

Thereupon, the Great Ancestor partitioned off a section of his residence with a small gate leading to the temple, entrusting the child to the Immortal (Xian) to care for and nurture. Later, when the Empress Dowager came to embrace him, she suddenly saw the child as a dragon.
He fell to the ground in alarm. The immortal cried out in distress, "Why have you struck and harmed my son? This will cause him to attain the throne of the world late in life.
When the Emperor had grown somewhat older, the immortal secretly told him, "In the future, you shall become greatly honored; [the Dharma] shall come from the East.

The Buddha-dharma will temporarily perish, but it shall flourish again because of you. When Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty suppressed the teachings, the immortal hid within his household, donned the dharma robes, and observed the precepts.
His devotion was even more profound. By this time, the Emperor had indeed entered from the east of the mountains to become the Son of Heaven and greatly promoted the teachings of Śākyamuni.
Xuán had passed away prior to this; the Emperor frequently mentioned the *ācārya* to his ministers as a point of conversation.

He also remarked, "My rise to power was due to the Buddha-dharma," and added, "I am fond of eating sesame and beans; my previous life must have been among the practitioners of the Way. When I was young, I resided in a monastery for a long time."
He was raised [in this way], and even until his later years, he delighted in hearing the sounds of the bells and stone chimes.

In the fourth year, a drought struck the region of Guanzhong. The Emperor led the people to seek sustenance in Luozhou. Previously, the Vinaya Master Lingzang had been a friend of the Emperor from their days as commoners;
upon this occasion, the Emperor commanded Lingzang to accompany him on the journey. Subsequently, those who flocked toward Lingzang became exceedingly numerous. The Emperor...
Upon hearing this, the Emperor issued a hand-written decree, saying: "I, your disciple, am a secular Son of Heaven; the Vinaya Master is a monastic Son of Heaven.
Those who wish to leave secular life may be ordained by the Master as he sees fit. From that time on, Huizang ordained people in succession, numbering tens of thousands.
When someone slandered him, the Emperor said: "The Vinaya Master transforms people toward goodness; I, your disciple, restrain people from evil. Though our words differ, our aims are one."
In intent, there was no difference.

Once, the śramaṇa Tánxún encountered two tigers fighting for a long time without ceasing. Xún held up his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) to separate them and used his own body as a shield, saying, "You dwell together in these woods and thickets;
there is no great cause for conflict. It would be fortunate if you each took a different path. The tigers then submitted.
Wu received the command and immediately drew in his breath and dispersed [the apparition].
At that time, when the Dharma Master Tanchong was approaching death, a lay youth appeared, standing to the right of his seat holding a radiant light in his hands. His disciples asked, "Who is this?

Tanchong replied, "The Sixth Heaven has frequently come to summon me. However, because the devas are attached to pleasure, which hinders the cultivation of the Way, I have ultimately refused them. After my passing, I wish—"
He was born in a place where the Buddha-dharma did not exist and taught sentient beings there; he cautioned them never to speak of it openly while alive, but to do so as they wished after his death.
In the eighth year, Li Shiqian passed away. Li Shiqian’s courtesy name was Yue. He lost his father in childhood and served his mother with such filial piety that it became renowned.
His clan elder, Bo Zhang, often sighed, saying, "This son is our family's Yan Hui. He was skilled in astronomy and the arts of divination, and considered himself...

Orphaned at a young age, he never drank wine or ate meat. Although the Li family was of long-standing nobility and their banquets were always filled with an abundance of exquisite delicacies set before them, Suiqian would first prepare millet for them and say to his kinsmen, "Confucius called millet the foremost of the five grains."
Xun Qing also said that eating millet and sacrificial grain first is what the ancients esteemed; how could one dare to contravene this? Young and old alike were struck with solemnity.
Later, he remarked to others, "Now that I have seen this gentleman, I realize for the first time the lack of virtue in my own kind.

Once, when an ox trespassed upon his field, Shen Qusheng led it away, placed it in a cool spot, and fed it until it was better cared for than by its original owner. He even saw a thief cutting his millet.
Whenever such things occurred, he would remain silent and avoid them. During years of famine, he distributed grain and combined various medicines to relieve epidemics.

He continued in this manner for thirty years. He was deeply devoted to the Buddha, and his conduct was restrained by the precepts and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*). Someone remarked that he was practicing "hidden virtue" (*yin-de*).
Sishen smiled and said: "Hidden virtue is like ringing in one's own ears; it is known only to oneself and cannot be known by others. Now...
"Those who practice benevolence, all know this. What 'hidden virtue' (yin-de) could there be? You are most skilled in profound discourse.

A guest harbored doubts regarding the Buddhist doctrine of karmic retribution (*vipāka*). Li Shiqian explained to him, saying: "The accumulation of good brings forth blessings; the accumulation of evil brings forth calamity. Is this not the very sign of fortune and misfortune?
The Buddha says that one revolves through the five realms of existence without end. And Jia Yi also said: 'A thousand...'"
The transformations of myriad phenomena have never had a limit. For instance: Gun became a yellow bear; Du Yu became a *tí-fú* bird;
King Bao became a dragon; Niu Ai became a tiger; the gentleman became a crane; the commoner became a monkey; Peng Sheng became a boar; Rui Yi became a dog;
Huang Mu became a soft-shelled turtle; Xuanwu became a snapping turtle; Deng Ai became an ox; Xu Bo became a fish; and Yang Hu [became a sheep].
He was previously the son of the Li family. These are all verifications of the Buddhist doctrine regarding the transformation of forms as retribution for one's karma.

A guest further remarked, "Xing Zicai said that in this world there are cases where pine and cypress trees transform into *chū* and *lì* trees; I believe this to be true. Lü Shuqian said, "This is a discourse on things that do not correspond.
Transformation arises entirely from the karma of the mind; how could it have anything to do with wood? He was then asked about the relative merits of the Three Teachings.
Shiqian said, "The Buddha is the sun; the Daoist Way is the moon; Confucianism is the five planets. The guest was unable to refute him and departed. The *Lun* says:
The Northern Dynasties historian Jiang Shen and others recorded the deeds of Master Li in such detail.
Was this not because he harbored the virtue of the Buddha and exhausted his own sincerity, not daring to deceive or mislead those who would come after? Master Shi—
I humbly compare [these] to the sun, moon, and stars—the three luminaries of the Three Teachings. At first glance, they appear to have degrees of superiority or inferiority;

yet, when it comes to illuminating the world and sustaining the life-force of sentient beings, their virtue is one and the same. If even one of these three were missing, the establishment [of the world] could not be achieved.
Thus, the *I Ching* says: "The Way of Qian undergoes transformation, and each thing rectifies its own nature and destiny. How worthy is Master Li! I have observed you...
He was profoundly learned in the great source of human nature and destiny.

In the thirteenth year [of the reign], the Second Patriarch, Great Master Huìkě, passed away. The Master was a native of Húláo; in his youth, he extensively studied a vast array of books and was particularly adept at the profound principles of metaphysics (*xuánlǐ*).
Upon reading Buddhist scriptures, he attained a transcendent realization on his own and subsequently left the household life, taking refuge at Mount Xiāng in Lóngmén.
When Chan Master Baojing had received ordination and attained full precepts, he was only forty years old. One day, while in meditative concentration, a spirit informed him:

"You are about to realize the fruit of sainthood; do not be obstructed by this place. Immediately thereafter, he suddenly felt a headache as piercing as thorns. Desiring to go seek medical treatment, he prepared to depart.
A voice from the air said, "This is merely changing your bones; it will not be without great pain.
He reported this to his master, who observed that five peaks had protruded upon his crown and said, "Since the spirits have already assisted you, you may go forth to seek the Way.
I have heard that Bodhidharma of India has recently arrived at Shaolin; you should go there to rely upon him. The Master went to Shaolin, where he attained the Dharma through the meeting of minds.
The details of this account are found in the "Dharma" chapter. When the [First] Patriarch of Shaolin entered nirvana, the Master (Huike) succeeded him in propagating the profound teachings.

Once, while traveling in Northern Qi, he encountered a lay devotee who would not disclose his surname or name, saying only: "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic wind ailment; I pray that you, Master, will perform a rite of repentance for my transgressions."
The Master said, "Bring forth your offense so that I may repent it for you. After a long while, the layman said, "I have searched for my offense, but it is utterly unobtainable.

The Master said, "I have finished repenting your offense for you; you should now dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The layman said, "Now that I have met the Master, I already know what this Sangha is."
He asked, "I do not yet understand what is called the Buddha-dharma. The Master said, "This mind is the Buddha; this mind is the Dharma. Dharma and Buddha are non-dual; so too is the Sangha-treasure.
[The student] said, "Today I have finally realized that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
The mind is likewise so; the Buddha and the Dharma are non-dual. The Master held him in high esteem and immediately shaved his hair, saying, "This is it."
"He is my treasure. He should be named Sengcan. Having completed the bestowal of the full precepts, he then told him:
"Master Bodhidharma came from India and secretly transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to me. I now entrust it to you, along with Bodhidharma’s robe of faith.
You must protect and uphold it so that it does not come to an end. Listen to my verse: 'Originally there is the ground of conditions; because of the ground...'"
"Seeds give rise to flowers, yet fundamentally there are no seeds; the flowers, likewise, have never been born. You should receive my instruction:

you ought to dwell in the deep mountains and not yet go forth to transform others. There will be national calamity. He asked, "Since the Master already knows this in advance, I pray you will grant me your guidance. The Master said:
Formerly, Bodhidharma transmitted the teachings of Prajñātāra, whose prophetic record stated: "Though auspicious within the heart, there is misfortune on the outside;

it falls precisely upon your person when I calculate the years. You must carefully consider these previous words and avoid the calamities of this world. However, I too have karmic debts from former lives."

"Now I must repay this debt. The Master then traveled through the capital of Ye, teaching and transforming others as circumstances required. After thirty-four years had passed, he concealed his traces and mingled with the common folk.
Sometimes he would pass by a butcher’s shop, or enter a tavern. To those who questioned him in wonder, he replied:
"I am merely disciplining my own mind; it has nothing to do with your affairs. Finally, at the triple gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guancheng County, he sat and spoke.
Regarding the Unsurpassed Way, listeners gathered like clouds. There was a Dharma Master named Bianhe who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* within the monastery.

When his disciples heard that the Master was preaching the Dharma, they gradually drifted away. Bianhe could not bear his indignation and instigated a slander against the district magistrate, Zhai Shen.
Shen was obstinately deluded by those arguments and unjustly accused the Master. Consequently, the Master remained serene and submitted to his fate; he was one hundred years old.
Seven. One who recognizes the truth is called a master who settles his debts. He was buried seventy li northeast of Gan County in Cizhou.
The Tang Emperor Dezong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Taizu.
In the seventeenth year, an imperial decree summoned the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai.

Upon arriving at Shan County, he manifested illness and expounded for his disciples such teachings as the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), the four non-arisings, the ten dharma-realms, the three contemplations, and the four wisdoms.

When a disciple asked about the stage of spiritual attainment he occupied, he replied: "I do not lead a multitude; I shall surely purify my six sense faculties. I have sacrificed myself to benefit others."

Having attained the rank of the fifth stage, he took up his brush and finished writing out the *Guanxin jie* (Verses on Contemplating the Mind), after which he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Zhiyi was born into the Chen family;

his eyes possessed the rare feature of double pupils (*dvyakṣi*). Initially, he visited Master Zhiyi (Huisi), who instructed him in the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s place of practice and expounded the Four Practices for Peaceful Bliss.

Delighted, Zhiyi withdrew to a secluded chamber to study and savor the profound principles of the *Lotus Sūtra*. When he reached the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," he realized it was the true essence of diligent practice.
Upon reaching these words, he attained great enlightenment; his concentration and wisdom were seamlessly integrated. He immediately informed Huìsī, who said:
"It was not that you could not realize it, nor that I could not recognize it. This is the *Sūtra-entrance Dharani* (Xuan-tuoluoni) manifested before one through the *Lotus Samādhi*.

Even if there were ten million masters of letters, none would be able to exhaust your eloquence. You may continue the transmission of the Lamp; do not become the last one to sever the seeds of the Buddha."
Huiyi respectfully accepted this entrustment. After a long time, he took his leave to travel to Jinling, where he stayed at Wagong Temple.
One night, he dreamed that he ascended a high mountain and looked down upon the vast ocean, where he saw a bhikṣu named Dingguang who beckoned him with his hand.
Later, when Huiyi led his disciples to Mount Tiantai, Dingguang came out to meet him and said, "Do you perhaps remember our mutual invitation from days past? Huiyi gazed intently...

He looked, and it was indeed what he had seen in his dream. Guang said, "I already possess the golden ground at this location; the Silver Ground at Luoxi on the northern peak of Fulong would be a suitable place for practicing the Way.
After some time, Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty issued an imperial decree [summoning him], but Huiyi remained firmly reclined and did not rise.

The messenger returned seven times. Emperor [Wen] dispatched Prince Yongyang to convey his earnest intentions. Having no choice, Zhiyi went to the capital. He was invited into the Taiji Hall to lecture on the scriptures;

the Emperor treated him with the etiquette due to a disciple and appointed him as National Teacher. By imperial decree, he was provided with a carriage drawn by rams and a ceremonial escort, and was given the honorary title "Zhizhe" (the Wise One).
Not long after, the Emperor dreamed of a sovereign whose retinue was most magnificent, and who was hailed by attendants as "Guanda" (Crown Attainer) as they came to welcome him.
Dharma Master Zhiyi resided at Sanqiao. Upon awakening, he sighed and said, "The Dharma-name bestowed by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty was 'Guanda' (Crowned Sage).
Sanqiao is now Guangzhai Temple. He immediately moved Zhiyi to reside there. When the Sui dynasty conquered Chen, Emperor Yang, while still a prince, requested that he receive the five precepts.

Zhiyi then took his leave and returned to Fulong Mountain, where he composed commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), the *Xiuxan Fa* (Methods for Cultivating Dhyāna), and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

His commentaries (*shu*) numbered over one hundred fascicles; all were composed extemporaneously as they issued from his mouth. His attendants transcribed them by hand, yet he did not retain a single character himself.

He established thirty-six great *dàodǎng* (Dharma-halls), ordained fifteen thousand monks, copied fifteen sets of the Buddhist canon (*kāṇḍa*), and fashioned eight hundred thousand images of gold, copper, wood, and earth. Once, while he was preaching the Dharma, the śramaṇa Huìróng...
This man was renowned in the world as the "Tiger of Meaning," and his eloquence was celebrated as a "Suspended River. Having heard that Huiyi was lecturing on the Dharma, he came to pose questions;

his numerous inquiries and investigations were all profoundly subtle and recondite. Huiyi’s responses, however, elucidated the principles and facts with such clarity and precision that Yao Rong sighed in admiration, saying, "The power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is truly irresistible.
Thus, the general outline of his system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) takes the body and mind as the basis for establishing both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
His discourses elucidate liberation; from the initial arousal of the bodhicitta until the attainment of the Way, his stages of practice are clearly illuminated.
Consequently, those throughout the world who speak of the Buddha-dharma take Tiantai as their compass.

In the third year of the Renshou era, after Wang Tong, known as Wenzhongzi, had reached the age of majority, he was filled with a profound resolve to save the world. He traveled west to Chang’an to have an audience with the Emperor.
The Emperor, seated in the Taiji Hall, summoned him for an interview, whereupon Tong presented thirteen memoranda on the strategy for achieving Great Peace.

He honored the Way of the King and promoted the strategies of the Hegemons; examining antiquity and verifying it against the present, he encompassed the governance of the world as easily as turning it over in his palm.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and said, "How late I have been to obtain you! Heaven did not grant me your birth earlier. He then issued a decree for the high officials and ministers to deliberate upon this matter.
The high officials were displeased; at that time, there was the looming threat of internal rebellion within the palace walls.

Realizing that his plans were not being adopted, he composed the "Song of the Eastern Expedition" and returned home. Thereupon, he continued the *Shi* and *Shu*, rectified the rites and music, compiled the *Yuanjing*, and expounded upon the Way of the *Yi*.
Within nine years, the Six Classics were largely completed. Disciples came to him from afar, including Dong Chang of Henan and Yao Yi of Taishan.

Du Ruhui of Jingzhao, Li Jing of Zhaojun, Cheng Yuan of Nanyang, Dou Wei of Fufeng, Xue Shou of Hedong, Jia Qiong of Zhongshan, Fang Xuanling of Qinghe, Wei Zheng of Julu, Wang Gui and Wen Yanbo of Taiyuan, Chen Shuda of Yingchuan, and others—all addressed him as their teacher.
They faced north to receive his instruction in the Way of the Royal Assistant; the rest came and went as disciples.
Those who received his teachings numbered over a thousand. During the Daye era, he was repeatedly summoned by imperial decree but did not comply.
In the thirteenth year, while suffering from illness, he heard of disturbances in Jiangdu. He rose with tears in his eyes and said, "The common people have long been weary of chaos.

Heaven may perhaps be about to open the era of Yao and Shun; yet I shall not participate in it—this is my fate. He subsequently passed away. His disciples posthumously conferred upon him the title Wénzhōngzǐ (Master of Literary Profundity).

I once composed the *Zhongshuo* (Discourse on the Center) as a counterpart to the *Lunyu*. Its chapter on the Duke of Zhou states: "The flourishing of the *Shi* and *Shu* led to the destruction of the Qin dynasty;
this was not the fault of Confucius. The growth of metaphysical emptiness led to the chaos of the Jin house; this was not the fault of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
The observance of fasting and purification led to the fall of the Liang state; this was not the fault of Śākyamuni. Does the *Yi* not say: 'If it is not the right person'?"
"The Way does not travel in vain. Someone asked about the Buddha, and [Tong] said, "He was a sage. [The questioner] asked, "What is his teaching like?

[Tong] replied, "It is the teaching of the West; in China, it would be mired in stagnation. He further remarked, "If one examines the *Huangji dangyi* (Discourse on the Imperial Ultimate), the three teachings are therein seen as one.
Tong’s younger brother, Ji, also authored a work titled *Donggaozi*.
The Master of Wén was lecturing on the Way at Bǎiwǔ Creek. His disciples held their books and stood in rows facing north, encircling the hall.
When the lecture concluded, Chéng Shēng withdrew to reflect beneath a pine tree. As the conversation turned to the *Zhouyī*, Xuè Shōu sighed and said, "Is it not inferior to that of Fúxí?
Why such an abundance of words? Shortly thereafter, a man carrying a load of fungi appeared, looking white-haired and aged, as he set down his burden.
Xī said, "My son, why do you sigh? Xuē Shōu replied, "Old man, what are you doing that you inquire about my sighing?
The one who carried the fungi said, "That which is near red becomes red; that which is attached to black becomes black. This is obtained through gradual influence.
Now, you, my son, serve the Dao, yet you still sigh. This means your six bowels and five viscera cannot receive it. That is why I asked."
Xue Shou said, "I have heard from my teacher that the *Yi* is the repository of the Way.
When Fuxi drew the hexagrams and King Wen appended the lines, he did not even bother to examine the wording. This is why I sigh. The one who carried the fungi replied, "King Wen was merely ill;
Fuxi was gravely ill indeed. In the past, before Fuxi had drawn the hexagrams, the Three Powers were not yet..."

If these four seasons were not established, would they not fail to proceed? If these hundred things were not produced, would they not fail to flourish? If these myriad phenomena were not manifest, would they not fail to appear in their full splendor?
Why such restless striving and the waste of painting? Ever since the Lord Fuxi divulged the secrets of the Way and leaked the subtle workings of the spirit.
The Great Harmony was divided and the primal Qi was rent asunder. This caused the wise men of the world to employ deceptive paths and act in opposition, saying:

"I am skilled in speaking of signs and images and in discerning the nature of things. They spoke of Yin and Yang grinding against one another and of the distant and the near taking from each other, creating theories of hardness and softness, sameness and difference, to startle the wills of men.
Thus, those who were supposed to know became ignorant, and the Great Simplicity was dispersed. This is what is meant by "lying low."
As for Xi Shi, who first portended the onset of chaos: how could one have sighed in distress over the weak and lamented for King Wen? He carried his medicinal herbs upon his back and departed;
though pursued and questioned as to his dwelling and name, he did not answer. When Wenzhongzi heard of this, he said, "He was a man of hidden virtue."
The Treatise says: The late Sima Wenzheng of our dynasty said, "Wen Zhongzi stated that the Buddha is a sage.
If Wen Zhongzi’s words are indeed accurate, then the mind of the Buddha can be discerned.

However, those who speak of Chan nowadays are fond of using obscure language to bewilder one another and making grand claims to surpass others, leaving students wandering aimlessly (tāng-tāng, meaning the appearance of having lost one's way)."

Furthermore, you are deluded; indeed, you are entering further into confusion. Therefore, expanding upon the intent of Wenzhongzi (Zhongyong), I have composed six verses on the "Exegesis of Chan" (*Jiechan song*).
If it is truly as these words suggest, then this [teaching] may be practiced even in the Middle Kingdom. Otherwise, it is something I do not understand. The final verse says:
"His words shall be the teacher for a hundred generations; his conduct shall be the law for the world. He is a sage."
He is a Great Sage; thus he is called a Buddha or a Bodhisattva. Alas! Lord Wen Zheng succeeded Confucius, Mencius, Xunzi, and Yangzi as a Great Virtuous One.
How could he have been ignorant of the Buddha? Observing his eulogies, it is clear that all the deeds performed by Lord Wen Zheng throughout his life were the very mind of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.
Even within our own school, the single dharma of Chan is held up as a model.

They regard this as a "separate transmission outside the teachings. Unless one has spent twenty or thirty years extinguishing the mind and severing discursive thought, one cannot fathom its essential meaning.
To call it "cryptic language" or "grandiloquence" is to mistake the appearance for the reality. Why is this?
Even Donggaozi considered Fuxi’s drawing of the hexagrams to be a divulgence of the secrets of the Way and a leakage of the mechanisms of the spirit, thereby fragmenting the Great [Unity].
This harmonizes with and tears apart the primal qi, causing those who know it to remain ignorant while the Great Simplicity dissolves.

How much more so for the Chan of "not establishing words and letters," which points directly to the human mind beyond language and outward traces—how could its expressions be sought through ordinary principles of meaning?
This is not only the case for Wen Zheng Gong, Wenzhongzi, Yang Meng, and others...

The worthy ones have not yet had the leisure to apply their minds. Among our own ranks of Dharma Masters who transmit the teachings, there are certainly those who, out of ignorance, give rise to slander.
Thus, the former masters said: "Out of thousands or tens of thousands of people, one may only fish out a single individual or half a person.
How indeed can this be easily believed?
Formerly, when Emperor Wen was still a prince in concealment, he encountered a foreign monk who presented him with a packet of śarīra relics, saying:
"Donor, you shall one day become the compassionate father of all under heaven. These are the remaining spiritual remains of the Great Awakened One; I have therefore left them for you to venerate.

After the monk had departed, the Emperor sought them but could not find their location. Following his accession to the throne, the Emperor once placed the śarīra relics separately with Dharma Master Ru and Dharma Master Tanqian.
He held them in his palms and counted them, yet whether they were few or many, he could never determine the exact number. Xuanzang said, "The Dharma-body of all Buddhas transcends numerical measure;
it cannot be fathomed by the world. The Emperor then began to place them in a casket made of the seven precious gems.
When the realm within the seas attained great peace, the Emperor recalled this matter and consequently erected śarīra stupas in thirty prefectures, including Qizhou.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued, stating:

"Looking up with reverence to the Perfect Enlightenment, who possesses great kindness and great compassion to rescue and protect all sentient beings, serving as a bridge and raft for the myriad classes of beings, I, the Emperor, take refuge in the Triple Gem and restore the Holy Teaching.
I intend to cause all people within the four seas to together resolve upon Bodhicitta and collectively cultivate meritorious deeds, so that both those currently living in this present age..."

To ensure that in future lives you may forever establish the causes for goodness and together ascend to the wondrous fruit [of Buddhahood], it is fitting that you invite thirty śramaṇas who are well-versed in the characteristics of the Dharma and capable of acting as guides.
Each shall be accompanied by two attendants and one subordinate official, along with one hundred and twenty *jìn* of frankincense (*guggulu*).
These shall be sent along various routes to erect stūpas in the aforementioned thirty prefectures; in each prefecture...

There shall be three hundred and sixty monks who, for seven days, shall perform the Way on behalf of me, the Crown Prince, the various princes, the officials of the inner and outer courts, and all the common people.
Let each person be permitted to give alms, limited to ten coins at most. The money so donated shall be used to provide for the construction of the stupa.
If it is insufficient, the labor may be conscripted from the local population or treasury funds may be employed. This shall apply separately to the monks and nuns of other provinces and commanderies.
A vegetarian feast shall be established for Śāriputra for all people. On the fifteenth day of the tenth month at the hour of the horse (noon), the stone casket shall be enshrined together.

From the Regional Commanders and Prefectural Governors down to the County Magistrates, all shall suspend their regular duties for seven days—unless there be military exigencies—and devote themselves exclusively to supervising the performance of the Way, exhausting their sincerity and reverence to accord with My intention.
On this day, the Emperor shall personally offer a casket of the seven precious gems to [the relics].
Ten *śarīra* relics emerged from within and were placed upon the table of the imperial throne. Together with the various *śramaṇas*, he burned incense and prostrated, vowing:
"May this disciple always protect and uphold the Triple Gem through the True Dharma and deliver all sentient beings.
He then took thirty gold jars and thirty lapis lazuli jars, placed the gold jars inside the lapis lazuli jars, and deposited the *śarīra* relics therein.
They used frankincense as a paste for the covering and impressed it with seals. Each of the śramaṇas reverently carried the śarīra relics as they proceeded.

Upon first entering the borders of the province, the regional commander, the provincial governor, and various officials lined the roads, escorting them on foot. The fourfold assembly maintained majestic deportment, solemn and pure.

Together, they brought jeweled canopies, banners, pennants, flower pedestals, Buddha images, palanquins, Buddha curtains, scripture carriages, incense mountains, incense bowls, and all manner of musical instruments to offer worship, surrounding him while chanting praises.

Following the method for enshrining the *śarīra* in the city of Kuśinagara as recorded in the *Āgama* sūtras, the śramaṇa then addressed the fourfold assembly, proclaiming: "The Most Honored One, by means of the Bodhisattva..."
His great compassion was boundless and limitless; his pity for sentient beings pierced to the very marrow of his bones.

For this reason, he distributed the relics so that they might serve as a common cause of merit for all under heaven. Furthermore, he cited various scriptural passages to reprove them through manifold skillful means and to instruct them, his profound sincerity reaching such a point that tears flowed down his face.
When the text of the repentance was being recited, and as the relics were about to be placed into the casket, the sand...
The gate was tall, and precious vases were respectfully carried forward and paraded before the great assembly. Everyone rubbed their eyes and gazed intently, all beholding the radiance together.
Their cries of grief and longing resounded, shaking the earth. It was the same at every location where [the relics] were enshrined.
At noon on the fifteenth day of the tenth month, the Emperor stood holding a jade scepter in the southwest courtyard of the Daxing Hall within the Daxing Palace.
It was thus established. An image of the Buddha and three hundred and sixty śramaṇas were invited;
with banners, canopies, incense, flowers, hymns, and music, they arrived from Daxingshan Temple and took up residence in the halls.

The Emperor burned incense and prostrated himself, then descended the eastern corridor and personally led the civil and military officials to observe a vegetarian fast and maintain ritual purity. Once the śarīra had been enshrined in the stupa, the Emperor said:

"The Buddha-dharma will surely experience a resurgence when there is a corresponding spiritual response. Subsequently, memorial petitions submitted from various locations all came to pass exactly as he had said (as recorded in Wang Shao’s *Sheli Ganying Ji*).
The treatise states: In the second year of the Taiping Xingguo era of our dynasty, Qian Chu, the King of Wuyue, offered his territory to the imperial court.
Emperor Taizong commanded that the Buddha’s *śarīra* be taken into the palace to construct an eleven-story pagoda on the northwestern grounds of Kaiyuan Temple.
A celestial palace was built at its base to enshrine the *śarīra*. On the day of the interment, the Grand...
The Emperor traveled incognito in a sedan chair and personally took charge of the arrangements. A white light emerged from a corner of the stupa;
the Great Emperor wept at its exterior, and the myriad people of the capital all shed tears. Countless individuals burned incense upon their fingers, arms, and palms.
Dozens of eunuchs expressed their wish to leave the secular life to sweep and water the base of the stupa, and they were all ordained as monks.
[Seng]—Emperor Taizong said to his close ministers: "In my previous lives, I have often sat personally before the Buddha;
it was only because I had not yet attained the knowledge of past lives that I could not see him clearly. This is recorded in Yang Wen Gong’s *Tanyuan*.
Yet, what exactly was our Buddha, the World-Honored One? And as for the majestic power of his relics, they have manifested auspicious signs throughout two thousand years.

It should be regarded as being like something new. Thus, the eminent emperors and illustrious kings of both ancient and modern times have revered and yearned for it with such depth that they were unaware of the reasons why, yet their inclinations naturally accorded with one another.

Although the Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty was not even ten-thousandth part capable of being compared to the divine achievements and sagely virtue of Taizong, all of them nonetheless possessed the power of past aspirations and transcendental resolve, and thus each reached the pinnacle of excellence.
*General Chronological Treatise on the History of Buddhism during the Lōngxìng Era*, Scroll Nine and Scroll Ten.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zǔxiù of Shíshì Monastery in Lōngxìng Prefecture.

In the first year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "The Emperor respectfully inquires after the Chan Master Zhishun of the southern valley of Mount Zhanghong.

As the winter months are extremely cold, we hope you remain in peace while savoring the Way. We urge you to exert yourself for the sake of all living beings and to bring the holy enterprise to fulfillment through the power of your compassionate vows."
I truly admire this. I have now dispatched the Grand Master of the Household, Lu Yuanshou, to convey my intention and summon Dhyāna Master Shi to the imperial court.

Śūṇa declined on the grounds of illness and did not go. Initially, when Śūṇa left home to follow Dhyāna Master Tanyu and practiced meditative concentration, he would sometimes perceive the arising of deluded thoughts;
he would immediately prick his thigh with an awl so that worldly dust would not enter. Only when it was unavoidable would he utter a single word.
It was nothing more than the practice of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. After some ten years or so, Chou Qi said to him, "You seem to have no concern at all for human affairs;
from this day forward, you may be spoken of as one who understands the Way. Later, he took his leave and entered Zhanhuang Mountain.
Those who were fond of virtuous deeds offered him rice and flour, but Shun avoided them and would not accept a single thing. When someone asked the reason, Shun replied, "I dwell in the mountains..."

"Acorns and chestnuts are sufficient to ward off hunger; why trouble yourself with meat? Such was his simplicity. Whenever he saw someone eating meat, he would invariably show a look of distress and warn them, saying:
'The six realms of existence have diverse forms, yet there is none you have not passed through.
All living beings have been your parents; all sentient beings have been your former selves. To eat their flesh is to eat your own parents.'"
His mind was one of profound forbearance; those who heard him were without exception moved to repentance and reform.

The Dharma Master Tanqian was deeply versed in such scriptures as the Avataṃsaka, the Vimalakīrti, and the Laṅkāvatāra. He once suffered from a chronic internal fever. One night, he dreamed that the moon fell into his lap;
he tore it apart and ate it, perceiving it upon waking to be cool, crisp, fragrant, and delicious. Once he awoke, his ailment was suddenly and completely cured.
Later, when he preached the precepts to his disciples, he would invariably say: "In the presence of Yue-de (Moon Virtue), I have three times recited these precepts.
At that time, he was known as the Bhikṣu Yue-de and was held in especially high esteem by Emperor Wen.

At the beginning of the Renshou era, when the Emperor was about to select prominent provinces to erect śarīra-stūpas, [the Master] was appointed to assist in their completion. Subsequently, auspicious signs and radiant light appeared throughout various prefectures; the local authorities reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor asked Daoxian, "The common people have obtained such auspicious responses, yet within my palace, we serve the Buddha with nothing lacking in devotion or rigor.
Why is it that we alone do not behold such extraordinary signs? He replied, "In this world, there are three Honored Ones who together bring peace to the realm."

The Emperor said, "A Buddha is called 'World-Honored One' (Shizun); the Way is called 'Heavenly Honored One' (Tianzun); and the Sovereign is called 'Supreme Honored One' (Zhizun). For those whose karmic obstructions are severe, the Buddha manifests compassionate light to gather them in.
Your Majesty’s light now dwells over the four seas, and the myriad states are all at peace. Since this light is identical [to that of the Buddhas], there is no difference to be seen.
The Emperor was delighted.

In the winter of the second year of the Daye era, Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty performed sacrifices at the Southern Suburb. He issued an edict that monks and Daoists should both bow in accordance with secular custom.

Among the Daoist practitioners, none dared to speak out. The various śramaṇas, however, as a rule did not comply with the edict. The Emperor interrogated them, saying, "The decree has been promulgated for a long time.
Why is it that you, sirs, persistently do not obey my command? Dharma Master Mingzhan replied, "If Your Majesty would have us conform to—"

"If you decree the abolition of the Way, this humble body dares not fail to obey your command. However, if you recognize that the Great Dharma is worthy of veneration, then beneath the dharma-robes, there shall be no ritual of monks bowing to the laity.
Emperor Wu asked, "What caused King Wu of Zhou to perform such prostrations? Sengzhan replied, "King Wu of Zhou relied on intimidation and indulged in violence;
he did not practice benevolence and virtue. He is not a model for those who possess a state. Your Majesty’s sagely governance is rooted solely in benevolence."
He was not unjustly accused of a crime. Thus, the贫道 (poor monk) was able to exhaustively offer his loyal words. The Emperor remained silent and ended the matter.
The officials, however, intended to punish Zhan for defying the imperial decree. Zhan said, "The one at fault is Zhan alone; I pray that you do not apply improper laws to my followers.
The Emperor admired his unbending integrity, set him aside without further inquiry, and from this point on, all discussions regarding the veneration of the sovereign ceased.
In this year, the Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, passed into nirvana. Regarding the Master [Hongren], some say he was a native of Xuzhou. Initially, as a layman, he visited Master Ke;
having received the robe and the transmission of the Dharma, he traveled between Mount Sikong during the period when Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou suppressed the Buddhist teachings.
After more than ten years had passed, no one recognized him. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he settled on Mount Wangong.
There he encountered the śrāmaṇera Daoxin, who paid respects to the Master and said, "I pray that the Upādhyāya, out of great compassion, will grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Master asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Master said, "Why then do you seek liberation? At these words, Daoxin attained great enlightenment.

After he had served with diligent labor for a long time, [Huiyuan] conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*). Having repeatedly tested him through profound and subtle matters, he knew that his karmic conditions were ripe;
he then spoke a verse and entrusted him with the dharma-garment. He further said, "Since I have obtained you, my task is complete.

Thereupon, he traveled leisurely through the regions along the Yangtze River, visiting Mount Luofu and various other mountains, before returning once more to his former residence. The local officials and commoners rejoiced at his return and led one another to present offerings, which the Master accepted.

He preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly. Thereupon, he stood solemnly in the midst of the gathering, joined his palms, and passed away. During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Jingzhi (Mirror-Wisdom).
He composed a single chapter titled "The Inscription on Faith" (*Xinxin Ming*), the text of which says:
The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear.

A difference of a hair’s breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth. If you wish for it to manifest before you, do not maintain compliance or resistance. To contend with compliance and resistance is the sickness of the mind.

Failing to recognize the profound essence, one merely exerts oneself in the effort of contemplating stillness. When [the mind] is perfectly identical to the great void, there is neither deficiency nor surplus.

It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting that one falls short. Do not pursue conditioned objects; do not dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single state of equanimity, all things are naturally exhausted in oblivion.

When stillness seeks to return to stillness, that very stillness becomes increasingly restless. To be stuck in either extreme, how can one know the single essence? If this single essence is not penetrated, both sides fail in their efficacy.
To dispel existence and non-existence is to follow emptiness while turning one's back on it. Excessive words and excessive deliberations only lead further away from accord with reality.
Cut off words and cut off thoughts; there will be no place that is not penetrated. Return to the root to attain the essential meaning; follow after illumination and you lose the source.

If you reflect back for even a moment, it surpasses the previous emptiness. That previous emptiness underwent transformation entirely due to deluded views. Do not seek the truth; simply require the cessation of views.

The two views do not abide; be careful not to pursue them. As soon as gain or loss arises, one becomes distracted and loses the mind. Since duality exists because of unity, do not even cling to that unity.
When the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. When there is no fault, there are no dharmas; when there is no arising, there is no mind.

The capacity can follow the object to extinction; the object follows the capacity to sink. The object exists because of the capacity for the object; the capacity exists because of the object for the capacity.

If you wish to know these two segments, they are originally one emptiness. This one emptiness is identical to the two, equally containing the myriad phenomena. When neither the refined nor the coarse is seen, how could there be partiality or factionalism?
The essence of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult. With narrow views and doubt, one becomes increasingly anxious and ever more slow.

To cling to it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path; to let it be of itself, its essence has no going or staying. Following one's nature accords with the Way; in carefree wandering, all afflictions are severed.

If your mindfulness is bound and deviates from the truth, you will fall into the dullness of torpor. This state is not good; it is not good to weary the spirit. What use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the intimate?

If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects. If you do not loathe the six sense-objects, you will be identical to perfect enlightenment. The wise act without contrivance; the ignorant bind themselves.
In the Dharma there is no separate dharma; how could there be attachment? To employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error?

Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation; awakening is free from likes and dislikes. All dualistic extremes arise from one’s own deliberations. They are like dreams, illusions, and empty flowers—why labor to grasp them?
Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast aside all at once. If the eye does not sleep, all dreams will vanish of themselves; if the mind does not vary, the myriad dharmas are but one suchness.
This suchness is profound in essence; in its state of stillness, one forgets conditions. When all conditions are viewed as equal, one returns once more to spontaneity.
The means by which they are extinguished cannot be compared or measured. In stillness there is no movement; in movement there is no stillness.
Since duality is not established, how could there be a unity? Reaching the ultimate limit, no rules or patterns persist. The mind accords with equality, and all conditioned activity ceases.

Doubt is completely exhausted; right faith becomes harmonious and upright. Nothing remains, and there is nothing to be remembered. Empty clarity illuminates itself without taxing the mind or strength.
This is a realm beyond deliberation, difficult for the conscious intellect to fathom. In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self.

It is essential to correspond with urgency; speak only of non-duality. Where there is non-duality, all are the same, encompassing everything without exception. The wise of the ten directions all enter this school.
This school is neither constricted nor expansive; a single thought-moment is ten thousand years. There is no place it is not present, yet it is present before the eyes of the ten directions.
The extremely small is identical to the large; forgetting and severing all boundaries. The extremely large is identical to the small; not perceiving its limits or surface.
Existence is itself non-existence; non-existence is itself existence. If it were not thus, one would certainly have no need for guarding. One is identical to all; all is identical to one.

If one can simply act in this way, why worry about not reaching completion? Faith and mind are not two; the non-dual mind of faith cuts off the path of words and is neither of the past, future, nor present.

The Treatise says: I have heard that when the ancient patriarchs bestowed instruction upon their disciples, they would invariably recite the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) by the Third Patriarch several times each morning as they rose.
Truly, these words are so! Indeed, since antiquity, there have been many compositions that explicate the Way.
As for thoroughly penetrating the source of the Dharma and wondrously exhausting the ultimate of the school, nothing surpasses this treatise. Its words are concise yet its meaning is abundant;
its purport is profound yet its diction is elegant. Thus, he succeeded to the ancestral position as a Great Dharma King, his true body dwelling in the world.
Is it not the case that this is no mere empty claim? Some say that once the Great Master had entrusted the Great Dharma to the Fourth Patriarch, he made this vow:
"Be careful never to say that you received the Dharma from me. Recently, Song Mingjiao remarked:
"This was likely because the Patriarch considered fame and traces to be a hindrance to the Way; thus, even regarding his own lineage of transmission, he wished to sever them. And Jue...

Fan also said: "At that time, the Great Master [Huineng] was mindful of the hardships with which the Second Patriarch, Bodhidharma, propagated the Dharma, as he suffered persecution from heterodox teachers;
therefore, he was extremely cautious. However, the explanations of these two masters are likely not correct. As it is said in antiquity:"
One must believe that matters spanning vast ages are not transmitted from the Pamir Mountains. Furthermore, Master Xian-sha said: "Dharma did not come to the Eastern Land;
the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. One should know that one must not say that the Dharma was obtained from one's own place;
this is surely the entrustment of a transmission without transmission, and the purport of the final, total upholding of the Way.
In the fourth year, when Shi Ping was pacified, the Magistrate Yang Hong led Daoists and renowned Confucian scholars to initiate a Dharma assembly at Dazhi Zang Temple.
He commanded Master Huìjìng to debate on doctrine with the Daoist Yú Yǒngtōng. Yǒngtōng wished to establish his thesis first.
Jing said, "The Master enters the temple; in principle, there is host and guest. How can you come first? Thereupon, Jing asked:
"Laozi said, 'There was something formless yet complete, born before heaven and earth. I do not know its name; I give it the designation Dao.

Now, is the substance of Dao 'complete' because it is one, or is it 'complete' because its substance is manifold? If it is 'complete' because its substance is one, then at the very moment of that completeness—"
Once it has already become one, then this "one" would not have arisen from the Way. If their essences were different, they would be mixed;

yet even before they were mixed, it had already become two. In that case, these two would not have originated together. Yongtong Fan was utterly at a loss for a response and withdrew without speaking.
The divine monk Faxi was of humble appearance and about forty years of age. The elders of the regions south of the passes all said they had seen him since childhood;
he spoke of events from the Jin and Song dynasties with such clarity that his words were worth listening to. He also claimed to have once traveled with Master Huiyuan of Donglin.
His speech and silence were inconsistent, yet both invariably served as omens of good or ill fortune. When Emperor Yang visited Weiyang, he heard of him...

Someone else summoned him; in a short while, one day, he was seen searching everywhere throughout the palace for a sheep's head. The Emperor loathed this and handed him over to the Minister of Justice (Tingwei).
His hands and feet were bound with silver shackles, and the guards were extremely strict. Yet Huiji daily begged in the marketplace, eating and drinking as if nothing were amiss.

The officials reported this to the Emperor, who ordered an investigation. The seals and locks were found to be as they had been before. When the door was opened and he was inspected, only his *kāṣāya* robe was seen covering [the body].

His bones were golden in color, and his skeletal structure was entirely interconnected. He immediately reported this to the Emperor, who issued an edict to Prince Da of Chang’an to investigate the matter;

it was confirmed to be as described. By imperial decree, the bones were fashioned into a statue using fragrant clay. That evening, Xi rose and walked from the clay image, speaking and laughing just as before.

He subsequently released them from their confinement. Not long after, he manifested illness. He commanded those close to him to remove his mats and place his body upon a wooden frame, beneath which burning charcoal was set to roast it.
After several days, half his body had become red and festering when he died. He was buried beside Xiangshan Temple.
Several years later, someone returning from south of the sea saw that Xi was unharmed. That person opened the tomb to look inside and found nothing but an empty coffin.
Calculating by this time, Xi had already lived for over three hundred years. This occurred just as Emperor Yang was assassinated at Jiangdu.
Only then did he realize that this was the fulfillment of the omen regarding the request for a sheep’s head.
The *Lun* says: Du Mu of the Tang dynasty remarked, "In the past, there was a physiognomist who declared that Emperor Wen would possess the empire;

later, he indeed usurped it and obtained it. At the end of the Zhou, the Yang clan held the rank of the Eight Pillar States (Bazhuguo), and their dukes and marquises succeeded one another for a long time. (1)
If a man in the morning steals the title and position [of another], within thirty years neither the elderly, the robust, nor the infants will meet their natural deaths.
One who knows the methods of physiognomy would say, "This shall bring calamity to the Yang family"; only such a person can be called a skilled physiognomist.
Mu Zhi’s argument is indeed truly incisive. Nevertheless, Emperor Wen unified the world and brought the entire realm under one rule, presiding over ten thousand nations for twenty-four years.
He established the rites, music, laws, and institutions that were largely adopted by the Tang.
During the Renshou era, the households in the empire reached eight million seven hundred thousand; considering the territorial expanse of the Tang...
Extensively speaking, from the beginning of the five dynasties until the end of the Tiānbǎo era, there were barely more than nine million households.

Emperor Wén of the Sui dynasty opened the way for his reign and personally attained a period of great peace; he was truly an eminent sovereign of his age. It is a pity that in the final years of his life, he entrusted power to one Yang Sù and did not see it through to its conclusion.
Alas! This is true not only of Emperor Wén of the Sui, but of all those since the Wei and Jin dynasties.

The rise and fall of thirteen dynasties—the Fu, Shi, Yao, Liu, the two Xiao, Chen, Gao, Yuwen, and Yang—serve as proof that the cycle of cause and effect is verified down to the finest detail, without the slightest discrepancy.
It is for this reason that my teaching spreads throughout the six directions, providing great benefit to the world, the state, and the family;
for its discourse on the matters of karmic retribution and the Way of Heaven is [in perfect accord with reality].
This is appropriate. There are those who assist Heaven by providing encouragement or deterrence. Therefore, the Grand Scripture and its extensive discourses are profound, penetrating, and clear;
they insist that every person must have self-confidence, for as the cause is, so shall the fruit be, and there is no way to evade it.

Although the Confucians say, "The matter is such that it returns to its source," they have not yet fully articulated the principle of encouragement and deterrence. This is why [the Buddha] alone is able to govern them.
While he censured the Sui Emperor Wen, he failed to trace back the accumulated evils of successive dynasties and their cyclical decline.
Only the rise of the Tang dynasty was different from those; thus its mandate was long-lasting and auspicious, providing all the more as the ultimate mirror for the world.
The Tang Gaozu, whose personal name was Yuan and courtesy name Shude, was surnamed Li. He was a native of Chengji in Longxi.

His body possessed three nipples, and his family had served as prominent officials during the Zhou and Sui dynasties. He inherited the title of Duke of Tang. In the thirteenth year of the Daye era, Emperor Yang embarked on a southern tour.
In Jiangdu, as bandits rose up throughout the empire, Gaozu’s son, Shimin, knew that the Sui dynasty was certain to fall. He plotted to launch a great undertaking, and Gaozu followed his counsel.
In the seventh month of autumn, he raised an army of righteous soldiers; in the eleventh month of winter, they captured the capital.

In the fifth month of summer the following year, the Sui Emperor abdicated the throne. Gaozu ascended the imperial throne in Chang’an and changed the dynastic name to Tang. He established [the new reign].
The Yuanwu De era lasted nine years. He abdicated the throne to Taizong. Taizong was a Son of Heaven with a Buddha-mind.

He founded the state, stabilized its enterprises, and brought the quarters of the world to vast tranquility. For twenty generations, spanning a total of two hundred and ninety years, no dynasty since the beginning of time has ever matched the great prosperity of the Imperial Tang.
The flourishing and decline of our Teaching has always been in accord with [the fate of the state].

The imperial way was maintained in succession; thus, in terms of the abundance of sages and worthies who provided protection both within and without the court, as well as the completeness of its institutions and statutes, none surpassed this dynasty.
Therefore, this comprehensive account of the Tang era is widely regarded as a complete record.
It is my hope that gentlemen of the Way and those among our later generations who are worthy will examine and verify it.

On the day of Ding-si in the second month of the seventh year of Wude, the High Ancestor performed the ritual of Shi-dian at the National Academy and summoned renowned Confucian scholars, Buddhists, and Daoists to debate the principles of their doctrines. The Daoist Liu Jinxi questioned the śramaṇa Hui-cheng, saying:

"When Prince Siddhārtha practiced austerities for six years seeking to realize the fruit of the Way, this implies that the Way can produce the Buddha and that the Buddha is accomplished through the Way. Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'Seeking the Unborn...'"
The *Shangdao* (The Superior Way) further states: "One who embodies and understands the Great Way gives rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Judging by this, it would seem that the Way ought to have preceded the Buddha. [Zheng] Chenggong said: "China’s relation to India is like that of the Ringed Sea to the Scaled Continents.
Laojun and the Buddha were separated by more than three hundred years; how could the Buddha have existed in the time of King Zhao, while the Way was sought out in the time of King Jing? Jin Xi said:
The Most High Great Dao was born before heaven and earth. It surged forth within the profound mystery and shone brilliantly above the Jade Purity.
This is the teacher of the Buddha. Cheng said: "According to the seven canons and nine currents of the classics for governing the state, the fundamental source is the Book of Changes."

The five phases generate one another and the two polarities unfold; that which wondrously transforms all things is called the Spirit (śūnyatā), and the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way (mārga).
How could it be said that there exists a separate Great Way born before heaven and earth? Since the Way is nameless, by what means could it give birth to the Buddha?
The *Zhongyong* says: "Following one's nature is called the Way. Che Yin said: "That which resides within oneself is virtue; that which reaches out to things is the Way.

How can it be considered erroneous for one who wears a golden crown upon his head, dons saffron robes, has white hair hanging down, and holds a jade *zhang* scepter in his hand, to dwell atop Mount Dalar and claim to be the sole possessor of the Great Way?
Jinxi had no reply. Shortly thereafter, the *Boshi* of the Imperial Academy...
Lu Deming established interpretations according to each school and analyzed their essential points thoroughly. The Emperor was pleased and said, "These three men are all formidable adversaries;
yet Deming has consistently eclipsed them in every instance. He may truly be called worthy. Thereupon, he bestowed silk upon each of them.
In the eighth year, Yu Jian, the Director of the Grand Historian’s Office, felt ashamed to hold his post by means of his technical skills and recommended Fu Yi to replace him.

When Yi became the Director, there was a Daoist named Chuan Renjun who was quite proficient in calendrical studies; Yi appointed him as Assistant Director of the Grand Historian’s Office and subsequently aligned himself with him.
They submitted a memorial requesting the abolition of Buddhism, stating: "The Buddha is in the Western Regions; his words are strange and the road is distant. During the Han..."
