They translated foreign books, allowing themselves unrestrained license and fabrication; thus, they caused those who were neither loyal nor filial to shave their heads and bow to their sovereign and parents.

They led idle lives and lived off the labor of others, changing their attire to evade taxes and levies. They propagated their demonic scriptures and expounded their heterodox teachings, falsely opening up the three miserable realms and erroneously manifesting the six paths of existence.
Fearing to intimidate the ignorant and deceiving the common masses, they ensured that among all the common people, those with true discernment were rare indeed.
Investigating the root source, one must recognize that such [practices] are but pretenses and delusions. They involve pursuing past transgressions while vainly speculating on future blessings;

there are even those who personally commit acts of rebellion and defiance of the law, only to encounter punishment, whereupon they perform prostrations to the Buddha within prison and recite Sanskrit mantras day and night without weariness, seeking to evade their crimes.
Furthermore, birth and death, longevity and premature demise, fundamentally arise from the natural order; as for punishment and reward, majesty and fortune—[these too are determined by nature].
Regarding those who serve as rulers, foolish monks falsely claim that all [authority] originates from the Buddha; they thus usurp the power of the sovereign and seize the principles of creation.
That such a thing harms the administration is truly lamentable. The Book of Documents says: "Only the ruler may exercise favor;

only the ruler may wield authority; only the ruler may enjoy fine food. Let no subject presume to exercise favor, wield authority, or enjoy fine food, for it brings ruin to his house and calamity to his state."
From the Five Emperors and the Three Kings onward, there was no Buddha-dharma at all. Rulers were enlightened and ministers were loyal, and their reigns were long-lasting.
It was not until the time of Emperor Ming of the Han that a shrine for the "Hu" (foreigners) was first established, and śramaṇas from the Western Regions were permitted to transmit their teachings.

Prior to the Western Jin, it was forbidden for people of China to shave their heads and leave the household life; however, following the chaos caused by the Fu and Shi clans who ravaged China, this prohibition was lifted. Yet, the administration remained tyrannical and the mandate for the dynasty’s longevity...
All these calamities have resulted from Buddhism. The cases of Emperor Wu of Liang and Emperor Xuan of Qi are particularly worthy of being taken as warnings.

In the past, the single woman Bao Si deluded King You until he lost his kingdom; how much more so now, with a hundred thousand monks and nuns carving silks and molding clay to exhaust the resources of the empire?
If Your Majesty were to allow this multitude of one hundred thousand to marry among themselves, their offspring would increase tenfold within ten years.

If you provide such annual instruction, you will naturally possess sufficient food and troops; the four seas will be spared from the calamity of being devoured like silkworms, and the people will know the source of both their authority and their blessings.

Thus, the winds of sorcery and delusion will subside, and the transformation of pure simplicity will return. Furthermore, throughout antiquity and the present, there have been few who offered loyal remonstrance without meeting with misfortune.
Recently, Zhang Qiu Zhituo of the Northern Qi submitted a memorial stating that monks and nuns waste and deplete the resources of the state.

Stupas and monasteries waste gold and silk; for the sake of various monks and nuns, [the subject] associated with high ministers and relied upon imperial consorts and princes, while slandering them openly and covertly.
He was executed in the marketplace by his own son. When Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou entered Qi, he first sealed the foundations and graves [of such figures].
Although this servant is not talented, he has privately aspired to follow their example. This memorial was submitted but received no reply.
In the ninth year, Fu Yi, the Director of the Grand Historian’s Office, submitted seven successive memorials requesting the abolition of the Śākya [Buddhist] religion;

his words were consistently vehement and urgent. Although the Emperor was advanced in years and possessed a yielding, indecisive nature, he was somewhat inclined toward them. He entrusted the memorials to the various ministers for collective deliberation.
The high officials all stated: "The Buddha-dharma has flourished since successive reigns; it promotes goodness, restrains evil, and provides secret assistance to the state. Its principles—
There was no one who opposed [the proposal] except for Zhang Daoyuan, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Grooms, who sided with Li Yi. He praised his memorial, saying it was reasonable.

Prime Minister Xiao Li rebuked Li Yi in court, saying: "The Buddha is a sage. For Li Yi to propose such a theory—where there is no law for those who are not sages—I request that he be subjected to severe punishment.
Li Yi replied: "Ritual is rooted in serving one's parents and culminates in serving one's sovereign; this is the ritual of loyalty and filial piety."
[This is] a transgression. The way of a minister and a son is thus established. Yet the Buddha left the city to become a renunciant, fleeing and turning his back on his father;

he opposed the Son of Heaven as a mere private individual and acted with rebellion toward his own kin as the successor to the throne. It was not that Li [the founder of the Li clan] emerged from the hollow mulberry tree, yet he returned to honor a teaching that lacks a father.
"Your servant has heard that those who are not filial have no kin; this refers to Li. Li joined his palms and said: 'Hell was indeed established for such a person as this.
(The above is found in the Old History of the Tang).
The Emperor again circulated Yi’s memorial to all the monks, asking what benefit the monastic life provided to the state.
At that time, the Dharma Master Falin composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresies) in two fascicles.

He extensively cited maps, histories, and Daoist scriptures to broadly clarify that Buddhism penetrates the source of all phenomena, whereas Confucian filial piety and its doctrines merely address the governance of this world alone and do not fully expound upon the ultimate.

These [previous] writings do not exhaustively reach the ultimate principle. Generally, those who have left the household life maintain their resolve and clarify the Way, propagate goodness and promote merit, enlighten the ignorant and deluded, and benefit the state to no small degree.
Master Minggai composed the *Juedui* (Decisive Refutations) in eight articles concerning the slander against the Buddha and the Sangha;
Master Huisheng composed the *Bianzhenglun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct) with ten parables and nine admonitions, refuting the Daoist Li Zhongqing’s *Shi*.
To rectify the errors of the nine heterodox schools, Senglin and others submitted a memorial to the Emperor and presented a letter to the Prince of Qin.

Furthermore, Li Shizheng, the Director of Ceremonies at the Gate of the Palace (Menxia), composed the *Neide lun* (Treatise on Inner Virtue) in three chapters to expound upon the benefits of Buddhist transformation; he then wrote a preface himself and presented it, the text of which says:
"As for the One of Ten Powers who acts as a charioteer, he steers the Dharma-boat across the sea of suffering. The Three Vehicles draw [the water]..."
It leads one along level paths through the burning house; its encouragement of goodness and advancement of virtue is so vast that it exceeds what is found in the Seven Classics.

Its prohibition of evil and prevention of calamity are so profound that none among the Nine Schools can compare with it. Yet, in its exhaustion of the spirit and comprehension of transformation, its words are grand and startling;

in its removal of delusion and severance from the mundane, its path is pure and remote, difficult to tread. Thus, whether among the officials and commoners of China and the barbarian lands, or the scholars and literati of court and countryside—
Each person adheres to what they find most comfortable, rarely finding true flavor in this Way.

Were it not for those who have refined their essence to examine the true and the false, and contemplated deeply to discern suffering and emptiness, there would be no way to establish a root of faith as steadfast as rock, nor to remove the cover of doubt that feels like one's very life is vanishing.

In the distant past, Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī propagated the Way with such excellence that others were moved to diligent service; in more recent times, Asaṅga and Nāgārjuna realized the truth of principle with such sincerity that they were filled with profound joy.
The profound learning of Kumārajīva and Dao’an led them to exhaustively investigate the Mystical Source (the *Mādhyamika*), causing their reverence to increase;
the faith of Sengrui and Huiyuan remained steadfast until their final years. They surpassed Shi An in his pursuit of licentious books and rivaled Confucius in his study of the *I Ching*.
A thousand pieces of gold could not startle them, nor could the eight musical tones alter their hearing; their erudition was so vast that their delight in it grew ever deeper. Thus they contemplated.
The more profound it is, the more sincere one’s faith becomes; all desire to desist, yet they cannot. Thus, it is certain that this is not false.

Our Sovereign has grandly received the Mandate of Heaven to extensively rescue the realm. His protection is equal to the azure heavens, and his support is as level as the broad earth. He has swept away the miasma of the atmosphere.

It clears the eight directions and rescues those mired in the mire and fire; it brings peace to the myriad people. The five teachings are widely disseminated and the nine merits are brought into order.
It encompasses the auspicious principles of ten thousand ages and reforms the lingering abuses of a hundred kings. It gathers all that is good, honoring the Three Jewels as a bridge and raft;

it eradicates all that is evil, weeding out the tares and weeds among the fourfold assembly. Following the bequeathed instructions of the final charge, it propagates and upholds the essential path of prosperity.

The merit [of the Buddha] is sublime; the Great Heaven cannot adequately describe it. Yet, among the gentry, there are many lineages of tradition, each following what they have studied, and divergent arguments arise like swarms of bees.
Some claim that the Three Kings lived long ages without a Buddha, while the Two Shi dynasties were tyrannical despite having monks.

They argue that serving the Buddha diminishes the fields of transformation, whereas abolishing the monks would benefit the state. If one merely clarifies such biased views, they have not yet presented [the full truth].
This principle is universally applicable. A broad examination of the rise of scholars is sufficient to prove the prevalence of superficiality and falsehood.

Why is this so? It was Hu Hai who destroyed the Qin dynasty; at that time, there were no Buddhists, yet the land collapsed like crumbling earth. It was Emperor Ming of the Han who promoted Buddhism; in his era, there were monks, yet the state was well-governed. When the Zhou removed Buddhist temples, the mandate of Heaven did not endure long;
when the Sui dynasty propagated the teachings of Śākyamuni, the edicts of the Kaihuang era were not tyrannical. Whether a reign flourishes or declines depends upon its distribution [of virtue].
Governance: Whether there is order or chaos depends upon the various officials. To cast blame solely upon Buddhists and monks is truly not a comprehensive argument.

Furthermore, the Buddha propagates only goodness and does not encourage evil among his subjects. His precepts are fundamentally for the prevention of wrongdoing; how could they harm the administration of the state?
If every person observes goodness and every household honors the precepts, then how could punishments increase, and how could calamities arise? Though a qíjì (a fine steed) is—
A swift horse cannot travel far without being ridden; medicinal herbs may be abundant in quantity, yet how can they cure an illness if one does not take them?
That Xiang Yu lost his army was not because Fan Zeng lacked strategic calculations; that the Shi clan rose to tyranny was certainly not because the Buddha was unkind.
It is simply that people became violent and chaotic by violating [the teachings], never by following them. From this, it is sufficiently clear. Furthermore...
There are those who claim that the Perfectly Awakened One is a demonic spirit, comparing him to the Pure Abodes as if they were licentious sacrifices; they disparage and slander him without limit.
While the Sagely Court encourages goodness by establishing *ārāmas* to honor merit, deluded people incite slander, turning acts of virtue into causes for reproach.
This is a profound derision of the Sovereign and not merely a destruction of the Buddha; it is for this reason that I, in my folly, beat my breast and sigh deeply, giving rise to indignation.

As for those who hold the writing-brush, I have been unworthily favored by Imperial grace and have already been moistened by the Dharma-rain. The feelings stirred within me through constant refinement have accumulated here for many years.

Indeed, doubts arose as soon as I heard [the teachings], but those doubts were extinguished through understanding. Formerly, I would have treated them with contempt and lacked faith; now, however, I believe them firmly and harbor no disparagement.
Recently, I have applied this to myself and extended it to measure others: all those who slight and disparage [the teachings] without reverence do so because—

This discussion has not yet reached its conclusion. If one were to probe the profound and seek out the hidden, such that one’s merit equaled that of Kumārajīva and Sengzheng, then all would surely possess deep faith and sincere reverence, and their aspirations would equal those of the renowned monks.
As for my own teacher, his learning does not delve into the depths, nor does his insight reach the sublime.

Having heard a little, I have slightly removed my delusions; thus, I have respectfully composed three treatises based on my humble abilities. The first, "Discerning Delusions" (*Bianhuo*), clarifies what is heterodox.
Section Two: On the Pervasiveness of Obstructions and the Destiny of Life—discerning how calamity and blessing alternate and rely upon one another.

Section Three: On Emptiness and Existence—shattering the dogmatic views of annihilationism and eternalism. I have verified these matters through various sayings and examined them through manifold virtues.

Above, I manifest the pure blessings of the Sagely Court; below, I analyze the empty falsehoods of licentious sacrifices. Though I harbor these intentions, I truly lack the requisite talent; my composition is vulgar and crude.
My citations and evidence are superficial; though I have exhausted my humble efforts, how could they proclaim the Sage’s virtue?
It is my hope that those who share my ailment but have not yet recovered may hear these shallow parables and attain profound realization.

May these weeds from the garden fence perhaps dispel the maladies of the heart and mind, and may this meal of wild herbs and beans perhaps save me from starvation in the ditches and ravines. Were the Elixir of Gold within my sight and the Jade Feast filling my table, I would still gaze upon these meager offerings with eyes full of longing.
This is truly lamentable. *The Discourse on Inner Virtue*, Chapter One: Dispelling Delusions. Its summary states:
A clever and eloquent scholar addressed a loyal and upright gentleman, saying: "I have heard that Śākyamuni was born in India, and the Sūtras originated from the Western Hu regions."
His fame and title have no peers among the Duke of Zhou or Confucius; his merit and virtue cannot be fully extolled even in the Classics and Odes.

He is truly one whom the distant barbarians revere, rather than a teacher or scholar of the Central Kingdom. This reached its height when Kāśyapa Mātanga entered the Han and Kang Senghui traveled to Wu.
The śarīra relics were displayed in the southern lands, and the caityas (zhāotí) were erected in the eastern capital. From that time onward, the Buddhist faith was esteemed;

the śramaṇas became as numerous as those in the waters of the Mò and Sì rivers, and their vihāras were more magnificent than the residences of kings and lords. Having constructed them upon high and dry ground, they were established there.
Furthermore, they were supported by fertile lands; tall flagstaffs were erected to shine upon the sun, and grand residences were modeled after the finest mansions facing the main thoroughfares.
Princes, dukes, and great officials assisted them with gold and silk, while wealthy families of farmers and merchants contributed fields and dwellings.

Wherein lay the merit of such blessings? How could their veneration and honor ever be sufficient? Yet this does not compare to the merit of melting down images and ending the casting of new ones; [thus] the currency can be...
To avoid waste, they prohibit the copying of scriptures so that pens and paper are no longer valued;

they abolish the monastic order to bring it under the common household registers, collecting taxes on the surplus of millet and grain; and they demolish stupas to provide for the needy, expanding the practice of benevolent charity.
Desiring to approach the imperial court to offer my humble loyalty, I submit this memorial to present this plan, which I believe can benefit the state and bring prosperity.
"You are a man of the people. What do you think of this? The loyal and upright gentleman said: 'How can such words be considered excessive?
In the past, I devoted my will to the groves of Confucian scholars and applied my mind to the gardens of literature; my discourse was largely in accord with yours.'"
This is truly due to the lateness with which I heard the Dharma; I rely on this guide to dispel my delusions. Fortunately, I have not yet wandered far from the path.

Whenever I reflect upon my transgressions and reproach myself, I forget to eat even when facing my meal. If you were to investigate thoroughly and deliberate deeply, you too would surely repent your confusion and know how to return.
I have heard that there is a person named Mr. Zhuan, the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy, who surpasses what I was like in former days.
...this delusion. When I reflect inwardly upon my former confusion, I find that it accounts for five out of ten [of my past errors].
I request that you distinguish the deluded words of Master Zhuan in order to release my misguided attachments. Master Zhuan claims: "The Buddha-dharma originally originated from the Western Hu;
it should not be venerated in China. In the past, I shared this same delusion, but now I have realized that it is not so. For...

I am of the Western Rong tribes; assisting Duke Mu of Qin, I helped him establish his hegemonic enterprise. Li Dayi was born among the Northern Di; serving Emperor Wu of Han, he eliminated threats and dangers.
Since I have been such as this, it is fitting that my teacher should also be so. Why must one take what accords with one's own customs while discarding what comes from a different region?
My teacher regards the greatness of the Way as supreme, making no distinction between "self" and "other. As for the Dharma...

Virtue is supreme; it does not reckon with distance. Now, to esteem benevolence as beauty and to abandon desire as loftiness—to warn against the lingering calamities of accumulated evil and to exhort the practice of goodness in pursuit of blessing—this is what all a hundred schools agree upon, and nothing in the Seven Classics can alter.

Yet, these views are narrow and shallow rather than profound, and pedantic rather than comprehensive. If one were to broaden this principle of extending one’s own self-restraint to others, who could [dispute it]?
How vast is his teaching compared to that of the Buddha! How distant is he from the Buddha in his ability to perceive the root through its branches!
How broad is his exhortation to good and punishment of evil compared to that of the Buddha! How profound is his elucidation of emptiness and analysis of existence compared to that of the Buddha!
Viewed from this perspective, his Way is indeed subtle; how could the virtue of any sage surpass it? How could he have been born in a foreign land?

Yet they disparage that Way. To come from afar and yet discard one's treasure—surely a horse of exceptional breed is not produced solely in the central cities, nor must a treasure of rare antiquity be a product of the Middle Kingdom alone. Thus, the Han dynasty sought the famous horses of the Western Regions.
Wei Shou [was like] a bright pearl from the South Sea. Rhinoceros and elephant tusks and horns were offered as tribute; the feathers and plumage of the *feiwei* bird were gathered.
When things produced in distant regions are still considered treasures here, how can the Way that emerges from remote lands alone be discarded?

It is like medicinal substances originating among the tribes of the west and north, or incantations arising among the Hu and Yue peoples: if they can truly dispel evil influences and cure diseases, they are to be valued.
How could one fail to employ that which has come from afar? To extinguish the three poisons and realize the unconditioned (*asamskṛta*)—its cleansing of evil is vast indeed.
To eliminate the eight sufferings and attain eternal bliss—its removal of affliction is profound indeed.

How can one be so constrained by the distinction between the "barbarian" and the "Chinese," or calculate intimacy and estrangement? Moreover, within the three thousandfold world-system beneath the ten billion suns and moons...
[The truth] resides in that realm and not in this land. Fu [Yuan] reckoned that what the *Shi* and *Shu* do not speak of was insufficient to be honored as *sūtra*.
In the past, I too shared this delusion; now, however, I have realized it is not so.

Indeed, regarding the secret profundity of celestial astronomy and calendrical phenomena, the extraordinary wonders of terrestrial geography and mountain rivers, and the diagnostic signs of the channels, vessels, and acupuncture points—needle...
The methods of medicinal charms and incantations are not recorded in the Odes or the Documents, nor have they been explicitly elucidated by the Duke of Zhou or Confucius.
Nevertheless, when examined, their auspicious and inauspicious effects manifest at times; when observed in practice, they frequently prove efficacious.

Furthermore, the things that the Duke of Zhou and Confucius did not speak of are as infinite as the teeming multitude, and the principles not recorded in the Odes and the Documents are as boundless as the vast expanse. This is indeed true.

"Writing does not exhaust speech; speech does not exhaust intention. How can one confine oneself to the limited teachings of the Six Classics while turning one's back on the universal principles of the Three Vehicles?
Indeed, when human affairs had not yet flourished in antiquity, the Sages established practical functions for later generations.
Thus, buildings replaced the habitations of nests and huts, and written characters supplanted the system of knotted cords. [Only then did people cease] drinking blood and eating raw fur."
Regarding these preparations, those used first are not necessarily the most precious; though the labor of fire-refining grain-based food may be performed later, it is not inferior.
Whether such things are employed or discarded first is not a matter of the universal or the partial in principle and teaching.

How could one claim that because the *Shi* and *Shu* were disseminated early they should be exalted, while the *Sūtra* (Xiudu) arrived late it should be superseded? A person might eat coarse herbs as a child and fine rice with meat as an adult; yet, when young...
To encounter the rank of a noble while formerly being a commoner is like obtaining wild herbs and greens; how can this be considered superior to the flavor of fine meat?
Is the late attainment of noble status not as honorable as the earlier dignity of a commoner? All things undergo change, yet the Three Jewels are eternally abiding.

Quiescent and unmoving, they respond to conditions and are encountered by all. The transformation body manifests traces of concealment and appearance, while the Dharma-body transcends the cycles of arising and perishing.
He was not born for the first time in a royal palace, nor did he pass away for the last time between the twin *śāla* trees.

How, then, can one discuss his birth and extinction in response to stimuli, or calculate the length of his coming and going? Mr. Zhuan praised Laozi and disparaged Śākyamuni, lauding the Daoist scriptures while denigrating Buddhism.
In the past, I shared this delusion; now, however, I have realized that it is not so. As for the [teachings of] Śākyamuni and Laozi—
They constitute a single essence, one and not two. Both alike eliminate the burdens of worldly desire; both together manifest the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

While the teachings of Laozi are clear yet not fully integrated, the scriptures of Śākyamuni reach the ultimate limit. If the Way were truly right, then the Buddha is certainly the same in being right and without error.
If the Buddha were truly wrong, then the Way could likewise be wrong and without truth. This is not a matter of logical contradiction; it is a difference in the perspectives of people.
Your mind wavers between attraction and repulsion; you are like the monkeys who react with either joy or anger at the same stimulus, and your affection and fear resemble those of Duke Gong of Ye.

As for the principles of the *Daodejing* from beneath the pear tree and the essays on the inner and outer realms from the Garden of Lacquer, they are profoundly subtle and difficult to surpass, pure and lofty, worthy of admiration.
I have personally studied them repeatedly and found no flaw in them. How could I, merely because I faithfully uphold the Buddhist scriptures, disparage them in a superficial manner?

Furthermore, let us consider the principle that birth and death are without end, and the doctrine that karmic retribution is imperishable—these were first elucidated by the Śākya school and were not even mentioned by the followers of Huang-Lao. I do not know for what reason the Daoist scriptures of today resemble Buddhist sūtras, discussing the three periods of existence to provide exhortations and warnings, and transcending the tracks of the Nine Schools. If one were to speak of this based on direct observation: [The text continues with a description of the physical body and its eventual decay, contrasting it with the immortality of the spirit, and concluding: ...it is as if one were to see it with one's own eyes. If one were to speak of this based on direct observation, how could one say that the Daoists have not yet reached this point? It is simply because they have not yet encountered the Buddha’s teachings. If they were to encounter them, they would surely realize that the Daoists’ doctrines are incomplete. Thus, we know that the Buddha’s teachings are truly profound and vast, while the Daoist scriptures are merely derivative and secondary. This is why the Buddha’s teachings are called the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna), whereas the Daoist scriptures are merely called the "Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna). How could the Lesser Vehicle ever compare to the Great Vehicle? It is like comparing a single drop of water to the great ocean, or a grain of dust to Mount Sumeru; there is no way they can be equal. Therefore, the Buddha’s teachings alone are the ultimate truth. They are the foundation upon which all other teachings depend. Those who wish to transcend the world must rely upon them. If one relies upon them, one will surely attain liberation. If one does not rely upon them, one will surely remain bound in the cycle of birth and death. This is the reason why the Buddha’s teachings are so uniquely supreme. One must not fail to understand this. If one understands this, one will naturally come to respect the Buddha’s teachings and abandon the Daoist scriptures. This is the way to resolve the matter. Do not harbor further doubts. If you have any more questions, please ask. I shall explain them for you. Do not be hesitant. Thus, I have finished my discourse. You may now depart. Be careful on your way back. Do not forget these words. Take them well to heart. Do not let them be lost. If you practice them, you will surely attain the Way. If you do not practice them, you will surely fall into the abyss. This is the law of cause and effect. It is not something that can be avoided. One must be diligent and earnest. Do not be negligent. This is the final word. Take it seriously. Do not treat it lightly. Thus, I have concluded my teaching. May you all be well. May you all attain peace. May you all attain happiness. May you all attain liberation. May you all attain the Way. Thus, to be identical with the Buddha is to equalize one’s illumination with his; if one hears with the ears and then lets go [of attachment], then to take the Buddha as a teacher is to follow his teachings.
If one’s illumination is the same, then that which is the same should not be criticized; if one takes him as a teacher, then that teacher must not be defamed.

To praise the Way while slandering the Buddha—how can this be such an extreme delusion? A tradition states: "The Buddha is the breath of a malevolent spirit, and the temple is a shrine for licentious and depraved rites. This is...
This is a profound lack of reflection. Demons bring only calamity; how could they propagate the transformation of the ten wholesome deeds?
Spirits must rely on the heterodox; how could they give rise to the Way of the Eightfold Path? Demons fear dogs, and spirits likewise dread cats.
How then could they humble the lofty pride of Śakra or displace the divine power of the celestial Māras? Furthermore, consider those such as Buddhabhadra and Kumārajīva, or Daōan and Huiyuǎn.
O peers! Those of lofty virtue and high renown are neither intoxicated nor deranged. How could they permit themselves to abandon love and decline glory to seek the heterodox path of *chimei* demons?
Or to toil their bodies and mortify their wills to serve the malevolent spirits of *wangliang* ghosts? Furthermore, from the Eastern Han dynasty down to our Great Tang...
Generation after generation, they have prohibited heterodox speech; everywhere, they have severed licentious sacrifices.

How could they permit the squandering of wealth and labor or the alienation of their own people to construct halls and stupas for demons, or to join the ranks of those who consort with malevolent spirits?

Furthermore, there were high ministers and eminent figures who served as the ornaments of human society—men such as Wang Dao and Xie Liang, and those like Dai Kui and Xu Xun—who set their hearts upon the realm of the divine.
At that time, those who stood apart from the world amidst mists and clouds all received the teachings and took refuge; they all set their minds upon reverent faith.

How could they have allowed themselves to be humiliated by honoring demons or serving malevolent spirits? This was truly because, upon beholding the subtle, they came to know the True, which led them to act in this way.
Furthermore, the ancestor of the Fu clan was Fu Yi, whose courtesy name was Wuzhong. He was a man of eminent talent and profound learning, renowned in his time as a "comprehensive scholar" (tongren).

He discerned the auspicious signs of Emperor Xianzong’s dream and verified the mystical significance of the golden man. Moved by the fact that Buddhism and Daoism were spreading in the East, Fu Yi rendered great service to them.

I venture to judge that the talent and insight of the current Mr. Fu cannot yet equal that of Wuzhong; why then does he destroy the Buddha and slander the Dharma, bringing such disgrace upon his own ancestors?
Is this not the opposite? Kan Ze, the Grand Master of the Secretariat of Wu, replied to Emperor Sun Quan:

"The superiority and inferiority of the teachings of Confucius and Laozi compared to those of the Buddha and the Dharma are vast indeed. Why is this so? The teachings established by Confucius and Laozi take Heaven as their model to regulate practical application."
"I dare not disobey Heaven. When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, Heaven receives and practices it; I dare not disobey the Buddha.

Speaking from this perspective, it is truly not a matter of mere comparison. I, the fool, believe that Kanzi’s discourse provides insight into one corner of the distinction between superiority and inferiority.
How can all you gentlemen of virtue fail to reflect upon these words? Indeed, the Great Beings and eminent monks have contemplated the principle profoundly, while the enlightened sovereign...
The wise ministers’ counsel for the state was loyal; yet why have successive dynasties treasured it as a great lesson?

It is because they knew that its principles exhaust all truth and its nature reaches the ultimate limit, such that no Way could surpass it. Master Fu’s contemplation was not as profound as that of the renowned monks, nor was his thought as refined as that of the sages of old.
He followed only his own mind while turning his back on the Dharma, recklessly severing blessings and giving rise to calamity. How can this be?
Is it that they plan for the state without loyalty? Or do they consider only their own persons without foresight? One must have great awakening to exhaust the mysteries and understand transformation;
one must observe deeply the faults and afflictions to provide for them in advance. Alas, the hundred years of life are easily exhausted; sigh, the five blessings are difficult to maintain constantly.
Life flows like a river and flashes like lightning; karma endures upon the earth as long as heaven itself. The three miserable realms are utterly treacherous and profound.
The four currents of existence are boundless and vast; one relies upon the boat of the Dharma for salvation and soars upon the wings of faith.

It is fitting to transform misfortune into fortune; why then indulge in thoughtlessness and become deranged? The tradition states that there were monks who rebelled during the Zhao and Liang dynasties;
yet to say, "Moreover, there are now two hundred thousand monastics and nuns throughout the realm," is a statement made without reflection.

If one were to reject the present monastic community because there were those who opposed the Sangha in the past, how could one discard the eminent scholars of today because there were rebellious ministers in antiquity?

Or, because there was a wayward son in a neighboring household, could one cast out one’s own obedient child? Or, because there were lawless people in the past, could one fail to sustain the commoners of today?
Indeed, as for the multitude of those who have left the household life throughout the realm under heaven, they are not gathered here like clouds...
A single commandery is truly divided among nine districts, which are further organized into prefectures and counties and delimited by passes and rivers.

Herein lies no authority for conscription or mobilization, yet there exist the prohibitions and regulations of the legal code. Even if there were two or three of the most wicked and dangerous individuals, or one or two icchantikas, [they could not prevail].
Since there is no basis for a mere gathering of crows, why worry about a swarm of ants? Furthermore, when a śramaṇa enters the Way, how could he harbor schemes for flight;
when a woman leaves the household life, how could she seek the use of armor?

Why, then, do you confuse the numbers of monks and nuns, aligning yourself with the faction of the "owl and mirror" [the wicked], fabricating falsehoods to disorder the truth, and concealing the good while praising the evil? O Gentleman!
There are three fears; how could it be appropriate for them to be thus? Now, if those in blue collars commit crimes, it does not concern the fault of Confucius;

if those in black robes act wrongly, how can this be the blame of the Buddha Śākyamuni? When monks violate the imperial laws and nuns offend the secular statutes, it is like reciting the Vinaya while engaging in burglary, or reading the Book of Rites while acting with arrogance and insolence. It is simply because these people possess the nature of stubborn vessels and do not transform themselves.
Regarding goodness: this scripture does not open the source of rebellion and disorder to cause one to become stained by evil. People are not all virtuous, yet the Dharma is truly and solely good.

For what reason would one, out of anger toward evil, turn away from goodness? Blaming others while abandoning the Dharma—this is like speaking of Yi Yin and Hui Zhong with one’s mouth while practicing the deeds of Jie and Zhi with one’s body;
or listening to Jie and Zhi with one’s ears while discarding the Odes and Rites with one’s mouth. If such were the case, then among people there would be those who...

The crime of executing him cannot be excused by the law’s failure to prevent it; rather, one should prohibit what is improper to propagate the Dharma, and one must not disparage the Way because of the person.
I privately hold firm faith in the wondrous Dharma and do not seek to form factions with the śramaṇas.

As for weeding out the tares and weeds to cultivate the noble seedlings, and sternly suppressing the treacherous and perverse to purify the Great Teaching—this is my deepest wish, my deepest wish. (Recorded in the *Fozu tongji*)
[The opponent] says: "To claim that *dàorén* (sages) and earth owls (*tǔxiāo*) are both evil species characterized by greed and perversity is a thoughtless statement.
For one who abandons the secular world to cultivate the Way is called a *dàorén*. One studies the Way to depart from greed and perversity.
If you say they 'covet the path of Bodhi' and 'oppose the flow of birth-and-death,' then Fu Zixing’s words do not even reach this point. Observe the disciplinary conduct of the *shāmen* (śramaṇas)."
It is that which practitioners cannot practice and that which those who seek cessation cannot bring to rest; it may be thoroughly investigated through the various Buddhist scriptures.
Even toward wriggling insects, one does not inflict harm, let alone engage in the acts of an owl and a mirror.
Even the rites of marriage and betrothal are still abandoned and not performed, let alone harbor the hearts of birds and beasts. Why, then, do you cite the supreme state of freedom from desire?

Humans are the most esteemed among all gathered creatures; yet you compare the virtuous and eminent who follow the Way to ignorant commoners, and liken the assembly of those practicing great compassion to inauspicious evil birds.
You call practitioners of the Way "the offspring of rebels," and with the heart of a beast from the north, you seek to harm the good.
How can such malice toward the virtuous be so extreme? How can such perversion of the truth be so sudden? In the past, I have often cited the *Classic of Filial Piety*...

[They] did not cause [it] to be destroyed or injured. [The critics] reviled the Dharma of the śramaṇas for removing the beard and hair, claiming it was contrary to the Way of the former kings and a loss of the principles of loyalty and filial piety.
Now, however, I have realized that this is not the case. As for serving one's sovereign or parents and exhausting one's devotion—

Though one may sacrifice their body, they are called benevolent; though they fail in loyalty and filial piety, they merely preserve their lives. To vainly maintain the integrity of one's skin is not righteous. When discussing excellence, we see those who risk their lives in times of peril;

according to the rites, when facing danger, one should avoid it at all costs. How can one criticize everyone indiscriminately? To condemn all equally for mutilating their bodies is to treat them as the same as those who cherish their skin and hair.
To cut the flesh from one’s thigh or offer up one’s liver—such injury is extreme; to shave the beard or pluck out the hair—the damage is likewise [severe].

It is subtle. To establish loyalty without sparing one’s life—those who debate this do not know how to find fault with it. To seek the Way without begrudging one’s own fur—how can this alone be considered an error?
When Tang took pity on the common people, he was still willing to burn his body to pray for their blessing;

when Mozi emphasized universal love, he wished to grind away his feet until they reached his head. How much more so for one who serves as a sovereign or a father, seeking profound merit and benefit: what is there to regret in the shaving of beard and hair?

Now, the teachings of the sages have diverse paths yet lead to the same destination. When the Way of the gentleman sometimes reverses conventional norms to accord with righteousness, Taibo was such a person.
He abandoned his filial duty to provide for his parents at home, feigning the gathering of medicinal herbs instead of returning;

he discarded the vestments and insignia of the Central Kingdom, adopting the shaving of the head as his adornment. Nothing could more profoundly reverse convention or contravene ritual propriety than this; yet—

Yet Confucius praised him, saying: "Tai Bo may be called one of supreme virtue. What is the reason for this? Although his outward actions seemed to turn his back on his ruler and parents, his heart remained loyal to his family and state;
though his physical form was altered in the lands of Ba Yue, his virtue remained complete through his three acts of protection.
Thus, although Tai Bo discarded the regulations of robes and caps, he did no harm to his supreme virtue; likewise, the śramaṇa abandons the appearance of a scholar-official.

What harm is there to the wondrous Way? Although changing one’s dress and altering one’s appearance violates the ordinary etiquette of a minister or a filial son, by believing in the Way and devoting one’s heart, one wishes for the sovereign and parents to enjoy manifold blessings.
By mortifying body and mind to cultivate the manifold virtues of the monastic life, one leaves behind [worldly ties] to ensure the profound merit of the sovereign and father for kalpas to come.
Is this not a great deal of loyalty and filial piety? To recklessly label such people as "śramaṇas" (monks) [is a shallow judgment].
This would be unfaithful; it cannot be trusted. The *Biographies* (Chuan) further state that Western barbarians were born from mud (*ni*), and therefore they serve mud and tiles.

This, too, is a statement made without reflection. In establishing sacred images and modeling their venerable forms, the materials used are mostly plastered coatings, not merely mud and tiles; sometimes they are carved or cast using iron, wood, gold, or copper.
As for painting them or embroidering them, these are done upon pigments and silk; could one then say that the men and women of the Western Regions are all born from these materials?
Furthermore, the ancestral temples of China take wood as their primary substance; does this mean that the gentlemen who established the rites were all nurtured by wood?
Because one must not forget one's parents, one establishes ancestral temples; because one must not forget the Buddha, one establishes [monasteries].
Its physical form serves to represent the boundless [filial piety], while the heart is employed to express reverence as if the Buddha were present.

To revere the Sage and look up to his virtue—how could there be anything lost herein? Indeed, those who regard goodness as a fault would likewise regard evil as merit. Furthermore, the *Biographies* state:

To say that if emperors lack the Buddha, the state will be well-governed and their reigns long, whereas if they have the Buddha, the administration will be tyrannical and their mandates short-lived—this is yet another statement born of unreflective thought.

It implies that the teachings established by the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) all promote licentiousness and tyranny, and that the words set forth by the Bodhisattvas are solely intended to propagate the deeds of Jie and Zhou.
To judge this by actual fact, it is most certainly not so. Indeed, when the Yin dynasty lost its great treasure, calamities arose.
The words of Daji caused the Zhou to lose its feudal lords; the calamity arose from the laughter of Bao Si.

The fall of the Three Dynasties was due to these very things. How could the teaching of the Triple Vehicle be comparable to such? The Way of the Buddha consists of compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity.

It treats all things as equal, regarding enemies and kin alike; it bestows peace and happiness while rescuing those in peril and suffering. This is how the ancients won the hearts of their people—the Buddha [does likewise].
Since this has been propagated, the scriptures strictly warn against the reasons why the people might flee from their superiors.

The virtues of Fuxi, Xuanyuan, Shun, and Yu are encompassed within the Six Perfections (Ṣaṭpāramitā), while the transgressions of Yi, Zhuo, Jie, and Xin are summarized in the Ten Evils (Daśākuśala) to be prevented and prohibited.

Had Jie followed the teaching of few desires, and Zhou followed the Way of Great Compassion, then Yi Yin and Lü Shang would have had no use for their schemes, and Tang and Wu could never have carried out their punitive expeditions.
Thus, Mingtiao could have been spared from the calamity of national ruin, and Muye could have seen the end of the chaos of overturned halberds.
Xiahou could have followed the song at Luorei, and the Lord of Chu could have avoided the disaster at Qianxi. Such being the case, [one should] renounce...

The transformation brought about by [the Buddha] into the benefit of others is no small matter. It extends blessings and prosperity to infinity and prevents peril and ruin before their signs even appear.

Fu [Yuan] claims that the existence [of the Buddha] is a detriment and his absence is a benefit. What kind of words are these? What kind of words are these? What enmity does the Buddha have that he is so falsely slandered?
What offense has the Buddha committed that he is loathed as an enemy? Furthermore, Fu says: "There has never been a Buddha..."
That "before the Dharma, all people were pure and harmonious, and the world was free of usurpation and rebellion," is yet another statement made without reflection.
Now, when the Nine Li disordered virtue, was that not an age without the Buddha? When the Three Miao rebelled against the mandate, did they not exist during the time when the Dharma was present?

How could there have been such purity and harmony during the final years of the Xia and Yin dynasties? Could it be that there were no usurpers and rebels during the Spring and Autumn period? Bandits, thieves, and traitors... [arose].
The officers received their mandates from Gao Yao. When the Xianyun barbarians were fiercely rampant, Ji Fu was dispatched to suppress them with his labor.

Yet the *Shuowen Jiezi* claims that the Buddha arose during a period of usurpation and rebellion; if the Buddha even cautioned against such theft of the Dharma, how could he ever encourage the chaos of usurpation and rebellion?

Even regarding a single word of contention, the Buddha likewise guarded against it—how could he destroy the Way of pure harmony? Indeed, as for the Buddha’s teaching, it exhorts ministers to loyalty and...

It encourages the son through filial piety; it encourages the state through order; it encourages the family through harmony. It propagates goodness by demonstrating the bliss of heaven, and it restrains wrongdoing by manifesting the suffering of hell.
It does not merely employ a single character to offer praise, nor does it stop at the five punishments to establish admonitions.
To claim that this "harms harmony and fosters chaos" is surely an extreme form of slander. Furthermore, how could such a thing harm the sun of the Buddha?
"Yet you have merely submerged yourself in the sea of suffering. To hold such views lightly and fail to avoid them is truly lamentable.

Thereupon, the scholar bowed his heart in submission and felt shame in his countenance; rising from his seat, he apologized, saying: "I was born into the ways of custom and have often strayed from the Way to indulge myself.

I neglected what remains to be investigated and took pleasure only in what had already been recounted. I turned my back on the True Dharma with divergent arguments and accepted false words as if they were the same [as the truth]."

I have been lost. Now, having heard of the profound and remote nature of the Buddha’s wisdom, I have come to know the loyalty and integrity of the Śākya teachings. My spirit has suddenly awakened and my principles have been laid bare;
this is sufficient to wash away delusions and dispel maladies. Although I followed the heterodox in years past, I now beg to return to the correct path this very day.
I shall reverently recite the precepts that have been sent to me, making them the sustenance of my daily life.
The commentary states: Formerly, Lord Sima Wenzheng criticized Cui Hao of the Northern Wei for his ignorance regarding the selection of methods (*yǔè*).

If those who transmit commands are not skilled in selecting methods, they are all the more to be censured. Just as Heaven’s will was about to greatly open the mandate of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Taizong appeared in the world as a manifestation of a sage with great authority, becoming a sovereign of profound virtue and brilliance for a thousand years.
How rarely encountered is such a person! There was one named Wenzhongzi, who took upon himself the role of a teacher for a hundred generations.

Emerging from the region between the Yellow River and the Fen River, all the ministers and counselors of Emperor Taizong’s time—such as the various dignitaries on the Lingyan Pavilion—turned their faces northward to address him as their teacher.

To receive the Way of being a royal assistant—at such a time—if one were to have been sent as a messenger and gradually come to know the direction of the Way, or had already emerged from the gate of the Wang family, then even if his appointments were not for the offices of high ministers or dukes, he would still not fail to achieve renown. As for men of talent in the countryside who merely rely on the low arts of divination and astrology, since their status and appearance are humble, they have no means to manifest their abilities; thus, it is said: [The text continues: ...therefore, when the Duke of Zhou was about to establish the rites, he first sought out those of great virtue. When Confucius was about to spread the teachings, he first sought out those of great wisdom. When the Yellow Emperor was about to unify the world, he first sought out those of great strength. When the Duke of Tang was about to pacify the barbarians, he first sought out those of great courage. Now, the Way of the Sage King is the most profound and subtle of all ways; its governance is the most difficult of all governance. Driven by long-standing private resentment, he slandered and defiled the Great Teaching in order to pilfer a reputation for himself.

Yet, when Emperor Taizong ascended the throne and the world was bathed in civil brilliance, these gentlemen occupied the imperial court, discussing the Way and governing the state while establishing rites and music;
their achievements were such that even the reigns of Yao and Shun could not surpass them. At this time, Li Yi’s learning had long been neglected and his skills were utterly exhausted.

Filled with shame, he withdrew from public life to his home; it is evident that he perished there in a state of profound despondency. How marvelous is Mr. Li’s “Discourse on Inner Virtue” (*Neide lun*);
having examined it thoroughly, I find it to be a work of refined insight and sagacious argument among all under heaven. As for its chapter on "The Destiny of Life" (*Tongming pian*):

Taking what the Confucians call "fate" (ming) and what the Buddhists call "karma" (karman), he traced their origins and examined their conclusions, synthesizing them into a comprehensive understanding; this was particularly profound and striking.
It is a pity that, due to the abundance of his phrasing, it could not be recorded in its entirety.
