In the fourth month of the summer in the ninth year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, Crown Prince Jiancheng and Prince of Qin, Li Shimin, had already formed a deep enmity and were about to incite internal strife.
Furthermore, as the borders were repeatedly disturbed and military affairs were urgent, [the Emperor] received a memorial from Zhuan Yi, who recklessly proposed the destruction of Buddhism. I beg...

He submitted a petition requesting the abolition of Buddhism; though he repeated his arguments at length, no decision was reached. Subsequently, the monks Falin and others composed treatises to refute him.
Together with Li’s *Discourse on the Inner Virtue of the Palace Gentleman*, these were presented to the court.

The Emperor thereby realized that Yi and his associates had praised Daoism and slandered Buddhism to align themselves with the will of the high ministers. Having no other choice, he ultimately proscribed both religions simultaneously. (5)

On the day of Xin-si of the month, an imperial edict was issued, stating: “The teaching of Śākyamuni takes purity as its priority. It involves distancing oneself from dust and defilement and eliminating greed and desire.
Thus, one propagates sublime deeds and cultivates roots of goodness; it guides the ignorant and deluded, serving as a bridge for all classes of beings.
For this reason, the scriptures and teachings are expounded to discipline students, to subdue body and mind, and to relinquish all attachments, including those regarding clothing and food.”
Food is fundamentally provided for the fourfold assembly. Since the Great Awakened One passed away and the Way and Dharma have spread, the final age has seen decline and gradual deterioration.
Consequently, there have been those of vulgar and debased character who schemed to exalt themselves, as well as people of idle and fallen conduct who merely sought to evade corvée labor.
They falsely undergo tonsure and assume the title of "leaving home," yet they indulge in desires without satiety and pursue gain without ceasing.

Consequently, they frequent the villages and roam the marketplaces; they drive livestock and amass wealth, making their living through farming and weaving and pursuing their careers through buying and selling.

Their affairs are identical to those of common households, and their traces are no different from those of ordinary people. Thus, they violate the texts of the precepts in their advancement and lack the rites of propriety in their retreat.

As for these instructions: there are those who personally engage in plunder and robbery, break into homes by tunneling through walls, commit fraud and deceit, and collude with the powerful and the wicked.
They frequently fall into the net of the law and tread upon heavy punishments themselves. Thus they defile True Suchness (Tathatā) and impair the Sublime Dharma.
This is like weeds and tares that sully the fine grain, or like mud that muddies clear water. Furthermore, the grounds of a *saṃghārāma* are originally called "pure."
As for dwelling, the mind should find its refuge in a place where the principles of reclusion are esteemed and the environment is profound and pure.

In recent times, however, many have established monasteries not in secluded and expansive locations, but solely in areas of clamor and confusion. They construct colorful buildings on rugged terrain with roofs and eaves in chaotic disarray;

they expand their reach into hidden vices, luring in the wicked and depraved. Some even extend their premises to adjoin market stalls or butcher shops, such that dust fills the rooms and the air is reeking with stench.

Fragrances fill the roads, which merely fosters frivolity and superficiality while undermining the principle of reverent veneration. Furthermore, the teachings bequeathed by Laozi fundamentally prize emptiness and stillness;
they nurture the will through non-action and cast aside attachment to external things. To preserve the truth and maintain oneness—this is what is called the Mysterious Gate.

To be preoccupied with worldly affairs is even more contrary to our fundamental purpose. I, the Emperor, have responded to the auspicious timing to govern the realm and cause the teachings to flourish;

my resolve is set upon benefiting all beings, and my heart’s intent lies in their protection. I wish to distinguish between jade and stone, and to discern between the fragrant and the putrid, so that the wondrous Way may endure long and the Field of Merit remain eternally firm.
To rectify the root and clarify the source, a thorough culling is appropriate. As for those monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and female adepts who are truly...
Those who diligently practice and maintain the precepts shall all be accommodated in large monasteries and observatories; they shall be provided with food and clothing so that they lack for nothing.

Those who are unable to be diligent, who have no religious practice, and who cannot endure the support of offerings, shall all be dismissed from the religious life and return to their respective hometowns.
The authorities shall clearly establish regulations and rules, ensuring they strictly follow the teachings of the Dharma; any matters that contravene these ordinances must be eliminated.
[The construction] was halted. Three temples were retained in the capital, two at Guan, and one temple was retained in each of the other prefectures throughout the empire;
all others were destroyed. On the fourth day of the sixth month, Prince Qin used his palace guards to suppress the internal rebellion and executed the Crown Prince and Prince Qi.
Gaozu appointed Prince Qin as the Crown Prince and entrusted him with the administration of both military and civil affairs. In this month—
On the day of Guihai, a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire. The previous edict regarding the purge of the two religions was rescinded.

On the day of Jiazi, the High Ancestor abdicated the throne and assumed the title of Taishanghuang (Retired Emperor). The Crown Prince ascended the throne at the Eastern Palace; he was known as Taizong.
The treatise states: The *Old History of the Tang* records that although Fu Yi had thoroughly studied the books on yin and yang, he himself did not believe in them.
It further says that initially, Yu Jian served as the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy; feeling ashamed to advance his career through such arts, he recommended Yi to replace him.
When Yi became the Director and stood in the same rank as Jian, he repeatedly exposed Jian’s shortcomings, yet Jian harbored no resentment. Those with discernment praised him greatly for this.
Frugal yet envious, Yi was fickle and censorious. Alas! Yi’s character was so shallow and narrow;

yet later, those who styled themselves great Confucian scholars would secretly appropriate his secondary arguments and treat them as their own masterpieces. Furthermore, he defiled and corrupted the commentaries on the Śākya teachings.
At that time, the righteous ministers all despised his doctrines; only the eunuch Zhang Daoyuan claimed they were reasonable. Gao—
Although the Patriarch said he would grant permission, when one examines his edict from beginning to end, it is seen that throughout he extols our Way;

he merely sought to purge the false and the profane that had brought damage to the Great Teaching. Once the order was issued, within a month Emperor Taizong ascended the throne as the Crown Prince and immediately suspended the edict.
There is truly a profound reason for both this divine will and human affairs.
In the first year of the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong sighed to his assembled ministers, saying, "Now that we are in the aftermath of great chaos, will it not be difficult to govern?
The Counselor Wei Zheng replied, "Great chaos is easy to govern; it is like a hungry person being easily fed. The Emperor said:
"Does not the ancient saying go thus: 'If a virtuous man governs a state for a hundred years, only then can he overcome the remnants of cruelty and eliminate the need for execution'?
Zheng said, "This is not the discourse of a sage or a wise man. The governance of a sage or a wise man responds as quickly as an echo; it is certainly not so difficult.

Fu Degui (the second character pronounced with the initial *jì*) of the Bureau of Ministers said, "Not so. Since the Three Dynasties, decadence and guile have increased daily. The Qin relied on laws and statutes, and the Han..."
The various hegemonic paths all desire to bring order but lack the capacity; it is not that they have the capacity but do not desire it.

To summon scholars who delight in empty discourse merely serves to confuse the state and is not worth listening to. Zheng said: "The Five Emperors and Three Kings did not change the people to teach them.

By practicing the Way of the Emperor one becomes an Emperor; by practicing the Way of the King one becomes a King—it simply depends on what one practices. Even the Yellow Emperor fought against Chiyou."
At seventy, one conquers disorder through battle and thereby attains non-action (*wuwei*). When the Nine Li harmed virtue, Zhuanxu campaigned against them;
having conquered them, he brought order. Jie caused chaos, so Tang exiled him; Zhou was devoid of the Way, so Wu attacked him. Tang and Wu personally reached the Great Peace.
However, if people gradually become corrupt and deceitful, no longer returning to simplicity, and instead become ghosts and specters now, how could they still be transformed?
Fu Yi could not respond. However, in his heart he considered it untenable. The Emperor had always regarded Fu Yi’s responses as being correct.
On another occasion, the Emperor summoned Fu Yi, granted him food, and said to him: "The Way of the Buddha is subtle and profound; its sacred traces are worthy of emulation.

Moreover, the retribution of karma is manifest and has repeatedly been verified by evidence. Why is it that you alone do not realize this principle? Fu Yi replied: [The text continues with Fu Yi's response.]

He said, "The Buddha is a clever deceiver of the barbarians from the West. Since his teachings entered China, those who revere them are all petty and depraved men who have copied the abstruse words of Zhuangzi and Laozi to embellish their own demonic delusions. They benefit the state in no way, yet they bring harm to the common people.
The Emperor loathed these words and did not answer him; from then on, he would never speak with him again for the rest of his life.
In the seventh month of the third year, locusts ravaged the crops. While the Emperor was in the imperial garden, he gathered the locusts and said:
"The people take grain as their very life, yet you harm it; this is to harm my people. If the people have faults, they rest upon me alone.
If you possess a spirit, you should eat me instead of harming my people. He was about to swallow them when his attendants, fearing he would fall ill, hurriedly begged him to desist.

The Emperor said, "What is most precious is that the calamity be shifted from my person; why should I avoid this illness? He then swallowed it. Consequently, throughout the remainder of the Emperor's reign, locusts caused no further harm.
On the *guiyou* day of the twelfth month of winter, he issued an edict, saying: "The Sui dynasty lost the Way, and the nine provinces were in turmoil.
I personally commanded the supreme army to inflict these manifest punishments. Among them, there were those who were like the dogs of Jie caught in Tang’s net, or those who bit their own whiskers."

Their righteous indignation led them ultimately to grasp their staffs and each sacrifice themselves for what they served; all of this is truly praiseworthy. As days pass and months come, the flowing river has grown distant;
I fear deeply that beneath the nine springs they may still be submerged in cauldrons and boiling water, and within the eight difficulties they may forever be entangled in water and fire.
With a somber countenance and a heart burdened with grief, I have not ceased to think of this whether waking or sleeping.

To establish fields of merit and to rescue their wandering spirits, you should, at the sites where battles were fought since the commencement of the righteous cause, construct monasteries for each of the righteous men and the fallen enemies who lost their lives on the battlefield.
You should invite eminent companions [to reside there], hoping that where the Dharma drum resounds, the blazing fires may be transformed into blue lotuses, and where the pure *brahman* chants...

Hearing that the ocean of suffering is easily crossed by means of the nectar of immortality, the relevant authorities were charged with determining the site, establishing the name of the monastery, assigning the monastic community, and repairing the buildings;
they were instructed to submit a detailed report on these matters to express the Emperor’s compassionate intent.
Thereupon, he commanded Yu Shinan, Li Boluo, Chu Suiliang, Yan Shigu, Cen Wenzhen, Xu Jingzong, and Zhu Zisha [to carry out the task].
[He] composed an inscription for a stele to record these meritorious deeds (the above is found in the Old History).
The commentary states: In the past, when King Wen of Zhou rose to power, he first bestowed grace upon the bones of the deceased, and thus the world turned toward benevolence.
Now, as Emperor Taizong establishes the Great Peace, he likewise inaugurates the construction of Buddhist temples to offer posthumous merit to those who perished in the ranks of battle.

Fortunate! Alas! Emperor Taizong may truly be said to have established instruction through the Way of the Spirits; his virtue permeated both the realms of the unseen and the seen, far surpassing the mere practice of burying bones.
In the tenth month of the fourth year, there were twenty-nine persons sentenced to death for crimes under the empire’s judicial system, from the eastern seas to the west.

It reached to the mountain ridges. To the north, it extended to the remote frontiers where the people were not familiar with customs and travelers did not carry provisions, obtaining their sustenance along the way;
a bushel of rice cost only five coins. The empire was thus greatly pacified. The chieftains of the barbarian tribes donned robes and caps and carried swords as they stood guard at court.
The Emperor, delighted, said to his ministers, "This is the effect of benevolence and righteousness that Wei Zheng urged upon me. It is a pity that I did not let Feng Deyi live to see this."
Upon seeing this, he recalled that when he first pacified the empire, he had personally executed over a thousand people without enjoying the resulting peace and prosperity.
He immediately bestowed his imperial robes upon various temples and commanded the monks to perform liturgical repentances to dedicate the merit for their posthumous advancement.
In that year, the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, was traveling at Mount Kuang. Ascending the summit, he gazed toward Mount Niutou and saw purple clouds like a canopy;
beneath them, white vapors split into six horizontal bands. The Patriarch, deeming this a sign of a person of extraordinary character, went there to seek him out.
At that time, Chan Master Farong resided within it; whenever he sat in meditative contemplation, he would not rise even upon seeing someone. Or...

Even when prostrating before him, he would not turn his head to look back. The world called him "Lanrong" (The Lazy One). When his grandfather entered the mountains and saw him, he asked, "What are you doing here?"
Rong said, "I observe the mind. The Patriarch asked, "Who is it that observes? What is this mind? Rong was struck dumb with astonishment and had no reply.
He rose abruptly and asked, "From where have you come, Great Virtue? Have you ever known Master Daoxin? The Patriarch replied, "I am he.
Rong bowed twice and requested instruction on the Dharma of the Mind. The Patriarch said, "Now, the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the heart-mind."

The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are entirely within the source of the mind. All gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are fully possessed by you;
they do not depart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning.
All causes and effects are like illusions and dreams. There is no triple world to escape, and there is no Bodhi to seek. As for the nature and characteristics of humans and non-humans—
Equanimity. The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation. Such a Dharma as this you have now attained; there is nothing further lacking.
How does this differ from that of the Buddha? You need only allow the mind to be at ease and free; do not engage in contemplative practices, nor do you need to still the mind.
Do not give rise to greed or anger; do not harbor sorrow or anxiety. Vast and unimpeded, move freely as you will.

Neither performing good deeds nor committing evil acts, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—whatever meets the eye and whatever encounters the conditions—is all the wondrous function of the Buddha.
Joyful and free from worry, this is therefore called the Way. Rong asked: "If the mind is already complete, then who is the Buddha? And what is the mind?"
The Patriarch said: "If it is not the mind, one does not inquire about the Buddha; if one inquires about the Buddha, it is not that the mind is absent. Rong asked:

"Since you do not permit the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), how should one counteract when objects arise? The Patriarch said: "Objects and conditions have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind."
If the mind is not given the name "strong," from what cause would deluded sentiments arise? Once deluded sentiments no longer arise, the true mind is free to exercise its universal knowledge.
You need only follow the mind with ease and spontaneity; without further applying antidotes, this is called the eternally abiding Dharma-body, which is subject to no change or transformation.
"I have received the Dharma-gate of the Sudden School from Master Daman Hongcan. I now entrust it to you. You must receive my words with careful attention and remain on this mountain.
There shall be five Great Beings who will carry forward your profound transformation. Having received the Dharma, the Patriarch returned to Shuangfeng.

In the seventh year [of the Zhenguan era], the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang traveled to India to seek the Dharma. He arrived at the city of Rājagṛha. Xuanzang was born in Yanshi, Luozhou, into the Chen family.

During the final years of the Sui dynasty, he left the household life and received full ordination. He had extensively mastered the scriptures and classics, yet he often lamented that the translations of the sutras from previous dynasties contained many errors and omissions.
He resolved to travel to the Western Regions to seek out different versions for collation and verification. In the third...
In the winter of that year, he submitted a memorial to resign his office, but the Emperor would not permit it.
He then secretly departed, traveling from Yuanzhou through the Yumen Pass to reach Gaochang. King Qu Wentai of Gaochang provided him with travel funds and escorted him as far as Kaśmīra.
There, he studied the *Abhidharmakośa*, *Hetuvidyā*, and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* under the master Saṃgha. Upon reaching Mahāvana, he followed a Brahmin...
He studied the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and the scriptures of heterodox schools. At that time, the Brahmin was over seven hundred years old;
he went to the country of Pukhti and studied the *Abhidharmakośa*, *Nyāyānusāra*, *Tarkamukha*, and other treatises under Dharma Master Fu Guang.
He went to the country of Nāgārāṣṭra and studied the *Sarvāstivādavinayavibhāṣā* under the Master Candramas. He went to the country of Lūna and [studied] under Jñānakṣetra...
He extensively studied the Sautrāntika-vibhāṣā and various treatises such as the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Kucha, he studied the two Vibhāṣās under the Tripiṭaka Master Viśeṣamitra. The king possessed a superior army of one hundred thousand men.
He was a preeminent figure in the Western Regions. Xuanzang crossed the Gaṅgā River with about eighty Hu merchants.

According to their local custom, they sacrificed humans to the gods. Xuanzang and the merchants were captured; because Xuanzang’s dignified bearing was particularly extraordinary, they intended to execute him as a sacrifice.

Suddenly, a great wind arose, raising dust and sand until it filled the sky, and the bright day turned into darkness. The multitude was struck with terror and, regarding Xuanzang as a holy man, [ceased their intent].
To explain this: Upon reaching Central India, he encountered a Mahāyāna lay devotee who expounded the *Yogācārabhūmi* for Xuanzang. He then entered the city of Rājagṛha.
Having heard in advance of Xuanzang’s arrival, the King prepared with full ceremony to welcome him from the outskirts and established him at Nālandā Monastery.

The monastery was constructed of the seven precious gems and housed ten thousand monks. When Xuanzang saw the Venerable Śīlabhadra, the Master of Śāstras, the latter was one hundred and six years of age.
One hundred and six. [Xuanzang] was the preeminent master of the Way and its Virtue in the Western Land, titled "Treasury of the True Dharma.
The sovereign of that country offered him the revenues of ten cities. When Xuanzang expressed his intention to seek the Dharma, Paramārtha sighed with emotion and wept, saying:
"Recently, while I was ill and near death, I suddenly dreamed that the Great Being Mañjuśrī said to me: 'You should not yet weary of this world; three years hence, in China...'"

"A great śramaṇa has received the Way from you; since that time until now, three years have passed. At this, [the King] was filled with a mixture of consolation and joy, as if they shared a long-standing bond.
When Xuanzang saw the King, the King provided him with an elephant carriage and thirty attendants, and daily supplied him with the finest delicacies.
These delicacies included agarwood, milk, ghee, honey, and "Great Man" rice (*mahāpuruṣa-śāli*); the fragrance of the rice could be smelled from a hundred paces away.
However, those produced within the country are not many; only the sovereign and his consort, as well as the preeminent masters of the Dharma, partake of them.

Paramārtha resided in that kingdom, where he followed the Dharmaguptaka (Zhengfǎzàng) to exhaustively investigate the secret profundities of the Mahāyāna, such that his daily wisdom and realization increased. Thus it is said.

In the tenth month of the ninth year, the Dharma Master Xuǎnwǎn passed away at Yánxīng Temple. In his final memorial, he petitioned that the sage emperors and enlightened kings should ensure that rewards and punishments regarding the Three Jewels are not applied indiscriminately;

he lamented that śramaṇas who violate the law should not be subject to the same penal codes as the common people, requesting instead that they be handed over to their proper authorities to be governed according to the monastic discipline (*vinaya*).
He also submitted one scroll each of the *Ān-yǎng-lùn* (Treatise on the Land of Peaceful Nurturing) and the *Sān-dé-lùn* (Treatise on the Three Virtues). The Emperor praised him.

He was enshrined. An imperial edict was issued expressing grief and lamentation, and the Crown Prince was dispatched to pay his respects. The authorities were ordered to provide the funeral requisites.
This was the first instance of a śramaṇa being granted an imperial burial in the Tang dynasty, beginning with Youwan.

In the eleventh month, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "The three vehicles follow a common path, with salvation as their priority; the Eightfold Noble Path takes refuge in compassion as its core.
They flow like an ocean of wisdom to nourish all living beings, and they clear away the forest of afflictions to serve as a bridge for all things.

Abiding in reality and embodying the Way, their principles accord with supreme benevolence; through wondrous fruits and superior causes, their deeds correspond to the accumulation of goodness. I, the Emperor, reverently emulate the Golden Wheel."
Receiving with reverence the precious mandate, the teachings of supreme virtue reach every corner without exception; the regulations of the Great Sage penetrate every hidden realm without oversight.

It is my desire that all people may be freed from the entanglements of worldly existence and that their families may attain benevolence and longevity. Lately, however, due to the turmoil of war and rebellion, the ranks of the monastic community have diminished.

The flowered terraces and jeweled stupas stand with no one to look through their doors; the dark-blue hair and blue lotuses are weathered by wind and drenched by rain. Reflecting upon this decay and ruin, I am truly grieved.
He was despondent. He decreed that in all the provinces throughout the realm where there are temples, the number of ordained monks and nuns shall be limited to three thousand.

Whether a province is large or small, and whether the land is inhabited by Chinese or barbarians, the local authorities shall determine the exact number to be ordained in each location, with the relevant ministries to deliberate and finalize the figures.

One must strive to select those whose virtue and practice are refined and brilliant. Regarding those who previously reduced their status, returned to lay life, or privately ordained as white-robed commoners:

if their conduct and deeds are praiseworthy, they shall all be included within the quota. Even if there are no individuals available to fill the number, it is permissible for the count to remain deficient.

Recently, I have heard that many members of the Sangha are immersed in worldly customs; some falsely claim to represent spirits and deities to spread base and monstrous tales, while others are deluded...

Those who practice medicine or sorcery through heterodox paths to seek profit, whether by branding or piercing their own bodies to alarm the common folk and deceive the ignorant, or by visiting government offices to solicit bribes—all such categories severely undermine the holy teachings. My heart is set upon their protection and preservation; they shall certainly receive no leniency.
From now on, the relevant authorities must rely upon the internal monastic codes and supplement them with the Golden Precepts (the Vinaya) to establish clear regulations.
The treatise says: Formerly, Dong Hu recorded that Zhao Dun had murdered his sovereign. Upon hearing this, Confucius said, "It is a pity;

one is exempt from such a charge if they have crossed the border. This implies that once one has crossed the border, the sovereign can no longer claim them as a subject, and thus the law cannot be applied.
Likewise, we who belong to the śramaṇa community initially obey our fathers' commands and leave the household. Although we have left the household, we still remain within [the fold].
Upon receiving imperial edicts, we immediately alter our physical appearance and change our attire to demonstrate that we have no further use for the secular world;
thus, we are called recluses who have shed the dust of the mundane and severed ties with the profane. How could this be merely a matter of crossing a border?
For this reason, successive dynasties have placed us outside the four classes of commoners and have not treated us with the rites due to subjects or sons.
Although this is fundamentally the Vinaya of the Tathāgata, it is in fact also the law of an enlightened monarch.
When Master Yuǎn made his request at the time of his death, Emperor Taizong specially issued a clear edict.

Examining its principles for refining those who enter the path and for prohibiting and suppressing those who are like pestilence and ruiners of the Way, they all accord perfectly with the bequeathed teachings of the World-Honored Buddha of former times.

As for the application of legal codes to administer punishments, it particularly accords with the principle of the *Chunqiu* regarding crossing borders, providing our followers with a means to govern themselves.
Alas! Only a sage can comprehend the wills of the world and bring to completion its ceaseless endeavors; Emperor Taizong was such a one.
In the tenth year, the Crown Prince asked Zhang Shiheng, "What is the response when one serves the Buddha to cultivate merit?

He replied, "Serving the Buddha lies in purity, benevolence, and forbearance. If one is greedy, lustful, arrogant, and tyrannical, then even if one exhausts their wealth to serve him, it will not diminish their calamities.
Furthermore, good and evil must be requited, just as a shadow follows a form; the words of the Sages on this matter are complete. For the sake of the ruler—
It is clear that if one is loyal as a minister and filial as a son, then blessings and prosperity will endure; conversely, if one acts otherwise, calamity will arrive.
At that time, the Crown Prince harbored rebellious intentions; therefore, Shi Heng used this response to admonish him.
In that year, an imperial decree was issued summoning the Vinaya Master Huixiu of Xiangzhou to the capital to lecture on the Dharma. Huixiu declined the invitation on the grounds of illness.

Initially, Huixiu had lectured on both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, yet he was not yet proficient in the Vinaya section. He believed that the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* could be applied according to specific circumstances without the need for formal instruction from a master.

However, upon opening the scrolls and delving into their profound mysteries, he found himself utterly bewildered regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not. He subsequently went to Vinaya Master Hong to study under him.

Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, he found that although there were thirty fascicles, they did not yet fully exhaust the profound meaning. He sighed, saying: "Principle may be sought through abstraction, but practice is difficult to harmonize and realize.
I have personally observed that among the renowned masters of our school, there has never been one who did not revere the Dharma and follow the Way.
How can I fail to aspire to emulate them? From then on, his practice during the six periods of the day became even more diligent. He did not discard a single pair of shoes for thirty years.
Whenever there was even a small patch of mud, he would walk barefoot. When people asked him about this, he said, "The mud is soft and easy to tread upon;

I simply do not wish to damage the offerings of the faithful. In his later years, his observance of the Vinaya became even more rigorous. When some urged him that one of such advanced age could no longer endure such strictness, he replied, "The mind of indolence arises easily, and the realm of sensory dust is difficult to dispel.
Having escaped from the jaws of a tiger, I have sworn to serve the Dharma unto death; how could I allow my physical decay to cause a deficiency in my practice?"

This was his original aspiration. He once admonished his disciples, saying: "Whenever I listen to the sūtras and śāstras, even after twenty recitations, I still regret that my efforts are insufficient.

I wish to study various other schools as well, yet I have not had the leisure to engage with them extensively. Nowadays, scholars who possess a mere superficial knowledge of the words and phrases quickly desire to model themselves for others, yet they lack comprehensive mastery.
Consequently, when confronted with difficult inquiries, they do not know the underlying origins of the teachings. Whether this Dharma perishes or endures depends on such individuals."
I have long lamented this in the deep night; how much more so now that in my declining years you have opened my mind and directed my will toward becoming a vessel of the Dharma.
This is merely like sharpening a blade upon a whetstone; how could it suffice to smelt and refine the raw jade itself? You all should reflect deeply upon this.
My former great teaching has been fulfilled, and I shall die without regret. He passed away at the age of ninety-eight.
In the eleventh year, an imperial edict was issued stating that the status and title of Laozi, as a progenitor of the state, should rank above those of the Śākya clan.
At that time, the Dharma Master Zhishi led ten like-minded colleagues to the palace gate to present their petition, but the decree refused their request.

When the Emperor’s carriage traveled to Luoyang, Zhishi and his companions followed him there to voice their opposition, arguing that the Daoists venerate the Three Zhangs and rely on talismanic water, sacrificial offerings, and registers.

This matter does not originate from Laozi; it is inappropriate for him to rank above the Śākya clan. The Emperor praised his resolve regarding the teachings and dispatched the Chancellor Cen Wénbèn to convey his decree and send him away.
Sīshí remained obstinate and refused to obey the imperial edict. The Emperor was struck with rage and had Sīshí flogged in the court courtyard.
Sīshí submitted to his punishment and was exiled to the regions beyond the Ling Mountains. Sīshí subsequently died, having failed to achieve his aspirations, at the age of thirty-nine.
Eighteen. Initially, Daoxuan was indeed guilty of an offense. Some criticized him for failing to weigh his own advancement and retreat. Daoxuan said:

"I certainly knew that an imperial edict already issued could not be altered. The reason I contended was simply because I wished for future generations to know that there were monks in the Great Tang."
Upon his death, those who heard the news from near and far could not help but lament and grieve.

The *Lun* states: "According to the principles of the *Chunqiu*, those of different surnames are placed last. That Emperor Taizong elevated the title of Laozi above that of Śākyamuni was likely derived from this principle.
Indeed, Master [Dao]xuan took the propagation of the teachings as his heart's purpose; he risked offending the Emperor’s countenance to debate and argue for them. Although...

The principle cannot be subverted. Yet, when the Great Teaching suddenly suffers such a decline in its reputation and status, how can any member of the Śākya lineage, with a sagacious ruler presiding over them, sit idly by and fail to utter a single word of protest? Confucius said, "The man of resolve sacrifices his life to fulfill benevolence;
he does not seek to save his life at the expense of harming benevolence. This is truly what you have done. How virtuous you are!
In the twelfth year, Yu Shinan, Minister of the Interior, passed away. The Emperor personally issued an edict to Prince Tai of Wei, saying: "Yu Shinan was to me like my own body.
He would rectify omissions and remedy errors without a single day’s neglect. He was a renowned minister of our age and a standard for human relations.
Whenever I committed even the slightest error, he would inevitably confront me and remonstrate. Now that he has perished, [the traditions of] Shiqu and Dongguan..."

There was no longer anyone within [the tomb]. How can the depth of our grief and regret be described? Not long after, the Emperor composed a poem on the rise and fall of past dynasties and sighed with lamentation:
"When Zhong Ziqi died, Boya never again played the zither. To whom shall this poem of mine be shown?
He then ordered Chu Suiliang to take it to Shenxuan’s funerary shrine; having finished reading it, he burned it, hoping that [Shenxuan] might...
The divine consciousness was moved by this realization. The following year, he dreamed that Yú Shìnán presented him with upright counsel as if they were in their usual state.
Consequently, he issued an edict stating: "The late Minister of Rites, Duke Wényì Yú Shìnán, possessed a pure and complete virtue and was a preeminent master of literary composition."

From dawn until dusk, he devoted his heart and mind, his ambition set upon loyal service and beneficial counsel. Suddenly, he followed the transformation of all things, and in an instant, the seasons have shifted.
Yesterday, I encountered this man in a dream; moreover, he presented forthright words as if it were a day from our former lives. Recalling his enduring virtues, I am deeply moved by grief and sorrow.
To provide him with merit for the afterlife and to express my sentiment of longing for the past, you shall immediately perform a vegetarian feast for five hundred monks at his home.
An image of the Buddha was commissioned (according to the *Jiushi* [Old History], Basic Annals).
In the eighth month of autumn, an edict was issued for the eminent scholars of the Three Studies to engage in debate at the Hongwen Hall.

The Daoist Cai Zihuang asked the Dharma Master Huìjìng: "The *Lotus Sūtra* designates the 'Introductory Chapter' as the first. I do not understand to which section this 'first' refers. Huìjìng replied: [text continues]

The Tathāgata entered meditative absorption and emitted light as an auspicious omen; by extending the remote to reveal the proximate, he established the great foundation for transcending duality and opened the way to the principle of the single reality.

This is the introduction. "Chapter" (*pin*) denotes a section; "first" (*di-yi*) denotes the beginning. Therefore, it is called "The First Chapter of the Introduction. Huáng raised an objection, saying: "The character 'di' means 'younger brother.
If one is a younger brother, it is inappropriate to call oneself 'one' (*yi*); yet if one says 'one,' it is not [appropriate to call oneself a younger brother]."

[The opponent] should have said "di" (younger brother). How can these two contradictory statements be reconciled? Jing said, "Did I not just say that 'di' means 'to dwell' and 'yi' means 'the beginning'?
You, Master, do not understand the meaning of the characters; how can you challenge others? Wang Huang was flustered and offered a convoluted excuse.
Jing took advantage of the momentum to crush his argument, whereupon Wang was overcome with shame and withdrew. Jing was on particularly close terms with Fang Xuanling. Furthermore...

He was held in high esteem by Chu Liang, the Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Taichang). Liang once remarked to others: "Jing looks down upon Dao'an; he regards Daosheng and Sengzhao with contempt. He is truly a peerless figure in his time.

Later, when the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Prajñāruci, translated the *Mahāvyutpatti* (Great Ornament Treatise), an imperial edict ordered Jing to serve as the scribe for the oral transmission (*bishou*).
Furthermore, the Prince of Zhaojun, Xiao Gong, and the Chief Secretary Du Zhenglun were both commanded by decree to oversee the project together.
In the thirteenth year, the court sorcerer Qin Shiying slandered the Dharma Master Huilin, claiming he had authored a treatise that insulted the imperial lineage.

An edict was issued to arrest Huilin. Huilin, becoming aware of this, changed his attire, bound himself, and went to the palace gate to request punishment. The imperial decree stated: "According to your treatise..."
Those who maintain mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara are not harmed even when facing execution. Now, it is detailed that your crime merits the death penalty;

I grant you a seven-day reprieve so that you may diligently practice this mindfulness, so that you may be spared from execution at the time of your sentencing. Senglin received the imperial decree but did not practice any mindfulness at all.

When the appointed time arrived, the Emperor inquired as to how his mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara had manifested. He replied, "At the end of the Sui dynasty, the virtue was lost and the four seas were in turmoil."
Teng: "Your Majesty has cleared the realm of all impurities and your Way has permeated all living beings. Since the seventh day, I have not thought of Guanyin; I have thought only of Your Majesty.
The Emperor marveled at these words and dispatched the Censor Wei Cong to inquire about the circumstances of Ling’s thoughts regarding him.
Ling replied: "Guanyin is the Most Holy One, manifesting forms within the six realms of existence. From the heavens above to the earth below, he serves as a teacher and savior for all."
Your Majesty presides over the imperial throne; the myriad nations rejoice in your heart, and your civil governance has reached the height of peace.
Your spiritual discernment extends beyond all bounds, such that your sanctity is equal to that of Avalokiteśvara. This is why we think only of Your Majesty.

Furthermore, Senglin has resolved to widely propagate the Dharma of Śākyamuni to assist the imperial transformation, hoping that the people will fear retribution and dread punishment, thereby keeping far from evil. What does Senglin seek?
