[The author] excludes various histories. As for the criticism of Emperor Taizong’s restoration of Buddhism—claiming that his fondness for the grand and his ambition for achievement, as well as his mobilization of troops in distant lands, were the deeds of mediocre and ordinary rulers and thus not to be emulated—I maintain that Wenzhong’s (Ouyang Xiu) censure was overly severe and that he was deceived by his own likes and dislikes.
During the era of Zhenguan, all insects and plants throughout the world were covered [in grace].
As for its influence: throughout all the lands reached by the sun, moon, frost, and dew, everyone knocked at the gates to offer their tribute and fulfill their duties;
only the Mo-li-zhi of Goryeo remained rebellious and obstructed the imperial mandate.

Emperor Taizong was a sovereign of moral heroism whose virtue would endure for a thousand years—how could he have sat idly by, leaving this as a source of anxiety for his descendants, without lending even a slight degree of strategic effort?
Indeed, this was due to the abundance of their majesty and virtue, and the inevitability of their momentum; it was not a matter of seeking grandeur or boasting of military achievements.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor pacified Chiyou, winning the chaos after seventy battles; Gaozong campaigned against Guifang.
It took three years before he could subdue them. Emperor Taizong raised a mere division of troops and the Yin Mountains were pacified; he arrived at his imperial halting place and Goguryeo submitted.
Yet, although the Yellow Emperor and Emperor Gaozong passed through the scrutiny of Confucius without ever being slightly disparaged, Wenzhong specifically regarded Taizong’s conduct as a flaw.
Could this not be an instance of excessive criticism? Considering Taizong’s magnificent virtue and greatness—

Such is the nature of karma; yet [Wenzi] still disparages it with such severity. I fear that future gentlemen, apprehensive of the difficulty of avoiding such censure, will have no intention of pursuing fame and achievement.
Wenzhong merely wished to exalt the matter, yet he did not realize that he was himself falling into the error of "loving the grand.
As for his re-establishment of the *futu* (Buddhism), this was precisely a means to harmonize and accord with the Way.

His virtue was such that he aligned himself with the hearts of Heaven, Earth, and the spirits, thereby providing salvation for the people of the world and future generations, resulting in benefit that is inexhaustible.
If Wen Zhong considered this inappropriate, then Taizong was ignorant in his choices.
Had Taizong truly been ignorant in this regard, then those of the caliber of Fang Xuanling, Du Jing, Wang Shichong, and Wei Zheng would likewise have [been excluded].
Is this not one who, following the example of those who seek only emolument, has become ignorant regarding what should be accepted or rejected?
Some say that because Wenzhong admired the character of Han Yu, he was compelled to act thus. Alas! How could Wenzhong have been so heartless?

To admire a man for disparaging the Buddha while simultaneously abandoning the moral virtue of Emperor Taizong—is this not to be deceived by one’s own likes and dislikes? Confucius established the teachings of name and reality (mingjiao).
Laozi, however, disparaged and rejected it. Yet when Confucius edited the *Book of Rites*, he said, "I heard this from Lao Dan.
Did Confucius then discard words based on the person? Or was it merely like the preferences and aversions of worldly sentiment?
How much more so for the True Buddha? This refers to the fundamental essence inherent in both the sage and the ordinary person.

To destroy it is to destroy oneself; how could it possibly harm the True Buddha? I have heard that once, during the night, Wen Zhong dreamed that he was led by several brave warriors to the court of Emperor Taizong.
Taizong, filled with anger, rebuked him, saying: "My military and civil merits and achievements are such as..."
This cannot escape the censure of his son. Why? When Wenzhong was startled awake by fear, he later wished to revise his work;
however, as the book had already been submitted and promulgated, he was unable to make the changes. He once sighed with regret, saying, "Equanimity is the most difficult thing to achieve.
This was certainly not said merely in passing.

In the ninth month of the second year of the Yonghui era, the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, entered parinirvāṇa. His surname was Sima; his family had resided in Henei for generations and later moved to Qizhou.

From birth he was extraordinary and transcendent; from childhood he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the various gates of liberation appeared to him as if they were skills mastered in a previous life.
Having succeeded to the Patriarchal position, he restrained his mind without sleep, his side never touching the mat for nearly sixty years. [This occurred during the] Sui...
At the end of the Daye era, he led his followers to Jizhou. There they encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city for seventy days without resolution.
The multitude was terrified, and the Master took pity on them; he instructed them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.

Shortly thereafter, the rebel forces saw what appeared to be divine soldiers within the battlements and said to one another, "There must be extraordinary people within the city," whereupon they withdrew. This occurred at the beginning of the Wude era.

He resided at Mount Pòtóu, where disciples flocked to him from all directions. Once, while traveling on the road to Huángméi, he encountered a young boy whose physical features were exceptionally refined and extraordinary.
The Master asked, "What is your surname? The boy replied, "I have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one.
The Master asked, "What is this surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The Master asked, "Do you have no nature? He replied, "Because nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
The Master silently recognized that he was a vessel for the Dharma and ordered an attendant to go to his mother to request his ordination.

Because of their past karmic affinity, the mother showed no sign of reluctance. Eventually, the Master transmitted the robe and entrusted the Dharma to him with this verse: "The nature of the lotus seed exists; Because of the ground, the lotus grows.
When great conditions unite with faith, Birth after birth, there is no birth. Thereupon, he entrusted his disciples to him.
One day he addressed the assembly, saying: "I once traveled to Mount Lu and ascended its peak.
Looking toward Mount Pòtóu, I saw purple clouds like a canopy, beneath which white vapors divided transversely into six paths. Do you understand this? The assembly remained silent.
Master Rèn said, "Could this not be the Dharma that the Master will later propagate as a separate branch? The Master said, "Excellent. This was during the Zhèngguān era.

At the end, Emperor Taizong, having long admired the Master’s flavor of the Way and wishing to behold his dignified bearing, issued an edict for him to come to the capital. The Master submitted a memorial declining the invitation.

Though this was repeated three times, he ultimately declined on the grounds of illness. On the fourth occasion, the Emperor commanded a messenger, saying, "If he truly does not rise, then bring his head here.
When the messenger arrived at the mountain to convey the decree, the Master extended his neck toward the blade; his expression remained serene. The messenger was struck with wonder.
Hui reported the circumstances to the Emperor, who marveled at him all the more with deep admiration. He subsequently bestowed precious silks upon him so that he might fulfill his aspiration.
At this time, [the Master] suddenly issued an admonition to his disciples, saying: "All dharmas are entirely liberated. You each must protect and mind yourselves."
His influence flowed on into the future. Having finished speaking, he sat peacefully and passed away at the age of seventy-two. His stupa was erected at his native mountain.

On the eighth day of the fourth month the following year, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord for no apparent reason; his physical appearance remained as if he were alive. Thereafter, his disciples did not dare to close it again.
Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dajian.
*Comprehensive Chronicle of the Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Longxing Era*, Scroll 12 and Scroll 13.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of Shishi Monastery in Longxing Prefecture.

In the fourth year of the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, Dhyāna Master Huìkuān passed away. Huìkuān was born into the Yang family; his father was the Daoist Wei Sāndòng Xiānshēng, and his elder sister was Xìnxiāng.
From birth, she knew the Way and remained in meditative stillness throughout the day. When Huìkuān was five or six years old...

He engaged in discourse with Xiangxin; their conversation was entirely unrelated to worldly affairs. Within the family, everyone followed the Way except for Kuan, who alone did not take pleasure in it.

His father scolded him harshly and ordered him to prostrate before the Celestial Honored One. Reluctantly, Kuan knelt before it. Suddenly, the iron image toppled over and shattered. The entire clan was struck with wonder and amazement.
I have therefore recorded the words and phrases from my discussions with Xinsiang. Previously, when the Dhyāna Master Tansiang of Longhuai Monastery was on his deathbed, he said to his disciple Hui:
"My karmic conditions dictate that I shall be reborn in the family of the Yangs atop the Peak in Mianzhu, Guanghan."
"Seven years from now, you shall come to see me. Having finished speaking, he passed away. Subsequently, Daohui somewhat forgot this.
One night, he dreamed that [Huikuan] reproached him for breaching their agreement. Startled awake, Daohui immediately went to the mountain peak and knocked on the door.
Huikuan asked, "Who is knocking at the door? Daohui replied hastily, "I am your disciple, Daohui. Huikuan laughed and said, "How do you know it is I, yet call yourself my disciple?"

Hui said, "The Master’s voice is just like it was in the past. They then met face to face. Hui’s father brought out the records he had compiled of his various discussions with Xiang and showed them to him;
these were primarily the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* and other treatises. Hui immediately took leave of Yuanwan and returned to Longhuai Temple to undergo tonsure.
From then on, his spiritual wonders became increasingly manifest, and the laity called him "Master Sheng" (the Holy One). His sister, Xiang, also followed him.
He left the household life. Once, while a strange monk from Jinghui Temple was entering meditative absorption, red flames filled the entire temple and blazed forth, yet no one recognized them.
Xinxiang said, "This mass of fire is simply the Venerable One entering the Fire-Light Samādhi.

Because that temple was flooded with water during his practice of the Water-Contemplation, the entire room became a profound stillness of water alone, and his physical form could not be seen. The strange monk marveled at him, believing he had attained the fruits of the path.

At that time, she was also titled the "Venerable Nun. During the reign of Emperor Kōten (Kō), her tenth-generation descendant became a *daisō* (fully ordained monk). The records of her ten successive incarnations still exist today. She has been granted various posthumous titles by successive dynasties.
In this year, the Dharma Master Xuanzang was about to construct a great stupa at Ci'en Monastery to enshrine the scriptures and treatises he had obtained.
The Sanskrit manuscript was presented for imperial review. An edict issued by Li Yifu, Secretariat Drafter, stated:

"Regarding your wish to construct a stupa, we have now ordered that the clothing and belongings of the deceased from the Imperial Palace, the Eastern Palace, and the seven掖庭 (掖庭) shall be used to assist you, Master, in its completion.
Thereupon, the Dharma Master provided the architectural standards of the Western Regions and personally carried earth and transported bricks; before long—
It was completed; it stood two hundred feet high. A stele was erected on its upper level, upon which the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Two Sages" was inscribed and enshrined.
In the fifth year, the Mahābodhi Temple in Central India dispatched a monk bearing a letter from Master Xuanzang.

Presenting local products. The inscription reads: "From the Venerable Huitian, who dwells at Mahābodhi Monastery by the side of the Vajrāsana—surrounded by a multitude of learned ones in this subtle, wondrous, and auspicious world—to the Upādhyāya Mokṣa in the Great Country of Mahācīna, who has perfectly exhausted the subtlest refinements of the immeasurable Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras: I respectfully send these greetings."

"I hope you have little illness and little affliction. I, the bhikṣu Hietian, have now composed the *Praise of the Great Supernatural Transformations of the Buddha*, as well as various sūtras, śāstras, and works on inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*).
I am now entrusting these to the bhikṣu Fachang to deliver to the immeasurably learned Great Elder, the Venerable Ācārya. Zhi Guang also sends his greetings as before. Mabasoka Rishou bows."
First, I pay my respects. I now send with this letter a pair of *pāṭa* (woolen cloths) to show that my mind has not been absent from you, though the distance between us is great.
Do not take offense at their smallness; I hope you will accept them. You must include the titles of the sūtras and śāstras you require in your letter, and I shall transcribe and forward them for you.
May the Upādhyāya Mokṣa know this. Furthermore, as Dharmadīrgha is departing to return home, I, Xuanzang, reply to the Elder Jñānaprabha. The summary of it says: "Last year, the envoy..."
I have returned. Having received the news of the passing of the Great Master Zhengfazang, my grief is so piercing that I cannot restrain myself.

Alas! The boat upon the sea of suffering has sunk; the Eye of Humanity and Heaven has been extinguished. How can one not express the pain of such a loss? Long ago, when the Great Awakened One’s radiance was hidden...

Kāśyapa succeeded to his great enterprise; Śāṇakavāsin passed away; and Kuṭadanta propagated his sublime teachings. Now that the General of the Dharma has returned to the Truth, the Dharma Master shall next undertake this task.
I pray that your pure words and wondrous eloquence may flow far and wide throughout the four seas, and that your adornment of merit and wisdom may endure forever upon the Five Mountains.
As for the sūtras and śāstras brought by Xuanzang, those such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* have already been translated.
The *Dilun* and other treatises, totaling more than thirty works of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, have been translated.

On this very day, may the Great Tang Emperor’s person enjoy ten thousand blessings and the entire realm be at peace. With the compassion of a Wheel-Turning King, he spreads the transformation of the Dharma-King;

all the sūtras and śāstras produced have received his divine pen in composing prefaces, and he has ordered the relevant authorities to transcribe them for circulation throughout the kingdom. This has extended even to neighboring states, which likewise all revere and uphold them.

Although we dwell at the end of this age of semblance, the teachings remain radiant and flourishing, harmonious and solemn; this is no different from the transformation wrought in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī.
I humbly pray that you will take note of this. Recently, one pack-load of scriptures was lost while crossing the Indus River.
I have recorded their titles below; should there be an opportunity, I request that you forward them. I also send a small gift as an offering, which I hope you will graciously accept.
In that year, by special imperial decree, the śrāmaṇera Kuiji was ordained as a bhikṣu. He entered the Great Ci'en Monastery to participate in the correct translation of the scriptures.
Kuiji was the younger cousin of Wei Zheng (Yuchi Jingde); his father was Zong, General of the Right Golden My Guard, and his mother was Pei.
In a dream, he swallowed the lunar disc with his palm and became pregnant. On the evening of his birth, divine light filled the room. At the age of six, he was already capable of composing writings.
Initially, Dharma Master Paramārtha had obtained a young boy in the Western Regions whose intelligence and insight were peerless;

he brought him to Sengzong. Sengzong called Daoki out to pay his respects. Paramārtha then commanded him to recite several thousand words from a military treatise he had composed. Paramārtha watched him closely with repeated glances.
When the boy and Jī finished reciting it, Xuanzang deceived him, saying, "This is merely an ancient book. Jī did not yet believe him, so Xuanzang had the Western boy recite it over again;
there was not a single character that differed. Jī was greatly enraged, thinking that Jī had stolen an ancient book to deceive him, and he intended to kill him.
Xuanzang then begged to leave the household life. Jī said, "If you agree to let me eat meat and strong-flavored evening meals, then I shall grant your request."

He requested ordination. Paramārtha said, "It would be better to submit to the sword and die than to die of starvation. Xuanzang, admiring his brilliance, granted him permission. He subsequently entered the monastic path.

Whenever he read commentaries or records, he could recite them from memory after a single glance, and their meaning was also understood instantaneously. He was proficient in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Having participated in the translation of scriptures, he received the core tenets of the *Yogācāra* and *Vijñaptimātra* from Xuanzang. He authored approximately one hundred treatises, for which he was then known as "The Hundred [Treatise Master]."
The Master of this treatise was naturally grand and extravagant; whenever he went out, he invariably prepared three carriages, for which reason he was also called the "Master of the Three Carriages.
In the fifth month of the sixth year, when the Dharma Master Xuanzang translated the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, the śramaṇa Shentai and others each composed commentaries (*yi-shu*) to explain it.
The Master Qixuan showed this treatise to Lü Cai, the Attendant Physician to the Imperial Medical Bureau, who [was deeply...].

He was a man of artistic talent who extensively disparaged its [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] literary style and composed the *Inming zhujie poyi tu* (Illustrated Chart for Refuting the Meaning of the Commentary on the *Hetuvidyā*). Those of frivolous character listened to and believed him.

In the seventh month of autumn, the Dharma Master Hui-li, who was translating the scriptures, sent a letter to the Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, Qian Zhi-ning, refuting his errors with these words:
"I have heard that when the Buddhas established their teachings, the words and phrases were profound and remote, while the essential meanings were subtle and deep. They were equal and perfect..."

The vast expanse of the void resembles the surging waves of the deep blue sea. To discuss the nature and characteristics of True Suchness (Tathatā), one may still remain confused despite dwelling on the tenth stage (bhūmi).
To explain the causes and conditions of even a small blade of grass, one may yet be ignorant despite abiding in the state of non-arising (anutpāda).

How much more so for those entangled in the net of the eight heterodoxies and submerged in the current of the four inversions—how could they hope to investigate the fundamental cause or discern and manifest its principles? There is no such possibility.

How deluded we are! I have personally observed that the Dharma Master of the Tripitaka Translation Bureau at Great Ci’en Monastery has established the foundation of wisdom early and achieved intellectual maturity in his youth.
His conduct is as pure as jade and his integrity surpasses the pine and cypress; thus he was able to travel in person to the Holy Land to inquire and receive the subtle teachings.
He holds the Tripiṭaka within his breast and encompasses the four Āgamas within the palm of his hand. He succeeds to the pure legacy of former sages and fans the wind of their enduring models.
In the present age, he is truly a vessel for the common people and a mirror for the monastic community.

Of the sacred teachings he has translated, there are already more than three hundred fascicles; among them is a minor treatise titled *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), which elucidates the essential principles of debate and refutation.
The principles for refuting heterodox paths, though not the most profound mysteries of the Profound Gate (the Buddhist tradition), are nonetheless not something to be understood in a moment of haste.

Recently, I have heard that Lü Fengyu, the Attendant of the Superior Medicine Bureau, relying on the capacity of an ordinary man and pilfering the doctrines of various masters, has composed a diagram of *hetuvidyā* (logic) to explain the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*).
He is unable to achieve refined awakening and delights in initiating heterodox views; he seeks fame and reputation at the expense of acting recklessly.

They engage in forced and artificial interpretations, setting aside the orthodox explanations of the multitude of virtues and indulging in the arrogant mind of self-conceit to peddle their views before high officials.

Amidst the clamor of the streets and alleys, they feel no shame for their thickened faces nor grow weary of their exhausted spirits; though the seasons of heat and cold have changed many times, their minds remain unsated.
Yet, having served in secular affairs with little leisure, they conclude that the True Doctrine can be mastered.

How is this different from a field mouse seeing that it can climb onto a cauldron or stove and claiming Mount Kunlun is not difficult to reach, or a spider seeing the ease of traversing a thorny forest?
Luo thus believed that the Fusang tree could be caught in a net; his failure to measure his own limits was no different from this.

Moreover, the Great Sound is silent and Great Eloquence is like stammering; this is why Vimalakīrti remained silent at Vaiśālī in accordance with the Truth, and why Confucius, though of lofty virtue, was humble among his fellow villagers.
We have never heard of anyone who gained the esteem of the scholarly class through boasting, self-aggrandizement, or self-promotion. [The Emperor] then composed a letter.

When those matters had somewhat subsided, on the *dingyou* day of the tenth month of winter, Liū Xuān, a Doctor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*tàicháng bóshì*), composed a letter of "Returning Reverence" (*guījì shū*) together with verses (*gē*).

He issued this as a proclamation to the virtuous masters (*dédé*) who were translating the scriptures, requesting that their work be brought to completion. Thereupon, the Dharma Master Míngjùn replied, returning the letter and composing a hymn (*sòng*) in response.

A postscript: The Great Teacher was extremely majestic and dignified, yet he reprimanded Lü Cai for his presumptuous conduct. Upon receiving the letter, Xuán de immediately impeached Lü Cai and submitted a formal report on the matter.
By imperial decree, the high officials and scholars were assembled to lead Lü Cai to Ci'en Monastery to see the Dharma Master.
There, Lü Cai received his reprimand, apologized, and withdrew.
On the *bingyin* day of the first month in the first year of the Xianqing era, Crown Prince Da Wang Hong was established as the Heir Apparent.
On this day, five thousand monks were provided with a vegetarian feast at Ci’en Monastery; the Imperial Messenger (Huangmen Silang) Xue Yuanchao was charged with presiding over the matter.

Thereupon, he questioned the Dharma Master Xuanzang regarding the precedents for translating scriptures in former dynasties. The Master replied: "The Han and Wei periods are distant, so it is not possible to discuss them in detail."
Since the Jin and Song dynasties, there have always been officials appointed to supervise, review, and meticulously edit the translation of scriptures.

Thus, when Dharmānandi translated scriptures during the time of Fu Jian, the eunuch Zhao Zheng held the writing brush. When Kumārajīva translated scriptures during the time of Yao Xing, Yao Xing himself and Yao Song held the writing brush.
During the Later Wei, when Bodhiruci translated scriptures, Cui Guang, the Palace Attendant, received the dictation. This continued until the Liang dynasty.

The same was true during the Chen, Zhou, and Sui dynasties. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, when Paramārtha translated the scriptures, the late Emperor commanded Prince Xiao Gong of Zhaojun and Chief Secretary Du Zhenglun to oversee the project; yet now, these records are particularly missing.

Furthermore, the Great Ci’en Monastery is magnificent and grand, with no peer in antiquity or modern times, yet a stele has not yet been erected. It is for these two reasons that this humble monk harbors this concern.
[The Emperor] said, "I wish to hear of this from Your Majesty. Yuanchao reported these words [to the Emperor], and an imperial decree was granted.
On the *renshen* day of that month, during the court assembly, Cui Dunli, the Director of the Secretariat (*Zhongshu Ling*), proclaimed the edict, saying:

"The Dharma Master Xuanzang of Da Ci'en Monastery has newly translated the scriptures and treatises; their textual meanings must be refined. It is appropriate to command Yu Zhirning, the Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Zuo Puye*), and..."

Minister of the Ministry of Works Lai Ji, Minister of the Ministry of Rites Xu Jingzong, Palace Attendant Xue Yuanchao, and Secretariat Drafter Li Yifu and Du Zhenglun were present at the time to review [the text].
Wherever there were passages that seemed unstable, they polished them according to the context.
When the court session concluded, the Inner Eunuch Wang Junde was sent to inform the Dharma Master, saying: "We have learned that you require the assistance of friends in the translation."
The Sūtra states: "I have already issued instructions to Yu Zhining and others that I hope to compose the inscription for the Ci'en Monastery myself;

I do not know what your thoughts are on this matter, so please report back to me. Upon receiving these imperial edicts, Xuanzang led the assembly to the palace to submit a memorial requesting [the Emperor's compliance].
Before long, Emperor Gaozong personally composed the inscription for the Great Ci'en Monastery and dispatched Changsun Wuji to show it to the various high officials.

The text read: "In the beginning when heaven and earth first formed, and at the start when all things first emerged, there was nothing that did not take shape upon the broad earth or find shelter beneath the vault of the heavens.
Thus, while the two luminaries shine in the sky, their waxing and waning remain unfathomable..."
As for the four oceans that record the earth, how could they fathom the limits of its waves? How much more so when the Dharma-gate is empty and still, arising before the point of non-extinction;

and the holy teaching is all-encompassing, manifesting beyond the formless realm of existence and non-existence. Thus, through the light of the Way, it has shone throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, and its transformation has permeated all living beings.
Reflecting deeply upon the manifestation at the royal palace, where the lotus blossomed beneath his first steps, and the divine pool emitted radiance as he planted his tree.
The lofty strains [of the Dharma] form the backbone of the embankment; the virtuous sounds are performed at the Deer Park.

A great assembly of scholars gathers at the Dragon Palace to bring blessings to sentient beings burdened by transgressions and to revive a human age on the verge of extinction. Thus, even those of the lowest intelligence can embrace the Way, though their bones may crumble in the wilds of the Cold Forest;
and those of the highest wisdom revere its wind, though they perish amidst the verses of the Snowy Mountains. Like threads, the rain of Dharma flows forth, purifying the burning house with its words.

The Wheel of Fire ascends as the Sun of Wisdom; it illuminates the layered darkness and restores the day. I have examined the annals of the past with great care and scrutinized the principles of the Way.
Is there anything that bestows blessings for eternal kalpas like the Teachings of Śākya? Empress Dowager Wende relied upon the jade tree as her trunk, from which the source of the spring flows forth.

Her virtue shone over Tushan and her radiance extended to the banks of the Gui and Rui rivers. Her fragrance spread through the vermilion records, manifesting noble models throughout the eight directions.

The instructions bestowed from the Purple Palace have fanned the auspicious Way through ten thousand ages; yet suddenly the essence of Heaven has obscured the moon, forever extinguishing its pure radiance, and the cords of Earth have snapped, eternally sinking its lush branches.
Gazing at my coiffure mirror, my grief increases; looking toward the distant mountains, how can I seek to follow you?
Zhong You gave vent to his sighs over the thousand *zhong* of grain; Yu Qiu expressed his grief over the three failures. My own boundless remorse is indeed poignant for the rest of my life.

Therefore, cherishing these thoughts, I have initiated the construction of this Golden Land. To the rear, it turns its back upon the suburbs of Bin, where the trees of a thousand manors are dyed like brocade;
to the front, it faces Mount Zhong, from which peaks a hundred *ren* high unfurl like lotuses. To the left, the eight rivers flow, their clear waters reflecting the light.

Yet it divides the mirror-like landscape; to its right, nine roads converge. Flying feathered canopies connect with the clouds, truly a profound region of the Heavenly Treasury and a magnificent site of the Imperial Capital.
Observe how its carved balconies span the heights and its ornate pavilions soar into the void: at dawn, vermilion birds illuminate the palace of the sun as they float in splendor;
at the start of day, the white-hued hare reflects in the moon-palace as its radiance clears and shines. Along the fragrant paths, autumn orchids grow in sparse beauty.

The pavilions are adorned with purple; fragrant crags hold dense winter cassias, and the private chambers are thick with vermilion. The lamps shine with profuse brilliance; as their flames swirl, they resemble cranes within the heart.
The banners mark the lofty spires, their colorful streamers winding like rainbows across the heavens. The tiered steps rise and fall, holding patterns of dew and resting upon jade.
The light curtains unfurl and fold, their lattices like lotus faces strung with pearls. The rosy clouds lower over the red peaks, and the vast pool reflects—
The green smoke blends its resonance with the chime of tinkling ornaments and the evening bells; the gentle breeze shares its harmony with the morning chants.
How could it merely be that the true Fragrant Accumulation Heaven Palace is far surpassed in its magnificent splendor, or that the immortal palaces of Langfeng are humbled in their ornate beauty?
There was the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who was truly the crown of True Suchness. His presence was profound and serene, like a pure breeze in solemn stillness.

Longsong’s refined thoughts were luxuriant and profuse like embroidered silk; his brilliance soared through the Milky Way. His wisdom, which illuminates both the present and the past, emerged from innate knowledge.

His sincerity, which harbors tranquility and embraces the truth, manifested from his very childhood. A solitary standard for his generation, he surpassed Daosheng and Huiyuan to shed light upon the past;

a towering excellence for a thousand years, he outstripped Sengcheng and Kumārajīva to glorify the future. He considered that the pure customs of antiquity had declined and the world had become turbid.
The customs have shifted with the times. I grieve that the great night of ignorance is so long and dark; I lament that the subtle words of the Buddha have been obscured for so long.

Consequently, I cast my lot in foreign lands to widely partake of the secret teachings. I boarded a boat upon the Milky Way beyond the clouds, and shook my mendicant’s staff amidst the mists and vapors above the peaks.

I wandered as a guest across the vast, surging waves of the sky-reaching great ocean, and traveled alone through the piercing chill of the earth-spanning frost. Upon the level plains, I paused to record these accounts.
Clad in single robes amidst the winds of the Snowy Ranges; with wheels lowered in the wilderness under the sun that scorches the shifting sands.
On distant journeys through moonlit paths, one’s shadow briefly becomes a companion at night; traversing perilous peaks far away, one’s form remains forever solitary at dawn.

Exhausting thought within the wondrous realm, one probes the mysteries of the Ultimate Truth; emptying the mind at the profound ford, one investigates the secrets of the subtle arts. Thus one attains what the sages of old could not reach and awakens to...

What had never been heard in the ancient scriptures was now realized: the golden tablets flowed eastward to continue the teaching that was on the verge of extinction, and the precious verses traveled westward to supplement the texts that were already incomplete.
At that time, I turned my gaze toward this sacred foundation and settled my mind in this place to propagate its profound principles.

Thus, the leaves regained their lush green upon the Jetavana grove; thereby, the remote and hidden gates were opened wide, and the waters of meditative concentration were purified once more. Such is the devotion of my heart.
The Eightfold Path is solemnized at the Twin Trees; may we hope for the extension of auspicious blessings and rely upon the aid of the unseen realm.

We respectfully pray that the Empress Dowager may roam freely through the Six Perfections and her spirit travel before the Vermilion Gates, while she rests in the Four Dhyānas and her soul ascends to the Purple Pole of the Ultimate.
Alas! The Jade Candle passes swiftly, hastening the four seasons through heat and cold; the Golden Arrow is difficult to detain, as the Six Dragons race across the dial of time.

Fearing that the waves might shift the trees and the ocean transform the mulberry fields, and that the earth’s topography might change so that high cliffs sink into deep valleys, we have reverently carved this upon a solid stone to commemorate this sacred site. The inscription is not recorded here.

On the gengshen day of the third month, the various officials presented a memorial extolling the excellence of the Emperor’s composition. A separate edict was issued for Xu Jingzong, Minister of the Court of Rites, to deliver the inscription of the stele to the Dharma Master Xuanzang.
On the jiazi day, Xuanzang led his disciples to the palace gate and submitted a memorial of thanks, stating: [The text continues with the content of the memorial.]
The work of creation has spread through all things to establish its teachings; likewise, the Way of the Sage reveals its true intent through words.

Thus, while the drawing of trigrams and the transmission of texts may seem like empty talk when viewed from the perspective of physical form, the establishment of hexagrams and the differentiation of images do not, in fact, transcend the realm of the world.
The virtue of Fuxi (the Sovereign of Xīhuáng) is still praised in antiquity, and the legacy of King Jī (King Wen) likewise stands uniquely lofty.
As for later generations, how could they compare to those who opened up things and accomplished affairs, elucidating the Eightfold Noble Path to manifest its elegance;

who explained the Way through their words to testify to the Three Insights and guide the common people; whose principles reached beyond the surface of heaven and earth, and whose sentiments encompassed all that lies outside the sun and moon?

When comparing their excellence, this [present work] is truly magnificent. We humbly observe that Your Majesty, with the Golden Wheel in motion and riding upon the auspicious Jade Calendar, has spread your transformative influence throughout the four continents.

Your benevolence extends throughout the nine realms; your Way encompasses the sages of antiquity, and your merit flourishes as divine. You possess manifold talents through innate knowledge, and your natural endowment is derived from the ultimate Heaven.
At first, moved by sorrow, you established a temple (zhāotí) before her bridal mirror; soon after, having erected the victorious banner, you spread the literary precepts.

If one’s celestial blossoms burst forth in brilliance and their sagely compositions surge like waves—swallowing the ocean of brushes and conceiving the Dragon Palace; eclipsing the forest of words and encompassing the Crane Tree;
internally mastering the Eight Baskets and externally verifying the Six Classics; profound yet classical, vast yet subtle—then [one has truly attained this].

Thus, may the vestiges of Jetavana be further exalted by being entrusted to your precious thoughts, and the lingering fragrance of the Nandanavana remain imperishable through the medium of your jade-like compositions.
These works will not merely serve to elevate the realm of dreams or illuminate the path for the lost; they will surely provide a mold for the four heavens and encompass the three realms.
Xuanzang, deeming that such a text deserved to be written by the Imperial Hand himself, submitted a memorial to urge this request, but the Emperor did not grant it.

He granted permission. A second memorial was presented, and he finally consented. On the eighth day of the fourth month, Xuánzàng led the monks and nuns of the capital, prepared banners, precious litters, incense, flowers, and Buddhist rites, and knocked at the gate of Fánglín Monastery to welcome the imperial stele.

By imperial decree, the nine divisions of music from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng*), as well as the musical performances of the two counties of Cháng’ān and Wànnián, along with the nobility, princes, dukes, and elders, escorted it. On that day...
It rained and they were unable to proceed. On the fourteenth day, they finally went to welcome him. The *Jiushi* (Old History) *Benji* (Basic Annals) states:
"The Emperor ascended the Anfu Gate tower to observe Master Xuanzang welcoming the Imperially Composed Stele for the Great Ci'en Monastery; he was escorted with Indian ritual protocols."
His followers were very numerous, and the Emperor looked upon this with great delight.

In the fifth month, the Dharma Master Xuanzang fell ill. An imperial decree was issued for Jiang Xiaozhang, Director of the Imperial Medical Office, and Shanggong Cong, a master of acupuncture, to attend exclusively to his illness.
Furthermore, messengers from the North Gate were dispatched to monitor his condition and report updates in turn. Xuanzang then submitted [a memorial].
In former times, the ranks of the Buddhist clergy were placed below those of the Daoist stream. In the final years of the late Emperor’s reign, he granted permission to rectify this.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the Yonghui era, an edict was issued that monks and nuns whose offenses were difficult to ascertain according to their inner state should be investigated according to secular law.

Xuanzang, fearing that his illness and exhaustion might forever prevent him from beholding the Emperor’s countenance, reported this through an imperial messenger. On that very day, the messenger returned with an imperial decree stating: "As for..."
Chen merely mentioned the titles and ranks of the Buddhist clergy. Regarding the matters settled by the previous dynasty, it was necessary to deliberate upon their integration with secular customs;
thus, an imperial decree was issued to eliminate them immediately. The Master was advised to rest his mind and recover his health, and his illness soon abated.

During the month of the Empress Dowager’s confinement, he was summoned to the palace to pray for blessings and assist in the delivery. A divine light filled the palace, shining from the courtyard up to the heavens. Consequently, the child was named Prince Fuguang (who was later Emperor Zhongzong).

Previously, the Emperor had once said to Paramārtha, "If a son is born to you, I shall permit him to leave the household life. Upon this occasion, Paramārtha submitted a memorial requesting permission for Prince Fuguang to enter the monastic order so as to ensure the flourishing prosperity of the Triple Gem; the Emperor issued an edict granting his request.
In the fourth month of the summer of the second year, twenty-seven monks and twenty-seven Daoists were summoned to the palace to engage in debate.
The Daoist Li Rong established his thesis based on the *Benji* (The Fundamental Limit). The Dharma Master Yibao questioned him, saying:

"Since you have cited the *Benji*, does the Dao originate from the limit, or does the limit originate from the Dao? Li Rong replied, "Both are possible. Yibao said: "If the Dao originates from the limit, then the limit must be the Dao."
Baopu zi said: "The fundamental can thus take its limit in the Dao; the Dao serves as the source of that limit. Sengrong said:

"It is simply a matter of mutual penetration. Baopu zi said: "If the fundamental limit and the Dao can mutually penetrate, then spontaneity (*ziran*) may likewise be modeled upon the Dao. Sengrong said: "The Dao takes spontaneity as its law, but spontaneity does not model itself upon the Dao.
Baopu zi said: "If that is so, then the Dao is fundamentally rooted in the limit, and the limit is..."

This failure does not stem from the Way itself. Bao Rong took offense at the errors in his previous remarks and no longer adhered to the principle; instead, he used other words to mock and disparage [the author].
Bao Zheng sternly said, "When establishing a thesis before the presence of the Son of Heaven, one must clarify what is heterodox and what is orthodox in order to simplify the Emperor's mind."

"How could I presume to trouble Your Majesty’s hearing with further words? Rong was both honored and abashed. The Emperor praised him and ordered him to lead Rong away from his seat, then gestured for Huang Yi to come forward to face Bao and engage in discussion.
They continued until the end of the day before finally concluding.

In this year, the Dharma Master Xuanzang submitted a memorial to decline [the imperial invitation] and retired to Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, where he devoted himself exclusively to the translation of scriptures.

The Emperor issued an edict in reply, stating: "I have examined your memorial and understand your desire to conceal your traces in the profound waters, emulating the reclusive spirit of Zhi Dun and surpassing the past;

entrusting your thoughts to divine stillness, you seek to set a standard for the present like Fotudeng and Kumārajīva. I look up to your exemplary conduct with the deepest admiration. As for me, my studies are centered on the Void (Śūnyatā)."
I am personally unable to fathom its lofty profundity; yet, with my shallow understanding and meager learning, I have not seen anything in it that is worthy of praise.

The Dharma Master serves as a bridge for the three realms and a guide for the four modes of birth. His wisdom is as bright as the lamp of the mind, and his concentration is as still as the water of the will. He is not obscured by the dust of sensory objects; how could he be startled by the waves of consciousness?
If one may dwell in the Way and its Virtue, why need it be amidst the layered peaks of Mount Taihua? If one may abide in emptiness and stillness, why—

"Only at Shaoshi, amidst its layered peaks, may you kindly withdraw these words and no longer insist on such requests. Then, the 'great recluse in the marketplace' will not be the sole prerogative of former sages;
rather, the vast benefit of your insights and learning shall be even more precious for our own generation. Sengrou submitted this letter of thanks, which stated in brief:
"In the past, Ji Zhong received the courtesy of the Wei ruler, yet they spoke only of their separation. Huiyuan was honored by the letters of the Jin sovereign..."

I have only just been granted rice for my sustenance, yet I have not yet seen your words that expound the principle of "emptiness and stillness" as something to be relinquished, nor the instruction regarding the "great hermitage within the marketplace.
Thus I know the intent of the Sovereign: he exhausts the truth and fully encompasses the mundane; he integrates the existent and embraces the non-existent.
He surpasses the heights of Fuxi and Xuanyuan, and outstrips the distance of Cao Cao and Ma Yuan. At that time, Master Sengrou’s path shook the world, and he intended to prohibit...

The old scriptures were being set aside while only the new translations were being propagated. There was a meditation master named Fachong who was well-versed in the essential tenets of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and was highly esteemed by Lord Fang Liang.
Upon meeting Xuanzang, he admonished him, saying: "I have heard that you intend to abolish the old scriptures and prohibit their propagation;
this is not permissible. The Master entered the path based on the old scriptures in recent years; if you now discard the old to exalt the new..."

"If the new [translation] is correct, then the Dharma Master should also return to his original [status]. Would it be permissible for you to renounce the world again in accordance with the new scripture? Paramārtha realized the point and desisted.

In the fourth year, while the Emperor was at the Hebi Palace, he convened monks and Daoists to debate doctrinal principles; the Dharma Master Huiyin established the doctrine of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The Dharma Master Shen Tai established the doctrine of the "Nine Cognitions of Severance" (*navavidha-jñāna*). The Daoists Li Rong and Huang Shou did not understand its meaning or terminology;

they were as bewildered as if lost in a sea of dreams. Although they engaged in debate, they were left desolate and without recourse. Consequently, an imperial edict was issued for the Daoists to establish their own doctrines.

Thereupon, Li Rong established the doctrine that "the Dao gives birth to the myriad things. The Dharma Master Huili asked him, saying: "Master, you have established that the Dao gives birth to the myriad things..."

Wu asked, "I have not yet discerned whether this Dao possesses consciousness or is devoid of consciousness. Rong said, "Man models himself after Earth; Earth models itself after Heaven; Heaven models itself after the Dao.
Since it is the model for both Heaven and Earth, how could it be said to be without consciousness? Li said, "If it necessarily possesses consciousness, it ought to produce only good.
For what reason does it also produce evil? Since good and evil, ascent and descent, arise in such a tangled and chaotic mixture," [how can you say it has consciousness?]
Then you would have no knowledge [of these things]. Allow me to attempt a more detailed exposition.

Why did the Sage and Enlightened One not appear early on during the time before the ancient world was opened and established? Why did he not bestow prosperity and joy upon the common people from the beginning?

Instead, why did he first give birth to figures such as Gonggong, Chiyou, Jie, Zhou, You, and Li, who brought ruin and injury to the masses? Among all ministers of state, why did he not instead give birth only to Houji?
Why did [Heaven] produce figures such as Qi, Kui, and Long, yet cause those like Fei Lian, E Lai, Jin Shang, and Xin Mang to flatter their sovereigns and bring about the ruin and chaos of the state?
Among the feathered tribes, why did it not produce only auspicious birds such as the phoenix and the luan, but instead further produce evil birds such as the owl and the mirror-bird?
Among the hairy herds, why did it not produce only the qilin and the huailiu, but furthermore...

[How could they] produce beasts of prey, wolves, bristling porcupines, and the like? Furthermore, as for the various categories of plants and trees, their qualities differ—some beautiful and some vile.

Since these grow together in a chaotic mixture without distinguishing between good and evil, it follows that the Dao lacks cognition and cannot produce things. How, then, can one claim that Heaven and Earth take [the Dao] as their model to generate the myriad things?
According to the teaching of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, which exhausts principle and fully realizes nature, then [the relationship between] Heaven, Earth, and the myriad...

Objects are the result of karma. Because sentient beings possess different karmic forces, what they experience varies accordingly. Those with superior wholesome karma find lapis lazuli for ground and gold for paths;
beryl trees shade the streets and jade leaves hang from the pavilions; nectar serves as food and exquisite robes serve as seats.
For those with much unwholesome karma, sandy soil forms the ground and tiles and rubble form the roads; they must satisfy their hunger with weeds and hemp.

"His clothes barely covered his body; he traveled through mud, slept in the rain, harvested in the frost, and plowed in the heat—all of which were the results of his own karma, with no one forcing him to do so.
Yet you, my son, are deluded in mind and fail to recognize this, recklessly claiming that 'Heaven produced him alone. How pitiable! " Rong was startled and did not know how to respond.
Huili took advantage of the opportunity to taunt him, and Rong fell silent. He then felt ashamed, descended from his seat, and bowed toward Huang Shou.
The Master of the Law, Huiyin, established the names and meanings of Laozi. Since he considered Laozi to be the ancestral progenitor of the state, he feared that using his name might cause offense.
He thereupon submitted this memorial: "Huang Shou has long been enrolled among those wearing the yellow caps; he is unaware of taboos regarding names.

Even the foxes of city walls and the rats of shrine altars still rely upon them for support. Our state inherits distantly from the lineage of the Dragon Virtue; Your Majesty is a descendant of the followers of Laozi."

How could one publicly discuss the taboo names of one's ancestors while in the presence of their descendants? As for the many excellent meanings within the *Five Thousand Words* (*Pañcavimśatisāhasrikā*), you were unable to list them;
yet you spoke the name of the Sage. When calculating the offense and deliberating the punishment, death would be a lenient penalty.
The Emperor nodded and said, "You must certainly establish a distinct doctrine. Having been thus thwarted and humiliated, Zhishou was overcome with shame and perspiration, losing his composure;

although he continued to engage in verbal debate, his arguments were disordered and inconsistent. When the session concluded, the Emperor remarked, "I have observed that the essential tenets of these two schools remain ultimately unclear.
As soon as this was said, Huili stepped forward and replied abruptly, "That the essential tenets of the two schools remain unclear is indeed true."

A Clear Decree. Why is this? When the assembly of monks established their doctrine, the Daoist practitioners did not understand its source. Being ashamed of having no argument, they resorted to deceitful and mendacious speech.
For instance, when Huiyin established the doctrine of the five *skandhas*, Huangyi attempted to challenge it using the term "shelter" (*yìn*).

Now, "shelter" takes covering as its primary meaning, whereas "aggregate" (*skandha*) takes accumulation as its definition. For example, there are eleven types of form; they are gathered together within the category of form.
Below this [heading], there are eight kinds of consciousness that accumulate within a single name; taking them collectively as a whole to encompass them is the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*).

If one uses the term "shelter" (*āyatana*) instead, it would be difficult to perceive [the meaning], and the underlying principles would be entirely contradictory. Furthermore, Shen Tai established the doctrine of the "nine knowledges of abandonment" (*navajñāna-prahāṇa*);
since the Daoist had never heard of this name since birth, although he ascended the seat of debate, he did not know where to pose his questions, leaving him with no way to avoid embarrassment.
Consequently, you have indulged in irrelevant discourse; thus, the essential tenets remain obscure, and you have profaned the imperial hearing. The fault lies with you, the Daoist.

However, among the great principles of the Buddha-dharma, dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is paramount; hence it is said that there has never been a single dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions.
Furthermore, for instance, seeing a palace pillar requires five conditions: first, a conscious mind that is not distracted; second, an unimpaired faculty of sight; third, the presence of light;
fourth, the object appearing before one; and fifth, the absence of obstructions between them. Only when these conditions are fully met can the pillar be seen.
If the sunlight has already set and the dragon-candles have not yet been lit, how could one possibly see the vermilion pillars, even if they were there?
Furthermore, it is like fine grain: in the months of spring warmth, provided with earth, water, and human labor, it can sprout;
yet if placed in a jar during summer or buried in the ground during winter, it will ultimately not grow because the necessary conditions are incomplete. Human beings are the same:

internally, karmic retribution acts as the cause, and externally, parents act as the condition; only when these factors coincide does a body come to be born. If the parents are discordant, birth will never occur.
This principle applies even to the feathers and fur of the myriad species; all are likewise so. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Deeply penetrating dependent origination, one severs all false views.
Through the Buddha’s wisdom, one exhaustively realizes the true mark of phenomena. This is called Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment, and he is the Teacher of Gods and Humans."
The followers of external paths do not act in this manner. Some calculate that all phenomena arise spontaneously, which is identical to the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi in this land;
others claim there is no cause, or speak of past karma. These are all heterodox schools that do not understand the fundamental source of the Dharma.

Furthermore, he explained before the Emperor the meaning of the three natures—paratantra, parikalpita, and pariniṣpanna—and shortly after departing the palace, issued an imperial decree for an attendant to follow him.
The King issued a proclamation through his officials, saying: "The meaning of the masters' exposition on dependent origination is excellent. Why did you not discuss it sooner?

He then sent an imperial edict to the Daoist Li Rong and others, saying: "Why do you not study the Buddhist scriptures? Thereupon, Li Rong and his followers were abashed and shrank away, their spirits stifled with shame.
In the second month of the first year of the Linde era, the Dharma Master Xuanzang fell ill.

He instructed his disciple Dachengguang to record all the sūtras and śāstras he had translated, totaling one thousand three hundred and thirty-five fascicles, and to create ten koṭis of Maitreya images.
When his illness became critical, he recited aloud: "The aggregate of form is unattainable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unattainable.
The eye-element is unattainable, up to and including the mind-consciousness-element. Ignorance is unattainable, up to and including awakening.
Even 'unattainability' is itself unattainable. He further had those around him chant in unison three times: "Namo Maitreya."
"To the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya: I pray that I may swiftly behold his compassionate countenance. Homage to the inner court where the Tathāgata Maitreya dwells;
I vow that after relinquishing this life, I shall surely be reborn therein. Having thus spoken, he passed away while lying on his right side.
He was sixty-three years old. That evening, four white rainbows stretched from north to south, piercing the *Jing* lunar station and passing directly through the pagoda of Ci'en Monastery.
When the news of his death reached the court, the Emperor wept with profound grief and said to those around him, "I have lost a national treasure.

He suspended court for three days. From the time of his death until his burial, he issued five imperial edicts, collecting and recording his remaining works and showing diligent compassion in his mourning.
During the funeral rites, a strange monk suddenly arrived carrying powdered sandalwood incense. He requested that the Master’s body be anointed according to the Indian ritual.
Dachengguang and the others, as the sarcophagus had been closed for many days, were reluctant to open it.

The monk said, “I have received a special imperial decree; if you refuse, I shall submit a formal report. Thereupon, they opened the sarcophagus, and his countenance appeared as if he were still alive, while a fragrant aroma wafted forth. His...
When the monks had finished applying the ointments, he suddenly vanished from sight. Those who recognized him believed him to have been a person from the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven.

In the fourth month of summer, by imperial decree, it was ordered that in accordance with the precedent of the Buddha, Śākyamuni, his remains be enshrined in a golden outer coffin and a silver inner sarcophagus, and a stupa erected at the Eastern Gate of the Sǎn River.
His disciples Shen Tai, Xi Xuan, Huìyǐn, Huìlì, Míngjùn, Yìbāo, Dàchéngguāng, and others were all [pillars] of the Dharma gate.
They were truly dragons and elephants among men.
The commentary states: Since the Great Teaching flowed eastward, there was Master Yuan whose conduct equaled that of the ancient sages;
there was Kumārajīva who exhaustively mastered the source of the Dharma; and there were Louyue and Fashang, whose virtue and morality were so revered that they served as teachers to the emperors.
Gentlemen, while all [these masters] failed to encounter a sovereign of great brilliance, Xuanzang alone appeared during the era of the True Observation (Zhen Guan) reign’s supreme governance.

His realization accorded with Emperor Taizong’s restoration of the Buddha-dharma; when one traces his achievement in translating and proclaiming the ultimate teachings, his merit rivals that of Kumārajīva.

His character and conduct were lofty and beautiful, nearly equaling those of Huiyuan; his influence shook the age, and his honor surpassed even that of Dao’an. From antiquity, such merit and virtue...
That both [the secular and the sacred] flourish together has not occurred since the time of Teng and Lan.
Thus, the Great Teaching became majestic and sublime, allowing future generations to find peace in its established forms. Alas! It may truly be said that he was already a sage.
In the eighth month of the second year of the Qiandeng era, the Vinaya Master Daoxuan of the Southern Mountains passed away.

An imperial edict was issued in his honor, and it was further decreed that all monasteries throughout the empire should depict his likeness and fashion statues of him to serve as models for emulation. His surname was Qian;

his father was the Director of the Ministry of Personnel, and his mother conceived him after dreaming that a lunar disc pierced her womb. Subsequently, she again dreamed of a Buddhist monk who spoke to her, saying: "That which..."

The one who was pregnant was Master You. He wished for [his mother] to cherish herself. When Huiquan reached adulthood, he withdrew from the world with a sense of detachment, having no desire to engage in worldly affairs.

His mother recalled her dream and permitted him to leave the household life. By nature, he was in harmony with the Way; wherever he went, he invariably moved divine beings to provide protection and service, and celestial food was offered to him.
A man from Yunshi once visited Huiquan and saw that those around him were all celestial youths serving as attendants. None...
In that year, because the ordination platform did not conform to the Vinaya, [Daoxuan] personally carried earth to rebuild it according to the rules.

On the day the platform was completed, an extraordinary bhikṣu arrived and prostrated before it, saying: "Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Semblance Dharma has remained in the world; the revival of the Vinaya depends solely upon you, Master.
Furthermore, a venerable elder with thick eyebrows and white hair descended to the platform and engaged in a long discourse on the Way with Daoxuan.
He departed. His disciples followed in his footsteps, but they did not know where he had gone; at that time, they believed it was Piṇḍola.

Furthermore, once while practicing the Way in the middle of the night, he stumbled and fell against a stone step. A youth in armor caught hold of him and asked, "Who do you take me to be, that you show such virtue toward me?
He replied, "I am your disciple Zhang Qiong, the Prince of Baxia. Because of his master...

"Because his virtue of the precepts is lofty and sublime, he has come to provide protection and service. Xuān then extensively inquired about the events during the time when the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, was in the world and after his parinirvāṇa.
Jué recounted each of these matters for Xuān. Furthermore, he personally bestowed upon Xuān two objects—a Buddha’s tooth and a precious palm—as tokens of faith, and then withdrew into seclusion.
Moreover, he frequently moved a mysterious person to pose difficult questions regarding the relative gravity of the Vinaya rules, and he also bestowed [the answers] upon him.
The *Jihuan tu* (Diagram of Jetavana) and the *Fuzhu yi* (Ritual of Entrustment) in ten fascicles were both previously unknown in the world;

thus, the *Nanshan lüshu* (Commentary on the Vinaya of the Southern Mountain) exhaustively elucidates the meaning of following phenomenal forms (*suixiang*), for it penetrates the divine intelligence.

After his passing, his disciple Wengang propagated his teachings, which the world revered as its master. This was designated as the School of Conduct for Preventing Transgressions and Stopping Evil, known as the Nanshan [School].
In the Mountain Teachings, a Vinaya Master once asked a celestial deity about the origins of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara. The deity replied:
"In a past kalpa of long ago, there was a king named Śrīgarbha and a queen named Ratnapratibhāsa. They gave birth to three daughters; the eldest was named Sunetrā."

The middle son was named Miaoyin (Wondrous Sound). The youngest was named Miaoshan (Wondrous Goodness). When Miaoshan first became pregnant, the lady dreamed that she had swallowed the moon. On the night of her birth, the earth shook violently;

extraordinary fragrances and celestial flowers pervaded both the interior and exterior of the palace. The people of the nation were struck with wonder. Upon being born, she was fresh and pure without having been bathed;
her features were as dignified and majestic as those of a Brahma. A five-colored cloud covered her body, and the people said, "A sage has appeared."

This was a sign of the world to come. Although her parents regarded her as extraordinary, their minds became perverse and they eventually grew to dislike her. As the Bodhisattva matured, she was naturally compassionate and gentle;
her clothing was always fresh and bright, and she ate but one meal at midday. The women of the palace called her "The Princess of Buddha-Mind.

Through her transformative influence, the palace ladies all turned toward goodness and abandoned desire. The King gradually came to detest her and intended to find a husband for her. Miaoshan, possessing clear insight, said:
Wealth and nobility do not endure; glory and splendor are like bubbles and illusions. Although he was subjected to menial servitude, he felt no regret whatsoever.
When the King and his consort summoned him and enticed him, he replied, "If you can exempt me from three afflictions, I shall comply with your command.
The King asked, "What are these three afflictions? Miaoshan said, "First, when people are young, their faces are like white jade or the moon, but in old age, their hair turns white."
First, the face becomes wrinkled; in walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one is in every way inferior to when young.
Second, while the limbs were once robust and one’s gait was like flying, suddenly illness arrives; lying upon a bed and pillow, there is not a single thing to be rejoiced in.

Third, while relatives gather and kinsmen fill one's presence, in a single moment of impermanence, though father and son are close, how could one replace the other? If these three afflictions can be avoided, then from marriage...

"It may be attained. If you are unable to do so, it would be better for you to leave the household life and devote yourself to the Way, thereby thoroughly realizing the fundamental mind so that all afflictions are naturally extinguished.

The King was enraged; he ordered her to tend the gardens and reduced her food and drink. Her two elder sisters also went privately to dissuade her from her resolve, but Miaoshan remained steadfast and would not turn back.
The Lady personally exhorted her, to which Miaoshan replied: "All the world is bound by the fetters of affection and love."
"There is no end to this cycle. Since our flesh and bones must inevitably meet and then part, I pray that my mother will comfort herself. Fortunately, there are two elder sisters to attend upon you;
please do not have any concern for Miaoshan. Thereupon, the lady and her sisters petitioned the King to release her so she might leave the household life.
The king grew angry and summoned the nuns to reprimand them, intending to inflict harsh punishments upon them to force them to abandon their resolve.

The nuns were terrified and assigned them menial tasks such as gathering firewood and water, and tending the pestles, mortars, and garden vegetables. Moved by this, the garden vegetables flourished even in winter, and a spring gushed forth beside the kitchen.

After some time, Miaoshan remained without any intention of retreating. When the king heard of these wonders regarding the spring and the vegetables, he was greatly incensed and dispatched warriors to seize her head and—
The executioners were led there to kill the assembly of nuns. Suddenly, clouds and mist arose like mountains, such that even objects a mere cubit away could not be distinguished.
When the weather cleared, Miaoshan alone was missing; she had been carried by a deity to another cliff to settle her dwelling. The deity said, "This ground is thin and cannot support you.
After moving three times, they finally reached this present Mount Xiangshan. Miaoshan resided there, eating wood and drinking from mountain streams. After a long time, King Daka... [text truncated]
King Māra suffered from a disease; his entire body became putrid and he ceased all eating and sleeping. None of the physicians in the kingdom were able to cure him.
As he was about to die, a monk said that he was skilled in healing, but that he required the hands and eyes of a person free from anger. The king found this very difficult to obtain.

The monk said, "In the southwest of your kingdom, on Mount Gandhamādana, there is a Bodhisattva practicing austerities. If you send an envoy to seek them, you will certainly obtain those two things. The king—
Having no other choice, he dispatched an inner attendant to convey his meaning. Miaoshan said, "My father does not revere the Triple Gem and destroys the True Teaching;
he has executed an innocent nun—this is the retribution he has invited. She then joyfully gouged out her eyes and severed her arm, handing them to the messenger.
She further instructed him to urge the King to reform his past ways, turn toward the good, and not be deluded by heterodox teachings, as well as to offer the two items to the Sangha.
He prepared a medicine, which the King took and was immediately cured. The King offered a generous reward to the monk-physician, who said, "Why thank me?

You should thank the one who gave his hands and eyes. Suddenly, the monk vanished. The King, realizing it was divine assistance, ordered his carriage and entered the mountains with his consort and two daughters to offer thanks to the Bodhisattva.
Before they could speak, the Consort recognized him as Miaoshan and could not help but choke back her sobs.
Choking with sobs and tears, Miaoshan said, "Does my lady remember Miaoshan? Out of gratitude for my father the King’s kindness, I have repaid him with my hands and eyes.
When the King and the lady heard these words, they embraced her and wept bitterly. The lady wished to lick her eyes with her tongue;
before she could do so, suddenly auspicious clouds covered the sky, celestial music resounded, shaking the earth, and flowers rained down. Then—
The sacred image of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed One appeared majestically in the sky, accompanied by ten thousand followers;
the sounds of joy and sorrow resounded through the mountains and valleys. In an instant, the Bodhisattva returned to his original form and passed away with solemn dignity.

The King, the Queen, and the two sisters cremated him and collected the relics, immediately constructing a stupa upon the mountain. Xuan asked again: "The Bodhisattva manifests emanations everywhere; how could this be..."
"Should I remain alone on Mount Xiangshan? The deity replied, "Within the borders of China today, Mount Xiangshan is the most preeminent.
The mountain lies two hundred li south of Mount Song. It is this very Mount Xiangshan in present-day Ruzhou.
The celestial deity further proclaimed that there are nineteen locations within the borders of China where King Aśoka’s stūpas containing Buddha-relics are situated; subsequently, they were all...
The *Xianyan* (Manifestation and Verification) states: The treatise says that Master Xuanchang of Nanshan was the reincarnation of Vinaya Master Liangyou.

Because his reputation for upholding the Vinaya resounded throughout the Five Indies, saints of the fruit-stage repeatedly descended and manifested themselves to him to discuss and clarify the meanings of the Dharma.

They reached the Celestial Kitchen to present offerings, where celestial youths attended upon them. During the Xiangfu era of our dynasty, there were still foreign monks who traveled from afar to pay homage at the Xuanzang Pagoda.
Were it not for the ancient Buddha-Dharma acting as a means of elevation and salvation, how could the divine spirits have been capable of such things?
As for the celestial deities discussing the locations of the Śarīra relics and the miraculous pagodas, and [the manifestation of] Avalokiteśvara...
This is merely a trace of the Bodhisattva’s manifestation; yet, as he universally manifests throughout the inexhaustible worlds via the Gate of All Doors, how could words ever suffice?
This wondrous excellence is but a single instance among the number of atoms in all lands. It is the body obtained as the fruition of the Bodhisattva’s myriad practices.
Manifesting in accordance with conditions, they initially possess no fixed characteristics of male or female;
this is surely the fundamental causal origin of the Great Being, as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding those who enter samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
