In the first year of the Zongzhang era of the Tang dynasty, the Buddhist and Daoist clergy were summoned to the Baifu Hall to determine the authenticity of the *Huahu jing* (The Scripture on the Conversion of the Barbarians).
The various officials presided over the proceedings. A monk named Faming was selected to participate; at that time, as the head seats of the three teachings engaged in heated debate, Faming—

Examining this, he found it to be incorrect. He immediately dismissed the crowd and declared: "When Laozi transformed the Hu people and became a Buddha, did he convert them using Chinese (Huayan) speech, or did he entice them using the Hu language?
If he had used Chinese, the Hu people would not have been proficient in it; therefore, he must have used the Hu language.
Since this was transmitted to our land, it necessarily required translation. I do not understand the meaning of what you Daoists call the 'Scripture on Transforming the Hu'."
"Under which dynasty was this translated? Who served as the scribe and who verified the meaning? At this, the entire assembly was struck with astonishment, and no one could respond.
The high officials and courtiers were all convinced by the accuracy of his words; they rose from their seats in great joy and departed.

An imperial edict was issued to search throughout the empire for the *Huahu jing* (Scripture on Converting the Barbarians) to be burned and discarded, as it was no longer to be counted among the canonical Buddhist scriptures. Subsequently, at the capital of Luoyang, the *Heng*... [text continues]

Dao Guan, Huan Yandao, and others submitted a memorial requesting that he remain. The Imperial Edict stated: "The Three Sages have shed their radiance once more, and the profound origin has been brought into orderly succession.
How could I forget the teachings of Laozi or harbor partiality toward the school of Śākyamuni? My will is sincere in returning to simplicity, and my heart dwells upon the removal of falsehood.

Where principle is violated and practice is elevated, even those who are close are eliminated; where the meaning accords and the name is appropriate, even those who have grievances must be recorded. From this point on...

Now, all records and accounts concerning the "Conversion of the Barbarians" (Hu-hu) found within various Daoist scriptures should be expunged, and the relevant authorities shall establish regulations to treat such matters as offenses.
The *Lun* states:
Initially, during the Northern Wei dynasty, the Daoist practitioner Jiang Bin and others composed what was known as the *Taishang Kaitian Jing* (The Scripture of the Supreme Opening of Heaven).
Sheng spoke extensively on the matter of Laozi converting the Hu, as well as his debates with Tanmuzu. Sengbin perceived the absurdity of these claims;

furthermore, the renowned minister Wang Ruan composed the *Xiaodao lun* (Treatise on Laughing at Daoism) in thirty-six chapters, which vehemently attacked the fallacy of Laozi becoming a Buddha to convert the Hu.
This work is now included in the Buddhist canon. During the Sui dynasty, the Chancellor Yang Su remarked that the Daoist scriptures claim that Lao—

It is said that the Master transformed the Hu people; however, the Hu people did not accept his transformation. Thereupon, he commanded Yin Xi to assume the form of a Buddha to transform them, and only then did the Hu people begin to accept his teaching.
If this were indeed the case, it would be clear that Laozi was unable to transform the Hu, and that the Hu people had long been devoted to Buddhism.
Furthermore, [the Master] once entered a Daoist temple, pointed to an image of the "Transformation of the Hu," and asked the practitioners of the Way, "Where is Laozi?"
"Using the conversion of the Hu as a pretext—why did the Buddha not convert the Hu to the Dao?

When the follower of the Dao offered no reply, these words were more than sufficient to fully expose his fallacy. Now, observing that Faming’s refutation is so precise, incisive, and appropriate, it far surpasses what I had previously considered;
thus, this delusion and falsehood should be extinguished and no longer persist. This has been the case since the Huichang era. [...]
How is it that even such teachings still delude the world?
It was in the second year of the Shangyuan era that the Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren, passed away. The Master was the son of the Zhou family of Huangmei in Qizhou.
From birth he was precocious and extraordinary. As a child, a strange monk sighed and said, "This boy lacks seven of the marks [of a Buddha] and thus falls short of the Tathāgata.
Later, he encountered Master Xìn and became his Dharma heir, propagating the teachings on Mount Pòtóu.

During the Chénghéng era, there was a layman named Lú Huínéng who came from afar to visit the Master. The Master asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From south of the Ling Mountains. The Master...
[The monk] asked, "What do you seek? He replied, "I seek only to become a Buddha. The Master said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you hope to attain Buddhahood?

He replied, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could the Buddha-nature be so? The Master recognized him as an extraordinary person and rebuked him, saying, "Go and work in the fodder shed!
Huineng prostrated at his feet and withdrew, then entered the rice-hulling workshop to perform manual labor. There, amidst the pestles and mortars—
After several months had passed, the Master knew that the time had come to transmit the Dharma. He then addressed the assembly, saying, "The True Dharma is difficult to understand;
one must not merely memorize my words and take them as their own responsibility. Each of you should independently compose a verse according to your own understanding.

If the meaning of your words accords with the profound truth, then both the robe and the Dharma shall be transmitted to you. At that time, there were over seven hundred people in the assembly, and Shenxiu occupied the seat of first rank. He studied...
He was esteemed and looked up to by both monastics and laypeople alike. Xiu also prided himself on being such that no one could surpass him;
without further reflection, he inscribed a verse upon a wall in the corridor, saying: "The body is the Bodhi tree; / The mind is a stand for a bright mirror.
/ At all times diligently wipe and polish it, / And let no dust or grime remain. When the Master (Huineng) saw this verse while walking about, he knew in his heart that it was Xiu’s work.

Huineng, for his part, feigned ignorance and said, "Those of future generations who practice according to this shall also attain the fruits of the Way. When the assembly heard these words, they each began to recite them. Later, Huineng heard the gāthā while at the rice-hulling shed and asked his companions, "Who composed this? His fellow practitioners replied, "The Master intended to transmit the Dharma and had everyone compose a verse; this was written by the Venerable Xiu. Huineng then said, "I too have composed one. He then recited it. The Master was deeply pleased. He then summoned Huineng to his quarters and said, "I have long known that you were my successor, but I did not reveal it to you because there were many obstacles. Now I am transmitting the robe and the Dharma to you. You must go far away and dwell in seclusion; do not remain here. Huineng prostrated himself and departed. The Master then sent someone to follow him, instructing him to say, "The Master has fallen ill and wishes to see you. Upon hearing this, Huineng fled even further away. The Master passed away on the eighth day of the twelfth month of that year. At the time of his passing, he told his disciples, "The Dharma will be transmitted to Huineng. After the Master’s death, the disciples went to the rice-hulling shed and found Huineng there. They informed him of the Master’s final instructions, and Huineng subsequently went to Caoqi. It was there that he established a monastery and propagated the teachings. This is the account of the transmission of the Dharma from Huineng to Huinong. Thus ends the record of the Sixth Patriarch. He said, "It is beautiful, indeed, yet it is not yet fully realized. His companions all censured him for his error and delusion.
When it reached late evening, Hui-neng ordered a youth to lead him to the corridor. Hui-neng personally held a candle and had the youth write a verse beside Xiu’s verse, saying:
"Bodhi originally has no tree; The bright mirror is also not a stand. From the beginning there is not a single thing; How can one borrow a duster?"
"Chen'ai. The Master saw this again and thought silently to himself, "This must be what Neng is capable of.
Consequently, he spoke these words: "Who made this? You have not yet seen your nature. Because the Master did not approve, the assembly all ceased looking at him.
That very evening, he secretly sent someone from the millhouse to summon Neng, telling him: "The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of one great matter."

According to conditions, he guided and transformed beings according to their individual capacities, whether small or great; thus, there arose the teachings of the Ten Stages, the Three Vehicles, and the Sudden and Gradual methods as gateways to the Dharma.

Nevertheless, the subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and truly authentic Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma was entrusted to the Venerable Kāśyapa, the foremost disciple, who transmitted it in succession through twenty-eight generations until it reached the Great Master Bodhidharma.
Arriving at this land, you shall be able to inherit the lineage down to me. I now transmit it to you, together with the robe passed down as a token of faith.
You must protect and uphold it well so that it does not come to an end. Listen to my verse:
"When sentient beings come to sow seeds, The fruit arises from the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, They lack nature and thus have no birth. [Then he] knelt.

Having finished receiving [the precepts], he said, "Now that the Dharma has been received, to whom shall the robe be entrusted? The Master replied, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him;
therefore, he transmitted this robe to manifest his attainment of the Dharma. Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention."
"Keep this within your own person and do not transmit it further. For now, you must withdraw to a distant place and wait for the time to manifest your transformation.

As it is said, the life of one who receives this robe is like a thread hanging from a string. Huineng asked, "Where should I go to remain hidden? The Master replied, "When you meet with Hui, stop; when you encounter Hui, hide.
Huineng prostrated at the Master's feet, took the robe, and departed that very night toward the south. None of the assembly knew of his departure. From this point on, the Master...

For three days he did not ascend the hall, which caused the assembly to wonder; they therefore questioned him. The Master said, "My Way shall proceed. They asked again, "To whom will the robe and Dharma be transmitted?
The Master replied, "He who is capable shall receive them. The assembly thought that the layman Lu was named Neng, and that this must be the person.
They searched together with all their might, but he was no longer there. Some even led one another in pursuit, seeking him by his physical description.

After the Master had transmitted the Dharma, four years passed before he entered nirvana. He was enshrined in a stupa on East Mountain, and Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Daman.

The *Jiù Tángshǐ* (Old History of the Tang) states: Toward the end of the Later Wei dynasty, there was a monk named Bodhidharma. Originally a prince of Central India, he left the household life to renounce his kingdom.
Having traveled to the South Sea, he obtained the sublime Dharma of the Chan school, which he said had been transmitted from Śākyamuni Buddha himself.

There were a robe and bowl serving as tokens of this transmission, passed down through successive generations. Bodhidharma brought these robes and bowl across the sea; upon first arriving in the state of Liang, he met Emperor Wu.
The Emperor questioned him regarding matters of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*). Bodhidharma was displeased and departed for Wei, where he lived in seclusion at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.
He encountered poison and passed away. That same year, the Wei envoy Song Yun was returning from the Pamir Mountains when he saw him.
When his disciples opened the tomb, there were only his robes and shoes remaining. Bodhidharma transmitted the Dharma to Huike; Huike once severed his own arm to seek [his instruction].
The Dharma was transmitted to Sengcan; Can transmitted it to Daoxin; and Xin transmitted it to Hongren. Ren’s secular surname was Zhou, and he was a native of Huangmei.
He and [Dao]xin both resided at Dongshan Monastery; thus, the world refers to his teaching as the Dongshan School.
The commentary states: Although the old histories’ accounts of the various patriarchs are brief, their essential points accord with the narratives found in the *Baolin zhuan* and the *Chuan deng lu*.
As for the claims that Bodhidharma died from poisoning and that a Chinese envoy subsequently encountered him again at the Pamir Mountains—did such poisoning and death actually occur?
The world also says that the former life of the Fifth Patriarch was that of Daoxin, who planted pine trees.
He went to see the Fourth Patriarch, who was about to entrust him with the robe and the Dharma. Suddenly, the Patriarch regretted this, saying: "You are already advanced in years;

though you may succeed me in the propagation of the teachings, how much longer can you do so? It would be better if you were to come again. Consequently, the Fifth Patriarch took up residence in the womb of a woman of the Zhou clan;
he was born without a father. His mother nearly suffered calamity, but she narrowly escaped death. Thus, the Fourth Patriarch truly endured his own life to wait for him.
"Come! [I shall] indeed [entrust you with] the Great Dharma. Alas! Our Patriarch’s coming and going within birth and death was nothing but a sublime play.
Were it not for a sage who has attained the stage of fruition (*phala*), who could participate in this?"
In the first year of the Yifeng era, the Venerable Buddhāpālita from North India arrived at Mount Wutai, the Cool Mountain.
There he encountered an old man who asked him, "For what purpose have you come? Buddhāpālita replied, "I have come seeking to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.

The old man asked, "Have you brought with you the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī? He replied, "I have not. The old man said, "The sentient beings of this land are increasingly wicked, yet they still go forth as monastics."
"Those who commit the four *pārājika* offenses are exceedingly numerous. What benefit is there in traveling so far without maintaining this dhāraṇī?
Would it not be possible to have it brought back and circulated in this land? Boli paid his respects and returned. In the fifth year of the Kaiyao era, he took the dhāraṇī to Chang’an.
An imperial decree was issued ordering the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman to translate it. The Emperor, having heard that this dhāraṇī was efficacious and miraculous, treated it with special regard.
He concealed this secret within the inner palace. Wolun repeatedly petitioned for it to be disseminated throughout the realm; Emperor Gaozong had no choice but to comply.
Wolun then took his leave and entered Mount Wutai, after which his final whereabouts remained unknown. At that time, there was Bodhiruci from South India.
He practiced the dhūta austerities and received the Way from Yaśoghoṣa, becoming a preeminent master of the Western Regions whose fame resounded throughout China.
When the Emperor heard of his reputation, he was delighted and consequently issued an imperial edict to summon him from the Western Regions.
In the first year of the Yongchun era, the Dharma Master Kuiji of Ci’en Monastery passed away at the age of fifty-one.

An imperial edict was issued in mourning for him, and the Emperor composed a eulogy for his portrait. He was granted a state funeral at Beiqu in Fanchuan, near the burial site of Master Xuanzang. Kuiji’s appearance was robust and his stature stood eight feet tall; his spirit and bearing surpassed those of ten thousand men.
He possessed a "jade pillow" on the back of his neck, and the patterns on all ten of his fingers were coiled and folded like seals. Thus it was seen.

He was struck with awe and submission. Nevertheless, his heart was kind and compassionate, and he instructed others with benevolence. In his later years, he prayed to be reborn in the Inner Court (Tuṣita Heaven). He observed the precepts with ever-increasing devotion.
He once commissioned a statue of Mañjuśrī made of jade and a copy of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written in gold; both yielded auspicious responses.

Initially, Vinaya Master Xuan of Nanshan had become renowned throughout the five regions for his propagation of the Vinaya, such that he was moved by the offerings of celestial kitchens. He constantly humbled himself before the foundation of the Three Vehicles...
He was playful and did not observe proper etiquette. Once, when Sengji visited Xuanchang, it was past noon and the celestial food had not yet arrived;

only when Sengji took his leave did the deity descend. Xuanchang reproached him for being late, but the deity said, "Just now I saw that a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva was here, and his retinue was so formidable that I could not enter on my own.
When Xuanchang heard this, he was greatly astonished; consequently, his reputation spread far and wide.
I pay my respects. Previously, Master Paramārtha had personally received from the Western Region’s Master Śīlabhadra the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the Vijñaptimātra school;

Xuanzang fully grasped its subtleties. He expanded upon its source and stream, such that later generations throughout the world revere it, designating it as the "School of the Manifestation of Principles through the Dharma-characteristics of the Three Vehicles" and calling it the "Cien Teaching. In this year, the recluse Sun Simiao passed away at the age of one hundred.
As for the rest: Sun Simiao was proficient in the arts of Zhuangzi, Laozi, yin-yang, calendrical calculation, and medicine; he held the Buddhist scriptures in especially high regard.
The world honored him as "Zhenren Sun" (the Realized Man Sun).

In the second year [of the Zhenguan era], Dharma Master Xuanyi passed away. Xuanyi’s courtesy name was Daoshi; some say his given name was Daoshi, having changed it to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Taizong.

He avoided his personal names out of filial piety and thus circulated under his courtesy name. He thoroughly mastered the three studies (*tri-śikṣā*) and once lamented that while the scriptural canon and the vast array of historical records from ancient and modern times were extensive, students found it difficult to investigate them all exhaustively.
Consequently, he compiled the *Fayuan zhulin* (Pearl Grove of the Dharma Garden) in one hundred fascicles, categorizing each entry by subject.
Those who discerned its merits praised him for its precision and breadth.
In the first year of the Hongdao era, the Emperor passed away. Several months after Zhongzong ascended the throne, Empress Wu deposed him as the Prince of Luling and confined him in Fangzhou.
Empress Wu then assumed the regency and ruled in the Emperor’s stead; she was known as Zetian.

In the seventh month of the following year, ten *śramaṇas* went to the palace gate and presented the *Dayun jing* (Scripture of the Great Cloud), extolling that Zetian was destined to ascend the imperial throne. Zetian was greatly pleased and bestowed [rewards] upon them.

Ten śramaṇas were granted purple square-cut robes and silver tortoise-shaped pouches. Scriptures were distributed throughout the prefectures and kingdoms of the empire, and a Great Cloud Monastery (Dayun-si) was established in each.
In the ninth month, Empress Wu altered the mandate of Tang, changed the dynastic name to Zhou, and styled herself the Holy and Divine Emperor (Shengshen Huangdi).
The commentary states: The *New History of the Tang* (Xin Tang shi) utterly condemned the spurious nature of the *Dayun jing*.
Nevertheless, later figures such as the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci, Amoghavajra, and the National Teacher Qingliang all failed to investigate its origins and reject it.
To this day, this scripture remains listed within the canon. Tracing its authenticity or falsity is truly not easy to determine in detail.

The "Revolution of Heaven" had already appeared in secret prophecies during the era of Emperor Taizong; why then would she present the *Dayun jing* while presiding over the throne and exercising imperial authority?
As for these ten śramaṇas, if one examines them according to the Vinaya, their crimes of manifesting heterodox wonders naturally merit expulsion;
they must not be included among the ranks of the Sangha. Empress Wu sought to fulfill her own private ambitions and show favoritism toward them.
To value this [the new era] was not only to overthrow the mandate of the Tang, but also to simultaneously destroy the Dharma of Śākyamuni. How tragic!
In the first year of the Yanchai era, Empress Wu added the title "Heavenly Sovereign, Golden Wheel Holy Divine Emperor.

She fashioned the seven treasures and again heard that the Sanskrit original of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* existed in the Kingdom of Khotan. She immediately dispatched an envoy bearing jade and silk to seek it, along with—
He requested that one person from that country, well-versed in the study of Brahma-sounds, accompany the scripture on its journey.

Thereupon, the ruler of Khotan dispatched Śikṣānanda, who was a master of the *Avataṃsaka* school, in accordance with the imperial command. Upon seeing him, Empress Wu was greatly delighted and issued an edict for him to enter Dàbiànkōng Monastery.
There, together with the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci, as well as the Dharma Masters Shenze, Xuānjing, and Fùlǐ, he translated [the text].
While he was translating the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Empress Wu Zetian visited his monastery and personally provided him with offerings of food.
In the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, she issued an imperial decree for the śrāmaṇera Kang Fazang to expound the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka* at Taiyuan Temple.
Just as he was about to introduce the title of the scripture, a brilliant white light emerged from his mouth; in an instant, it formed a canopy and remained suspended there.
After a long silence, the multitude raised a joyful clamor, marveling at the extraordinary event. The *dougang* (lecturer) Sengheng reported the matter to Empress Wu Zetian, who was delighted.

An imperial decree was issued ordering ten eminent monks (*dashide*) of the capital to confer the full ordination upon him as a *zang* (Tripitaka master). He was granted the title "Xianshou" (Worthy Head), and by imperial edict, he was summoned to enter Dabiankong Monastery to participate in the translation of scriptures.
In that year, an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Huian of Mount Song to the inner palace to inquire about the Way. He was held in equal esteem with Chan Master Shenxiu.
Once, Empress Wu asked An how many years he had been in his current incarnation (his *jiawu* age). He replied, “I do not remember. She asked, “Why do you not remember?
An said, “The body of birth and death is like a revolving cycle; since the cycle has neither beginning nor end, what need is there to record it? Furthermore...”
The flow of the conscious mind is continuous and uninterrupted. To perceive the rising of bubbles is merely deluded thought;
from the initial consciousness until the cessation of the signs of movement, it is exactly like this. How could one record it by year or month? Empress Wu marveled at this for a long time.
At that time, Huian was over a hundred years of age, and the people of the world admired him, calling him National Teacher Lao’an (Old An).
On the *wùchén* day of the fifth month in the first year of the Shènglì era (698 CE), the Tripiṭaka Master Yìjìng returned from the Western Regions.
He had obtained over four hundred Sanskrit texts of sūtras and śāstras, as well as more than three hundred grains of relics and a true likeness of the Vajrāsana.

Empress Wu halted her carriage at the Upper East Gate to welcome him and offer congratulations. He was then installed at Fóshòujì Temple. Not long thereafter, he was summoned by imperial decree to enter Dàbiàn...

At the Empty Temple (Kōngsì), together with Śikṣānanda and others, he translated and verified the meaning of the scriptures. In the tenth month of the following year, the translation of the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was completed.
Śikṣānanda and the others submitted a memorial to the throne; Empress Wu personally composed the preface, which was proclaimed to the hundred officials from the Taijidian Hall.
In the first year of the Jiushi era, an imperial edict was issued to collect one cash per day from the monks throughout the empire to fund the construction of a Great Image at Baima Pass.
The Chancellor Di Renjie submitted a memorial of remonstrance, stating: "The foundation of governance must first attend to human affairs.

Your Majesty, out of compassion for the masses who are deluded and lost like children who have strayed from home, desires to cause the Dharma of Images to be practiced alongside the True Dharma so that people may perceive the forms and give rise to wholesome thoughts."

Yet the monasteries of today surpass the imperial palaces in their construction; they exhaust luxury and reach the pinnacle of magnificence, with carvings and paintings executed to the utmost of skill.
Precious materials are spent on adornment, and rare timber is used to the limit for the grand structures. These works were not performed by ghosts, nor did the materials descend from heaven;

since they all derive from the people, how can the populace endure such burdens? Moreover, there is a proper time for production, yet expenditure is unrestrained; this is what the common households must provide.

They are often insufficient for their needs; though their skin is pierced with pain and they do not shrink from beatings, itinerant monks offer a single sermon on the deception of fortune and calamity.
They shave their hair and strip off their clothes, yet still feel shame that there is too little.

There are also those who alienate kin like strangers and take wives themselves as if there were no distinction between self and other—all of them rely on the Buddha-dharma to delude the ignorant. Throughout the streets and alleys, Buddhist temples are everywhere.

In the bustling markets, there are even more monasteries; their earnest exhortations to convert others exceed official summons, and their requirements for ritual services are stricter than imperial decrees.
They possess vast tracts of fertile land, watermills, and estates in great abundance, yet they know no satiety. Draft-dodgers and those evading punishment flock to the gates of the Dharma;
furthermore, if even one man does not plow, society suffers the resulting hardship, and when those who live on idle sustenance become so numerous, it leads to further ruin.

They plunder the people’s wealth and property. Whenever I think of this, I am truly and acutely pained with grief. In the past, Emperor Wu and Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty gave away their possessions in incalculable amounts;

yet when the waves boiled over the Three Huai Rivers and the smoke rose from the Five Ling Mountains, the monasteries lining the streets could not save them from the calamity of ruin, nor did the monks who covered the roads perform any service for the King.
How much more so now, as the winds of war and dust repeatedly disturb the land and military levies become increasingly frequent? Suddenly—

To undertake such an endeavor exceeds the capacity of our current strength. We humbly consider that your meritorious virtues are immeasurable; why must you establish a great statue merely for the sake of its renown?
Even if we were to collect monastic funds, they would not cover even one-hundredth of the cost. Since the sacred countenance is so vast, it cannot remain exposed to the elements.

Even if it were covered with a hundred layers [of structures], one would still fear that it would not be entirely protected. Your servant has now gathered the consensus of public opinion, which all maintains that the Tathāgata...
In establishing the teachings, he takes compassion as his primary principle; to universally rescue all classes of beings is the focus of his mind.
How could he labor people with empty ostentation? When the memorial was presented, Empress Wu did not accept it.
The Treatise says: The Dharma Master Zhi Dun stated, "The śramaṇa’s relation to the world is like an empty boat moored in the great abyss.
He comes without business and departs upon finding leisure; within the four seas, he ultimately has no fixed dwelling."

When the state is in chaos, we travel alone with our mendicant staff; when the Way flourishes, we joyfully gather together. This is because those of our school are, by nature, people who have no worldly affairs in this world.

As for those of the degenerate age who ruin the Way and merely seek security in food and clothing— (Note: The final clause functions as a transition to a critique of those who prioritize material sustenance over spiritual cultivation.)
Regarding the discourse of the Duke of Di (Li Jing), it is truly impossible to ignore its implications. Alas! Could this possibly have been the doing of a true śramaṇa?
The memorial states that the Tathāgata established his teachings with the universal salvation of all beings as his core intent;
how could he have exhausted the people with empty formalities? This not only rectifies the errors of Emperor Kuangzong, but also serves to assist [the state].

This is the true teaching of our Buddha. It is as different from those who, in later generations, indiscriminately disparage the Buddhas and Laozi merely to seek fame as the clouds are from the earth.
In the first year of the Chang’an era, Empress Wu was about to construct a Great Image; the Censor Zhang Tinggui again submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying:
Now, the Buddha takes awakening and knowledge as his defining characteristic; he is realized through the mind and cannot be perceived by means of various physical marks.
As the Sūtra says: "If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, this person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
This fruit of True Suchness (Tathatā) cannot be sought externally. Your Majesty has taken refuge with a faithful heart and has given rise to a vast aspiration.
As for his vows, he has long since strengthened the stupas and temples and expanded the majestic forms [of the Buddhas] throughout the world.
Indeed, giving performed while dwelling upon the marks of conditioned phenomena is not the most supreme or rarest of dharmas. How is this known? A sutra says:
"If a person were to fill the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and use them for giving, the merit thereof would be very great; yet it would not be equal to..."
If there is someone who, within this sutra, receives and upholds even a four-line verse and explains it for others, their merit shall surpass that of the former.

As the Buddha has said: "Even if Your Majesty were to exhaust the wealth of the four seas, expend the strength of ten thousand men, use all the timber of the mountains to build stupas and temples, and employ the finest refined gold to cast sacred images, the labor would indeed be great and the expenditure most excessive."
The merit he thereby obtains is not even equal to that of an ordinary man in a meditation hall. A Bodhisattva should not be greedily attached to the merit he creates;
for conditioned phenomena are not worthy of high esteem, especially since this project of construction depends upon earth and wood.
In some cases, they excavate rocky outcrops to construct foundations and tiered steps; in others, they block up caverns and hollows to facilitate transport and timber-cutting.

Under the pressure of these operations, insects and ants perish by the billions. How could this accord with the Buddha’s teaching on the meaning of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), which out of compassion for all wriggling creatures forbids the harming of their lives?
Furthermore, it is not right to employ spirits while employing only humans for labor. When calculated as a whole, the craftsmen are mostly impoverished and destitute. At dawn...
In the evening, laboring at our tasks, our sinews were exhausted and our bones were worn out. We ate from bamboo baskets and drank from gourds, cooking our morning meals under the stars.

The exhaustion of hunger and thirst caused various ailments to converge upon us. How could this be the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching on the "mere practice" (tuxing), which takes pity on domestic animals and cannot bear to exhaust their strength?
Furthermore, regarding the labor for construction projects, monks and nuns are subject to taxation. Although they beg from door to door, those who are impoverished remain numerous.

When prefectures and counties demand their levies with the urgency of a fire or a star, these monastics have no other recourse but to devise schemes or sell their property to fulfill the obligation. The sound of resentment fills the roads, and the atmosphere of harmony is not restored.

How could this be consistent with the Buddha’s teaching on the virtue of joyful relinquishment? Out of compassion for the ignorant and deluded, he would not have been unwilling to allow them to retain their possessions.

Indeed. Furthermore, as the frontiers and the north have not yet been pacified, military preparations are becoming increasingly urgent. The empire is depleted and the realm within the seas is exhausted and weary.
We humbly beseech Your Majesty to be cautious and grave; to reflect upon the conduct of a Bodhisattva for the benefit of all sentient beings, and to practice giving in this manner.
Then that merit and virtue would be as immeasurable as the emptiness of the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
I have reflected upon this. Why must you be so diligent in abiding by signs, thereby undermining the livelihoods of the common people and exalting urgentless pursuits?
Speaking in terms of current administration, it would be appropriate to prioritize the borders, replenish the treasuries, and sustain the labor force.

Discussing this from the perspective of Buddhism, it would be appropriate to rescue those in peril and suffering, extinguish all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and honor non-action (*wuwei*). I humbly entreat Your Majesty to examine my words and put them into practice.
The conduct of the Buddha takes principle as its highest priority; one must not reject words because of the person who spoke them. When this memorial was submitted, Empress Wu was greatly pleased.
She summoned Zhang Tinggui to an audience in the Changsheng Hall and bestowed upon him gold and silk.
In this year, by imperial decree, Dharma Master Fǎzàng of Xianshou was summoned to the Fóshòujì Monastery in the Eastern Capital to lecture on the newly translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
When he reached the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," he was moved by a great earthquake that shook for over an hour before subsiding.

That very day, he was summoned to an audience at the Chángshēng Hall, where the Emperor questioned him regarding the ten layers of the profound gates of the Imperial Net (*diǎngǒng*), the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*hǎiyìn sānmèi*), and the six aspects of mutual inclusion and distinction.

Regarding the principles of identity and difference, and of arising and ceasing, the Tripiṭaka Master had already expounded them with systematic order. As his profound purport was thoroughly penetrating, Empress Tianzao was suddenly struck with bewilderment and amazement upon hearing it.
She requested instruction repeatedly, and the Master then took a golden lion in a corner of the hall as an illustration for her.
When he reached the point concerning "a lion at the tip of a single hair" and "a lion at the tips of ten billion hairs," Empress Tianzao attained sudden and complete understanding. Thereupon—

This collection of his words is titled the *Jinshizi Zhang* (The Chapter on the Golden Lion). Initially, Venerable Yan of Linghua Monastery transmitted the Huayan school’s fundamental tenets of Dushun.
Zang served as Yan’s attendant and received the entirety of his teachings. Upon Yan’s passing, Zang preached the Dharma with a mind of pure sincerity.
Thereupon, the venerable elders of the capital city submitted a joint petition to the throne requesting that he be ordained as a monk. Thus, Zang shaved his hair.

His full ordination was entirely by the special decree of Empress Wu Zetian. Furthermore, he once arranged ten circular mirrors for Empress Wu, placing them in the eight corners and at the zenith and nadir, all facing one another.
He installed a Buddha image in the center and lit candles to illuminate it; thus, the image appeared in every mirror, reflecting and merging with one another.
To those who observed it, the reflections appeared interlaced and simultaneous, symbolizing that the ocean of lands and the ten realms universally contain all things without end.
The essential meaning of this [teaching] had been lost to obscurity until National Teacher Qingliang Chengguan took it as his primary doctrine.
Scholars throughout the land followed him, designating it the "School of the Perfectly Interfused Virtues in a Single Thought-moment" and referring to it as the Xianshou Teaching.
Three years passed, and the expenses for casting the image were nearly complete. Ji Qiao, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying:

"I have heard that the Dharma is compassionate and that Bodhisattvas provide protection; their sole intent is to benefit all living beings, not to rely on the construction and veneration of earthen and wooden structures.

I have humbly heard that for the creation of this image, taxes are being levied not from the household registers, but that the funds are to come from monks and nuns. It is not through the service of prefectures and counties that these efforts can be sustained."
[Daobian] continued: "Furthermore, among the commoners throughout the empire, those who are poor and weak are numerous. Some hire out their labor as day laborers to provide for their food and grain;

others sell their fields and dilapidate their houses to fulfill the king’s corvée service. Now, the amount of money spent on creating these images already totals one hundred and seventy thousand strings."
If one were to provide extensive relief for the poor through such scattered almsgiving, even a single person giving a thousand coins could sustain one hundred and seventy thousand households.

This would alleviate the hardships of hunger and cold, spare the toil of labor services, accord with the compassionate hearts of all Buddhas, and broaden the sovereign’s intent to nurture and transform the world.
Thus, both humans and spirits would rejoice, and the merit would be immeasurable. Yet, Heaven did not grant this; thus, in this winter, the image was completed.
He led the hundred officials in performing the ritual sacrifice.

In the first month of the first year of the Shénlóng era, the five princes—Ministers Zhāng Běizhī, Huán Yànfàn, and others—used military force to execute the treacherous ministers and restored the Crown Prince to the throne;
he was then the Emperor Zhōngzōng. They transferred Empress Wú Zetiān to the Shàngyáng Palace.

The Palace demoted the Chancellor Fang Rong to Gaoyou. In the fourth month of summer, while in Guangzhou, Fang Rong encountered the Indian monk Paramiti, who was carrying the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The Regional Inspector invited him to the Upper Daochang Monastery to proclaim and translate it. Fang Rong acted as the scribe for the oral transmission.
Once the ten fascicles of the translated scripture were completed, Paramiti took the Sanskrit original back to India.
In this month, the Emperor issued an imperial decree summoning Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, to the capital. The decree stated:
"I have invited the two masters An and Xiu to receive offerings within the palace. In my leisure time from the myriad affairs of state, I have constantly investigated the One Vehicle.
Both masters have recommended that there is a Chan Master Neng in the South who secretly received the robe and Dharma of Great Master Ren; you may go to him for instruction."
The Emperor dispatched the inner attendant Xue Jian with an imperial edict to invite him, saying: "I pray that Master will look upon me with compassion and hasten to the capital.
The Master declined the invitation in a memorial, citing his illness and expressing his wish to spend his final years among the forest slopes.

Xue Jian said, "The virtuous practitioners of Chan in the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate samādhi. It has never happened before that one could attain liberation without relying on dhyāna and samādhi."
"I do not yet know what kind of Dharma the Master teaches. The Master said, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? A sutra says:
'If one perceives the Tathāgata as either sitting or lying down, this is practicing a deviant path. Why is this? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, this is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata. That all dharmas are empty and quiescent—this is the Tathāgata."

"Pure sitting is ultimately without realization; how much less so is there anything to be attained through sitting? Jian said, "When your disciple returns to court, the Sovereign will surely question me.

I pray that you, Master, will out of compassion point out the essential heart-essence, so that I may now realize my nature and clarify the Way. The Patriarch replied, "The Way has neither light nor darkness."

Brightness and darkness signify the meaning of alternation. That brightness is inexhaustible is also [a case of] having an end. Jian said: "Brightness is a metaphor for wisdom; darkness is an analogy for afflictions (*kleśa*).
If a practitioner of the Way does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter the afflictions of birth and death, by what means can they attain liberation?
The Master said: "If one uses wisdom to illuminate afflictions, this is the 'small child' or 'sheep' of the Two Vehicles."

Regarding vehicles and such mechanisms, those of superior wisdom and great capacity do not view them in this way. [The student] asked: "What is meant by the perspective of the Mahāyāna? The Master said:
"Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual in their nature; this non-dual nature is itself the true nature. As for this true nature..."
It does not diminish when dwelling among the ordinary and ignorant; it does not increase when among the sages and saints. It remains undisturbed while abiding in afflictions;
it is not quiescent while residing in divine concentration. It is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither coming nor going; it is not in the middle, nor within or without.
The nature and characteristics of non-arising and non-ceasing are suchness (*tathatā*). That which is eternally abiding and unchanging is called the Way (*mārga*). Jian asked:

"When you, Master, speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, how does this differ from the heterodox schools? The Master said: "The heterodox schools seek to stop arising by means of cessation, and they manifest cessation through arising."
That which is extinguished is as if not extinguished; that which arises is said to be non-arising. I say that it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning and is likewise unextinguished now.
This is why it differs from the heterodox paths. If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever;

you will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally abiding, with wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Jianli took his leave and returned to the palace to present this memorial.

The Master spoke thus. The Emperor praised him for a long time. Shortly thereafter, he dispatched an envoy to bestow upon him a *kāṣāya*, a water bottle, an alms bowl, and other items, conveying the Emperor’s sentiments of deep admiration.
In the third month of the second year, Chan Master Daotong Shenxiu passed away. Zhang Yue, the Grand Secretary, composed an inscription for his stele, titled "Tuan."
Now, that which synthesizes the four great elements constitutes the body; that which establishes the myriad beginnings presides over the mind. The body is empty;

by perceiving the body as empty, one’s beginning coincides with wondrous function. The mind is not substantial; by contemplating the mind as an illusion, it becomes equal to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
When names and numbers enter, the wondrous source is alienated; when words and expressions emerge, the true principle is obscured. Therefore, the Tathāgata has an intention [to speak].

The essential path is transmitted through the power of upholding supreme virtue; after ten thousand kalpas, one encounters the seal of the Dharma-transmission. In a single thought-moment, one is suddenly bestowed with the Buddha-body.

Who was it that propagated this? It was truly Master Daotong who did so. The Master was honored as Daotong; his name was Shenxiu. His original surname was Li, and he was a native of Weishi in Chenliu.
His mind penetrated the nine schools of thought, and he possessed the intuitive realization of prior awakening. As for his person...
He was eight chi tall, with prominent eyebrows and large ears; his appearance bore the marks of a king or a hegemon, and his proportions accorded with the measure of sages and worthies.

In his youth, he was a scholar who traveled throughout the region south of the Yangtze River to seek instruction. He mastered the profound principles of Laozi and Zhuangzi, the great meanings of the Book of Changes and the Book of Documents, the sutras and treatises of the Three Vehicles, and the disciplinary codes of the Four Divisions (*Caturvarga-vinaya*).

His explanations were thorough in their philological analysis, and his pronunciation blended the dialects of Wu and Jin. He was as radiant as a peacock covered in gold and turquoise, and as resonant as the chiming of metal bells.

Master Yu had already attained solitary insight that emerged from within and possessed extensive learning applied to all quarters. Upon reaching the age at which one recognizes the mandate of Heaven, he withdrew himself from the mundane world.
He heard that in Qi Prefecture there was a Chan Master named Ren, a true successor in the Dharma lineage of the Chan school.
Since Bodhidharma came from India to the East, the Dharma was transmitted to Huike; Huike transmitted it to Sengcan; Sengcan transmitted it to Daoxin; and Daoxin transmitted it to...
Hongren succeeded to the light and inherited the profound traces through five generations. Thus, disregarding the remoteness of the journey, he traveled swiftly to pay his respects.

His empty receptivity met with the Master’s profound mind; his lofty awakening shared the same track as the True Vehicle. With the threads of thought severed and consciousness forgotten, he realized the tranquil fundamental mind.
Abiding in the realm of cessation, his practice was free from fixed points. Having attained realization through a teacher, he was now, at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, without dependence.
He preached this Dharma-gate of the King of Emptiness. For six years he served his master with diligence, never ceasing day or night.

The Master sighed and said, "The Dharma of the Eastern Mountain is entirely present in Xiu. He ordered him to wash his feet and invited him to sit beside him. Upon seeing this, [Xiu] wept and took his leave, withdrawing into seclusion.
During the Yifeng era, he finally registered at Yuquan Temple; its name was listed in the Monastic Records, and it was located seven *li* to the east of the temple.
Mount Ditu is majestic. He gazed upon it and said: "This is truly the solitary peak of Laṅkā, a hermitage that serves as a gateway for crossing over.
Beneath the shade of pines and upon the mats of grass, I shall grow old here. When clouds follow the dragon and wind follows the tiger, when the Great Way emerges, the worthy perceive it.

As for the lands of Qiyang, they have departed from Chengdu; as for the mountains of Huayin, scholars come there like a marketplace—yet this is not yet considered much. Those who come later shall attain [the Way].
With this, one brushes away the three realms of existence and transcends the four dhyānas. One ascends to the hall of the seventy [sages] and tastes the flavor of the Three Thousand [worlds].
This is nothing short of such excellence. As for the opening of the Dharma: in its general outline, one forgets mindfulness to still conceptualization and exerts all effort to restrain the mind.

In its entry, the categories are equal for both ordinary beings and sages; in its arrival, there is no sequence of before or after. Prior to entering meditative concentration, the ten thousand conditions are entirely closed off, and wisdom is brought forth.
Thereafter, all things were as they should be; in particular, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was venerated as the essential core of his heart. Beyond this, nothing further is known.
During the Jiushi era, as the Master’s years had grown advanced, an imperial decree invited him to court. He sat cross-legged in audience before the Sovereign.

Carried in a sedan chair to ascend the hall, he bowed his head in homage before the Sovereign of Ten Thousand Chariots; he washed his hands and took his ease within the Nine Layers of the palace. Those who transmit the Holy Way do not face north;

those who possess sublime virtue receive no rites of subordination from ministers. Thus, he was successively promoted to the title of Dharma Master of the Two Capitals and Imperial Preceptor of the Three Dynasties.
We look up to the Buddha-sun as it rises once more and rejoice at the rare appearance of the udumbara flower. Yet, while residing in the capital, its profound mysteries were kept concealed;
whenever emperors shared the seat and queens attended the assembly, the ranks of courtiers surrounded us like swans and cranes, and the great disciples encircled us like dragons and elephants.

At such times, we were like glowing coals awaiting the ore, so we remained silent before them yet their hearts were subdued; we were like those suffering from hunger who receive nourishment, so though our words were concise, they grasped the meaning. (1)
The rain falls universally upon all conditions; the myriad pipes each sound according to their own nature.

Were it not for one who dwells securely in fearlessness and possesses boundless adaptability, who could achieve such a thing? The Sage’s reverence increases daily, and imperial grace accumulates from generation to generation.
At the site of the initial assembly at Dangyang, a temple was established named Dumon; at the ancestral residence of the Wei clan, a temple was established named Baoen. — Su Shi.

The village was named Xiangbiao (Village of Virtue) because his character was exemplary; it was not merely a local designation, yet he grew weary of the clamor of the capital. With a mind ever fixed on the empty valley, he repeatedly requested to return to the mountains.
Having been granted permission to stay for a long time, he became frail and exhausted, though free from other ailments or suffering. His spirit remained whole while his physical strength failed him.

On the night of the twenty-eighth day of the second month in the second year of the Shenlong era, at the hour of midnight, he looked upon his end and sat in meditation, passing away as calmly as if entering a state of transformation. This is the account of his dhyāna.
The Master received full ordination at Tiangong Temple in the eighth year of the Wude era (the *wuyou* year). He passed away at this same temple in the *bingwu* year;
his monastic age was eighty. Born toward the end of the Sui dynasty, he lived for over one hundred years, yet he never spoke of it himself, so those around him could not ascertain his exact age.
The fires of the three realms burned his heart, and the waters of the fourfold assembly flowed against his back; now the rafters have collapsed and the beams have crumbled.
Thunder shook and rain fell as they wept. Since all these precious bodies produced such golden mouths, their loss was treated like the death of one's own parents.

An imperial edict sent envoys to offer condolences, and princes and dukes returned with gifts. On the second day of the third month, the posthumous title "Great Penetration" (Dàtōng) was conferred, fulfilling the rites for honoring the deceased.
On the fifth day of that month, the remains were temporarily enshrined at Que Sai, out of a longing to delay the time of the final interment. The Imperial Chariot—
When the moment of departure arrived at Wúqiáo, Duke Wáng escorted him sorrowfully as far as the Yī River. The ceremonial insignia were arrayed as far as the mountain grotto.
On the fifteenth day of the mid-autumn month, the imperial decree was finally issued; the Emperor granted his prior promise, and [the Master] thus fulfilled his long-held aspiration.

The Grand Master of Ceremonies led the way with the drum and flute orchestra, while the Commandant of the City Gates supervised the funeral rites. On this day, the Son of Heaven departed from Lóngmén, where he personally moistened the golden shrouds and ascended [the funeral bier].

The Emperor halted his carriage there; his gaze followed the returning palanquin until it vanished from sight. From Mount Yi to the Yangtze River, the way was lined with those who offered their condolences and waited in mourning.

Hundreds of carriages bore banners and flowers, and fragrant clouds spread for a thousand li. On the first day of the waning moon in the tenth month, the remains were enshrined behind the old residence on the ridge, and a stupa was erected.
The state treasury provided lavish decorations exceeding one million coins. The great bell was cast by the former Emperor, while the various scriptures were commissioned by the current Sovereign.

The golden plaque was inscribed by Imperial decree, and the magnificent banners were crafted within the palace. The stupa and temple were held in such high esteem that their renown spread far and wide as peerless monuments.
When the Master first passed away in Dongluo, his remains were seen at Nanjing; white mists gathered in dark gloom over Mount Chan, and white lotuses grew upon the tree where he sat.
Thus, the twin trees changed color and the Si River flowed backward; when a supreme being departs this world, even disparate signs accord with one another in resonance. One hundred...
On the day of the *sukravāsa* (the end of wailing), a great assembly was held at Longhua Monastery for eight thousand people, with twenty-seven individuals receiving ordination.

On the two occasions of the *xiang* and *lian* anniversaries, all attended the Ximing Dharma Hall; the numbers were as in the previous assembly. The Bodhisattva Wanhui requested alms from the inner palace;

precious robes filled the chests, their value rivaling that of a foreign state. The Empress herself, accompanied by her favored attendants, personally joined the offerings and circled the incense burner. Its magnificence was vast.
The causes of such vast blessings lie in this very existence and its cessation. As the sun and moon pass by, glory and decay push one another forward.
Alas! The Dharma-heir forever yearns for the ultimate source; he grieves that the Compassionate Vessel has so suddenly vanished, and laments that the surging stupa remains closed too long.
The sighs of Shicheng shall not be in vain, and the monument of Mount Lu may indeed be inscribed. I venture to compare this to the discourse of Master Gong on his Master—while he was still alive.
Regarding heaven and earth, they do not know their height or thickness; regarding the rivers and seas, they do not know their breadth or depth.
They give forceful names to their traces merely to comfort their own minds. The inscription says:
The pearl within the forehead is hidden; it cannot be reached without a finger. The dust upon the mirror of the mind is external; it cannot be reflected without polishing.

The oceanic treasury is tranquil, yet the winds of consciousness pull toward pleasure. If one does not enter the gates of liberation, who can explore the essentials of the Dharma? Splendid indeed is the Master of Chan, standing alone beneath heaven!

When merit is gathered, one approaches the secret; when names are dissolved, they are seen as provisional. Approaching that which is unattainable, even "dissolution" is entirely relinquished. Like the moon’s reflection in the void, it appears to those who have awakened.
To immeasurable multitudes of virtuous beings, he is father and teacher; he exposes the clarity [that dispels] feverish affliction, and his light pierces through darkened doubt.
I hoped he would remain in the world, his ten-thousand-year life-span without end. Alas, how could it be that like a fleeting glance through a crack, he departed in a single day?

Alas for my disciples, our grieving hearts broken and fragmented; looking up in reverence, we advance, yet reflecting on his final entrustment, we retreat. All remain inseparable from meditative concentration; emptiness is not the extinction of awakening.

"Keep this in mind; let it be kept in mind. I venture to inform those beyond further study [the *aśaikṣas*]. At that time, Prince Qi Fan and the Retired Scholar Lu Hong both had steles and monuments erected.
The *Old History of the Tang* contains a biography of him, noting that it was unprecedented in antiquity for a śramaṇa to receive such ritual respect from a sovereign.
In the third month of the first year of the Jinglong era, the National Teacher Huian instructed his disciples, saying: "When my life-force is exhausted, place my corpse in the forest."
In the midst of this, a wild fire broke out and consumed [the dwelling]. By chance, the divine monk Wan-hui arrived;

he grasped Dao’an’s hand and engaged him in conversation, yet his disciples, listening from the side, were all unable to perceive it. On the eighth day, he lay down with his body folded and passed away peacefully at the age of one hundred twenty-eight.
His disciples, following his instructions, carried his remains to a forest. Indeed, a wild fire arrived and cremated them, and they obtained *śarīra*.

There were eighty grains; five of them were exceptionally large, purple-red in color, and their radiant flames were dazzling to the eye. An imperial decree was issued for them to enter and remain within the inner palace, where it was said:
"In this year, a second decree was issued for the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan to arrive. The Emperor halted his carriage to welcome him and offer greetings, providing [him with] full..."
The ritual protocols of the two streets welcomed him with banners, streamers, and the music of drums and pipes; he was carried upon a blue elephant and installed at Jianfu Monastery.
Nanti was a wind deity of vast and expansive presence, with an elegant and refined bearing; he was proficient in both Mahayana and Hinayana teachings and mastered both Chinese and Sanskrit sounds.
