Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zǔxiù of Shíshì Monastery in Lōngxìng Prefecture.
In the third year of the Jinglong era of the Tang dynasty, there was a Chan master named Fayi, the son of Wang Langya.
Because Wang had joined Xu Jingye in raising troops to assassinate Empress Wu, his clan was utterly destroyed. At that time, Fayi was still young; he fled and hid among the common people.

He encountered a śramaṇa who took him into the monastic order and ordained him as a great monk (*mahāsaṃghika*). During this time, Emperor Zhongzong issued an edict seeking descendants of the Langya lineage.
The presiding official reported Shi Yi’s name to the Governor of Fufeng. Upon finding Shi Yi, the governor was delighted with him;
he lodged him in his rear hall and submitted his name to the court. Subsequently, the governor’s wife, captivated by Shi Yi’s refined demeanor, pressured him to abandon the monastic life.
The Lord of the Asuras wished to give his beloved daughter in marriage to Upatiṣya, but Upatiṣya firmly refused and would not consent.

One day, the lady took her daughter to see him, intending to have her approach him and bewitch him with charms so as to win over his heart. Having no other choice, Upatiṣya feigned compliance and said, "I have been traveling for a long time;
once I have had a bath, we may then perform the marriage rites. The lady rejoiced, believing this to be the truth, and hurriedly ordered everything to be prepared.

While bathing, Sengyi entered the chamber and immediately severed his own genitals with a sharp blade. A maidservant saw this in secret and hurriedly called out to the palace attendants to force open the door and rescue him;

he subsequently regained consciousness. The Prefect, admiring his integrity, took charge of his affairs. When Sengyi went to the capital for an audience, the Emperor ordered that he inherit the rank of Prince of Langya.
Sengyi declined the offer with earnest sincerity based on his original resolve, presenting his principles with great loftiness. The Emperor praised him highly.
He followed these instructions with ease. Subsequently, his meditative contemplation reached profound realization, and he was highly esteemed and saluted by the virtuous men of the age.
In that year, the Vinaya Master Dao’an was summoned to the palace to bestow the precepts of refuge upon the consorts and princesses; consequently, he remained within the inner quarters.

On another day when the Emperor arrived, all the other masters rose from their seats to show deference, but Dao’an alone hesitated and merely offered a long bow. The Emperor held his magnanimity in high regard.
This illustration was produced at the Lingguang Palace. The Emperor composed a eulogy for it, which says: "The pearl of the precepts is bright and pure; the stream of wisdom is clear and serene.

The body is confined by the five categories of offenses, yet the mind merges with the eight meditative attainments. He studies the wondrous True Doctrine and his contemplation penetrates the ultimate nature. He maintains the affairs of the Dharma and upholds the principles of virtuous governance.
May the Vinaya-piṭaka transmit its fragrance afar, and thereby may the teaching of the Image Age shine in great prosperity. At that time, this was considered a source of great honor.

In the sixth month of the first year of the Jingyun era, Empress Wei incited a rebellion and Emperor Zhongzong passed away. In the seventh month, Prince of Linzi raised troops to quell the internal turmoil.
His Imperial Brother, the Prince of Xiang, ascended the throne as Emperor; this was Ruizong. On the day of Gengchen of that same month, an edict was issued stating:

"The scriptures of Śākyamuni and the profound principles of the August Way are equal in essence though different in manifestation; they rescue humanity and transform customs through distinct teachings yet identical merit. From now on..."
Whenever monks, nuns, Daoists, or female Daoist adepts gather for matters concerning the Dharma, they should assemble in a unified procession.
Initially, Emperor Taizong ranked Laozi as a member of the imperial clan and placed him above Śākyamuni; however, during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he was again placed below Śākyamuni.
From this point forward, this has become the permanent protocol, and it is ordered that they assemble in a unified rank.
On the day of Yimao in the eighth month, the persimmon tree at Xingxing Monastery— the former residence of the High Ancestor— which had withered during the Tiangshou era,

suddenly flourished once more. Consequently, a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm, the officials were granted titles and ranks, and tens of thousands of monks, nuns, and Daoist priests were ordained.
In the ninth month, an imperial edict was issued for the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci to translate the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* at the Gānlù Pavilion by the White Lotus Pond in the Northern Garden.
The Secretariat Director Lu Xiàngxiān, the Minister of the Court of Civil Office Guō Yuànzhèn, and the Chancellor Zhāng Shuō were commanded to provide literary revisions.
The scripture was completed in fifty-nine assemblies, totaling one hundred and twenty fascicles.

In the tenth month, an imperial edict summoned the divine monk Wanhui to the palace; he was granted the title Duke Fayun and lodged at the Jixian Academy, where two beautiful women were provided to serve him.
After a short while, he suddenly requested water from the River Wei; his attendants were flustered and unable to obtain it.
He further said, "The ground before the hall can be used as a burial pit. Once it was prepared, he returned, drank some water, and passed away in deep stillness.

He was posthumously granted the title of Duke of the State, and his portrait was enshrined in the Jixian Academy. When he was young, he was able to deliver letters to his elder brother three thousand *li* away, departing in the morning and returning by evening;
thus, he was named Wan-hui (Ten Thousand Returns). Emperor Gaozong heard of his reputation and issued an edict for him to enter the palace, where he was ordained as a monk.
When Empress Wu was on the throne, she summoned him to the inner palace, bestowed upon him a brocade robe, and ordered palace attendants to serve him.
When Crown Prince Zhuanghui was first born, Empress Wu held him up to show him to Xuanhui. Xuanhui said, "This is the essence of a Western tree spirit; he should be raised as a brother.
Later, when Princess Anle, relying on Empress Wei, plotted treason, Xuanhui encountered her. Seeing her from afar, he spat toward the dust and said, "Blood!"
One must not approach him when he is raw [or tainted]. Before long, Anle was indeed executed. When Xuanzong was in the frontier regions, he once visited Huai in private;

Huai patted his back and said, "In fifty years, you shall be a Son of Heaven in a time of great peace. When Ruizong was the Prince of Chang’an, whenever he was about to go out, Huai would invariably announce to the market folk, "The Son of Heaven is coming!
A short while later, the Prince of Chang’an would arrive. His divine and extraordinary nature was of this sort.
The Treatise says: Master Fayun once composed a verse: "When light and darkness are both forgotten, the Buddha-eye opens;

Unattached to a single dharma, one emerges from the lotus grove. True emptiness does not destroy the nature of numinous wisdom; Sublime function is eternal, its merit unconditioned. Noble wisdom is inherently the path to Buddhahood;
The light of stillness is non-illuminating, yet spontaneously pervasive. If one savors the meaning of this deeply, it is truly [the teaching of] the Great...
This is the expression of one who has attained realization. Yet Fǎyún specifically manifested through the miraculous wonders of the Hīnayāna.
As for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appearing in the world to propagate the great, orthodox Dharma-eye, they must invariably conceal their radiance and blend with the mundane;

they never begin by revealing their secret mechanisms, but only at the very end of their lives do they grant their final entrustment. Thus, while Fǎyún’s manifestations of the extraordinary were numerous, was this not [the work of] a sage?

Was this perhaps the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Venerable One? In the third year, an imperial edict summoned the Great Being (*mahāsattva*) Saṃgha from Sizhou to the palace for offerings. He ordained three men—Huian, Hu'an, and Muksha—as his attendants.
The Emperor personally inscribed the plaque for the temple where he resided with the characters "Puguangwang" (Universal Radiance King). Not long after, [Saṃgha] moved his residence.
At Jianfu Monastery, the following year, the capital region suffered from drought. By imperial decree, the Great Master was ordered to bring rain.

Śāṅgha sprinkled water from his flask, whereupon thick clouds surged forth from his dwelling and heavy rain poured down. In the third month of the following year, he passed away at the age of eighty-three.
His countenance remained as lifelike as ever. An edict was issued for his body to be sculpted at Jianfu Monastery and a stupa to be constructed.
Immediately, a foul stench filled the city. The Emperor burned incense and offered prayers for him, promising to send him back to the Huai River.

As soon as he had finished speaking, a wondrous fragrance wafted through the air. The entire capital marveled at this marvel. He was then escorted with his whole body back to Puguangwang Temple in Sizhou, where a pagoda was erected for him.
The Emperor once asked Master Fayun about Wanhui, saying, "What kind of person was Saṃgha? He replied, "He was an emanation of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara."
The details of his spiritual transformations and deeds are fully recorded in the biography authored by Jiang Yingshu.

In the third month of that year, an imperial edict was issued to Wei Anshi, the Guardian of the Eastern Capital, ordering him to carry a decree to summon the śramaṇa Yixing from Mount Song to the imperial court.
Yixing declined on the grounds of illness and did not go, instead fleeing to Mount Dangyang in Jingzhou. The *Jiushi Tangshu* (Old Book of Tang) states:
His secular surname was Zhang. Originally named Sui, he was the grandson of Lord Gongjin of Shan and the son of Zhan, the Magistrate of Wugong.

From his youth, he was intelligent and quick-witted; he perused the works of the sages and the histories. He once visited the Daoist master Yin Chong to borrow the *Taixuan jing* (The Book of Great Mystery) to read it.

After several days, he returned it. Yin Chong said, "This scripture is subtle and profound; though I have sought its meaning for many years, I am still not fully enlightened. You should investigate it thoroughly."

"Do not be negligent. Xing said, "I have already thoroughly investigated its meaning," and thereupon presented the *Taoyan Xuantu* (Mysterious Diagram of the Grand Derivative) and the *Yijué* (Decisions on the Meaning) that he had composed.
When Wang Chong examined them, he was greatly astonished; he subsequently discussed their profound depths with him and, upon retiring, remarked to others, "This is a contemporary Yanzi.
From this, Xing became renowned throughout the world. Initially, Wu Sansi admired his learning and conduct and went to request a friendship with him. Xing...
He fled to hide from them and soon left the household life. He traveled throughout the world seeking out extraordinary arts.
Upon arriving at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, he saw dozens of ancient pines in a detached courtyard with a stream flowing through its gate.

Standing by the screen at the entrance, he heard the sound of a monk calculating with counting sticks in the courtyard as he spoke to his disciples, saying: "Today, a disciple shall come from afar seeking [instruction]. I..."

"The calculations have already reached the gate; surely there is no one to guide me? He then removed one counting bead and said, "The water before the gate shall flow westward; my disciple has also arrived.
As he walked back, he looked behind him and saw that the stream had indeed begun to flow west. He followed these words and hurried inside immediately.

Prostrating himself twice, he requested instruction in the method. The other bestowed it upon him in its entirety, whereupon he thoroughly mastered the principles of calendrical astronomy and the movements of the yin and yang.

Yang mastered the science of astronomical calculation (*tuībù*). He then entered Mount Song to rely upon Chan Master Pují, where he investigated and resolved the fundamental tenets of the Chan school.

Later, while secluded on Mount Dāngyáng, he further studied the Vinaya under Master Huìwù. Regarding all the scriptures and classics, he would not forget anything after reading through them even once throughout his life.
In the first year of the Tianxian era, the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng of Caoxi, addressed the assembly, saying:

"Good friends, each of you listen with a pure mind to what I say. You all should know that your own minds are Buddha; do not harbor further doubts. There is not a single thing outside that can be established;
everything is the original mind giving rise to all manner of phenomena. Therefore, a sutra says: 'The mind gives rise to all manner of...'"

When dharmas arise, the mind perishes; when various dharmas perish, [the mind likewise ceases]. If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñā), one must attain the samādhi of a single mark and the samādhi of a single practice.

If, in all places, one does not dwell upon marks, and among all dharmas, one gives rise to neither aversion nor affection, nor does one engage in grasping or rejecting, nor dwell upon matters such as benefit, success, or failure, but remains at ease, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene—[this is the way].

This is called the Samādhi of One Characteristic. If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely upright mind without wavering from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one immediately accomplishes the Pure Land; this is called the Samādhi of One Practice.

If a person possesses these two samādhis, it is like the earth which, having seeds, can contain, nurture, and bring them to fruition; the Samādhi of One Characteristic and the Samādhi of One Practice are likewise so.

My preaching of the Dharma now is like seasonal rain that universally moistens the great earth. Your Buddha-nature is like a seed; encountering this soaking moisture, it shall all sprout and flourish.
Those who receive my words will certainly attain Bodhi; those who follow my practice will surely realize the wondrous fruit.
As the Master preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, the number of students coming and going constantly exceeded a thousand. In the seventh month of the following year...
Yue took his leave and returned to his old residence at Guoen Temple in Xinzhou. His disciples wept and asked, "When the Master returns, will you come back again?
The Master said, "When karma falls, one returns to the root; when I come, I shall have no mouth. They asked further, "To whom did the Master transmit the Dharma-eye?"
The Master said, "That which has the Way is transmitted; that which is without mind penetrates. Upon arriving at Guoen Temple, on the third day of the eighth month, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have received the robe and Dharma from Master Ren. Now I shall preach the Dharma for you, but I do not transmit the robe.
This is because your roots of faith have already matured; you are resolute and free from doubt, capable of undertaking the great task. Listen to my verse: The Ground of the Mind..."
"Containing all seeds, when rain falls everywhere, they all sprout. Once the essence of the flower has been fully realized through sudden awakening, the fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously attained.
He further addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma is non-dual; the mind is likewise so. The Way is pure and free from all marks.
You need not contemplate stillness or emptiness regarding this mind. This mind is fundamentally pure, with nothing to be grasped or rejected. Each of you must exert yourselves."
"Go as you please according to conditions. The time for my nirvana has arrived; take care. Having said this, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Thereupon, the mountains and forests turned white, birds and beasts wailed in grief, and colored clouds and fragrant mists remained unbroken for days.
Subsequently, Wei Ju, the Governor-General of Guangzhou, led the officials of the two prefectures of Shao and Xin to welcome his entire remains back to Baolin Monastery at Caoxi.

A stupa was erected; his true body remains there to this day. The *Old History of the Tang* states: When Empress Wu heard of Shenxiu’s reputation, she issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital.

She had him carried into the palace in a sedan chair and personally prostrated herself before him in worship. By imperial edict, Dumen Monastery was established on Mount Dangyang to commemorate his virtue.

At that time, from princes and dukes down to the commoners and gentry of the capital, all were moved by his reputation and vied with one another to come and pay their respects, bowing even at the sight of his dust.
I prostrate myself. My eyes behold them by the tens of thousands. Initially, Shenxiu and Huineng were disciples of the same master, Hongren, and their religious practices were equal.
When Hongren passed away, Huineng resided at Guangguo Temple in Shaoguo. In the mountains of Shaoyang, there had long been many tigers and leopards.
In a single night, they all vanished; those far and near were struck with wonder and sighed in admiration, and all submitted to him in reverence.

Xiu once memorialized Empress Wu Zetian requesting that Huineng be summoned to the capital, but Huineng firmly declined. Xiu again composed a letter himself to invite him earnestly, to which Huineng said to the messenger:
"My appearance is short and ugly; I fear that if people of the northern lands see me, they will not respect my Dharma. Furthermore, my late master [foretold] that I would be in the south..."
The circumstances were such that he could not disregard them. When the Emperor Zhongzong summoned him, he ultimately did not cross the mountain pass and passed away.
His teachings were circulated throughout the world; thus, Xiu was called the Northern School and Neng was called the Southern School.
The Commentary states: Although the old records have been lost and the Way of our ancestors remains unclarified, there are accounts therein worthy of praise.
For instance, when Huixiu was favored by two successive reigns, he nevertheless declined the invitation to Caoxi; while Caoxi remained steadfastly recluse and did not go.
Thus, Huixiu did not conceal the virtues of others, and Caoxi was diligent in internalizing his teacher’s teachings, fearing that others might...
To treat the Dharma with contempt based on outward appearance—these are all matters concerning the great principles of what the worthy accept or reject.

Now, this *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) fails to record the beauty of the mutual deference shown by former sages; instead, it contains much of the language of mutual animosity between the two schools.

It is only natural that those of shallow character in later generations, upon obtaining even a slight position or reputation, would become haughty and self-important, regarding the whole world as being inferior to themselves.

Among the younger generation, there are often those who devote themselves solely to refutation as their primary goal. Alas! The transformative rites and exemplary models of the founding masters have utterly vanished.
How can those who come after them possibly provide a description?
In the tenth month of the second year of the Kaiyuan era, Chan Master Xuangjue of Yongjia entered nirvana.

The Master had extensively mastered the Tripitaka and was refined in the perfect and wondrous Dharma-gate of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Together with Chan Master Ce of Dongyang, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch.

Upon arriving, the Master shook his staff, carried his water jar, and circumambulated the meditation seat once. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa must possess the three thousand dignified demeanors and the eight..."
[The Master] performed ten thousand subtle practices. "Virtuous One, from what direction have you come, that you give rise to such great conceit?

The Master said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising? Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness? The Master said, "Realizing it is non-arising;
understanding it fundamentally has no swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. The Master then assumed the full dignified demeanor and paid his respects. He must...
Yun took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Is your return so soon? The Master replied, "Since it is fundamentally without movement, how could there be 'soon'?

The Patriarch asked, "Who knows that it is not moving? The Master said, "The benevolent one himself gives rise to discrimination. The Patriarch said, "You have grasped the meaning of non-arising very well.
The Master said, "If there is no arising, how can there be 'meaning'? The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who would engage in discrimination? The Master replied, "Discrimination..."

Nor was it the mind. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for one night. At that time, he was called "One-Night Enlightenment" (Yi-xiu-jue). Upon his return, students flocked to him from all directions.
The Master composed a work titled *The Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*), which a foreign monk transmitted back to India;

there, everyone held it in high esteem and regarded it as a Mahāyāna sūtra of the Eastern Land. He also composed the ten chapters on the Perfect Meaning of Awakening and Cultivation in the Chan School, as well as the *Guan*... [text ends].
The *Xin shimen* (Ten Gates of the Mind) and other works were widely circulated throughout the world.

In the eighth month of the third year, Emperor Xuanzong dispatched Zhang Qia, Director of the Court of Ceremonies, bearing an imperial edict to Mount Dangyang to summon the śramaṇa Yixing to the capital.
Yixing, having received this second summons, did not permit himself to decline and proceeded to the court. By imperial decree, he was installed at Guang...
In the Tai Dian (Hall of Great Peace), the Emperor frequently consulted Xingqi on the essentials of securing the state and governing the people. Xingqi presented his views without concealment.
Not long after, Princess Yongmu was to be married off; the Emperor issued an edict to dispatch her with exceptional generosity, following the precedent set for Princess Taiping.
Xingqi remonstrated, saying, "During the final years of Gaozong, there was only this one daughter, which is why she was treated with such special courtesy. Yet, in the end, Princess Taiping..."

"Arrogance and usurpation bring about offense; one should not cite such cases as precedents. The Emperor accepted his words and immediately rescinded the edict, decreeing that only the usual protocols be followed.

His loyal remonstrances were mostly of this kind. Some said that his practice of virtue surpassed his memory of the scriptures. One day, the Emperor ordered him to bring out the palace registers to show them to him.
After Xing had finished reading them, he commanded an inner attendant to hold the original text before the Emperor while he recited it back; he did not miss a single character. The Emperor—
Filled with wonder, he looked at his attendants and said, "This is a sage. From that time on, he summoned him repeatedly to consult him regarding the essentials of the Buddha-mind.

His conduct was dignified and refined as he offered sage counsel and instruction; his imperial favor grew daily more profound. The people of the world, seeing that the Emperor followed him to inquire about the Way, came to call him the "Celestial Master" (Tianshi).
In the fourth year, Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song passed away. The Master had resided at Pangwu on the mountain, where one day a strange occurrence took place.
A man arrived, wearing a tall cap and fine robes, surrounded by an entourage. Huiguang said, "Welcome, benevolent one! Why have you come?
He replied with a harsh voice, "Do you not recognize me? Huiguang said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal;
I view them all as one. How could I make such distinctions? The man said, "I am the deity of this mountain. I can bring life and death upon people. How can you, Master, claim to be one with me?"

The Master looked at him. Gu said, "I am fundamentally unborn; how can you kill me? I regard my body as equal to empty space, and I regard myself as equal to you. Can you destroy empty space or yourself? Even if you could do so, I would still be neither born nor extinguished. How much more so since you cannot? How then could you give rise to the act of killing me? Shen bowed his head and said, "I am dull-witted and ignorant. The Master said, "It is precisely because you are dull-witted and ignorant that you have not yet perished. Shen said, "I am intelligent and upright. The Master said, "It is precisely because you are intelligent and upright that you will surely perish. Shen asked, "Why is that? The Master replied, "The dull-witted and ignorant person does not know to cultivate themselves. Because they do not cultivate themselves, they do not fear death. Because they do not fear death, they do not seek to avoid calamity. Because they do not seek to avoid calamity, they are not bound by worldly affairs. Because they are not bound by worldly affairs, they are not moved by external things. Because they are not moved by external things, they are not harmed by them. Therefore, although they encounter the five poisons, they do not perish. As for the intelligent and upright person, they know to cultivate themselves. Because they cultivate themselves, they fear death. Because they fear death, they seek to avoid calamity. Because they seek to avoid calamity, they are bound by worldly affairs. Because they are bound by worldly affairs, they are moved by external things. Because they are moved by external things, they are harmed by them. Therefore, although they do not encounter the five poisons, they nonetheless perish. Shen said, "I am dull-witted and ignorant. The Master said, "It is precisely because you are dull-witted and ignorant that you have not yet perished. Shen said, "I am intelligent and upright. The Master said, "It is precisely because you are intelligent and upright that you will surely perish. Shen asked, "Why is that? The Master replied, "The dull-witted and ignorant person does not know to cultivate themselves. Because they do not cultivate themselves, they do not fear death. He surpassed all other deities; how could he have known that his teacher possessed vast and great wisdom? He prayed, "I wish for you to bestow upon me the true precepts so that I may cross over the world.
Guī said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you already possess them. Why is this? Because there are no precepts apart from the precepts themselves."
Furthermore, what precepts shall I observe? The spirit said, "This is the principle. I have heard of it only vaguely; I seek only the Master’s instruction. I wish to become your disciple.
Kui then spread out a seat, held up an incense burner, and straightened his desk, saying, "I shall confer the Five Precepts upon you.
If you can [observe them], say 'I can'; if not, say 'No'. The spirit replied, "I respectfully accept your instruction. Kui asked, "Can you refrain from sexual misconduct? The spirit said:
[The Master] also married. [The disciple] said, "I do not mean this; I mean that there is no desire for sin. The spirit said, "I can.
[The Master] said, "Can you refrain from stealing? The spirit said, "I have no lack of anything; how could I steal? [The Master] said, "I do not mean this;

I mean that you grant blessings to the licentious while bringing calamity upon the virtuous when offerings are not made. The spirit said, "I can. [The Master] said, "Can you refrain from killing? The spirit said, "Indeed."
"You hold the handle of authority; how could you not execute him? Yangzi said: "I do not mean this. I mean that there may have been excess, error, suspicion, or confusion.
The spirit said: "I am capable. Yangzi said: "Can you avoid being arbitrary? The spirit said: "I am solely upright; how could I be arbitrary? Yangzi said: "I do not mean this.
I mean that your actions before and after did not accord with the Will of Heaven. The spirit said: "I am capable. Yangzi said: "Will you not be ruined by wine?"

[The Master] said, "Can you do it? [The disciple] replied, "I can. [The Master] said, "As described above, this constitutes the Buddha-precepts. To uphold them with a conscious mind yet without a mind of restrictive attachment;

to act for the sake of others with a conscious mind yet without thoughts of one's own body—if one can be thus, then though born before heaven and earth, one does not become a mere vital essence (*jing*);
though dying after heaven and earth, one does not become subject to decay; though undergoing transformation all day long, one does not undergo agitation. This concludes [the precepts]."

Ultimately, though one is in a state of quiescent extinction, one does not rest therein. To awaken to this is to realize that though one marries, it is not a wife; though one feasts, it is not an act of taking;
though one holds office, it is not power; though one acts, it is not out of habit; though one is intoxicated, it is not delusion. This is simply to be without mind. Without mind, there is no precept.
Without precepts, there is no mind, no Buddha, and no sentient beings. There is no "you," and there is nothing at all.
"I am here. Without you, who would observe the precepts? The spirit asked, "How far is my supernatural power from that of the Buddha?
He replied, "As for your supernatural power, you can accomplish five out of ten things, whereas the Buddha can accomplish seven out of ten and cannot accomplish three.

The spirit stood up in awe, withdrew from his seat, and said, "May I hear more of this? Huiguang said, "If you could turn the Supreme Lord upward, cause the eastern heavens to travel westward, and make the seven luminaries move to the east—"
[The interlocutor] said, "I cannot. Guī said, "Can you strip the earth-spirit of the Five Peaks and bind the Four Seas?
[He] said, "I cannot. Guī said, "This is called the five 'cannots. A Buddha can empty all phenomena and perfect the wisdom of the myriad dharmas, yet He cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma.
A Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaustively recall the events of kalpas past, yet..."

It is impossible to transform and guide those for whom there is no affinity. Although a Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, he cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings; these are called the three impossibilities.
Furthermore, even fixed karma is not eternal, and the absence of affinity is likewise limited to a single lifetime. The realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease.

It is vast and empty, such that not a single person can act as a master over conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). That conditioned phenomena have no master—this is what is meant by [the ultimate truth].
There is no dharma. That there is neither dharma nor a master is what is called "no-mind. As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*);
he is simply able to penetrate all dharmas through no-mind. The deity said: "I am indeed shallow and ignorant; I have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
"The precepts bestowed by my master, I shall faithfully practice. Now I wish to repay his compassionate virtue by manifesting what I am capable of.
The Master said, "I contemplate the body as having no substance; I contemplate all phenomena as impermanent. Being thus clearly realized, what further desires could there be?

The Spirit said, "The Master must surely command me to perform deeds for the sake of the world, to display my divine power, so that those who have already resolved to attain enlightenment, those who have not yet resolved, those with faith, and those without faith [may all be transformed]."

When people see my divine traces, they will know that there are Buddhas and there are spirits; that there are those with power and those without, and that there are things that are spontaneous and things that are not.
The Master said, "I have no need for such things. They replied, "Even the Buddha causes dragons and spirits to protect the Dharma.
How could you, Master, rebel against the Buddha? The Master, having no choice, said, "The obstruction at Dongyan Temple."
"It is desolate and treeless; there are trees only on the northern peak. However, that peak does not provide a protective screen behind you.

Can you move the trees from the north to the eastern ridge? The deity replied, "I have received your command. I fear that there will surely be clamor and commotion during the dark of night; I pray that you, Master, do not be alarmed."

He immediately paid his respects and took his leave. The Master saw him off at the gate and watched him depart. He observed that the ceremonial guards moved in a long, winding procession like those of a sovereign;
mists, vapors, smoke, and clouds swirled and intermingled, while banners, streamers, rings, and pendants vanished into the air.

That very evening, there was indeed a violent wind and a clap of thunder, with rushing clouds and flashing lightning. The buildings shook and swayed, and the roosting crows cried out in alarm. The Master said:

The assembly said, "Do not fear; the deity has made a covenant with us. At dawn, when the sky cleared and became bright, the pines of the northern mountain had all been moved to the eastern ridge, standing there in dense, orderly rows.
The Master admonished his disciples, saying, "After my death, do not let outsiders know of this.
If it becomes a subject for idle talk, people will regard me as a sorcerer. The Master was a native of Ique, surnamed Li. He entered the monastic order in his youth and was fully ordained.
He received the Dharma of the precepts from National Teacher Lao’an;
he was seventy-three years old at his death. The treatise states: Lord Wen of Jing once asked Lord Wen-ding Zhang:
"A hundred years after Confucius there arose Mencius. After this, who has been equal to Confucius and Mencius? Why is our Way so desolate?"
Wendeng pondered for a long time and said, "I only fear that some have surpassed him. Wenzi asked, "Who?

Wendeng replied, "Nanyue Huairang, Shuangfeng Daogui, Mazu, Shitou, Danxia, and Wuye—people such as these could not be restrained by the reins and bits of Confucius and Mencius, and so they turned to the teachings of the Śākya clan. Master Wen deeply approved of this. Thereafter...
When Zhang Gong Wujin heard this, he sighed and said, "This is the discourse of an enlightened person. Yet Mount Song was a secondary branch of the ancestral temple;

that its spiritual resonance is so transcendent and its preaching so abundant—this clearly shows that the successive masters of the Zheng and Xu lineages descending from Mount Nanyue could not be restrained by the bridle of worldly teachings. (2)
How could the candid discourse of the Three Dukes not be believed?
In this year, the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Amoghavajra (Wuwei), arrived at the capital. At the beginning of the Emperor’s reign, one night he dreamed of a Buddhist monk coming to visit him;
the monk’s demeanor was extraordinary and magnificent. Upon waking, the Emperor recalled the vision incessantly and consequently commissioned a skilled artisan to create [an image].
He had a portrait of the monk painted on the wall of the palace hall. When the time for the audience arrived and [the monk] entered to face the Emperor, the Emperor gazed at him intently;

it was indeed the monk he had seen in his dream. Startled and struck by this wonder, he lodged him at Ximing Monastery. Princes Ning, Xue, and others all lowered their status to show him courtesy and held him in high esteem.

Later, there was a drought in autumn. The Emperor, having learned through investigation that Wúwèi was capable of summoning dragons, dispatched an inner court messenger with an imperial edict to request rain.
Wúwèi hesitated and submitted a memorial stating that the frequency of droughts was but natural; if he were to forcefully summon the dragons, he feared it might cause harm to living things.

The Emperor sent him again with a personal decree, saying: "The people suffer from the autumn heat; even a violent wind and torrential rain would be sufficient to bring them relief. Wúwèi gave his consent. The officials made preparations.
The altar’s decorations were magnificent and radiant. Fawei remarked with a smile, "Is this how one brings rain? He ordered them all removed.
Holding a full bowl of water alone, he stirred it with a small knife and recited incantations over a hundred times.

Immediately, a tiny creature resembling a coiled dragon emerged from the bowl, its head rising above the surface of the water. After a short while, it sank back down. Fawei chanted again to send it away, and white vapor rose from the bowl.
The water surged upward. He said to the imperial envoy, "Return quickly; the rain will arrive immediately. The envoy galloped out and looked back;
there was a cloud like a length of silk coiling up from the lecture hall. In an instant, wind roared and lightning flashed. The envoy hurried inside to report this.
His robes and headcloth became soaked through. Thereupon, a violent wind and torrential rain lashed the dwellings, leaving the officials and commoners in terror for many days before it subsided.
On another occasion, when heavy rain persisted for over a period of time, he was summoned by imperial decree to bring it to an end.

Fearing [the deity], he fashioned five clay female figures in the temple and addressed them in Sanskrit as if scolding or reviling them; immediately, the rain cleared. His spiritual efficacy was consistently like this.

The Emperor revered him as if he were a deity. Before long, he had mastered the Chinese language and translated more than ten sūtras, including the *Gaganagañja*, the *Vairocana*, the *Sukhāvati-vyūha*, and the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*.
The Chan Master Yi-xing, the Tripiṭaka Master [Amoghavajra], Bao-yue, and others participated in these affairs.

Wei was simple and serene by nature and delighted in meditative contemplation; he constantly exhorted his students to practice it. He repeatedly submitted petitions requesting to return home, but the Emperor remained firm.
He declined the invitation.

That year, Song Jing, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, entered Caoxi to pay homage at the Patriarch’s stupa. He made a vow, saying: "I, your disciple, wish to protect the Great Dharma throughout my life.
I pray for a single auspicious sign to serve as proof. As soon as he finished speaking, a gentle breeze wafted a fragrance that spread in dense, pervasive waves.
Suddenly, sweet rain poured down, falling only within the confines of a single temple. Xingjing was filled with joy and departed after composing a poem.
Before long, he was summoned back to court and, together with Yao Yuanchong, served in succession as chief ministers. The world acclaimed Yao and Song as the virtuous ministers of the Restoration.
In the fourth month of the ninth year, the court found that the solar eclipses predicted by the *Linde* calendar did not correspond with reality.

An imperial edict was issued for the Chan Master Yixing to revise and compose a new calendar. Having received the decree, Yixing deduced the numbers of the *Dayan* (Great Expansion) system and established its methods to respond to the requirements.

He compared the records of solar terms, intercalary months, days, names, degrees, and numbers found in the classics and histories; all those verifiable were found to be in agreement, and he recorded them. After some time, a Daoist...
Xing Hepu said to Yin Qin, the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy: "Is Yi Xing not a sage?
Formerly, Lu Xianghong, while creating the *Dachu* calendar, once recorded that eight hundred years later it would be off by one day, and that a sage would surely appear in the world to rectify this.
Now the appointed period has been fulfilled, and Yi Xing has rectified it by calculating the *Dayan* numbers."
"The errors of the various schools of calculation are not unfounded, as Hong’s words attest. Yin also agrees with this.

Furthermore, he wishes to know the progression and retrogression of the ecliptic, yet the Bureau of Astronomy lacks an instrument for the ecliptic. He submitted a petition requesting that one be newly established," and the imperial decree was granted.
In that year, the śramaṇa Zhisheng submitted the *Shijiao jinglü lun mulu* (Catalogue of the Scriptures, Vinayas, and Treatises of the Buddhist Teachings) in twenty fascicles.

He arranged and cataloged the scriptures of the Great Canon and the treatises composed by sages and worthies, totaling five thousand forty-eight fascicles; from this point on, these figures became the established standard.
On the day of Guiyou in the tenth month of the eleventh year, the Dhyāna Master Yixing completed the construction of the Huangdao Instrument (Yellow Path Instrument).

The Emperor himself composed an inscription for it and issued an edict to display it in the courtyard of the Anwu Chengdian Hall for all officials to see. This instrument was modeled after the shape of the celestial sphere, featuring the positions of the fixed stars, the equatorial coordinates, and the degrees of the entire heavens.
Water was poured to drive the wheel so that it would rotate automatically, completing one full cycle in a single day and night.
The celestial mechanism revolves externally, bound by two wheels. These are joined by the sun and moon, which enable their movement.
As each day the heavens travel one full circuit to the east, the sun travels one degree to the west, and the moon travels thirteen degrees plus seven-nineteenths of a degree.
After twenty-nine rotations and a fraction, the sun and moon meet; after three hundred and sixty-five rotations, the sun completes its circuit through the heavens. By means of wood...

The frame was made level with the ground, causing its upper structure to be half-submerged beneath the earth; thus, the phases of darkness and light, the new and full moons, and the variations in speed were all regulated accordingly.
Two wooden figures were erected upon the level ground; one was placed in front of a drum to signal the passing of each hour, striking it automatically when the time arrived.
One of them was placed in front [of the tower] with bells to mark the hours; when each hour arrived, it would strike itself.
All were arranged within the ground with wheels, axles, and interlocking locks set in complex patterns. At that time, they were praised for their ingenuity and regarded as a divine achievement.
However, after a short while, the copper and iron became increasingly stiff and could no longer rotate on their own, so they were subsequently stored away in the Jixian Academy (Ji xian yuan).
In the twelfth year, there was a śramaṇa named Niu Yun who had been dull-witted since his youth. He traveled to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
Upon first arriving at the Eastern Terrace, he saw an old man who asked him, "For what purpose have you come? He replied, "I wish to see the Great Sage and seek wisdom.
The old man said, "Mañjuśrī resides on the Northern Terrace; go there to see him. Yun followed these instructions and hurried toward the Northern Terrace. The old man...
The man was also there. Huiyun thought that he must be Mañjuśrī and prostrated himself before him. The old man said, "You are a śramaṇa; you should not pay obeisance to a worldly person.
Huiyun did not cease his prostrations. The old man took pity on him and entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He observed that Huiyun’s previous life had been as an ox;
because he had once carried scriptures on his back, he had now obtained the retribution of being a bhikṣu. The old man arose from concentration and [spoke] for Huiyun.
He spoke thus. He added, "Your nature is dull from sitting too long; there is a mass of stagnant flesh within your chest. I shall now strike it away for you.
Consequently, he instructed Yunxian not to open his eyes at all. Yunxian followed these instructions. He felt as though the old man were using a pickaxe to dig into his chest.
However, it was not particularly painful. After a short while, his mind became clear and expansive, suddenly different from how it had been before.
When he opened his eyes, he saw that the old man had manifested as Mañjuśrī, his wondrous features upright and majestic. Mañjuśrī said to Huiyun, "I have bestowed my wisdom and eloquence upon you.
Huiyun leaped for joy and prostrated; as he rose, Mañjuśrī vanished from sight. From that time on, Huiyun possessed sharp memory, eloquence, and insight. He became...
At that time, the Master was known as "Ox-Cloud" (Gyūun) due to his past causes and conditions.

In the fourteenth year, the Japanese śramaṇas Eiei and Fushō arrived in Yangzhou, presenting ten *saṃghāṭī* robes upon which were embroidered the forms of mountains, rivers, and exotic objects of their land; these had been sent by the sovereign of that country.

He bestowed [these items] upon a śramaṇa of noble conduct from China. At that time, the Vinaya Master Jianzhen accepted the robes and marveled that people of foreign lands possessed the Buddha-nature (buddha-gotra), wishing to go there to transform them.
Coincidentally, Ruyi (also written as Rui) and Zhao and others also urged him to do so; he accordingly boarded a ship and sailed eastward.
However, they were driven by a malignant wind into the "Sea of Fishes and Serpents. Because his practice of the True Vinaya was sublime, they all escaped the calamity.
Upon his arrival in Japan, the King, having anticipated his coming, personally went out to welcome him with great honor. He was lodged in the Vairocana Hall.

Before long, he requested the authentic transmission of the *śīla* (precepts). The Queen and the ministers all received the transmission in succession. From that time forth, the Vinaya teachings first appeared in Japan.
In the fifteenth year [of the Kaiyuan era], the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci passed away at the age of one hundred and fifty-six.
Bodhiruci was the son of the King of South India; having abdicated the throne, he entered the monastic life. When Emperor Gaozong heard of his reputation, he issued an imperial decree summoning him.
He arrived at the capital during the Chuigong era. Over the course of forty years, he produced translations of such scriptures as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The Emperor and his high ministers revered him as if he were a living Buddha. On the day of his funeral, they specially provided him with a ceremonial procession and insignia of rank.
His stupa was erected on the western plain of Longmen, and he was posthumously granted the title "Tripitaka Master Kaiyuan, Omniscient One. Such was his fame and virtue.

Such a thing had never occurred before in the height of antiquity. At that time, there was a monk known as Puzhuo Duoheshang of Mount Song, whose name and lineage were not recorded and whose words and deeds were unfathomable.

Initially, he met with National Teacher Lao’an and attained realization of the essential point of the mind. He lived in seclusion on Mount Song, where there was a shrine of great spiritual power. Inside the temple hall stood only a single hearth;
people from far and near offered sacrifices there, and the slaughtering of animals for cooking never ceased for a single day. The Master led his disciples into [the temple].
At the shrine, he struck the hearth three times with his staff and said: "Tut! This hearth is composed of clay and tiles;
from where does the 'sage' come? From where does the 'spirit' arise? Yet you thus slaughter living beings! He struck it another three times, and the hearth immediately collapsed and fell apart.
A moment later, a man appeared wearing a green robe and a tall cap, who bowed before the Master and said: "I am originally the Hearth God of this shrine. For a long time..."

"Having received the retribution of my past karma, I have now been graced by your teaching on the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). I shall be liberated from this place and reborn in the heavens;

I have come specifically to pay my respects and express my gratitude. The Master said, "This is your own inherent nature; it is not something I have forcefully asserted. The spirit bowed twice and departed.
A short while later, the disciples asked the Master, "We have long been by your side, Reverend, yet we have not received your instruction. How did the stove god obtain [this realization]?"
"What direct and essential method is there to attain rebirth in heaven? The Master said, "I simply tell them it is composed of clay and tiles;
I have no other principle to impart to them. The assembly was silent. After a long while, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The assembly replied, "We do not understand. The Master said:
"Why does the nature that has existed from the beginning not function? The assembly then prostrated themselves. The Master said, "Broken! Broken! Fallen! Fallen!
Thereupon, the entire assembly realized the profound principle. Later, Zen Master Yifeng raised this question to National Teacher An.
The National Teacher sighed and said, "This man has fully realized that things and self are one and the same; he may truly be called a bright moon."
He dwells in emptiness; there is no one who does not see him. It is simply that it is difficult to catch his verbal pulse.
Feng asked, "I do not know what kind of person can catch his verbal pulse. An said, "One who does not know. Furthermore, a monk asked, "When all things are formless, what then?
The Master said, "If you bow, it is only you and not I. If you do not bow, it is only I and not you. The monk bowed in gratitude. The Master said:
That which exists fundamentally is not a thing; it is a non-thing. Thus it is said: "If one can turn things over, one is identical to the Tathāgata.
A monk came from the place of Niutou. The Master asked, "From whose Dharma assembly have you come? The monk stepped forward, joined his palms, circumambulated the Master once, and departed.
The Master remarked, "There should be no such person as this under the assembly of Niutou. The monk then returned to Niutou.
The monk stood to one side with his hands joined in *añjali*. The Master said, "As expected, as expected. The monk then asked, "When responding to things without depending on another, how is it?
The Master said, "How could it not depend on another? The monk said, "If that is so, then one follows the correct path back to the source."
The Master said, "What is it that accords with returning to the source? The monk replied, "If it were not for you, Master, I would have nearly committed an error.
The Master said, "That is still the principle before one has seen the Fourth Patriarch. Bring forth the principle after having seen him. The monk then circumambulated the Master once and departed.

The Master said, "The Way of accordance and correctness is thus from ancient times to the present. Furthermore, while another monk was standing in attendance, the Master said, "Patriarch after patriarch, Buddha after Buddha..."
"It is simply this: as with a person's original nature and original mind, there is no other principle besides this. Understand it! Understand it! The monk bowed in thanks.
The Master struck him with his whisk and said, "If it is thus in one place, it is so in a thousand places. The Master's final whereabouts were unknown.
On the *jichou* day of the eleventh month in the fifteenth year, the Chan Master Yixing fell ill at Huayan Temple.
The *Old History of the Tang* records that one night the Emperor dreamed of visiting the temple, where he saw a room with a rope bed and bamboo windows, its atmosphere desolate and forlorn.

When he set out at dawn, his illness became known. The Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to inquire after him. Upon his return, the messenger reported that the conditions of Xing’s dwelling matched exactly with what had been seen in the dream.
The Emperor sighed for a long time. An edict was issued ordering ten eminent monks (*da-de*) of the capital to establish a ritual altar for Xing to pray for blessings.
Soon thereafter, Xing’s illness subsided slightly, and by imperial decree, he accompanied the Emperor on a tour to Xinfeng. Not long after, Xing’s illness grew critical.

The Emperor personally went to inquire after him. [The Master] then bathed, sat upright, and passed away at the age of forty-five. The Emperor mourned him with profound grief and suspended court for three days.
An imperial edict was issued expressing deep sorrow and allowing the remains to remain in the shrine for twenty-one days so that those from both the inner and outer courts could pay their respects.
His countenance remained as if alive, and his hair and beard grew longer each day. The Emperor personally composed an inscription and had it engraved upon stone. It was then brought forth.
Fifty thousand coins from the inner treasury were used for the original foundation of the pagoda and the bronze statue. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dahui.

The Emperor once asked him in a relaxed manner, "How long will the national mandate last? Will there be any obstacles? Xing replied, "The imperial carriage shall undertake a journey of ten thousand *li*, yet the altars of state will ultimately meet with good fortune.
The Emperor asked him why he did not answer directly; he withdrew and presented a small golden casket, saying, "It reaches ten thousand *li*."

He immediately opened it. One day, the Emperor opened the casket to look inside; there was but a small amount of *angui* (angelica) within. During the rebellion of An Lushan, the imperial carriage traveled to Chengdu and reached Wanli Bridge.
Suddenly, he realized the meaning. Before long, the Emperor indeed returned. When Emperor Zhaozong was first enfeoffed as Prince Ji, the Tang dynasty perished because of him;
thus it is said that "in the end, there is good fortune. There was a village matron who had long provided offerings for his travels, and she had a son who was imprisoned...

A man was sentenced to execution for murder. His mother wept piteously, pleading for his life. Xing took pity on him and ordered his disciples to capture living creatures; they obtained seven pheasants and pigs.

Each day, Xing hid one of them in a jar and recited a mantra in the Sanskrit language (*brahmavāc*) over it for seven days. When the Big Dipper had completely vanished from the sky, the imperial court was struck with alarm.
The Grand Astrologer submitted a memorial stating that a great change was imminent and requesting that the Emperor avoid the main hall and perform rites of expiation. The Emperor [acted] in secret.
Xing was asked about this and replied, "There is nothing else to it; it is surely a demonic spirit. Generally, a mind of anger destroys all goodness, while a mind of compassion subdues all demons.
If you were to grant a general amnesty to the empire, the demon would be unable to act. The Emperor agreed with this and subsequently issued a great amnesty.
Because of this, the old woman’s son was spared. Every day Xing produced a pig, and for each one, a star appeared; this continued until the seventh day.

The celestial pole returned to its former position. His secret arts were largely of this kind. He authored the *Yi lun* (Treatise on the Changes) in twelve fascicles, the *Dayan lun* (Treatise on the Great Divination) in twenty fascicles, the *Kaishan Dayan li* (Kaiyuan Great Divination Calendar) in fifty-two fascicles, and the *Qizheng changli* (Long Calendar of the Seven Luminaries) in three fascicles.

Furthermore, he compiled the *Shishi xilu* (Record of the Buddhist Lineage), the *Dayan xuantu* (Mysterious Diagram of the Great Divination), the *Xinji suanshu* (Arithmetic of the Mental Mechanism), the *Kuodun jia shiliu ju* (Compendium of the Sixteen Sections of Dunjia), and the *Liuren lianzhu ge* (Song of the Linked Pearls of Liuren).

The *Liuren Suijing* (Essential Scripture of the Six Heavens), the *Tianyi Taiyijing* (Scripture of the Celestial Unity and Great Unity), and the *Taiyu Jundajing* (Scripture of the Grand Bureau of the Nine Palaces) each consist of one fascicle.

The *Wuyin Dilijing* (Scripture of the Five Tones and Geographical Divisions) consists of fifteen fascicles. The *Yixing Zhuan* (Biography of Yi Xing), compiled by Chancellor Li Jifu by imperial decree, consists of one fascicle. All of these are recorded in the "Bibliography of Arts and Literature" (*Tang Yiwenzhi*) of the Tang Dynasty.

In the sixteenth year, an imperial edict was issued for Zhang Shuo, a *tetejin* (special advance), Chen Xuanjing, a calendrical official, and others to compile and implement the *Dayan Lì* (Great Derivative Calendar) composed by Yi Xing.
In the third month, the Emperor traveled to the Warm Springs (*Wēnshāng*). On his way, he passed by the site of Yi Xing’s stupa.

The Emperor halted his carriage there and lingered in contemplation, ordering the palace attendants to inform the stupa of his intention to depart on tour. He bestowed fifty bolts of silk upon it and commanded—
He planted pine and cypress trees before the stupa; such was his sacred devotion. The court historian Ou-yang Wen-chung said:
"From the Tai-ch'u era down to the Lin-te calendar, there were twenty-three schools of calculation;
though they were close to the heavens, they were not yet precise. It was with Yi-hsing that precision was finally attained. His reliance on numerical data to establish his system was indeed [firm]."
There is nothing that can surpass it. Although there may be those in later generations who attempt to revise or compose new versions, they will all merely be imitations.
There was a śramaṇa named Daohong, born in Huangzhou, who was close friends with the Court Gentleman Zhang Jingzhi; he was skilled at speaking of good and ill fortune.

There was no lack of clear evidence. Once, while serving as a Grand Secretary, he went to inspect the residence of Zhang Yue and cautioned him, saying, "Do not dig into the northeast, the *ren* sector.

On another day, he saw Yue and remarked, "The vital energy (*qi*) of this residence has become desolate; why is this? He and Yue went together to inspect it and found three pits over a zhang in depth in that corner.
Hong was startled and said, "Your Excellency shall enjoy wealth and honor for only one lifetime; your sons will likely not reach their natural ends. Yue was terrified. He intended—
He leveled it. Hong said, "Distant soil lacks vital energy and is not connected to the local earth veins; it is like a wound on the body—patching it with flesh from elsewhere will be of no benefit.
Later, he advised his sons that they would all be defiled by Lu Shan and consequently exiled and executed; indeed, it turned out exactly as he had said.
The treatise states: The Duke Wenzhong of Ouyang harbored a profound resentment toward our Buddhist tradition and never once showed it the slightest concession.
Yet, he alone among them honored the work of Yi Xing, "The Great Expansion" (*Dayan*), within the *Tang Shi*.

Furthermore, Song Jingwen excised the biographies of Yi Xing, Xuanzang, and others from the section on "Arts and Techniques," while singularly recording the geographical theories of Dao Hong. Some have attributed this to the Tang...
The Buddhist practices and deeds [recorded here] offer nothing for the two gentlemen to adopt; therefore, I have stopped at this point. But could it truly be so?
It is because the *Dayan* (Great Divination) system governs celestial timing, whereas the principles of geography are intimately connected to human affairs;

thus, they are worthy of being recorded by the historian’s brush. As for the flourishing of our Śākya teachings, none was more magnificent than during the Tang dynasty. Throughout those three hundred years...
Those who served as masters for the world in terms of morality are too numerous to count.

Because the people of the Ou and Song dynasties regarded him as a follower of a foreign teaching, they avoided his name and did not record it. This is like the Spring and Autumn Annals, where even though Lao Dan and Tanzi were sages, they were not mentioned;
whereas the people of Jiang and Huang were recorded in the canon. Is this because the teachings of Laozi are insufficient to be valued? No.
This is indeed the fundamental canon of state governance: all matters concerning ritual, music, law, and administration, involving both the noble and the humble, must be recorded.
As for our Buddhists, who have utterly severed worldly entanglements and emerged with exceptional clarity beyond the mundane world—how could they possibly be concerned with laws and administration?

It is therefore fitting that they do not participate in the secular records of the state. From this perspective, when the states of Ou and Song excluded our Buddhist followers, their underlying intention was precisely this.
This was out of reverence for him. How magnificent! One Xing (Xuanzang) personally fulfilled the prophecy of Luo Xiahong made eight hundred years prior.
At that time, the Son of Heaven knelt before him and hailed him as a sage; yet when his compositions were applied to later generations, [the Emperor] treated them with even greater honor.
It envelops heaven and earth and penetrates both the hidden and the manifest; though several hundred years have passed, its efficacy has only increased.
Whether he was truly a sage or merely a worthy one, I cannot know.
*The Comprehensive Chronological Treatise on the History of Buddhism* (Lǒngxīng Fójiào Biānián Tōnglùn), Scroll Fifteen;
*The Comprehensive Chronological Treatise on the History of Buddhism*, Scroll Sixteen.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zǔxiù of Shíshì Monastery in Lǒngxīng Prefecture.

In the seventeenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, Zhang Yue, the Grand Preceptor and Duke of Yan, passed away. As a preeminent minister of the Tang, the great literary compositions of the court were largely his handiwork.
His writings were characterized by refined and powerful thought, and he was particularly adept at the Buddhist scriptures. He had once been exiled to Yue...

While in the province, his poetry became even more sorrowful and elegant. People of the time said that he had received the assistance of the mountains and rivers. Throughout the world, he was not addressed by his surname, but simply called "Lord Yan.
He composed a preface for the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (Heart Sutra) inscribed on stone, which says: "The myriad practices arise from the mind;

the mind is the sovereign of man. The Three Vehicles converge into the One; the One is the source of all dharmas. To know that the mind has nothing to be attained is true attainment. To perceive the One..."
That which is unobstructed is profound penetration. The Tathāgata said that the five aggregates are all empty; thus, the person is fundamentally empty.

The Tathāgata said that the characteristic of all phenomena is emptiness; thus, phenomena are also empty. To know phenomena is to illuminate emptiness; to see emptiness is to relinquish phenomena. Are these two—knowledge and vision—not themselves empty?
Therefore, both concentration and wisdom are within the dharma of emptiness. One who enters this gate is called "enlightened."
Gate. Those who travel this path are those who transcend all paths. Who but one who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* could realize this?
The Imperial Son-in-law, Zheng Wanjun of Rongyang, was a man of profound artistic talent. His learning was vast and his calligraphy reached the level of "cursive sagehood.
He thus took up his brush to transcribe the *Heart Sūtra* and had it carved into stone, establishing a precious sanctuary for the holy and good, and opening [enlightenment] for those yet to come.
Regarding these magnificent achievements: the Buddha taught that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn through the mark of non-reliance;
I have transmitted that they are now unceasing through the mind of non-attainment. Thus, while the Way abides in written words, their meaning remains as constant as heaven itself.

Upon hearing this, the State Elder Zhang Yue praised it and extolled these Buddhist deeds, inscribing them upon a stone monument. He further composed two eulogies for the Dharma Hall and the Practice Hall of Fachi Monastery.
Preface: The West Three Refuges Hall and the two Dharma Halls of Fachi were constructed by the Elder Chushang Chan Master.
The Chan Master’s surname was Peng and his given name was Zhi. He was profoundly filial by nature; upon observing the mourning period for his parents, he did not eat for seven days.

His words were subtle and his conduct secret as he resolved his will upon the Way and explored its mysteries. He investigated the principles of the *I Ching*, Laozi, Zhuangzi, and Taiyi, and was skilled in the correct script of calligraphy.

He uniquely embodied the refined character of Wang Xizhi and Wang Xianzhi; his strokes were elegant and exquisite, with every fine detail clearly visible—like breaking a withered lotus stalk or polishing a fine stone.

His calligraphic structure was so fluid and spirited that it truly transcended human effort. Among the eminent scholars of the Central Court, he was as revered as a mountain or a marsh, his noble character inspiring those both near and far.
In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to Chan verses, setting aside all worldly affairs of his life.
My karma has been liberated as if only a trace of dust remains. I have often sighed that the Emperor, my father, and mother permitted me to leave the household life;

the grace of their nurturing, like rain and dew, is of one and the same measure. Relying upon the teachings of the Tathāgata, I have initiated this meritorious deed—could it be even a ten-thousandth part [of their kindness]?

I offer this blessing to the two palaces and provide secret protection for the seven ancestors, intending that all beings together shall ascend to the site of enlightenment. Thus, in the first year of Chang’an, the Three Refuges Hall was established.
It was established on the full moon day of the tenth month of the year *xinchou*, the *gui-mao* day.

The Hall of Good Dharma (*Śubhadharma-śālā*) was constructed on the full moon day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Kaiyuan era, the *gui-chou* year, the *wu-chen* day. The Master’s younger maternal brother, Renwan; his disciple Qiyi;
and the novice Śrāmaṇera Lingzhe—these individuals exerted real effort in support of this undertaking. He then composed a eulogy, saying: "I respectfully address all sons of the Buddha. One.
The Contemplation of the Purity of Mind: One who seeks the True and Right Path should enter through the faculty of faith.
This is the Buddha’s mark of emptiness; this is the subtle and wondrous light of the Dharma. Concentration and wisdom are never separate; this is the meaning of the harmony of the Saṅgha.

Persons are empty and phenomena are also empty; even these two kinds of emptiness are themselves empty. Abiding the mind within these three jewels of emptiness is called the place of the Three Refuges. How sublime is the Primordial Superior One who has established [this path]!

He established the Hall of Wholesome Dharmas and painted the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Adorned with pure vision, he was able to exercise an unimpeded mind that universally enters into all things.
Seeing without being stained by objects, and knowing without grasping at consciousness—this is called true seeing, and it is also called the knowledge of liberation.
The Buddha’s contemplation transcends arising and ceasing; all phenomena are thus.

On the first day of the eighth month of the twentieth year, the cyclical date being *rénshēn*, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi informed his disciples, saying, "When the white moon is full, I shall pass away.

When the time arrived, he circumambulated an image of Vairocana, placed a volume of the *Brahma-scriptures* upon its crown, and returned to his chamber. There, sitting in the *paryaṅka* posture, he passed away.

He was posthumously granted the title of State Preceptor Guǎngdìng, and an imperial decree was issued for Du Hóngjiàn of the Secretariat to compose a stele commemorating his virtues. Vajrabodhi was from the Western Regions.
The Master was of royal lineage and had renounced the world. He received the Esoteric Teachings from the Ācārya Nāgabodhi and subsequently traveled to the Eastern Land (China).

Upon his initial arrival at Guangzhou in the South Sea, the Regional Inspector reported his presence to the Court. By imperial decree, he was sent by rapid post to the capital for an audience with the Emperor.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and provided him with quarters at the Great Ci’en Monastery. Not long after, a summer drought occurred, and the Emperor issued a mandate for Vajrabodhi to pray for rain. Vajrabodhi established a ritual altar and depicted the Seven... [deities].
There were ten million images. It was said that as soon as his eyes opened, rain would fall. After three days, the images indeed opened their eyes;

a cloud arose from the altar and filled the sky, and in a brief moment, it rained. The Emperor specially issued an edict to praise him. The following year, he requested leave to travel to Yanmen, but this was not granted. He subsequently moved to Jianfu Temple.
In all matters—whether speaking or remaining silent, rising or sitting—his demeanor was composed and refined, and neither joy nor anger was ever manifested on his countenance.
Regarding his physical form, no observer could fathom its limits. Wherever he went, he invariably established consecration mandalas (*abhiṣeka-maṇḍala*).
His disciple Amoghavajra transmitted his teachings; initially, Amoghavajra served Vajrabodhi, who bestowed upon him the Sanskrit *Siddham* script and the treatises on grammar (*śabda-vidyā*).
Within ten days, he had mastered the recitation. Fazhi marveled at his extraordinary talent and led him into the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala to test him by having him cast flowers.
Fazhi believed that Amoghavajra had surpassed him. Consequently, Amoghavajra requested to be instructed in the Yoga of the Five Families, but Fazhi did not grant his permission.
Amoghavajra then prepared to travel to India to seek it out. One night, Fazhi dreamed that all the Buddha statues in the capital were walking toward the east; upon waking, he [realized the omen].
Amoghavajra reported this to the Emperor, who then revealed his intention to travel westward. Amoghavajra said, "You possess the potential to receive the Way; why should I be parsimonious?
He immediately transmitted to him the five sections [of the Yoga Tantras], as well as the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra* and the ritual manuals for the *Svastyayana-vidhi*.
After Amoghavajra passed away, Amoghavajra followed his final instructions to travel to India, where he further expanded his learning.
The Treatise says: Since the Great Teaching flowed eastward, various monks have occasionally assisted in the transformation of beings through spiritual wonders.

These were all instances where their meritorious practices had matured and they had reached the source of the mind; it was the manifestation of noble wisdom through self-awakening and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and by no means the result of the power of mantras or illusory arts.
Beginning with Śrīmitra during the Eastern Jin dynasty and continuing thereafter, secret mantras were proclaimed and translated. To summarize their essential point:
Their great purpose does not exceed the worship of spirits and deities to expel the heterodox and the delusive; they merely perform rites for others to avert calamities and relieve distress.
Among them, there have often appeared pseudo-monks who come from foreign lands, employing occult arts to startle the ignorant.
What they call the "Dharma of the Arhats" is nothing more than a trivial and inferior form of heterodox sorcery, much like the thunder magic of the Daoist school.
This belongs to the category of secular law. How could it possibly be ranked alongside those who possess lofty paths, vast virtues, and who propagate the teachings of Chan?
It was only during the Kaiyuan era that the three great adepts from the Western Regions—Vajrabodhi, Amoghavajra, and Bukong—first transmitted the Esoteric Teachings.

By means of profound words and virtuous auspiciousness, he opened the way for the protection and guidance of His Majesty; thus his divine efficacy and manifest power were nearly equal to the force of the Creator itself.
Therefore, although the Three Great Sages propagated the esoteric teachings, was it not because they manifested their fundamental wisdom and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that they became sages?
I have often lamented that the *Zizhi Tongjian* records that during the Zhenguan era, there was a monk who came from the Western Regions and was skilled in incantations.
This art could cause a person to die instantly, yet by reciting incantations over them again, it could cause them to revive.

Emperor Taizong selected handsome men from among the *feiqi* (flying cavalry) to test it, and they all responded exactly as described. He then questioned Fu Yi about this. Fu Yi said, "This is a heterodox art.

As I have heard that the heterodox cannot affect the orthodox, I request that you command him to cast a spell upon me; it will certainly not take effect. The Emperor ordered a monk to cast a spell on Fu Yi. At first, Fu Yi...
There was no sensation; he suddenly collapsed stiffly as if struck by some object, and did not recover his consciousness.

This is likely a fabrication devised by those who wish to promote their cause. Why? If such a thing truly occurred, then the monk would not be a true monk and the incantation would not be a true incantation;
it would simply be a demonic artifice. It certainly does not suffice to remedy the flaws of our teaching.

Moreover, such a thing is utterly impossible. Had he been able to travel from the Western Regions all the way to Chang’an, and if his art had truly been capable of reviving the dead, he would have had no leisure even to protect his own person;

yet he died stiff and lifeless before ordinary people for no apparent reason, an occurrence that not even a child would believe. Furthermore, at that time, although those three Great Beings—*mahāsattvas*—though...

Neither had arrived. As for the great virtuous monks of the capital—Huisheng, Xuawan, Falin, Mingzhan, and others—how could they have sat idly by while pseudo-monks in a remote region destroyed the gates of the Teaching, failing to request stern measures against them?
It was only because they hesitated to issue an imperial edict that Fu Yi was left to debate the matter.
According to the Buddha’s ordained precepts, even if weeds grow along a spring path, a bhikṣu is not permitted [to harm them].
One would even avoid treading upon them for fear of harming their lives; how much more so, then, could one advocate for the taking of human life by transmitting such incantations to the world?
Therefore, I maintain that those who delight in such matters have merely fabricated pretexts for it, which is clearly evident.
In this year, the Chan Master Yifú passed away. The *Jiù Táng Shǐ* (Old History of the Tang) states: Fú received the Dharma from Chan Master Shénxiù.
Initially residing at Huàgǎn Temple in Lántián, he remained in his chamber for over twenty years, never once venturing beyond the confines of the monastery.
He once accompanied the imperial entourage when it visited the Eastern Capital; the Prefectural Governors of Pú and Hé, as well as the officials, scholars, and commoners, all brought [offerings].

Banners and flowers were used to welcome him, such that the roads along his route were completely filled. Upon his death, an imperial edict was issued bestowing upon him the title "Great Wisdom Chan Master" (Dazhi Chanshi), and he was buried atop Mount Ique.
Those who escorted him numbered in the tens of thousands, and Yan Tingzhi of the Secretariat composed an inscription for his tombstone.

Although Shenxiu had been a preeminent figure in the Chan school for his virtuous conduct and had received the profound respect of the Emperor, he had never gathered disciples to establish a formal teaching center.
As for the transmission of the Dharma within the monasteries, it was from Yifú Pùjì that the teaching began to be propagated in the capital for over twenty years;
all people looked up to him with reverence.
In the twenty-first year, Wéi Jì, the Prefectural Governor of Héngzhōu, submitted a memorial stating that the master of arts Zhāng Guǒ possessed secret methods for attaining longevity.
He claimed to be several hundred years old. Empress Wu once summoned him; Guo feigned death and did not go. Now he was seen again.

Upon hearing this, the Emperor dispatched Xu Jiao, the Vice Director of the Secretariat, carrying an imperial letter to welcome him. Guo arrived. Hearing that his transformations were unfathomable, the Emperor grew suspicious of him.
At that time, there was one named Xing Hepu who was skilled in calculation and could know whether a person’s life would be long or short. The Emperor ordered—
Fagu was utterly bewildered and could not discern his own birth year. There was also a master named Yeguang who was skilled at seeing ghosts.
The Emperor summoned Fagu and sat with him in secret, ordering Yeguang to look at him; however, Yeguang was unable to see him.

The Emperor had heard that those who drink the juice of *gynandra pentaphylla* (jin-zhi) without suffering any harm are truly extraordinary men. As it happened that the weather was cold, the Emperor bestowed the *jin-zhi* upon him. Fagu drank three cups and became pleasantly intoxicated.
As if intoxicated, he looked left and right and said, "This is no fine wine. Shortly thereafter, he took a mirror to examine his teeth and found them all scorched black.

He commanded his attendants to fetch an iron *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) and strike his teeth until they all fell out. He then applied a divine elixir to his gums, and after a short while, his teeth were as brilliant as before.
The Emperor finally believed him and intended to give him his daughter, a princess, in marriage; however, he foresaw this and declined with great earnestness, thereby escaping the match.
Later, he requested leave to return to the mountains, and the Emperor issued an edict stating: "The Honored Master Zhang Guo of Hengzhou is a man who wanders through all quarters..."
