He was one of the outsiders. His traces were established in the lofty heights, and he had entered deeply into the profound darkness. Having long since merged with the mundane dust, he responded to the imperial summons at the palace gates;

yet no one could determine the number of his years, for he was regarded as a transcendent being from the era of Fuxi and Huangdi. When questioned about the pivot of the Way, he fully comprehended its ultimate source.

Now, specifically performing the rites of court, he has been granted an exalted mandate: he may be appointed as a Silver Light Court Gentleman (Yinqing Guanglu Dafu) and titled Master Tongxuan (Tongxuan Xiansheng).
In that year, he indeed entered Mount Heng. His final whereabouts thereafter were unknown.

In the twenty-third year [of the reign], the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi passed away at the age of ninety-nine. By imperial decree, Li Xian, Director of the Bureau of State Ceremonies, was appointed to supervise the funeral arrangements.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Guanghua Temple on the western mountain of Longmen. This concludes the biography of Vajrabodhi.
He was originally of the Śākya clan, a descendant of King Amṛtodana. Having abdicated the throne to renounce the world, his virtue and reputation were preeminent throughout India.
Wherever he went to preach the Dharma, extraordinary signs invariably appeared.
Initially, while expounding the Vairocana Sūtra in the kingdom of Oḍra, the assembly suddenly beheld four golden characters of Vairocana appearing in the sky; each person sought out the text.
He arranged them in order, and after a long time, he passed away. On another occasion, while crossing the Long River, a camel carrying scriptures fell into the water.
Fearing he would lose the texts, he suddenly followed it into the water. Thereupon, the Dragon King invited him into his palace to preach the Dharma;

though he did not grant the request, the Dragon King insisted so firmly that he stayed for three nights. When he emerged with the Sanskrit manuscripts he had carried, not a single character was wet. Such was his divine wonder.
Many cases are like this.
The *Śāstra* says: Initially, Master Xuán of Nanshan’s reputation for his observance of the Vinaya resounded throughout the Five Indias.

Some said that when Wúwèi first arrived, Xuán did not pay him much respect. One night, Xuán picked a louse from his bedding and placed it on the ground. Wúwèi called out from across the room, saying, "Vinaya Master!"
"How could one who is unable to regard sentient beings with compassion strike a son of the Buddha? Xuān was struck with awe and submitted his heart in submission.

The next day, he adjusted his robes and apologized for his regret. This account is an error of the transmitter. Xuān died in the second year of Qiánfēng (667 CE), a total of fifty-one years before Wúwèi first arrived.
Furthermore, according to the "Treatise on Portents" (*Wǔxíngzhì*) of the *Jiù Tángshǐ* (Old History of the Tang), in the ninth year of Tiānbão (750 CE) in Luóyáng...
A giant serpent emerged from beneath Mount Mang; it was over one hundred *zhang* in length, and anyone who encountered its breath would die instantly.
An imperial edict ordered Wufei to recite incantations over it. Wufei said in alarm, "This is the creature that will turn Luoyang into a stagnant pool.
After he had chanted for three days, the serpent died. Thus, from the time Wufei passed into *nirvāṇa* until the ninth year of the Tiānbǎo era, fifteen years had elapsed.

This must have been the Venerable Amoghavajra’s subduing of the snake through mantras. Because his records of fearless divine traces were particularly abundant, each instance was attributed to him by name.
Nevertheless, as one who had attained the fruit of realization, he took the Buddha-mind as his own mind;

he must have exercised his supernatural powers to guide the serpent's consciousness, enabling it to escape its evil form and be reborn in a favorable realm. It does not mean that [the snake] was simply...
He cast a spell upon a snake, causing it to die instantly.

In that same year, the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra traveled to Siṃhala Island (Sri Lanka) to seek from Ācārya Samantabhadra the rites for the eighteen assemblies of the Vajra Consecration and the construction of the altar for the Mahākaruṇā-garbha-dhātu. One day, the king was taming an elephant.
Shortly thereafter, a herd of elephants broke loose; none dared to resist them. Amoghavajra sat calmly in the middle of the road.

When the mad elephants rushed toward him, they saw Amoghavajra and immediately came to a halt, kneeling and prostrating themselves. After a short while, they departed. Consequently, the entire nation came to revere him with divine awe.
In the twenty-sixth year, a śramaṇa named Faxiu dreamed that a strange monk exhorted him to provide five hundred kaṣāyas and dedicate them as offerings to the monks of Huixiang Temple.
Upon waking, he marveled at the wonder and proceeded to beg for alms to have them made. However, though he searched everywhere for the so-called Huixiang Temple, he could find no trace of it.
One day, while traveling on the road, he encountered a monk who came toward him and asked, "I entrust you with these kaṣāyas."
"Is it finished now? Xiu replied, "It is finished. The monk said, "I shall lead you to Huixiang Temple.
You must pack provisions and carry a fire-starter; follow me there. Xiu agreed. The next day, he followed him into Zhongnan Mountain.
After traveling for two days, they reached a deep and secluded place where all that was visible were drifting clouds and craggy caves. As they proceeded, they encountered a stone altar. Together—
He stopped atop it. The monk ordered Xiu to drill for fire with a fire-drill, light incense, and bow toward the high heavens. Suddenly, the clouds parted and a cliff was revealed;
halfway up, there was a vermilion gate, with a pagoda and banners soaring aloft. Delighted, Xiu climbed upward with him.
Gradually, the pure and resonant sounds of midday chanting were heard, with bells and stone chimes sounding in harmony. In a short while, he caught sight of the temple, which bore an inscription:

[The master] performed the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). The monk immediately hurried inside and ordered the gatekeeper to grant Xu (秀) access to the quarters. He then proceeded with full ceremony to pay his respects to the senior elder of the Upper Hall.
Next, he met the various monks, all of whom were remarkable and dignified; they greeted one another with great cordiality.

The following day, Xu took out his *kāṣāya* robe and distributed it throughout the monastery. After the senior elder had finished expressing his thanks, he led Xu into an empty room and called for an attendant to fetch a *śīla-bhāṇaka* flute (*rìbā*).
After a short while, an attendant arrived carrying a jade flute. The elder said, "This was the chamber where the former Emperor of Tang resided.
Because he delighted in fine music here, he descended as a sovereign of men; after a long time, he shall surely return. Xiu stayed for only two nights and was not permitted to remain longer.
The elder bestowed upon him the jade flute and a *kāṣāya*, entrusting them with these words: "Take these back and present them to the Emperor of Tang. Immediately—
The Emperor dispatched a monk to escort Xiu out of the monastery. Before they had traveled far, he looked back and saw clouds and mist closing in from all sides;

Xiu sighed with emotion and returned. He went to the palace gate and submitted the items he had been entrusted with. When the Emperor examined them, he took up the jade flute and played it; it sounded exactly as if he had been playing it for years.
Later, while feasting at the Scented Pavilion, the Emperor summoned Li Bai to compose a poem. The Emperor blew the jade flute and Yang Guifei performed a dance.
He was greatly delighted and suspected that [the monk] had ascended as an immortal amidst the swaying [trees].

The *Lun* says: In Zanning’s *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, it is recorded that while Xiu was conversing with an elderly resident of the Upper Hall at Huixiang Temple, a spirit suddenly appeared in full armor standing below the hall. Startled, Xiu asked, "Who is this spirit? The elder...
The record states: "In no time, he will bring great chaos to the state of Tang. Later, An Lushan indeed threw the world into turmoil. Alas!
To record this [as a prediction] is an extreme error. Why is this? Li Xiu obtained the jade flute and presented it in that year;
sixteen years later, Lushan rebelled. Thus, at the time Xiu beheld the deity, Lushan did not yet exist.
I have been reflecting on this for thirty or forty years. Truly, had Xiu appeared with his spiritual essence before An Lushan was even born, there might still have been some hope.
But how could there be a spirit existing elsewhere while he himself is already alive in this world?
Although the matters of ghosts and spirits since antiquity—vague, strange, and wondrous beyond measure—cannot be fathomed, there are indeed certain aspects that can be understood.

There are things that appear trustworthy yet cannot be trusted. If An Lushan had possessed even a hair’s breadth of what distinguishes him from ordinary men, one might still have excused him by considering his movements as those of a ghost or spirit, difficult to fathom. Yet An Lushan was utterly ignorant and profoundly unrighteous;
father and son murdered each other, and he died at the hands of his own domestic slave, Li Zhuer, who cut open his belly. How could such a man be a divine immortal?
"Or does it manifest within the objective realm? Zan Ning recorded this; how could he not deeply tarnish the reputation of the various gentlemen of Huaihui Temple?
Therefore, I have now deleted it. Relying on [Zan Ning] to conceal his great error, I am constrained by necessity to provide this clarification.
In the third month of the twenty-eighth year, the Elder Li Tongxuan passed away. In the seventh year [of his travels], the Elder arrived at Yú County in Taiyuan.
There was a man named Gāoxiānnú who recognized him as a man of worth and provided him lodging.
In his chamber, he would daily consume only ten grains of jujube and a single large spoonful of cypress-leaf cake. Throughout the day, he dipped his brush and faced his paper, never ceasing.

He engaged in human affairs in this manner for three years. He then moved to the side of the Ancient Buddha Hall of the Ma clan, where he built an earthen hut to dwell in, remaining in a precarious, upright meditation posture throughout the day.
After ten years had passed, he suddenly took his scriptures and books upon his back and departed. After traveling twenty *li*, he encountered a tiger blocking the path; it lay down submissively.
The Elder stroked it and said, "I am about to compose a treatise to explain the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Can you..."
To determine whether he had found a place to settle, [the tiger] immediately took the scripture bag upon its back and followed him.

Upon reaching the earthen cave at the foot of the Shenfu Mountain ridge, it crouched and waited before it. The elder took the bag and placed it inside the cave; the tiger then tucked its tail and departed.
That cave was brilliant and clean, measuring six or seven cubits in width, circular both above and below, and described as being "as vast as the sky. Thus it was established.

"Bi! There is a Way; it is not something produced by human effort. On the evening when the Elder composed his treatise, his mind plumbed the profound mysteries, and white light issued from his mouth to serve as lamps and candles.
At that moment, two women appeared whose beauty was unsurpassed in the world;

both were of marriageable age, dressed in plain cloth garments, with their heads wrapped in white kerchiefs. Those who saw them were struck with awe, as they drew water from the spring and lit incense to offer [to the Elder].
He used paper and ink. Every day between the hours of the Rabbit and the Dragon (5–7 a.m.), he would prepare pure offerings and place them before the Elder.

Once the meal was finished and the vessels removed, he would depart; no one could fathom where he went. This continued for five years until, upon the completion of the Elder’s treatise, he vanished without a trace.
The Elder had a handsome beard and mustache, bright eyes and eyebrows, red lips, and purple skin. He wore a birch-bark hat and garments of hempen cloth.
Wearing a long skirt with wide sleeves and a loosened waistband, he walked barefoot. He lived in a state of carefree liberation among humans and devas, unconstrained by anything.
Once, while leaving the mountain, he encountered a local gathering where people were feasting and enjoying themselves. The elder approached him and said, "May you all dwell in happiness."
"I am about to depart," he said. The assembly was startled by his departure; some escorted him into the mountains, but once they reached the grotto, he thanked them and sent them away.

That very evening, mist and clouds gathered and spread, and the rocky valleys shook and trembled. Two white cranes soared through the air, crying out mournfully, while other birds and beasts filled the mountains with their lamentations.
The next day, the villagers went together to await him, only to find that he had already sat upright, manifesting [parinirvāṇa].

He passed away peacefully within his shrine-casket at the age of ninety-five. He authored the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* in forty fascicles, the *Deciding Doubts Treatise* (*Jueyi lun*) in four fascicles, the *Synthetic Commentary* (*Huishi*) in two fascicles, and one fascicle each for the *Prolegomena to the Ten Gates* (*Shimen xuanyi*), the *Exegesis of the Outline*, the *Explanation of Dependent Origination*, and the *Ten Clarifications for Dispelling Delusions*.
He also composed the *Ten Mysterious Gates and Six Aspects*, the *Ocean of Meaning of the Hundred Gates*, the *Vows of Samantabhadra*, and the *Contemplation on the Conditions of the Avataṃsaka*.
Verses, hymns, and poetic compositions were gathered by the local people at the Jetavana Hermitage on Mount Fang.
During the Dali era, the śramaṇa Chaoguang first obtained them, and they subsequently circulated throughout the world.

The Commentary states: The Avataṃsaka Mahāyāna teaching is the ultimate discourse of our Buddha. It was first fully translated during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, at which time its textual form was finally complete.

At that time, the National Teacher Xianshou deeply investigated its fundamental tenets. It was not until the Zhenyuan era that the National Teacher Qingliang composed the new commentary on the Avataṃsaka.
Although the Treatise of the Elder (Li Tongxuan) was completed by Qingliang, [the lineage continued].
Previously, it was not manifest in the world; only after a long time did it finally emerge as a standard for comparison.

Observing its fundamental principles and great meanings, its distinctions of essential purpose, it reveals the primordial function of the *dharmakāya* and manifests the capacity for attaining Buddhahood through the very mind.
It causes the immovable wisdom of Mañjuśrī and the profound realm of Samantabhadra to be fully disclosed, so that they may all be seen instantaneously and without obstruction.

As for the reliance on numerical systems to represent dharmas, he utilized the hexagrams of the *I Ching* to assist in this endeavor. Consequently, many practitioners of the profound teachings of the Chan school (Zongmen) came to admire him greatly;
furthermore, scholars of the official class in later generations likewise came to recognize the sublimity of the Great Teaching through his work.
Some have claimed that the Elder was a member of the Tang imperial clan and that in his youth he had extensively mastered a vast array of books.
Thus, Empress Wu, having revolutionized the mandate of heaven, eventually departed for the mountain forests; of her, no one in the world has left a record. Alas!
Were it not for sages and worthies manifesting their traces to propagate the Great Teaching extensively, who else could have been capable of such a thing?
In the twelfth month, Zen Master Qingyuan Xingsi passed away. When the Master first met the Sixth Patriarch, he asked, "What should one attend to so as not to fall into stages?
The Patriarch replied, "What have you ever done? The Master said, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths."
The Patriarch asked, "In what rank do you fall? The Master replied, "I do not even accept the Noble Truths; how could there be any rank? The Patriarch held him in high esteem.
Later, while residing at Qingyuan, he met the śrāmaṇera Xiqian. The Master asked, "From where have you come? He replied, "From Caoxi.
The Master asked, "What have you brought back? He replied, "Even before reaching Caoxi, I was not lacking anything. The Master [was deeply impressed].
[The Master] said, "If that is so, what is the use of going to Caoxi? [Zhao] said, "If one does not go to Caoxi, how can one know that [the Dharma] has not been lost?
Qian asked, "Does Caoxi recognize you, Master? The Master said, "Do you recognize me now? [Qian] said, "Even if I were to recognize you, how could I truly attain it?
The Master said, "Though there may be many horns, a single麒麟 (qílín) is sufficient. On another day, he asked Qian again, "What do you think?"
"Where have you come from? He replied, "From Caoxi. The Master then held up his whisk firmly and said, "Does Caoxi also have this?
He replied, "Not only does Caoxi lack it; even in the Western Heavens, there is none, Master. The Master asked, "Have you perhaps been to the Western Heavens?
He replied, "If I had been there, then there would be one. The Master said, "That will not do; speak further. He replied, "The Master must also speak at least half of it yourself; do not..."
"It all depends on you, my student. The Master said, "I would not refuse to tell you, but I fear that in the future there will be no one to take up this responsibility.
He then ordered Xuanzhe to travel to the Venerable Huairang at Mount Nanyue and deliver a letter, saying, "Once you have delivered the letter, return quickly.

I shall give you an axe with which to dwell in the mountains. Upon arriving there, Xuanzhe did not present the letter but asked immediately: "Do you not value your own spiritual nature? Do you not seek it?"
"How are the various sages? Nanquan asked. Xuefeng said, "Your question is too high, sir. Why not ask about those below?

Xuefeng said, "I would rather sink into the cycle of rebirth for eternal kalpas than envy the liberation of the sages. Nanquan then desisted. When Xuefeng returned, the Master asked, "You have come back very quickly.
Did you deliver the letter? Xuefeng said, "The message was not conveyed, nor did the letter arrive. The Master asked, "How so?"
After Changjing had finished recounting his previous story, he said, "When I departed, I was granted a hatchet by the Master; please accept it.
The Master lowered one leg, and Changjing prostrated in thanks before taking his leave for Shitou. This refers to Master Shitou.
When the Master passed into nirvana, his disciples all honored him as the Seventh Patriarch.
In this year, Pujì, the State Preceptor of Xingtáng Monastery in the capital, passed away. The *Jiù Táng Shǐ* (Old History of the Tang) states: Pujì was born into the Mǎ clan of Hédōng.
In his youth, he traveled extensively to seek out eminent monks to study the Sūtras and the Vinaya. He served as a disciple under Shénxiù for six years;
Shénxiù marveled at him and transmitted the entirety of his teachings to him. When Shénxiù entered the capital, he recommended Pujì to Empress Wǔ Zétiān, who granted him ordination as a śramaṇa.

After Xiu passed away, all those throughout the land who were fond of the teachings of Śākyamuni took him as their teacher. When Emperor Zhongzong heard of his noble conduct, he issued a special decree ordering him to succeed Shenxiu in presiding over the assembly of his dharma-disciples.
In the thirteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict was issued to move Huairang (Ji) to reside in the capital.

At that time, princes, officials, and commoners vied with one another to come and pay their respects; yet Huairang maintained a grave and dignified demeanor and spoke seldom, making it difficult for those who came to him.

Seeing his serene and joyful countenance, people from both near and far held him in especially high esteem. Upon his death, all the officials and commoners of the capital who had once visited him donned the mourning attire of disciples.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Dazhao (Great Illumination).

On the day of his burial, Pei Kuan, the Governor of Henan, along with his wife and children, wore hempen garments and took their place among the ranks of the disciples. The officials and commoners likewise did so.
The women of the city wept as they escorted him to his burial, causing the marketplaces to nearly come to a standstill.
In the ninth month of the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, Yán Tǐngzhī, the Grand Master for the Crown Prince, passed away. Since his youth, Tǐngzhī had possessed refined character and integrity.
He rose through successive prominent appointments, each marked by distinguished achievements. The people of the realm looked up to him, hoping he would become Chancellor;
the Emperor likewise recognized his worth and intended to appoint him as such. However, in his later years, he was suppressed by Li Linfu and remained frustrated, unable to fulfill his ambitions.
At this time, he composed his own epitaph, stating: "In the first year of the Tianbao era, Tingzhi, serving as the Prefect of Jizhou, submitted a memorial petitioning [for retirement]."

By imperial grace, he was granted permission to retire from service to convalesce; concurrently, he was appointed as Grand Master of the Crown Prince (Taizi Jianshi). Throughout his career, he held thirty-five successive offices.

Having constantly received the sagely favor of the Emperor, he was repeatedly promoted beyond his merit. How could he, driving on with his decrepit and sluggish steed, find a way to repay the Emperor’s vast bounty?
At seventy years of age, he had no further means to serve, a source of sorrow for his superiors. In the ninth month of that year, he fell ill.
In his private residence in Luoyang, [he was] buried on the [day of the] [month of the] [year], to the west of the stupa of Venerable Dazhao.

His rites fulfilled loyalty in serving his sovereign; he was granted entry into the National History. Striving in his duties with humble ability, he may record human legends and the changes of hills and valleys for his own chronicle.
Why use literary embellishment? Initially, Tingzhi served as a disciple to Chan Master Dazhao.
Huiyi was profoundly learned in the Buddhist scriptures. His posthumous instructions regarding burial next to the Dazhao Pagoda demonstrated that he did not forget the master’s virtue;
this is recorded in the *Old History of the Tang*.
In the second year [of the reign], the Emperor dispatched the Palace Messenger Yang Tingguang to Mount Sikong to gather *changchun* (immortal) pine seeds. While there, Tingguang...
He went to Wuxiang Monastery and asked Chan Master Benjing, saying, "I, your disciple, have long admired the Way.
I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will briefly grant me some instruction. The Master said, "The great scholars of the Chan school throughout the land are all assembled in the capital.

You, Celestial Messenger, would be well-advised to consult them for a definitive resolution. This poor monk dwells by the mountains and beside the waters, having no concerns to occupy my mind. Tingguang bowed twice. The Master said, "Celestial..."
He told him to cease his formalities and address the poor monk as "Master. [The messenger] asked, "Does the celestial messenger seek the Buddha or inquire about the Way?
He replied, "I, your disciple, am ignorant and dim-witted; I have not yet discerned the meaning of 'Buddha' and 'the Way. What do they signify?

The Master said, "If you wish to seek the Buddha, then the very mind is the Buddha. If you wish to realize the Way, then no-mind is the Way. [The messenger] asked, "In what way is the very mind the Buddha? The Master said, "The Buddha awakens through the mind."
"The mind is manifested by means of the Buddha; if one awakens to the state of no-mind, even the Buddha does not exist. [The Emperor] asked, "How is it that no-mind is the Way?
The Master said, "The Way is fundamentally no-mind; no-mind is called the Way. If one realizes no-mind, then no-mind is itself the Way. Ding Guang knelt to receive [the teaching].

He returned to the palace and reported in detail what he had encountered in the mountains. The Emperor immediately issued an edict for Ding Guang to carry the imperial summons to rouse the Master from his retreat.
In the twelfth month of that winter, he arrived at the capital and was settled at the White Lotus Pavilion.

On the first day of the Lantern Festival in the first month of the following year, he invited renowned monks and eminent scholars from the two streets to the Imperial Inner Sanctuary to join him in expounding the principles of Buddhism.
A Master named Yuan asked, "According to what you have realized, O Master, what constitutes the Way? The Master replied, "A mindless state is the Way. Yuan said, "The Way..."
"If it exists because of the mind, how can you say that no-mind is the Way? The Master said: "The Way is originally nameless; it is because of the mind that it is named 'the Way.

If the name 'mind' were real, then the Way would not be empty. Since the mind, when investigated to its limit, is non-existent, upon what could the Way rely to be established? Both are equally empty and illusory."

[Zhao] Yuan always used provisional names. He asked, "Does the Chan Master perceive that body and mind are the Way? The Master replied, "The mountain monk’s body and mind have been the Way from the beginning.
Yuan said, "A moment ago you said that no-mind is the Way; now you say that body and mind are originally the Way.
Is this not a contradiction? The Master said, "No-mind is the Way. When the mind is extinguished, the Way is non-existent; mind and the Way are one."
Therefore, it is said that no-mind is the Way. Body and mind are originally the Way, and the Way is also originally body and mind.
Since body and mind are fundamentally empty, the Way is likewise exhausted at its source and non-existent. Yuan said, "The physical form of Meditation Master Guan is very small."
[Daoyuan] nevertheless understood this principle. The Master said, "You see only the mountain monk’s form; you do not see the mountain monk’s formlessness.
Daoyuan said, "I request the Chan Master to explain formlessness based upon form. The Master said, "The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: 'The four great elements have no master.'"
"The body is also without self; it is free from the view of 'mine. Only by being in accord with the Way can one attain it.

Venerable Sir, if you hold that the four great elements have a master who is the 'self,' and if you maintain such a view of self, you will not be able to realize the Way even after the exhaustion of kalpas. Yuan was deeply ashamed and withdrew.

There were seven others like Yuan who went back and forth to debate the Way, yet the Master’s eloquence flowed forth freely, overwhelming them all. The Emperor and the fourfold assembly [were likewise moved].
Everyone praised his excellence and ceased [their criticisms].
In the third year, Chan Master Huairang of Nanyue passed away. During the Yuanhe era, the renowned scholar Zhang Zhengfu composed his stele inscription, stating:
"In the third year of the Tianbao era, the Great Master Guanyin reached his end at Mount Heng. He was sixty-eight years of age. [He was a] monk.

The forty-eighth year of the Xila era. In the tenth year of the Yuanhe period, the disciples of the late Master, Daoyi, namely Weikuan and Huahui, were moved by the realization that the kalpas of dust had suddenly passed and the trees around the stupa had already reached the height of two armspans.

Fearing that the words of the elders would perish and causing anxiety for future students, they sought to propagate the master’s legacy and honor his ancestral virtue. Thus, they recorded his exemplary conduct, entrusting it to this neglected writing.
To provide some consolation for my boundless grief, I shall offer these words, though they are but forced names that leave no trace:

Since the teachings were spread in this land by Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmarakṣa, nearly a millennium has passed. When Bodhidharma transmitted the Mind-Teaching to its sixth successor, it split into two schools;
one entered the Buddha-wisdom directly without relying on gradual stages. It is from this that the school of Caoxi’s doctrine was propagated and believed. As for Guanyin—his...
He was a man whose master’s name was Huairang. He was of the Du clan of Jingzhao; his ancestors had lived in Ankang, so he was a native of that commandery.
From his childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and perceptive, far surpassing all others in speech. Whatever he encountered, he grasped completely upon a single reading without omission.
He was always composed and never given to playfulness; though among the vulgar, he could not be approached with levity. Once, while silently observing still water, he beheld his own reflection.
His dignified appearance was as vividly present as if reflected in a mirror; three times his image remained as it was before. Suddenly, his heart felt a profound sense of personal realization.
Before he had even finished turning back his steps, a voice was heard from the air, saying: "The Dharma of the Buddha is a bridge and raft that awaits you to make great.

Since you have been entrusted with this mission, why do you not exert yourself? Thereupon, he deeply severed the ties of worldly affection and swiftly underwent tonsure. Using the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Jingzhou school...

This is its subtle and profound mystery. The Great Being Zhijing was present there. He adjusted his robes and followed him; having advanced, his deportment was solemn and orderly, surpassing his peers.
Since Mount Song was a sea of fountains for Chan, the Elder Chang’an was present there. He bowed his head and consulted him;
once he had received the instruction, his body and mind became autonomous, transcending worldly defilements. Disgusted with and detached from words and letters, he sought to realize the truth.
Zongyuan searched the Dharma-realm in profound stillness and soared far toward Caoxi. When Master Neng was spreading the gift of the Dharma, students flocked to him like those returning home;
thirteen of them crossed the threshold of his teaching, and eleven more ascended into his inner chamber.
Our Master, though a junior scholar in his youth, sat at the end of the row; he was empty within as if receiving nothing, yet he was skilled in...
He kept [the scripture] closed, fearing even the sound of it being heard. Nengong found this extraordinary and placed it to his right as a seat-pillar.

When a single sound blows forth the myriad existences, and what is contained within a square inch pervades the great chiliocosm, those who are alike find their branches flourishing, while those who differ find themselves in perfect accord. Having together received the secret seal, he became a patriarchal master;
he then ascended Mount Wudang and lived in seclusion for ten years. Later, he came to Mount Heng, where he finally settled to spend the remainder of his life.
Within the eminent precincts of Prajñā, there is the Avalokiteśvara Hermitage. Because he resided in this edifice, it became his title.

Sometimes, when he analyzed subtle doctrines and principles, scholars would follow like the wind, their mouths silenced; at other times, as he prepared to depart with staff and sandals, the mountain spirits, regretting his departure, appeared to him in dreams.
From afar, those from Liang and Yi, and more recently from Jing and Wu, flocked to him like clouds gathering in shadow or rivers flowing with the wind, drawn by his spiritual influence.
The assembly of sages on this mountain unites the ancient and the present in a single moment. How sublime! Such a thing has never been heard before.

Master Yi (Yigong) realized his nature and, together with Master De (Degong), propagated the Teaching in Zhongling, where they became renowned as a distinguished lineage. Subsequently, Master Yang (Yanggong) struck the wooden clapper, and his influence extended to Master Kuan (Kuanghui).

Together they transmitted the lamp of the mind, jointly stabilizing the land. Now, having carved and polished this jade tablet, it is displayed upon the old mountain to illuminate their radiant light for all to see.
In future kalpas, his disciples who receive the Dharma shall likewise be listed here on the left, so as to clearly demonstrate that my teaching has been opened up.
In this year, He Zhizhang, Director of the Imperial Library and Guest Attendant to the Crown Prince, dreamed of wandering through the imperial palace for several days.

Upon waking, he requested to become a Daoist and return to his hometown; the Emperor granted his request by decree. He converted his residence into the Yuqiu Observatory and lived there, further requesting—

He converted several *qǐng* of the Lake of the Zhou Palace into a sanctuary for the release of living beings (*fangsheng chi*). An imperial edict was issued granting him the Mirror Lake (*Jìng hú*) and a bend of the River Shàn.
Once these were completed, the Emperor composed a poem for him; the Crown Prince and the hundred officials saw him off. He lived to the age of eighty-six.

In his later years, Zhīzhāng became increasingly unrestrained and eccentric, wandering and enjoying himself through the village lanes. He styled himself the "Madman of Sìmíng" and the "External Supervisor of the Secretariat. Whenever he was drunk—

Whenever he composed a text, his brush never ceased its movement. His calligraphic works were all worthy of admiration, yet he never polished or embellished them. He was skilled in both cursive and clerical scripts; those who appreciated the arts would bring brushes and inkstones to follow him.
If his mind was satisfied with the work, he would not refuse them. On a single sheet of paper, there might be only a few dozen characters.

The world regarded him as a treasure. His courtesy name was Jizhen. Lu Xiangxian was close friends with him from his youth and once said to others, "Jizhen’s refined conversation and elegant demeanor are such that if I do not see him for a single day, feelings of vulgarity and avarice arise within me."
In the fourth year, the Emperor summoned the retired scholar Wu Yun to an audience at Dading Hall. The Emperor inquired about the essentials of the Way (*Dao*).

Yun replied, "Regarding those who have reached a profound depth in the Way, none can compare with the Five Thousand Words of Laozi; all others are merely a waste of paper and ink. The Emperor further asked about the methods for the refinement and cultivation of immortals.
Yun replied, "These are the concerns of common recluses. One must accumulate years and months to pursue them; they are not matters upon which a sovereign should bestow his attention."—Wu Yun.

Whenever he expounded his teachings, they invariably concerned the principles of name-and-teaching (mingjiao) and worldly affairs. He used subtle words to admonish the world, and the world held him in high esteem.
Monks were jealous that he was so well-received, and since Gao Lishi had long been a devotee of Buddhism, they joined together to slander Zhìyún before the Emperor.

Realizing he could no longer remain, Zhìyún took his leave to return to the mountains. An imperial edict was subsequently issued to establish a Daoist monastery for him. Later, he moved to Mount Yá in Shànzhōng, Kuàijī, where he passed away.
Initially, Lü Yún had been expelled by the *li-xi* (wrestlers) because he treated them with contempt; consequently, his writings severely reviled the followers of Śākyamuni.

Critics censured him for this reversal of direction. At that time, Chen Shàoyóu, the Regional Inspector of Xīzī, greatly detested what Yún had done and therefore commissioned the Dharma Master Shényōng to compose a treatise to refute him.
Shényōng wrote the *Fánmí lùn* (Treatise on Overturning Delusion) to correct his errors, and Yún’s treatise was subsequently discarded.
When Secretariat Drafter Dou Shao saw Yong’s treatise, he sighed in admiration, saying: "Yong may truly be called a *maṇi* jewel beyond the mundane world, a lion among treatises.

In the fifth month of the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, an imperial decree was issued ordering that monks and nuns throughout the empire be granted certificates by the Ministry of Sacrifices (*Cíbù*). Now it is said:
The establishment of the Sacrificial Bureau (Cibu) began from this point onward.

In that year, the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra returned from the Western Regions; by imperial decree, he entered the palace to establish a ritual altar and perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) for the Emperor, being granted the title of State Preceptor Zhizang.
At that time, a court sorcerer named Lu Siyuan had gained favor through his arts, and an edict was issued ordering him to [join]...
Amoghavajra tested their relative merits. On another day, they met in the private chamber. Amoghavajra held a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) toward him.

During the course of their conversation, Amoghavajra reached out, took the *cintāmaṇi*, and threw it to the ground. He then commanded Wuxuan to pick it up. Although Wuxuan possessed great strength, he could not move it.

Thereupon, the Emperor concentrated his mind upon the profound essence of the teachings.
On the day Jichou of the third month, an edict was issued that each prefecture throughout the empire must establish a pond for the release of living beings (*fangsheng chi*).

In the tenth month of winter, Yan Zhenqing, the Prefectural Governor of Shenzhou, composed the "Epigraph and Preface to the Pond for the Release of Living Beings Throughout the Empire under the Tang" (*Youtang Tianxia Fangshengchi Beiming Bingxu*), which states:
"In the seventh generation of the August Tang, our Emperor Qianyuan Dasheng Guangtian Wenwu Xiaogong, Your Majesty, possesses the character of supreme sagehood..."
Amidst a period of hardship and peril, he lacked even the force of a single company of troops like that of Shao Kang.

Yet, at the onset of Lu Shan’s tyranny, he exercised diligence and humility in his governance; through sincerity, the myriad states rejoiced together, and by self-restraint, the world turned toward benevolence.

His kindness and trustworthiness equaled the four seasons, and his brilliant majesty reached the eight quarters of the earth. His meritorious achievements reached Heaven and Earth, and his filial piety moved the spirits.

It penetrates to the divine intelligences. Thus, the Hu-hi, Xi-xi, Qidan, Da-shi, Xun-man, and other tribes prostrated themselves from ten thousand *li* away, vying with one another to risk their lives.

The armies of Shuofang, Hedong, Pinglu, Hexi, Longyou, Anxi, Qianzhong, Lingnan, and Henan have roared for five years, pushing forward their spearheads to offer up their lives. The great evildoers were subdued as if snapping twigs.

It is truly a matter of great antiquity. To cite the two capitals as examples, they were like things merely picked up from the ground. An Qixu had already fled and been subjected to the execution of his entire clan;
Shi Siming was cowering in hiding, soon to meet his death in a boiling cauldron. You have rescued the imperial framework that had fallen and secured the ancestral altars once more.
You welcomed the Retired Emperor from Western Shu to extend filial piety at the Central Capital, where you attended him three times a day, brilliantly manifesting the majesty of the Son of Heaven.

Filial piety: in inquiring after his well-being and attending to his meals, he did not alter the rites of a common household. He was reverent and respectful—truly the supreme model for emperors and kings, beyond the reach of mere proclamations or oaths.
Since the practice of abdication began in antiquity, from the dawn of humanity until the Sui dynasty, there has never been one like our Emperor.
Yet he still nurtures all creatures with maternal warmth and remains anxious and diligent for the sake of the four classes of living beings. Thus...

On the day of Jichou, in the third month of spring in the second year of the Qianduan era, the cyclical year being Jihai, the Imperial Edict was issued by the Left Commandant of the Household Cavalry,
Right Langjiang Shi Yuanchong, and the Palace Attendant Zhang Tingyu, to proclaim the virtuous decree. Beginning from Xingdao in Yangzhou,
it extended to the various circuits of Shan-nan, Jian-nan, Qianzhong, Jing-nan, Ling-nan, and Xi-xi, reaching as far as...

At Jiangning, Qinhuai, and Taiping Bridge in Shengzhou, spanning five li from the riverbank to the city walls, eighty-one sites were established as *fangsheng chi* (pools for the release of living beings).
This was intended to proclaim imperial brilliance and extend compassionate love. Does the *Book of Changes* not say, "Trust reaches even the pig and the fish"?
Does the *Book of Documents* not say, "Down to birds, beasts, fish, and turtles—all attain their natural state"? Thus it was in antiquity.

Who else but Your Majesty could possess such sagacity, wisdom, and divine prowess while refraining from taking life? In the past, King Tang of Yin was so profoundly benevolent that he left one side of his net open;
Emperor Wu of Han bestowed such grace that he received only the response of a bird returning a pearl.

Although the flowing water rescued the parched and the name of Bao-sheng was invoked, these matters were limited to their respective times; yet they still brought blessings that endure to all eternity. How much more so for us today!

Those who move in the sun’s light and those who are rooted, whether dwelling in water or on land—throughout the entire world, it is made a single pool. Within the bounds of the realm, all receive blessings.
By riding upon the power of the *dhāraṇī* empowerment, the ocean of afflictions and the fords of birth and death are dried up.

When measured against antiquity, how could there ever have been even a faint resemblance? This humble servant, though his office is but that of a regional governor, has lived during this magnificent era and has received profound grace. [He is] without...

This is submitted for Your Majesty’s consideration. In accordance with the principles of Gao Yao’s and Xi Si’s songs praising the virtue of Yu and Lu, I have composed this single chapter, an inscription for a World-wide Pond for Releasing Living Beings.
Although it does not equal even one ten-thousandth of what is required to honor the sagely brilliance of Your Majesty, it is nonetheless the sincere devotion of your servant.
The full text of the inscription is not recorded here.

In the first year of the Shangyuan era, Wang Wei, the Vice President of the Left for the Department of State Affairs, passed away. His courtesy name was Mojie. At the time of his death, he suffered no illness;

he wrote several scrolls of letters to his relatives and friends, then set down his pen and passed away. He was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts and excelled at seal script. His fame flourished during the Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras.
Distinguished elites and nobles would leave their seats vacant to welcome him, while the various princes of Ning and Bing treated him as a teacher and friend. He was a master of calligraphy.

His contemplation entered the divine realm. As for the mountains and waters, their depth and distance, the formations of the clouds, and the colors of the rocks—painters consider these to be reached through celestial inspiration (*tianji*), not attained through study.
A guest once showed him a picture of musicians with no title or inscription. Wei said, "This is the first beat of the third variation of the 'Ni裳' (霓裳) dance.
The guest did not believe him. When he led a master musician to play the melody, the guest was convinced. [He shared this] with his younger brother, Jing.
All were devoted in their resolve to serve the Buddha; they abstained from pungent foods and wore no ornate garments.
He possessed a villa at Wangchuan, a place of extraordinary beauty, featuring Huazigang, Gegu, Zhuli, Guanliu, Liulang, Zhuyuyu, Panyan, and Xinyiwu.

There he would roam with his friend Fei Di, composing poems and exchanging verses as a source of joy. After the death of his wife, he did not remarry and lived in solitude for thirty years until the death of his mother.
A memorial was submitted requesting that the Wangchuan residence be donated to establish a Buddhist temple.

On the gengxu day of the fourth month in the first year of the Baoying era, the nun Zhenru of Longxing Temple in Chu Prefecture had a vision in which she was seemingly escorted by someone into the heavens to see the Heavenly Emperor.
The Emperor bestowed upon her thirteen treasures and said to Zhenru: "In the Middle Kingdom, there is..."
Calamity. It is appropriate to suppress it with the second treasure. On a *jiǎzǐ* day, Cui Shēn, the Regional Inspector of Chū Prefecture, presented a memorial to the court offering these treasures:

the first was the "Mystic Yellow Celestial Talisman" (shaped like a ritual tablet, eight inches long and two inches wide, made of yellow jade; it bore an inscription reading "After the Destruction of Armies"); the second was the "Jade Cock" (its plumage and markings were all complete, made of white jade);
the third was the "Grain Disc" (six inches in diameter, with grains of millet formed naturally, made of white jade); and the fourth was the "Ring of the Queen Mother of the West."

(Two pieces; seven cun in diameter; made of white jade). Five: the emerald-colored jewel (round and lustrous). Six: the wish-fulfilling pearl (shaped like an egg; its light is like that of the moon). Seven:
the red musāragalva (as large as a giant grain of millet). Eight: the *laṅkāna* pearl (two pieces; two cun long). Nine:

the jade pendant (like a ring with one-quarter missing). Ten: the jade seal (bearing an inscription like a deer; when used to seal objects, the form of a deer is impressed upon them). Eleven: the Empress’s silkworm-harvesting hook.
(Six inches long; its shape is like that of a bent ring at its tip; its color is like gold and also like silver). Twelve: The Axe of Leigong (two inches long and two inches wide).

Thirteen: [Name lost] (the historian has lost its name). When the Emperor examined them, he was greatly pleased. If placed in the midst of the sun, white vapors would extend to heaven. He named them the "Treasures that Stabilize the State.
The Emperor received these offerings from Chuzhou, which is the state where the Crown Prince was first invested with his fief. Furthermore—

Hearing that there was a calamity in the Central Plains, it was deemed appropriate to suppress it with the second treasure. He subsequently issued an edict for the Crown Prince to assume the affairs of government, granted a general amnesty throughout the realm, and changed the era name to Baoying.
In the fifth month, the Retired Emperor passed away at the age of seventy-eight. From spring until summer, the Emperor had frequently been unwell;
upon the death of the Retired Emperor, he was so overcome with grief and wailed so bitterly that he fell ill. Fourteen days later, he passed away at the age of fifty-four.
The Crown Prince ascended the throne; he was Daizong.

The Treatise says: At the outset, when National Teacher Zhong answered Emperor Suzong’s questions regarding the ten bodies of the Tathāgata and other matters, he maintained a lofty and austere standard for his school, allowing not the slightest concession. Although the Emperor had not yet fully understood the matter, he posed ten questions;

only then did Zhong respond with composure, exhaustively conveying the full meaning in nine hundred thousand words. Thereupon, the Emperor attained a profound resonance with him. This was truly a master of the lineage.

This is the general principle of transmitting the Way. When the Heavenly Emperor bestowed the Thirteen Treasures upon Zhenru, he informed him that a calamity was imminent in the Central Plains and that the second treasure should be used to suppress it.
When that treasure entered the court, it was not long before Suzong passed away and Daizong ascended the throne. From Suzong to Zhaozong, there were thirteen emperors, and then the Tang dynasty fell.
Thus, it is clear that the High God announced his mandate with such precision.
Yet the New History records the thirteen treasures in the Basic Annals and lists them again in the Treatise on the Five Elements, without ever clarifying why they were considered prophetic omens.
Alas, how strange!

In the ninth month of the first year of the Yongtai era, a golden bronze Buddha image was cast at Guangshun Gate, and the Emperor led the hundred officials to pay their respects and offer sacrifices to it.

In the tenth month, the Tibetan forces invaded and pressed upon the capital. The Emperor issued two carriages carrying copies of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) and sent them to the Ximing and other monasteries, where they were placed upon high seats one hundred feet tall for recitation.
When the invaders were pacified, the Emperor dreamed that the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, requested his robe.

The bowl was returned to Caoqi. The following day, an imperial messenger was dispatched to escort it back. At that time, the threat of banditry was repeatedly pressing in, and the Emperor grew increasingly anxious.
The Chancellor Wang Jin said, "The fortune and mandate of our state are long-lasting and auspicious; this is due to the reliance upon meritorious retribution.

Although times are currently fraught with many hardships, they are not worth mentioning. An Lushan and Shi Siming’s poison has spread and is now flaring up, yet both have met with calamity through their own sons. Pu... [text ends]
Gu Huaien collapsed when facing the enemy; the various tribes came to invade but withdrew before battle could even begin. This was not due to human effort.

Consequently, the Emperor became deeply devoted to Buddhism and Daoism, renovated sacrificial shrines, and issued an edict that no government officials throughout the realm were permitted to whip or humiliate monks and nuns.
Within the imperial palace, the *Renwang huguo jing* was recited and lectured upon. An edict was issued commanding the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra to retranslate the old version.
The Emperor personally composed a preface for it and appointed Amoghavajra as the Extraordinary Rank of Tetei (Tetjin) and Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Qing).
In that year, an imperial edict was issued for the Dharma Master Liangben to compose a new commentary on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* at the Peach Garden of the Daming Palace.

Once the commentary was completed, Ben presented it to the Emperor with a memorial, which stated in brief: "With a cleansed mind and purified thoughts, I have struck the silence to seek its resonance.

This illumination and revelation has originated from the celestial palace; I rely upon the Buddha’s power for this empowerment. All [the explanations] are based upon the sūtras and śāstras to expound the True Doctrine, much like a compilation..."
A multitude of jewels are gathered at Mount Jing; the hundred rivers are bound within the vast ocean. Fire arises from wood and shines together with the two luminaries;

consciousness transforms within the Tathāgata-body, illuminating equally within the single mark. That which brings about the realization of the Way is the Dharma; that which carries the Dharma is the Sūtra.
To extensively deliver all beings toward the Great Pervasion is to fulfill the Bodhi-mind, just as Your Majesty intends. Upon reading this, the Emperor was pleased.
This was praised as excellent.
On the *renwu* day of the seventh month in the first year of the Dali era, the *alabana* (Ullambana) assembly was first established within the imperial palace.

Altars were set up for the seven successive emperors beginning with Gaozu and Taizong; imperial carriages were prepared and great banners erected, each inscribed with the respective imperial title at its top.
He was welcomed from the Imperial Ancestral Temple into the Inner Sanctuary amidst the sounds of *nāḍa* and *chuī* music, with drums and dances, and banners and streamers reaching to the heavens.

On that day, the hundred officials stood in attendance at the Gate of Radiant Compliance (*Guāngshùn mén*) to welcome and pay their respects as he was escorted. From then on, this became an annual custom.

On the day of *guǐwèi*, two varieties of divine mushrooms (*língzhī*) grew in two chambers of the Imperial Ancestral Temple; the Emperor composed a poem to celebrate them, and the hundred officials all joined in harmony with his verse.
In the seventh month of the second year, the Chancellor Du Hongjian went out to pacify Ba and Shu.
Upon arriving in Yizhou, he dispatched a messenger to Mount Baitia to invite Chan Master Wuzhu to enter the city and inquire about the Dharma, saying:

"Your disciple has heard the Venerable Jin expound the three-phrase Dharma-gate of 'no recollection,' 'no thought,' and 'do not be deluded. I do not yet know whether these three phrases are one or three. Wuzhu [replied:]...
He asked: "Is it not said that 'non-recollection' is called precept (*śīla*), 'non-thought' is called concentration (*samādhi*), and 'not being deluded' is called wisdom (*prajñā*)?

Thus, when the single mind does not arise, one possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom; they are neither one nor three. He asked: "In the last phrase, is the character for 'delusion' (*wang*) not derived from the radical for 'heart' (*xin*)?

Wuzhu replied: "That which is derived from the radical for 'woman' (*nü*) is correct. He asked: "Is there scriptural authority for this? Wuzhu replied: "The *Dharmapada* says: 'If one arouses diligence...'"
"The mind: if it is deluded, it is not true diligence. If one can ensure the mind is not deluded, diligence will be boundless.

He asked again, "Does the Master still employ the three phrases to receive students? He replied, "For beginners, I still require them to cease their discursive thoughts and settle the waves of consciousness."
When the reflection appeared in the clear water, he realized the essence of non-thought (*amanyana*), and quiescent extinction manifested; even "non-thought" could no longer be established.

At that time, a crow cawed in the tree in the courtyard. The Master asked, "Teacher, did you hear it? He replied, "I heard it. [The Master continued,] "The crow has gone now; do you hear it now, Teacher?"

[The monk] said, "I heard it. The Master said, "The crow flew away without making a sound; how can you say you heard it? He then turned his gaze toward the fourfold assembly and said, "The True Dharma is difficult to hear.
You should each listen with careful attention. Whether one hears or does not hear is not related to the nature of hearing. Originally it was not born, and now it is not extinguished.
When there is sound, it is the auditory object that arises of itself; when there is no sound, it is the auditory object that ceases of itself."
Yet this nature of hearing does not arise following sound, nor does it perish following sound. To awaken to this nature of hearing is to escape the wandering through the sensory object of sound.
This is likewise true for visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles. You should know that hearing is without arising or ceasing; hearing is without coming or going.
The official and his subordinates were filled with joy and praised him as excellent. He asked again, "I have recently composed a commentary on the *Awakening of Faith*."
"Two fascicles. Is it appropriate to call this 'Explaining the Buddha-Dharma'? He replied, "In composing commentaries, one always employs the mind to deliberate and discriminate;
they can only be written to form a tradition for the benefit of beginners. According to the treatise, it says:

'Know that all dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of written words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; they are ultimately equal, without change or variation, and are solely..."

Because it is single-minded, it is called *tathatā* (suchness). Now, you, Excellency, are attached to the characteristic of verbal expression, attached to the characteristic of names, and attached to the characteristic of mental objects.
Since you are attached to these various characteristics, by what means can you realize and understand the Buddha-dharma? The Excellency bowed his head and said:

"Master, your current discourse based on principle accords with the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground; it is truly inconceivable. However, by what means can one attain the seal of non-arising and non-ceasing?"
"Attaining liberation. He replied, "When the mind does not arise upon encountering objects, this is called non-arising. Non-arising is itself non-extinction.

Since there is neither arising nor extinction, one is not bound by external sensory realms; this is liberation in the very place where one stands. The Master asked, "What is meant by 'recognizing the mind and seeing the nature'?
He replied, "All practitioners of the Way drift along with their thoughts because they do not recognize the true mind and do not see..."
The fundamental nature, the true mind, does not follow along with the arising of thoughts, nor does it rely on stillness when thoughts cease.
It neither comes nor goes; it is neither fixed nor chaotic. It neither grasps nor abandons; it neither sinks nor floats. It is unconditioned and signless, vividly alive and agile.

In his daily life he was composed and at ease. This essence of mind is ultimately ungraspable; there is nothing that can be known or perceived. Everything encountered by the eye is suchness (*tathatā*);

there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the Buddha-nature (*dharmatā*). From this point on, Hongjian settled his mind in the joy of *dhyāna*. He once wrote a poem that says: "I long to pursue the principles of *dhyāna*;

how could I ever bow before the source of transformation? Later, due to illness, he resigned from the position of Chancellor. Three days after relinquishing his office, he passed away. At his bedside—
Finally, he bathed, solemnly donned his court robes over his *saṃghāṭī*, shaved his beard and hair, and passed away. His final testament was that he be buried according to the dharma of a śramaṇa.
The commentary states:
"His preaching of the Dharma was free from attachment, concise, clear, and subtle, perfectly accordant with what is called 'hearing nothing' in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*."

The principle of arising and ceasing is such that those who hear it ought to awaken with joy and attain faith and understanding. Hongjian, a meritorious official who served during the establishment of the Lingwu regime, was a family whose generations had venerated the Buddha.
At the time of his death, he bathed, shaved his hair and beard, and donned monastic robes; thus, he came to resemble Wang Wenzheng Gong Dan of the Sacred Court.

Although Wang Wenzheng Gong possessed great virtue and was a man of eminent merit, [his end] was complete... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. The final character "完" (wán) suggests the sentence may have continued to describe the completion of his virtuous life or legacy.)
His fame was lofty and his integrity eminent, standing as a model for the most distinguished ministers; yet even the "Grand Progression" (*hongjian*) could not rival him.
Nevertheless, in his later years, he entrusted his instructions to his sons and his friend Yang Wengong Dainian with earnest and detailed exhortations.

These are recorded in great detail in Wengong’s *Tanyuan* (Garden of Discourse). From this, one can perceive the depth of his understanding of the Buddha and the clarity of his realization of the Way.
Alas! In our school, the direct pointing to the person—that great matter of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—is fundamentally and spontaneously present.
How is it that people themselves abandon and obscure it? Time and again, they spend their entire lives busily engaged in trivial matters for others, remaining forever in ignorance;
those who are thus mediocre throughout the world are all like this. If the two masters here can turn their heads back and preserve this mind for future generations...
To thoroughly penetrate this great matter—how could it be easily attained?
After three years, the Emperor summoned National Teacher Huizhong to the inner palace and introduced the Man from Taibai Mountain to him. The Emperor said, "This man possesses considerable insight;
I ask you, Master, to examine him. Huizhong asked, "What abilities do you possess? The man replied, "I am fortunate enough to have some understanding."
The mountain man was skilled in geography, divination, and mathematics. He said, "As for the mountain where we dwell, is it a male mountain or a female mountain?
The mountain man was bewildered and could not answer. Chong asked, "Do you know geography? He replied, "I do. Chong pointed to the ground inside the hall and asked, "What kind of terrain is this?
He answered, "Allow me to calculate it first, and then I shall know. Chong asked, "Do you know how to read and write? He replied, "I do."
Chung drew a single horizontal line upon the ground and said, "This is the character '甚' (shen). The mountain man said, "This is the character '一' (one).
Chung said, "A single stroke above the earth is the character '王' (wang). Why do you call it the character '一'? He asked again, "Can you calculate? The man replied, "I can.
Chung said, "What is three times seven? The mountain man said, "The National Preceptor is teasing his disciple. Is three times seven not twenty-one?"
Wŏnch’ŏng said, "But it was the mountain man who was playing with this poor monk. Seven times three is twenty-one; why do you say twenty? He asked again, "What other abilities do you possess?
Wŏnch’ŏng replied, "Even if your disciple possessed such abilities, I would not dare open my mouth before the National Teacher.

Wŏnch’ŏng said, "Even if you had such abilities, they would still not be sufficient. The Master then said to the Emperor, "To ask about the mountain while not knowing the mountain; to ask about the earth..."

He did not recognize the characters when asked about them; he did not know how to read. When asked to calculate, he could not solve the problem. "Your Majesty, from where have you obtained this ignorant fellow? [The ministers asked].
The Emperor said to the mountain man, "I possess the imperial throne, yet it is not a treasure. You, Master, are truly a national treasure."
The mountain man said, "Your Majesty is truly one who recognizes treasure.
That year, an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Daoqin of Mount Jing to the capital. The Emperor personally paid him homage and worship.
One day, while the Master was in the inner court, he rose upon seeing the Emperor. The Emperor asked, "Master, why do you rise? Daoqin replied, "How can a donor [address]..."
While the Emperor was observing the Master in his four modes of deportment, he was pleased and said to Minister Zhong, the State Preceptor, "I wish to bestow a name upon Master Qin.
Zhong joyfully accepted the imperial decree, and the Master was subsequently granted the title Chan Master Guoyi. Later, he took his leave and returned to his mountain home.
Master Mazu instructed his disciple Zhizang to ask, "In the twelve periods of the day, what do you take as the objective realm? The Master replied, "Wait for you..."
When he was about to return, there was a message [sent to him]. Huizang said, "I shall return this very moment. The Master said, "In conveying my words, you must ask for Caoxi's instruction.
Furthermore, a monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Your question is improper. The monk asked, "How can it be made proper?
The Master said, "Wait until after I have passed away, and then I will tell you. He entered nirvana in the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era.
He was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Dajue.
In the fourth year, Chan Master Niutou Huizhong passed away. The Master had received the Dharma from Master Wei and served as the sixth patriarch of the Niutou school.
Throughout his life, he never changed his single robe, and his only utensil was a single cauldron. He once possessed two measures of grain for the support of monks.

At the granary, thieves were spying about; the tiger acted as its guardian. When the district magistrate Zhang Xun entered the mountain to pay his respects, he asked the Master, "How many disciples do you have?
The Master replied, "There are three or five. Xun said, "May I see them? The Master struck the meditation bench three times.

Three tigers emerged, roaring and snarling; Xun retreated in terror. Later, when he moved to reside at Zhuangyan Temple and was about to construct a Dharma Hall, there was an ancient tree with a colony of magpies nesting upon it.
The Master said to the nest, "A hall is to be built on this site; you may depart at once.
As soon as he had finished speaking, the flock of magpies moved their nests to another tree. When the foundation was being laid, two divine beings appeared and fixed its four corners.
Jiǎo secretly provided resources for night labor, and it was completed in a single day. Consequently, students gathered like clouds. The Master had a verse on settling the mind that said:
"When both person and phenomena are purified, good and evil are forgotten; with a straightforward mind and true reality, this is the site of Bodhi.

When he was about to pass away, he hung his cauldron before the stone chamber and suspended his robes from a tree; the wisteria vines died off without cause. Having assembled the community for the *poṣadha* ceremony, the Master finished his duties.
He cleansed his hair and bathed his body. That evening, auspicious clouds covered his courtyard, and the sound of celestial music resounded from the sky.

At dawn the following day, he sat peacefully and passed away. In a brief moment, wind and rain burst forth violently, shattering the trees and forests, while a white rainbow pierced through the cliffs and ravines.
In the fifth year [of the Tianbao era], the Tripitaka Master Dairi arrived at the capital from the Western Regions. He claimed to have attained the wisdom-eye of knowing others' minds.
The Emperor ordered him to enter Guangzhai Monastery to request the National Teacher Huizhong to test him. Huizhong asked, "Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds?
The Tripitaka Master replied, "I dare not say so. Huizhong said, "Tell me, where is this old monk right now? The Tripitaka Master said, "The Master."
"You are the national teacher of this land. How can you go to Tianjin Bridge to watch monkey performances? Zhong asked again, "Where is the old monk now?
The Tripitaka Master replied, "You are the national teacher of this land. How can you go to Xichuan to watch the boat races?
Zhong asked the question for a third time, using the same words as before. After a long while, the Tripitaka Master remained ignorant of where he was.
Zhong shouted, "You wild fox spirit! Where is his penetration of the mind? Tripitaka had no reply. The *Lun* says:
"Under the Fourth Patriarch, Master Rong spoke both horizontally and vertically, yet he still did not know the pivotal point of the 'upward' direction.
This is the speech of Huangbo Yun. It was because of Huangbo’s great capacity and great function, his extraordinary and unconventional methods.
To speak in this way is indeed correct. At other times, there have been students who mistake mere superficial talk for the Way of Chan;
in fact, the disparagement and denigration of various regions has often gone even further than this. Alas! It is said that learning does not skip levels.
How much more so for our school, which transmits the single seal of mind (cittamudrā) to bring an end to birth and death—how could one possibly [treat it with such levity]?

Is this not a case of leaping over the stages? Observe how the Way of the various patriarchs of Oxhead flourished at one time; their spiritual efficacy was manifest and clear at the moment of death and rebirth.

There were those who, while still alive, had flowers brought to them by hundreds of birds and were attended by tigers and wolves; there were those whose passing caused birds and beasts to wail for over a month before ceasing;
there were those for whom extraordinary fragrances lasted for ten days before fading; and there were those for whom mountains and forests were transformed.
That the stream of the White Brook was cut off, that divine banners appeared in the sky coming from the west and circling the mountain several times,
and that the trees in his old residence turned white for seven days before returning to normal—
all these things experienced by Master Zhong are inconceivable matters that transcend the realm of natural creation. Were it not for his divine virtue and subtle...
Acting thus, they do not feel shame even if they obscure heaven and earth, nor do they feel abashed before a hundred sages; how could they have reached such a state?

For instance, when the Tripitaka Master Mahakarṇa, who had partially realized the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle and attained the five supernatural powers, went to see the National Preceptor, he perceived the Preceptor’s location clearly on the first two occasions because his mind was directed toward an object. However, on the third occasion, the National Preceptor— [text continues] —perceived him.
He entered the gate of the profound, secret, and great samādhi of tranquility, while Dà'ěr stood there utterly bewildered and ignorant.
Thus, it is not at all false that there are gradations in the realization of the fruits [of the path] and degrees of depth in the Great Way.

As for those who claim that Wúxián’s contemplation of Hú Zǐ could be compared to that of the National Teacher (Guóshī)—how can such limited arts and calculations possibly equal the perfect penetration of one's own nature?
To speak of them as being on the same footing would be a grave error. *Lōngxīng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Seventeen;
*Lōngxīng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Eighteen.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Zuxiu of the Stone Chamber in Longxing Prefecture.

In the fifth year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Amoghavajra, the Tripiṭaka Master of Great Universal Wisdom, manifested illness and instructed his disciples, saying: "The practice of Samantabhadra..."

"I vow to bring forth boundless Dharma gates. You all should practice them with diligence. You should contemplate the Bodhicitta, the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) of the Honored One, which directly explicates the letter A.
By realizing that all phenomena are unborn, you shall realize the body of Great Enlightenment.

He further commanded his disciple Zhao Qian to take up the brush and record the *Nirvāṇa-vidhi* he had composed to bequeath to future generations, so that they might follow it in conducting funeral rites and thereby express their final farewells.

The Emperor issued an imperial decree dispatching an inner envoy to bestow medicinal decoctions and offer inquiries after his health. He was further conferred the rank of Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si and the title of Duke of Xiao with an appanage of three thousand households.
Although Amoghavajra declined these honors four times, they were not granted. Amoghavajra sighed and said, "I have sought to save the world through the Dharma;
I never imagined that as I approach death, I would be defiled by such honorary titles. Thereupon, he took the ritual implements entrusted to him by his former teacher, Vajrabodhi...

During the cremation, his cranial bone remained unbroken; it contained śarīras whose radiance dazzled the eyes. Yan Ying, the Censor-in-Chief, composed an inscription for the Monument to His Virtues, and Xu Hao, the Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, engraved it upon stone.

The Master’s name was Amoghavajra (Bukong). He was a native of the Western Regions; as his clan and lineage were not known within the Middle Kingdom, they are not recorded here.

Emperor Xuanzong, who possessed an intuitive understanding of the Ultimate Way, held him in exceptional esteem. Throughout the three reigns of Emperors Suzong, Daizong, and Dezong, he served as the State Preceptor for Consecration (*guǎngdìng guóshī*).

By means of profound teachings and virtuous auspices, he provided spiritual protection to the Sovereign. At the beginning of Dezong’s reign, [the Emperor] appointed him as Tèjìn (Special Advance) and Dàhónglù (Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial).

He was honored with official commendations. When he manifested illness and ceased his activities, the Emperor further conferred upon him the title of *Kaifu Yitong Sanchi* and the rank of Duke of Xiao within the palace quarters;
however, he firmly declined both honors, which were not granted. He was specially bestowed with the Dharma name "Great Vast Wisdom Tripitaka Master.

On the day of Guiwei in the sixth month of summer in the fifth year of the Dali era, he passed away at Da Xingshan Temple in the capital. Emperor Daizong decreed the suspension of court business in his honor.
On the third day of the month, he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works (Sikong). He was conferred the posthumous name Da-bian-zheng Guangzhi Sanzang Heshang.

On the day of his cremation, an imperial edict dispatched a palace attendant to carry a written prayer for the ancestral sacrifice, expressing the utmost reverence as if he were still present. The Emperor’s words were profound and sincere, and the offerings presented were exceptionally fragrant.
This ceremony surpassed all others in its magnificence, with nothing else to compare it to. In the ninth month of the following year, an edict was issued to enshrine his relics.
The stupa was enshrined in his former residence at the temple. The Master’s nature was keen and brilliant; he extensively surveyed the essential tenets of the Dharma-treasury of the past Buddhas.

Standing alone among the assembly of monastics (*śramaṇa*), he was vast and peerless. Examining the regulations for the ritual forms of the *mantra* syllables and the procedures for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and ascent to the altar, as well as the swiftness of attaining Buddhahood in this very life and the wondrous bestowal of blessings upon hearing his voice—it was celestial and magnificent.
Its breadth and depth are vast and profound; it is certainly not something that those of superficial learning can fully elaborate upon.
Nevertheless, I venture to provide a general overview and set forth its grand purport. In the past, Vajrasattva personally received the meaning of the Yoga Mahāyāna before the Buddha Vairocana.
Several hundred years later, it was transmitted to Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva. Nāgārjuna, in turn, after several hundred years, transmitted it to... [Nāgabodhi].
The Ācārya Jñāna transmitted it to the Ācārya Vajrabodhi. The Ācārya Vajrabodhi came from the East and transmitted it to the Upādhyāya.
The Upādhyāya, in turn, traveled west to India, Siṃhala, and other lands, where he visited the Ācārya Jñāna and propagated the teachings of the eighteen assemblies.
Thus, the lineage of Dharma transmission has been handed down from Vairocana Tathāgata down to the Upādhyāya.

He confronted it with his spiritual power; before a single moment had passed, the sea became calm and waveless. At his birth, there was an auspicious sign of a ray of light illuminating his mother.
At his passing, there was a marvel of the pond water in the vihāra drying up completely. He lived for fifty summer retreats as a monk.
He lived to the age of seventy. From his childhood until his later years, he constantly prepared ritual offerings and sat in the *bodhimaṇḍa*.

Formerly I received his subtle words; now I behold his cane and staff. His radiant countenance is faint and distant, yet the sacred precincts remain pure and serene.

He explored the Way and beheld its profound mysteries, rising above his peers and excelling among the eminent. Within a single month, his reputation shook the capital. The Great Master’s character was as lofty and steep as a cliff, yet his spirit was open and expansive;

his physical bearing was dignified and mature, and his practical application of wisdom was empty and luminous. He grasped the hidden subtleties of the Tripiṭaka and investigated the sources of all schools.

Furthermore, he was naturally proficient in both the profound teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism, and extensively mastered the calendrical systems and esoteric sciences. Upon hearing of his reputation, the elders were delighted and submitted to him;

high officials lowered their couches to receive him with the etiquette due to a guest. Consequently, he formed a circle of scholarly and religious discourse with Lu Xiangxian, Duke of Yanyang and Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent;

He Zhizhang, Court Guest Attendant; Li Yong, Governor of Beihai; Xu Anzhen, Secretariat Drafter; and Chu Tinghui, Censor-in-Chief. Together they were known as the [Circle of] Confucians and Buddhists.

He roamed as a companion with whom there was no opposition. In guiding the world, he always placed literary conduct at the forefront and propagated it through the cultivation of *śīla* (precepts) and *samādhi* (concentration).
Upon entering a chamber of orchids, his fragrance naturally emanated; facing a mirror by the water, even the finest hair was clearly reflected. One could not know how this came to be.

A torch dispels the thick darkness; myriad streams flow toward the ravines and marshes. When he first arrived, his practice of transformation was like that.

Born through conditioned existence, he ceased by riding upon transformation. Like grasses and trees silently moistened by rain, his cloud of compassion was without artifice. When he finally departed, it was likewise.
To dwell in accordance with the Way is thus. Human life shifts and turns; the Path remains while fortune passes away. Gazing toward him, he is no longer seen; only the silent, empty mountains remain.
How lamentable! The inscription says: The waters of Yue stretch far and wide; the lofty mountains encircle one another. The Great Master has entered extinction; thus a spirit-stupa is erected.
