The Stele for the Posthumous Title, composed by the Provincial Inspector Du Guji, states: According to previous records, the Chan Master was styled Sengcan. It is unknown where he was from;
he appeared during the Zhou and Sui dynasties and transmitted the teachings to the Great Master Huik'e. He followed [Huik'e] as his teacher in Ye.
He attained the Way on Mount Sikong. Believing that physical form is not the truth, he manifested sores and ailments.

Believing that dharmas have no self, he did not choose his dwelling place. Taking the illnesses of sentient beings as his own illness, he invariably preached the Dharma to deliver people wherever he went.
Since the single characteristic does not reside within, without, or in between, he insisted on teaching without relying on written words. The general outline of his teaching was as follows:

The wondrous function of tranquil illumination encompasses all categories of beings and the flowing succession of arising and ceasing. Contemplating the four quarters, above and below, one perceives no phenomena, no body, and no mind;
even the mind is free from names and designations. The body is equal to the realm of space, and phenomena are identical to dreams and illusions.
There is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized; only then is it called liberation. The Chan Master follows this very path. Having received the entrustment from above, he [descends]...
He rescued those in darkness and doubt; as the great clouds cast their shade, the entire realm was transformed.

Subsequently, he entrusted his *kāṣāya* along with the Dharma to one who had attained awakening. The Way remained while his physical form faded away, and his remains were left upon this mountain; two hundred years have now passed.

The ancient terrace of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* remains dignified in its foundation, yet its eaves and steps have crumbled and fallen into ruin.

A monk of lofty conduct and ascetic practice, Zhìqīng, took the lead in the restoration and settled there as its resident abbot. In the seventh month of the autumn of the following year, Zhēnqīng’s term of service was nearing completion.
There was the Surveillance Commissioner, Minister and Grand Master of Remonstrance, Duke Wei of Zhao.
He wished to dedicate the anniversary of our Emperor’s birth as the Baoying Temple, and further requested that thirty-seven monks of lofty conduct from the mountain forests be supported there.

On the twenty-third day of the tenth month of winter, His Majesty graciously granted permission. Thereupon, the temple was renovated with magnificent halls and pavilions; its restoration flourished with great vigor.

He then invited the Dharma Masters Fayuan and Faquan of Zhi Guan Monastery, Chengjue of Xiangyang, Shanhong of Qingliang, Yuanjue of Luofu, Benyu of Foti, Huida of Yuhang, as well as Haitong and Hai'an of the local prefecture, to dwell together in cultivation and practice to augment his auspicious fortune.
They all considered that although the number of disciples had increased, the Vinaya had not yet been established. In the third month of the following year...

Yue then requested Qin to ascend the dais and direct the wooden clapper; he further commissioned Longgang Dao Gan, Tiantai Fazai, Zhaoti Zhirong, Baima Fayin, Hengyue Zhijue, Sidé Yiying, Xiangcheng Cangxuan, Longxing Cangzhi, and Kaiyuan Mingche to jointly preside over the Dharma rites.
Thereupon, those from near and far flocked to the assembly like swift horses.
The precincts of the site of enlightenment were so crowded that there was no space to move. For forty days, the sacred images emitted light, yet the Dragon King did not send rain.
Among the three hundred and fifty-seven monks and nuns, the scholar Zhengyi Dafu and former Weiwu Shaqing Zhang Tinggao left the secular life to return to the truth;
his dharma name was Huigang, and he was the foremost among them. Furthermore, since this year, [the Emperor] has held him in high esteem.

The number of those who received full ordination totaled more than ten thousand people. Across the regions of the Yangtze, the hills, the lakes, and the seas—spanning a territory of a thousand li—the various transformations of the Semblance Dharma were all due to the power of his transformative influence.
In Linchuan, situated at the edge of the mountain ranges, the Vinaya had never been propagated;
thereupon, more than three hundred members of the dual assembly requested that Faye expound upon it and serve as their preceptor. Later, there was one from the Capital...
The eminent monks of Zisheng Monastery said, "We have returned to the original Vinaya Master. They marveled at his great eloquence, deeply sighing in admiration and praising him.

They established the Puguang Unobstructed Chan Cloister to the southeast of the monastery and founded the Guanzhou Guanyin Sanctuary within it, inviting Shanhong to reside there to illuminate the essentials of the mind.
His senior disciple, Tanyi, said, "Zhifeng maintains [the precepts] with refined diligence."

In accordance with the precedents of past assemblies of the honored multitude, he then commanded Zhìhuǎng and others to establish a Vinaya-piṭaka Hall to the east of the Pǔtōng Dàochǎng and to inaugurate a *śīlā-maṇḍala*.

This was done to commemorate the arrival of Master Xíngqīn and to ensure that this inaugural record would endure imperishably. Before long, the construction was completed and the halls and pavilions rose majestically;
solemn and awe-inspiring, they were like the life-preserving raft crossing the sea, where even the slightest fraction of negligence would have invited the Rākṣasas.
Adorned with necklaces that shine with the light of *maṇi* jewels, he enters the rank of the Buddhas and dons the *kāṣāya*;
his name and fragrance spread everywhere, and his spiritual powers (*ṛddhipāda*) are infinite. Can even half a month suffice to record them without end?
Written and inscribed by Yan Zhenqing, Duke of Kaiguo of Lu Commandery, Acting Prefect of Fuzhou during the Xinhai year of the Dali era of the Great Tang.

The *Lun* (Treatise) states: The inscription on the Stele of the Duke of Lu records that in the first year of the Jian-ning era of the Han dynasty, an Indian śramaṇa translated the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and conferred full ordination upon the great bhikṣus.

However, both the *Liang Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks of the Liang Dynasty) and the *Sui Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels of the Sui Dynasty) maintain that it was during the Jia-pi era of the Cao Wei dynasty...
In the mid-Heian period, Tánkēluó first brought the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* from the Western Regions.
I read the account of Zè Róng in the *Hòuhàn shū* and noted that during the final years of the Han, every year on the Buddha’s birthday, Zè Róng would provide abundant food and drink.

He would spread out mats and hang banners over an area of five or six li in circumference, and those who came to partake of the meal or to witness the spectacle always numbered in the tens of thousands. Judging by this, it appears that [the formal monastic discipline] did not yet exist in the Han era.
There are precepts. Generally, the ritual for the fast resembles that of a sacrificial offering. It is indeed true that the precepts first arrived during the Wei period.
Thus, the account of Lord Lu is likely an error by those who transmitted it; one should take the *Monastic Biographies* as authoritative.
In the ninth year, the Daoist Shi Hua gained favor through his arts. He consequently requested permission to set up a blade-ladder to compete with the śramaṇas in a contest of methods.

An imperial decree was issued for monks from the two monastic districts to be selected to compete on a fixed date. A śramaṇa named Chonghui, whose origins were unknown, had regularly recited the Śūraṅgama-mantra;
he submitted a memorial requesting to defeat [Shi Hua]. The Emperor led his hundred officials to witness the event. In a moment, Shi Hua stepped onto the...
He set up a ladder of blades and commanded Huì to climb it. Huì stepped upon the blades and ascended, returning and going back forth without injury.
Taking advantage of this success, he ordered wood to be piled in the courtyard and set it ablaze with fierce flames. Huì entered the mass of fire and called for Shìhuá to enter as well.

Shìhuá was so overcome with shame and perspiration that he did not dare look directly at him. The Emperor was greatly pleased and concluded the proceedings, bestowing upon Chónghuì the title of State-Protecting Tripitaka Master. Afterward, nothing more was known of him.

End. The treatise states: The records of Shi Hua and Chonghui are found in the *Táng Fódào lúnhéng* (The Balance of Buddhism and Daoism during the Tang Dynasty) and the *Gāosēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
Is this not indeed true? Formerly, during the time of King Mu of Zhou, a transformed man came from the western extremity; he entered and emerged from fire...

He gathered [the materials], leaped through the window, and passed through the wall; his myriad transformations were beyond description. The world suspected he was an emanation sent by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

It is not without reason that Master Chonghui said: "Those who have realized the fruit of Arhatship possess the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the three insights (*trividyā*), and the eighteen transformations (*aṣṭādaśavikurvaṇa*).
They dwell eternally in the world, responding to beings according to their capacities. This must surely be one of such a class.
Indeed it was so.
Toward the end of the Zhenghe era of our dynasty, there was a Daoist named Lin Lingsu, a native of Wenzhou, who was skilled in sorcery and supplemented his arts with the methods of the Thunder God.
He once traveled through Xuzhou, Haozhou, Huai, and Si, wandering among the monasteries and begging for food. Among the crowds...

The monk treated him with contempt. Upon arriving in Chu Prefecture, he engaged in a physical altercation with Hui-shi. They brought their dispute before the local authorities, where the deputy magistrate Shi Zhong-wen questioned him.

Delighted by his eloquence, agility, and brilliance, Shi released him and took him into the guest quarters. There, he inquired after the arts of *tuna* (breath cultivation), *shaolian* (alchemical refinement), and the flight of the spirit.
In the first month of the seventh year, Shi led him to the capital to have an audience with the Chancellor Cai Jing. Cai Jing introduced him to the Emperor. Ling...
Su spoke boastfully, saying: "In the heavens there is the Shenxiao Yuqingfu (Palace of the Jade Purity of Divine Clarity), presided over by the Emperor Lord of Eternal Life.

His younger brother is the Emperor Lord of Green Florescence; both are sons of the Jade Emperor. Next are the Left Minister, the Immortal Lord, along with the punishing immortal officials such as Chu Hui and more than eight hundred other officials.
[He claimed] that the Zhezong Emperor was the Emperor Lord of Eternal Life, and Zhang Jing was the Left Minister, the Immortal Lord."
Ling-su was none other than Chu Hui. The Emperor received him with joy and faith, granting him the title "Immortal Guest of the Golden Gate" and establishing the Tongzhen Palace for his residence.

Soon thereafter, he renamed the great monasteries and observatories throughout the empire as "Shenxiao Yuqing Wan-shou Palaces" and installed images of the Lord of Eternal Life and the Azure Flower Emperor.
He established a curriculum for Daoist studies. Whenever Ling-su appeared before the Emperor, he invariably exerted himself in denouncing the followers of Śākyamuni.
"Please remove them.

On the *yǐmǎo* day of the first month in the first year of the Xuānhuá era, an imperial edict was issued to abolish the old names of the Śākya (Buddhist) tradition and to prohibit bronze ritual bells, stupas, and statues.
In the third month, a great flood occurred in the capital; *yuán* and *táo* creatures emerged from the houses of the city's inhabitants. The Emperor dispatched Língsù to manage the waters.
After a long time, there was no sign of efficacy at all, and the officials and citizens grew increasingly fearful. One day, the Great Being Saṃgha suddenly appeared within the palace.
The Emperor immediately commanded him to perform a rite for averting the flood. The Great Being shook his staff, ascended the city wall, and recited secret mantras.

In a short while, the water level suddenly decreased until it was completely exhausted. Ling Su was somewhat disheartened by this. Shortly thereafter, he did not avoid violating the Imperial Prince’s festival; the Prince—

He was beaten. He appealed to the Emperor. In the eleventh month of winter, on the day of Yimao, the Emperor detested him and exiled him specifically back to Wenzhou, where he subsequently died on the road.
Alas! In the cases of monks such as Śāṅgha and Chonghui, it is truly evident that they do not enter parinirvāṇa but abide eternally in this world;
that they protect the land and bestow blessings upon the people can indeed be seen here.
The śramaṇa Yuanze resided at Huilin Temple in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). He was a close friend of the recluse Li Yuan; indeed, Huilin was the former residence of Yuan’s family.
Yuan’s father, Li Cheng, had served as the governor of the Eastern Capital when he was killed by An Lushan. For this reason, Yuan did not enter public office.
He resided constantly within the monastery, where he would engage in conversation and laughter with Sengze all day long. Once, they happened to set out together to travel to Mount Emei.
Daoyuan intended to go by traveling upstream from Jingzhou through the Gorges, while Sengze wished to take the route via Chang’an and the Xiyu Valley.

Daoyuan, feeling that human affairs had been severed for too long, was unwilling to enter the capital again; however, Sengze was persistent and strong-willed, so they eventually departed from Jingzhou. As their boat reached Nanpu, Daoyuan saw a woman.

Zu saw a man wearing a brocade apron, carrying a water jar on his back as he drew water from the spring. Zu gazed at him and wept, saying, "That which I did not wish for has come about because of this.
Yuan was startled and asked the reason. Zu said, "This woman has been pregnant for three years, waiting for me to become her son.

Had she not encountered me, it would have been that; but now that she has seen me, there is no way to escape it. You should assist me with your talismans and incantations so that she may give birth quickly."

"On the third day, we shall bathe the child; I pray that you, sir, will deign to look upon him. Let a smile serve as my token of faith. Thirteen years hence, outside the Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou, I shall meet with you, sir.
Yuan bathed the child with deep sorrow. By evening, Ze had passed away. After the mother had nursed him for three days, Yuan went to see him.
Upon seeing Yuan, the child indeed laughed with a joyful expression. Yuan then related this in full to his wife.
After the funeral was completed at home, Yuan returned to the monastery. Later, as previously arranged, he traveled from Luoyang to Wuxing to attend the wedding ceremony.
Upon arriving at the site by the well of Ge Hong, he heard a cowherd boy tapping on a cow horn and singing: "Upon the Stone of Three Lives, our former spirits dwell;
Whether we praise the moon or chant in the wind, let us not debate it. I am ashamed that my lover has come from afar to visit; Though this body is different, our nature remains the same."

[The monk] remained constantly present. Yuan asked, "Is Master Ze in good health? He replied, "Master Li is a man of true faith; however, his worldly ties are not yet exhausted. Do not approach him for now.
Only when you have practiced diligently without indolence shall we meet again. He then sang this song: "The affairs before and after the body are vast and obscure;
To speak of their causes and conditions would break one's heart. Having searched through the mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue, I now turn back toward the mist..."
As he was rowing across the Qutang Gorge, [the monk] suddenly vanished from sight. Huìyuǎn returned to Huílín Temple; by the beginning of the Chángqìng era, he was eighty years old.

Lǐ Deyù, the Vice President of the Court of Judicial Review, presented a memorial recommending him, stating: "Huìyuǎn was endowed by Heaven with supreme filial piety and had severed his ties to official service."
For over fifty years, he constantly maintained silence. His realization accorded with the profound essentials; a single word of his exhortation would wash away a hundred anxieties.

Clinging to this true integrity while living in a refined age, I, your servant, privately lament for Your Majesty on his account. Emperor Muzong issued an edict appointing Yuan Shou as an Advisor to the Council (Jianyi Daifu), but he did not go to serve.
Shortly thereafter, he passed away at the end of his natural life.
Ten years later, National Teacher Huizhong was about to pass away. Danyuan asked him, "After a hundred years, if someone asks about the ultimate matter, what will you say?
Huizhong replied, "Fortunately, I am already pitiable enough; why must I have a talisman for protecting my body? He then entered his final leave-taking with Emperor Daizong.
Daizong said, "After the Master’s passing, by what means shall your disciple remember you? Huizhong said, "Tell [the Emperor]..."
A donor was constructing a seamless stūpa. The Emperor asked, "Please show me the model for the stūpa. Zhong remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand?
The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. Zhong said, "After I have passed away, my attendant Yingzhen will know this matter."
On the ninth day of the twelfth month, he entered nirvana while lying on his right side.

His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa at Dangzi Valley and were granted the posthumous title of Great Realization (Dazheng) Chan Master. The Emperor soon summoned Yingzhen to the inner palace and questioned him, repeating the previous words.
Zhenru remained silent for a long time and then asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand. Zhenru then recited a verse:
"To the south of Xiang, to the north of Tan, In between lies a land filled with gold. Beneath the shadowless tree, all share one boat; Upon the crystal palace, there is no one to guide.

Wŏnch’ŏng said, “Chao’en also understands a little of the Buddha-dharma. Chao’en then asked Wŏnch’ŏng, “What is ignorance (*avidyā*), and from what does ignorance arise?
Wŏnch’ŏng replied, “The signs of the decline of the Buddha-dharma are manifesting now. The Emperor asked, “Why is that?
Wŏnch’ŏng said, “That even a slave like me understands how to ask about the Buddha-dharma—is this not the manifestation of its decline? Chao’en’s expression turned violently angry. Wŏnch’ŏng said:

Wuzhong replied, "When those at court say that you are the Son of Heaven, is that true?
Zhao En prostrated himself on the ground and said, "I am guilty of death, I am guilty of death! I am truly not the Son of Heaven. Wuzhong said, "I am not a Buddha. What I... [text ends]

"Is your surname not Yu? Chao'en prostrated himself on the ground once more and said, "A capital offense! A capital offense!
From now on, I truly dare not discuss the Buddha-dharma with you, Master. Zhong said to the Emperor, "I was just afraid this slave would kill me."

One might say that his power equaled that of the sovereign and his wealth and status shook the world; yet Wonch’ŭk addressed him by the title of "slave.

During the Zhide era, he received ordination and the full precepts. He immediately exhorted himself with ten points, saying: "In body, I shall not discard the outward appearance of a śramaṇa;

He did not tread upon the dust of a nun’s convent; his ribs did not touch the couch of a lay devotee. His eyes did not discern colors that violated propriety;
his tongue did not savor delicacies served after noon. His hands never released the *cintāmaṇi* bead; he never stayed overnight apart from his robes and bowl.
Following Niu-tou Chung and Chin-shan Chin, he inquired into the fundamental principle of the Western Transmission and received the perfect teaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at the capital.

Chan Master Dushen was summoned by Emperor Daizong in the third year of the Dali era to enter the palace and serve as a *runwen dade* (virtuous master for refining translated texts) alongside the Tripitaka Master Dabianzheng.
Subsequently, he took his leave and entered Mount Wutai at the Great Huayan Monastery.

There, he contemplated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with profound thought, reflecting that while the sages of the fifth stage abide within the Buddha-realm and their minds embody *tathatā* (suchness), they still rely upon subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

He gave rise to a mundane mind and studied worldly knowledge. From this, he extensively read the Six Arts, maps and histories, the nine schools of divergent learning, the glossaries of China, the Indian scriptures and Sanskrit characters, as well as the holy teachings of the four Vedas and five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and various secular classics;

there was nothing he did not master thoroughly. In the fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era, when he was about to take up the brush to compose his commentary, he first sought an auspicious response. One night—
In a dream, he beheld the golden countenance of the Buddha, its radiant features majestic and imposing as a mountain rising before him. He then cupped his hands and brought them to his face.
Upon awakening, he was filled with joy, believing it to be a sign that he had attained the realization of the Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka*). From then on, his pen never paused.

He subsequently divided the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* into four major sections—Faith and Understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), Practice (*caryā*), Realization (*abhisamaya*), and Verification (*pratyakṣa*)—such that no principle remained unencompassed. He often lamented the shortcomings of previous commentaries.
The purport of the sūtra had not yet been fully exhausted; only the National Teacher Xianshou had somewhat delved into its profound source, and thus he took it as his primary lineage.

He composed the commentary, which took four years in total to complete. Furthermore, he dreamed that he became a dragon, with its head raised at the Southern Terrace and its tail coiled at the Northern Terrace;

it undulated through the void, its scales and fins gleaming in the sun. In an instant, it transformed into hundreds and thousands of forms, slithering through the azure heavens and dispersing in all directions.

He then departed. Those who understood him considered this to be a manifestation of the Dharma’s circulation. Initially, while lecturing on it for the assembly, he was moved by the appearance of auspicious clouds that gathered and suspended themselves in the air before the courtyard of the lecture hall.

Furthermore, for the sake of the monk Rui and others, he composed forty fascicles of *Yanyi* (Exposition of Meaning) following his commentaries and one hundred fascicles of *Shoujing* (Hand Mirror) following the text. It is said thus.
In the first year of the Yuánxīng era, there was a Chan Master named Míngzàn of Nányuè. His origins were unknown.
Initially, when Prime Minister Lǐ Bì retired to Mount Héng during the Qiányuán era, Míngzàn was living in seclusion at Shàngfēng. When Bì went to visit him, Míngzàn was reciting a sutra.
The sound of his voice was first sorrowful and then joyful. Bi, who possessed a refined knowledge of music, said to him, "Is it not that you, a recluse, harbor ambitions for the clouds and the sky?
Zan spat at him, saying, "Do not harm me! Do not harm me! Bi’s expression did not waver.
After a long while, seeing that Bi stood waiting without flagging, Zan said, "Has your meal not yet been served? Bi replied, "It has not. Zan pushed him aside.
Fire issued forth and a sheep ate it. Li Mi spoke with him for a long while before taking his leave. Zàn patted his back and said, "You will serve well as a prime minister for ten years.
When Mi came to power, he spoke of Zàn’s noble conduct to the Emperor, and an imperial decree was issued to summon him.

When the messenger arrived at Shiku, he proclaimed the edict, saying, "Venerable One, rise and give thanks. Zàn sat motionless, his cold tears dripping down his chin, showing not the slightest sign of movement.
He kept this in mind. The messenger marveled at his sincerity and integrity and did not press him further; he returned to report the matter to the Emperor.
The Emperor praised him repeatedly, more than four times without ceasing. Zàn once composed a song, the lyrics of which say: "Utterly still and without affairs, there is no change or alteration."
When there is nothing to do, why need one discuss a single segment? With a direct mind free from distraction, there is no need to sever other matters.
The past has already passed; the future need not even be calculated. Sitting upright and doing nothing—when has anyone ever called for you?
To seek spiritual effort outwardly is to be a fool or a blockhead. Not storing a single grain of rice, one simply knows how to swallow it when meeting food. The world is full [of such people].
Serving people, they chase after one another without ever catching up. I do not delight in being born in heaven, nor do I cherish the fields of merit.
When hunger comes, I eat; when weariness comes, I sleep. Fools laugh at me, but the wise understand. This is not because I am dull-witted; my fundamental nature is simply thus.
If I wish to go, I go; if I wish to stay, I stay. On my body I wear a single tattered robe, and on my feet I wear the trousers given by my mother. Much...

To speak further is merely to add more words; from the beginning, we have only been misleading one another. If you wish to deliver sentient beings, there is no better way than to first deliver yourself.
Do not vainly seek the "True Buddha," for the True Buddha cannot be seen. As for the wondrous nature and the numinous hall, when have they ever been subject to conditioning or refinement?
The mind is a mind of non-action; the face is the face given by one's mother. Though the kalpa-stone might be moved, that which lies within it never changes. There is nothing.
The matter is fundamentally without a matter; why must one read words? Eradicate the root of self and other, and you will darkly merge with the meaning within.
All manner of straining the sinews and bones is not as good as sleeping soundly beneath the forest trees. When you lift your head and see the sun is high, go from door to door to beg for food.
To apply effort upon effort leads only to increasing confusion; if you grasp at it, you do not get it, but if you do not grasp, you naturally penetrate it. I have one...

The words are: "Cut off thought and forget conditions; they cannot be skillfully explained, but are transmitted only through the heart-mind. There is yet one more phrase: there is nothing better than to give it directly.
Subtle as a fine hair-tip, vast beyond any location, it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected, requiring no laborious weaving.
Worldly affairs are wearying; they are not as good as the mountain peaks. Green pines shade the sun; azure streams flow forever. Mountain clouds serve as curtains; the night moon is the lamp."
A hook. Reclining beneath the wisteria vines, with a block of stone for a pillow, I do not court the Son of Heaven; how could I envy princes and lords?
With no anxiety regarding life or death, what more is there to worry about? Water-moon has no form; I am always simply at peace. All phenomena are thus; they are fundamentally unborn.
Sitting naturally without affairs, when spring comes, the grass grows green of its own accord.
*General Chronicle of the Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Lōngxìng Era*, Scroll Eighteen;
*General Chronicle of the Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Lōngxìng Era*, Scroll Nineteen.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zǔxiù of Shíshì, Lōngxìng Prefecture.

In the first year of the Yuanxing era of the Tang dynasty, Chan Master Zhànrán of Jīngxī addressed his disciples at the time of his death, saying: "The Great Way has no fixed direction and no substance.
Whether one is born or dies, its underlying principle is one and the same. I shall lay my bones on this mountain; tonight, my karmic retribution comes to an end. Thus he spoke briefly.

I shall discuss the Way with you and reach a definitive conclusion. A single thought-moment devoid of marks is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that no dharma is not fully contained within it is called the provisional (*upāya*).

That which is neither identical nor different is called the Middle (*madhyama*). In the state of ordinary beings, these are the three causes; in the state of the Sages, they are the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
When burning a wick, the beginning and the end share the same nature; when crossing the sea, the shallow and the deep flow differently. Self-benefit and benefiting others both reside herein.
"Take this to heart! Having finished speaking, he passed away. Liang Su of the Hanlin Academy inscribed the following on the back of his stele:

"When the Sage does not appear, there must surely arise one destined for the world. Since the Dharma was entrusted by the Wisdom-King (Jñānaprabha) to Guanding, it has reached Zuoxi after two generations.
The Way was clear yet appeared obscure; it awaited this Master to be revealed. Riding this precious vehicle, he has caused a brilliant revival."

Among those who received his instruction and attained mastery of the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) were thirty-nine individuals. Furthermore, dozens of gentry scholars (*jinshen xiansheng*) of high rank and eminent reputation humbled themselves to receive his teaching.

His teacherhood was solemn and his Way was revered; those both far and near turned toward him with benevolence. This could not have been the case unless he were a sage of the highest order, second only to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
How was this achieved? In the second year of the Zhenguan era, Liang Su of the Hanlin Academy completed his *Commentary on the Tiantai Practice of Stopping and Contemplation* (*Zhiguan lun*).

He composed the "General Preface to Stopping and Contemplation" (*Zhiguan tongli*), stating: "What is the purpose of stopping and contemplation? It is to guide the principles of the myriad transformations and restore them to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Reality...
What is this "limit"? It is the fundamental nature of things. That which prevents things from returning to their source is caused by darkness and movement.
To illuminate darkness is called clarity; to arrest movement is called stillness. Clarity and stillness are the essence of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

In the causal stage, they are called *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; in the resultant stage, they are called wisdom (*jñāna*) and concentration (*samādhi*). The causal stage is called practice. The resultant stage...
This is called "accomplishment" (*cheng*). The practitioner is one who practices this; the accomplished one is one who realizes this. To trace its origin:
the Sage perceived that delusion is sufficient to ruin the will and movement is sufficient to lose one's direction.

Thereupon, he ceased [the flow] to observe it and remained still to clarify it, so that when there was movement, there could be stillness, and when there was stillness, there could be clarity. Thus, by relying on their mutual dependence, he established the Dharma. This is...
He illuminates the fundamental by transcending all dependencies; he drives the great chariot to maintain rectitude.

He rides upon the great enterprise to consolidate sovereign power, attuning himself to the field of non-duality and inspiring others within the realm of the three teachings. Reaching the utmost subtlety, he exhausts his nature; reaching the utmost complexity, he embodies the spirit.
Speaking of the near, even a single hair’s worth of goodness can lead one through; speaking of the far, there is the gate of the double mystery.

It may be glimpsed. By employing the ultimate in circularity to make it round, things are free from partiality. By employing the ultimate in substantiality to make it real, things are free from delusion.
The Sage raises up his words to provide demonstration; he broadens his perspectives to provide instruction. He treats them with ease and gentleness, causing them to seek the truth for themselves;
he provides models for deliberation, causing them to arrive at realization on their own. This is the origin of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
It is thus. Now, what are the Three Truths? They are the One. What are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle? These are the names for the One.

Emptiness and the provisional are terms of mutual relation; the Middle Way is the name for attaining the One. This is an explanation based on conceptual thought, not the ultimate principle of the One.
When one reaches the One, it is the Three; when one reaches the Three, it is the One. It is not a matter of mutual containment.
It is so because it is so. It is not so because of mutual generation; it is not a matter of numerical categories; it is not a forced designation.
It is the principle of spontaneity (*ziran*). That which is spoken and transmitted is the trace (*ji*); the principle is called the root (*ben*), and the trace is called the branch (*mo*).
The root is the ground reached by the sages; the branch is the teaching demonstrated by the sages. By means of the root...
As for the manifestation of traces, they may be categorized as small or great, common or particular, sudden or gradual, manifest or secret, provisional or real, fixed or unfixed.

By following these traces back to the source, they become one and great, perfect and real, non-abiding, the Middle, the Wondrous, and the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*). This is the synthesis of the "one" and the "three. What is...

That which is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā) is spoken of in reference to the universal permeation of all phenomena. That which is called "provisionality" (upāya) is spoken of in reference to the establishment of all phenomena.
That which is called "the Middle Way" (madhyamā-pratipad) is spoken of in reference to the wondrous perfection of all phenomena. In destroying all delusions, nothing is more effective than emptiness.
In establishing all phenomena, nothing is more effective than provisionality. In ultimately realizing all natures, nothing is greater than the Middle Way. Thus it is said:
In the midst, there is no dharma that is not the Middle Way; from the perspective of the provisional, what dharma is not provisional?
To cite emptiness, there is no dharma that is not empty. To perfect these is called the Three Virtues; to cultivate them is called the Three Contemplations. To state their essence:

is this not the teaching of the sages who fathom the profound, investigate the subtle, exhaust principle, and exhaust nature? It causes the ignorant to become enlightened and the obstructed to become unimpeded. Through such unimpededness, one attains awakening.

Awakening leads to arrival; arrival leads to constancy; constancy leads to exhaustion [of phenomena]. Clarity leads to illumination; illumination leads to transformation; transformation leads to fulfillment; fulfillment leads to oneness.

The Sage has a means by which he encompasses all dharmas without error, pervades ten thousand kalpas without contradiction, sustains as many worlds as grains of sand in the Ganges without attachment, and returns to the state of non-substantiality without being nothingness. He is given the provisional name "Buddha."

It is forcefully designated as "Awakening. To investigate its essential meaning: is there any virtue greater or more sublime than that of liberation and sovereign mastery? Such is the accomplishment of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). What is called "Perfect and Sudden" (*yuan-dun*) is neither gradual nor indeterminate; it refers to the meaning of the ten chapters of the treatise. These ten chapters expand upon the beginning and end, serving as the gateway to the Way. As for the five summaries (*wu-lüe*): [The text continues with the five summaries:

1. The Summary of the Three Contemplations 2. The Summary of the Ten Modes of Practice 3. The Summary of the Ten Profound Gates 4. The Summary of the Ten Suchnesses 5. The Summary of the Ten Realms of Sentient Beings These five summaries are the essence of the ten chapters. They are like a single thread that binds the ten chapters together, or like a single finger pointing to the moon. By means of these five summaries, one can understand the ten chapters; by means of the ten chapters, one can understand the five summaries. Thus, they are mutually inclusive and interdependent. This is the principle of the Perfect and Sudden teaching. It is not that the Perfect and Sudden excludes the Gradual or the Indeterminate; rather, it encompasses all three. Therefore, the Perfect and Sudden is the ultimate vehicle, the supreme path, and the most profound doctrine. Those who practice according to this teaching will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood. This is the definitive conclusion of the *Mohe Zhiguan*. May all sentient beings, through this, realize the Great Enlightenment. [End of excerpt]

To cite its grand framework, it is the ferry for crossing the stream. The ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) are the pivotal mechanisms that trigger [awakening] and the truths upon which contemplation is established.
The ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) are the gates for the practice of manifesting conduct through sublime function.

It begins with right contemplation and culminates in the manifestation of the objects, because the full meaning is thereby complete. To omit any of these is not essential to cultivation. What, then, are the "vehicles"?
It is that which carries all things and moves them. What are these ten? They are the matters that complete the task of carrying.
To know the subtlety of the realm and arrive there without traveling is the pinnacle of virtue. It relies solely on the One; how could it depend on the nine?
These nine are nothing other than the doctrine of mutual generation, a path trodden by those who have not yet arrived. Therefore, one who gives rise to the mind does so from nowhere.
To "arouse" [the mind] means to settle the mind where there is nothing to be settled; to "pervasively shatter" means to shatter everywhere where there is nothing to be shattered.

Even down to the other vehicles, all are spoken of only because there is no alternative. As for distinguishing their principles and categories, organizing them into chapters and headings, expanding upon them does not constitute prolixity, and synthesizing them does not result in deficiency. They are like linked rings that cannot be untied, or like pearls strung together.

They must not be confused. Like a mirror suspended on high, it cannot be obscured; like a flowing river, it cannot be dammed. The various schools of debate have many gates, yet this is no mere wrangling;
following the correct meaning of the scriptures, these are no empty words. In distinguishing the shallow and deep of the four teachings, there is a source;
in establishing the causes and conditions of a single matter, there is no omission in principle. Alas! *Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are the means by which the Way is clarified to save the world.
Is this not a book? Were it not for one whose sage wisdom is transcendent, standing alone and eminent, who could have composed it?

Were it not for one whose intelligence is profound and far-reaching, who has grasped the meaning and forgotten the symbols, who could have understood it? Yet people today exclusively employ chapter-by-chapter commentaries and literal characters to explain it;
how can they be so negligent and superficial? Or when they speak of the "inconceivable realm" (*acintya-viṣaya*) and the "un... [the text here is incomplete].
Matters that can be contemplated belong entirely to the realm of the most holy; even the Perfectly Enlightened Sages have not yet exhausted them.

If an ordinary person, with a mind subject to arising and ceasing and the three delusions raging within, attempts to infer the supreme and subtle principle through verbal discourse, it is like a dung beetle attempting to describe the Great Peng bird, or a summer insect debating the layered ice of winter—the impossibility of its clarity is evident. Now, regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:
The explanations regarding the myriad characters of the written word may be extensively sought, yet they offer no benefit to a beginner.
How can this compare to practicing in quietude for oneself, where merit arrives of its own accord? Why must one make premature calculations a matter of concern? This is most certainly not so.
For what is called the realm of the supreme sages—is it not separated by vast distances and utterly severed from the ordinary world? It is simply a single nature.
To attain it is called awakening; to lose it is called delusion. It is but a single principle. Through delusion one becomes an ordinary person; through awakening one becomes a sage.

The deluded person isolates themselves, but the principle does not isolate itself. The one who loses it loses it of their own accord, but the nature is never lost. This is the purpose of the composition of *Zhi Guan*.
Therefore, by transcending difference and identity, one investigates the sagely and spiritual; this causes the true nature of all living beings to accord with principle.

That true nature accords with principle so that one may traverse the path of awakening and reach the wondrous realm. If one does not understand this teaching, then into what shall one's learning enter?
Where shall one's merit be applied? From where shall wisdom be elicited? It is like being without eyes, obscured regarding the sun and the moon.
"O Light! To travel through places of profound peril and then to stumble and fall—how could this be endured? Alas!

Since the Sage departed long ago and no worthy sages have appeared, the masses of common and ignorant folk possess only consciousness. This has allowed demonic and heterodox delusions to flourish, with various factions burning fiercely together.
Amidst empty and profuse talk, they create pits and traps. Some are so bound by the literal words that they dare not move; others..."
Those who drift upon the vast surging waves and cannot remain steady include: those who are too far away and willingly accept not reaching their goal;
those who are too near, being their very own selves; those who mistake a withered tree for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and those who mistake a hollow sound for wisdom (*prajñā*).
There are those who run headlong along paths that are not the Way yet speak of "expediency" (*quán*); those who rely on ghosts and spirits yet speak of "penetration" (*tōng*);

those who let their minds wander yet speak of "broadness" (*guǎng*); those who rarely speak yet claim it is "secrecy" (*mì*); and those who transmit [teachings] through whispers from tooth to tongue, claiming them to be "oral instructions" (*kǒu jué*).
All such types establish themselves as patriarchs and, succeeding those patriarchs, form distinct lineages. They subvert the Classics and disparage the Sages; those who are ignorant [follow them].
It was not realized. Confucius had a saying: "The Way is not clearly understood; I know the reason for this—it is because of entanglement with external things. How tragic!

From the year of the passing of the Great Master Zhi (Zhiyi) in the eighteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty until the Jianzhong era of our present dynasty, nearly two hundred years have elapsed.
This tradition was transmitted through five masters in total. The first was Guanding; next was Jin’yun Wei;
followed by Dongyang Xiaowei; then Zuoxi Master Lang; and the fifth was Jingxi Master Ran.
Among his fellow disciples, Guanding was foremost in wisdom and understanding; he was able to follow his master’s instructions and compile this work.
This is because they did not take literary composition as their primary concern. At times they fell into prolixity; at other times, when they achieved success, it was crude.

During the period between the two Wei dynasties, they merely transmitted the teachings in sealed secrecy. Thus, their Way did not flourish. It was only during the Tianbao era that Zuoxi first began to propagate and explain them, yet those who understood them were few.
Jingxi then expanded upon them through several hundred thousand words of biographies and commentaries, laboriously weaving together the remnants of the Dharma.
It is complete. After the passing of Jingxi [Zhiyi], those who understood his teachings were merely three or four people.
An ancient said: "To know by birth is the highest; to know through learning is next; to be distressed by it yet not learn is the lowest.
Now, one who knows by birth is one whose nature possesses the inherent virtue (*xingde*); one who knows through learning is one whose celestial mechanism (*tianji*) is profound.
If one’s sensual desires are deep and their ears and eyes are blocked, they will not understand despite studying; this is the lowest [grade].

It causes the student to be afflicted internally by obscurations and externally enslaved by distractions, such that throughout their life they cannot master the texts, and after several years they cannot obtain any benefit.
Thus, the pursuit of literary studies becomes like wearing shackles and clogs upon one's feet; the entanglement of phrases becomes like winnowing chaff.

It is like having grit in one’s eyes. Because teachers were incapable and disciples failed to comprehend, it is for this reason that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* have not yet been fully illuminated in the world.
You have long been distressed by this; therefore, you have rectified the grand framework and grasped the essential pivot.
Regarding where the principles reside and where the teachings are urgent, you have either rearranged them or expanded upon them. As for those meanings that were circuitous...

The language of these words is vulgar; some have weeded them out, while others have polished them. Generally, nine-tenths of the faults of superficiality and looseness have been cured, and of the requirements for expansion and brevity, one-third remains.
Thus, having removed vulgarity and stagnation to guide the ignorant, I dare not say I am bestowing this upon others;
yet for those who share my vision and practice, may they not hold me guilty of failing in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and may I have no secrets to hide from them.

To you! This undertaking began on the first day of the Jiazi year of the Shangyuan era of the Zhongzheng period; after three years, when the year reached the Zhi-mu (the Tidal Ford of the Splitting Wood), the work was completed.
The Discourse says: Liang Su’s Collected Works consist of twenty fascicles, for which his friend Cui Gong composed a preface, praising Su as a man of Heaven... [text continues].
He was a disciple of the Great Master Yuanhao of the Tiantai school. He served in successive official capacities as Palace Lecturer, Compiler for the History Bureau, and Hanlin Academician.
He passed away at the age of forty-three. Regarding all his Buddhist compositions, they were so refined, profound, and far-reaching that none in the world could rival them.
Beholding his work, "Tongli" (The Comprehensive Precedents), one truly believes this statement.
More than fifty years later, Li Ao (styled Xizhi) composed the *Fu xing shu* (Treatise on the Restoration of Human Nature).
He had profoundly investigated its origins and sources, for his work emerged from that same framework;

often, the initial formulations and underlying principles coincide, differing only in the citations and the arrangement of categories. Thus, Sui’s literary style was deeply derived from the Master’s instruction.
He was far beyond compare. They studied under him and emulated his example. Among his teachings were what are known as the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*).

Might these two masters not have shared in the profound and subtle generosity and kind speech? By integrating and transforming their peers—those extraordinary and eminent individuals—they restored their original nature, allowing them to realize the natural radiance of their fundamental ground (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), did they not?
In the second month of the fourth year of the Yuanzhen era, the Great Master Mazu Daoyi of Jiangxi entered nirvana. The Master was a native of Shifang in Hanzhou;
his appearance was robust and imposing. He had the gait of an ox and the gaze of a tiger, his tongue could extend past his nose, and beneath his feet were the marks of two wheels.
He encountered Chan Master Huairang and attained a secret realization of the mind-dharma. He first resided at Jianyang, then moved to Linchuan, and subsequently to Nankang;
wherever he went, he gathered disciples, preached the Dharma, and established Chan monasteries. During the Dali era, he began residing at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang.
He once addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, believe that your own mind is the Buddha. This very mind is the Buddha. [This was] Bodhidharma the Great...
The Master has come here from Southern India to transmit to this Middle Kingdom the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle’s Single Mind, so as to cause you all to attain awakening.
Furthermore, he cites the text of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the ground of the minds of sentient beings.

Fearing that you might be deluded and lack self-confidence regarding this Dharma of the Single Mind—which each and every one of you possesses—the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Buddha’s word takes the mind as its essence."
The Gateless is itself the Dharma-gate. It is further said: "One who seeks the Dharma should have nothing to seek. Outside the mind there is no separate Buddha;
outside the Buddha there is no separate mind. Do not grasp at good, do not grasp at evil; rely on neither of the two extremes of purity or defilement.
Realize that the nature of offenses is empty, for in every thought-moment they are ungraspable and lack intrinsic nature. Therefore it is said: 'The triple world is but mind. The myriad phenomena..."
And all myriad phenomena are sealed by this single Dharma. Whatever forms one perceives are themselves the perception of the mind.

The mind does not exist as a mind of its own accord; it exists because of form. These are merely conventional expressions according to the occasion. Whether in terms of phenomena or principle, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
It is the same with the fruit of the Bodhi path: that which arises within the mind is called "form. Because one knows that form is empty, what arises is itself non-existent.
"Born! If you understand this meaning, you may then wear clothes and eat food according to the occasion to nourish the holy embryo, passing the time with effortless spontaneity.
What further matters are there? You have received my instruction; listen to my verse: 'The mind-ground is explained according to the occasion; Enlightenment is likewise only peace.
When phenomena and principle are both unimpeded, That which is born is, in truth, unborn. The Master passed away at Kaiyuan. First...
This master once traveled through Shimen at Letan in Yuzhang.

Admiring the extraordinary beauty of the mountains and waters and the level expanse of the caves and gullies, he looked back at his disciples and said, "When my decrepit body returns to the dust, let my bones be laid here.
Consequently, when his time came, his disciples enshrined his remains and *śarīra* relics and established a *dharmaparyāya* site at Shimen. The Chancellor Quan Deyu composed an inscription for it.
Emperor Xuanzong bestowed upon him the posthumous title of Chan Master Daji. His disciples who received the Dharma numbered one hundred and thirty-nine in total;
each became a patriarch in their own region, effecting endless transformation. By this time, the Chan school had reached its peak of flourishing throughout the world.
Chan Master Dazhu Huihai was a native of Jianzhou. He first visited Mazu, who asked him, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From Dayun Temple in Yuezhou. Mazu asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here? He said, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma."
The Patriarch said, "Do not look away from your own treasure storehouse. Why do you abandon your home and wander about? Here, I have not a single thing; what Buddhist Dharma do you seek?
The Master then prostrated himself and asked, "Which one is this, O Wisdom-Ocean, that is my own treasure storehouse?
The Patriarch replied, "That which is now questioning me is your treasure storehouse. It is fully possessed in its entirety, with nothing lacking."
Since mastery is inherent, why falsely seek it elsewhere? Under the Master’s words, he recognized his own original mind without relying on intellectual cognition.
After completing his prostrations and expressions of gratitude, he served the Master for a long time. Later, because his preceptor had grown old, he returned to provide for him.

He then concealed his traces and hidden his abilities, appearing outwardly dull and mute. He composed one scroll titled *The Essential Gate to Sudden Enlightenment and Entry into the Way* for those who were interested in the Dharma.

He secretly departed. When Mazu saw him, he immediately addressed the assembly, saying, "In Yuezhou there is a great pearl; it is perfectly round and bright, its light penetrating through, free and unimpeded.
Among the assembly was one who knew that the Master’s original surname was Zhu (meaning "pearl"), so they went together to search for him.
From this point on, the Master’s reputation for the Way became prominent. His preaching of the Dharma surged like billowing waves and surging seas, vast and unimpeded.
The *Dunwu men* (Gate of Sudden Enlightenment) and the *Guangyu* (Extensive Discourses) were circulated in the world.
In the sixth year [of the Dali era], Chan Master Shitou Xiqian passed away. Having received the Dharma from Qingyuan, he resided at Nan Temple on Mount Heng during the Tianbao period.

Many spirits and deities of the Southern Peak often appeared before him to listen to the Dharma, and the Master would bestow the precepts upon them all. During the Dali period...
In the central Yangtze region, Mazu was the master; in Hunan, Shitou was the master. Travelers came and went in great numbers, flocking to the gates of these two Great Beings.
Once, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The dharma-gate of my teaching was transmitted by the Buddhas of the past. It does not concern itself with meditative concentration or diligent effort."
One realizes only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision: mind is itself Buddha. Mind, Buddha, sentient beings, bodhi, and afflictions differ in name but are one in essence.

You should know that the substance of your own spiritual mind is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; its nature is neither defiled nor pure. It is profoundly still and perfect, equal for both ordinary beings and sages.
Its application is boundless, transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness. The three realms and six paths are nothing but yourself.

The mind manifests. How could the moon in water or an image in a mirror have arising or ceasing? You all should know that there is nothing it does not encompass. When the Master first read the *Zhao lun*, he saw the passage:
"Only the sage can take the myriad things as himself. He then attained a sudden enlightenment and said: "The sage has no self; there is nothing that is not his own self.
Thereupon, he composed the *Cantong qi* (The Mysterious Agreement), the opening lines of which say: "The mind of the Great Immortal of the land of India..."
The East and West have transmitted the secret seal; human faculties are either sharp or dull. The Way has no Northern or Southern patriarchs;

the spiritual source is bright and pure, while its branches and streams flow on in obscurity. To cling to phenomena is fundamentally delusion; to accord with principle is likewise not awakening. In every gate, in all circumstances—

Mutual interpenetration and non-interpenetration: when they interpenetrate, they mutually involve one another; otherwise, they abide according to their respective positions. Form originally has distinct substances and images; sound fundamentally lacks pleasure or pain.
Darkness accords with the words of superior, middling, and inferior; clarity and turbidity are manifest in their phrases. The natures of the four great elements return to themselves.

Like a child finding its mother; fire is hot, wind is movement, water is moist, and earth is solid. The eye perceives form, the ear perceives sound, the nose perceives fragrance, and the tongue perceives saltiness and acidity.
Yet, though each phenomenon depends upon these [senses], they are distributed according to their roots and leaves; from beginning to end, they must all return to the fundamental source.
The noble and the humble employ their respective words. Within light there must be darkness; do not meet with darkness alone.
Within darkness there must be light; do not gaze upon light alone. Light and darkness face one another, like successive steps. All things possess their own inherent efficacy.

One should speak of both function and locus. In practice, it is like the meeting of a box and its lid; in principle, it is like the point of an arrow’s tip. When receiving words, one must grasp the source; do not establish your own arbitrary rules.
If you do not realize the Way upon seeing it before your eyes, how can you know the path as you take your steps? Advancing forward is neither far nor near.
Delusion obstructs the mountains and rivers; I respectfully address those who investigate the profound mystery: do not let your time be spent in vain. The Commentary states:
Regarding the *Stonehead Chanmen Cantong Qi* (The Stonehead Chan School’s Verse on Accordance with the Truth), Qingliang Dafayan provided a commentary upon it.
Its profound meditative verses and wondrous phrases cause the reader to sigh three times in admiration without end. Huang Shan谷 once asked the monastics: "What did Mugu say?"

What kind of words were these songs? I was unable to explain them at all. Later, I saw that when Liu Mengde served as the Prefect of Kuizhou, there was a *yuefu* (court music) titled "Muhugē" (Song of Muhu), which appeared to be a ritual song for propitiating deities; yet even this remained unintelligible to me.
While in Qianzhong, I heard those propitiating the gods singing a song at night, which said: "Listen to our Muhu arriving," and so on until the end.

"Do not burn paper money for the dead; go back home. Thus we know that Su Xi, a native of Jiazhou, intentionally composed this song to emulate the melodies of the Ba people. It is like Shitou studying Wei Boyang’s *Cantong qi*.
I say that while Huangbo’s account of the "Muhou" song is already established as such, the *Cantong qi* is what profoundly elucidates the esoteric intent of Caoxi.
Thus he established the school of the Stonehead (Shitou) tradition; it is truly an imperishable classic for ten thousand generations.

In the twelfth year, Li Si, the Minister of Rites and Regional Inspector of Hedong, prepared the full ceremonial rites to welcome the Dharma Master.

Chengguan entered the capital. Upon his arrival, an imperial decree was issued ordering him to collaborate with the Kasmirian Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā in translating the Sanskrit manuscripts of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (the "Later Section") presented by the Kingdom of Uḍḍiyāna.
The Emperor personally attended the translation assembly for one day; when he failed to appear, he immediately dispatched the monk Jiguang to convey his intent, stating:

Jingguan received the Imperial decree and, having completed the translation and proclamation, presented it to the Emperor. The Emperor commanded him to expound the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The assembly of ministers gathered in great numbers. Jingguan ascended the high seat and said: "Our Sovereign governs the realm; his virtue harmonizes with Heaven and Earth, and his glory dwells throughout the myriad regions."

Re-translations were brought as tribute; with the east wind entering the seasonal laws, the Western Heaven offered across the sea its sincerity. With imperial calligraphy from South India, the Northern Palace received the reverence of a tributary state.

Chengguan, reflecting upon his great good fortune and feeling deep devotion to this glorious era, received the imperial decree at the translation hall to assist in the profound elucidation of the text according to the Emperor’s intent.
With hands clasped in joy and trembling with awe, I have read this three times, exhausting my own meager wisdom. A drop of dew falling upon heaven and earth contains the flavors of a hundred rivers;

a grain of dust added to Mount Hua increases its height by no more than ten thousand *zhang*. To reach the very limits of emptiness and space, its essence is boundless—this is what is meant by "Great."

This constitutes the magnificent framework of this one scripture, which manifests the radiance of true light. To accord with one's original nature, there is no stage that can be reached without practice;

All of these were like ancient brocade embroidered with gold, fashioned according to the capacity of each vessel.

He authored the *Lüzong xingyuan* (The Source of Practice in the Vinaya School) in twenty-one fascicles. Initially, when Jue traveled to the capital, his fame resounded throughout the imperial precincts.

In the past, Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu and Master Fayue of Mount Zhong both used literary composition to broaden the minds of others and to assist later students, enabling them to reach the ultimate through principle and attain awakening by means of words. Could this not be considered one branch of the profound discipline?
The Elder Fazhao of Wuxing extracted the essence of the Six Arts and stood preeminent among those beyond the secular world; those who entered his chamber were...
The Venerable Che of Wozhou: The mind of this Master was merged with the void and non-being, yet his traces were entrusted to written words;

Its transformations were like the alternating tones of wind through pines or the clashing of ice and jade; like a thousand-fathom peak where golden and azure hues shine beneath the layered cliffs, they startled the eyes of this vulgar man.
At first he did not dare to look at him; after three repetitions, however, he became serene. A natural harmony was hidden within him;

thus, by observing his countenance and examining his words, one could know his mind without waiting for the environment to become still. This being so, how much more so must it be for Mount Guiji, whose mountains and waters have been preeminent and sublime since antiquity?
During the Eastern Jin dynasty, many recluses sought refuge here from the world. In the fifth month of summer, the Master returned to this region from Mount Luofeng.
I know that as he brushed aside his monastic robes and sat upon a light boat, tracing the river against the mirror-like surface of the water, he must have found exquisite verses in his stillness.
Thereafter, one enters further into emptiness and stillness until all worldly concerns are washed away; thus, the objects and realms of the former state are but mere weeds and tares.
A person of humble station like myself is currently occupied with emulating his exemplary conduct and looking up to him with longing; how could I dare lament being separated from his company?
De-yu was also on close terms with Meditation Master Xuan. When Xuan took his leave to return to Tianzhu Temple, De-yu composed a preface to see him off, saying:

I have long savored this Dharma and have long desired to discuss it with someone. Eventually, I encountered Master Xuán; indeed, the Master—

His bodily discipline, mind, and wisdom are united with the boundless. Having come from the sublime landscapes of Mount Gui and the waters of Wu, he now proceeds to the pure realm where the Tianshi [Indians] once practiced their itinerant life.

Is it not that his true substance lies beyond mere names? The people of Hangzhou revered him so much that they did not address him by name, but called him "The Master of the Western Ridge.

On the fourteenth day of the fourth month in the fifteenth year, on the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, an imperial decree was issued for the relevant authorities to prepare ceremonial carriages to welcome Professor Master Chengguan into the inner palace to expound the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka*.
As Chengguan ascended the high seat, he declared: "How great is the True Realm! Ten thousand..."
The Dharma initiates all things; it encompasses both emptiness and existence while transcending all marks. It enters the realm of words and images yet leaves no trace.

Those who attain this wondrous existence do not find it to be existent; those who attain this true emptiness do not find it to be empty. Birth and cessation find within it true permanence; dependent origination finds within it mutual illumination.
Our Buddha attained this and wondrously practiced true awakening, utterly purifying the habitual tendencies of defilement, remaining serene amidst the myriad transformations.

Within this realm, activity and function unfold within a single void; bodies and lands are harmonized so that they contain one another, while sounds and light flow forth to illuminate the far reaches.

Our Sovereign has attained this, his spiritual discernment reaching the ultimate void and his being preserving the great harmony. His sagely writings eclipse those of a hundred lifetimes, and his pure influence fans out across the myriad nations.
He spreads the profound transformation to awaken the dreaming world and bestows the natural truth upon our innate nature and feelings. Thus we know that—
There is a great void that unfolds boundless illumination; were it not for the true realm (*dharmadhātu*), how could the mind be as pure as space?

The *Avataṃsaka* teaching exhaustively explores this profound purpose and fully traces its source and flow; thus, it is vast and far-reaching, encompassing the profound and subtle, beyond the reach of thought or calculation.
To point to its source: the sensory dust of the passions has its own scriptures, yet the ocean of wisdom is without exterior.
Delusive confusion is not grasping; the profound mystery is not empty. It cannot be consumed by the fires of the four propositions, yet it enters all gateways of the myriad dharmas.
It darkens the two limits into non-duality, and though it moves through a thousand transformations, it is not manifold. Phenomena and principle interpenetrate so that both are forgotten;
nature and characteristics fuse together without end. It is like the clear reflection of the Qin mirror, or like the mutual containment of the celestial pearls—layer upon layer.
The interpenetrating lights appear vividly and simultaneously; thus, one attains perfect realization in an instant and perceives the realm of the Buddhas within a speck of dust or a single hair.
Within the minds of all Buddhas, sentient beings newly and continuously become Buddhas; within the minds of sentient beings, all Buddhas realize the Truth moment by moment.

The Dharma-gate of a single word could not be exhausted even if written with ink as vast as the ocean; a single hair’s worth of goodness is inexhaustible even if the realm of space were to come to an end. Speaking of its meditative concentration:
it unifies the one mind within the mindless state, remaining eternally tranquil amidst the ten thousand movements. The ocean-like stillness of true wisdom contains the light of the nature-emptiness;
the star-like array of the Dharma-body casts its reflection upon the water of the mind. Its perfect sound unfolds eternally without being struck. Thus, the fruit...

The ocean transcends thought as it transmits through the mind; the myriad practices forget illumination yet are cultivated in unison. Gradual and sudden approaches are attained simultaneously without acquisition.
Although the four bodies extend widely and the eight difficulties are instantly transcended, the singular ultimate is proclaimed so loftily that the two vehicles are left beyond hearing.

He acts as a friend to all; everyone takes him as a friend. Encountering the three poisons, the three virtues become perfect; entering a single speck of dust, the one mind becomes pure. Through a thousand transformations, his contemplation remains unchanged;

The commentary states: The Confucian scholar Han Yu composed a poem titled "Seeing Chengguan," which, while praising his talent, was nonetheless very haughty in its tone of address.
All our predecessors who were senior to us have maintained that Chengguan was a teacher to the gatekeepers of seven successive emperors; thus, Han Yu ought not to have behaved in such a manner.

To treat the teacher of one’s sovereign and father with such contempt is incorrect. It appears that [the title] was first bestowed as "National Teacher" (Guoshi) upon his summons in the thirteenth year of the Zhenyuan era;

at this point, Tu Moxi had already served as a secretary to the two regional commanders of Xuanwu and Wuning, entered the capital to serve as a Lecturer of the Four Gates, was subsequently promoted to Censor of the Court of Judicial Review, and was later demoted to the post of Magistrate of Shanyang after being accused of an offense. One should examine the circumstances of their emergence and obscurity, and the relative weight of their significance will then become apparent. This applies generally to all those from the position of Guoshi onwards.

He was indeed capable of such attainment. Thus, during the middle watch of the night, he sighed repeatedly; a divine being then stroked his back, appearing with a form so extraordinary it startled all who saw it, before departing after a brief moment.
From that time on, he exhaustively investigated the sutras and śāstras, refining the essentials of the mind.

Furthermore, he maintained the monastic discipline with such purity and tranquility, and applied himself so diligently to its observance, that the responses of spiritual resonance are too numerous to be fully recorded. Thereupon, he established the Lingyun Hermitage as a place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). He diverted nearby springs to wash away the dust of delusion and frequented the pine-covered ravines to seek coolness.
The red cliffs and cloud-shrouded peaks rose like screens and windows; thus, those who sought his teachings flocked there.
Gazing at the landscape from precarious heights, those who followed his heavy carriage with wings-like urgency were too numerous to count.

For over ten years, he dwelt in the hermitage of Dàlín, whetting the blade of the Dharma and kindling the torch of wisdom, so that those who gathered around him in reverent devotion might sever their bonds, guide their delusions, and attain a state of serene self-realization.
During the Zhèngyuán era, he returned to the Jìtán Temple of Dōnglín, where, by means of my...

The Way was perfected, and my teaching had been disseminated. In the seventh month of the autumn of the fifteenth year, he summoned his disciples and said, "I shall follow the transformation and return.
In an instant, he entered nirvana. He was fifty-seven years of monastic age and seventy-one years of secular life.
