How much more so for this bird, which has propagated the Way extensively and whose sacred realization is manifestly clear—how could one remain silent?
Therefore, without shame, I have recorded this directly in these words.
In the eighth month of that year, Emperor Shunzong abdicated the throne. The Crown Prince ascended the throne, becoming Emperor Xianzong.
Previously, while still in the Eastern Palace, Shunzong had asked Chan Master Fuguang Rumang: "From what direction does the Buddha come? To what direction does he go when he passes away?
Since it is said that he dwells eternally in the world, where is the Buddha now? The Master replied: "The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); his passing..."
He departs toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it eternally abides in the state of no-mind.
Where there is thought, one returns to non-thought; where there is dwelling, one returns to non-dwelling. He comes for the sake of sentient beings; he goes for the sake of sentient beings.

In the pure ocean of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the essence is profoundly still and eternally abiding. The wise should contemplate this well and no longer give rise to doubt or hesitation. The Emperor asked again: "The Buddha, toward—"

Born in the royal palace, he passed away toward the twin śāla trees; he remained in the world for forty-nine years. Furthermore, it is said that there is no dharma to be taught. Mountains, rivers, and the great ocean;
heaven and earth, as well as the sun and moon—when their time comes, they all return to extinction. Who can say they are not subject to birth and death?
Such are the lingering doubts. The wise should discern this well. Manfu replied: "The Buddha-body is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is delusion of nature that is false."
Discrimination [is such that] the Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it has never undergone arising or ceasing. When conditions are present, a Buddha appears in the world;
when conditions are absent, a Buddha enters extinction. He transforms sentient beings everywhere, like the moon reflected in water—neither permanent nor annihilated, neither born nor ceasing.
Birth has never truly been born, and cessation has never truly ceased. One clearly perceives the state of no-mind, which is spontaneously non-existent.
The Dharma was thus preached. When the Emperor heard it, he was greatly delighted. On another occasion, he once asked the National Teacher Qingliang for the essential point of the mind.

The National Teacher replied to him, the gist of which was as follows: "The ultimate Way is rooted in the mind; the dharma of the mind is rooted in non-abiding. The essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous awareness that is never obscured.

Its nature and characteristics are quiescent, yet it encompasses all virtues and functions, subsuming both the internal and external. It is able to be profound and able to be vast. It is not... [text ends]
There is that which is not empty: it is neither born nor extinguished, without end and without beginning; one seeks it but cannot find it, and though one abandons it, one cannot be separated from it.
If one is deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then confusion and suffering will be in disarray; if one awakens to the true nature, then emptiness will be luminous and all-pervading.

Although this is "mind itself is Buddha," it is known only by those who have realized it. Yet, if there is realization and there is knowing, then the sun of wisdom sinks away into the realm of existence.

If there is neither illumination nor awakening, one remains in a state of delusion and obscuration within the Gate of Emptiness. If not a single thought arises, then the boundaries of past and future are severed;

the essence of illumination stands alone, and both things and self are equally suchness. One directly reaches the source of the mind, where there is no wisdom and no attainment, nothing to grasp and nothing to abandon, and neither opposition nor cultivation.
Nevertheless, delusion and awakening depend upon each other, and the true and the false stand in mutual relation. If one seeks the true and abandons...
Delusion is like discarding one’s shadow while exhausting oneself; if one realizes that delusion is itself the truth, it is as if one stands within the shade and the shadows vanish.
If one is without-mind yet forgets not to reflect, then all myriad concerns are cast aside. If one allows the spontaneous flow of tranquil awareness, then all practices are thereby initiated.

Be expansive and let go of whether things come or go; with still, mirror-like discernment, perceive their source and current. Whether speaking or remaining silent, do not lose the profound mystery; whether moving or still, never depart from the Dharma-realm.
When speaking of cessation, both knowing and stillness vanish; when discussing contemplation, both stillness and knowing are illuminated. To speak of realization, it cannot be shown to others;
to explain the principle, it is not understood except through realization. Therefore, awakening to stillness means there is no stillness; true knowing means there is no knowing.
By means of this single mind in which knowing and stillness are non-dual, one accords with the Middle Way in which both emptiness and existence are simultaneously transcended.
In the second year of the Yuanhe era, an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Dayi of Mount Ehu to the Linqide Hall to debate the Dharma. The Emperor attended in person to listen.
A Dharma Master asked, "What is meant by the Four Noble Truths? He replied, "The Sovereign is the One Truth; where then are the other three truths? The Master asked again.
"The desire realm has no dhyāna; dhyāna abides in the form realm. Upon what, then, does this land rely? He replied, "The Master only knows that the desire realm has no dhyāna;
you do not know that the realm of dhyāna has no desire. [The Master] asked, "What is dhyāna? Yì pointed to the empty space with his hand.
The Dharma Master was speechless. The Emperor laughed and said, "The Dharma Master has expounded upon endless sutras and treatises, yet he cannot even manage this one point.
Yì then asked the assembly of masters, "In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, what ultimately constitutes the Way?
One replied, "Knowledge is the Way. Yì said, "It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness. How, then, can there be a 'knower'?"

"This path" refers to having objects of perception while being without conceptual discrimination. The meaning is: one who is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
How could it be that "non-discrimination" is the path? "Having objects of perception" refers to the four dhyānas and eight samādhis as being the path. The meaning is:
the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into any numerical categories. How could the four dhyānas and eight samādhis be the path?
Furthermore, several people came forward to engage him in debate; he refuted them all by seizing upon their own logical vulnerabilities.
He then cited an instance where Emperor Shunzong once asked Chan Master Śīla, "How can the sentient beings of this great earth see their nature and attain Buddhahood?

Śīla replied, "Buddha-nature is like the moon in the water: it can be seen, but it cannot be grasped. Thereupon, [the Master] said to the Emperor, "Buddha-nature is not something that is seen, yet it must be seen. It is like the water..."
"How can one grasp the moon within? The Emperor then asked, "What is Buddha-nature? He replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has just asked.
Emperor Xianzong intuitively grasped the profound meaning; consequently, he came to hold the Chan school in even greater esteem.
As for the man known as Hanshanzi at that time, his clan, lineage, and native village were unknown. He lived in seclusion on Cold Cliff (Han-yen) in Tangxing County, Taizhou;

thus, the local elders referred to him as Hanshanzi. By nature he was emaciated and rustic, fond of wearing a birch-bark hat and wooden clogs, with a fur robe so tattered and frayed that he appeared like one driven mad by the wind. Yet he laughed and sang with composure. His dwelling was near Mount Tiantai.
At Guoqing Temple, there was a monk named Fenggan who was likewise no ordinary man.
He personally fetched water and wood and labored at the pestle and mortar to provide for the needs of the community. He was a friend beyond the mundane world with Hanshanzi.
Previously, while Fenggan was walking along the road to Chicheng, he happened to hear a child crying amidst the weeds; going to look, he saw a boy approximately ten years of age.
When asked about his hometown, he offered no reply at first. [Fenggan] found him extraordinary and led him back to the monastery, ordering him to sweep the grounds.
Because he had been found in the wilds, he was named Shide (The Picked-Up One). Once grown, Shide’s ascetic practices were peerless in their intensity and diligence;
he was esteemed by Fenggan and Hanshan, with whom he traveled. The three of them were exceedingly fond of one another, and the monks of the monastery—

Everyone marveled at this; yet, though they harbored doubts in their hearts, none could discern its meaning. Shide (Shi-de) used to wash the dishes daily, hoping that some leftover rice might remain so he could set it aside as bait.

Both Hanshan (Han-shan) and his companion were capable poets; they would occasionally play among the villagers, and whenever moved by circumstances or inspired by emotion, they would immediately compose poems to express their thoughts.
These were sometimes inscribed on stone walls, sometimes between the leaves of trees, or in wine shops.
His discourse was always transcendent and beyond the mundane; even the renowned masters of antiquity could not approximate it. He described himself as follows:
"Originally, I am no recluse, yet I style myself a 'Man of the Mountains and Forests. When in Lu, I wear a white cap; moreover, I love to wrap my hair in a loose cloth turban."
The Way possesses the integrity of Chao Fu and Xu You; they were ashamed to serve as ministers to Yao and Shun. A monkey wearing a cap is not practicing to avoid the wind and dust. It is also said:
"If you wish to find a place of peaceful dwelling, Cold Mountain can be preserved forever. When a gentle breeze blows through the secluded pines, the sound is even more pleasant when heard up close.
Were it not for those with graying hair who prattle on about Huang-Lao, one would not have failed to return for ten years and forgotten the way back."
At that time, Daowu said: "The presence of a body and the absence of a body—this is both 'I' and 'not-I. Having thus reflected with careful deliberation, he lingered and sat leaning against a rock.
Grass grew between his feet; red dust fell upon his head. He saw people of the world setting out wine and fruit at the spirit’s bed.
He further said: "In the jade hall hang pearl curtains; within it dwells a beautiful maiden, her countenance surpassing that of a goddess."
The Immortal’s countenance was as radiant as peach and plum blossoms. "When the spring mist gathers in the eastern house, the autumn wind rises in the western neighbor's;
were you to live another thirty years, you would be no more than the dregs of sugarcane. Passages such as these were exceedingly numerous. Shidi once served as the master of offerings.
When it was time for the meal, he ate facing the Buddha. Furthermore, before the image of Kauṇḍinya, he rebuked him, saying, "You of inferior roots and ruined seed—what are you doing here?
The monks of the monastery were deeply suspicious of him and would not allow him to receive direct offerings.

Moreover, much of the gruel and rice from the temple deity was left over and scattered by crows and ravens; Śikṣānanda took up his staff, struck the deity, and reviled him, saying, "Even your food is not enough!"
"Can he protect it? How can he protect the monastery? A deity appeared in a dream to the monks of the temple and said, "Shide has whipped me.

When dawn arrived, [the monk] reported this, and every detail was exactly as described. Thereupon, the assembly was struck with wonder. Fenggan departed to wander among the clouds. Toward the end of the Zhenyuan era, Lü Qiu Yin was appointed to govern Taizhou.
As he was about to depart for his post, he suddenly suffered from a headache so severe that even renowned physicians could not cure it. Fenggan...
Gan happened to visit his home and claimed that he was skilled at treating this illness. When Lüqiū heard of this, he went to see him. Gan ordered water to be sprayed over him;
in a short while, the ailment was suddenly eliminated. Consequently, Lüqiū was greatly delighted and showed him profound respect.

He asked where he had come from, and Gan replied, "From Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. Lüqiū asked, "Are there any worthy and enlightened masters there? Gan replied, "There are, but they cannot be sought through worldly [standards]."
Therefore, I seek you out. Hanshan, Shide, Jili, and Puxian have manifested their traces; these two sons are mingled among the monks at Guoqing.

When you go on your official tour, you should come to see them; it would not be right to delay. Not long after Lüqiu arrived from the south on his mission, he entered the temple to visit the remains of Fenggan.
He saw only thatched huts in a desolate state with tigers crouching beside the dwellings. He then re-entered the temple to pay his respects to the two [sages].
The Great Being (Mahāsattva) was led by the temple monks to the rear kitchen. When Lü Qiu paid his respects twice, the Great Being rose and ran away, saying, "Chatterbox Amitābha!
Do you not know me? Why do you bow to me? He then hurried back to the Cold Rock. The following day, Lü Qiu sent gifts to him.
When Han Shan saw the messenger arrive, he cursed him, saying, "Thief! Thief! and then hid away among the rocky cliffs. Shi De also slipped away in secret.
Their final whereabouts were never known thereafter.
The commentary states: In the past, Chan Master Baojue Xin once commissioned the Grand Historian Huang Tingjian (Shan谷道人) to harmonize with the verses of Han Shan.
The Master of Poetry (Su Shi) promised this to Huang Shan-gu. However, after ten days had passed, he had not yet produced a single verse.
Later, upon meeting Baojue, Su remarked, "If you continue to read books and compose poetry for another ten years, you might perhaps rival Tao Yuanming;
as for someone like Han-shanzi, even if you were reborn twice, you could never equal him. Baojue considered these words to be insightful, remarking, "Huang Shan-gu is our Song dynasty's Xiao Ling."

Such are his words. Generally speaking, the intentions of the sages and worthies are profound, subtle, and far-reaching; were it not for one of penetrating insight and clear vision, they could not be discerned.
Having deeply savored the phrasing of these passages, I find them to be like celestial nectar or sweet dew—naturally pure and sublime.
They are by no means comparable to the worldly concoctions seasoned with salt and plum. Lately, those who are deluded...
Vulgar people have sometimes increased their numbers and defiled the ranks with impurities. Alas, what a pity!
In the third year [of the reign], the Chan Master Rūhai of Long’an Temple in Changsha passed away. Liu Zongyuan, the Sima of Yongzhou, composed a stele inscription for him, which states:
"The Buddha was born far from the Middle Kingdom, at a distance of nearly thirty thousand *li*. Since his passing until the present day..."
It has been only two thousand years; thus, the transmission of the Way has become increasingly subtle, and the discourse on Chan has suffered the greatest ailment.
To be restrictive is to be mired in phenomena; to be extravagant is to depart from the truth. As one departs from the truth, extravagance becomes ever more prevalent.

Therefore, those of today who are empty-minded, foolish, deluded, licentious, arrogant, and self-centered all misrepresent Chan to disorder their teachings. They brazenly exploit the dull and ignorant, casting them into remote valleys and wildernesses. This is what makes them different.
To the south of Changsha was the Master Long’an. The Master’s words were: “From Śākyamuni to Siṃha, twenty-three generations passed before they became separated.
Having separated, there arose Bodhidharma; from him to Huike, five generations passed before they became further separated. Having separated, there arose Xiu and Neng.
North and South reviled one another, acting with perversity and fighting with ferocity; thus their Way became obscured. Alas! I shall reunite them.”
Furthermore, those who transmit the scriptures of the world all follow the paths of Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna. The writings of these two masters still exist in their entirety;
by examining them, one finds they accord with his own intent, so there is no need for concern. Thereupon, he studied in the north under Huìyǐn and sought instruction in the south from Mǎsù.
They both rejected what was eccentric to tread upon the level middle way; though their paths diverged, they became increasingly identical—empty and void.

Yi Shi composed the *Anchan Tongming Lun* (Treatise on the Penetration of Illumination through Peaceful Meditation). He argued that by extending the One to reach the myriad things, there is no phenomenon that is not the Real;

and by merging the myriad things back into the One, there is no reality that is not a phenomenon. Because he extended [the One] yet never truly extended it, there was nowhere to which he went; because he merged [the myriad] yet never truly merged them, there was nowhere to which he returned.
Sitting solidly in meditative absorption for ten days or more—this is what is called the application of practice. It is a state of vast, undifferentiated unity.
The mundane is ultimately characterized by flux; this is what is called the "True Constant. While he resided in Changsha, he remained in meditative concentration for fourteen days.
People established a dwelling at that very spot, which subsequently became Baoying Temple.
To the west of Xiang, people further followed his example, carrying large timbers and quarrying fine stones to expand the residence, whereupon it became Longan Temple as well. Minister Pei Gong...

So-and-so, Li Gongso-and-so, Palace Attendant Lü Gongso-and-so, Minister Yang Gongso-and-so, and Censor-in-Chief Fáng Gongso-and-so all honored the Way of their Master and observed the rites of disciples.
He was eighty-one years old in total, having been a monk for fifty-three years.
He passed away on the ninth day of the second month in the third year of the late Yuánhé era. His disciples Xuánjué, Huáizhí, Hào-chū, and others—
Describing his master’s conduct, he requested me to compose an inscription for a stele, saying: "The Master’s surname was Zhou, and his given name was Ruhai. By family tradition, they were scholars.

His father was named Zhejiao, who served as the Judicial Assistant (Lu-shi Can-jun) of Tongzhou. His uncle was named Zheceng, who served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites (Shang-shu Li-bu Shi-lang)."
The Master originally followed the teachings of Śākyamuni, but his father seized his resolve and compelled him to serve as a *zhubó* (magistrate) in Chengdu; he took no pleasure in this.

During the chaos of the Tiānbǎo era, he returned to his original aspiration. He resided for a time at Xīmíng Monastery in the capital and later at Mount Gǔlǚ, finally passing away at Lóng'ān Monastery and being buried at that site.
The inscription reads: "In the cultivation of the Buddha’s path, its profound essence is *dhyāna*. [Yet] they belong to different realms and distinct eras."
Who received its transmission? The Way became obscured and fragmented; it drifted and dispersed, with no means to verify its lateral course.
People merely listened to false words and engaged in empty strife, with the north and south destroying one another—who could reunite them? In Chu there was Long’an; such was the virtue of Long’an.

I contemplate that awakening alone is the principle. Encompassing all within the well, it transcends the extraordinary; manifesting rectitude, it eliminates delusion. Its appearance is obscure while its form is tranquil; its merit flows infinitely.

When movement or speech arise as conditioned phenomena, one remains profoundly still and silent. As for the solemnity of shrines and temples, my dwelling is unadorned. Whether noble or base come to me—
My Way knows no attainment; when it departs, there is nothing to pursue; when it arrives, who can restrain it? It is but the mechanism of the world and the subtlety of the Dao.

Having been set forth and made manifest, it then departs and returns. Phenomenal forms are merely contrived; the true source has no dependence. For those of later generations, whom shall they take as their teacher?
Alas, regarding this stele:
my disciple Haochu was on friendly terms with Zihou. Zihou composed a preface for Haochu’s departure, in which he wrote:
"The Confucian scholar Han Tui-zhi is a friend of mine; he once lamented that I was fond of the words of the Buddha and censured me for associating with Buddhists."
Recently, Li Sheng Chu of Longxi came to me from the capital. After he departed, he sent me a letter reproaching me, saying:

"I observed that in the preface you wrote for Yuan Sheng, you did not condemn the Buddhists. Indeed, there are aspects of Buddhism that cannot be condemned; they often accord with the *Yi* and the *Lunyu*. I truly delight in them.
Their teachings on human nature and emotion are consistent with [Confucianism]; they do not differ from the Way of Confucius."—Tuō-mó (Mencius).
He was fond of Confucianism, yet he was unable to surpass Yangzi. In Yangzi’s writings, there is much that is drawn from Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, and Han Fei.
Is the Buddhist not even more eccentric, perverse, treacherous, and cruel than Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, and Han Fei?

If one says this is because [the Buddha] is a "barbarian" (*yi*) and thus rejects him for being a barbarian while failing to believe in the Way, then would one instead befriend the evil Eral and the robber Zhi, while deprecating Ji Lai?
As for Zhuang Zhou and Yu, they were not what is meant by those who discard names to seek reality.
What I have adopted accords with the *I Ching* and the *Analects*; even if a sage were to be reborn, he could not refute it. What I condemn in them is their outward manifestation:
namely, shaving the head and wearing black robes, having neither husband nor wife, nor father nor son, and living without engaging in agriculture, sericulture, or mulberry cultivation.

If a person were such as this, even I would not find them pleasing. To withdraw in resentment from their outward appearance while neglecting what lies within is to know the stone but not the jade it contains. This is why I delight in the words of the Buddhists.
Those who associate with such people do not necessarily need to master their language; moreover, all who practice that Way do not crave official rank, nor...
They compete for ability; those who delight in mountains and waters and crave peace and leisure are many.
I am weary of the world’s frantic pursuit, where people take only rank and emolument as their task, vying with one another to crush each other. Thus, I have abandoned this path—where else could I go?

This is why my fondness lies in wandering with the Buddhists. Now Hao-chu has stilled his nature and settled his emotions; he reads their scriptures and has mastered the *I Ching* and the *Analects*. Only...
The joy of mountains and waters is refined by literature; furthermore, father and son together practice this Way to sustain themselves and dwell therein.

To remain detached and free from seeking is far superior to those who compose the doctrines of Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, or Han Fei, and who busily pursue rank and emoluments, vying with one another for advancement. Li Sheng Chu and Haochu also...
"It is well that you are going there now. Show them my words, using the northern man Yu as an intermediary, and observe what happens. The commentary states:
Regarding Zihu’s stele inscriptions for the monks of the Southern Peak,东坡 (Dongpo) considered them to be peerless throughout all ages.
This was because their essential purpose accorded with the intent of our Buddha, the Sage’s teaching. [I] have previously compared the New and Old Tang Histories...

I have examined [the records]. Although even the memorials of Wei Zheng, Luo Binwang, and Lu Xun were reduced by more than half in the *New History*, the writings of Zihu (Liu Zongyuan) and Han Yu remained unchanged, not a single word being altered. As for all other matters, their phrasing was entirely transformed while only their underlying intent was preserved.
This is especially true regarding such discourses as those on the feudal system and revenge. Once these arguments had passed through Zihu’s...

Hou Pují utterly refuted all these various theories. Alas! The inscription on the Stele of Master Hǎi states that those who are "empty and foolish, lost in delusion, arrogant and self-centered" all misrepresent Chan to disorder its teachings.
Considering that the Chan school was at its height during his time, it is unlikely that this was universally true;
yet, nearly four hundred years later, it has indeed come to pass exactly as he foretold. How marvelous! [This concludes] the "Sending off Hào."
That the Confucian scholars of the world treat us in this manner at the very outset—how unfortunate it is!

The fourth year [of the reign]. Emperor Xianzong asked his attendants: "Between leniency and severity in governance, which should take precedence? The Chancellor Quan Deyu replied: "The Tang dynasty succeeded the cruelty and oppression of the Sui;
therefore, it should prioritize benevolence and generosity. Emperor Taizong, upon seeing a diagram of the Mingtang Hall, immediately prohibited the punishment of flogging on the back.
All successive sagacious emperors have followed this precedent, holding virtue and instruction in high esteem. Consequently, although the great rebels of the Tianbao era broke out suddenly—"

They were subsequently exterminated. This was likely because the transformation brought about by our dynasty deeply moved the hearts of the people. The Emperor said, "It is truly as you say. De-yu was skilled in debate;

he elucidated the origins and developments of antiquity and the present to awaken the sovereign. As a high minister, he was broad-minded and harmonious, not seeking to be overly scrutinizing or ostentatious in reputation.
His literary works were elegant, correct, and abundant for his time. Regarding the meritorious deeds of the dukes, ministers, marquises, and kings—

Those who were exceptionally outstanding were all commemorated with inscriptions. Although his conduct was free from outward affectation, his refined elegance and natural grace were inherently admirable.
During the Zhenyuan and Yuanhe eras, he served as a paragon for the scholarly elite. Li Deyu once composed the "Record of Chan Master Caiyi’s Seated Meditation," which states:
"In Nanyue of Xinzhou, there is a place of pure seated meditation, and the Chan Master resides there."
As for the origins of this Master, they cannot be detailed with certainty. Initially, a local woodcutter encountered him in the wilds;

his form was solid and motionless, like a clod of earth, as if he were one with the grasses and trees. When the matter was reported to the Prefect, the Master was invited to settle in this place, where he has remained for thirty years.
The people of the prefecture do not know how he came to be there, and thus they called him by the name "Cloth-Clad" (Cao Yi). His feet never touch the ground.
The mouth does not taste flavors; days have no distinction between day and night, and time has no distinction between cold and heat. In the realm of silent stillness, there is but a single rope bed.
While the myriad phenomena are clamorous, this body remains unmoving. Internally, one realizes that the three periods of time and the five aggregates all arise from delusion.
Thereafter, one uses the existence of dharmas to clearly contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, thereby attaining true permanence and the true self within right wisdom.
Within the square inch of the heart, there is profound stillness and emptiness; both body and wisdom are equally pure. Subtle words and gentle speech are occasionally heard.
Whether one traverses the far or near reaches of this realm, or follows the high or low capacities of one's faculties, it is like rain moistening the myriad things or wind moving through the air.
All who step across its threshold attain entry. This is not possible unless one wields the profound mechanism within the formless...
To exhaustively reach the source and bottom of the true nature (*dharmatā*), the four seasons will assail from without and a hundred ailments will arise within.
As for what the ancients called "leaving behind things and distancing oneself from people to stand alone," the Chan Master has attained this. Alas!

Worldly people allow their minds to roam by being moved by external objects; when the mind is shifted by objects, profit and loss arise, and good fortune and misfortune take form. Thus they are led astray and bound by the bridle.
It is fragmented and chaotic, with no return [to the source]. The Perfected Person, however, returns stillness within movement and restores the nature within emotion;
it is from this that the distinctions between early death and longevity, or benevolence and vulgarity, arise. This is merely one explanation according to worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
To the Way of the Chan Master, it is like weeds among grain. In the second year of the Jiànzhōng era, while I was on official duty through Shàngrǎo, the Left Assistant Director Cui—
The Duke went out to serve as an assistant in the commandery; he had probed the flavor of the Chan Master’s teachings. Having mastered them, he recounted them to me in detail.
He brushed away the dust from my collar and joined his hands at my feet, purifying me with goodness through the Master’s physical presence.

Furthermore, he believed that the wondrous intent of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the secret application of Vimalakīrti were both contained herein. How could he have known that this very place of seated meditation would not become [a site of such realization]?
Is this not the preaching of another land? Therefore, I have roughly recorded what I have heard and seen to inscribe upon this stone.
*Lōngxìng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Twenty;
*Lōngxìng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Twenty-One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of the Stone Chamber in Longxing Prefecture.

In the fifth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang Dynasty, the Emperor asked the National Teacher Chengguan: "Regarding that which is expounded in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, what is meant by the 'Dharmadhātu'? He replied:
It is said: The Dharma-realm is the fundamental substance of all sentient beings. From the very beginning, it has been spiritually luminous, vast and penetrating, expansive, empty, and still;
it is nothing other than the single realm of ultimate reality. It possesses no form or appearance, yet it manifests throughout the great trichiliocosm;
it has no boundaries, yet it encompasses all phenomena. It shines brightly within the space between the heart and mind, yet its form cannot be seen.
It shines brilliantly within the realm of sensory objects (*rūpa-dhātu*), yet its principle cannot be divided.

Without the eye of wisdom that penetrates all phenomena and the clear intelligence free from discursive thought, one cannot perceive such spiritual penetration of one’s own mind. Therefore, when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed:
"How marvelous! I now see that all sentient beings universally possess the wisdom and virtue of the Tathāgata."
[The Buddha] explained the marks [of existence], yet because people cling to them through false conceptualization, they are unable to realize them.

Thereupon, he proclaimed the nature of the Dharma-realm and preached the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which, by means of absolute emptiness, eliminates emotional attachments and integrates principle and phenomena in a pervasive, tranquil stillness.

The Emperor, endowed with sagely brilliance, attained a vast realization upon hearing this profound discourse. He then commanded the relevant authorities to prepare the rites for casting seals and transferring the capital.
The Master presided over the monastic community throughout the empire and was titled the State Preceptor Qingliang, Chief Administrator of the Sangha (Sengtong).
On the Bingshen day of the third month of this year, an imperial edict appointed Meng Jian, Counselor-in-Attendance, and Xiao Mian, Assistant in the Secretariat,
to oversee the translation and editorial refinement of the scriptures at Liquan Temple (as recorded in the Old History, Basic Annals).

The Treatise states: From the Han dynasty through the Jin, the Southern and Northern Dynasties, and the sixteen kingdoms until reaching the Tang, there were always Indian monks who came from India as well as Chinese who were proficient in Indic languages, who translated [the scriptures] in alternating succession.
By the Kaiyuan era, Zhisheng’s catalog of the sutras, vinayas, śāstras, and collections compiled by sages and worthies totaled five thousand forty-eight fascicles;
this served as a relatively fixed number. Subsequently, during the Zhenyuan era, another two hundred or so fascicles of new translations by Amoghavajra and others were separately cataloged.
By the time of the Yuanhe era and thereafter, the translation of scriptures was finally discontinued.
At the beginning of the Taiping Xingguo era of our dynasty, three Indian monks—Dharmabhadra, Amoghavajra, and Dānapāla—arrived from Western India.

They were highly proficient in the Chinese language. Emperor Taizong, who had long ago received a prophecy from the Buddha, established a translation bureau at Taiping Xingguo Temple and ordered these three Indian monks to select all the Sanskrit manuscripts stored in the national treasury that had not yet been translated.
Regarding the translation of the scriptures: monks specializing in the study of doctrine from both monastic districts were assembled to carefully determine and finalize the translations.
Furthermore, fifty youths were recruited to practice the Sanskrit script. Among them was Li Weijing, the son of the Prince of Jiangnan;

his quick intelligence surpassed that of others, and he was thoroughly proficient in Indic literature. After some time, he too became capable of translating. Emperor Taizong personally composed the *Newly Translated Sacred Teachings*.
Preface. Upon the accession of Emperor Zhenzong, Chen Nu first submitted a proposal suggesting that the expenses for the translation of scriptures be discontinued.

The Emperor, however, refused to grant his request, as he held the previous reign’s devotion to this cause in high regard. By the time of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, more than five hundred fascicles of newly translated sūtras and śāstras had been produced.
Emperor Zhenzong then composed the "Continuation of the Preface to the Holy Teachings" (Jì Shèngjiào Xù). Thereupon, the translation [work]...

The monks petitioned for the compilation of a catalog similar to that produced during the Kaiyuan era. An imperial decree was issued ordering Zhao Anren and Yang Yi to revise the translations and compile them into twenty fascicles.
Shortly thereafter, the Emperor granted the texts on Buddhist matters composed by Taizong himself, instructing that they be included in the catalog.

Anren and his colleagues submitted a second memorial requesting the inclusion of the Emperor’s own writings on the teachings of Śākyamuni; the Sovereign then bestowed these *dharmas* [teachings] upon them.

The *Yin qian ji* (Anthology of Preceding Sounds) in seven fascicles is appended following the *Tàizǔ Wénjí* (Collected Works of Emperor Taizong), placed at the head of all compilations by the sages and worthies of the Eastern Land.
Alas! Since the era of Emperor Zhenzong, the world has been far removed from the passing of the World-Honored One;
though the scriptures and teachings have indeed been translated in great numbers, they were truly not strictly necessary. For all that is intended for students, even if...
Thus, amidst these thousands of sutras and myriad treatises, I have been led astray by worldly glory and profit; I have idly failed to take them even into my eyes.
I have utterly neglected to reflect upon the hardships with which the former sages established them. It is for this alone that I have never ceased to shed tears.
At that time, the meditator Wuzhuo entered Mount Wutai seeking an audience with the Great Being Mañjuśrī.
Upon reaching the entrance of the Vajra Cave, he burned incense, prostrated, and sat in meditation with his eyes closed. After a short while, he heard the sound of someone shouting at an ox.

Wuzhuo suddenly opened his eyes and saw a mountain-dweller of extraordinary and rugged appearance leading an ox to drink at the stream. Wuzhuo rose and bowed; the mountain-dweller asked, "For what purpose have you come?"
He said, "I wish to see the Great Being Mañjuśrī. The old man replied, "The Great Being cannot yet be seen.
Have you finished your meal? He replied, "Not yet. The old man led the ox back home. He followed in his tracks and soon entered a temple. The old man called out, "Kuntī!
and a young boy came out to greet him at the sound of the voice. The old man released the ox and led him up into the hall. The halls and buildings were all constructed of gold and jade. The old man—

The old man sat upon his couch, pointing to an embroidered stool and commanding the youth to sit. The youth immediately advanced with a mother-of-pearl cup containing a substance like clarified butter or curd;
he bowed and they drank together. As the youth tasted it, he suddenly felt his mind and spirit become exceptionally clear and bright. The old man asked, "From where have you recently come?"
Zhao said, "The South. The Old Man asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the South? Zhao replied, "In this degenerate age, few bhikṣus observe the precepts.
The Old Man asked, "How many followers are there? Zhao said, "Either three hundred or five hundred. Zhao then asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained here?
The Old Man replied, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages dwell together. Zhao asked, "How large is the assembly?"
The old man said, "Three times three before, and three times three after. Thus they conversed until nightfall. Zhe wished to remain, but the old man would not permit it.
Zhe lingered with longing and did not depart immediately. The old man threw back his sleeves and rose, shouting to a servant boy to lead Zhe out.
Zhe could not stay; having walked no great distance, he asked the boy, "Which temple is this? The boy replied, "It is Prajñā Monastery. Zhe was filled with sorrow.
The one who realized this was Mañjuśrī himself. He could not be seen again, so [the elder] prostrated at the youth’s feet and requested a single word as a parting gift.
The youth vanished from sight and sang: “Absence of anger on the face is the offering;
Absence of anger in the mouth emits wondrous fragrance; Absence of anger in the heart is the precious jewel; Stainless and untainted—this is the eternal truth.”
He resided at Mount Wutai due to his devotion, and it was said that he frequently encountered Mañjuśrī there.
During the Yuanfeng era of our dynasty, the Grand Marshal (Taishou) Lü Gong Huìqīng, styled Jífǔ, was a scholar well-versed in both Buddhist and Confucian classics.

He once annotated the *Dharmadhātudarśana* and offered innovative interpretations of the *Zhuangzi*. Taking advantage of his leisure from official duties, he traveled to Mount Tai daily; upon reaching its central peak—
Suddenly, clouds and mist closed in from all sides; a violent wind and thunderous rain roared through the forests and valleys. His attendants were struck with terror and hid themselves.

After a short while, a creature appeared, resembling a dark azure dragon, half-emerging from amidst the clouds and mist. The Grand Commandant was greatly alarmed. After some time, the weather cleared slightly.
Looking outside, he saw a young boy whose body was black and whose hair hung loose. He had wrapped *phoṭī* grass around himself from his feet up to his shoulders and stood bare-chested.
On his right shoulder, he held a *pustaka* (Brahmanic manuscript). He asked the Grand Marshal, "Sir, what have you seen that causes you such terror?
The Grand Marshal replied, "I have long had karmic obstacles; I have encountered this evil realm. The youth said, "Now they are all extinguished.

What do you seek, sir, that brings you here? The Grand Marshal said, "I wish to see the Great Being (*Mahāsattva*). The youth asked, "What is the purpose of wishing to see the Bodhisattva? He replied:
I have perused the Great Teaching of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; its purport is profound and its meaning vast.

I hope that you, O Mahāsattva, will give rise to the mind of understanding and provide an annotated commentary for circulation in the world, so that those in the darkness of night may suddenly attain illumination and those with great resolve may achieve awakening.

The youth said: "The sublime intent of the Buddhas accords perfectly with both principle and phenomena; it is simple, clear, and can be understood by paying close attention to the insights of the former masters.

For instance, in a single chapter such as the 'Ten Stages' (Daśabhūmika), the commentary on the text does not exceed a few sheets. Yet nowadays, the commentaries have become overly prolix, extending to nearly a hundred fascicles."
Yet the Sage’s intent becomes ever more remote; this is truly what is called "shattering the Great Way.
The Grand Marshal said, "A youth with such a countenance as yours dares to rebuke his seniors? The youth smiled and said, "Sir, you are mistaken.

Here, every blade of grass and every tree is none other than the realm of Mañjuśrī. As for your daily activities, if you do not become deluded when encountering things, this is truly Mañjuśrī himself."
"Why have you allowed ordinary sentiments to disturb my thoughts? The Grand Marshal repented of the error in his previous words and immediately prostrated himself with his head to the ground.
Just as he rose, the youth manifested the form of a Great Being (Mahāsattva), mounted upon a lion, and vanished into the clouds without a trace.

From that time forth, the Grand Marshal was filled with remorse and his mind became dazed and confused. When his family members asked for the reason, he replied, "I wish to exhaust my sincerity in repentance."

After some time, he went again to see the Boy in the Reed-Rug. He immediately prepared incense and lamps, vowing to practice this morning and evening until he had seen him, and only then would he stop.
After a long while, he suddenly saw the boy on the incense table scolding him, saying: "Why do you remain attached with such extreme greed for signs?
The Grand Marshal replied: "I simply wish for all people in the world to see the true manifestation of the Great Being’s transformation."
He granted permission and immediately ordered a skilled artisan to paint it. Within moments, [the image] vanished.
Six years later, an imperial decree was issued for Chan Master Huaiyun of Changjing Temple in Jingzhao to move and reside at the Upper Temple (Shangsi).

Disciples from afar flocked there like spokes converging on a hub. Huaiyun addressed the assembly, saying: "The ultimate truth transcends words, yet people of this age do not understand it; they instead force themselves to practice other matters, taking them to be [the goal]."
Its function is such that its self-nature is fundamentally not an object of the sensory realms; it is a subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation.
All its discerning awareness is neither defiled nor obstructed; such radiance has never ceased or been abandoned.
From past kalpas until now, it remains eternally unchanged, like the solar disc which shines upon both the distant and the near. Although it reaches all forms, it does not become fused with anything.
The numinous candle is wondrously luminous and does not require artificial refinement. It is because of a lack of understanding that one grasps at external objects and forms;

this is merely like pressing on the eyes so that illusory flowers appear in the sky—only to exhaust oneself in vain throughout kalpas. If you can reflect back upon yourself, there is no second person.
His actions were such that they did not deviate from the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Layman Pang Yun, courtesy name Daoxuan, was a native of Hengyang. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he visited Master Shitou and attained a wondrous resonance beyond words. One day, Shitou asked him: "Since you first saw me, what have you been doing in your daily life?"

Seven years later, Liu Zongyuan, the Imperial Secretary of Yongzhou, composed the Stele Inscription for Venerable Mita of Mount Nanyue. Its text reads: [The inscription follows.]
During the reign of Emperor Daizong, there was a monk named Fazhao who served as State Preceptor.
He declared that his master, the Great Elder of Mount Nanyue, possessed extraordinary virtue. The Emperor turned southward to pay him homage.

As it was impossible to summon him to court, the Emperor named his dwelling the "Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sanctuary" (Banzhou Daochang) to honor his station. The Master first resided beneath a rocky cliff to the southwest of the mountain. People...
If food was offered to him, he would eat; if not, he would eat earth and mud and consume grasses and trees. His manner of obtaining clothing was likewise.
Those who came from the southernmost reaches of the ocean or the northernmost depths of Youdu seeking his Way might encounter him at a precipice or in a valley;

with emaciated bodies and soiled faces, they would personally carry firewood and fuel as his servants, and it was only through such familiarity that they could approach the Master. All these transformed beings established themselves in the Middle Way.
Yet through the skillful means (*upāya*) of his teaching, he enabled them to arrive swiftly; thus he manifested the power of single-minded devotion.

He inscribed [his teachings] upon the streets and alleys and carved them into the mountain torrents, laboring with great diligence to guide and assist those below. Without seeking it, the Way was perfected; without speaking, all things were accomplished.
People all carried cloth and silk, hewed wood and stone, and deposited them at the mountain retreats. Without resistance or effort, the temple halls were completed, extending even unto...
Emperor Dezong issued a renewed edict to honor and establish the monastery, which was named Mida Temple. Any surplus from these endowments was distributed to those suffering from hunger and illness;
the Master did not take credit for this achievement. The Master first studied under Master Tang of Chengdu, followed by Master Xian of Zizhou.

Master Xian had studied under Master Ren of Dongshan, both of whom were men of the Way. Upon reaching Jingzhou, the Master advanced his studies under Master Zhen of Yuquan, who then transmitted the teachings to him.
He appointed Hengshan as the leader of the teaching, and those who followed him and were transformed by his influence numbered in the tens of thousands. Initially, Fazhao resided at Mount Lu;

while in the meditative state of *samādhi*, he journeyed to the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and saw a man clad in coarse garments attending upon the Buddha. The Buddha told him, "This is Chengyuan of Mount Heng.

Upon emerging from meditation, Fazhao sought him out and found that he was indeed the likeness of the one he had seen. He then studied under him, and it was through this master that the teaching was transmitted throughout the world.
This is his instruction. He served as a monk for fifty-six years; his lifespan was ninety-one years.

On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the eighteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away at the temple. He was buried on the southern ridge of the temple, and a stone inscription was carved to the right of the temple’s main gate.
The epitaph reads: "The single breath of Qi revolves and thins out, vast and without end; Above it there is no beginning, and below it there is no end."
Separated yet unified, obscured yet penetrating; though beginnings and ends may differ, now they are one. In the void and the dark mystery, the Way is harmonized.
The Sage-Spirit leaves no trace, yet manifests the merit of instruction. You lead the multitudes with severity, yet embrace them with tolerance; you establish sincerity by relinquishing the center.
Clad in the protection of grass and water, you shelter the vault of heaven; reaching upward to grasp and looking downward to take.
Eating to sustain the form, he roamed to the infinite, meeting the Great Hero. The Son of Heaven raised his head to follow him as his teacher;
from the four quarters they rushed forward like clouds following the wind. Beginning with a mere cubit, he established the Spirit Palace. Starting from the road of Shu, he reached Linhong;

His transformative influence flowed through ten billion generations, revered by all; he enshrined his dwelling upon the Southern Ridge. His younger brother, named Hong-won, was filial and respectful;
this stone was erected to record his profound traces.

In that land, the three poisons and the eight difficulties do not exist; it is adorned with various jewels, and its people are without...
There are ten fetters and nine afflictions; the multitude of sages take these as their companions.

If there are those who can, with sincere heart and great vows, turn their minds toward this land, provided they possess sufficient power of mindfulness, they shall be born in that country. Thereafter, they shall transcend the three realms and never retreat from the path of Buddhahood.
These words are not deceptive. During the Jin dynasty, Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu composed this *Nian* (Invocation).

The *Buddha-samādhi-yong* was widely encouraged at that time. Subsequently, the Great Master Tiantai Zhiyi composed the *Shi-jingtu-shiyi-lun* (A Treatise on Resolving Ten Doubts Concerning the Pure Land), extensively proclaiming its teachings with thoroughness and subtlety; those who were deluded all relied upon it.
Indeed, there were many who left behind extraordinary traces before departing. Among them were Li Chengzhi, the Prefectural Archivist of Longxing Temple in Yongzhou, and the monk Falin.
The Pure Land Hall was situated to the east of the temple and has been constantly maintained for more than twenty years until now.
Its corners and walls have fallen into ruin, and its images have collapsed. It happened that the Venerable Xun resided beneath this building and first began to restore it.

This Venerable cultivates the Supreme Vehicle and understands the Ultimate Truth; he has transcended the traces of analyzing form through the realization of essence-less emptiness and has reached the ultimate state.

The True Source (Zhenyuan) penetrates the provisional names of existence and non-existence to enter into the ultimate reality (lakṣaṇa). Therein, the objective realm and wisdom merge, and phenomena and principle coincide;
thus, even the causes for rebirth in the Pure Land do not abandon their mutual functioning. He vowed to repair this monastery to enlighten future students.
A lay devotee commissioned a Buddha image, the features of which were most complete. Now, Prefect Feng has constructed a great [hall].
I erected gates to mark its positions and subsequently extended the four eaves all around, encircling it with a wide corridor.

I had images of the two Great Beings painted there and completed the work with silk canopies, banners, and streamers. Alas! Those who seek the birth that is non-arising should know that the raft exists for this purpose.
Thus, I inscribed the *Ten Doubts on the Tiantai Teachings* upon the walls and pillars, so that those who behold them might understand.
Faith was thereby aroused.

In the eighth year, the Dharma Master Zhibian possessed an understanding that was peerless and had composed many works; however, as he had few disciples, he abandoned his lecture hall and resided at Hengyue Temple.
Whenever he read his own compositions, he would invariably sing them once and sigh three times, considering them to be the expression of his own realized understanding.
Thus, he did not encounter anyone who could appreciate his music. One day, an elderly monk arrived and borrowed Bian’s writings to read them.
He remarked, "Your realization is supreme and accords well with the Buddha's intent. That you currently have few disciples is merely due to a lack of karmic affinity with people."
"If even the Buddha could not save those with whom he had no karmic affinity, how much less so a beginner? You may prepare food and offer it as alms to the birds and beasts;
twenty years hence, you shall naturally have a following of your own. Having spoken these words, he vanished suddenly. Dao-bian then followed his instructions:

he sold his clothes and bedding to exchange them for rice, cooked it, and scattered it outside the city. A great flock of crows gathered, pecking at the food before departing. Dao-bian offered a prayer:

He said, "Those who eat my rice shall become my Dharma companions. Twenty years later, when Bian went to the city of Ye to give lectures, there were more than a thousand people in his assembly; they were indeed all young bhikṣus.
In this year, Chan Master Daoshu passed away. The Master had initially studied under Chan Master Shenxiu and attained the essential meaning [of the teachings].
He then settled in a thatched hut on Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou. There was a rustic man there, whose appearance was simple and unadorned, yet whose speech was strange and unconventional.

At times he would manifest the forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, or celestial immortals; at other times he emitted extraordinary light or produced various sounds. He displayed hundreds of such miraculous transformations.
The Master’s disciples were constantly struck with awe; none were able to fathom him. In this manner, he remained for ten years before finally vanishing from sight.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The rustic man employs limitless wiles to dazzle and delude people, yet it requires only that this old monk neither see nor hear them.
His wiles have their limits, but my non-seeing and non-hearing are inexhaustible. Thereupon, he departed into the distance.
Recently, I have heard that there is no one who does not revere him. As the saying goes: "If one does not find strange what is strange, the strangeness will naturally perish.
In the first month of the ninth year, Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai entered nirvana at the age of ninety-five. The Master was a native of Changle in Fuzhou;
he left the secular world in his childhood and thoroughly mastered the three studies. At a time when Mazu was propagating the teachings in Jiangxi, the Master...
With wholehearted devotion, he became a close disciple and entered the inner sanctum alongside Master Xitang Zhizang.
At that time, there were thousands of students gathered at Mazu’s gate, and these two great masters stood out as peerless pillars. When Mazu passed away, the Master went to Mount Baizhang in Xinwu;
before even a month had passed since his arrival, disciples seeking the profound teachings flocked to him from all directions. Although the Master was advanced in years, whenever...
His daily routine was always shared equally with the community; he once said, "If one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day.
A monk asked, "What is the Mahāyāna teaching on sudden enlightenment? The Master replied, "First, you must bring all conditions to rest and let all affairs subside.
Regarding all dharmas—whether wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane—do not remember them, do not dwell upon them, and let them go."

One relinquishes body and mind, allowing them to be autonomous. The mind is like wood or stone, devoid of discrimination; the mind has no place of activity, and the ground of the mind is as empty as space.
The sun of wisdom manifests of itself, like the sun emerging when clouds part; such a person is called one who has attained liberation.
Facing all objects, the mind is neither still nor turbulent, neither constrained nor dispersed. There is no obstruction regarding any sounds or forms. This is...
Neither beauty nor ugliness constitutes principle or non-principle. When all cognitions and views are completely exhausted, one is no longer bound;

dwelling with mastery over the mind, such a person is called a Bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment and has already ascended to the stage of Buddhahood. If both defiled and pure minds are exhausted, one dwells neither in bondage nor in liberation.
Being free from all conditioned and unconditioned states of bondage and liberation, one abides in the measure of the mind (cittamātra) within birth and death with equanimity.
Their mind is sovereign; ultimately, it never unites with the illusory defilements of the aggregates, elements, realms of birth and death, or the sense bases.
It stands aloof and without dependence, entirely unrestrained. There is no obstruction in coming or going; traversing through birth and death is like the opening of a door.
Should they encounter various circumstances of suffering or pleasure that do not accord with their wishes, their minds suffer no retreat or dejection. They do not dwell upon fame or clothing.
Eating, he does not crave the merit or benefits thereof; he is not obstructed by worldly dharmas. Although his heart is close to others, suffering and pleasure do not disturb his mind.
He eats like a deer merely to sustain life, mending his robes to ward off the cold. Thus, he is like one who is foolish and like one who is deaf.

If one possesses even a slight degree of attachment within the cycle of birth and death, then despite extensive study and intellectual understanding, seeking blessings and wisdom will be of no benefit to the ultimate principle;
one will instead be swept away by the winds of conceptual objects and return once more to the sea of birth and death. The Buddha is beyond seeking; if people seek him, they deviate from him.
The Principle is beyond seeking; if one seeks it, one loses it. If one attempts to grasp this "beyond-seeking," one again becomes identical to those who possess seeking.

This Dharma is neither real nor unreal. If one can give rise to the realization that it is like wood or stone, and is not swept away or submerged by the aggregates (*skandha*), the realms (*dhātu*), the five desires, or the eight winds, then the causes of birth and death are severed; one is free to go or stay as one pleases. A monk asked:
"If one now receives the precepts, with body and mind pure and already endowed with all virtues, will one attain liberation? The Master replied: "One attains a small portion of liberation."
[He is] liberated, yet has not yet attained liberation of mind. It is asked: What is liberation of mind? The answer is: Not seeking the Buddha, not seeking knowledge or understanding;
when the sentiments of defilement and purity are exhausted, one neither clings to non-seeking nor dwells in the state of extinction.
Furthermore, one does not fear the suffering of hell nor crave the bliss of heaven. Being unrestrained by any phenomena, this is for the first time called unimpeded liberation.

Do not say that possessing even a small portion of the precepts is sufficient. There are as many gates of untainted morality, concentration, and wisdom as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, yet you have not yet entered even a hair’s breadth of them.
Exert yourselves with fierce effort! Do not wait until your ears are deaf, your eyes grow dim, your head turns white, and your face wrinkles;
do not wait until the suffering of old age has overtaken your body, tears flow from your eyes, and your heart is filled with terror, having no place to go. When it reaches such a state—
At that time, one cannot even manage one's own hands and feet. Even if one possesses merit, wisdom, and extensive learning, they are of no use at all.
Because one’s thoughts are preoccupied with various external objects and one fails to practice inward reflection, one does not perceive the Buddha-way.

All the evil karma accumulated throughout one's life manifests before one, transforming into seemingly pleasant scenes. One is reborn according to whichever of these visions appears most intense, having no freedom whatsoever. [One becomes] a dragon or an animal.
Whether one is noble or base is likewise not yet fixed. Question: How does one attain freedom? Answer:

It is like being currently confronted by the five desires and the eight winds, yet having no grasping or rejecting in one's mind, where defilement and purity are both forgotten. It is like the sun and moon in the sky, illuminating without depending on external conditions;
or like a fragrant elephant crossing a torrent, proceeding without further doubt or obstruction. Such a person cannot be encompassed by either heaven or hell.
Furthermore, whenever you read the scriptures or examine the teachings, you must always turn them back toward yourself.
However, all verbal teachings merely clarify that the nature of awakening within oneself is never turned by any phenomena of existence or non-existence;
this is called being a "Guide. Being able to illuminate and shatter all phenomena of existence and non-existence is called "Vajra" (the Diamond-like); this is precisely what constitutes true freedom.
This is the section on Independence. If you cannot act in this way, even if you can recite the twelve Vedas, you will merely fall into increased arrogance;

you will instead be slandering the Buddha rather than practicing the Way. While reading scriptures and studying the teachings may be considered a good and virtuous deed according to worldly standards, if measured against those with clear vision, these are people who create obstructions. Even a person of the Tenth Ground would not tolerate this.
Go! Flow into the river of birth and death. Do not seek after intellectual understanding, verbal explanations, or the meanings of phrases.
Depart from all dharmas of existence and non-existence; by passing beyond the three propositions, you will naturally be no different from the Buddha.

Since you are already the Buddha yourself, why worry that the Buddha does not understand your speech? One only fears not being the Buddha, being turned around by all dharmas of existence and non-existence, and thus failing to attain liberation.
Freedom. Thus, if principle is not first established, one is carried away by blessings and wisdom, like a lowly servant serving a noble.

It is better that principle be first established; then, when blessings and wisdom arise, one can act as a master in the moment, turning soil into gold, changing the waters of the sea into ghee and curd, breaking Mount Sumeru into fine dust, and deriving infinite meanings from a single meaning, and [infinite meanings] from infinite meanings.

He established this as a single principle. Whenever the Master finished preaching the Dharma and the great assembly was descending from the hall, he would call out to them. The assembly would turn their heads back, and the Master would ask, "What is it?
This became known throughout all quarters as "Baizhang’s phrase for descending from the hall."

The Master observed that since the inception of the Chan school at Shaoshi, its adherents had mostly resided in Vinaya monasteries; yet, there was no established protocol for preaching the Dharma or for the administration of the community.
He therefore conceived the plan to establish separate Chan residences. Those who possessed the eye of the Way and were endowed with venerable virtues were titled "Elders" (Changlao).
Once they became the masters of the transformation, they would occupy the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang). No Buddha Hall was established; instead—

The Dharma Hall of the Tree represents the transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is honored as supreme in the present age. Regardless of the number of students, whether many or few, there is no distinction of high or low.
All enter the Sangha Hall, where they are arranged according to the order of their seniority (*kṣaṇa*). Long benches are provided, along with racks for hanging robes and other requisites.
When lying down, one must always lean the pillow against the edge of the bed, for this is merely a brief rest after long periods of seated meditation. With the exception of...
Entering the room to request instruction, he accommodated the diligence or indolence of his students; their progress varied from superior to inferior, as he maintained no fixed standard.

When the entire assembly gathered for morning and evening sessions, the Elder would ascend the hall to take his seat as the presiding master, while the disciples stood in a single file like geese, listening intently by his side.

The master and guests engage in dialogue to stimulate and clarify the essential tenets of the school. At the two times of the midday meal and the morning gruel, they join the assembly to ensure equal distribution.

The practice of *fǔqǐng* (collective labor) is observed so that those of high and low rank may exert equal effort. Ten administrative offices (*shíwù*) are established, each employing one leader to manage communal affairs and ensuring that each official attends to their respective duties.
Should there be those who assume false names or conceal their true identities to mingle with the pure assembly, they shall be separately placed in a noisy and distracting location.
The matter was then investigated by the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina). The offender was removed from his seat, his robes were taken down, and he was expelled from the monastery.
Alternatively, if he had committed a transgression, he was struck with a staff. The assembly was gathered to burn his robes, bowl, and requisites;

he was then driven out through a side gate to demonstrate his disgrace. Such were the essential procedures. Thereafter, as the monastic communities flourished daily, it was during the reign of Emperor Daizong...
The Master followed this and expanded upon it; what is now known as the *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules for the Chan Garden) is fully contained therein.
The Discourse says: Confucius said, "If Qi undergoes one transformation, it will reach the level of Lu; if Lu undergoes one transformation, it will reach the Way.
This is not true only of the Confucians; we Buddhists are the same. Since the Great Teaching flowed eastward, it flourished under Fotudeng. From Fotudeng...
Thus Dao’an attained the Way; through Dao’an, Huiyuan emerged. The disciplinary framework of the Dharma-gate was thereby rendered brilliant and fully complete.
As for the School of the Lineage (Zongmen), since the passing of Caoxi, the Way has resided throughout the world.
Huiyue emerged and revitalized it; from Huiyue came Mazu; from Mazu came Baizhang. At the time of Baizhang...
During the Zhenchang era, the flourishing of Chan studies throughout the empire surpassed that of Caoxi by a hundredfold.
Hai took advantage of this prosperity to establish rules and regulations to ward off depravity and to set forth laws and standards to govern it;

thus, the monastic communities have maintained these for four or five hundred years as if it were but a single day. All of this was achieved through three stages of transformation before reaching its great perfection. Alas!
Without Baizhang, how could the monastic forests of the world have reached their present state?
In the ninth year [of the Tianbao era], Liu Zhitou of Hedong composed the "Stele for Master Daming of Nanyue. Its inscription reads: "The Confucianist establishes himself through ritual;
without benevolence and righteousness, he perishes. The Buddhist maintains himself through the Vinaya; without meditative concentration and wisdom, he is lost. Therefore..."

One who departs from ritual in favor of benevolence and righteousness cannot be spoken of as a Confucian; one who diverges from the precepts in favor of meditative concentration and wisdom cannot be spoken of as a Buddhist.
Only a Great Enlightened Master can master this Way. This Master’s surname was Ouyang, and his title was Huikai.
He was born in the twenty-first year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty. He first became a monk in the eleventh year of the Tianbao era. In the tenth year of the Dali era...
In the first year [of his ordination], he ascended the platform to become a *Mahāvinaya-dhara*. He passed away on the tenth day of the eleventh month in the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era.

In the first month of the ninth year of the Yuanhe era, his disciples Huixin, Daosong, and the nun Wuran, among others, commissioned the monk Lingyu of eminent virtue to compose his biography (*xingzhuang*), requesting that his deeds be inscribed upon this stele. Zongyuan now extracts from it...
The Elder said: "Master, you were formerly a government official; your family was a great clan in Tanzhou with distinguished merit and noble rank.
These matters need not be discussed here, for you are now a Great Bhikṣu. Generally, when the Way of the Bhikṣus declines, its followers inevitably diminish the Vinaya and abandon the Sūtras."
Da Ming was apprehensive about this. Thereupon, he followed Sengjun and Faji to investigate the Vinaya, whereby the Great Dharma was established.
Furthermore, he followed Huixiu and Daoyu to master the scriptural teachings, whereby the profound meanings were cultivated. Thus, these two paths emerged and receded, appearing and disappearing;
later students were no longer confused, and those who came seeking found what they had gained. In the third year of the Guangde era, Daming Temple was first established.
At Mount Heng, by imperial decree twenty-one monks were selected to reside at the monastery, with the Master as their leader.

In the third year of the Qiannian era, an order was issued to establish a Vinaya collection at Mount Heng; seven monks specializing in the Vinaya were summoned to lecture on the precepts, and the Master was included among their number.

In all matters concerning his clothing, utensils, and conduct, he followed the teachings of the masters; his speech and movements served as a model for others. He attended to them by holding their towels and basins.
He had several hundred attendants carrying staffs and sandals; tens of thousands of students cut their hair and received his instructions and precepts.
He was as if alone despite being among the multitude; he was honored yet remained humble; he was obscured yet radiant; he was solitary yet vast. His grandeur was unsurpassed.
His stupa is at the western foot of Mount Zhurong, and the stele is to the east of the stupa. The inscription reads: "The Confucianist acts through ritual; the Awakened [Buddhist] acts through..."
The Flourishing of the Vinaya: All return to the True Source, wherein there is neither Great nor Small Vehicle. This Vinaya of the Great Ming is both concentration and wisdom;
it exhaustively investigates the scriptural teachings to serve as a Dharma for transcending the world. It transforms immeasurable people and bestows boundless bounty.
By imperial decree, those of venerable virtue and majestic deportment are succeeded; the Way pervades the great continent, and its illustrious reputation shall never fade. Zhurong (Agni) to the West.
At the foot of Mount Dongting, in its southern reaches, there are stone and metal inscriptions whose words shall endure for ten thousand years.
Zishou further inscribed the back of the stele, saying: "In general, when burying great *buddhas*, no burial pit or grave is used.
Thus, the use of a stele is not appropriate. In ancient times, the noble houses were permitted by ritual to use steles for burials; subsequently, their descendants followed this precedent."

He departed and subsequently inscribed [the master’s] virtuous conduct, intending it to endure for a long time in the world. When the Qin dynasty engraved characters upon mountain rocks to proclaim their meritorious deeds, these were also called *bei* (steles), and thus the practice was established.
Consequently, even for Buddhist monks (*futu*), such monuments are appropriate. Whenever a great Buddhist monk is buried, if his disciples are numerous, they are able to erect a stele.

During the Jin and Song dynasties, the Dharma was highly esteemed; therefore, those who composed stele inscriptions mostly followed the Buddhist teachings. During the Liang dynasty, the Dharma was likewise esteemed...
In the past, stele inscriptions mostly concerned the Dhyāna school, as its methods were not widely disseminated; thus, while Dhyāna did not flourish extensively, the Vinaya remained preserved.

Consequently, in recent times, most stele inscriptions concern the Vinaya. Generally, when burying a great *buddhaputra*, it has never happened that a *bhikṣuṇī* presided over the matter of the stele.
Now, however, Wúrǎn herself has come, weeping, to request this. Her resolve is increasingly firm, and she is moreover able to recount her teacher’s other virtues in full detail.
Therefore, I have inscribed this upon the back of the stele. The Master presided over the affairs of the precepts for twenty-two years.
Prime Ministers Qi Gong Ying, Li Gong Bi, and Zhao Gong Jing; Shangshu Cengzhong Gao, Fei Gong Zhou, and Shilang Lingfu Gong Hu were either his teachers or his friends.
Qi Gong personally held the texts to receive the great principles as a disciple. Furthermore, it is said that when the Master was first a child...

At that time, he dreamed of a great man wearing a white cap and white robes who came to tell him: "He who shall dwell on Mount Nanyue and expand my Way must surely be you. Subsequently, this proved to be true.
As his end approached, there was light in the night and the sound of *sheng* and *qing* bells; the entire assembly witnessed and heard it.

Instances such as these were very numerous, but because they are not spoken of by Confucian scholars, I have recorded them here at the request of those who, free from worldly taint, were diligent in their pursuit. Thus ends the final transmission.
...untainted. The daughter of the Wei clan was of illustrious and noble lineage; she has now presided over the precepts and dharma of Mount Heng for ten years.

Ma Zong, the Regional Commander of Nanhai, petitioned the court because the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi had not yet been granted a posthumous title. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Great Mirror" (Dajian).
Ma Zong then commissioned Liu Zongyuan of Hedong to compose the inscription for the posthumous title stele. Its text says: "The Duke of Fufeng is upright and incorrupt..."
It was reported to the Emperor that for three years in Lingnan, the Sixth Patriarch of the Buddha-dharma had not yet received a formal title.

Consequently, he was posthumously titled the Chan Master Dajian, and his stupa was named the Lingzhao Stupa. On the thirteenth day of the tenth month in the tenth year of the Yuanhe era, the official decree from the Ministry of Rites reached the provincial capital.
The Duke ordered the clerks of the ministry and the officials of the provincial office of merit to announce it.
At his memorial service, banners, canopies, bells, and drums filled the mountains and valleys; ten thousand people gathered as if they had heard of ghosts and spirits.

At that time, there were over a thousand students who leaped for joy and exerted themselves as if their teacher had been reborn, yet they were moved to grief and wept with longing as if their teacher had just passed away.
Thereupon he said: "Since the beginning of sentient life, beings have delighted in fighting, seizing, and killing one another, thereby losing their..."

The fundamental reality has become perverse and chaotic, flowing into depravity so that it can no longer return to its original state. Although Confucius did not hold a high position of authority, he sustained the world with his remaining teachings after his passing;
yet, these were further complicated by Yang Zhu, Mo Di, Huang-Lao, and others, until their doctrines became fragmented. It was only later that our Buddhist teachings emerged.

Pushing away [phenomena] to return to the source is what is meant by "being born yet remaining still. Master Bodhidharma criticized Liang Wu-di for his fondness for conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*), whereby the art of Emptiness became increasingly manifest.

After six transmissions, it reached Dajian (the Sixth Patriarch). Dajian initially employed Huineng as a servant despite his laborious service, but once he heard Huineng’s words, they were rare and profound;
the Master was moved by them and subsequently entrusted him with the dharma-vessel. Huineng then withdrew and lived in seclusion in the South Sea.
The Superior Man remained without further fame or renown for another sixteen years. Only when he deemed himself capable did he reside at Caoxi to serve as a teacher for others.
Students gathered from all quarters, numbering several thousand at any given time. His Way took non-action (*wuwei*) as its reality and the void as its substance.
He took vastness without dissipation as his ultimate refuge. In instructing others, he began with the inherent goodness of human nature and concluded with its inherent goodness;

he required no weeding or tilling, for he rooted his teaching in primordial stillness. Emperor Zhongzong heard of his fame and sent a favored courtier twice to summon him, yet could not bring him to court;

however, he adopted the Master’s words as the core of his own mental practice. His teachings remain fully extant today and are disseminated throughout the world; indeed, all who speak of Chan trace their lineage back to Caoxi.

One hundred and six years have passed since the passing of Dajian (Dajian Huineng). There have been dozens of individuals who governed the region of Guang and were renowned by name, yet none were able to receive a formal posthumous title.
Now, for the first time, it is announced to all under heaven that he has obtained a grand posthumous title. He enriched and assisted our Way; how could there not be words [to commemorate him]?
When the Duke first entered court service, he did so as a Confucian scholar. He successively served as the Inspector of Qianzhou and the Protector-General of Annam, traveling across the great sea.
The various tribes from the west of Śiṇdhu, sailing by ship and submitting to your command, have all been graced by your virtue.
