Having received your transformative influence, they have suspended their banners and halberds to come under your governance. Your dependencies in the South Sea are as numerous as a forest; you inspire awe through non-killing and non-anger, and your benevolence truly shines forth.
To manifest the Great Mirror [of Wisdom], none is more worthy than you. Thus, the elders among your disciples have replaced the stone [stele].
From beneath the eaves, a messenger was sent to present this petition. Its words were as follows: “Dharmatrāta, ever-vigilant, transmitted the Buddha’s words and mind;
six generations received his mandate, and the great banner descended upon them. Through diligent toil and profound silence, they ultimately bowed into the depths.

Carrying that vessel of faith, he traveled to the north of the sea. His Way was thus spread among the marshes of the valley. The masses gathered in vast numbers, yet they did not level his loftiness. Thus it was proclaimed to all.”

Chen Weidao praised him, saying: "Innate goodness is present at birth and inherent in all things. Yet when one wanders into the wild currents and gallops toward excess, ten thousand divergent paths emerge.
Without reflection, disorder increases; without awakening, error proliferates. Through the Master’s internal mirror, all have recovered their original nature.

Without planting roots or weeding sprouts, the center is unified and the exterior is harmonized, resulting in a refined brilliance that shines through. Thus, even the Emperor Zhongzong sought his counsel."

In the morning, [the Master’s teachings] secretly assisted the royal ordinances, enabling people to dwell in leisure. One hundred and six years passed, yet his title and posthumous name were not recorded.
Through the memorial of the Duke of Fufeng, the Heavenly Book and the Imperial Edict have now been restored and widely promulgated; thus, his glory is eulogized throughout the southern lands.

The Dharma has arisen once more, and its followers, numbering in the tens of billions, mourn together while rejoicing in unison. This is solely because the Master’s teachings have reached them, extending even to the Duke of Fufeng.
All beneath heaven revere the Son of Heaven. The Son of Heaven, in his gracious mandate, praises the overflowing virtue and beauty of your merit, which extends even to the barbarians of the seas.

You regard the Buddha as your model; you transmit benevolence as a teacher, and you govern with benevolence as a ruler. Your petitions and words are firm and enduring; may your legacy continue forever without end.
In the second year of the Shaoxing era of our dynasty, the Layman Dongpo visited Caoxi and inscribed this: "Śākyamuni taught through literature;
its translation in the Middle Kingdom necessarily relied upon Confucian scholars capable of eloquent expression. Thus it was transmitted far and wide.
Therefore, among the Mahāyāna sūtras that have arrived here, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* is uniquely sublime, exhaustive in its detail and perfection, owing to the transcription by Fang Rong."

It is for this reason. When Liu Ziqiu was exiled to the south, he began to investigate the Buddha-dharma, composing inscriptions for Caoxi, Nanyue, and other sites that remain unsurpassed in excellence throughout past and present;

yet, the *Nanhua* [Zhuangzi] currently lacks a stone inscription. The Elder Master Chongbian is a master of both Confucianism and Buddhism, possessing a complete mastery of the Way of Learning (*Daoxue*).
He has observed that from the Tang dynasty until now, there have been many who have composed eulogies and accounts of the Patriarchs, yet none have been as lucid and authoritative as this.
Thus, as for one such as Zihou, it appears that when his words are traced back to their source, they accord with those of Mencius.
How could we not cause students to see and recite them daily? Therefore, I have prepared the stone and requested that you inscribe this text upon it.
The Treatise says: The *Zhongyong* states, "That which is luminous through sincerity is called nature; that which is sincere through luminosity is called instruction.
It further states, "Heaven has four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter; rain, wind, frost, and snow are all forms of instruction. The earth bears wonders and marvels."

The wondrous manifestations of all phenomena appearing before us are none other than the teaching. Our tradition’s *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable. The Sixth Patriarch said:
"This refers to the profundity of the Principle (*li*). It further states: "The gateway to this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "This refers to the profundity of the Teaching (*jiao*). Nevertheless, our school points directly to the Dharma of the Mind.
One must say: the mountains, rivers, the great earth, form and emptiness, light and darkness—all such phenomena are manifestations of the nature.
To see the nature is to find truth in every encountered object. When truth is found in every encountered object, the self and objects merge into one, and there is no longer any "object" at all.
Because there is no separate entity, whatever the eyes behold and whatever the mouth speaks is none other than the Teaching.

As for "the Teaching being self-evident through sincerity" and "nature being self-sincere through luminosity," luminosity and sincerity are merely different names for wisdom and stillness, or illumination and quiescence.
For this reason, the principles of nature are extremely profound and the gates of the Teaching are difficult to enter; yet once one enters, it is said:
This teaching—seeing [the mind] and calling it "nature" (xing)—how great! My ancestor’s discourse on nature and teaching seems to accord perfectly with the *Zhongyong*.
Thus, Zihou composed the stele for my ancestor, and Dongpo praised him, saying that tracing back the roots of his words, they accord with those of Mencius.
Alas! Zihou was indeed not one who distinguished between Confucianism and Buddhism...
This serves as a distinct category. Is it not a marvelous teaching regarding the nature of things?
How virtuous! *Lōngxīng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Twenty-one;
*Lōngxīng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Twenty-two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of the Stone Chamber in Longxing Prefecture.
In the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, Chan Master Yinfeng of Mount Tai traveled from Hengyue to Wutai; his route passed through Huai...
[The above] refers to when Wu Yuanji obstructed the military at Caizhou and defied the imperial mandate.

As the government troops and the rebels were engaged in combat and had not yet determined victory or defeat, the Master said, "I shall briefly alleviate their distress. He then struck his alms-bowl against the air and flew across it with his body.

The officers and soldiers of both armies looked up in wonder and sighed in amazement; their hearts of combat were instantly stilled, and by this means the government army was able to achieve its success.
The Master’s surname was Deng. As a child, he appeared dull-witted, so his parents permitted him to leave the household life. Once he had received full ordination, he went to attend upon Mazu.
Under Mazu’s words, he attained realization of the essential meaning. One day, while pushing a cart, Mazu stretched out his legs across the path; the Master said, "Please withdraw them."

[The Master] stepped forward. The Patriarch said, "Once extended, it cannot be withdrawn. The Master said, "Once advanced, there is no retreating. He then pushed the cart over [the Patriarch], injuring the Patriarch's foot.
Returning to the Dharma Hall, the Patriarch took up an axe and said, "Come forth, you who have just now crushed the soles of this old monk's feet!

The Master immediately stepped out before the Patriarch and held out his neck to him. The Patriarch then set down the axe. Thereafter, he traveled extensively throughout all quarters, wherever he went...
He frequently displayed miraculous and extraordinary feats. After some time, as his divine wonders became quite prominent, he feared they might delude the masses.
He then entered the Vajra Cave on Mount Tai and, intending to manifest his final passing, asked the assembly: "In various places, I have seen those who pass away while sitting or lying down.
Is there anyone who passes away while standing? The assembly replied, "There is. The Master asked, "Is there anyone who passes away while inverted?"
The assembly said, "We have never seen such a thing before. The Master then stood upright and passed away; his body remained perfectly erect, and his robes likewise clung to his form.
The assembly carried the corpse to cremate it, yet it remained motionless and firm. Those from near and far came to gaze upon it in worship, marveling at the wonder.
The Master had a younger sister who was a nun; she was also there at that time. She approached him and rebuked him, saying, "Brother, you used to trouble and disturb everyone during your lifetime..."
He was not following the laws of the state, and even in death he continued to delude people. [The official] then pushed him with his hand, and he fell down lifeless.
Thereupon, he was cremated and the śarīra were collected; it is said they were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Wutai.

Chan Master Guizong Zhichang had double pupils. He would rub his eyes with his hands using medicinal ointment, until after a long time both the corners and the whites of his eyes became entirely red. Thus, he was popularly known as "Guizong the Eye-Wiper. When Li Bo, the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou, asked him, "In the scriptures it is said that Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed; I have no doubt of this. But as for a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru—is that not mere idle talk? The Master replied: The Master replied: "The scriptures say that Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed; I do not doubt this. But as for a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru, is that not mere idle talk? If you can see the mustard seed within Mount Sumeru, then you will know that there is no falsehood in the saying that Mount Sumeru contains a mustard seed. If you cannot see Mount Sumeru within the mustard seed, then you will never understand why it is said that a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru. Li Bo was greatly enlightened by these words. Later, when Li Bo was about to retire from office, he sent a messenger to ask the Master for a verse. The Master wrote: "Mountains are mountains, waters are waters; The sun rises in the east, the moon sets in the west. The official who once questioned me has now departed; I sit alone, leaning on my staff, watching the clouds. Li Bo read this and sighed, saying, "This man truly possesses the Way. He subsequently composed a poem in praise of the Master. Later, when Li Bo passed away, he left instructions to have his remains interred at the foot of the mountain where the Master resided. The Master then composed a memorial inscription for him. It is said that upon reading this, Li Bo’s spirit appeared in a dream to the Master and thanked him profusely. Afterward, he sent a messenger to request the Master to perform a funeral rite for him. The Master then composed a gatha, which read: "From the beginningless beginning, The nature of mind is originally pure. Since birth and death are but illusions, Why seek liberation elsewhere? If you wish to see the Buddha, Look directly at your own face. When the face is seen, the Buddha is realized; Then you will know the meaning of 'no-thought'. Upon reading this, Li Bo’s spirit appeared again in a dream, weeping and thanking the Master. He then sent a messenger to inform the Master that he had already been reborn in the Pure Land. The Master then composed another gatha, which read: "Leaving the human realm, He has ascended to the Western Paradise. Though his body has perished, His Dharma-body remains eternal. If you wish to meet him, Seek him in the West. Li Bo’s spirit appeared yet again in a dream, bowing deeply and thanking the Master. He then vanished. This account is recorded in the *Guizong Chanshi Yulu* (The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guizong). It is said that after the Master’s passing, his disciples erected a stupa for him at the foot of Mount Lu. Whenever the weather cleared, one could see the Master’s image sitting upright atop the stupa. Those who witnessed this were filled with awe and reverence. His disciples later compiled his teachings and titled it the *Guizong Chanshi Yulu*. It is said that those who read it would immediately attain realization. Thus, his influence continued to benefit sentient beings even after his physical life had ended. His legacy remains a testament to the power of the Chan tradition.
People were circulating the report that Master Shi had read ten thousand scrolls of books; whether this was true or not, Zhibo replied, "It is so.

The Master said, "From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet, you are no larger than a coconut. Where would you place those ten thousand scrolls? Zhibo lowered his head and remained silent.
The Master asked again, "What do you understand from the entire Tripitaka? He raised his fist and showed it to him, saying, "Do you understand? Zhibo said, "I do not."
The Master said, "This scholar does not even recognize his own fist. Huo said, "I request the Master’s instruction. The Master replied, "If you understand, it is for your use on the road;
if you do not understand, it is merely worldly discourse. The Master once addressed the assembly, saying, "The ancient worthies of old were not without knowledge and understanding;
they were men of noble character who differed from the common run. People of today cannot [attain this] themselves..."
I have spent my time establishing independent emptiness. My disciples, do not misapply your minds. No one can take your place, nor is there any place for you to apply your mind.
Do not seek it from others. From the past until now, you have merely relied on others to form interpretations;

thus, every word you utter is obstructed, and your light does not penetrate through, simply because there is something before your eyes. A monk asked, "What is the profound principle? The Master said, "No one."
The monk said, "I understand. The Master asked, "How was it just now? The monk said, "If there were a 'just now,' it would already be a deviation.
The monk asked, "Is there no skillful means by which you might enable a student to enter? The Master said, "The subtle power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can save the world from suffering.
The monk asked, "What is the subtle power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom? The Master struck the crown of his head three times and asked, "Did you hear that? The monk said, "I heard it."
The Master said, "Why do I not hear you? The monk was speechless. The Master drove him away with his staff.
On another day, he ascended the hall and said, "I now wish to speak of Chan; all you sons, come forward together. The assembly came forward.

The Master said, "Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara, which skillfully responds to all places. A monk asked, "What is the practice of Avalokiteśvara? The Master then snapped his fingers and said, "All..."
"Did you people hear it? The monk replied, "I heard it. The Master said, "What are you all seeking here?
He drove them away with his staff, laughed loudly, and returned to his quarters. After the Master passed away, the worthy Xian praised his portrait, saying:
"How lofty was his insight! Wiping his eyes, he avoided the imperial throne. Turning back to look at those who washed their ears— For a thousand ages, he remains beyond reproach."

Wu Yuanqing, who served as an attendant, possessed an intelligence and insight that far surpassed others. Emperor Xianzong was particularly pleased with him. One day, while at Zhaoyang Palace, he beheld the various flowers in full bloom;
he lingered there, admiring them, when suddenly he heard a voice from the air saying: "The marks of emptiness and illusion open and fade without ceasing;
they can destroy one's roots of goodness. How can a benevolent person indulge in them? Yuanqing was suddenly awakened to this truth, and his resolve was firm.
He had escaped from the secular world. One day, the Emperor asked him while at court, "Why are you not happy? He replied, "Since my youth, I have abstained from eating meat;

my vow has been to follow the teachings of Śākyamuni. The Emperor said, "I regard you as a brother. If there is anything regarding wealth or status that you desire beyond the ordinary, I shall not refuse you;
however, leaving the household life is not permitted. After ten days had passed, his appearance became emaciated and haggard. The Emperor took pity on him and...
The Emperor issued an edict, saying: "As you wish, you may choose the distance of your journey; report back when you have selected the date. Yuanqing, having received this grace, offered his thanks.
Shortly thereafter, he received news that his mother was ill and requested leave to visit her. The Emperor generously provided him with provisions for the journey and saw him off.

Upon arriving home, Yuanqing encountered Dharma Master Taoguang, who urged him to visit Chan Master Niaoke. Yuanqing addressed him, saying: "Since I was seven years old, I have eaten only vegetarian food; at eleven, I received the five [precepts]."
Jie was twenty-two years old this year; he resigned from his official post for the sake of leaving the household life and requested that the Venerable Master confer upon him the appearance of a monk.

Niaoke said, "In these times, those who become monks rarely possess diligent austerity; their conduct is mostly superficial and excessive. Yuanying replied, "Fundamental purity does not require polishing;
original brightness does not follow after illumination. Niaoke said, "If you realize that pure wisdom is wondrously perfect, its essence is inherently empty."

"Quiescence is itself true renunciation; why rely on external appearances? You should become a lay bodhisattva who cultivates both precepts and giving, like the likes of Sun Xu. Yuanqing said, "Although the principle is thus, it is not my original intent. If I might receive your compassionate acceptance, I vow to follow my teacher's instructions. Thus he requested three times, but [Tao Guang] did not grant his request.

Tao Guang then urged him on behalf of the Palace [officials], saying: [The Palace official said: "Your Reverence, you have long been renowned for your virtue and wisdom. Your fame has spread throughout the four seas. Now, the Emperor and the Empress Dowager deeply respect the Dharma and cherish the Triple Gem. They desire to see you enter the capital to serve as a model for the people. If you do not comply, we fear that the imperial decree will be issued by force. We pray that you will consider our plea and respond with compassion. Tao Guang replied: "I am a man of humble talent and shallow learning. How could I dare to presume upon the imperial favor? However, the Emperor’s benevolence is vast and his grace is profound. If I were to refuse, I would surely bring shame upon myself. But I am already over seventy years old; my life is at its end and my strength is exhausted. I am weary of the world and have no desire for worldly affairs. Furthermore, I am currently suffering from illness. If I were to go, I fear I would only trouble the state and fail to benefit the Dharma. I beg you to reconsider this matter and report it to the Emperor once more. [The Palace official said: "Your Reverence, your intention is noble, yet it is difficult to carry out. The Emperor’s command is firm and cannot be altered. We pray that you will set aside your personal concerns and accept the imperial summons. Tao Guang remained silent and did not answer. The Palace official, seeing that his words had no effect, withdrew. He reported the matter to the Emperor, who then sent another envoy to urge him again. Tao Guang finally consented. When he was about to depart, he told his disciples: "I have lived here for many years, relying on your support. Now I am leaving to travel to the capital. You must all maintain the precepts and cultivate yourselves diligently. Do not let your virtue decline. Upon arriving in the capital, he stayed at the Xingfu Temple. The Emperor and the Empress Dowager received him with great honor and provided him with all necessities. Tao Guang, however, remained focused on his practice, never neglecting his daily recitations and meditations. He passed away there at the age of eighty-one. His remains were returned to his hometown, where they were interred according to Buddhist rites. His disciples erected a stupa to commemorate him. His reputation for piety and integrity remained celebrated for generations.
He had never married nor kept any female attendants. The Chan Master said, "If I do not receive you, who else can deliver you?

Niaoke then shaved his head, conferred the full precepts upon him, and gave him the Dharma name Hetong. Day and night he applied himself with diligence, reciting Mahāyāna sūtras and practicing the *ānāpāna* samādhi.
One day, he suddenly took his leave to travel to other regions. Niaoke asked, "Where will you go? He replied, "To meet [the Buddha]."

Tong had left the household life for the sake of the Dharma, but because his preceptor did not bestow compassionate instruction upon him, he said, "I am now going to various regions to study the Buddha-dharma.
Baizhang (Kuo) said, "If it is the Buddha-dharma, I too have a small portion of it here. Tong asked, "What is the Preceptor’s Buddha-dharma?
Baizhang plucked a tuft of cloth from his own body, held it up, and blew upon it. Tong thereupon awakened to the profound principle. At that time, it was called "The Tuft of Cloth" (Pumo).
The attendant said:
"In that year, Chan Master Bāiyán of Zhāngjìng Monastery passed away. The Chancellor Quán Deyú composed his epitaph, which states:
'The master of the Elder of the Chan School, the Great Master Bāiyán, was Chan Master Dájì. The transmission of the Buddha’s words and mind began with him.'"
From Bodhidharma down to Huineng, Neng’s transformative teachings flourished in the southern regions and spread throughout the world.

Generally speaking, he held that the five aggregates, the nine consciousnesses, and the eighteen realms are all empty, like the clarity of a mirror. Although the myriad phenomena are fully manifested, the nature of light remains untainted;

the mind is void, though the ten thousand images appear therein. Although it does not abide across the three periods of time, its awakening and contemplation remain profoundly still. To attain this is the essence of his teaching.
This is precisely how the ordinary becomes the sage. Otherwise, if even a single speck of dust momentarily arises, the six sense bases become hardened;
one revolves and returns within the cycle of birth and death, where wind, waves, and wheels of fire cause delusion to never cease. The transmission and reception are perfectly harmonious;

the Great Master attained this, and with a single word his fundamental principle was penetrated, entering deeply into unimpeded liberation. The Master’s name was Huaiyun, his surname Xie. During the chaos of the Eastern Jin dynasty, he...
He sighed deeply and said, "Where now are my ancestors? Who is it that causes these four limbs and hundred bones, this seeing, hearing, moving, and acting?
He wept tears like falling rain and vowed to don the black robes of a monk, setting his mind upon the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and his practice upon the path of Caoxi.
He attained the foundation of perfect clarity and purity, and cast off the habitual tendencies of delusive thoughts and攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to objects).

The meaning of the one hundred and eight phrases illuminated his body and mind; his mind transcended words and was transformed beyond fixed location. Thereupon he reached Qingliang, descended to Youdu, ascended Culei, and entered Taihang.
Everywhere he went, those who encountered him were bathed in the flavor of the Dharma. He eventually stayed at Boyan Temple on Mount Taihang. The Gate.
People thus came to know him by the name Bāyán (Póyán). In the third year of the Yuánhé era, an imperial edict summoned him to the capital, where he sat in meditative retreat at Zhāngjìng Temple.
Every year, he was invited to enter Lín徳 Palace to lecture on the teachings. Later, he declined the summons firmly due to illness.

On the twelfth month of the tenth year, he manifested his passing with a serene countenance; he was sixty years old, having spent thirty-five summers [in the monastic life]. His disciples Zhìlǎng and Zhì...

In the first month of the following year, Cao erected a stupa at the Baling Plain. Those who were moistened by a single rain and entered the Dharma-realm through the transmission of a single lamp are too numerous to be recorded in writing.
He composed a single volume titled *The Biographies of Masters and Disciples*, which traces the lineage from Mahākāśyapa of Kukkuṭapāda Mountain down to Huineng and Xiu;
its chronological arrangement is detailed and authentic. When someone asked about the essentials of the mind, he replied: "The mind..."
It is fundamentally pure and devoid of objective realms. It does not involve the rejection of objects to realize the mind, nor the removal of defilement to attain purity.

Transcendentally wondrous and independent, it does not coexist with phenomenal things. One who can awaken to this is not burdened by habitual tendencies, the cycle of birth and death, or illusory aggregates.
Therefore, many scholars and gentlemen who know the Way and enter into its principles frequent this path. Allow me to attempt to speak of it.

By means of the *Zhongyong*’s progression from sincerity to illumination (*cheng-ming*) to exhaust the nature of all things, and by means of the *Great Changes* (*Dàyì*)’s state of "tranquil and unmoving, yet upon being stimulated, it penetrates all," the long-robed monk and the one in ceremonial robes reach the same ultimate goal.

Had the Master been contemporaneous with the Sage Confucius, would he not have been ranked among the likes of Yan Hui and Min Dun? If the Buddha Śākyamuni had lived in his time, would he not have been the Great Wisdom?

Is he not one of those who clarify the fundamental principles? As for the sequence of his following a teacher and receiving full ordination, the honor and faith bestowed upon him by high officials and ministers, and the extraordinary manifestations surrounding his birth and parinirvāṇa—these I shall not record here. Thirty years ago, De-yu once heard the Way from Daji;
when I later came to the capital, I had the opportunity to converse with the Master at length. It was through recent grief that I attained awakening and entry into realization.
Thus one knows that afflictions do not conflict with Bodhi. Although the cycles of birth and death have no fixed end, they ultimately converge upon the other shore.

The Inscription says: The teaching of the West and the subtlety of the Southern School shine together with the sun. Baizhang of Bóyán attained it and became a Great Teacher. His brilliance was like lapis lazuli;
yet he bound fire to burn his own nature, drowning the current of craving within the Right Path, and rushing toward the darkness of ignorance. This is the very Mind.
This is the Buddha; form itself is emptiness. The Master’s penetration is such that there is no going and no coming, no bondage and no liberation.
The Master’s transformation is such that this numinous stupa stands revealed, its vermilion and white colors encircling it, manifesting the kalpas of the mundane dust.

The treatise states: The inscription for the Quanwen Pavilion at Zhangjing Temple by the Chancellor, Mr. Quan Wencong, is profound and subtle in its principles and flows with the profound purport [of the Dharma].
Furthermore, his own claim that he recently attained awakening through grief is truly not deceptive.
I have observed that the Grand Preceptor of our dynasty, the Duke Zhongshu Waiwei Fu, once sent a letter to the Guardian of Luoyang, inquiring after and seeking out [the Master] He.
Master Ze [wrote] a portrait inscription. Shou replied with a verse. The Duke responded to him, saying: "I have received your admonition in verse;

it is indeed beautiful, yet its principle is not yet silent. Regarding what is called 'neither permissible nor impermissible,' whether one attains it or does not attain it—if, within that, one regards the portrait as 'not attained,' then for one who does not regard the portrait, where would they fall?"
In his conduct, he seemed to take neither existence nor non-existence as an obstacle; he was close to attaining universal penetration (*tong*).
Thus, there is a verse that says: "To cling to appearances is truly false; to negate appearances is likewise delusory. To neither cling nor negate—this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Alas!
Although these two masters were separated by nearly two hundred years, each served as a model for the gentry of their respective eras in both literary talent and moral virtue. As for...
Entering the Gate of Nonduality and realizing the ultimate truth, they experienced a state of vast, spontaneous freedom, their radiance ever-renewing day by day.
For this reason, among the eminent and virtuous great ministers of the Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties, the two masters alone are held as preeminent.
In the eleventh year [of the Yuanhe era], the Dharma Master Chongxun traveled from Xiangxi at the request of his uncle, the Minister (Zhongcheng).
Liu Zhitou presented him with a preface, saying: Someone asked Zongyuan: "I have heard in full detail what you have attained from the Venerable Master Xun.
What, indeed, is the nature of his Way? Zongyuan replied: "Since my youth I have studied Buddhism, seeking its Way for thirty years."
For many years, those who speak of the world have rarely been able to penetrate its teachings. It is only in Lingling that I alone have attained understanding.
Furthermore, the words of the Buddha can no longer be heard by us; what remains in the world are merely his surviving books.
If one does not seek within these books, there is no way to grasp his words. If the words themselves cannot be grasped, how much less so his underlying intent?

Ah! Now this superior man has exhausted their scriptures, grasped their words, and elucidated their meanings; he expands upon them beyond ten thousand characters without prolixity, and summarizes them in a single phrase without omission.
This stands in contrast to those of the world who merely analyze chapters and sentences or scrutinize individual characters;
for when they speak of the ultimate void, they become so dissipated that they lose their mooring, and when they debate the multiplicity of all existing things, they fall into confusion.
That they have all survived despite being submerged in the mud—is this not because they were not far from the truth?
According to what I have heard, among those in the world who speak well of the Buddha, there was Master Huicheng in Wu, Master Haiyun in Jingzhou, and Master Chongxun in the south of Chu.
If the Master’s words were preserved, the Way of the Buddha would not be far off. Now that Master Huicheng has passed away, those who speak of the Buddha have become even fewer.
Among them, the one who attained a thorough understanding through the Confucian tradition was Zheng Zhongshu.

When Zhongshu met with the Venerable Man, seeing him holding the scriptures and receiving instruction from him, he remarked: "Through this Middle Way, I am able to achieve further progress. This was the statement of Zhongshu of Changzhou.
He replied: "They are born from the Buddha-dharma and have attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma; it is by virtue of their teachers and friends that they are so designated.
Now the Commander-in-Chief, the Minister of the Interior, has prepared a boat to welcome you and prepared lodgings to await you, desiring that the Way may be propagated far and wide.
How could this be in vain? For the Minister of the Interior is upright, pure, and dignified; the Secretariat is eloquent and erudite; and the Governor of Changzhou is quick-witted."
Even those who have attained [enlightenment] still revere his Way; how much more so for one as ignorant as I? Now, the harmony of the multitude arises from the lead of the great man.
To the south of Mount Dongting, reaching all the way to the South Sea, the scholars there are vast and profound.
Those who seek the Way constitute half the world; with a single lead, it spreads widely to distant lands. Thus, when such practice exists, harmony follows.

This is like the thunder that cannot be suppressed when it arises during hibernation. Thus, I have written this as a preface to the Elder Śūnya’s departure to respond to the summons of his uncle, the Minister of the Household.
Regarding the "Maiden of the River Ma," her origins are unknown. During the height of the Tang dynasty, when Buddhism flourished greatly, such was the local custom in the region west of the Pass.

They are skilled in mounted archery; by nature they are grave and fierce, delighting in combat. They have never heard the name of the Triple Gem and know nothing of the rules for performing virtuous deeds.
Their wives pity their stupidity and go to where they are. When people see these young women with single children, their elegance and charm are truly transcendent.
Her appearance was elegant and refined. Taking advantage of the fact that she had no attendants and no kinsmen, [a man] wished to seek her as his consort.
She said, "I have no parents, nor do I have many brothers, and I too wish to find a refuge. However, I do not desire worldly wealth.
If there is a wise and virtuous man who can recite the sutras I uphold, then I am willing to serve him. Many men vied with one another to seek an audience with her.
The woman gave him the "Chapter on Universal Renown" (*Pumen pin*), saying, "If you can master this in a single night, then I shall return to you.
When dawn broke, more than twenty people had mastered the recitation. The woman said, "I am a woman of a family whose lineage has been pure for generations;
how could I be matched with all of you? You must recite it again from another text. She then gave him the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* under the same conditions as before.

There were still about ten or so who had attained general proficiency. The woman further gave him the *Lotus Sūtra* in seven fascicles, stipulating that anyone who mastered it within three days would certainly be granted her hand in marriage.
When the deadline arrived, only the son of the Ma family succeeded in mastering it.

The woman said, "Since you have surpassed everyone else, you may inform your parents; once the formal mediation and betrothal rites are completed, we can proceed with the marriage. This was indeed a living person.

How could his great principles be the same as those of the vulgar and unrestrained men of the lanes? When Ma Shi arrived according to their agreement and prepared the rites to welcome him, the wife said to him as he entered:
"I have just been attending to my physical ailment; please do not stay here, but remain in another room.

Wait until I am somewhat recovered before you see me; I have not yet removed my [mourning] garments. Ma Shi’s son was delighted and moved him to another chamber. Before the guests had dispersed, the wife gave her command.
In the end, the body decayed and rotted away. Looking about, there was nothing that could be done; thus, they divined a site and buried it.

Not many days later, an old monk arrived, wearing a purple *kāṣāya* robe and carrying a staff. He claimed to be a kinsman of the deceased woman and went to the Ma family to inquire about the circumstances of her death.
The Ma family led him to the burial site, where a great crowd of onlookers had gathered. The monk [struck] with his staff...

He pushed it aside and saw that the corpse had already transformed, leaving only a skeleton of golden chain-mail. The monk went to the river to bathe it, lifted it onto his *khakkhara* staff, and said to the assembly:
"This holy one, out of compassion for you who are burdened by heavy obstructions and entangled in craving, has manifested this skillful means to transform you."

"You should contemplate the causes of goodness so as to avoid falling into the ocean of suffering. Having said this, she suddenly flew into the air and departed. The multitude, seeing this, wept with grief and prostrated themselves in worship.
From that time on, those who venerated the Buddha became numerous in the region west of the Pass; this was due to the transformation brought about by the woman.
In this year, the Vinaya Master Shanghong of Jingyun Temple in Fuzhou passed away. Bai Juyi, the Judicial Secretary of Jiangzhou, composed an inscription for him, which states:

"In the spring of the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era, twenty monks from Donglin Temple on Mount Lu—including Daoshen, Huaizong, Ru Jian, and Chongqi—along with over a thousand monastics and laypeople, gathered together to uphold the legacy of the late [Master] of Jingyun."

A certain person, bearing a memorial of the virtuous deeds of the Great Virtue Master Hong and ten thousand coins as an offering, came to Xunyang to request that Sima Bai Juyi compose an inscription for his late teacher.
However, due to unforeseen circumstances, this was not accomplished. In the summer of the twelfth year, when the stone burial mound was completed, he came again to request it;
yet, due to illness, this too was not accomplished. In the winter of the thirteenth year, when the stone pagoda was finished, he came once more to request it, and only then did he comply.

Thereupon, the monk returned to the mountain, the assembly returned to the village, and the money returned to the temple treasury. Within a month, the text was completed; the following year, the stele was erected. Its inscription reads:

"I have heard that the ancient masters of India [Gandhāra] taught the Dharma for transcending the world. The essentials of this Dharma are threefold: namely, precept (śīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).
Precepts give rise to concentration; concentration gives rise to wisdom; and wisdom gives rise to the eighty-four thousand gates of the Dharma. This is it.
Third, they function as mutual supports for one another. If we speak in terms of sequence, then precept is certainly the cause of concentration, and concentration is the root of wisdom.
When the root is planted, the sprout flourishes; when there is a cause, the fruit is fulfilled. Without a cause, fulfillment is like a fruit in a dream;
seeking flourishing without a root is like pulling up a seedling. Although the Buddha encompasses the three fruits through his knowledge of all modes, he must necessarily employ the precept first.
The Buddha transformed the four modes of birth through the six pāramitās, yet he could not abandon the Vinaya.
Whether the utility of the Vinaya can be measured or cannot be measured, among the ten principal disciples of the Tathāgata, Upāli was renowned for his skillful mastery of the Vinaya.
After Upāli passed away, Master Nanshan obtained it; after Nanshan passed away, Master Jingyun obtained it. The master’s name was Shanghong.
He was born into the Rao clan. His great-great-grandfather was Junya; his grandfather was Gongyue; and his father was Zhigong. He was a native of the south of Linchuan City.
Possessing intelligence from childhood, he conceived the aspiration for renunciation at the age of fifteen and first underwent the tonsure under his maternal uncle.
Having attained maturity and established himself in virtue, he formulated the vow for Bodhi at the age of twenty-five and received full ordination from the Vinaya Master Dayuan of Mount Nanyue.
Because he was born of joy, during the Dali era, he did not leave his parents' homeland; he registered at Jingyun Temple in his native prefecture to cultivate the Way.
Because his virtue responded to the state of non-abiding, during the Zhenyuan era, he departed from the notions of "self" and "mine" and moved to Longxing Temple in Hongzhou to preach the Dharma.
Because he drew near to spiritual friends, he [associated with] Fazhen of Kuangshan and Lingyou of Tiantai.
He associated with five elders, including Faye of Jingmen, Xingguo, Shenzhou, Huijin of Jianchang, and others.

Because he entrusted the Buddha-dharma to kings and ministers, he was on friendly terms with four gentlemen: Chancellor Jiang Gongfu, Grand Preceptor Yan Zhenqing, as well as the local Circuit Intendant Yang Junping and Wei Jundan.
To revitalize the prohibitions and precepts, he lectured on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Regarding the Vinaya: those who followed the good and distanced themselves from transgressions were beyond counting. In accordance with the conditions for transformation, he sat upon the Amṛta Precept Altar and swore an oath to sentient beings for twenty years.
Because he bore the great burden of affairs, he ascended the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) stage eighteen times to bestow the Śīla precepts.
For the sake of rescuing and delivering sentient beings, men and women of the Sahā world attained liberation through me.
There were fifteen thousand five hundred and seventy-two people [in attendance]. He manifested birth as impermanent;
thus, on the *jihai* day of the eleventh month in the tenth year of the Yuanhe era, he passed away at Donglin Monastery, manifesting that cessation has a locus.

On the *bingyin* day of that same month, his remains were interred at the stone tomb on South Hill. He dwelt in the world for seventy-seven years and observed the summer retreat for sixty-five years. From...
From birth until extinction, he followed the traces [of the Way] to provide instruction; whether walking, standing, speaking, or remaining silent, everything was nothing other than Buddha-work.
Now, when one bestows bounty upon others, the return from oneself is abundant. Thus, his disciples and officials repaid him as if they could not do enough.

Consequently, they planted pines until they formed a forest and carved stone into stupas. The stupa has an inscription stone, and the stone bears an epitaph, which says: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Campaka..."
The fragrance of the *mṛdvīkā* has faded; the flavor of the *sarpis-maṇḍa* has grown thin. Who shall restore this fragrance? Who shall revive this flavor?

When Master Jingyun was born, he alone rectified the bhikṣus and revitalized the *vinaya*. Now that Jingyun has passed away, upon whom shall the assembly rely for peace? Upon whom shall the Dharma generals depend?
Formerly, when Jingyun came, those who practiced the Way followed him and those who entered his chamber returned to him. Now that Jingyun has departed, they ascend...
Those remaining in the hall reflect; those who have entered the chamber grieve. To the west of Mount Lu and to the south of Tiger Creek stands a towering stone pagoda.
There is one who has recorded its history, inscribing these words of truth upon the pagoda’s stele.
In this year, the eminent monk Lingche passed away. His collected works comprise twenty fascicles. The Prefectural Secretary Liu Yuxi composed a preface stating:
"It has long been the case that Buddhist disciples have excelled at composing poetry. The Venerable Xiu’s 'Parting Lament' and Master Yue’s 'Lament for Minister Fan' are examples of this."

He was universally admired and praised by the talented scholars of his time. Such individuals appeared frequently thereafter. Shangren was born in Kuaiji; he was originally the son of the Tang family.

Intelligent and quick-witted, he was devoted to learning and refused to remain an ordinary man. Consequently, he took leave of his father and elder brother to enter the monastic life, adopting the name Lingche and the courtesy name Yuancheng.
Although he studied the sutras and treatises, he single-mindedly preferred literary compositions. He followed a traveler from Yue...
He studied poetry and consequently became widely renowned. Upon his death, he traveled to Wuxing, where he engaged in extensive study and discussion with the elder poetic monk Jiaoran.
Jiaoran wrote a letter of recommendation for him to the literary official Bao Ji, Minister of the Board of War.

Upon receiving it, Bao was greatly delighted and further sent a letter introducing him to Li Shu, Minister of the Board of Civil Office. At that time, Li presided over the realm of literature and aesthetic refinement.
Those who formed alliances with him included Li Bao; thus, the reputation of these superior men was spread abroad by the two masters, like clouds catching the wind or branches and leaves unfurling.
He engaged with literary talent through his writings and delighted those of high character with his Buddhist philosophy. His demeanor was exceedingly elegant, and his conversation was full of flavor.
During the Zhenyuan era, he traveled west to the capital, where his fame resounded throughout the imperial city. Monastics grew envious of him.
He spread slanderous rumors to incite the high-ranking court officials; eventually, he was falsely accused of an offense and exiled to Tingzhou.
He entered Kuaiji and returned to Dongyue, where many local lords from the regions of Wu and Chu treated him with great hospitality and welcomed him.
In the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era, he passed away at Kaiyuan Temple in Xuancheng at the age of seventy-one. His disciples moved his remains and erected a stupa on a mountain in Yue.
He resided at the foot of Mount Zhuzheng during overcast days. Initially, the Master lived on Mount Ke in Wuxing, where he was a companion to Master Zhaou.
At that time, I, while still with my hair tied in two tufts, held brush and inkstone to accompany him in his poetic compositions; they both remarked, "This youth may be instructed.

Later, we met again in the capitals of Jing and Luo, forming a bond like that between Zhi Dun and Xu Xun. Seventeen years after the Master’s passing, I— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
Wujun. His disciple Xiufeng brought the writings of his late master to request a preface to commemorate them. He further stated:
"The Master once composed nearly two thousand poems while in Wujun; these have now been edited down to three hundred pieces and compiled into ten fascicles.
Furthermore, from the Dali era through the Yuanhe era, over a period of fifty years, the verses exchanged with literary patrons and writers have been separately compiled into another ten fascicles."
Now, as I contemplate practicing in this enlightened age, I seek a single word to serve as its winged support. He therefore granted my request, saying:
"Among those who speak of 'poetry-monks' today, most emerge from Jiangyou. Lingyi led the source; Huguo inherited it; Qingjiang raised its waves; and Fazhen followed along.
Yet these are like the sound of a single small string or a solitary melody that merely pierces the ear; they are not the music of the Great Odes. Only...
Wuxing Zhu’s daily attire was complete with every requisite. After Master Zhu, Master Che inherited his legacy.

As for his "Poem on the New Temple in Fuyong Garden," which says: "The scripture came from the White Horse Temple; the monk arrived in the year of the Red Bird (223–253 AD)," and his "Poem Sent from Tingzhou," which says:
"Blue flies act as mourners; yellow dogs carry home letters"—these may be called entering the inner citadel of the masters. How could he be merely preeminent in [one area]?
Regarding the Buddhist monk Jian-xie:
When Chanche passed away, Han, the Prefect of Zhangzhou, sent a letter to Liu Zitong, the Regional Inspector of Liuzhou. Zitong composed a poem in response to Han; the first stanza reads:
"In my youth, I heard the 'Yue' songs in the capital; Hearing of you, my affinity for the rivers and seas grows ever deeper. The other... [text continues]
If you were to transcribe the *Lanting* gathering at this time, do not depict the eminent monk Zhi Daolin. The second verse says:

Frequently I grasp the jade-like letter from within my sleeve, Alone I chant its lingering lines as the autumn wind rises. The Gui River flows day and night for a thousand li; When will my tears reach Yongdong?
Zi-thou (Liu Yuxi) again sent a poem to Minister Yang, lamenting for [Hui]che: "In Dongyue he became a monk..."
He returned to the Tang clan name. For how long have the jade pendants touched the sounding rings? Once the empty flowers have scattered, their place is unknown;
who will gather the golden blossoms for the Minister?
In the twelfth year, the monk of no surname passed away at Mount Yue. Liu Zongyuan, the Regional Inspector, composed a stele inscription for him, which begins: "It is thus..."
On a certain day of a certain month in a certain year, the Great Monk of Yuezhou passed away at Sheng’an Temple.
He had been a monk for [blank] years and was [blank] years of age. He had a name but no surname; no one in the world knew his village, locality, or clan.
When asked about what he had established, he replied: "My nature is my surname. Its source has no beginning, and its lineage has no end. I inherit this surname."
Regarding "Shi": my master bound me to the Way; originally, I have no surname. As for "Fajian" (Dharma-Sword), it is my given name. In truth, I do not even possess a name;
how could I maintain that I have a name? "Xinghai" (Nature-Ocean) is my courtesy name, and "Fajie" (Dharma-Domain) is my style name.
Precepts serve as its walls; wisdom serves as its doors. To guard with them is secure; to dwell within them is peaceful.
Is my neighborhood not thus complete? The categories of the Path (mārga) are infinite in number; the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas is boundless.
I am intimate with them and not alien to them—is my clan not thus vast? Such is what can be heard of his Way.
He ceased [other activities] and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* more than ten million times.

Some mocked him for engaging in "conditioned" acts; he replied, "I have never performed them. Alas! As the Buddha-way grew distant and heterodox views vied to arise, only the Great Master of Tiantai attained its true teaching.
The Upādhyāya inherited this fundamental lineage to accord with the Middle Way; all who received his instruction did not lose it.
The school [teaches] that the flow of sentient beings tends toward disorder; only the true path of the Land of Ultimate Bliss allows them to find their destination.
The Preceptor diligently sought what was upright and beautiful to fulfill his vow. All who heard and believed him were not deluded by his way.

Some criticized him for having a visible trace [of worldly involvement], saying, "I have never seen him act so. Initially he resided at Longxing Temple in Fangzhou, later he moved his residence to this province, where he established the Way.
He established his seat on the northern peak of Mount Laṅkā and did not cross its threshold for fifty years. Of all those whom the Upādhyāya venerated, they were all men of high virtue in the world.
The one he first served upon leaving the household life was Master Zhuoran; he resided at Mount Li in Nanyang and was buried in Yuezhou.
The one from whom he received the full precepts was Master Daoying; he resided in Jingzhou. The foremost among his disciples was Huaiyuan.
The Master resided at Anguo Temple in Changsha, where he established the precept-dharma of Mount Nanyue. [The disciple] came annually to attend upon the Master;
having met with his passing, he was subsequently buried on such-and-such a day, some several paces to the east of the stupa of Master Zhuoran. The inscription reads: "The Way is rooted in the One."

To depart from [conventional] categories is to enter another door; to take one's nature as one's clan is to return to the root. To have no name yet possess a name is because the Teacher’s instruction is most honored.

These are employed provisionally to instruct beings, yet they are not what I maintain. The high official does not dwell [in status], the great clan does not seek intimacy; profound and elegant, he is radiant within.

Vast and empty, outwardly benevolent—these are the remaining words of the Sage. To investigate them and apply oneself to them, whether in motion or in silence; they have passed away like drifting clouds. As the teachings grew old, they became increasingly subtle.
The world’s rulers investigated and set them forth, until there appeared one of great wisdom who emerged through the Gate of Truth. The Master revealed them clearly.
To cause the people to be renewed. When emotions stir, change arises; as things sink into obscurity, he bestowed upon them a land of music, participating in the source of transformation.

The Master used it to guide them toward the Way, so that the people would not fall into confusion. The Way functions without being contrived; its divine operation leaves no trace. Darkness and light are both as they are.
Life and death have both entered quiescence; the Dharma is entrusted to future students. Bestow it without weariness. As for the burial, follow my teacher’s example; do not forget the true abode.
To offer this clear inscription, it is carved upon this enduring stone.
Zi-thou again inscribed the back of the stele, saying: "Since the Monk of No-Surname has taken up residence on this mountain, he says:

'Whatever I seek is not found outside; I shall remain unmoving. When Yang Gong Yan of Hongnong was summoned from Daozhou as a minister of state, he passed by here and considered that [the monk] should reside in the capital.
He urged him to go, but [the monk] would not comply. Yang Gong intended to report this to the throne, saying: 'I wish to intercede...'"
The year passed; the following year, Yang left his post as Chancellor and was exiled to the south of the South Sea, where he ultimately fulfilled his own aspirations.

Li E of Zhao County was a man of erudition and eloquence; while serving as the Governor of Yuezhou, he initially intended to humble him with his haughty demeanor, yet upon hearing a single word from him, he submitted as his disciple.
The entire clan of Pei Zangzhi of Hedong received his instruction. Furthermore, the Prefect of Jingzhao, the Duke of Hongnong, Yang Gong [name omitted],...

He used his secluded dwelling as a site for the Way. When Zhang Weijin, the Regional Inspector of Hezhou, purchased the Western Peak to expand his residence, all the goods and wealth offered at the hall could not be fully recorded. Yet he accepted them without a word.
As he approached the end of his life, he instructed his senior disciple Huaiyuan in the profound mysteries of the Way, never revealing his own surname. Some say he was a man from the Zhou state.
Li Ke, the Prefectural Governor of Xinzhou, composed his biography; Xie Chu of Changsha wrote his life account (*xingzhuang*);
and Cui Xingjian of Boling wrote "On the Preservation of One's Nature. Those who have extolled the Venerable’s meritorious deeds through literary compositions are too numerous to mention in full.
The Duke of Hongnong sent the life account from Yuhang, and Master Huaiyuan brought the biography from Changsha.
The messenger requested that I compose an inscription for it. Having already written the text, I have further utilized the reverse side of the stone to record this.

In this year, Liu Zhou restored Dayun Temple; Li Zhi厚 (Zhitou) wrote its commemorative record, stating: "The people of Yue believe in omens and easily resort to killing; they disdain transformation and turn their backs on benevolence.
When they fall ill or are distressed, they gather spirit-mediums to perform chicken divinations. At first, they kill small [animals]..."
If the small sacrificial animal is unsuitable, they kill a medium-sized one; if that is unsuitable, they kill a large one.
If even that is unsuitable, they bid farewell to their kin and prepare the funeral rites, saying, "The spirits will not accept me. Thereupon, they cease eating, blindfold themselves, and die.

Consequently, households easily decline and fields easily fall into ruin, while livestock and offspring fail to multiply. If they are exhorted with ritual, they remain obstinate; if they are constrained by law, they [resist].
I fled. Only the Buddhists serve the divine with grand discourse; therefore, I entered their ranks to assist in the work of transformation.
When I first arrived in Liuzhou, I established four temples by official decree; three were located north of the river, while Dayun Temple was situated south of the river.
To the north of the river, there were six hundred households surrounding the administrative seat; to the south of the river, there were three hundred households.

Suddenly, a fire broke out on the southern bank, and Dàyún Monastery was consumed by flames and not rebuilt for nearly a century. The three hundred people lost their place of refuge and support, so they established a spirit and sacrificed to it.
In the tenth year of the Yuánhé era, when Prefect Liu Zòngyuán first arrived, he subsequently enshrined the spirit at Yǐnyuǎn.
He took possession of that land. Beside it was a small monastic dwelling; he cleared it out to create a vast thoroughfare leading to crossroads, extending northward to the river.
He petitioned the provincial government for the former name of the temple and erected a great gate inscribed with those characters.

He established east and west corridors and enshrined the Buddha hall as a residence for students. He gathered his disciples and entrusted them with the provision of food, ordering them to strike the chime and drum.
The bell was used to solemnize the Way and transmit its teachings; thus, people began once again to distance themselves from ghosts, cease killing, and strive toward benevolence and compassion.
When they were ill or in distress, they sought counsel and acted accordingly. This was likely because the teaching of Yi was appropriate for the times.
In total, the buildings erected numbered several dozen bays; the land cleared measured several mu in length, breadth, and depth;
there were several hundred trees, thirty thousand stalks of bamboo, and a vegetable garden of a hundred plots with several ridges of paddy fields.
The monks who oversaw these affairs were named Tuisi, Linghuan, and Daojian. Two years later, on the [blank] day of the tenth month, the temple was fully restored.
In the thirteenth year [of the reign], Chan Master Yuanho passed away. Yuanho propagated the teachings of the Tiantai school.

Liang Su of the Hanlin Academy once requested that he compose a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Yuanho consented; that night, he was moved by a miraculous dream and rejoiced at it as an auspicious sign.
He immediately took up his brush to record what he had realized, stating in brief: "I have heard the enlightened ones say: 'The unchanging radiance of the Great Jewel is called the Eternal.'"
The grand ceremony of allowing all things to rest in ease and spreading harmony is called "Teaching" (Jiao). That the entire realm knows where the transformation returns is called "Practice" (Xing).

That the mutual resonance of the human heart reaches its ultimate limit is called "Realization" (Zheng). Thus, by means of the Way, one governs the times; by means of the Dharma-nature, one accords with the movement.
At the moment of responding to things, one shares its radiance with both manifestation and concealment. In magnifying the supreme transformation, both self and others are made clearly manifest.
That his vast fame was truly disseminated is because his reverent literary genius and supreme harmony were brought to their ultimate expression, such that the Four Virtues were fully manifested;

this is truly due to the existence of his wondrous essence. That he transformed the various schools and examined all past practices, such that the fundamental canons were cultivated and the myriad achievements were accomplished, is truly dependent upon his fundamental source.
Truly, in transmitting the Great Illumination of the ultimate source to others, its purport and its subtle movements provide great benefit.

That which will truly exist for those to come lies in its wondrous application; that it synthesizes the myriad mysteries to establish sincere instruction, and that its influence spreads throughout the ten directions so that all follow and submit, truly lies in its wondrous teaching.
Commentators have compared Hào’s commentary to that of Wang Fǔjì on the *I Ching*, and they rank it as a peer to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* commentaries of Qingliáng.
The treatise states: Liu Ke of the Tang dynasty recorded the monk Huangshiyan, while Prime Minister Xue Quan recorded Master Caiyi;
both praised them as if they were their own inferiors. Upon examining this, I find that such behavior is but what is natural for impoverished monastics.
By entrusting themselves to the writings of these two gentlemen, they have thus achieved immortality. As for Zhongxun’s propagation of the teachings and Jingyun’s upholding of the Vinaya—
Lingche’s literary talent, Wuxing’s eminent conduct, and Yuanhao’s compositions were all great figures of our school in their respective eras; yet,
as the monastic biographies (*Sengzhuan*) are incomplete and insufficient to illuminate them for the world, I have compiled the writings of these various worthies and recorded them here,
hoping that those of later generations who aspire to follow in their footsteps will take note.
On the *dinghai* day of the first month in the fourteenth year, an imperial edict was issued to welcome the Buddha’s relics from Famen Temple in Fengxiang to the capital.
The Emperor personally went to Anfu Gate to receive and prostrate before them. He kept them within the palace for three days of offering before they were sent to various temples.

Princes, dukes, officials, and commoners all hurried to pay their respects. Full ritual protocols of the Buddhist section were employed, along with the musical ensembles of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and those of Chang’an and Wannian.
Banners and standards fluttered, and the sounds of drums and wind instruments resounded along the roads. Han Yu, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, submitted a memorial stating:
"Buddhism is merely one teaching of the barbarians. It flowed into China from the time of the Later Han dynasty; it never existed in antiquity.
Formerly, the Yellow Emperor reigned for a hundred years and lived to the age of one hundred ten. Shao Hao reigned for eighty years and lived to the age of one..."
Bai-sui (Hundred Years) reigned for seventy-nine years and lived to the age of ninety-eight. Di Ku reigned for seventy years and lived to the age of one hundred five.
Emperor Yao reigned for ninety-eight years and lived to the age of one hundred eighteen.
Emperors Shun and Yu were both one hundred years old. At that time, the world was at peace and the common people were secure and happy.
They lived to an advanced age. However, Buddhism had not yet appeared in the Middle Kingdom. Subsequently, Tang also lived for a hundred years;
his grandson Da Wu reigned for seventy-five years, and Wu Ding reigned for fifty-nine years. The historical records do not state their lifespans.

Inferring from their ages, it appears they were no fewer than one hundred years old. King Wen of Zhou was ninety-seven years old; King Wu was ninety-three years old; and King Mu reigned for a hundred years.
At that time, the Buddha-dharma had not yet reached China; it was not because of their worship of the Buddha that such longevity occurred.
It was only during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty that the Buddha-dharma first appeared. Emperor Ming’s reign lasted only...
In the eighteenth year [of the dynasty], thereafter, chaos and ruin succeeded one another and their reigns were not long-lasting.

From the Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties down to the Northern Wei, the practice of worshipping the Buddha gradually became more earnest, yet the duration of these eras was particularly brief. Only Emperor Wu of the Liang reigned for forty-eight years;

during his time, he thrice "shed his body" to serve the Buddha. He did not use sacrificial animals in the offerings to the ancestral temples, and throughout the day he took but one meal, consisting solely of vegetables.

...and [the Emperor] died of starvation in Taicheng after being pursued by Hou Jing. The state also perished shortly thereafter. Having sought blessings through the worship of the Buddha, he instead obtained only calamity.
From this we can see that it is clear the Buddha is not to be trusted. When the High Ancestor first received the abdication from the Sui, he proposed to abolish [Buddhism].
At that time, the vision of the ministers was not far-reaching; they were unable to deeply understand the wisdom of the former kings.

The Way is that which is appropriate for all times, past and present. To propagate and expound upon sagely wisdom in order to remedy its abuses was a task that was subsequently halted—a circumstance for which I have always felt regret.
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty, the Emperor, Sage, Martial, and Cultured, is divinely sagacious and heroic, unequaled in the many hundreds of thousands of years since antiquity.
At the very beginning of Your Majesty’s reign, You did not permit the ordination of persons as monks, nuns, or Daoist priests, nor did You permit...
Separate temples and monasteries were established. At that time, I, your servant, believed that the will of the High Ancestor would surely be carried out by Your Majesty.
Although it may not yet be possible to implement it immediately, how could you allow it to flourish unchecked?

Now Your Majesty has ordered the various monks to welcome the Buddha’s relics from Fengxiang, to view their procession from atop the imperial tower, and to bring them into the inner palace, further commanding the various monasteries to provide successive offerings. I, your servant—
Though I am extremely foolish, I must know that Your Majesty is not deluded by Buddhism in making these offerings to pray for blessings and auspiciousness.

You simply do so because, in times of abundant harvests and when the people are happy, you follow their inclinations by providing extraordinary spectacles for the officials and commoners of the capital.
These are merely objects for play and amusement. How could one as sagacious and enlightened as you be willing to believe such matters?

Nevertheless, the common people are ignorant and easily deluded, yet difficult to enlighten. If they were to see Your Majesty act in this manner, they would assume it was done with sincere faith in the Buddha.
They would all say, "If even the Great Sage Emperor directs his whole heart toward faith, how much less should we, the lowly and humble subjects, begrudge our devotion to the Buddha?"
Regarding their bodies and lives, they have gone so far as to burn their heads and sear their fingers in groups of hundreds;

they strip off their clothes and scatter their money from morning until night, emulating one another, fearing only that they might be late. Both old and young rush about, abandoning their livelihoods.

If you do not immediately impose prohibitions and restraints, then as they visit temple after temple, there will surely be those who sever their arms or cut their flesh as offerings, thereby ruining social customs and bringing ruin to the state.
The popular tradition that the *Gupta* [scriptures] were spread in all four directions is no small matter. The Buddha was originally a person from among the "barbarians" (Yidi);

his language did not coincide with that of the Middle Kingdom, and his clothing followed a different system. His mouth did not utter the legal words of the former kings, nor did his body wear the legal garments of the former kings.
He knew nothing of the righteousness between ruler and subject or the affection between father and son. Even if his person were still present, were one to serve him...

When foreign envoys come to court at the capital, Your Majesty receives them with composure, allowing no more than a single audience in the Xuanzheng Hall, a single reception by the Court of State Ceremonial, and the bestowal of a single set of robes, before escorting them out of the borders so as not to confuse the masses. How much less should this be the case for one whose life ended long ago—whose withered and decayed bones are but the remnants of the foul and impure. How could it be appropriate for such remains to enter the imperial palace? Confucius said: [“Respect the living, and extend that respect to the dead. Yet, even when a ruler’s father or elder brother dies, they do not allow their bodies to remain within the inner quarters; they place them in a separate chamber outside the palace walls. This is because the body is the vessel of the spirit, and the spirit is what animates the body. Since the spirit has already departed, the body is merely a hollow shell. To bring such things into the palace would surely cause the people to harbor doubts and suspicions. Furthermore, the deceased king was a man of low birth who usurped the throne through force. He was not a sage-king like Yao or Shun, nor a benevolent ruler like Tang or Wu. His reign was short-lived and his rule was marked by disorder. To allow his remains to enter the palace would surely provoke resentment among the people. If the people are resentful, the state will suffer calamity. Therefore, it is most fitting to bury him in the wilderness, where he may rest in peace, far removed from the sacred precincts of the imperial city. This is the way to honor the deceased while ensuring the stability of the realm. It is the principle of the sages and the practice of the wise kings. May Your Majesty consider this and act accordingly. Thus, the state will be preserved, and the Way of the ancestors will be upheld. This is the ultimate duty of a ruler. I pray you grant my request. Confucius said: “The Master said, ‘To bury the dead according to their rank is the way of the sages. This is precisely why the rites of burial must accord with the status of the deceased. To treat a usurper with the honors due to a sovereign would be to violate the principles of propriety and righteousness. I hope Your Majesty will weigh these matters carefully and act with circumspection. This is for the sake of the longevity of the dynasty and the peace of the people. I humbly submit this memorial. Confucius said: “The Master said, ‘The way of the gentleman is to be reverent in his conduct toward others. To be reverent in this manner is to ensure that the state is not brought into disrepute. I pray you, Your Majesty, take heed. Confucius said: “The Master said, ‘The way of the gentleman is to be careful in his speech. To be careful in speech is to avoid causing confusion. I pray you, Your Majesty, consider this well. Confucius said: “The Master said, ‘The way of the gentleman is to be frugal in his expenditures. To be frugal is to conserve resources for the benefit of the people. I pray you, Your Majesty, act with restraint. Confucius said: “The Master said, ‘The way of the gentleman is to be loyal in his service. To be loyal is to serve the state with sincerity. I pray you, Your Majesty, uphold these virtues. Confucius said: “The Master said, ‘The way of the gentleman is to be filial in his family. To be filial is to honor one’s ancestors. I pray you, Your Majesty, honor the legacy of the former kings. Confucius said: “The Master said, ‘The way of the gentleman is to be fraternal in his relations. To be fraternal is to maintain harmony. I pray you, Your Majesty, promote unity among the people. All deluded movements of thought and perception are, in their very manifestation, your own true mind. This mind has no interaction whatsoever with external objects or with the state of maintaining stillness;

"This is not yet the truth. One must constantly realize that all is empty; not a single dharma should be grasped by the mind. This is the place where the Buddhas apply their minds. You should practice this with diligence.
