Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zǔxiù of Shíshì Monastery in Lōngxìng Prefecture.
In the fourth year of the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, the carving of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* into the stone walls at Yongfu Temple in Hangzhou was completed.
Prime Minister Yuan Zhen composed a record for it, the text of which states: "According to the account of the śramaṇa Shi Huìjiǎo regarding these matters himself, at Yongfu Temple..."
The first is named Gushan Temple (Solitary Mountain Temple). It is situated atop Mount Gu on the heart of Qiantang Lake in Hangzhou.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* carved into stone walls exists within this temple. Its inception began when Yan Hufu served as Prefect in the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era;
its completion was achieved when Bai Juyi served as Prefect in the fourth year of the Changqing era. [End of] Upper Volume.
The depth of the stone was six chi and five cun. Its length was fifty-seven chi and six cun. A pedestal surrounded the base of the stone;
a canopy surrounded the stone; and a paved walkway surrounded the hall. In total, the cost for hiring artisans to perform the carving amounted to sixty-nine thousand two hundred and fifty coins.
Once the work on the ten pillars was completed, two additional stone monuments were erected, one of which—
Regarding those who contributed money for the stele, anyone donating ten *qian* or more was entitled to have their name inscribed upon it.
Among those whose contributions were particularly generous were Yan Xiufu, Prefect of Hangzhou; Bai Juyi, Palace Secretary and Prefect of Hangzhou;
Cui Xuanliang, Minister of Justice and Prefect of Huzhou; and [Minister of Justice and] Prefect of Muzhou.
The historian Wei Wenwu; Wei Xingli, Prefect of Chuzhou; Zhang Wei, Prefect of Hangzhou;
Li You, Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review and Prefect of Suzhou; Yuan Zhen, Grand Master of Remonstrance and Prefect of Yuezhou;

and Chen Hu, Director of the Right Bureau of the Ministry of Personnel and Prefect of Chuzhou—besides these nine prefects, there were also those among the gentry who traveled through Hangzhou, such as Xuan... (text truncated).
From Jia Su, who was appointed as Director of the Kuubu Bureau and Editor of Imperial Edicts, down to others, there are few who are not included in the ranks of those inscribed upon the stone stele.
Their placement is invariably determined by the sequence of their monetary contributions, rather than by status, age, or the amount donated.

As for one particular monument, its monastic followers sought to enhance their own reputations; they composed literary accounts of his deeds to magnify themselves. Regarding this, I— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
In the second year of the Changqing era, I served as a high official under the late Emperor. Without cause, I was banished to Tongzhou, and the following year I was transferred to Kuaiji.

On my way, I passed through Hangzhou; the people there vied with one another to see me. They asked in astonishment why they were looking at me, and all replied, "We are not here to see the Chancellor, but rather to see the Yuan and Bai we have heard of in the past. Because of this, the monks mistakenly took me to be the famous man of that name.
The people together attacked the Provincial Governor day and night. [The Governor] requested that I provide a text for him.

I observed how the followers of the Sangha cause their teachings to be inscribed upon stone and carved upon steles; this is surely because they wish to achieve immortality and also because they wish to magnify their own fundamental doctrines.

Now, since the steles have already been inscribed with texts and the scriptures have already been engraved upon stone, and furthermore, the nine feudal lords have led one another to contribute funds to their object of veneration—from this point onward...
To speak of this: it may also be said that he has come from a different school and yet achieved immortality.
Speaking from a remote perspective, beyond tens of thousands of years, heaven and earth grind against one another; yin and yang surge against each other; fire and wind shoot at one another.
When names and forms perish, the four seas and nine provinces are but a single mote of dust within emptiness; how, then, can one know whether they decay or not?
Nevertheless, Yang叔子 (Yang Xiu) recognized an ancient ring within a withered tree; Zhang Sengyou was a master calligrapher for generations;
the spirit of Liyang remains to this day as city walls and moats; and a dog’s single bark transported it to another age—yet in the end, [it did not].

It can be refined through cultivation. If you, my son, practice counting the breaths, success will be easily achieved. This, moreover, shows that nature and matter interact with one another, such that they can never be entirely forgotten by each other.

Furthermore, how could one know that the sixty-nine thousand characters engraved upon stone—formed eternally through the aggregation of many names—could not alone become an imperishable vessel for containing [the teachings] throughout ten million kalpas? From this it follows that...

Reflect upon this: thus the followers of the monastic order will achieve their purpose. As for the profound mysteries of the Buddhist scriptures, it is the monks who ought to speak of them to me, not I who should speak of them to the monks;
moreover, since this writing merely records [the event] upon stone, I have not gone so far as to expound its meaning.

During this year, Wang Zhixing, the Palace Secretary (Zhongshu Ling), requested that a *vaipulya* ordination platform (*jietan*) for monks and nuns be established in Sizhou, so that those wishing to receive the tonsure could do so during the month of the Emperor’s birth.
The imperial decree granted permission. Subsequently, Li Deyu, the Inspector of Zhexi, submitted a memorial stating:

"Wang Zhixing has established an ordination platform in Sizhou and recruited those wishing to be ordained, requiring each person to contribute two thousand coins; consequently, he no longer conducts any further investigations [into their eligibility]."

I submit this for consideration. [The Emperor] universally ordered the tonsure of all. To the right of the Huai River, every third male household had one son tonsured, on the pretext of exempting them from corvée labor;

those ordained numbered in the tens of thousands. Your servant has observed that several hundred men cross the river daily, and among the commoners of Suzhou and Changzhou, ten out of eight or nine have done so.
If this is not prohibited, by the time the year reaches its final month, the Jianghuai region will lose hundreds of thousands of able-bodied males, which is no small matter.
This was the matter. The Emperor did not accept it. Previously, Emperor Xuanzong had repeatedly issued edicts forbidding the private ordination of commoners as monks, nuns, or Daoist priests.
By this time, Zhi-xing had defied these prohibitions in his petition; consequently, the common people became confused and flocked to shave their heads and don the robes.
Zhi-xing thereby acquired several hundred thousand strings of cash, for which he was greatly despised by the pure discourse of the literati.

"Who is this traveler you have encountered that speaks in such a manner? Zhan praised him, saying, "Yesterday I received a pointer from Master Baizhang regarding a place of rest.
Thereupon, the Master gathered the assembly and invited [Zhan] to ascend the hall to preach the Dharma. Zhan cited the tradition of Baizhang’s school, saying:
The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects; it manifests the true and eternal, unconstrained by words or texts.

The nature of mind is unstained, fundamentally perfected from the beginning; simply by detaching from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness. Upon these words, his teacher attained awakening.

In the tenth month of the second year of the Dàhé era, Shen Chuānshī, the Inspector of Jiangxi, submitted a memorial requesting that, on the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, a *vaipulya* ordination platform be established in Hóngzhōu to ordain monks for the purpose of generating merit. The Imperial Decree replied: "The ordination of monks and nuns has been repeatedly prohibited by imperial edict.
You, Chuānshī, having been entrusted with the governance of a province, have violated these prohibitions in your petition. You shall be penalized by a one-month reduction in your salary."

The Treatise says: When Emperor Taizong of the Tang ascended the throne, he first deliberated on the matter of frequent amnesties, concluding that they were a detriment to loyal and virtuous officials.

I [the author] say: For the state to bestow indiscriminate favors upon all is likewise not to the benefit of the Dharma-gate. In the past, at the end of the Northern Wei, the number of monks and nuns who received general ordination reached several million;
ultimately, this resulted in the calamity of Emperor Wu of the Zhou. During the reign of Emperor Jingzong, Wang Zhixing schemed for personal gain.

The ordination of monks likewise met with the calamity of the Huichang era; however, it was only during the three reigns of Taizong, Xuanzong, and Xianzong that the private ordination of monks and nuns was absolutely prohibited.
Could it be that they were stingy toward our Way and failed to fully promote it? No, it could not.

The concern lies with those who are mired in superficiality, vulgarity, and a mere pursuit of food and clothing; they only defile the illustrious virtue [of the Sangha] without contributing to the teachings.
Thus, during the Zhenguan and Kaiyuan eras, eminent monks who served as imperial teachers and friends were found in great numbers.
Is this not because the Dharma-gate was honored and noble, remaining neither redundant nor corrupt? As the proverb says: "When things are rare..."
This is what makes it honorable. It merely requires that there be successors in the future; then, though few in number, there will be no harm.
In this year, Chan Master Weiyen of Yaoshan in Lǐzhōu passed away. The great Confucian scholar Táng Xēn composed a stele inscription for him, which states:
"The following year after [the Emperor] ascended the throne, the Śākya Master of Yaoshan in Lǐyáng Prefecture passed away on the sixth day of the twelfth month."
Eight years after [the Master’s passing] at his place of mental cultivation, a disciple recorded the deeds of his late teacher and traveled to the capital.
He informed the Virtuous One of Chongjing Temple, seeking a means to manifest his late teacher’s radiant light so that it might endure imperishably.
The Venerable Chongjing was my maternal uncle. He once visited Mount Jing and attained its essential heart-mind.

Since the passing of Master Xingshan Kuanjing, among those from all quarters who followed the Way and sought to resolve their doubts or transmit its subtleties, there were none who did not go to Chongjing for instruction.
He once said to Shen: "The Way of our school is as clear at Yaoshan as your own teachings are propagated."
At the banks of the Shu and Si rivers, although the torch of wisdom has been extinguished, the thunder of the Dharma still resounds.
How could it be that such illustrious virtue fails to illuminate and such supreme conduct remains buried? It is recorded that the Great Master was born in Xinfeng, Nan’gang;
even as a child, he never joined in the games of other boys, often sitting alone as if lost in thought or contemplation. At the age of seventeen, he crossed the Dayu Pass to the south, arriving at...
On Mount Xi at Chaozhou, he met Chan Master Huizhao; he then shaved his head, donned the black robes, and served him with reverence.

During the Dali era, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Xicheng of Mount Heng. His release of formal etiquette and observance of ritual decorum were as if they had been habitual practices for a long time.
One day, he said: "A great man should transcend phenomena to attain natural stillness; how could he deign to labor over trivial details regarding robes and conduct?"
At that time, there were Xian in Nanyue, Ji in Jiangxi, and Hong in Zhongyue; all had awakened to the mind and reached a profound accord.
Thus it was known that the substance of a great jade scepter does not require polishing, and the brilliance of a pearl worth a carriage cannot be obscured.
From then on, Ji became renowned throughout the four quarters for the Mahayana Dharma; as for his pointing to the mind to transmit the essentials, this was something no one else could do.
As for the one who has attained [enlightenment], the Master must recognize him silently and understand him intuitively, not differing from him even as he appears ignorant.
He dwelt in a chamber of stillness for nearly twenty years. Huiji said: "What you have attained may be called permeating the inner workings of the mind and extending through the four limbs.

You wish to benefit others yet find nothing to benefit; you wish to know yet find nothing to know. All is a浑然 (hún rán) harmony with Heaven, in accord with primordial non-being (běn wú). I have nothing further with which to describe it."
He taught them thus: "The Buddha takes it as his great task to reveal the truth to the blind masses, and his great virtue to deliver them from all evils.
You should, by means of such merit and virtue, universally rescue the deluded; you ought to serve as a bridge and a vessel. Do not linger here for long.

Thereupon, he ascended Mount Luofu and crossed Mount Qingliang; he traversed the Three Gorges and traveled through the Nine Rivers. At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, while resting at Yaoshan, he sighed deeply and said:
"My life is but a temporary lodging in this world, like a floating duckweed or a drifting reed. Why then should I emulate their tossing and turning?
Having cleared away the brushwood and built a hut merely to shelter my meditation seat, the local people who learned of it brought food and drink, running to visit me in haste.
The Master said, "I have bestowed no virtue upon these people; why should I trouble them? He declined all of it with thanks and would not accept it. The villagers knelt and said, "We pray that..."

When he heard that the daily expenses were being calculated, he said, "One *sheng* of rice will suffice. From then on, he would regularly supplement his meals with several varieties of mountain vegetables.
Once the meal was finished, he would take his seat and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras.

Day and night were as one, and he continued in this manner from beginning to end for nearly thirty years. Disciples who traveled to seek further instruction realized that the teaching resided in him. Several years later...
The monastic community dwelt there, their meditation halls roofed together in overlapping rows; their number was beyond counting.
From the way they cultivated the mind amidst worldly bustle and guided the source to form a stream, one could see the clarity of Master Ji’s prescient wisdom.
Suddenly, one day, he said to his disciples: "One who travels by post stops when evening falls; there has never been anyone who travels long without resting."
"I have reached my destination; I shall now rest. The spiritual source is inherently pure; it is the various marks that cause confusion.

One who can extinguish all marks is without form. Exhausting the root and severing external attachments—you must fully comprehend this. Having finished speaking, he leaned on his armrest and passed away.
He was eighty-four years old and had sixty summer retreats (*varṣa*) as a monk.

His入室 disciple Chongxu and others moved his seat and constructed a stupa to the east of Chanju Temple, following the original teachings. Formerly, the Master had always worn robes made of coarse hemp cloth and used bamboo vessels as sandals;
he shaved his own hair and prepared his own food. Although there were several hundred disciples at his gate and many young attendants...
He never changed his labor, though it was extensive; he never changed his food, though there were a hundred varieties of delicacies and fresh fruits set out in rows;

he never changed his clothing, though he wore heavy furs for warmth in winter and light, airy garments in summer; his magnificent chambers were serene and deep, and his fragrant couches were solemn and pure.
He never altered his posture; though deer circled him and fierce beasts crouched before him, he never changed his gaze.
Noble and humble alike came in succession to prostrate themselves at the foot of his bed, yet he never altered his manner of receiving them.

Were it not for one who has exhausted all phenomena to realize true emptiness, transcended the ailment of dependent origination, and whose innate nature is pure beyond all things—how could he have cast aside his physical form, forgotten his desires, and remained so long?
As for those who are of one mind: other eminent ministers and high officials have taken refuge in and practiced the Way of the Master, yet none have even reached his threshold;
therefore, they are not included in this chapter. The inscription says: When a single object is within, it stirs upon contact with external conditions.
I reveal its source: neither the condition nor the stirring exists. The Sage of the West spoke truly of its essential point. That essential point—

Once attained, one may speak of its subtlety. My source is self-sufficient; my true nature is inherently numinous. It encompasses the myriad existences in its vastness and emerges from the formless in its minuteness.
What was transmitted at Caoxi remains merely hidden in secrecy. When both body and world are empty, how could there be any substantial thing?

To perceive this for oneself is called "clarity"; this is the ultimate essence. Its appearance and disappearance depend on me alone; who can speak of death and birth? Engraving this upon jade tablets, I establish it here.
At Yanxiu, the author of the stele, Shen, aspired for it to be imperishable.
The commentary states: Both the *Chuandeng lu* and the Cao-Dong lineage records maintain that Yaoshan succeeded Shitou Xiqian;
yet this stele now claims he received the Dharma from Daji Mazu. This assertion has circulated for three hundred years, and no one in the world has yet corrected it.
The reason for this is that one must know that eight years after Yaoshan passed away, his disciples collectively erected a stele.
How could disciples fail to examine what their teacher had inherited? I maintain that the stele should be taken as authoritative.

Furthermore, it is commonly said that Li Ao, the Minister of the Secretariat, heard the Way from Mount Yao. Li Ao once composed the *Fu xing shu* (Treatise on the Restoration of Human Nature) in three chapters, which are now recorded here on the left.
The first chapter of the *Fu xing shu* states: "That by which a person becomes a sage is their nature. That by which a person..."
That which deludes one's nature is emotion (*qing*). Joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, and desire—these seven are the manifestations of emotion.
Once emotion is turbid, nature is thereby concealed; it is not the fault of nature itself. These seven circulate and arrive in succession, so that nature cannot govern them.
When water is turbid, its flow is not clear; when fire is smoky, its light is not bright.
Brightness is not the fault of water or fire being turbid; if the sand is not stirred up, the flow will be clear.
If the smoke does not choke it, the light will be bright. If the emotions do not arise, the nature will be sovereign. Nature is the mandate of Heaven;
the sage is one who attains it without confusion. Does the sage lack emotion? The sage is tranquil and unmoving, yet he does not fail to respond.
They arrive [at their purpose] without speaking, yet they are trusted; they do not dazzle, yet they shine with light. Their creative works participate in Heaven and Earth;
their transformations accord with Yin and Yang. Although they possess emotions (*qing*), they have never truly possessed emotions. Thus, how could it be that the common people lack nature?
The nature of the common people does not differ from the nature of the Sage. Nevertheless, it is where emotion is clouded that confusion arises.
Their mutual conflict has no beginning and will have no end; thus, even throughout one's entire life, one does not perceive one's own nature.
Fire hidden within mountain rocks and forest trees is not without fire; the terminal currents of the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji rivers that spring from the mountains are not without water.
If the stone is not struck and the wood is not rubbed, they cannot burn down their respective forests and mountains.
It dries up the myriad things. If the source of the spring is not cleared, it cannot become the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, or the Ji;
it cannot flow eastward into the great abyss in vast surges and billows to reach unfathomable depths.
If the movement of the emotions does not cease, one cannot restore one's nature to illuminate heaven and earth with boundless brilliance. Therefore, sincerity is the nature of the sage.
It is thus: quiescent and unmoving, vast and luminously clear, it illuminates heaven and earth; stirred, it penetrates the affairs of the world.

Whether walking or stopping, speaking or remaining silent, there is nothing that does not reach its ultimate state. Those who restore their nature are the worthy ones who follow this path without ceasing.
By not ceasing, they are able to return to the source. The Sage knows that the nature of all people can [be restored].
Following this path without ceasing leads to the state of sagehood. Therefore, rituals were established to regulate it, and music was created to harmonize it.
To abide in benevolence (*ren*) is the root of music; to move with centrality (*zhong*) is the root of ritual. Thus, when in a carriage, one hears the sound of the *he* and *luan* bells;
when walking, one hears the resonance of the jade pendants. One does not set aside the *qin* and *se* lutes except for specific occasions. This applies to both sight and speech.
One acts by following ritual and law. This is the means by which one teaches people to forget their cravings and desires and return to the Way of nature and destiny (*xing-ming*).

The Way is ultimate sincerity that never ceases. When there is ultimate sincerity that does not cease, there is emptiness (*xu*). When there is emptiness that does not cease, there is clarity (*ming*).
When there is clarity that does not cease, there is illumination. When there is illumination that does not cease, it illuminates heaven and earth without omission. It is nothing other than this.
This is the ultimate way of exhausting the nature and destiny (xing-ming). How lamentable! Every person is capable of reaching this state; yet none stop themselves from failing to do so.
Is this not delusion? In the past, the Sage transmitted it to Yanzi. Yanzi attained it and cherished it so earnestly that he never lost it;
his mind returned to its source before he had gone far. For three months he did not depart from benevolence (ren). The Master said of Hui: "He..."
He was close to it. That he was often without provisions was because he had not yet reached the level of a Sage by a single breath’s distance;
it was not that he lacked the power, but rather that his life was short and he died prematurely. As for the others who "ascended the hall," they were all disciples.

They were nourished by the same spring of vital energy and moistened by the same rain, yet those who attained it varied in depth and shallowness; it was not necessarily uniform. This was the case with Zengzi.
At the point of death, he said: "What do I seek? That I may die upright—this is enough. These are words concerning the rectification of nature and destiny (*xing-ming*).
Zisi was the grandson of Zhongni (Confucius); having attained the Way of his grandfather, he composed the forty-nine chapters of the *Zhongyong* to transmit them to Meng Ke (Mencius).
Meng Ke said: "I am not moved by my heart until the age of forty. The disciples of Meng Ke were proficient [in these matters].

This refers to Gongsun Chou, Wan Zhang, and their followers, who indeed transmitted it. During the Qin dynasty’s destruction of the books, only one chapter of the *Zhongyong* (Doctrine of the Mean) survived that was not burned.

Consequently, this Way fell into neglect; those who taught it focused merely on parsing the characters, phrases, and sentences, while they took the arts of deportment and swordsmanship as their mutual masters.
As for the source of nature and destiny (*xingming*), I have been unable to transmit it.
When the Way reaches its extreme in *bō* (peeling away), it must necessarily return. Since I was six years old, I have studied books; however, I have only pursued the study of words and phrases.
It has been four years since I set my mind upon the Way, yet when speaking with others, there has never been one who recognized me as such.
I traveled south to observe the surging tides at the mouth of the Yangtze River and entered Yue, where Lu Can of Wuxing resided. When I spoke with him, Lu Can said: "As for your..."
It is said: "The mind of Confucius was such that if there were a sage in the East, he would not go beyond this;
if there were a sage in the West, he likewise would not go beyond this. It is simply that you must practice it without ceasing. Alas!

Although the books concerning human nature and destiny (xing-ming) still exist, scholars have been unable to clarify them. Consequently, they all turn toward the teachings of Zhuangzi, Liezi, Laozi, and Śākyamuni.
Those who do not understand this claim that the disciples of the Master (Confucius) were insufficient to exhaust the Way of nature and destiny;
those who believe this are indeed numerous. When someone questioned me, I transmitted to them what I myself knew. I have therefore committed it to writing in this book to open their understanding.
The source of sincerity and luminosity had been neglected, severed, abandoned, neither propagated nor taught, such that it was on the verge of being lost to posterity.

Thereupon, I entitled this work "Treatise on the Restoration of Nature" (*Fuxing shu*) to govern the mind and transmit it to others. Alas! Were the Master to be reborn today, he would not refute my words.

The second [section] says: Someone asked, "Human beings have been mired in delusion for a long time. To restore one's original nature, there must be a gradual process. May I venture to ask about the method?
He replied, "If one does not deliberate and does not reflect, then emotional states (*qing*) will not arise. When emotional states no longer arise, this constitutes correct reflection (*zhengsi*).
Correct reflection means neither thinking nor deliberating. The *I Ching* says, 'What is there to think about? What is there to deliberate upon? It also says:"
"Restrain the depraved and preserve one's sincerity. The *Odes* say: "Let there be no depravity. [The Master] said: "Is that all? [The Disciple] replied: "It is not yet.

This refers to one who has purified their mind through fasting and vigilance (*zhāijì*), yet they have still not transcended stillness. Where there is stillness, there must be movement; where there is movement, there must be stillness.

That movement and stillness do not cease is precisely what constitutes the emotional state (*qíng*). The *Changes* (*Yī*) says: "Good fortune, misfortune, regret, and shame arise from movement. How could one return [to the source]?
"Is this its nature? He asked. "How is it so? [The Master] replied: "When one is in a state of stillness and knows that the mind is without thought, this is *zhāijì* (fasting and purification).
To know that fundamentally there is no thought, to be detached from both movement and stillness, and to remain tranquil and unmoving—this is *zhíchéng* (ultimate sincerity).
The *Zhōngyōng* says, 'Sincerity leads to clarity. The *Yìjīng* says, 'The movements of the world are all rooted in the One. He asked: "Without deliberation..."
When one does not engage in such thinking, objects are perceived externally and emotions respond internally; how could this process be stopped? Is it possible to stop emotion with emotion?

He replied: "Emotion is a deviation from nature. If one knows it to be a deviation and fundamentally has no intention toward it, then through uninterrupted stillness, deviant thoughts will naturally cease.
Only when nature is luminously clear—where could deviation possibly arise? As for [the method]...
To cease emotion within emotion—this is the "Great Emotion. Is there an end to the mutual cessation of emotions? The *I Ching* says:
"The son of the Yan family was perhaps close to perfection; he never failed to know what was not good, and having known it, he never again practiced it.

The *I Ching* further says: "Returning before one has gone far; no cause for great regret; supreme good fortune. A questioner asked: "Fundamentally, there is no thought. Whether in motion or stillness, both..."
"Separated. Yet, when stillness arrives, is it not heard? When the form of things appears, is it not seen? He said:
"Not seeing and not hearing—this is not the work of man. It is sufficient that while sight and hearing are clear and vivid, they do not give rise to the act of hearing or seeing.
There is nothing one does not know; there is nothing one does not do. The mind is tranquil, its light illuminating heaven and earth. This is sincerity."
This is clarity. The *Great Learning* says: "To extend knowledge lies in the investigation of things. The *Book of Changes* says: "Without thought and without action, it is still and unmoving;
yet when stimulated, it immediately penetrates the affairs of the world. Were it not for the most supreme spirit in the world, who could participate in this? [The student] asks:
"May I venture to ask what is meant by 'to extend knowledge lies in the investigation of things'? [The Master] replies: "'Things' refers to the myriad things. To investigate..."
This refers to the arrival [of objects]. When objects arrive, the mind is clearly luminous and discerns them; yet that which does not respond to these objects is the perfection of knowledge.
This is the ultimate state of knowing. Because knowledge reaches its perfection, the intention becomes sincere; because the intention is sincere, the mind becomes rectified.

Because the mind is correct, the person is cultivated; because the person is cultivated, the family is harmonious; when the family is harmonious, the state is well-governed; and when the state is well-governed, all under heaven is at peace.
This is how one is able to participate in the Way of Heaven and Earth. The *I Ching* says: "Because it resembles Heaven and Earth, it does not conflict with them."

His wisdom encompasses all things and his Way benefits the world; thus he does not err. He moves in various directions without being carried away by them. Joyful in Heaven and knowing his destiny, he is free from anxiety.
At peace with his station and grounded in benevolence, he is able to love. He circumscribes the transformations of the earth without overstepping its bounds;
he brings all things to completion in their particularity without omission. He penetrates the Way of day and night and thereby possesses knowledge. Thus, the Spirit has no...
The Book of Changes is square yet formless; "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way"—this is what that refers to. [The disciple] said, "Please explain the Doctrine of the Mean for me.
[The Master] replied, "It does not go beyond what has preceded. [The disciple] said, "I have not yet understood it clearly. May I venture to ask:

what is meant by 'that which Heaven mandates is called nature'? [The Master] replied, "When humans are born, they are tranquil; this is the nature of Heaven. Nature is the mandate of Heaven. To follow one's nature...
"This is what is called the Way (Dao). [The questioner] asked, "What does this mean? [The Master] replied, "It means 'to lead' or 'to follow.
To follow its source and return to one's nature is the Way. The Way is supreme sincerity. Supreme sincerity is the Way of Heaven. Sincerity is stability; it is immovability."
"To follow the Way is what is meant by 'instruction' (jiao). What does this mean? It is said: Instruction is the way of humanity.
It consists in selecting what is good and adhering firmly to it. To follow this Way and return to its source is clarity. As for instruction, it can indeed be used to instruct the world.
Yanzi was such a person. The Way cannot be departed from for even a moment; it is something that cannot be departed from."
This is not the Way. The commentators say: it is because the mind must not be moved for even a moment. To move is to be far removed; it is not the Way.
Yet transformation knows no fixed direction, for it never departs from the state of non-movement.

Therefore, the gentleman is cautious regarding what he does not see and fearful regarding what he does not hear. For nothing is more visible than that which is hidden, and nothing is more manifest than that which is obscure.
It is subtle. Therefore, the gentleman is cautious regarding his solitude. Commentators say: "The seeing of that which is not seen is the greatest of all seeing;
the hearing of that which is not heard is the most profound of all hearing. When the mind does not stir, this is the seeing of the unseen and the hearing of the unheard.
His return [to the Dao] will not be far off. Thus, he is cautious regarding his solitude. To be cautious regarding one's solitude is to preserve the Center. Question.
[The Master] said: "Those who explained the *Zhongyong* in the past and what I have spoken are both different. Why is this? [The disciple] said:

'They explained it through phenomena (*shi*), whereas I have attained realization through the mind (*xin*). [The Master] asked: 'Did they also attain realization through the mind? [The disciple] said: 'I do not know. The question was thus posed.
"The nature of ordinary people is like the nature of the sages. From what do the hearts of desire, love, and aversion arise?
He replied, "Emotion (*qing*) is delusion; it is depravity. [The questioner] asked, "If it is depravity and delusion, then they must have no cause.

When delusive emotion is extinguished and ceases, the original nature becomes clear and bright, circulating through the six voids; this is why it is called 'being able to restore one's nature. The *Yi* says: 'The Way of Qian...'"
Through transformation, each is made correct in its nature and destiny (*xing-ming*). As the saying goes: "If one hears the Way (*Dao*) in the morning, it is acceptable to die in the evening.

This is because one is able to rectify one's nature and destiny. [The interlocutor] asks: "When the emotions (*qing*) cause confusion, the nature (*xing*) is extinguished. How can this be said to be like the nature of a sage?"
It is said: "The clarity of water is turbidified by sand and mud. While it is turbid, does its essential nature (xing) not still exist?
After a long time, when it is undisturbed, the sand and mud settle of their own accord, and the clear, pure nature reflects heaven and earth;
this does not come from without. Therefore, while it is turbid, the nature is fundamentally not lost; when it returns to clarity, the nature is likewise not newly produced."

The nature of human beings is also like water. A questioner asked: "If the nature of human beings is fundamentally good, yet their depraved emotions cloud it, may I ask whether the nature of the Sage will again be muddied by his desires?
[The Master] replied: "It is not muddied again. Emotion is fundamentally depraved and delusory;
when obscured by depravity and delusion, the nature cannot be restored. Since the Sage has already restored his nature, it is no longer subject to such obscuration."
Is it that which consciousness produces? Since what is produced by the perverse is already perceived by the enlightened, there is no perversity.
How, then, could perversity arise? He asked, "May I venture to ask where one goes after death? He replied, "This is that which the sages did not clearly record in their annals.
The *I Ching* says: 'Examine the beginning and grasp the end; thus one knows the discourse on life and death. Essential qi forms things; the wandering soul forms the spirit."
Transformation. Thus, the nature and circumstances of ghosts and spirits are fully understood therein. The Master said, "If you do not know life, how can you know death?
Therefore, by tracing its origin and returning to its end, one can fully exhaust the Way of life.
Once the Way of life is fully exhausted, the discourse on death will be understood without further study. This is not what is urgent. If you cultivate this without ceasing, its—
Know this for yourself. I cannot speak with such ostentation as to say that my words are not those of the books.
The third point is this: He who works by day and rests by night is an ordinary man. I do not work when others work, for I work together with all things;
nor do I rest when others rest, for I rest together with all things. Thus, I am not like an ordinary man; by day, I have no [activity].

Activity never ceases at evening; yet activity is not "my" activity. When there is activity, there is an object. Rest does not cease for me; yet rest is not "my" rest. When there is rest, there is an object.
Whether it be rest or activity, both are absent and do not exist. That which you preserve, my son, shall ultimately neither perish nor depart.
Those who do not exert themselves in the Way are muddled and lack reflection. Between heaven and earth, all things—
Life arises. Man is one with the myriad things. That which distinguishes him from birds, beasts, insects, and fish—is it not the completeness of his nature of *dao* and *de*?
Having received the single *qi* to form a body, one becomes a thing and one becomes a human;
this is attained with extreme difficulty. Born into this world, moreover, one does not possess a long life. Because it is not a long life...
At my age, though I possess this body so difficult to obtain, I do not devote myself single-mindedly to the Great Way, but instead act according to the whims of my own heart.
My difference from birds, beasts, insects, and fish has thereby vanished. I am muddled and lack reflection; being thus muddled, I shall never attain clarity.
I am now thirty-nine years old, yet when I think back to the time I was nineteen, it seems like the break of dawn.

It is so. When I reflect on the time nine years ago, it is as if it were only this morning. As for human beings receiving their life span, those who live longer than seventy, eighty, or ninety years are rare; those who reach a hundred years are even rarer.

When one is at the age of a hundred and looks back upon the time when one was ninety, how could the distance between that past and this present day not be vastly different? How could they not be poles apart?
Furthermore, how could one remain far removed from the time when the sun rises?
Thus, although a human being may enjoy a lifespan of a hundred years, it can be understood that this is like the sudden clash of thunder and lightning, or like the whirling of the wind.

How much more so, then, for among hundreds or thousands of people, not even one reaches the age of a hundred. Therefore, throughout my life, I have set my mind upon the Way and its Virtue (Dao-de), just as...
I fear it is too late. Who, indeed, is that person who has allowed his mind to run wild?
Li Ao, styled Xizhi, was a graduate of the jinshi examination and served successively as Minister of the Ministry of Revenue. He once governed Langzhou and admired the Way of Yaoshan;
though he repeatedly invited him, Yaoshan did not go. Consequently, Li entered the mountains to pay his respects. Yaoshan was reciting a sutra and paid no heed to him. An attendant said:
The Prefectural Governor was present there. Li, being impatient by nature, said, "Seeing someone in person is not as good as hearing of their reputation.
Yaoshan called out to the Governor, who responded. Yaoshan said, "How can you hold the ears in honor while treating the eyes with contempt?
Li bowed his hands in thanks and asked, "What is the Way? Yaoshan pointed up and down and asked, "Do you understand? Li said, "I do not understand. Yaoshan said, "Clouds in..."
"Venerable Sir! There is water in the pitcher. Li Xian replied with a verse, saying: "My body has been refined until it resembles the form of a crane;
Beneath a thousand pine trees lie two cases of scripture. I have come to inquire after the Way and have no other business: The clouds are in the blue sky, and the water is in the pitcher.
He further asked, "What are precept, concentration, and wisdom? Shanshan said, "There are no such idle furnishings here. Li did not understand. Shanshan—
He spoke again, saying: "If you wish to attain the assurance of this matter, you must simply stand atop the highest peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor.
If you cannot let go of the things within the inner chambers, they will all constitute leaks. Li took his leave.
One night, while climbing the mountain, Yaoshan suddenly saw the moon as the clouds parted; he let out a great laugh, the sound of which reached eighty or ninety li east of Liyang.
Upon hearing this, Ao sent another verse in reply, saying: "Having chosen a secluded dwelling that accords with my rustic sentiments, Throughout the year there is neither seeing off nor welcoming.
Sometimes I ascend directly to the peak of a solitary mountain, And beneath the moon, parting the clouds, let out a laugh.
Li also once asked a monk, "What sayings did Mazu have? The monk replied, "Sometimes he spoke of 'this very mind is Buddha,' and sometimes he spoke..."
"It is neither mind nor Buddha. Li said, "In general, pass right through here. Later, he again asked Chan Master Xitang Zhizang, "What sayings or phrases did Master Mazu have?
Zhizang called out, "Li Ao! Ao responded, "Yes? Zhizang said, "The drums and horns are sounding."
Xiao sighed in admiration and departed.
The *Treatise* states: "The *Xi zhi fu xing* (On Returning to One's Nature through Practice) was likely derived from Buddhist scriptures; it differs only in its choice of terminology and citations.
This is because Xi had studied the art of composition under Han Changli (Han Yu), who authored the *Yuan xing* (On the Origin of Human Nature).

In truth, he had not yet seen his nature; he merely refined his rhetoric and established categories to differentiate it. At that time, the gentlemen who clearly understood the Way all found this unacceptable.

Xuzhi thereupon purified his mind through fasting and vigilance, investigating the principle of being detached from both movement and stillness, where quiescence and illumination merge into a single fusion.
He proceeded until emotions were extinguished and his true nature restored, reaching a state of utmost sincerity through which he beheld the Way. His...
His exposition largely accords with the general principles of the Tiantai *Zhi guan*. Although he does not explicitly cite Buddhist scriptures, how could his insights remain hidden?
Had he practiced them and gained entry into the chamber of Mount Yao, his teachings would have been even more profound. Yet, because his teachings were so remote, they were rejected;
they did not resonate with the common sentiments as closely as this book does.
In the third year of the Tàihé era, the carving of the stone-wall scriptures at Chóngxuán Monastery in Sūzhōu was completed. The Regional Inspector Bái Jǐyì composed an inscription for them, stating:
"The inscription is located to the east of the stone wall; the stone wall is situated in the southwest corner of the Guǎngdé Fǎhuá Cloister."
The monastery is located several paces west of Chongxuan Temple. The temple is located several li north of the city of Suzhou.

Buddhist scriptures were engraved here using the Chinese language and Tang-style calligraphy; from the titles of the sutras, their chapters, and the names of the various Buddhas onwards, the characters were inscribed with gold.
In revealing, instructing, awakening, and entering the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas, there is nothing more venerable than the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,

which delivers boundless beings through its definitive meaning and extends infinitely through its perfect teaching, totaling sixty-nine thousand five hundred and five words. In realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
composing the Gate of Non-duality, and abiding in inconceivable liberation, there is nothing more ultimate than the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
It consists of twenty-seven thousand nine hundred and twelve words. It brings the four modes of birth and the nine classes of beings into nirvana without remainder;
yet, in reality, there is no one who attains deliverance. Nothing is more preeminent than the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. It consists of five thousand two hundred and eighty-seven words.
It destroys transgressions, accumulates merit, and purifies all evil realms; nothing is more urgent than the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*.
The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra* consists of three thousand and twenty words; one should recite it with mindfulness and accord with one's vows, aspiring to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Do not consider the *Sūtra of Amitābha* to be more urgent than this; it consists of one thousand eight hundred words and employs right view to contemplate the true nature of reality.

Do not look further than the *Sūtra on the Method for Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva*; it consists of six thousand nine hundred and ninety words and elucidates the self-nature.
To recognize original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi), nothing is more profound than the *Śrī-mahābherī-haraka-nirghoṣa-sūtra*, which consists of three thousand two hundred and five words.
To empty the dust of dharmas and rely upon Buddha-wisdom, nothing surpasses the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, which consists of two hundred and fifty-eight words.
These eight sūtras comprise the twelve divisions of the canon; together they total one hundred eleven thousand six thousand eight hundred and five words.
These seventeen words exhaust the essential tenets of the Three Vehicles and the secret treasury of the myriad Buddhas.
This stone wall is four layers thick, three *xun* high, fifteen *zhang* long, and one *chi* and eight *cun* thick.
Stone lotuses spread over its top and bottom, and stone deities guard it before and behind. Fire and water cannot burn or float it away; wind and moon cannot shake it.
Extinguished. This refers to the bestowing of the unsurpassed Dharma throughout the limits of the future.

Composed in the winter of the second year of the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, it was completed in the spring of the third year of the Taihe era. The śramaṇa Qinghuang of the Vinaya school initiated the plan, and Qinghai succeeded to his resolve.
His disciple Nankè completed it. Dàozé finalized it. The monk of the monastery, Qi Yuán, set aside his artistic skills to transcribe it.
The Prefectural Governor, Yújì, offered his prose to compose this eulogy. The eulogy says: After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the world became empty and void;
only these scriptures remain together with sentient beings. Suppose there were someone who transcribed them upon palm leaves and stored them within a sandalwood shrine—this would not be enduring.

It will not endure for long; it is like a wax seal upon the void. Even if one were to use blood as ink and flayed skin as paper, it would perish and vanish instantly, like a drawing made with a brush upon water.
Alas! A drawing on water does not compare to an inscription on stone, nor does a wax seal compare to characters engraved in gold.
Their merit shall be imperishable, and their meaning most profound. Therefore, I say that the merit of the Stone Classics accords with the Tathāgata’s heart of entrustment.

In that year, Chan Master Danxia Tianran was about to pass away. He ordered his attendants to prepare a bath. Having finished bathing, he donned his bamboo hat, took up his staff, and put on his sandals.
He extended one foot, which had not yet touched the ground, when he entered nirvana. He was eighty-three years of age.

The Master was originally a Confucian scholar who had been preparing for the imperial examinations. Once, a Chan practitioner asked him, "Where are you going now, sir? He replied, "I am going to select an official. The Chan practitioner...
He asked, "How does the selection of officials compare to the selection of Buddhas? He replied, "To select a Buddha, where should one go?
The Chan practitioner said, "Mazu of Jiangxi has appeared in the world; he is the very field for selecting Buddhas. The Master then went to see Mazu, who placed his hand upon the Master’s forehead.
The Patriarch gazed at him for a long time and said, "Nanyue Shitou is your teacher. When the Master arrived at Nanyue, he presented himself with the same intention.
Shitou said, "Go to the stable and work there. Thereupon, he bowed in gratitude and entered the hall of the practitioners to take up his duties.
Later, while participating in a communal labor of weeding grass, the Master alone washed his head and knelt before Shitou.
Shitou joyfully shaved his hair for him and proceeded to explain the precepts to him. [Nanquan] immediately covered his ears and departed, returning to Jiangxi to see Mazu again.
Before even paying his respects, he entered the monks' hall, mounted the neck of the sacred statue (sheng-seng), and sat there. The assembly was astonished and reported it to Mazu.

Mazu entered the hall and saw him, saying, "My son is truly natural. The Master immediately descended from his seat, prostrated himself, and said, "I thank the Master for bestowing upon me a Dharma name.
After some time, he traveled extensively throughout all quarters. Later, while lying across the Tianjin Bridge, the Imperial Commissioner Zheng came out and rebuked him, but he did not rise.
When the officials asked the reason, he replied, "I am a monk with no affairs. Zheng was struck by his strangeness and provided him daily with rice.
[The Master] was called Mian. He was widely revered in Luoyang. Residing at Danxia in Dengzhou, he gathered several hundred followers.
He once addressed the assembly, saying: "You, as a whole family, must protect this one spiritual essence. This is not something you can create or describe by name.
What more need be said about 'recommending' or 'not recommending'? In the past, when I saw Master Shitou, he too taught nothing other than to preserve it."
"Guard this matter; it is not something you can grasp through translated words. Each of you has your own patch of ground; what more is there to doubt?
Is Zen something you can intellectually understand? How could there be a Buddha to be attained?
The very word 'Buddha' is never pleasing to hear. Look for yourself: skillful means, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are not obtained from the outside."
Do not cling to the square inch of the heart. Skillful means is Mañjuśrī; expedient means is Samantabhadra.
What more do you intend to pursue? Do not rely on scriptures, yet do not fall into emptiness. Nowadays, students are in a state of constant turmoil, all of them investigating Zen and seeking the Way.
In my place here, there is no Way to cultivate and no Dharma to realize. With every sip of drink and every mouthful of food, each person is for themselves.
There is a share [of this]. Do not harbor doubts; such people exist everywhere. If you can recognize it, Śākyamuni is but an old ordinary man.
You must examine it for yourself. "One blind person leading many blind people together will fall into a fire pit."
In the darkness of night, how could one play at double-sixes for the sake of fortune? Be careful and take heed of what is not a matter.

The Master once composed two poems titled "Verses on Playing with the Pearl. The first says: "Once you recognize the treasure within your robes, The intoxication of ignorance awakens by itself. When the hundred skeletal members all crumble away,"

A single object eternally abides as the numinous; the realm of wisdom is fundamentally formless. The divine pearl has no fixed shape; when awakened, it is the Buddha of the Three Bodies, yet when lost in delusion, it is ten thousand volumes of scripture.
When present in the mind, the mind can fathom it; passing through the ear, the ear finds it hard to hear. It is like the "formless image" (wangxiang) that existed before heaven and earth.
The Mysterious Pearl emerges from the profound darkness; its primal hardness requires no forging. Its original purity needs no settling; vast and expansive, it circles the rising sun.
Delicate and resonant, it reflects the morning stars. Auspicious light flows on without ceasing; when touched by true qi, it is reborn. It mirrors the silence of Mount Kongtong.

The luminosity that encompasses the Dharma-realm does not diminish its power over the ordinary; transcending the fruits of sainthood, it is never full. The dragon girl offered it with heartfelt devotion, and the serpent king presented it from his own mouth.
The goose was restored to life through protection, yet the yellow sparrow’s intent remained light. That one understands speech has nothing to do with the tongue.
That which can speak is not sound; it transcends all boundaries and is utterly vast. Boundless and equal to space, its unfolding of the teaching is not for the sake of verbal explanation.

Hearing its name, do not mistake the name for the reality. Do not establish either of the two extremes, and there is no need to travel the Middle Way. When you see the moon, cease looking at the pointing finger.
"Return home and cease questioning the path; recognize the mind, and that mind is itself the Buddha—what further Buddha could possibly be accomplished?
At that time, there was a woman named Ling Xingpo who once visited Master Fubei.

While they were drinking tea together, the woman asked, "To whom do you entrust that phrase which cannot be expressed even with one's full strength? The Master replied, "Fubei has no superfluous words. The woman said, "I..."

"Not so," [Fubei] said. "How would you say it? The nun folded her hands and wept, saying, "Alas! Heaven above, how even more grievous is my suffering! Fubei was speechless. Furthermore, by imperial decree, he was appointed to attend upon the Crown Prince at the Eastern Court. Emperor Shunzong deeply admired his character and treated him with the affection due to a brother.
The Emperor treated him with exceptional kindness and courtesy, as if he had been his companion from childhood.

his eloquence and reasoning were swift and resonant, and in responding to the Imperial will, he always accorded with the True Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*). Even in moments of casual conversation, he never failed to propagate the Dharma.
This became his primary concern. Consequently, the Son of Heaven came to recognize all the more that the Buddha was a Great Sage and that his teaching contained great and inconceivable matters.

Throughout his life, he offered tens of millions of items in support and charity, all of which were used to embellish the temple halls with the most exquisite carvings and paintings.
