All who looked up to him in devotion—whether noblemen, warriors, artisans, or merchants—gazed toward him with reverence. They offered gold and jade to express their sincerity and prostrated themselves before his majestic and dignified form;
those who came daily numbered in the thousands, beyond what could be fully recorded. Yet the Upādhyāya regarded all sentient beings as the Buddha.
He cultivated goodness by remaining detached from the four marks [of self, person, being, and life]. His mind was as level as the earth, devoid of hills or mounds;

he received everyone, from kings and dukes down to common porters, with sincerity. Critics have maintained that the Master alone has truly accomplished the practice of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.

Indeed, those who wish to launch the great vessel across the vast ocean to rescue the deluded masses and bring them to the other shore must necessarily possess extraordinary merit and wondrous wisdom.
Was this the Way? On the first day of the sixth month in the first year of the Kaicheng era (836 CE), he passed away reclining on his right side facing west.

Though it was the height of summer, his venerable countenance appeared as if alive; throughout the night, an extraordinary fragrance pervaded the air. On the sixth day of the seventh month of that same year, he was transferred to the South Plains of Changle.
In accordance with his final instructions, he was cremated, yielding more than three hundred *śarīra* relics. As the flames reached their peak, a divine light shone forth.

The moon was bright; once his remains were consumed by fire, his spiritual bones were as perfect as a pearl. He was posthumously granted the title "Great Attainment" (Dada) and his stupa was named "Mysterious Secret" (Xuanyi).
His secular age was sixty-seven, and his monastic seniority was forty-eight. His disciples, consisting of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, numbered approximately one thousand.
Some expounded upon profound doctrines, while others oversaw great monasteries. Cultivating dhyāna and upholding the Vinaya, they became teachers of men, with fifty such followers.

All were men who had attained realization. Alas! Was not the Master truly a hero among those who have left the household life? Were it not so, how could such supreme virtue and extraordinary auspiciousness be so magnificent?
His successor-disciples, including Ziyue, Yizheng, and Zhengyan, have been able to shoulder the ancestral legacy and reverently preserve his inherited traditions.
They feared greatly that his illustrious influence might at some point be lost to oblivion; thus, the official Liu Gong of the Gemen [family]—whose karmic affinity for the Dharma...
Our deepest affinity with the Way has become ever more firm, and we likewise submit this request: we pray that you will spread your pure influence and deign to visit these precincts.

We shall record these events in full, rejoicing in them with praise; indeed, our words shall be free from shame. The inscription says: Among the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, the fourth is Śākyamuni.

Compassionately regarding us living beings, he brought forth the scriptures to shatter the dust of delusion. As the net of the teaching is spread wide aloft, who can discern and distinguish its depths?

There is a Great Dharma Master who has heard [the teachings] directly from the Buddha himself. Regarding the Tripitaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and the studies of Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom—whether deep or shallow, they share a common source; whether preceding or following, they mutually awaken one another.

The doctrines of divergent schools hold partial truths; which is correct and which is erroneous? There was a Great Dharma Master who acted as frost and hail against them. Those who incline toward the True are obstructed; those who engage with the False are carried away.
Like elephants in rut or restless monkeys, they cannot be restrained by hooks or cages. Even when suppressed or cut off like a blade, they still produce sores and afflictions.
There was a great Dharma Master who wandered with thoughts severed. When the Great Tang inaugurated its destiny, the Great Hero (the Buddha) bestowed his teachings;

a dark resonance occurred for a thousand years, and the Three Vehicles shone forth in succession. Cherished with honor and mindful of his kindness, he elucidated, propagated, praised, and guided the Way. There was a great Dharma Master who responded to the call of the times.
The gate of emptiness was just being opened; the hall of the Dharma was only now unfolding. Yet its towering halls and buildings collapsed in a single day.
Like the moon in water or an image in a mirror, it comes and goes without intention, leaving only those of later generations to gaze upon it with lingering reverence.
On the sixth day of the third month of the third year, the National Teacher Qingliang, the Unifier of the Sangha (Sengtong) Chengguan, was about to pass away.

He said to his disciples, Haishan and others: "I have heard that when the Great Transformation lacks merit, the former sages lamented it; when one’s substance lacks practice, the ancients were ashamed of it.

Without clarity in the relations of seniority or movement and stillness, and without the continuity of the thread of discourse, do not engage in the forced interpretation of heterodox views, nor follow what is wrong."
Discerning the false, do not allow yourself to be deluded or ensnared by an evil mind; do not engage in persistent strife.

Even the Great Illumination cannot dispel the darkness of the long night, and even a compassionate mother cannot protect her child after death. You should place your trust in the Buddha, and not place your trust in humans.
"The ultimate truth is profound and subtle; it is not something manifested by words and speech. It must be realized through deep resolve so that it appears clearly before one.
When facing objects without a mind and encountering conditions without being moved, you will not fail me. Having spoken these words, he passed away.

Throughout his life, the Master served nine successive dynasties as the preceptor to seven emperors. He lived to the age of one hundred and two, with eighty-three years of ordination seniority. His height was...
He was nine chi and four cun tall; with his hands hanging down, they reached past his knees. His eyes emitted light at night and did not blink during the day.

He could hold two brushes simultaneously, and his voice resonated like a bell. Because Emperor Wenzong revered him as a sage-ancestor, he specifically suspended court for three days, and the high officials wore white mourning garments.

The entire-body reliquary stupa was enshrined on Mount Zhongnan. Not long after, a monk from India arrived at the capital and submitted a memorial stating that he had seen two messengers passing through the air over the Pamir Mountains;
he had stopped them with a mantra and questioned them, to which they replied, "We are the deities of Mañjuśrī’s Hall in North India.
We have come to take the great tooth of the Bodhisattva Avataṃsaka back to our kingdom for veneration. An imperial decree was issued to open the stupa.
As a result, one tooth was lost, and only thirty-nine remained. He was subsequently cremated; the *śarīra* were radiant and lustrous, and his tongue was the color of a red lotus.

He was posthumously granted the title of National Teacher Qingliang (Cooling). A pagoda named Miaojue (Wondrous Enlightenment) was erected, and the Chancellor Pei Xiu composed the inscription by imperial decree.
Its epitaph reads: "The Jewel Moon is Cool and Clear; its tranquil illumination pervades the Dharma-realm. In the guise of a śramaṇa, he concealed..."

Knower of the World: His clarity is as profound as it is vast, containing all within its emptiness. His spirit is as pure as the bells and tripods of antiquity; his snow-like purity washes the Shanyang River.

As rosy clouds span Mount Guo, the True Chamber stands remote and sublime, and the Sacred Peak rises steep and towering. He merges with heaven and earth in his stillness, and towers above wind and thunder in his loftiness.

Departing from the subtle and the minute, he rests in the Great Mandate; the Ultimate Reality is vast and grand. He serves the seasonal governance of the Way, transforming that which is dark and ignorant. Radiant is the essence of Yu; the Primordial Sage conceives the numinous—his Virtue...

The spirit drifts and lingers; his fixed gaze conjures illusory forms. The valley echoes enter his ears, yet its nature cannot be grasped. Like a blue lotus emerging from the water, its depth is impossible to fathom.
Having just received the *śīla*, he upholds both the prohibitions and the prescriptions. From beginning to end, he achieves perfect harmony between the presence and absence [of phenomena].

His phoenix-like prose is exquisite and wondrous, expounding upon the secret mysteries. As he dips his brush, a wind arises; the offerings fill two pens. Desiring to construct the profound gateway, he swallows...
A single golden image, upon its completion, was about to be circulated. The dragon soared aloft, spreading new teachings across the five peaks; its radiance embraced the two capitals.

Leaping forth from the Dharma-realm, its merit equaled that of a hundred cities. The myriad practices were unfolded like blossoms opening upon ancient brocade. It enlightened the common people, providing them with the drink of nectar.

Harmonizing and supporting the golden verses, it protected and sustained all living beings. The Sage Lord and his disciples thus brought prosperity to the distant frontiers. [The] *pi* [scriptures]...

Ye Fanxuan was peerless in the translation hall; with a single stroke of his brush, he turned his gaze toward the heavens time and again. In the royal court he expounded the Dharma, pouring forth words like a surging spring.

His phrasing was eloquent and his arguments unfettered—profound, profound, profound, and profound. With purple robes as his formal attire, he soaked the name of the kingdom in the coolness of the Dharma.

Had it not been for our Master, who would have known our Way? His commands were transmitted throughout the nine provinces as he lit the lamp of the inexhaustible. A single person bowed before the bestowed gift, bringing all under his unified guidance.
The Sangha of the world: the Imperial Net is vast and harmonious, secretly penetrating ten thousand households. Traversing the heavens without end, they manifest and commune simultaneously;

they roll up and unroll with sovereign ease, coming and going without a trace. The insight of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) truly holds fast to the Mean. When the tooth-relics arrived from the Western Regions, the assembly of Brahmans quickly came forth.

They petitioned for a stone to serve as proof, and the auspicious wind of the Dharma blazed ever more brightly. By imperial decree, a portrait was commissioned; yet the form is itself formless. The Sea...

The Great Dragon of India coils its residence within the abbot’s quarters. The Sage has departed; what remains for us to study? The principle underlying these matters is such that the stupa is locked away in Zhongnan Mountain.
By imperial decree, a portrait of the National Teacher was painted and enshrined at Daxingtang Temple. Emperor Wenzong composed a eulogy, which begins: "I, the Emperor..."

Contemplating the Dharma-realm: vast, silent, and boundless. Responding to conditions to accomplish phenomena, it truly employs the empty faculties. National Teacher Qingliang embodied the ultimate reality to open the gateway;
he encompassed the entire Dharma-realm, and our Patriarch followed in his honor. His teaching harmonized the seas and mountains; his grace spanned heaven and earth.

He first renewed the legacy of the two Vasubandhus, uplifting those who were obscure and ignorant. With this rare spiritual essence now arrived, we reverently receive the Buddha-sun. Its light coalesces throughout the four seas, and its nine...

The state celebrates an abundance of blessings, overflowing upon the gate of the Golden Immortal (Buddha). You have taken the seat of the ancient sages; as a great hand and renowned official, you have crossed the sutras to seek further instruction.

You continue to serve as a teacher for the Great Rest (Mahāśānti), preserving my distant reign. Thus, I have exerted my humble brush to extol your flourishing achievements. True Emptiness (Śūnyatā) is inexhaustible; when the occasion arises, one mounts the vehicle.
As the white moon fills the empty autumn and the clear breeze suits the summer, the wondrous non-being does not shift; as conditions cease, transformation occurs. How remote!
Such was the ritual of Yu; how magnificent was his vihāra!

The commentary states: The flourishing or decline of the Buddha-dharma has always corresponded with the state of the imperial way. As for the flourishing of the Emperor, none surpassed that of the Tang.
The Buddha-Dharma flourished greatly in the Central Lands because of him. Indeed, it was through the mutual support of internal and external patrons that its excellence was achieved.

Master Qingliang Sheng served nine successive dynasties as the preceptor to seven emperors. Under Emperor Xianzong, he was specially granted a gold seal and bestowed with the titles of Sengtong (National Preceptor for Monks) and Guoshi (State Preceptor).
By examining his life in this world, the prosperity of both the imperial way and the Buddha-Dharma can be readily imagined.
By the time of his passing, the persecution of Huichang followed; the Buddha’s world fell into sorrow, and the Tang dynasty likewise ended in decline.
Alas! Rise and fall are the constant laws of nature, yet they are also so dependent upon the individuals involved.
On the sixth day of the first month of the fifth year, Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi entered nirvana. Prime Minister Pei Xiu composed an inscription for his Stele of the Transmission of the Dharma.
The Master’s surname was He; he was a native of Xichong in Guozhou and a thirty-ninth-generation descendant of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
During the eighty years that Śākyamuni dwelt in the world, he preached the various [teachings] for immeasurable devas, humans, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas.
This Dharma was finally entrusted by the Buddha to Mahākāśyapa, so that it might be transmitted from patriarch to patriarch and circulated separately in the world.
Behold this Dharma: it is the fundamental source of all sentient beings and that which all Buddhas have realized. It transcends all principles and is free from all marks;
it cannot be sought through words, intellect, consciousness, existence, non-existence, concealment, or manifestation. It can only be attained through the mutual resonance of mind and mind.
The seals, seals, and seal-marks are in perfect accord; they serve only for one’s own realization and the enjoyment of luminosity.
From Kāśyapa down to Bodhidharma, and from Bodhidharma’s arrival in the East at Caoxi, there were thirty-three generations in total. Caoxi transmitted it to Heze; Heze transmitted it to Rizhou Ru;
Ru transmitted it to Zhang of Jingnan; Zhang transmitted it to Yuan of Suizhou; Yuan transmitted it to the Master. As for the Master:
Heze was the fifth generation [from Bodhidharma]. From Kāśyapa, he was the thirty-eighth generation. Such was his lineage. The Master came from a noble family;

in his youth, he was well-versed in Confucian learning. One day, he went to pay his respects at Suizhou. Before they had even exchanged words, he withdrew and wandered among the assembly of disciples, where he saw [the Master] solemnly absorbed in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Overjoyed and filled with admiration, he subsequently shaved his head, donned the robes of a monk, and received the Way. Once, while attending a vegetarian feast, he received a scripture and obtained...
While reciting the twelve chapters of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. Upon returning, he informed his teacher, who gave him his seal of approval.
He then went to visit Zhao at Dongjing, who said, "He is a bodhisattva; who could have recognized him? Subsequently, he visited Guan at Qingliang.

Guān said, "Are you the one who can follow me to the Vairocana Flower Treasury (Vairocanābhisambodhi-kusumagarbha)? Subsequently, having received a new commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* from a monk of Hángshàng, he proceeded to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka*.

After a long time, he composed commentaries and sub-commentaries (*śāstra-ṭīkā*) on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, and the *Dharmadhātudarśana*.
He also compiled the *Lǐchàn xiūzhèng tútuán zǎnlüè* (Abridged Collection of Diagrams and Biographies on Ritual Repentance and Cultivation). Furthermore...
He compiled the Zen sayings of various schools into the *Zen-zang* (Zen Treasury), including verses and treatises, totaling over ninety volumes.

Some, however, did not maintain the practice of meditation but instead extensively lectured on the sutras and śāstras, traveling to famous towns and great capitals with the primary aim of promoting the establishment of monasteries.
Thus, one is merely enslaved by much learning; how could one have not yet forgotten fame and profit? He said: "Alas! The single mind is the totality of all dharmas.
When divided, it becomes precept, concentration, and wisdom; when expanded, it becomes the six perfections; when dispersed, it becomes the myriad practices.
The myriad practices have never been anything other than the single mind, and the single mind has never deviated from the myriad practices. Meditation is one of the six perfections."
This is merely one aspect; how could it encompass all phenomena? Furthermore, the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma-eye to Kāśyapa, yet not the dharma-practice.
Thus, that which is realized within one’s own mind is the Dharma, while that which arises following practice is practice. Practice is not necessarily identical [to the Dharma].
Therefore, the single mind is the source from which the myriad dharmas arise, yet it does not belong to the myriad dharmas. This is attained.
Those who practice this attain mastery over the Dharma; those who perceive it encounter no obstruction regarding the teaching.

Since the essence is not the Dharma, it cannot be explained through the Dharma; since the essence is not the teaching, it cannot be transmitted through the teaching. How, then, can it be sought by following mere tracks?
From Kāśyapa to Pūrṇayaśas, there were ten patriarchs in all, all of whom were Arhats; those they converted were likewise Arhats.
It was not until Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Vasubandhu that the Mahāyāna was first opened up.

They composed treatises to explain the sūtras and to suppress and destroy the non-Buddhists, acting as the vanguard for the Bodhisattvas. Among them, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin alone took the power of the precepts as his spiritual majesty;
the Venerable Upagupta alone took ascetic practice as the path to liberation. Other patriarchs either extensively propagated the Dharma teachings or...
They were single-minded in their meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Some departed like a cicada shedding its shell; some were extinguished by transforming into fire;

some clung to trees to demonstrate their passing; and some suffered harm to repay their karmic debts. This is because while the Dharma is necessarily the same, their practices are not necessarily identical. Moreover, those who merely follow tracks are not practitioners of good conduct;
those who strictly adhere to the compass and the ink-line are not masters of skillful means (*upāya*). Without swiftness, one cannot be considered a great ox.
Without transcending [these], one cannot be considered a Mahāsattva. Thus, for the Chan master in the cultivation of the Way, insight and vision constitute the wondrous gate;
tranquility constitutes the true flavor; loving-kindness and patience constitute the armor; and wisdom and severance constitute the sword and spear.

With these, he breaks down the high fortifications of internal demons and penetrates the solid ranks of external thieves. He pacifies and subdues the heterodox and the mixed, and releases those trapped in the cage. When encountering a destitute son...
Thus, he rebukes those who would return to their homes; he scolds the destitute woman and makes her illuminate her chamber.

That the impoverished son does not return and the poor woman does not become wealthy—our Master feels shame for this. That the Three Vehicles do not flourish and the Four Divisions [of the Sangha] do not thrive—our Master feels shame for this.
That loyalty and filial piety are not cultivated together and that the burden of responsibility cannot be sustained—our Master feels shame for this. Therefore, he is urgently intent upon salvation.
He was diligent and earnest in opening the way for and guiding others; he did not exalt himself on account of a single practice, nor did he pride himself on a single virtue.

When someone sought refuge in him, he would go to them without waiting for an invitation. When someone sought to increase their benefit, he would provide instruction before they even reached a state of frustration.

He did not treat children with disdain when receiving them, nor did he grow weary of encouraging those who were arrogant or stubborn. Thus, in his propagation of the teachings and his deliverance of beings...
The way in which they assist the transformation of the state is such as this. Therefore, those who apply the method of venerating the teacher—when greedy, they practice giving;

when violent, they practice restraint; when rigid, they practice compliance; when rebellious, they practice obedience; when muddled, they practice enlightenment; when indolent, they practice diligence; those seeking self-glorification become humble; those clinging to self-hardness are transformed;

those following private interests become public-spirited; and those immersed in emotion embrace righteousness. Thus, the customs of the scholar-officials undergo change: their livelihoods are revitalized, the consumption of animal flesh is severed, and they uphold [the Way].
Regarding those who take the precepts as their proximate dwelling: there are those who emerge from seclusion to cultivate governance and rescue others from suffering as their path;
there are those who withdraw to serve their parents, making abundant offerings their practice. Beyond these, there are those who come in great throngs and depart with joyful hearts;
they arrive with sleeves fluttering and return with full bellies. Their numbers in every location are beyond reckoning—truly like the Tathāgata.
He was a bodhisattva entrusted with the mission of salvation and an unsolicited, virtuous friend to all sentient beings. Was he one of the four reliances?

Or was he a person of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)? I do not know the breadth or narrowness of his spiritual realm and abode; how could those who debate know the ultimate destination of the Great Way?
Having lived through sixty-two years of the world and observed thirty-four years of monastic seniority, Emperor Xuan posthumously conferred upon him a title of honor.
Master Dinghui had four assemblies of disciples—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—totaling approximately one thousand people.
The commentary states: At the end of the Taihe era, the Chancellor Li Xun and Zheng Zhu plotted to assassinate the eunuchs but failed.

When their scheme was discovered, Li Xun fled to Mount Zhongnan to seek refuge with Master Mi. Fearing for their own safety, his followers would not admit him; however, Master Mi alone provided him protection and shelter.
The situation became urgent, and Xun fled toward Fengxiang, where he was captured by the troops of Luo. The eunuch Qiu Shiliang hid Xun in secret;
when the pursuers arrived and were about to kill him, Qiu remained composed and said, "I have been acquainted with Xun for a long time.
According to my dharma, one must rescue those in distress. Death is simply his lot. Qiu admired his steadfastness and released him. This is recorded in the *History of Tang*.
This is surely to praise his possession of great integrity. He secretly possessed the penetrating Dharma-eye and attained the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
With vast and unimpeded eloquence, he expounded the religious teachings; his spiritual power was fully realized.

That at the moment of encountering the unpredictable crisis of birth and death, he could thus have such self-confidence in the Way—formerly, Han Yu’s literary prowess was perhaps not necessarily superior to that of Liu [Zongyuan].
Zi-thou! That which later generations have come to extol him for is merely his singular excellence as a military commissioner under Wang Tingzou.
Yet, even that which Guifeng Shi records—merely one among the myriad practices—is still so brilliantly illuminated upon bamboo and silk.
How much more so when he opened the way for humans and devas and perpetuated the Dharma-path; would it not be most fitting to call him a Bodhisattva?
How profound it is! Thus, what my ancestor called "clarifying the Buddha-mind lineage through the correspondence of practice and understanding" was precisely Guifeng.
In this month, Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne; from his youth, the Emperor had disliked the teachings of Śākyamuni. In the ninth month of autumn, he summoned Daoist priests.
Zhang Guozhi and eighty-one others entered the inner palace to perform a *jīnlù* (Golden Register) ritual at the Three Palaces.
In the tenth month of winter, the Emperor visited the Three Palaces and ascended the Nine Immortals’ Mystic Altar, where he personally received the dharma registers.

Wang Zhe, the Left Reminder, remonstrated, saying, "At the commencement of your royal enterprise, it is not appropriate to place excessive reliance on such [Daoist] practices. The Emperor did not accept his advice.

In the sixth month of summer in the first year of the Huichang era, the Daoist Liu Xuanjing of Mount Heng was appointed as a Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guanglu Daifu) and installed as a scholar of the Chongxuan Academy.
He was ordered to reside within the imperial palace with Zhao Guizhen to practice the ritual registers (falü).

Liu Xuemu, a Left Assistant in the Office of Remonstrance, submitted a memorial offering earnest remonstrance; consequently, Xuemu was demoted to the post of Director of the Revenue Bureau (Hucucao) of Henan Prefecture.
In the first month of the fourth year, an edict was issued stating: "The prohibition of slaughter during the months of fasting originates in the Buddhist scriptures.

As our state’s founding is still relatively close to those of the Liang and Sui dynasties, some among the ministers and high officials may still be influenced by these harmful customs. From now on, only the first three days of the first month—the beginning of the growth of all things—shall be designated for the cessation of slaughter.
On the memorial days of each of the successive sagely emperors, one day shall be observed as a day of cessation. For other occasions, such prohibitions are not required. In the third month...

The Daoist Zhao Guizhen served as the Professor of the Way of the Gate (Daoism) for the Left and Right Quarters. At that time, the Emperor was intent on seeking immortality and took Zhao Guizhen as his teacher.

Taking advantage of his favor, Zhao Guizhen would invariably disparage and denounce the followers of Śākyamuni whenever he had an audience, claiming that Buddhism was not a teaching of the Middle Kingdom and that it harmed living beings;
he urged that it should be eradicated entirely. The Emperor deeply agreed with him. Zhao Guizhen further requested a debate with the followers of Śākyamuni.

Debate. An imperial decree was issued summoning the monk Dao to the Linqide Hall for a discussion. Dharma Master Zhixuan ascended the debating seat; his eloquence was swift and his arguments vigorous.
Dao could not best him. Zhixuan then submitted a memorial: "The foundation of a king's rule lies in ritual, music, and a unified system of laws; thus the world is governed.
As for practices such as breath cultivation and elixir ingestion, these are matters monopolized by solitary recluses in the mountains and forests. I pray that Your Majesty..."
The Emperor was displeased by this lack of deference. His attendants suggested that Xuan should compose a poem to explain himself.
Xuan immediately presented five stanzas, which included the lines: "The crane’s back is precarious and the dragon’s back is slippery; may Your Majesty remain for a thousand years.
The Emperor understood this as a satirical critique and specifically granted him leave to return to his native home.
The Treatise says: Formerly, when Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty abolished the Teaching, several dozen śramaṇas risked their lives to protest against him.
Although they were unable to rectify Emperor Wu’s delusions, it was sufficient to demonstrate that there were people within our Dharma.

When Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty deliberated on the purge of the monastic community, Huicheng, Xuawan, Zhishi, Falin, and others earnestly debated and cited scriptural principles in defense of the faith.
Magnanimous indeed, he did not fail in his duty as a true son of the Dharma King. From the Dali era onwards, as the ancestral Way flourished, many heroes of our school flocked to the Zen groves.
By the time Emperor Wuzong deliberated on the abolition of the teachings, there was only one person who truly understood the profound mysteries of the Dharma—Master Zhizhou.
Although Emperor Wuzong’s fervent intent could not be dissuaded, the fortune of the Buddha...
Fate cannot be escaped. As for those who call themselves sons of the Śākya, when faced with such times of upheaval, there is not a single word to record.
Though the Buddha-dharma is as venerable and vast as heaven, it is also the fault of our own followers for having neglected their studies.
In the fifth month of the fifth year, the Wangxian (Aspiring Immortality) Tower was constructed within the imperial palace. At that time, Zhao Guizhen was receiving exceptional favor.

Several memorial officials submitted memorials to remonstrate against this. The Emperor said to his ministers: "The memorial officials' discussion of Zhao Guizhen is intended to let you know that there is no business in my palace;
I have banished music, women, and sensual pleasures. This talk of 'entering the Way' is merely a pretext. Li De...
Yu replied, “Your servant does not dare speak of the merits or failures of previous dynasties; however, Guizhen once entered and exited the inner palace during the reign of Emperor Jingzong.
For this reason, the public sentiment is unwilling for Your Majesty to again keep her in close proximity.
The Emperor said, “I already knew this person at that time, though I did not know her name; I called her Master Zhao. During Jingzong’s reign, she was likewise—”
"There is nothing particularly wicked about this. I speak with him merely to wash away my mental fatigue. As for the affairs of state and the military, I discuss them only with you, the ministers;
why would I consult a Daoist? Consequently, the Chancellor no longer offered remonstrance, and Guizhen subsequently engaged in worldly discourse.
He then recommended the Daoist Deng Yuanchao of Mount Luofu, who possessed the arts of longevity. The Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to welcome him.
When Yuan Chao arrived, he joined with Liu Xuanjing, Gui Zhen, and others in forming a rigid alliance to slander and destroy the followers of Śākyamuni.

Consequently, their petition to dismantle the monasteries was carried out. In the fourth month, all Buddhist monasteries throughout the empire were inspected and enumerated, totaling four thousand six hundred.
There were two hundred and six thousand and five hundred monks and nuns in the *araṇya* (hermitages).

On the *gengzi* day of the fifth month, an imperial edict was issued to consolidate and reduce the number of Buddhist temples throughout the realm; this was submitted as a memorial by the Secretariat and the Chancellery, based on the relevant statutes and regulations.
Regarding the memorial services for the imperial ancestors in the various upper prefectures, officials shall offer incense at the temples.

One temple shall be retained in each of those upper prefectures, and all sacred images of the successive emperors shall now be moved into these temples. All temples in the lower prefectures shall be abolished.

In the two capitals, within the Left and Right Streets, ten temples shall be retained, with ten monks assigned to each. The Imperial Edict states: "The temples to be retained in the upper prefectures must possess exquisite craftsmanship."
Each [of these] shall be one site. Any dilapidated structures should be demolished and removed. On the days when incense is offered, officials should attend the Daoist and Buddhist monasteries.
In both the Capital (Chang’an) and the Eastern Capital (Luoyang), four temples each shall be retained, with thirty monks per temple. The Secretariat and the Chancellery further memorialized:

"Regarding the bells, chimes, and bronze statues from the temples abolished throughout the empire, they shall be entrusted to the Salt and Iron Commissioner to be cast into coinage. As for the iron statues, they shall be entrusted to the local authorities."

The provincial authorities were to cast [the metal] into agricultural implements. Images made of gold, silver, brass, and stone were to be melted down and delivered to the Ministry of Revenue (Du-zhi).
All images made of gold, silver, and other such materials were ordered by imperial decree to be surrendered to the government within one month.
The Eighth Month. An Imperial Edict stated: "I have heard that prior to the Three Dynasties, there was no mention of Buddha.
It was only after the Han and Wei that the teachings of the Image-Religion (Xiangjiao) arose and declined. From this, during these degenerate times, this foreign custom has been transmitted;

through the conditioning of causes and conditions, its proliferation has increased until it has come to consume and waste the resources of the state without our gradual realization, and to entice and delude the hearts of the people until the masses have become increasingly lost."

Throughout the nine regions, from the mountains and plains to the palaces of the two capitals, the ranks of monks have grown daily more numerous and Buddhist temples have become increasingly magnificent.
Human labor has been exhausted in the construction of earthenworks and timber structures, and human resources have been diverted from their natural uses for the sake of gold and jewel ornaments.

The relationship between sovereign and subject is displaced by that of teacher and disciple, and the bond of marriage is severed within the confines of the precepts. No path has caused greater harm to the Dharma or more injury to people than this one. Furthermore—
If even a single husbandman does not till his fields, there will be those who suffer from hunger. Today, the number of monks and nuns throughout the world is beyond counting;

they all depend on farmers for their food and silkworms for their clothing. As for monasteries and temples, their number is beyond reckoning; they are all constructed with cloud-like arches and ornate decorations that rival the imperial palaces.
That the material resources of the Jin, Song, Liang, and Qi dynasties declined and their customs became corrupt and deceitful was entirely due to this.

This is how it has come to pass. How much more so for my High Ancestor, the Great Emperor Taizong, who settled the calamities and rebellions through military might and governed the world through civil principles;
holding these two ends to manage the state, how could he have sought to rival the petty teachings of the West?
Even during the Zhenguan and Kaiyuan eras, attempts were made to reform and eradicate these abuses, yet they were not entirely eliminated; they continued to spread and proliferate.

I have extensively studied the words of former sages and sought out public opinion from all quarters. As for the corruption that must be reformed, my decision is firm and beyond doubt. Furthermore, loyal ministers both within and outside the court have harmonized with my righteous intent.
Since the proposed measures are most appropriate and ought to be implemented, I shall punish the source of this millennial pestilence and fulfill the legacy of the hundred kings.

"The administration of the Dharma is intended to save people and benefit the multitude; why do you, my son, decline it? As for the temples demolished throughout the empire and the monks and nuns who have returned to lay life, they have been conscripted as tax-paying households.
Alas! Such a thing was not practiced in antiquity, suggesting there must have been a time to wait for; yet now it has been abolished entirely—is this not because the time has come?
Some five hundred thousand idle and unproductive elements have been driven away, and the gaudy, useless buildings have been abandoned."
There are sixty thousand districts in total. From this point forward, you shall purify yourselves and instruct the people, aspiring to the principle of non-action (*wuwei*).

By simplifying and standardizing governance, you shall achieve the merit of unifying the customs of the realm. This is intended so that the commoners throughout the six directions may together return to the imperial transformation.
Yet, at the beginning of reforming abuses, people are often unaware of their daily conduct. Therefore, the subordinate officials of the brilliant court should embody my intent.
In the third month of the sixth year, the Emperor fell ill. He personally summoned Daoist practitioners to ingest cinnabar elixirs and receive dharma registers (*dharmaloka*).

By this time, he suffered from carbuncles on his back, agitation, and a loss of his usual composure. His condition eventually reached its final stage; for ten days he was unable to speak, and he passed away at the age of thirty-three.
The old history offers this encomium: Emperor Zhaosù abolished the teachings of the Buddha to punish the idle and indolent.

His ambition was to ascend the vermilion ladder and seek the pearl in the red water; yet he merely observed the scholarly pursuits of Xiao Yan and Yao Xing, failing to realize the vain quests of the First Emperor and Emperor Wu of Han.
Having been deluded by the words of heterodox paths, he consequently and one-sidedly repudiated the teachings of foreign lands. Moreover, as for his own person...

The poisonous Dharma that came from the West has for a millennium been practiced until it became a custom among the simple folk. They revere its teachings more than the laws of the state, and they delight in its followers no differently than those who have attained immortality.
It is like the customs of tattooing the body and cutting the hair of certain tribes, or like the spectacles of spitting fire and swallowing boats;
how can it be rectified by the music of the Xian and Shao, or regulated by the ceremonial cap of Zhang Fu? Furthermore, [the influence of] Fu and Rong [has only served to further this].
Flatterers like He Chong have not been lacking throughout the ages; even the worthies Xun Qing and Mencius could not have dared to oppose such arguments.
To suddenly ruin and deface golden images and burn and discard foreign scriptures would breed resentment among those who prostrate in worship and provoke the anger of common folk.
The actions of a wise monarch do not alarm the sentiments of the people; that previous dynasties preserved these matters without comment was truly for the sake of the Middle Kingdom.

As for the Way: wishing to reform these evils, one must await the clearing of the Yellow River. Although Emperor Zhaosù was renowned for his clear judgment, he nevertheless succumbed to such flattery (the above is found in the Old History).
The Commentary states: The old history, the *Wuzong ji* (Annals of Emperor Wuzong), records the beginning and end of the abolition of the Śākya [Buddhist] teachings in great detail.
Although at that time those in yellow caps [Daoists] took advantage of imperial favor to undermine our religion, it was also the great minister Li Deyu who assisted in accomplishing this matter.
The new history states: "Emperor Wuzong resolutely and with great vigor eliminated the teachings of the Buddha, and personally received..."
The Daoists follow ritual registers and take elixirs in their quest for longevity; by this, one knows they are not wise men free from delusion, but merely differ in their preferences.
Alas! Emperor Wuzong was not a wise man free from delusion; how could his differing preferences regarding Buddhism and Daoism alone suffice to define him?
His biased faith in Li Deyu, who monopolized power and dominated affairs, was likewise a sign of his partiality.
The factions were in mutual conflict; although he had the merit of suppressing rebels, success was not yet seen, and resentment among both the court and the commoners had already become extreme.
Had he been allowed to retain power for much longer, how would he have differed from Li Linfu?

In the third month of the sixth year [of the Dazhong era], Xuanzong ascended the throne. He was the thirteenth son of Emperor Xianzong. Outwardly reserved yet inwardly radiant, he was dignified and spoke little.
Once, while suffering from an illness, he was suddenly touched by a supernatural light; he sprang up and sat upright in a solemn posture.
When Emperor Muzong went to see him, he patted his back and said, "This is a blessing for the state. He bestowed upon him a jade *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) and transferred his fief to Guang...
O King, he once dreamed that he was riding a dragon ascending to heaven. Furthermore, at the pond within his residence, dragons were often seen sporting in its waters.
During the Taihe and Huichang eras, when groups gathered for banquets, he never spoke unless someone tried to provoke him;

when they succeeded in eliciting a word from him, the entire company would break into dancing and laughter as a form of entertainment, calling him "Guangshu. Emperor Wuzong was particularly fond of such boisterous and unrestrained conduct.

He did not observe formal courtesies. Upon reaching this point, his countenance was filled with grief as he received his various officials; yet, in his management of public affairs, both within and without the court were in full accord, and it was only then that his hidden virtues became manifest.

On the *xinmao* day of the fifth month, an imperial edict was issued sentencing twelve individuals, including the Daoists Zhao Guizhen, Liu Xuanjing, and Deng Yuanchao, for having deluded the late Emperor with demonic arts and slandered the followers of Śākyamuni.
All were granted a flogging at the court and banished to the regions beyond the ridges.

Gui-si (the tenth day of the fourth month). An imperial edict was issued that the eight great monasteries in both the Capital (Chang’an) and the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) were to be restored, and new plaques with their titles were bestowed.
In the intercalary third month of the first year of the Taizhong era, an edict stated: "In the final years of the Huichang period, the monasteries were consolidated and abolished.
Although it was said that the teachings of foreign lands provide a source for aiding governance, the people of the Middle Kingdom have long practiced these [Buddhist] ways. This excessive reform—"

This matter is indeed erroneous. As for the sacred sites of Mount Ling and the monasteries abolished during the Changwu era, the long-established senior monks shall continue to repair and maintain them as before.
Comprehensive Annals of Buddhism Compiled during the Longxing Era, Volume Twenty-five and Volume Twenty-six.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of Shishi in Longxing Prefecture.

In the first year of the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, the Minister of Revenue, Bai Juyi, passed away at the age of seventy-five. He was posthumously granted the title of Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Emperor Xuanzong composed a poem to mourn him. Having enjoyed the patronage of Emperor Xianzong, Bai Juyi spoke on all matters of state, cleansing and purifying the administration.
Xuemodu was seen to be fit for office and was granted an audience; however, he was resented by those in power and subsequently dismissed.

Unable to implement the principles he harbored, he gave himself over to literature and wine, finding contentment in whatever circumstances befell him. He took refuge in the Buddhist doctrine of birth and death, as if forgetting his physical form.
Later, he was promoted and employed again, yet once more he found himself at odds with the young and arrogant sovereign. Consequently, he became ill and resigned from office.

Consequently, he had no intention of establishing a reputation for merit or fame. Together with his younger brother Xingjian and his cousin Minzhong, he lived in friendship in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).

At his residence in Lüdào-lǐ, he dredged a pond, planted trees, built a stone pavilion on Mount Xiāng, and carved the Bājié Rapids; he styled himself the "Madman Who Sings in Intoxication" (*Zuìyín Xiānshēng*) and wrote his own biography.
In his later years, his devotion to Buddhism became even more profound, to the point that he would abstain from meat for as long as a month, calling himself—
The Layman of Fragrant Mountain (Xiangshan Jushi) hosted a banquet with Hu Gao and eight others; all were men of advanced age who had not served in office.
People admired them and painted them as the "Nine Old Men" (Jiu Lao Tu). Bo Juyi was precise and refined in his prose, while Ji was skilled in poetry;
at that time, scholars vied to recite their works. From the moment he was born, at only seven months old, he could open a book, though he lacked the two thumbs required for writing.
His characters were such that even after testing him hundreds of times, he never made an error. At the age of nine, he was already proficient in musical theory and its principles.
His devotion to literary talent was clearly a matter of innate endowment. After his death, the residence where he lived was converted into a Buddhist temple.

Emperor Xuanzong, never ceasing to think of his virtue, subsequently appointed his younger brother, Minzhong, as Chancellor. Once, when Bai Juyi was ill, he fashioned an image of Amitābha Buddha and offered prayers to it.
He composed a record for himself, saying: "My original teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, spoke thus:
'To the west of here, beyond a hundred trillion Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī (Ultimate Bliss), because it is free from the eight sufferings and the four evil realms.'"
That land is named Pure Land because it is free from the three poisons and the karma of the five turbidities.

That Buddha is named Amitābha because his lifespan, his vows, his meritorious qualities, his physical marks and signs, and his radiance are all immeasurable. Contemplate carefully the sentient beings of this Sahā world:

there is no distinction between the worthy and the foolish, the noble and the humble, or the young and the old; yet, if any among them give rise to the thought of taking refuge in the Buddha, [they shall be reborn there].

Whenever they raise their hands and join their palms, they invariably face the west. When encountering fear, calamity, or suffering, and opening their mouths to cry out, they invariably first recite the name of Amitābha.

Furthermore, whether it be images cast in metal, molded from clay, carved in stone, embroidered in thread, or even those made by stamping water or piling sand as children play—there is none that does not take Amitābha Buddha as its primary figure. One does not know how it comes to be so, yet it is thus.
Viewed from this perspective, it is clear that those Tathāgatas have made great vows regarding these sentient beings, and that these sentient beings possess great karmic conditions for those lands.
Were it not so, there are many Buddhas of the past, present, and future in the south, north, and east;
why would it be only thus? Why would it be only thus? [The text concludes with: Tang Zhongdafu Taizishao...
When Fu Bai (Bai Juyi) reached the age of decline and old age, he suffered from the ailment of a wind-stroke.

He then donated three hundred thousand *fèn* coins and commissioned the artisan Du Jingzong to paint a depiction of the Western World based on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*.
It was nine feet high and one zhang and three feet wide. The Venerable Buddha Amitābha sat in the center, while Avalokiteśvara...
The two Great Beings, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, attend to him on his left and right. Humans and devas gaze up at him, surrounded by his retinue.

Multi-storied pavilions, music, water, trees, flowers, and birds are adorned with the seven treasures and draped in five-colored silks; radiant and magnificent, they are the fulfillment of meritorious virtue.
The disciple Juyi burns incense and bows his head in prostration. Kneeling before the Buddha, he gives rise to a heart of compassion and makes this great vow:
"May these merits be bestowed upon all sentient beings. May all those who are as old as I am, and all those who are as sick as I am, leave suffering behind and attain happiness;
may they sever evil and cultivate goodness, and without even crossing the Southern Sea, behold the Western Paradise."
The great light from the ūrṇā-kośa shall respond to one’s thoughts and appear; through the highest grade of the blue lotus, one shall be reborn according to one’s vow.
From this present body until the end of the future, one shall always be able to draw near and make offerings. Desiring to reiterate this meaning, he spoke these verses of praise:
"In the Pure Land of the World of Ultimate Bliss, There are no evil realms nor any manifold sufferings. I vow that my own body, as it grows old..."
The sick person shall be reborn together with Amitābha Buddha.
The *Lun* (Commentary) states: The Tang history records that Bai Juyi was equal in fame to Yuan Zhen. Yuan Zhen sought dangerous shortcuts midway and lost his reputation as a prime minister;
his prestige collapsed entirely. When Li Zongmin was in power, Bai Juyi’s own influence was formidable and brilliant, yet he never aligned himself with him.
To distance oneself from worldly affairs, to strive for advancement while maintaining integrity, and to be self-sufficient in one’s virtue—how truly worthy is such a person!

I venture to say that Bai Juyi (Lètiān) was exceptionally virtuous compared to his contemporaries. His moral achievements were like those of our own dynasty’s Duke Huan of Wei (Mǎn Wèigōng), and his literary prowess was like that of Sū Dōngpō;
all admired them, and their fame is clearly inscribed in the records of the brush. Thus, Lètiān was more worthy than hundreds [of others].

This is indeed fitting for the world. Observing his dignified discourse on the Way, which penetrates deeply to the very source of the religious teachings, there were only a few individuals during the three hundred years of the Tang dynasty who could rival him—namely, Bo Juyi (Lètiān), Liu Zongyuan (Liǔ Zǐhòu), Pí Gōngměi, and Liáng Sù.

Although each was rooted in their own specific lineage of transmission, they all possessed an innate capacity for realization that emerged through natural genius; they were not merely bodhisattvas who had mounted the power of their vows.
Furthermore: "Who could possibly equal this?
In the second year, while the Provincial Inspector Pei Xiu was governing Xuancheng, he once met with famous monks for debate. Someone posed a doubt to test the Master, saying:
"The three realms are illusory and sentient beings are deluded; how can there be any practice capable of unraveling their entanglements? Who [could achieve this]?"
"To use wisdom to transform the ordinary and the ignorant—why do you act thus? You, sir, are merely vexing yourself in vain. The Master said, "Ah!
When pearls and jade are in a casket, one sees their preciousness upon opening it. When sages and worthies are at one's gate, one treads upon their threshold by practicing what they teach."
They diverge along their respective paths; there is only good and evil. Good and evil are like the directions of east and west.
If one pursues them without ceasing, one will surely arrive at their respective destinations. It depends on projecting the mind into non-attachment and guiding the horse upon no-path.
In this way, the three realms are truly as they appear, and sentient beings are not deluded. It is only that those who study cannot block desire, destroy greed, and depart from fame.

It is beneficial. One does not abandon the outflows (*āsrava*) merely by thinking of proceeding toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). However, their abandonment depends on oneself; their acquisition depends on others.
It is not through the application of wisdom that one unravels the bonds; rather, when one realizes that there is not a single thing capable of disturbing my true nature, [the task is accomplished].
On another day, a disciple said to the Master: "I venture to ask: before the term 'three realms' (*tridhātu*) had been established, people did not know how to practice cultivation."
They do not perceive cause and effect. Those who fear the records of their deeds (*yin-zhi*) do not commit many evils; those who seek great fortune do not diminish their virtues.

Disorder and prosperity, increase and decrease, depend upon the times. Since this teaching spread throughout the Central Lands, the foolish fear punishment and diminish their wickedness, while the wise look toward the divine and augment their goodness.
As this augmentation continues without end, it shall lead to ultimate perfection by the present day.
If one continues to diminish it without end, even until now there should be no evil; yet why is it that confusion, delusion, and tyranny have not decreased since the time of Qin and Han?
Why is it that blessings, wisdom, and intelligence have not increased since the era of Wei and Jin? Those who return to it converge like spokes in a hub from diverse paths;
those who establish it arise like clouds of myriad dharmas. Examining the heavens, its traces are not seen; seeking it in antiquity, it cannot be found.
There exists this Dharma, known as the Great Sage who acts as Teacher to Gods and Humans. It is fitting that we cause all people to ascend the path to enlightenment;
it is not fitting that the common masses remain ignorant and deluded. From antiquity until now, such has been their confusion.

Suppose the Semblance Dharma had not been practiced until this day—would we not have all fallen into the evil realms, becoming ghosts or *yu* (poisonous water-creatures)? Indeed, the Dharma never existed from the beginning; yet now...
"It exists. How could those who aspire to sagehood fail to know it? Is their stubborn adherence to it not a form of drowning? The Duke laughed and said to him:
"When the Great Light first began to dawn, the Dharma was not yet fully established. Sages arose in succession, acting as craftsmen on behalf of Heaven.

From the binding of cords to the drawing of seals, the balance between the ornamental and the substantial underwent gradual change. With each sage’s establishment, a corresponding Dharma arose; thus the Way of Heaven and the affairs of humanity became manifest."

If this were indeed the case, then before the time of Suiren, when fire had not yet been produced, there would certainly have been no stellar fire in the heavens, no fire for human consumption, no fire omens in the tortoise shells, and no fire disasters among things.

Likewise, before the time of Shaohao, when metal had not yet been refined, there would certainly have been no stellar metal in the heavens, no use of metal by humans, no metal omens in the tortoise shells, and no metal disasters among things. And so it was with the Sage.
By striking wood one brings forth fire; by forging stone one obtains gold. Thus, the essential radiance of the sovereign spirit surges and transforms throughout the upper and lower realms.

One thereby knows that worldly phenomena and temporal affairs follow the Sage. Examining the source of the spirit and exhausting the limits of nature and destiny, he creates great expedient means to protect all living beings;
yet the beings receive them without being aware of it, for this is due to the operation of the Way of Heaven.

All things flourish through life, yet everyone regards them as their own; who knows that this is so? Thereupon, the questioner attained a state of vast clarity and personally realized the flavor of the Buddha.

When the imperial decree permitted the establishment of monasteries to propagate the Dharma, officials and commoners encouraged one another by the tens of thousands, requesting that the first monastery be established within the outer walls of Xuanzhou.
Thus, the Xinxing Monastery was restored once again.

On the *xinhai* day of the ninth month in the third year, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "Li Deyu, the Sima of Chaozhou, was early enrolled among my disciples and in his youth attained positions of refined honor.
He repeatedly held the glory of the offices of General and Minister, yet he made treacherous and sycophantic conduct his sole profession. During the era of Huichang..."

Reaching the pinnacle of officialdom, he indulged in flattery and sycophancy to gain the favor of the sovereign; thus he acted with unrestrained arrogance in governing, monopolizing power, instigating affairs, envying the worthy, and harming the loyal.

His actions were frequently marked by deceitful schemes, and he secretly harbored ambitions of usurpation. Those who maintained integrity were inevitably discarded, and those inclined toward goodness were utterly excluded.
He slandered the faithful and virtuous, fabricating the reputation of factionalism, while giving full rein to his villainy and falsehood to further incite violence.

Among all acts of treachery, this exceeds the "pointing at a deer as a horse"; the guilt is truly manifest in its deception of Heaven. While you were presiding over the balance of state affairs, you showed no hesitation or avoidance;
you entrusted the National History into the hands of your beloved son-in-law and bestowed the secret imperial edicts upon the person of your young son.

Even when participating in the drafting of official correspondence, you displayed such intimacy that you respectfully promoted the *Yuanhe Shilu* (Veritable Records of the Yuanhe Era) as an immutable document.

He has dared to act with such audacity and changed the established order, showing no fear or restraint. He usurped the meritorious achievements of another to establish them as the glorious legacy of his own house;

he exploited the biased sentiments of Li Rong to fabricate the vindictive case against Wu Xiang. Even if one were to pull out every hair on one's head to count his crimes, they would not yet be exhausted.

Observing this closely, I discerned the origins of his ambition to usurp the throne; thus, I further verified his lack of loyalty to the sovereign. I have striven to preserve the integrity of the state and have long practiced forbearance.
Although I demoted him from his official rank and honors, I still wished to conceal his shameful conduct. Yet, his insolent glares did not cease, and his competitive agitation remained unheard of.

As his accumulated evils became manifest, public opinion could no longer be suppressed. He was accordingly appointed as the Administrative Assistant of Yai Prefecture. Not long after, Du Yu felt ashamed.
His anger did not subside; he then appeared in a dream to appeal to the Chancellor Linggu Tao, begging for permission to return and bury his corpse.
Those who understood him remarked that although his forcefulness and flattery differed from those of the past, they were no less persistent.
The treatise states: Li Xizhi of the Tang dynasty said, "When historians record events, they cannot obtain the facts; they must rely on biographies and posthumous title documents.
Generally, those who compose such biographies are former students or old subordinates; if they speak with empty praise, it is even less worthy of belief.
I have observed the preface to the *Huichang Yipin Zhiji* (Collected Works of the Chief Minister during Huichang) written by Zheng Ya, a former subordinate of Li Deyu, which exaggerates and...
Du Yu’s meritorious achievements are no different from those recorded in his biography in the *New History*.

However, the *Old History*, in its annals of Emperor Wuzong, records Du Yu’s malfeasance, which accords with the wording of the imperial edict. Thus, the *New History* relied upon the accounts of former officials.
"Would this not lead those who come after me astray?
Three years later, Pei Xiu, the Governor of Hunan, went in person to visit Chan Master Shanjue of Hualin. Xiu asked the Master, "Are there any who wait for you?
Shanjue replied, "There are one or two. Xiu asked, "Where are they? Shanjue then called out to them.
The great sky and the small sky. At that time, two tigers emerged from behind the hermitage. Xiu were greatly startled. Jue said to the tigers, "Go away for now;
there is a guest here. The two tigers roared and departed. Xiu asked the Master, "What kind of practice have you performed to evoke such a response?
Jue remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand? Xiu replied, "I do not understand. Jue said, "This mountain monk constantly recites the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra."
Upon hearing this, Xiū sighed in wonder and departed. Jue lived in seclusion and habitually carried his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff). At night, he would go out among the forest foothills;

every seven paces he would strike the staff once and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara. Once, a monk came to visit him. Just as the monk was spreading out his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), Jue said, "Wait, wait.
The monk asked, "What have you seen, Master? Jue replied, "It is a pity; you have nearly smashed the bell tower."
The monk attained realization from this.
Four years later, Chan Master Huangbo Xiyun passed away. The Master was a native of Fuzhou; he was of robust and imposing appearance.
Having traveled widely, he eventually went to Jiangxi to study under Mazu. Upon finding that Mazu had already passed away, he went to see Baizhang. He asked about Mazu’s daily life...
Regarding the karmic occasion: Zhaozhou brought up the story of his second visit to Mazu concerning the hanging of the whisk. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.
Zhaozhou said, "In the future, you shall succeed Mazu. The Master replied, "Not so. Today, because you raised this matter, I have come to see the great function of Mazu’s dynamic power.
If I were to succeed Mazu, I would lose my own lineage. Zhaozhou said, "So it is, so it is. You have seen what the Master saw."
One must diminish one's own virtue by half compared to that of the master; only when one’s realization surpasses that of the master is one fit to receive the transmission.

From then on, the Master blended his presence with the common crowd. Later, in Yuzhang, he met the Regional Inspector Pei Xiu; their karmic affinity was perfectly aligned, and he subsequently emerged from seclusion to preach the Dharma.
Once, addressing the assembly, he asked, "What do you all seek? He then drove them away with his staff, yet the assembly did not disperse.
He said to them, "You lot are all nothing but wine-dregs drinkers. Traveling like this, you only bring laughter upon yourselves.
You go as soon as you see eight hundred or a thousand people; you cannot simply seek out a place of clamor.
When I was traveling, if I encountered a man even beneath a blade of grass, I would strike him on the crown of his head with my staff to see if he knew."
"You could have offered him a bag of rice for his pain and itching; it would have been as easy as this.
Where else could such a thing happen today? Since you all claim to be itinerant monks (*caryā-yātrika*), you ought to apply some spirit.
Do you know that in the Great Tang there are no Zen masters? At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "As for those honored ones in all quarters..."
"How about when one stays in a village to propagate the teaching? The Master said, "I do not say there is no Chan; I only say there is no teacher.
Have you not seen that beneath the Great Master (Mazu), eighty-four men emerged and sat in the great Dharma hall, yet those who attained the Great Master’s true eye were only two or three?
Master Niu-tou Huizhong was one of them. Now, as for leaving the household life—"

People must know that there is a matter transmitted from of old. For instance, even though the Great Master Niu-t'ou Jung under the Fourth Patriarch spoke both horizontally and vertically, he still did not know the pivotal bolt of the higher realm.
Only with such vision and intellect can one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
Yet, regarding the immediate needs of one's own person, they are unable to realize them; they merely know how to study words and phrases to recite in their bellies.
You have tucked this inside your skin and everywhere you go you claim, "I am a master of Chan. But can you truly take charge of your own birth and death?
To treat an elder with such contempt—you will enter hell as fast as an arrow. As soon as I saw you step through the gate, I recognized you. Do you understand? You must exert yourself urgently;
do not spend a lifetime in vain, merely wearing a patchwork robe and eating the food provided by others. You who possess clear eyes—
People laugh at you, but in the long run, you will all be reckoned up by worldly people. You should examine for yourself how far this reaches:
whose business is it? If you understand, then understand; if you do not, then disperse.
In the fifth year [of the Kaiyuan era], an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Hongbian of Jianfu Monastery in Jingzhao to enter the palace.
The Emperor asked, "Why does the Chan school have the designations 'Northern' and 'Southern'? He replied, "The Chan gate originally has no north or south.

In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, and it was transmitted from one to another down to the thirty-first generation. In this land, there was the Great Master Hongren..."
He had two disciples: one named Huineng, who received the robe and the Dharma and resided south of the mountain range; the other named Shenxiu, who propagated the teachings in the north.

Although the Dharma they attained was one and the same, there were differences in their methods of guidance and the realization they inspired—namely, the sudden and the gradual. Thus it is said, "The South is Sudden, the North is Gradual.
This was not because the Chan school originally possessed the designations "North" and "South. The Emperor asked, "What are the names of precept, concentration, and wisdom? He replied:

Preventing what is improper and ceasing evil is called *śīla* (precept). When the six sense faculties encounter objects and the mind does not follow after conditions, it is called *samādhi* (concentration).
When both mind and objects are empty, and one possesses clear discernment free from delusion, it is called *prajñā* (wisdom). The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'expedient means' (*upāya*)?

He replied, "Expedient means is the gateway of skillful artifice that conceals reality and covers up appearances. It is applied to those of middling and inferior capacities, providing indirect guidance and instruction; this is called expedient means. Thus he established it.
Regarding those of superior capacity, to say that one abandons expedient means (*upāya*) and speaks only of the unsurpassed path is itself a discourse of expedient means.

Even the profound words of the Patriarchs, whose aspirations and achievements transcend all description, do not go beyond the traces of expedient means. The Emperor asked, "What constitutes the Buddha-mind?
He replied, "Buddha means awakening (*bodhi*). It refers to a person possessing wisdom and illuminating awareness; this is the Buddha-mind. The mind is the Buddha."
Its alternative names comprise hundreds of thousands of different appellations, yet its essence is but one. It is fundamentally without form or shape;
it is not characterized by blue, yellow, red, or white, nor by male or female. Appearing as a deva when among devas and appearing as a human when among humans, it can manifest as male or female.
It is neither beginning nor end, without birth and without cessation; therefore, it is called the nature of numinous awareness. It is just like Your Majesty.
"Responding to the myriad affairs of state is precisely Your Majesty’s Buddha-mind. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to transmit it together, there would be nothing else to be gained.
The Emperor asked, "If someone were to practice the recollection of the Buddha today, what would happen? He replied, "The Tathāgata appeared in the world as the Teacher of Gods and Humans;
he taught according to their capacities. For those of the highest capacity, he opened the way to the Supreme Vehicle for the sudden realization of the ultimate principle."

Those of middling and inferior faculties are unable to understand this all at once. For this reason, the Buddha opened the gates of the sixteen contemplations for Vaidehī, enabling her to attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī by means of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Thus the Sūtra says: "This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha. Outside of the mind there is no Buddha;

outside of the Buddha there is no mind. The Emperor asked: "Furthermore, if there are people who seek the Buddha by upholding the sūtras or reciting mantras, how should they proceed? He replied: [The response follows].

[The Master] said: "The Tathāgata’s various teachings of the Dharma are all for the sake of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), just as hundreds of thousands of streams do not fail to flow toward and merge into the ocean.

"Since the Patriarch has transmitted the seal of the mind (citta-mudrā), how is it that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of the 'Dharma of non-attainment'? He replied: "In the Buddha’s entire career of transformation..."
In truth, not a single dharma was given to him; it was merely said that the individual natures of all sentient beings are one with the Dharma-treasury.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara simply certified Śākyamuni’s original nature, and it was only upon having nothing to attain that he accorded with Dīpaṃkara’s original intent.
Therefore, a sutra says: "There is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span; this Dharma is equal. Cultivate all wholesome deeds without clinging to signs.
The Emperor asked, "Since you, Chan Master, have realized the meaning of the Patriarchs, do you still pay homage to the Buddha and read the sutras? He replied:
For śramaṇas to prostrate to the Buddha and recite the sūtras is indeed the constant law for maintaining the Dharma. There are four kinds of retribution:
by relying on the Buddha’s precepts to cultivate the body, seeking out spiritual friends, gradually practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and treading the path traversed by the Tathāgata.

The Emperor asked: "What is meant by 'sudden realization,' and what is meant by 'gradual cultivation'? He replied: "Sudden realization means clearly understanding that one's own nature is non-dual with the Buddha. However, there are..."

Because he had only recently begun his training, he was instructed to engage in gradual cultivation as an antidote, so that the functioning of his innate nature might arise in accordance with it. It was like a person eating a meal;

one cannot be full after a single mouthful. On this day, the practice lasted for seven *ke* (approximately forty-two minutes) before it concluded. The Emperor was delighted and bestowed upon him the title of Chan Master Yuanzhi.
The Commentary states: During the Kaicheng and Huichang eras of the Zongzhang reign, Xuansong once disguised his appearance to withdraw from the world and become a śramaṇa.

[The Emperor] asked, "Do you seek it? Do you not seek it within the Sangha? "Venerable Sir," Baizhang replied, "I always pay homage to such matters.

Therefore, Xuedou’s verse says: "His majestic wind is formidable, yet he does not boast; Sitting upright, he brings peace to the entire world."
"Dragons and snakes—the Great Zhong Emperor once lightly provoked them, and three times he personally encountered their claws and fangs. This refers precisely to that event.

Therefore, those of middling and inferior capacity hear these teachings and find them beneficial yet remain fearful. This is what is meant by "saving one drowning with a hand, or saving a fire with water";

That Way harms things; those who lose that Way lead their followers astray, and those who harm things overturn their own school.
Neither of these accords with the Buddha’s intention of using his hand and water. Those who govern a state should adopt only that which is beneficial to the people.
If one removes the disease caused by these parasitic elements, then [the Way] will be unimpeded. Throughout the Tang dynasty there were fourteen emperors;

had they observed its profound principles and refined it, yet the officials in charge had not failed to lead people back to their origins and to the source in order to bind the hearts of the people, then its Way would have been most formidable and nearly achieved a state of universal unity.
Now the Son of Heaven has adopted that which benefits the people and has partially restored its teachings; thus it is unimpeded.

Thus, it was diverted to provide for those of middling and inferior capacity. At that time, Jiangzhou received an imperial decree following this precedent; I was then serving as the Regional Inspector (Cishi).

When I previously visited this place, there were a thousand pine trees at the mountain gate, their misty light permeating the heavens. Cicadas chirped and the rapids roared, while the whistling of the pines was cool and clear.

I could have cherished them separately and refrained from cutting them down, visiting them profitably from time to time; instead, I rejoiced in the situation and restored them to their natural state.
