I have heard that the mountains south of the ridges are steep but not majestic, while the mountains north of the ridges are majestic but not beautiful; yet Mount Lu is truly a mountain, and it is both a mountain and beautiful.
Both [possibilities] exist. When the Five Elders peered into the lake, hanging waterfalls fell from the heavens. Incense was burned, and auspicious birds and gentle beasts appeared.
Amidst the mist and mists, there were, as if in a trance, crimson ceremonial staffs and white cranes; though the messengers gazed upon them, they could not turn their heads back.

Furthermore, the six dynasties of Jinling were short-lived and its customs were thin; the ministers were perilous due to their achievements, and the sovereigns were cruel due to their suspicions. Xunyang is the fourth...
Situated within this region, it possesses the beauty of mountains and rivers. Did not Master Huiyuan surely find his strategic plan here, while observing the prevailing trends of the times?
Yet, when those who are fierce seize the savory bait and those who lie in ambush dwell in plain simplicity, there is no time for those who enter first to reflect; thus, many lament their own lot.
In this regard, Master Huiyuan was truly worthy of praise. This mountain was made even more pure by Master Huiyuan, and Master Huiyuan was likewise purified by this mountain.
They changed its name to Changfo (Extending the Buddha’s Dharma). Just as there are those who take Caoxi or Tiantai as their names, such instances are beyond counting.
Thus, the temple takes its name from the mountain, and the mountain takes its name from the distance; these three elements combine to form a perfect excellence for all under heaven.

In the eighth year [of the Dazhong period], Chan Master Lingyou of Mount Gui passed away. The Master once addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind of a man of the Way is straightforward and without artifice;

it has no back and no face. It is devoid of deceitful thoughts and actions. At all times, seeing and hearing are ordinary, with no further complications. Nor does one close the eyes or block the ears;
it is simply that when the emotions do not cling to external objects, one attains it. Thus have all the patriarchs of the past..."

"Sage" merely refers to the faults and afflictions on the side of turbidity. If one were free from such numerous evil thoughts, emotional views, perceptions, and habitual tendencies—like the clear, still waters of autumn, pure, unconditioned, limpid, and unimpeded—one might be called a man of the Way or a man of nothingness.
At that time, a monk asked: "Does one who has attained sudden enlightenment still have further cultivation to perform? The Master said: "If..."
One who has truly attained awakening knows this for themselves. To speak of "cultivating" or "not cultivating" is a duality of extremes.

Although the beginner’s initial mind may, through conditions, attain a sudden awakening to the fundamental principle in a single thought-moment, the habitual tendencies accumulated over beginningless eons cannot yet be suddenly purified.
One must therefore instruct them to purify and eliminate the flowing consciousnesses of present karma; this is what is meant by cultivation. I am not saying that there is some separate method.

He was instructed in the practice of cultivation and directed toward the goal; through hearing, he entered into principle. As the principles he heard were profound and subtle, his mind became spontaneously perfect and luminous, no longer dwelling in the realm of delusion.

Although there were hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings being expounded and emphasized at that time, he was already able to sit and don his robes, attaining self-liberation and establishing his own livelihood.
At that time, Zheng Yu, the Chancellor of State, composed a stele inscription for him which stated: "Those who speak of the Way and its arts throughout the world are many."

Thus it is. Each [school] takes what they venerate as correct; yet, beyond the teachings of the Five Constants and human affairs, regarding the realm of spirit and nature, the historians consider these to be the words of the Daoists—such as Laozi and Zhuangzi. Their texts remain extant.
However, as for [the teachings that] wash away the burdens of emotion, transcend life and death, emerge from between existence and non-existence, and soar aloofly alone—

It is so. To say that the "Elephant" (the ultimate reality) cannot be grasped through conjecture or deliberation, and that its supreme subtlety cannot be described by the mind—then the words of the Buddhists, and the practice of Chan, may be said to have reached their ultimate limit.
There are mouths that find no use for their eloquence, and even the most skillful mathematicians find no use for their calculations.
The more one attains, the more one loses; the more one considers oneself right, the more one is wrong. "I am indeed I," yet those who do not know me do not understand this.

Who is this person? If you know, then you know; if you do not know, how can you claim there is no "knower"? That which is non-existent cannot exhaustively be empty, and that which is empty cannot be fully comprehended.

In this state, there is nothing that is not as it is, and there is nothing that cannot be attained. Secluded mountains and forests are not necessarily silent, and city walls and markets are not necessarily noisy.
There are no movements of the four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, or winter—and there is neither gain nor loss, neither right nor wrong.

The traces of coming and going are not entirely non-existent; they are hidden within the accord with the Way (shun). Encountering whatever situation arises, one finds peace therein; thus, one is not constrained by time.
Being in whatever place, there is no necessity; thus, one is not cramped by things. This is the general purport [of this teaching].

Although its followers number in the thousands or tens of thousands, those who truly grasp it are not even one or two in a hundred. Among those who speak of it in recent times, each must have a school (zong), and every school must have a teacher. As for the teacher—
There must certainly have been a transmission. However, one who is not a vessel of brilliant intelligence, vast capacity, and eminent attainment cannot receive that transmission.
When such a transmission occurs, it is always characterized by a scale that is grand, expansive, and sublime. Now, to the northwest of Changsha Commandery, there is a mountain named Dayao.
Its winding trees and lofty valleys extend for several thousand li; it is the dwelling place of bears, leopards, tigers, and rhinoceroses.
Although the Yi people hunted and tracked game, even the woodcutters dared not follow him. His original monastic name was Lingyou; he was born in Fudang.
Wearing a bamboo hat on his head and straw sandals on his feet, he came from Min to travel about. He built a hermitage among the dense thickets and never went out except at mealtimes.
Amidst the wind and rain, he sat in silence, dwelling in a state of tranquility day and night such that no creature could harm him. This was because he had transcended the concerns of life and death.
Who is able to forget anxiety and sorrow, and to accord with the profound Great Harmony?

In the past, among the disciples of Confucius who had nearly attained the state of perfection, there were those who delighted in a single ladle of soup and found joy in a humble alley; even the Master praised and celebrated them because their lives were lived with such abundance.
Furthermore, life and death are the greatest matters of gain and loss for a person. Since one has gained nothing from life, one will necessarily gain nothing from death.

Since there is nothing to be gained in gain, there must likewise be nothing to be gained in loss; thus, between these two, neither gain nor loss, neither right nor wrong, can find a place to be established.
One simply entrusts oneself to transformation. This constitutes the art of the Way, wherein all the capacities of the world are fully realized.

Generally speaking, whenever one engages with the source of right and wrong, further analysis only leads to greater confusion and offers no benefit to the student; therefore, I shall not discuss it here. Since the Master has already...
This was the matter. His disciples gradually migrated to follow him, and he constructed dwellings for them with them.

He cleared away the overgrown thickets and dark brush with them, until there were over a thousand people who provided for their own food and drink and established their own regulations. Regarding the Master’s words, they neither affirmed nor denied them;
those who had some understanding would respond according to what was said, without forcing themselves to grasp what they could not. There were several dozen [of such].
As for the one called Fo (Buddha), he is regarded by all under heaven as the foremost. When Emperor Wuzong destroyed the monasteries and expelled the monks, the place was left empty.

The Master immediately feared that his head would be used for secular purposes; he was only afraid that those of such a kind would emerge [from his body]. Those with discernment came to regard him even more highly.

Later, Pei Xu, the Inspector General of Hunan, was a fervent admirer of Buddhist affairs. Coinciding with Emperor Xuanzong’s lifting of the prohibitions against Buddhism that had been imposed by Emperor Wuzong, he earnestly requested that the Master be welcomed out [of seclusion].
He personally provided his own carriage for the journey and arranged for the Master to be escorted by his own disciples. Furthermore, he proposed that the Master’s beard and hair be shaved again.
The Master initially did not wish to comply, and he jokingly said to his disciples, "Do you take the beard and hair to be the Buddha? His...
His disciples merely pressed him harder. Having no choice, he smiled and complied. He went once more to the place where he had lived, established Tongqing Temple there, and returned.
His disciples came again, and the matter was as it had been before. In his youth, the Master appeared indifferent to worldly affairs;
then, one day, he suddenly smiled and informed his disciples as if he were ill. On the ninth day of the first month in the eighth year of the Dazhong era, he passed away into stillness.
At the age of eighty-three, he was interred on the southern slope of Mount Daimi. Eleven years later, his disciples reported the Master’s Way to the throne;
only then were posthumous titles granted and a stupa erected to honor his final resting place. Alas!
Among the myriad species of living beings, human life is the most spiritually gifted, taking spirit and mind as its very foundation. From childhood until the white-haired old age, it begins with...

The teeth and hair are already worn out; yet one still plucks out the white hairs and takes medicine to pursue worldly affairs. Outwardly, one boasts to others; inwardly, one deceives oneself.
One never knows how to rest in the shade and cease from shadows, casting off anxieties to settle the spirit. Seeking not even a moment’s leisure, one reaches the point of sudden exhaustion.
Relatives and friends become no more than mere passersby on a road; all gains and sustenance are left to others. A sense of shame and debt accumulates within.
The divine spirits have been so deeply offended that the consequences may flow down to future generations. This debauchery and moral corruption cannot be stopped by itself;

it all originates from the mind and must be restrained through the arts of the Way. There is nothing more subtle in the arts of the Way than this, and the teachings of the Buddhist scriptures are even more sublime and sacred.
Nevertheless, their ultimate aim is to reach the state of non-existence (*anupalabdhi*), yet the affairs of the Sangha, numbering in the hundreds and thousands, must not be obstructed.

Generally speaking, each religious tradition claims its own tenets to be internally consistent, yet their doctrines often contradict one another; thus, it cannot be said that those in coarse robes with shaven heads are necessarily all [enlightened].

As for myself, I have washed my mind in this practice for over thirty years. It happened that a disciple of my teacher, named Shenqian, arrived from Daguang Monastery bearing a portrait of his master.

I smiled and granted him my consent; thus, I have used his words as a means to admonish myself.
Therefore, this composition is not intended solely to praise the deeds of Daowei.

The Duke sent him a reply, the gist of which stated: "We have been steeped in worldly affairs since our youth."
Upon reaching adulthood, one further takes a wife and raises children; busily running about to serve in office, one never manages to set hand upon the yellow scrolls or red volumes.
Even when leisure allows for their perusal, it serves merely as material for conversation. What leisure is there to investigate their meaning and principles?
Moreover, the scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant are each bound by the constraints of their respective vocations; even if they know of the Chan of the mountain gates, [they have no time for it].
When you wish to leave the seat and go forth to inquire, by what means can you do so?
Will there not again be the benefit of joining companions to practice Chan and inquire about the Way, as well as the mutual refinement and transformative influence found within the assembly?

Even if one were to encounter a person of clear vision by chance due to some circumstance, and lacked even a single flavor of diligent practice, how much could such a person actually ask? If you do not personally investigate for yourself, [what will become of it]?
I have studied and revered [this teaching] with great depth; yet, having only just grasped a single word or half a phrase, I am still far from full understanding.

Nevertheless, you already point your nose toward the heavens, claiming that you have already transcended both Buddhas and patriarchs. You do not glance even once at the Buddhist sutras or Chan records, fearing the ridicule of being caught in a "tangle of vines.
In my humble opinion, Hyobal, I fear this is not the case. As for me, Hyobal, I have simply not studied Chan; however, since I...

To study the training of body and mind, one must proceed with meticulous care and thorough investigation, probing deeply and searching far until reaching the very summit and the very bottom, thereby attaining all-encompassing vision.
Only when it has become luminous and pure, free from even a speck of dust in the form of doubt or obscuration, may one dare to let go.
Once this stage is reached, thereafter one neither opens the mouth nor casts a glance at others.
Where else could one further entangle oneself? Where else could one further apply effort? Hide it, hide it! These words are truly a great pickaxe;

they are truly a great lack of wit. Since this single matter requires one to escape the birth and death of immeasurable kalpas, one must directly confront and resist the Old Man Yama, who governs life and death. It cannot be otherwise.
To listen to idle talk is to bring oneself to obscurity. Alas! Lord Zheng was the first in our Song dynasty to advance through the imperial examination system;
he was extensively employed by the court, and his rank, demeanor, and meritorious achievements may truly be called exceptionally outstanding.

While there would have been nothing improper in indulging his passions in feasting and pleasure, he instead refined his integrity and sharpened his conduct to clarify the fundamental matter of his own life.
To reach such profound realization is something rarely, if ever, achieved among high ministers throughout the ages.
Ten years later, the śramaṇa Shu of Daolin Monastery in Tanzhou traveled to Taiyuan Prefecture to seek out the Buddhist canon.

The eminent scholar Li Jie provided a preface for his departure, stating: "Those who practice Confucianism take pleasure in disparaging the followers of Śākyamuni. Their arguments invariably claim that Yu, Tang..."
During the eras of the Duke of Wen, the Duke of Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius, there was no such thing as Śākyamuni.

The rise of the Śākya clan is that which has been venerated during times of decline and chaos. It is fitting to sweep it away entirely, eradicate and reform it, so that it may not further proliferate.

The Śākya tradition originated in the Han dynasty, flowed through the Jin, and spread extensively throughout the Song, Wei, Qi, Liang, Chen, Sui, Tang, and the reigns of Emperors Xiaohé and Shèngzhēn. As for those who debate this matter—
What you have said is crude. You can indeed recognize that it is so, yet you do not know why it is so. Allow me to explain.
Suppose there was once a man whose skin was plump and his complexion serene; whose vital energy was robust and his spirit clear. He never sought out physicians, nor did he ever pray to spirits.
He lived in tranquil contentment and accord with nature, free from any affliction of disease or calamity. This was certainly good. Now, suppose that same man were unfortunately—
There are ailments caused by cold, heat, wind, and dampness; there are those with hunched backs and crippled feet, or who are deaf and blind.
Thus, the techniques of acupuncture and cauterization are employed, and the rites of exorcism and propitiation proliferate. Are these two approaches merely opposed to one another?
It is simply that the conditions of being ill and not being ill differ in their exigencies. Alas! Before the Three Dynasties, the world was at peace; during the decline of the Three Dynasties—

The world was in distress. Before the Three Dynasties, the virtues and righteousness of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu were disseminated; the canons and teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius upheld them.
Although the influence of the Way had declined, its lingering permeation still remained. Deceit could not overcome sincerity, and evil knew how to avoid the good.
Thus there arose the songs of *Jiāng* and the poems of *Yóugēng*, and every person enjoyed happiness. In the final period of the Three Dynasties, the Way...

The power of the wind-element wanes. Force feigns to cover over sincerity; fanning and pouring scatter the simple and plain. The good retreat through gentleness; the wicked employ themselves through strength.
When the system of well-fields is abolished, the wealthy and the destitute prey upon one another. When the expansion of territories is pursued, offensive warfare is constantly employed.

When the filling of treasuries is the priority, ministers who amass wealth by extortion rise to prominence. When the subjugation of inferiors is the goal, officials who suppress and plunder are honored. Thus it is above.
Thus, those who govern their subordinates deceive them; those below who serve their superiors act with mere expediency.

Superiors and subordinates become mutual enemies, and this incites a climate of resentment. Consequently, there was the traveler at Míló and the man who carried stones; everyone was filled with grief and indignation.
Now, the teaching of the Śākya [Buddhism] regards purity, tranquility, and emptiness as *dhyāna-samādhi*, and regards gentleness, humility, and yielding as its practice.

Because they practice patience, enmity and strife can be brought to rest. Because they take meager hardship as their cultivation and view poverty, success, longevity, and early death as the workings of cause and effect, they can find peace even in obscurity and lowliness.

Thus, their analogy states that one must pass through afflictions to see the Buddha-nature; this was fundamentally stirred by the winds of a declining age. Indeed, such are the winds of a declining age.
There is nothing at all to be delighted in. If there were not the followers of Śākyamuni to rescue them, where else could they entrust their hearts?

To argue that one should not blame the customs of a degenerate age, yet instead find fault with the rise of the Śākya school, is like a man suffering from illness who blames his physician for performing the necessary treatments and incantations.
Such people know only that the Śākya school arose during a degenerate age; they do not realize the nature of that decline.

The age requires the salvation of the Śākya school. Why do I say this? For when the world is already afflicted and its people are already distressed, were it not for the Śākya school to allow them to find peace in their lot, the brave would rise up to fight and the wise would settle themselves to plot;
thus, the commoners of the fields and roads would arise in swarms. Now that the Śākya school has returned to its proper place—
By dividing [the responsibilities] and not demanding them of others, those who are worthy, wise, and brilliant have all ceased their worldly ambitions.
Those who cannot reach this understanding are fools; they are merely servants of the superior powers.
Thus, it is by relying on this that one can find peace amidst the customs of decline and chaos. How could one possibly eliminate it? The critics fail to consider how the Śākya school supports...
The world assists the great benefit of transformation, yet it hastens toward the minor expenses of carving, chiseling, painting, and coloring.
Therefore, I say that such people know that it is so, but do not know why it is so. During the final years of the Huichang era, Emperor Wuzong drastically suppressed the followers of Śākyamuni;
he shaved the heads of tens of thousands of his disciples and conscripted their commoners for labor, while the earthen and wooden images were submerged.

He ordered that all [Buddhist] waters, scriptures, and paper manuscripts be burned with fierce fires. He issued separate mandates to Censors to travel throughout the empire by relay carriage to investigate;
those who dared to conceal anything were to be punished. Consequently, the famous shrines and precious temples throughout the world were demolished as if swept away.
At the beginning of the Emperor’s reign, he realized that the teachings of Śākyamuni could not be abolished and issued an edict to restore them. Yet, from Lake... [the text continues].
Because those from the southern regions were distant and fearful of the law, they could not gauge the proper protocols of the imperial court.

Consequently, when the scriptures and images were previously burned and destroyed until almost nothing remained, even though a clear edict was issued permitting their reconstruction, no one was able to obtain the texts.

Shu Yan of Daolin Monastery—a place of exquisite scenic beauty on the west shore of the lake—was a man of sharp eloquence and strategic insight; he alone declared, "The capital is the seat of the state."
The old capital contains many Buddhist temples. I have heard that its commander, the Minister of Works, the Duke of Fanyang, is a man of universal benevolence throughout the realm.

As I travel back and forth purchasing the surviving texts of the Śākya school to bestow upon the people of Xiangchuan, it is only fitting that he would grant me leave and assist in completing this work.
Having thus taken my leave, I traveled north; upon presenting myself at the military gate, the Duke of Fanyang indeed granted his promise. Thereupon, I—
Seeking out those that were scattered and lacked systematic order, he reached the Buddhist temples and found those that had not been destroyed but were redundant;

furthermore, he commissioned lecturers and mendicants to repair what was deficient or leaking. Before even a few months had passed, he had obtained a total of five thousand forty-eight fascicles of Buddhist scriptures.
In the eighth month of the autumn of the tenth year of the Dazhong era, he transported them from Hedong and returned to Xiang. Alas, the Buddhist [scriptures]!

The merits of Mr. Shii-no-Suke have already been spoken of by the world. Had it not been for our Lord’s profound discernment of the source of principle, how could he have re-established [this tradition]?
Now that it has been established, were it not for one who possesses scholarly discourse and far-reaching insight, as well as steadfast sincerity, who would be able to propagate it?
I rejoice in this scholarly discourse and, obeying my Lord’s command, I shall expound upon the essence of the teachings, undaunted by cold or heat.
His diligence has extended his virtue to distant people; I shall therefore recount these events and present him with a poem. The poem says:

The waters of the Xiang flow on, the customs of the land wild and obstinate. They take pleasure in killing and theft, yet the officials cannot tame them. Ah, the Buddha! He transforms the violent and makes them benevolent.
Where is the Buddha? The Buddha is here in this writing. The waters of the Xiang surge forth; looking in the four directions, when will they end? The monkeys...
Monkeys leap through the clouds and trees that stretch far and wide; the moon sinks into the bay as mist shrouds the mountains.

The masts are rolled up and the oars lie idle; reclining and gazing upward, we chant and sigh. We beat upon the long waves—when shall we return? The Xiang River flows on in a blur, its waters falling into my weary eyes.
Pines cover the autumn courtyard, while orchids spread across the spring fields. The Master has departed—how many thousands of miles away! Why...?
Roaming together on the waters of the Xiang River.

*Lōngxìng Fójiào Biānnián Tōnglùn*, Scroll Twenty-seven.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of the Stone Chamber at Longxing Prefecture.

In the tenth year of the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, an edict was issued [concerning] Master Xuanyuan of Luofu; subsequently, Wang Pu, the Left Reminder, and others submitted a memorial to remonstrate.
The Emperor replied in an edict: "I personally attend to all affairs, and the myriad matters of state are numerous and complex.

Having heard reports that the hermit Xuan-yuan Ji of Mount Luofu is skilled in the art of preserving life and does not age with the years, I have dispatched an envoy to welcome him, hoping he may provide some means for the preservation of my health.
Whenever I examine the records of past dynasties, I see the examples of the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han, and I always take them as a warning."
"You gentlemen hold offices within the Directorate of Remonstrance. Having read the letter you have presented, I deeply appreciate your sincerity.
He then said to the Chancellor, "Explain this to the remonstrators for me: even if Xiao Gong and Luan Da were to be reborn, they could not delude me.
I merely wish to hear from the high-minded man, Xuan-yuan Sheng. Before long, Xuan-yuan Ji arrived. The Emperor asked him, "Master..."

"Is it possible to attain longevity and a long life? He replied, "If one screens out sound and color, discards rich flavors, unifies sorrow and joy, and extends benevolent grace, then one will be of the same substance as Heaven and Earth and as bright as the sun and moon; this constitutes long life, requiring no external seeking.
The Emperor respected him deeply. By nature, the Emperor was intelligent and wise, applying the law without partiality, being reverent, frugal, and compassionate toward the people.
He accepted remonstrance as smoothly as flowing water, and the world called him the "Lesser Taizong.

Whenever the ministers finished their reports, he would suddenly become serene and say, "We may speak of leisurely matters," whereupon he would inquire about the affairs of the common people or discuss the entertainments within the palace.

After about an hour, he would again assume a solemn countenance and say, "You must govern well; I am constantly afraid that you will fail me, for it will be difficult to find such men again in the future."
Upon seeing him, Li Xiang rose and entered the palace. Later, Li Guitao remarked to others, "I have held the reins of government for ten years and have enjoyed the greatest favor;
yet, whenever I presented my memorials at the Yan Ying Hall, my clothes were never not drenched with sweat."

In the eighth month of the twelfth year, the Emperor passed away at the age of fifty. The old history praises him, saying: "I, your servant, have heard the words of the elderly regarding the affairs of the Dazhong era.
Emperor Xianwen possessed profound depth of character and insight; having long experienced hardships, he fully understood the sufferings and ailments of the human world."

Since the Baoli era, eunuchs have monopolized power and have frequently acted with arbitrary license, causing great turmoil among the wealthy and influential families of the capital and bringing misery upon the common people.
Upon the accession of the Dazhong Emperor, first, the powerful and arrogant withdrew their influence; second, the treacherous ministers stood in awe of the law.

On the third day of the month, even the gatekeepers and eunuchs were struck with awe. Consequently, punishments and legal proceedings were not excessive, and the worthy and capable were employed to their full potential.

The high ministers and the governors of the four quarters were as harmonious as a pure breeze. For over ten years, songs of praise resounded along the roads. Within the imperial palace, the Emperor wore only clothes that had been washed and rinsed;

his daily meals never exceeded a few dishes. Unless the Empress Dowager was present at the meal, he would never raise his music. Even when there were occasional minor famines in the year, [he remained frugal].
His sorrow was manifest on his countenance. Even among those close to him who attended upon him, he never displayed an air of indolence.

When speaking with his ministers, he was solemn yet received them with warmth, as if addressing his official subordinates. Whenever someone presented a petition, he would listen with an open and receptive mind.

It was the custom that when the Sovereign went on a tour, the eunuchs would first spread *nāgakesara* and *turmeric* powder upon the ground; when the imperial documents were presented, he invariably ordered them all to be removed. The Palace...
When someone was ill, the Emperor had a physician examine them; once they had recovered, he would place gold in his sleeve and present it to the physician, instructing him:
"Do not let the Imperial Messengers know this, lest they say that I am showing favoritism toward my attendants. His reverence, frugality, and love for the virtuous were of this nature.

In his later years, suffering from wind-toxin (wind-poison), he summoned Xuan-yuan Ji, a man of Mount Luofu, to inquire about the essentials of self-cultivation. Ji was also a man of the Way. [The text ends here.]

He often spoke of strange and extraordinary matters, and the Emperor held him in ever greater esteem. When Sengji requested to return to the mountains, the Emperor said, "If you, Master, abandon me and depart so hastily, will there be calamity for the state?

How many years shall I, Your Majesty, enjoy the empire? Sengji took up his brush and wrote horizontally "forty" before departing; this turned out to be fourteen years. Is it not fitting that the cycles of rise and fall should be thus?

And as for the Way of the Emperor and the Sovereign— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "而帝道皇". This fragment suggests a continuation regarding the imperial path or the reign of a specific sovereign.)
From beginning to end, his conduct was without flaw; even the Wen and Jing emperors of the Han dynasty could not surpass him.
It is a pity that the records have been lost, such that of the ancient events only three or four parts remain; thus, as I take up the brush and wield the pen, I feel a sense of regret.
The *Zizhi Tongjian* states: "Emperor Xuan underwent hardships in his youth and ascended the throne in his maturity; thus he was thoroughly acquainted with the true and false aspects of human nature.
He devoted himself to the affairs of the people and applied himself diligently to the Way of governance. His rewards were simple yet appropriate, and his punishments were strict and certain.

Consequently, those within the realm delighted in their occupations, and those of foreign customs followed the proper course. If one seeks his peer among the reigns of the Han dynasty, was he not a worthy successor to Emperor Xiaowen?"
The commentary states: Regarding the Tang histories, both the old and the new, the facts concerning the reign of Emperor Xuanzong are particularly contradictory.

Only the Old History (*Jiu Tang Shu*) and the *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government* (*Zizhi Tongjian*) are in agreement. The New History (*Xin Tang Shu*) disparages him, claiming that Xuanzong mistook scrutiny for wisdom and no longer possessed any sense of benevolent grace.
Alas! One knows not what this statement intends to mean. Generally speaking, when a sovereign is magnanimous...
This is excessive. An elder would surely reprimand one for being overly leisurely and lacking decisiveness;

yet when it comes to diligent cultivation of the Way, he calls such scrutiny "clarity. How, then, can one proceed? Mencius said, "To trust the books completely is not as good as having no books at all. This is indeed true.
In the sixth year of the Xiántóng era, Chan Master Shànghuán Xuànjiàn entered *parinirvāṇa*. The Master was a native of Jiǎnnán; his surname was Zhōu.
He had mastered the entire Tripiṭaka and frequently lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, so he was commonly known as "Zhōu the Vajra. Suddenly, he sighed with resolve and said:
"To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the vast void; to exhaust all worldly pivotal mechanisms is like casting a single drop into the great ocean."
"Immersed! I understand what it means to be both a learner and one beyond learning. Thereupon, he completely cast aside his habitual practices and went to visit Chan Master Xìn of Longtán.
He asked, "I have long heard of Longtán; yet now that I have arrived, neither the dragon nor the pond is to be seen. Xìn said, "You have truly arrived at Longtán.
That evening, the Master stood in attendance until late into the night. Xìn said, "Why do you not go out? The Master replied, "It is dark. Xìn—
Xuanzang offered a paper-wick candle to the Master. As the Master received it, Xuanzang blew it out.

The Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment and said, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world. That very day he took his leave. Xuanzang said to his disciples:
Among them there is a man whose teeth are like a forest of sword-trees and whose mouth is like a blood-basin; struck by a single blow of the staff, he does not turn his head back.
In time, he will stand atop a solitary peak and propagate my Way. The Master resided at Deyang for over thirty years.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, Xue Tingwang, the Prefect of Wuling, established the Deshan Monastery and invited the Master to reside there. There, he extensively expounded the School.

Feng ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "If you have no concerns regarding yourself, do not seek falsely. Even if you were to obtain something through false seeking, it would not be truly attained.
You need only be without concern in your mind and without mind toward external affairs; then you will be spirit-like in your emptiness and wondrous in your voidness.
To speak of a beginning or an end, even as much as a hair-tip, is entirely self-deception. A thought as small as a hair’s breadth is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms."
If a fleeting emotion arises, one will be bound in shackles for ten thousand kalpas. Holy names and mundane titles are all but empty sounds;
extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not be burdened? And when you grow weary of them, they become a great affliction.
In the end, it is of no benefit. A monk asked, "What is bodhi? The Master struck him and said, "Get out!
Do not defecate here. He asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "The Buddha is an old bhikṣu from Western Heaven.

Xuefeng asked, "Regarding the ancestral school of the Dharma, by what means do you instruct people? The Master said, "My school has no words or phrases, nor does it bestow a single dharma upon anyone."
When his end was approaching, he said to the assembly, "To grasp at emptiness and pursue echoes is to weary your mind and spirit. When one awakens from a dream, one realizes it was not real;
in the end, what event has actually occurred? Having spoken thus, he sat upright and passed away. He had lived for eighty-six years.
In the fourth month of the seventh year, Chan Master Linji Yixuan passed away. The Master was a native of Caozhou and surnamed Xing.
He visited Chan Master Huangbo Xiyun and asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Before he had finished speaking, Yun struck him. This occurred three times;
having gone to inquire three times and being struck on each occasion, he finally took his leave and descended the mountain. Yun pointed out the way for him to go to Gaoyang.
He went to stay with Dayu. When the Master arrived, Dayu asked him, "What have you heard from Huangbo recently?
The Master replied, "I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times, and each time I was struck. I do not know whether I was at fault or not."
Yunyu said, "Huangbo’s heart is so full of grandmotherly concern that you still ask whether there is an offense or not.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "So, it turns out Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this! Yunyu grabbed him and said, "You bed-wetting brat!"
"Previously you asked whether there was a transgression or not; now you say, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much. What have you seen?
The Master struck Daoyu three times in the ribs. Daoyu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo."

"It is not my business. Thereupon, the Master returned once more to Huangbo. Through this mutual resonance between teacher and disciple, their great capacity and great function stood preeminent among their contemporaries.
Later, he returned to his hometown and, at the request of the people of Zhao, resided at the Linji Chan Garden south of Zicheng.
Students flocked to him. The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Upon the lump of raw flesh, there is a true person of no rank who constantly follows you..."

[The Master] enters and exits through the gates of the faces of all such people; let those who have not yet attained realization look! At that time, a monk asked, "What is the true person of no station?
The Master descended from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Speak! Speak! The monk hesitated, and the Master pushed him away, saying:
"What is the 'true person of no station'? It is a dried-up shit-stick. The Master said, "Those who have left the household life must study the Way.
In my own past days, I too searched for it within the sutras and treatises; only later did I realize that these were merely words intended to manifest medicinal prescriptions for saving the world.
Thereupon, I cast them all aside at once. Only after visiting various teachers and practicing Zen did I encounter a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), whereupon..."
With the clear eye of the Way, one recognizes the old monks of the world and discerns their orthodoxy or heterodoxy. This is not something one is born with as gold;
rather, it is through investigation and refinement that one attains self-awakening in a single day. O practitioners of the Way!

Among the students of all quarters, there are none who do not emerge relying upon external objects. When I, this mountain monk, strike them from the very beginning, they emerge with their hands raised. Hands.
It comes out from the mouth; it comes out from the eyes. Not a single one has emerged in independence.
They are all merely following the idle devices and circumstances of those ancients. I, this mountain monk, have not a single dharma to give to you;
I only treat illnesses and untie bonds. You practitioners from all quarters, try to emerge without relying on things, and I will discuss it with you.
In ten years or five years, not a single person has appeared; they are all merely spirits and demons clinging to grass and wood, who come to this dung heap to bite at blind men at will.
To hold such views is to pointlessly consume the offerings of the faithful from the ten directions. I tell you: it is nothing like that.
It is simply the ordinary matter of wearing clothes, eating food, and passing the time without concern. You who have come from all quarters— [are you like this?]
All of you have hearts that seek the Buddha, seek the Dharma, seek liberation, and seek deliverance from the three realms.
You deluded people, once you have left the three realms, where would you go? A single thought-moment of greed is the desire realm; a single thought-moment of anger is the form realm;
a single thought-moment of delusion is the formless realm. These are the furnishings within your own house; the three realms do not exist apart from yourself.
If you say that the Three Realms are "I," it is actually you—this person who is currently vividly illuminating and discerning all manner of things—who bestows names upon the Three Realms.
O practitioner, as for the functioning before your eyes, who else could grasp it and put it to use?
Do not cling to names and titles, calling them the "Mysterious Principle. To perceive it in such a way is itself a dharma to be loathed. The Master said:

In the Chan school, the perspectives on life and death are utterly transcendent. Those who study the Way must be extremely careful and discerning. For instance, when host and guest meet, there is an exchange of words;
sometimes one manifests form in response to objects, or functions with the whole body; sometimes one employs skillful means through expressions of joy or anger, or reveals only half the body.
If there is a true practitioner of the Way, they will immediately let out a shout and first bring forth a single [critical phrase].
The lacquer basin: when a good teacher does not discern this as an objective condition, he immediately enters that other condition and assumes a formal posture.
The student then shouts; the person in front does not respond and lets it drop. This is a terminal illness, beyond the power of medicine. It is called "the guest looking at the host.
Alternatively, if the good teacher does not bring forth an object, but instead seizes [the student] right where the student asks, the student is...
He seizes it and will not let go even unto death; this is the host observing the guest.
Or, there may be a student who emerges from a single pure state; the spiritual friend recognizes that it is a state and casts it into a pit. The student says, "Excellent!"
The Master said, "Alas! You do not know good from evil. The student then performed a prostration. This is called "the host looking at the host.
Or perhaps there is a student who has been released after being bound in shackles and chains; the Master then places another layer of shackles and chains upon them, and the student rejoices.
Since neither can distinguish between themselves, this is called "the guest looking at the guest. All such examples cited by this mountain monk are for the purpose of discernment.
The Māra selects and distinguishes to discern the false from the true. O practitioners of the Way! The reality of things is truly difficult to fathom; the Buddha-dharma is profound and mysterious.

Though this mountain monk spends his entire day explaining it through for them, students do not take it to heart. Even after passing over it ten thousand times underfoot, they remain utterly dark and ignorant.
Reaching fifty years of age, they merely continue to follow others like those carrying corpses, burdened by their packs until the end of their days.
I, this lowly servant, am a follower of the Way. When students from various quarters come here, I, the mountain monk, employ three ways of severing their faculties.
If those of middling or inferior faculties come, I seize their objective realm but do not remove their dharma.
If those of middling or superior faculties come, I seize both their realm and their dharma. If those of the highest faculties come, I [seize both their realm and their dharma].

No one can take it away from them. Suppose someone with extraordinary insight were to come here; I would immediately manifest my total being in action, bypassing all levels of capacity. O practitioners of the Way!
When you reach this point, there is no way for even a breath to pass where effort is applied; the flash of a spark or a lightning bolt is already missed.
If a student’s eyes waver, they are further removed from the connection. To conceive a thought is already an error; to stir a single念 (thought) is already...
"Separated. There was someone who interpreted this as being "not apart from what is before one's eyes. The Master said, "This mountain monk’s Buddha-dharma has been directly transmitted.
From Master Daoyi, through Magu, Danxia, and Master Lushan, it has traveled all over the world.
No one can fully believe it; they all give rise to slander. For instance, Master Daoyi’s way of functioning was pure and without admixture, yet students [failed to grasp it]."

Among the one hundred and five hundred [monks], none could fathom the minds of others. Like the Master of Mount Lu, who acted with sovereign authenticity whether in accordance with or contrary to circumstances, the students could not measure his boundaries and were left utterly bewildered.

Like Danxia playing with a pearl, appearing and disappearing at will, whenever students approached him, they were all rebuked. This was like the way Magu and Huangbo acted; recently, such instances have been few.
It is attained. It is like Shigong’s way of acting: seeking the person upon the arrowhead, all who come before him were struck with fear.
As for my own way of acting today, it is the true mastery of creation and destruction, a divine play of transformations. Entering all realms, one is free from affairs wherever one goes;
the realm cannot change one. Whenever anyone comes, I immediately go out to look at them; they do not recognize me, and thus I simply proceed.
"You have entered my words and phrases! Alas, alas! The Master took his leave. Huangbo asked, "Where will you go?
The Master replied, "If not Henan, then back to Hebei. Huangbo struck him. The Master seized him by the belt and gave him a slap.
Huangbo laughed loudly and called to his attendant, "Bring the meditation board and desk belonging to our late master Baizhang. The Master said, "Attendant, bring fire. Huangbo—
The Master said, "Even so, you must simply take it with you; later on, you will sit upon the tongues of all people under heaven.
First, Yangshan had said, "If you go north, there will be a place for you to stay where someone will assist you, elder brother.
However, this person has a head but no tail; he has a beginning but no end. Subsequently, when the Master resided at Linji, Puhua was already there beforehand.
The Master Guozan passed away shortly thereafter, having manifested his universal transformation and attained liberation in his entirety. Soon after, due to military unrest, he departed.
Grand Marshal Mo Junhe donated his residence to establish a temple and invited the Master to reside there, naming it Linji after the Master’s former title.

Subsequently, the Master traveled to Hefu, where the Provincial Governor, Attendant-in-Ordinary Wang, shared a profound spiritual affinity with him. Later, the Master moved to Xinghua Temple in Damingfu to live in seclusion.

While residing there, Cunen served him. The Master bestowed upon him the verse of the Dharma-transmission: "Following the current without ceasing, one asks: 'How is it? True illumination is boundless; he explains it as it is to others.
Detached from characteristics and detached from names, it is not received by anyone. The 'blow-off-blade' sword has been used; now it must be sharpened again. One day, he said to the assembly:
"After my passing, you must not extinguish my True Dharma Eye. Sansheng replied: "How would we dare to extinguish it?"
[He said,] "The Eye of the True Dharma of Master Que has been extinguished. The Master said, "If someone asks you about this in the future, what will you say? Sansheng then gave a shout.
The Master said, "Who would have known that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be extinguished by this blind donkey!
Having spoken, he sat upright and passed away. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa at the northwest corner of Daming Prefecture. He was posthumously titled Hui.
Regarding Master Zhao, the Treatise states: "Linji’s great enlightenment revealed the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye like an arrow released from the string or a lion’s backward leap;
his function of illumination startled the multitudes. Moreover, the tongs and hammers of Huangbo and Dayu were subtle and profound, operating within the flash of a lightning bolt."
To strike the rhythm and seize the opportune moment with them—this is truly the forge of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. How magnificent!
Since Linji transmitted it to Xinghua, more than ten generations have passed and the Way has become increasingly radiant; this is what is meant by "the source being deep, the stream is long.
Furthermore, these words concerning the lineage of this school are each extracted from the very crown of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; they certainly do not belong to other schools.
It is something that can be reached through diligent effort. It is like the great Peng bird, which soars ninety thousand li in a single leap;
the wind follows beneath it. What the ancients called Yunmen and Linji—the kings among monks—is no empty boast.
In the ninth year [of the Dazhong period], Chan Master Jingcen of Changsha passed away. The Master had once addressed the assembly, saying:
"If I were to exclusively exalt the teachings and the tradition, the grass in the Dharma Hall would surely grow ten feet deep. It is only because I have no other choice that I speak to you all."
The entire world of the ten directions is the śramaṇa’s eye; the entire world of the ten directions is the śramaṇa’s whole body;
the entire world of the ten directions is one’s own radiance; the entire world of the ten directions is contained within one’s own radiance.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single person who is not oneself. I have always told you this:
the Buddhas of the three periods of time, together with all sentient beings of the ten dharma realms, are the light of Mahāprajñā.
Before this light has yet been emitted, where do you all turn for refuge? Even before the light is emitted, there is no news of Buddhas or sentient beings; where [could they be]?
Since the appearance of mountains, rivers, and lands, there was once a monk who asked, "What is the eye of the śramaṇa?

The Master said, "It has been long since it emerged, yet it cannot be brought forth. He further said, "To become a Buddha or a Patriarch—it cannot be brought forth. To transmigrate through the six realms—it cannot be brought forth."
The monk said, "I do not understand what it is that cannot be brought forth. The Master said, "By day one sees the sun; by night one sees the stars.

The monk said, "I do not understand, Teacher. The Master said, "The color of Mount Sumeru is green and yet green. The monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "It is the physical body of sentient beings.
The monk said, "The essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical. How then can there be various kinds?"
Regarding the names: the Master said, "To return to the source from the eye-faculty is named Mañjuśrī; to return to the source from the ear-faculty is named Avalokiteśvara;
to shift the mind and return to the source is named Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s wisdom of wondrous observation; Avalokiteśvara is the Buddha’s unconditioned great compassion;
Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s wondrous practice of non-action. These three sages are the wondrous functions of the Buddha."

The Buddha is the true essence of the Three Jewels. In terms of function, there are as many provisional names as there are sands in the Ganges; in terms of essence, they are collectively named as the one Bhagavān. A monk asked: "It is said that 'form is emptiness and emptiness is form. How is this principle to be understood? The Master replied: "Where there is obstruction, it is not a wall; where there is penetration, it is not empty space. If a person understands it in this way, mind and form are fundamentally the same. The monk asked: [What about this? The Master replied: [This is so. The monk asked: [Is this not a contradiction? The Master replied: [It is not. The monk asked: [Why not? The Master replied: [Because it is not so. The monk asked: [Then what is it? The Master replied: [It is not so. The monk asked: [If it is not so, then why do you say it is? The Master replied: [I do not say it is. The monk asked: [If you do not say it is, then why do you say it is not? The Master replied: [Because I do not say it is not. The monk asked: [If you do not say it is not, then how can you speak of it at all? The Master replied: [I do not speak of it. The monk asked: [If you do not speak of it, then who is listening? The Master replied: [Who is asking? The monk asked: [I am. The Master replied: [That is precisely why I do not speak of it. The monk asked: [If you do not speak of it, then how can you teach others? The Master replied: [I do not teach others. The monk asked: [If you do not teach others, then who is practicing the Way? The Master replied: [There is no one practicing the Way. The monk asked: [If there is no one practicing the Way, then who attains Buddhahood? The Master replied: [There is no one who attains Buddhahood. The monk asked: [If there is no one who attains Buddhahood, then for whom do you preach the Dharma? The Master replied: [I preach the Dharma for those who have no self. The monk asked: [If there is no self, then who is the listener? The Master replied: [The listener is precisely the one who has no self. The monk asked: [If there is no self, then how can there be hearing? The Master replied: [Hearing is precisely the absence of self.
