The monk asked: [If the ultimate truth is the absence of self, then what is the nature of reality? The Master replied: [The nature of reality is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the nature of reality is the absence of self, then what is the path to enlightenment? The Master replied: [The path to enlightenment is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the path to enlightenment is the absence of self, then what is the fruit of Buddhahood? The Master replied: [The fruit of Buddhahood is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the fruit of Buddhahood is the absence of self, then what is the dharma-body? The Master replied: [The dharma-body is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the dharma-body is the absence of self, then what is the sambhogakaya? The Master replied: [The sambhogakaya is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the sambhogakaya is the absence of self, then what is the nirmāṇakāya? The Master replied: [The nirmāṇakāya is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the nirmāṇakāya is the absence of self, then what is the three bodies in unity? The Master replied: [The three bodies in unity are precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the three bodies in unity are the absence of self, then what is the ten thousand phenomena? The Master replied: [The ten thousand phenomena are precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the ten thousand phenomena are the absence of self, then what is the one mind? The Master replied: [The one mind is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the one mind is the absence of self, then what is the myriad dharmas? The Master replied: [The myriad dharmas are precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the myriad dharmas are the absence of self, then what is the ultimate source? The Master replied: [The ultimate source is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the ultimate source is the absence of self, then what is the beginningless ignorance? The Master replied: [Beginningless ignorance is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If beginningless ignorance is the absence of self, then what is the end of suffering? The Master replied: [The end of suffering is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If the end of suffering is the absence of self, then what is nirvana? The Master replied: [Nirvana is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If nirvana is the absence of self, then what is samsara? The Master replied: [Samsara is precisely the absence of self. The monk asked: [If samsara is the absence of self, then what is the distinction between them? The Master replied: [There is no distinction. The monk asked: [If there is no distinction, then why do you speak of them? The Master replied: [I do not speak of them. The monk asked: [If you do not speak of them, then how can you guide sentient beings? The Master replied: [I do not guide sentient beings. The monk asked: [If you do not guide sentient beings, then who is the teacher? The Master replied: [There is no teacher. The monk asked: [If there is no teacher, then who is the disciple? The Master replied: [There is no disciple. The monk asked: [If there is no disciple, then who is the congregation? The Master replied: [There is no congregation. The monk asked: [If there is no congregation, then who is the assembly? The Master replied: [There is no assembly. The monk asked: [If there is no assembly, then who is the host? The Master replied: [There is no host. The monk asked: [If there is no host, then who is the guest? The Master replied: [There is no guest. The monk asked: [If there is no guest, then who is the master? The Master replied: [There is no master. The monk asked: [If there is no master, then who is the servant? The Master replied: [There is no servant. The monk asked: [If there is no servant, then who is the attendant? The Master replied: [There is no attendant. The monk asked: [If there is no attendant, then who is the practitioner? The Master replied: [There is no practitioner. The monk asked: [If there is no practitioner, then who is the cultivator? The Master replied: [There is no cultivator. The monk asked: [If there is no cultivator, then who is the seeker? The Master replied: [There is no seeker. The monk asked: [If there is no seeker, then who is the one who seeks the Way? The Master replied: [There is no one who seeks the Way. The monk asked: [If there is no one who seeks the Way, then who is the one who realizes the Way? The Master replied: [There is no one who realizes the Way. The monk asked: [If there is no one who realizes the Way, then who is the one who attains the fruit? The Master replied: [There is no one who attains the fruit. The monk asked: [If there is no one who attains the fruit, then who is the one who enters nirvana? The Master replied: [There is no one who enters nirvana. The monk asked: [If there is no one who enters nirvana, then who is the one who remains in the world? The Master replied: [There is no one who remains in the world. The monk asked: [If there is no one who remains in the world, then who is the one who transcends the world? The Master replied: [There is no one who transcends the world. The monk asked: [If there is no one who transcends the world, then who is the one who dwells in the dharma-realm? The Master replied: [There is no one who dwells in the dharma-realm. The monk asked: [If there is no one who dwells in the dharma
"What is Buddha-nature? The Master said, "Buddha-nature is majestic and dignified; it manifests and abides in its own form, yet sentient beings find it difficult to see.
If you realize that sentient beings have no self, how does my face differ from the Buddha’s face? Question: "What is the sphere of practice for those of the highest caliber?
The Master said, "It is like the eyes of a dead man. Question: "When those of the highest caliber meet one another, what is it like? The Master said, "It is like a dead [man]."
[The student] took hold of [the master’s hand]. He asked, "Why has it been that for immeasurable kalpas, the worlds within Samantabhadra’s body have not been pervaded?
The Master said, "Since immeasurable kalpas ago, have you ever traveled through them all? He asked, "What is the body of Samantabhadra?
The answer was, "If you are already inside the Han-yuan Hall, why ask about Chang’an? He asked, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go?"

[The student] departs. The Master says: "Failing to recognize the adamantine essence, you instead call it 'conditions for birth. Throughout the ten directions, all is true quiescence; who is there, and who is walking?
Because Linji had addressed the assembly, saying, "Upon this lump of flesh there is a true person of no station," the Master then composed a verse:
"The myriad dharmas are as one; there is no need for selection. In this oneness, who selects and who does not select? Right now in this life..."
"Death is fundamentally Bodhi; the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time share this same eye. Yangshan asked, "Everyone possesses this very thing, yet they simply cannot use it.
The Master said, "Precisely! I ask you to use it. Yangshan asked, "How would you use it? The Master then kicked Yangshan down.
Yangshan said, "Right now he is like a great tiger. From then on, the world called him "Cen the Great Tiger."

Ten years later, Chan Master Dongshan Jia passed away. The Master was a native of Kuaiji; his surname was Yu. He left home to become a monk in his youth and, at the age of twenty-one, went to Mount Song to receive full ordination.
His first visit was to Nanquan, whom he encountered just as Nanquan was presiding over a vegetarian feast for the anniversary of Mazu’s death.
Jianquan asked the assembly, "Today we have prepared a vegetarian feast; I wonder whether Mazu will come? The assembly had no reply.

The Master (Dongshan) then stepped forward and said, "He will come when he has a companion. Upon hearing this, Jianquan praised him, saying, "Although this boy is young, he is indeed worthy of being refined.
The Master replied, "Preceptor, do not treat the noble as the base. Next, he visited Guishan and asked, "I have recently heard from Zhong..."
The National Teacher [Huai-rang] said, "Inanimate things preach the Dharma; I have not yet fathomed its subtlety.
Yang-shan said, "I also have this here, but it is difficult to find someone for it. The Master said, "Then please let the Venerable One speak it.
Yang-shan said, "With the mouth born of my parents, I would never dare to speak it. The Master asked, "Are there others who admire the Way at the same time as the Venerable One? Yang-shan said:
"From here, proceeding to the Stone Chamber, there is the Wayman Yunyan. If you can part the weeds and gaze upon his wind, he will surely be someone you hold in high esteem.
When the Master arrived at Yunyan’s place, he asked, "Who is it that can hear the Dharma preached by the insentient?
Yunyan said, "The Dharma preached by the insentient is heard by the insentient. The Master asked, "Does the Master yourself hear it? Yunyan said, "If I were to hear it, you..."
“Then you would not be able to hear me preach the Dharma. The Master said, “If that is so, then Liang-jia does not hear the Venerable’s preaching of the Dharma.
Yanguan said, “If you do not even hear what I say, how much less can you hear the preaching of the insentient?
The Master then composed a verse, saying: “Great! How marvelous! How truly marvelous! The preaching of the insentient is inconceivable. If one were to listen with the ears, it would be as if...”
"It is difficult to meet. I shall only know [where you are] when my eyes hear your voice. He then took his leave. Yunyan asked, "Where are you going?
He replied, "Though I have left the Master, I have not yet determined where I shall stay. Yunyan said, "When will you return? The Master said, "I shall come as soon as the Master has a place to stay.
Yunyan said, "Once you have gone from here, it will be difficult to see one another again. The Master said, "It will be difficult not to see one another."
He asked Yan again, "After the Master has passed away, if someone were to ask whether it is possible to capture your true likeness, how would you respond?
Yan replied, "Simply tell them, 'This very one is it. After a long silence, the Master said, "To take up this matter requires great care and discernment.
The Master still harbored some doubt. Later, while crossing a stream, he saw his reflection and attained a great awakening to the previous teaching. Thereupon, there was [this verse]:
The verse says: I fear that seeking from others will lead me far away and distance me from the Self.
Now I go alone; everywhere I shall encounter Him. He is now precisely myself; I am now not He. One must understand it thus before one can accord with Suchness (*tathatā*).
At the end of the Dazhong era, he gathered and guided disciples at Mount Xinfeng. Thereafter, he flourished in his teaching at Gaoyang (Gao'an).
Dongshan was once performing a vegetarian feast on the anniversary of Yunyan’s death. A monk asked, “Master, you met Nanquan when you first set out on your path;
why then do you offer this feast for Yunyan? The Master said, “It is not that I value my late teacher’s virtue and wisdom, nor is it for the sake of the Buddha-dharma.
I simply value that he did not explain it all away. Another monk asked, “Master, do you still approve of your late teacher? The Master said:
[The Master] half-accepted and half-refused it. [The monk] asked, "Why do you not fully accept it? The Master said, "If I were to fully accept it, I would be failing my former teacher.
On another occasion, the Master gave this instruction: "Even if one says directly that 'originally there is not a single thing,' one has still not yet earned his bowl and satchel.
A monk asked, "Who is worthy to receive them? The Master said, "One who does not enter the gate. [The monk] asked, "As for that..."
"Does one who has not entered the gate still receive [the robe and bowl]? The Master said, "Even so, I cannot help but give it to him.
The Master spoke again: "To say directly that 'originally there is not a single thing'—even this does not yet suffice to dispense with his robe and bowl.
Here, one ought to deliver a turning word. Tell me, what word can be delivered? There was a senior monk who delivered ninety-six turning words.
His words did not satisfy the Master’s mind; it was only at the very end that his final turn of phrase finally met with the Master’s approval.

The Master said, “Why, Ācārya, did you not speak thus sooner? A monk who had heard this requested that the Master recount those words. Thus, for three years, he attended upon him, yet the Master did not grant him the teaching.
Because the Senior Monk fell ill, the monk said, “For three years I have requested that you recount those previous words, yet I have not received your compassion.”
He took it well and did not grasp it wrongly. He then bared his blade toward him and said, "If you do not speak, I shall kill you, Elder!
The Elder was struck with awe and said, "Wait; let me offer this for you. He then said, "Even if you were to bring it forth, there would be no place to put it."
The monk bowed in thanks. The monk asked, "I have often heard it taught that one should practice the 'Bird Path. I do not yet understand what this Bird Path is.
The Master said, "One does not encounter a single person. The monk asked, "How does one walk? The Master said, "You must simply go with no trace beneath your feet.
The monk asked, "If one is thus walking the Bird Path, is this not one's original face? The Master said, "Why do you ask?"
[The Master said: "What a perversion! [The monk] asked, "In what way am I perverse? The Master said, "If you were not perverse, how could you mistake a servant for a lord?
[The monk] asked, "What is the original face? The Master said, "Do not walk the path of birds.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying, "Only those who know the one above the Buddha have the right to engage in discourse. At that time, a monk asked, "What is..."
The Buddha is a person of the highest caliber. The Master said, "He is not ordinary. The Master asked a monk, "What thing in the world is most painful?
The monk replied, "Hell is the most painful. The Master said, "Not so. To fail to understand the Great Matter beneath these seams of the robe is the greatest suffering.
The Master asked a monk, "What is your name? [The monk] replied, "So-and-so. The Master said, "Which one there is that is your true host? [The monk] replied, "I see it."
In response, the Master said: "Alas, alas! People of the present age are for the most part like this;
they merely recognize the one before the donkey or behind the horse as themselves. This is precisely why the Buddha-dharma has sunk into oblivion.
When even the host within the guest is not yet clearly distinguished, how can one distinguish the host of the host? A monk asked, "What is the host of the host? The Master—
The Acharya said, "Speak for yourself. He replied, "I can speak, but I am merely the master among guests.
What is the master among masters? The Master said, "To speak thus is easy; to maintain continuity is very difficult.
When the Master was about to pass away, he said to the assembly, "I have a reputation for idleness. Who can rid me of it? No one in the assembly could answer. A novice monk said, "Please [speak]."

Regarding the Master’s Dharma name, the Master said, “I have long since discarded my name. A monk asked, “Master, you are unwell. Is there anyone who does not suffer from illness? The Master said, “There is.
The monk asked, “Does this one who is not ill look after the Master? The Master said, “The old monk has his share in looking after him.
The monk asked, “How can the Master look after him? The Master said, “When the old monk looks after him, he does not see any illness. Furthermore...
He said, "Setting aside this leaking shell, where would you go to meet me? The assembly had no reply. He then shaved their heads, donned their robes, and ordered the bell to be struck.
They became profoundly still and silent. At that time, more than a thousand disciples were filled with joy and admiration.

After some time, the Master suddenly opened his eyes and said, "For those who have left the household life, the mind does not cling to things; this is true cultivation. Toiling in life and resting in death."

"What is there to grieve for? he said. He then summoned the administrative monk and ordered him to prepare a single midday meal for the ignorant ones, ostensibly to reproach his disciples for their lingering attachment to worldly emotions.

When the provisions for the meal were finally ready on the seventh day, the Master joined the assembly for the meal. After it was finished, he again addressed the assembly, saying: "In the life of a monk, there is no cause for concern;
generally, at the moment of departure, one must not allow clamor or agitation. Tomorrow, after bathing, sit upright and..."
He passed away at the age of sixty-three, posthumously titled Chan Master Wuben.
In the fifth month of that year, the Emperor visited An Guo Temple and bestowed upon the National Teacher Zhixuan a precious throne two zhang high.
It was crafted from aloeswood and lacquered; its surface was inlaid with dragons, phoenixes, and floral patterns in fine gold, and it was furnished with a double seat and a scripture table.

At its four corners stood auspicious bird-deities and divine figures, several *chi* in height. One ascended by means of a stone staircase. In front were draped embroidered bags and brocade sashes, their precious beauty being utterly unsurpassed.
At that time, ten thousand monks were fed daily in the palace; the Emperor himself performed the *zàn* and *bài* chants. The Chancellor Sù Fǎng remonstrated, saying:
"The Dharma of India involves severing worldly attachments to attain extinction. This is not something for an emperor to personally practice. He then transcribed the Sanskrit [mantras].

Regarding his speech, it was the Brahma-voice. It was not like [the worldly practice of] investigating errors to grant rewards or imposing excessive punishments to bring calamity, nor was it for seeking blessings through prayer.

Furthermore, as for the Buddha, he is to be grasped through awakening; he cannot be sought through physical marks. Although Emperor Yizong did not accept [his advice], he nonetheless praised its excellence.

His surname was Chen, and he was popularly known as "Chen Pusa. He had mastered the three studies (*tri-vidyā*) and his reputation covered the age. His miraculous deeds were particularly numerous. This occurred during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong... [and so forth].
When Zong fled from the Chao rebels and took refuge in Chengdu, he dispatched the Censor Guo Zun with an imperial edict to summon him to the imperial presence.

The Emperor, who had long held his reputation in high esteem, received him in audience and was greatly pleased. He conferred upon him the title National Teacher Wuda and kept him at the temporary palace for a long time.

When he eventually took leave to return to Jiulong, he suddenly saw, within a state of meditative concentration, a Bodhisattva descend into his chamber, stroke the crown of his head, and intone profound and wondrous sounds.
He comforted him, and having finished speaking, he vanished immediately. Suddenly, a pearl entered the left thigh of Xuán, swelling up with excruciating pain;
upon it were the two characters "Cháo Cuò. Realizing this was his past debt, Xuán lay down on his right side and passed away.
His writings, totaling some two million words, have been circulated in the world. His disciple Sēngchē, and Chē’s disciple Juéhuī, both attained great renown.
He served as the Head of the Sangha throughout three lifetimes. Some say that Xuan’s previous incarnation was Dharma Master Zhixuan of Sanxue Mountain in Hanchuan;

while Zhixuan was alive, he once lectured on the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*), which caused the earth to miraculously turn golden, and at his death, he experienced a miraculous illness—circumstances that closely resemble those of Xuan.
The commentary states: The world claims that Master Xuan was the reincarnation of Yuan Ang of the Han dynasty; his habit of offering remonstrances was surely a remnant of his former character.
When Emperor Wuzong became infatuated with heterodox ways and intended to abolish the Great Teaching (Buddhism), Xuan remonstrated against it.

While it was appropriate for him to defend and clarify his own tradition, he went further by discouraging the Emperor’s practice of alchemy and dietetics, and instead urged him toward ritual, music, law, and governance. This was to oppose the Emperor’s inclinations while simultaneously providing him with what was beneficial.

This was indeed a matter of competition. Thus, [Zhang] Ang’s remonstrance against the relocation of the Prince of Huainan and his exclusion of Zhao Tan from the position of charioteer, as well as his refusal to allow Lady Shen to occupy her seat, were quite different from [the actions of others].
Nevertheless, from Emperor Wen of Han to Emperor Xi of Tang, a period of over seven hundred years, it would have been sufficient for Ang to repay the debt incurred regarding the matter of Chao Cuo.
Why then did he still suffer an evil retribution and die? It is likely because he had previously harbored a private grudge against Cuo.
Furthermore, when the proposal to eliminate the seven rebellious states was mishandled and those states rose in revolt, Zou Yang subsequently petitioned for Dong Chuo’s execution.
Yet, even after Chuo was executed, the armies of the seven states did not withdraw; thus, Zou Yang had merely exploited the majesty of the state to settle a private vendetta.
Consequently, through ten or more generations, the karmic retribution for this act has remained unabated. How can one not be cautious?
In the eleventh year of the Xiántóng era, the Chancellor Pí Xiū passed away. His courtesy name was Gōngměi, and he was a native of Méngzhōu.
From childhood, he lived in seclusion together with his brothers; by day he lectured on the sutras, and by night he composed writings, never venturing outside his door for years on end.

When someone presented him with a deer, his students recommended it to him, but Xiū would not eat it, saying: "Even my vegetarian diet is insufficient; if I were to swallow meat now, how could I sustain myself hereafter?"
He passed the jinshi examination and served successively in various internal administrative posts. He once served as the Prefect of Hongzhou.

One day, while visiting the murals at Longxing Temple, he sighed and said, "Their countenances and deportment are truly admirable; where are the eminent monks? At that time, several monks were present, but their responses did not satisfy him.
Xiu asked, "Is there no Chan practitioner here? A monk replied, "A monk arrived recently who seems to be a Chan practitioner. Xiu ordered him to be summoned.
When he arrived, it was Master Huangbo Xiyun, whose name had not yet become prominent. Pei Xiu approached him with his previous questions. Huangbo called out in a loud voice, "Pei Xiu!

Xiu responded, "Yes. Huangbo asked, "Where are you? At this, Xiu attained sudden enlightenment. Later, having realized this awakening, he invited the Master into his residence, where they discussed the Dharma morning and evening.
When Xiu was transferred to the commandery of Wanling, he also took the Master along with him; from that time on, [their relationship] grew ever deeper.
He thoroughly penetrated the source of the Dharma. Furthermore, his karmic affinity with Chan Master Mi of Guifeng was exceptionally close.

During the Dazhong era, he served in the administration for six years, after which he successively held the positions of regional commander (*jiedushi*) across various provinces. He passed away at the age of seventy-four. His literary talent was outstanding;

his calligraphy, both in regular and cursive styles, was forceful and elegant, adhering to the formal rules of the tradition. By nature, he was refined and composed, maintaining strict integrity in his conduct, and his movements were dignified and serene. Emperor Xuanzong once remarked:
Xuizhen was a Confucian scholar who, in his daily life, generally abstained from wine and meat. He authored several tens of thousands of words of Buddhist literature.

His "Preface to the Guifeng Collection of Explanations on the Source of Chan" states: "The Chan Master compiled the various explanations on the source of Chan into the Chan Canon and wrote a general preface for them."

Xuī said, "There has never been such a thing. Since the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he established teachings according to the capacities of beings, and Bodhisattvas were born in succession to prescribe medicines according to their ailments.
Therefore, the temporal teachings of a single lifetime open two gates—the profound and the shallow—and the One True Suchness Mind unfolds the distinct dharmas of nature and characteristics.
Both the 'Horse' and the 'Dragon' masters propagated the doctrines of the World-Honored Regulator, yet the schools of Emptiness and Nature differ."

The two masters Xiu and Er both transmitted the mind of Bodhidharma, yet they differed in their respective receptions of the sudden and gradual approaches. Tiantai relied exclusively upon the three contemplations; Niutou possessed not a single dharma;
Jiangxi [Hongren] maintained that the entire body is the absolute truth; and Heze [Shenhui] pointed directly at knowledge and vision.

Others, meanwhile, engaged in mutual refutation regarding emptiness and existence, attacked each other with regard to the real and the false, employed "taking by way of reversal" and "grasping by way of conformity," and utilized secret indications alongside explicit explanations. Thus, among those of the Western Regions—

In recent years, their various schools have become numerous. This is truly because illnesses have a thousand sources and medicines come in many varieties; one must apply them according to the specific case and the capacity of the individual, such that they cannot all be identical.
Although all are gateways to realization and are entirely the path of the True and Right, the followers of these various schools are for the most part narrow-minded rather than broad.
Consequently, over the past few decades, the methods of the masters have deteriorated further, with people making their own lineages of transmission into mere gateways for self-interest.
Each opened their own school, taking the sūtras and śāstras as their spears and halberds to attack one another. Their sentiments shifted and changed with the bow and arrow;
the Dharma rose and fell according to human ego. Amidst this chaotic tangle of right and wrong, no one could discern the truth.

Thus, the various teachings and lineages of the World-Honored One and the Bodhisattvas were merely sufficient to incite disputes among later generations and increase the disease of affliction. What benefit was there?
How greatly beneficial this was! After a long time, Chan Master Guifeng sighed and said, "I have encountered these times; I must not remain silent.

Thereupon, he used the three types of doctrinal teachings of the Tathāgata to seal the three Dharma-gates of the Chan school, fusing the vase, bowl, hairpin, and bracelet into a single piece of gold, and blending the cream, curd, and clarified butter into a single flavor. He shook the fundamental principles so that all who were raised up followed accordingly.
Based on the *Huìyào* (Essentials of the Teachings), those who come together follow the same path;

yet, fearing that students might still find it difficult to clarify, I have further directly demonstrated the beginning and end of the source of the school, the union of the true and the false, the concealment and manifestation of the nature of emptiness, and the distinctions among various doctrines and meanings.

Regarding the similarities and differences between the sudden and gradual [teachings], the mutual reversals of negation and affirmation, the depths of the provisional and the real, and the right and wrong of the universal and the particular—there is nothing that has not been told with a raised hand and pointed out as clearly as one’s palm. He roars with a frown and entices with gentleness;
he nurtures and administers medicine, fearing that life and nature might meet an untimely end; he protects and guards them, mindful of water and fire.
It is like being adrift and scorched; he waves his hand to scatter it. Alas for the stubbornness of strife!

The Great Illumination cannot shatter the darkness of the long night, and a compassionate father cannot protect his child after death. But my Master, holding up the sun of the Buddha, shines its light upon all with skillful means;

all doubts and obscurations are utterly removed. Following the Buddha’s mind, he extends his great compassion across all beings, so that even through the exhaustion of kalpas, they remain under its protection.
This is indeed the World-Honored One as the master who expounds the teaching, and my teacher as the person who synthesizes the teachings.

With the beginning and end in accord and the distant and near illuminating one another, it may be said that the essential task of all the temporal teachings of a single lifetime has been fully accomplished. Some may say:

"Since the passing of the Tathāgata, [this teaching] has never been widely propagated or synthesized; now, all at once, you depart from its fundamental intent and fail to uphold it, thereby abandoning it."
To maintain a defensive barrier without taking up [the truth] therein—does this not deviate from the Way of the Secret Treasury and the Esoteric Seal? The answer is:

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and at the assembly of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Buddha likewise fused [all things] into a single flavor (*ekarasa*). Yet, those who possess the flavor do not perceive it.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said: "The Buddhas have secret speech, but they have no secret treasury. The World-Honored One praised this.
It is said: "The words of the Tathāgata are revealing, manifest, pure, and free from obscuration. The foolish do not understand them and call them a 'secret treasury' (guhyakośa);

the wise, however, fully comprehend them and thus do not designate them as a 'treasury. This is the proof. Therefore, when the Way of Kings flourishes, outer gates need not be closed, yet defense is maintained against the barbarians;
when the Way of the Buddha is complete, all dharmas are held in total retention (dhāraṇī), yet protection is maintained against external māras."
One should no longer harbor biased attachments or wring one's hands in agitation over such matters. Alas! Later students should place their trust in the Buddha, not in other men;
they should seek verification in the fundamental Dharma, not in what they have not yet practiced.
If they can act in this way, they will be able to repay the diligent labors and virtues of Guifeng.
The treatise states: According to the Tang Shiyi, Xiu held office for six years.

One day, while Emperor Xuanzong was in his private chamber, Xiu entered the audience and respectfully requested that the Crown Prince be established. Xuanzong slowly shook his head and said, "As you request."
"I am but a man of leisure," he said. "Do not take offense at this. When he was granted a request for an external post, he was appointed as Chancellor (Pingchangshi) to govern a great province.

He passed away after more than ten years in office. When the historians recorded his character, they noted that he was refined and composed, maintained strict integrity in his conduct, and was dignified and serene in his movements.
Emperor Xuan once remarked, "Xiu is truly a Confucian scholar. This was because he...
He was a shadow and trace of the world. As for his mastery of the Six Arts and his profound penetration of the vehicles of the teachings, he possessed the Eye of the True Dharma;
thus, all the beauty of the world converged in this one man, such that none could compare to him throughout past or present.
At that time, only Master Pang possessed the eye of the school and exclusively upheld the "upward" direction, while Xiu adorned it with literary elegance and brought it to light.

They assisted the School of the Patriarchs. As for their two prefaces to the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* and the *Contemplation of the Dharma Realm*, as well as their "Exhortation to Generate the Bodhicitta," though there may be authors in later generations, none can surpass them. Regarding the spiritual rank of these two masters, one may deliberate thus: [text continues].
Is it not the case that the eighth [stage], being signless and effortless, possesses both merit and wisdom entirely as retributive attainments?

On the gengwu day of the third month in the fourteenth year of the Xiantong era, an imperial edict was issued for the monks of the two monastic districts to welcome the Buddha’s relics from Famen Temple in Fengxiang.
